units.la: EXhibemus heîc Tibi, BENEVOLE LECTOR, Johannis Morini aliorumq; Clarissimorum Virorum, de republ. literaria, in Orientalibus & Philologia S. præcipuè, immortaliter meritorũ, DISSERTATIONES EPISTOLICAS, quibus ANTIQUITATES ECCLESIÆ ORIENTALIS haud leviter enucleavére. Publici juris primùm factæ sunt Londini, repertæ inter libros R.P. Ameloti, Congregationis Oratorii Presbyteri, post illius obitum, & ex ipsismet autographis fideliter editæ. Cùm autem ex his insignem in rem literariam redundare utilitatem persuasum habeamus, nec exemplaria apud nos adeò sint freqven-tia, operæ pretium visum fuit, præ-
units.tr: Here, kind reader, we present to you the epistolary dissertations of John Morin and other most distinguished men, who have deserved immortal credit for the republic of letters, especially in Oriental studies and sacred philology, and who have not lightly elucidated the antiquities of the Eastern Church. They were first published in London, found among the books of Father Amelot, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, after his death, and faithfully edited from the autographs themselves. Since we are persuaded that these bring remarkable benefit to literature, and copies are not so common among us, it seemed worthwhile to submit them once more and make them available for the public good.

units.la: lo easdem iterum submittere, bonoqve publico communicare. Commendandæ hæ Epistolæ vel ideò, qvòd contineant varias ad historiam Versionum Biblicarum, rituum sacrorum, & Chronologiam Muhamedanorum pertinentes res, easq; non vulgares; inprimis verò demonstrat Johannes Morinus, qvô animi consilio non solùm Pentateuchum Samaritanum, & Exercitationes in illum ediderit : Sed & cur, anteqvam hunc publicaret, LXXviralem Versionem Codicis S. Græcam cum nova præfatione, & posteà alia opuscula evulgaverit. Inter omnes autem Epistolas curiosiores omninò sunt prima & secunda, qvarū illa est Synagogæ Samaritanorū, qvæ est in urbe Sichem sive
units.tr: These letters deserve commendation, if only because they contain various matters pertaining to the history of the Biblical versions, sacred rites and the chronology of the Muhammadans, and these are not commonplace things. Above all, John Morin shows with what purpose he published not only the Samaritan Pentateuch and the Exercitationes on it, but also why, before publishing it, he issued the Greek Septuagint version of the Sacred Codex with a new preface, and afterwards other short works. Among all the letters, the first and second are by far the most curious. The first is that of the Samaritan Synagogue which is in the city of Sichem, or

units.la: * Vid. Acta Eruditorum Lipsiæ publicata Cal. Jun. An. 1682. p.176. ve Napalous, ad Cl. Virum Josephum Scaligerum, interprete Johanne Morinô, quâ fidem ritusq; suos exponunt, & qua in re à Judaeis discrepent, simul declarant: haec verò est Samaritanorum in Ægypto commorantium,ad eundem Josephum Scaligerum, de eodem argumento. Quid praeterea B. L. in quâlibet Epistola sit expectandum, subsequens illarum cum suis argumentis index evidenter poterit docere. Praeter [?] notas etiam & animadversiones, quae epistolis subjiciuntur, his omnibus praemittitur Vita Johannis Morini, quae mores illius, tùm Romae, tùm Parisiis, studiorum [?] item rationem & alia bene multa complectitur. Praeter haec additur quoque librorum tam à se editorum, quam edendorum Critica. Et ut eò limatius hoc prodeat o-pusculu[?]pusculum, accuratâ diligentiâ revidere, & ab innumeris, qvibus Londinensis editio scatebat, mendis repurgare curavimus, indiceq; rerum & verborum locupletissimô adauximus. Vale & fruere!
units.tr: * See Acta Eruditorum, published at Leipzig on 1 June 1682, p. 176. Napalous, to the distinguished man Joseph Scaliger, translated by John Morin, in which they set out their faith and rites and at the same time declare in what respects they differ from the Jews. The second is that of the Samaritans dwelling in Egypt, to the same Joseph Scaliger, on the same subject. What else the kind reader may expect in each letter, the following index with its arguments will clearly show. Besides the notes and comments appended to the letters, all of these are preceded by a Life of John Morin, which embraces his character, both at Rome and at Paris, his course of studies, and many other things. In addition, a critical account of the books both published and to be published by him is added. So that this little work might come out more polished, we have taken care to revise it with exact diligence and to purge it of the countless errors with which the London edition abounded, and we have enriched it with a very full index of things and words. Farewell, and enjoy!

units.tr: A letter of the Samaritan Synagogue, which is in the city of Sichem, or Nablus, to the most distinguished man Joseph Scaliger, translated by John Morin: in it they explain at greater length their faith, morals and rites, and at the same time set out in what respects they differ from the Jews.

units.la: III. Andreas de Leon Samorensis, Cl. viro Michaeli le Jay. Regia Bibliorum Antverpensium editio, quæ magnam partem extat in Bibliis Parisiensibus, castigatur in plurimis locis; Paraphrasis Chaldaica ad antiqua exemplaria M.S.S. reformatur, specimen novæ e-ditionis Bibliorum Antverpensium correctioris, cui Biblia Pontificia, non verò Regia, nomen futurum erat.
units.tr: III. Andreas de Leon of Samora, to the distinguished man Michael le Jay. The royal edition of the Antwerp Bible, of which a large part is found in the Paris Bible, is corrected in very many places; the Chaldee paraphrase is reformed according to the old manuscript copies; a specimen of a new and more correct edition of the Antwerp Bible, which was to bear the name of the Papal Bible rather than the Royal.

units.la: VITA JOHANNIS MORINI, è Congregatione Oratorii in Francia, Cum Animadversionibus in illius Opera.
units.tr: THE LIFE OF JOHN MORIN, of the Congregation of the Oratory in France, with Remarks on His Works.

units.la: BLœsiæ, Galliæ oppido ad Ligerim,natus est Johannes Morinus, sub finem prioris seculi, Parentibus, qvi Religionem, qvam in hisce locis vocant Hugenoticam, profitebantur, in eaqve ab illis educatus, Rupellum,qvæ tunc munitissimum erat Hugenotorum præsidium, missus, ut Literis Humanioribus operam daret; deinde Lugdunum Batavorum, ubi linguam Græcam & Hebræam excoluit,animumque ad res Theologicas, imprimis ad eam Theologiæ partem, quam vulgò 'positi-vam appellant, applicuit. Postquàm autem in hoc studiorum genere non nihil profecisset, reversus in Galliam, Parisiis commoratus est, ubi captus nomine & eruditione Cardinalis Peronii, clarissimi Catholicorum Romanorum fidei defensoris, coepit cogitare de ejuranda eorum, qui Reformatorum nomen sibi sumunt, Religione. Ex eo tempore in Peronii familiam cooptatus, in illius Comitatu vixit aliquantisper, à quo postea cùm discederet, Lingonensi Episcopo se adjunxit. Sed ut Morinus modesti erat animi, & ab omni fastu abhorrentis, relictâ non solùm Cardinalis, sed & Episcopi domô, ut tranquilliorum vitam studiisque suis magis accommodatam ageret, Congregationi Presbyterorum Oratorii, quæ tunc in Gallia, potissimum Parisiis celeberrima erat, nomen suum dedit. Congregationis illius instituendæ autor fuit Petrus Berullns, Presbyter Parisiensis, qui postea ab Urbano VIII, ob singularem suam pietatem in Cardinalium ordinem adscriptus est. Institutionis autem ratio novæ illius Presbyterorum societatis in Bulla,{a} quam Paulus V. Reginæ Mariæ precibus largitus fuit, sic exprimitur: Nimirum ut disciplina Ecclesiastica undique fere in Regno Franciæ Hæresium bellorumque præteritorum injuria tùm in Religione, tùm etiam in Moribus, non parum depravata ac corrupta, in primævum ac pristinum suum statum, devotionisque & pietatis splendorem salubri aliquâ ratione restitueretur. Dicta autem fuit Oratorii Jesu Christi Domini Nostri Congregatio in Honorem Orationum, quas in diebus carnis suæ fudit, ut ii, qui ipsam ingrederentur, eundem Jesum Christum pro nobis in Oratione positum & pernoctantem revererentur, quorum principale Institutum esset, perfectioni sacerdotalis status totaliter incumbere, singulasque actiones ordini sacerdotali proprie convenientes amplecti. Hactenus ex Bulla Pauli V. & hæc fere ad verbum
units.tr: John Morin was born at Blois, a town in France on the Loire, near the end of the previous century. His parents professed the religion that is called Huguenot in those parts, and he was brought up in it. He was sent to La Rochelle, which was then the strongest stronghold of the Huguenots, to devote himself to the humane letters. Then he went to Leiden, where he cultivated Greek and Hebrew and applied his mind to theology, especially to that part of it which is commonly called positive. After he had made some progress in this kind of study, he returned to France and stayed in Paris. There, won over by the name and learning of Cardinal Perron, the most distinguished defender of the faith of the Roman Catholics, he began to think of abandoning the religion of those who take to themselves the name of Reformed. From that time he was enrolled in Perron's household and lived for some while in his service. When he later left him, he attached himself to the bishop of Langres. But Morin was a man of modest disposition, abhorring all show, and so, leaving the household not only of the Cardinal but also of the bishop, in order to lead a quieter life better suited to his studies, he gave his name to the Congregation of the Priests of the Oratory, which was then very famous in France, above all in Paris. The founder of that Congregation was Pierre de Bérulle, a priest of Paris, who was afterwards enrolled by Urban VIII among the Cardinals on account of his singular piety. The plan of the new society of priests is set out thus in the Bull of Paul V, which he granted at the prayer of Queen Mary: namely, that the church discipline, which throughout almost the whole kingdom of France had been not a little depraved and corrupted, both in religion and in morals, by the injury of the heresies and the wars of the past, should be restored in some salutary way to its original and pristine state and to the splendour of devotion and piety. The Congregation was called the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus Christ our Lord, in honour of the prayers which he poured out in the days of his flesh, so that those who entered it might revere the same Jesus Christ, who for our sake gave himself to prayer and spent the night in it. Its chief purpose was to devote itself wholly to the perfection of the priestly state and to embrace each action that properly belongs to the priestly order. So far from the Bull of Paul V, and these things are taken almost word for word.

units.la: {a} Bulla Pauli V. An. 1613. bum sumpta sunt ex Literis Regiis {b} quibus Regina Maria erigendae societatis illius tam Parisiis quàm in aliis Regni locis facultatem concesserat. Itaque Morinus adhuc Juvenis, genus istud vitae amplectitur, de perficiendo sacerdotali ordine & ad pristinum statum revocando, uti Berullus sibi proposuerat, minimè cogitans, sed quod illud esset studiis suis maximè commodum, videretque in ea Societate Presbyteros, qui sub praetextu perficiendi ordinis sacerdotalis nullo Religionis voto adstricti, nullisque functionibus Ecclesiasticis occupati, pingvi otiò fruebantur. Berullus ingenium eruditionemque Morini plurimi faciens, illum dedit Mironio tunc Andegavensi Episcopo, ut assiduus studiorum illius comes esset. Is postea factus Archiepiscopus Lugdunensis: & ab ejus latere vix recessit Morinus usque ad illius obitum. Tunc Parisios reversus vixit in domo Oratorii Parisiensis una cum
units.tr: {a} Bull of Paul V, 1613. These words are taken almost verbatim from the Royal Letters {b} by which Queen Mary had granted permission to found that society both in Paris and in other places of the kingdom. Thus Morin, still a young man, embraced this kind of life, with no thought of perfecting the priestly order and restoring it to its former state, as Bérulle had proposed for himself; rather, because it was most convenient for his studies. He saw that in that society there were priests who, under the pretext of perfecting the priestly order, were bound by no vow of religion, were occupied with no ecclesiastical functions, and enjoyed a rich leisure. Bérulle, valuing Morin's talent and learning very highly, gave him to Mironius, then bishop of Angers, so that he might be a constant companion of his studies. Mironius afterwards became archbishop of Lyons, and Morin scarcely left his side until his death. Then he returned to Paris and lived in the house of the Paris Oratory, together with Bérulle, who by his uprightness and frankness of character had won the favour of the Queen Mother.

units.la: {b} Lettres de la Reyne Regente, An. 1612, le 2. Jan. cum Berullo, qui ob probitatem suam morumque candorem Reginæ Matris gratiam sibi conciliaverat. Cùm autem domus illius Presbyteri vitam planè otiosam agerent ac tranquillam, cantandis solum Litaniis quibusdam occupati, Literarum studio se totum dedit. Cantus ejusmodi Litaniarum apud Oratorianos putatur autor Cotonus Jesuita sagacissimus, qui exemplo Societatis suæ Berullum commonuit, necesse prorsus esse, ut Congregationis suæ homines functionis alicujus Ecclesiasticæ beneficio domi retineret, alias per urbem quotidie errabundos fore.
units.tr: {b} Letters of the Queen Regent, 1612, 2 January. Since the priests of that house lived a wholly idle and quiet life, occupied only with the singing of certain litanies, Morin gave himself entirely to the study of letters. The singing of such litanies among the Oratorians is thought to have been devised by Coton, the very shrewd Jesuit, who, following the example of his society, warned Bérulle that it was absolutely necessary that he keep the men of his Congregation at home by means of some ecclesiastical office, otherwise they would wander through the city every day.

units.la: MORINUS ratus scire suum nihil fo-re, nisi & se scire alii cognoscerent, publici juris jam fecerat librum de Patriarcharum & primatum origine, & antiqua Censurarum in Cleros praxi, dicaveratque Urbano 8. summo Pontifici.{c} Operis istius Morinum non longo post tempore tanquam festinantius à se editi poeni-
units.tr: MORIN, thinking that he knew nothing unless others also recognised that he knew it, had already made public his book on the origin of the patriarchs and primates and the ancient practice of censures against the clergy, and had dedicated it to Pope Urban VIII. Morin soon repented of having published this work too hastily, since in it many things

units.la: {c} Edit. Parif. apud Anton. Steph. in 4to. An. 1626. poenituit ; adeo multa in hoc extant,quae: illum tunc in rebus Ecclesiasticis Infantem manifestò produnt. Ut enim dicendi illius genus præterea,quod nimis luxurians Juvenem sapit, abundatq; phrasibus ac similitudinibus longius petitis, primorum Pontificum Epistolas, quae haud dubie suppositae sunt, tanquam genuinas interdum laudat; Dionysioque Areopagitae tribuit Libros de Hierarchia ; & quod his omnibus deterius videtur, Morinus magis accedit sententiæ Romanensium aulicorum de suprema Episcopi Romani potestate,quam saniori Theologorum Catholicorum, imprimisque Gallorum doctrinis, qui illud argumentum erudite pertractârunt. Urbanum Pontificem Maximum superbis hisce titulis statim à limine ornat {d} Divinitus constitueris Thesauri Ecclesiæ Custos & Præses, æternitatis dispensator, mentis divinæ Interpres, legum Christianarum arbiter, omnium Mortalium Judex, unicus tui dominus & vindex. Deinde in contextu ope
units.tr: {c} Paris edition, by Antoine Estienne, in quarto, 1626. clearly reveal him to have been then a novice in ecclesiastical matters. For besides his style of speaking, which, being overly luxuriant, smacks of youth and abounds in phrases and comparisons drawn from far away, he sometimes praises as genuine the letters of the first Popes, which are undoubtedly spurious, and he ascribes to Dionysius the Areopagite the books on the Hierarchy. And, what seems worse than all these things, Morin inclines more to the opinion of the Roman courtiers about the supreme power of the Roman Bishop than to the sounder doctrine of Catholic theologians, and especially of the French, who have treated that subject learnedly. At the very outset he adorns Urban, the Supreme Pontiff, with these proud titles: {d} Divinely appointed guardian and president of the treasury of the Church, dispenser of eternity, interpreter of the divine mind, arbiter of Christian laws, judge of all mortals, sole lord and avenger of thee. Then, in the course of the text, he

units.la: {d} In Epist. Dedic. ad Urb. VII. operis {e} verbis sesquipedalibus & ho-mine gravi haud dignis affirmat, vincula quibus tanquam habenis membra Chri-sti Pontifex moderatur, & velut alter Hercules Gallicus Christianos omnes ab ore pendulos & è sinuosis errorum an-fractibus in ovili revocat, quatuor esse Episcopalis Jurisdictionis ordines. Epi-scoporum, Primatum, & Patriarcharum: Praeterea scribit Morinus, {f} Apostolos, qviqve eos secuti sunt, Pontifices, in Pro-vinciis creasse Archiepiscopos: Episco-pos in sua ditione Monarchas esse. {g} Regimen, inquit, omne Ecclesiasticum est Monarchicum; dioecesis Episcopi dioecesim regunt; Monarchicus igitur. En Morini acumen, dum non modo Pa-pae Romano, sed & aliis Episcopis adula-tur. Verum his & aliis ejusdem naturae plurimis valere jussis, satis erit annotasse, Morinum postea tam inepti operis pu-disse, saepiusque de illo castigando cogi-tasse. Mirum tamen est, quam avide il-lud à Theologis Parisiensibus exceptus fue-
units.tr: {d} In the dedicatory epistle to Urban VII of the work. {e} asserts, in words too pompous and unworthy of a serious man, that the Pontiff, like another Gallic Hercules, governs the members of Christ with the bonds by which they are held as with reins, and calls back all Christians, hanging on his lips, from the winding paths of error into the sheepfold; and that there are four orders of episcopal jurisdiction: of bishops, of primates, and of patriarchs. Moreover, Morin writes that the Apostles, and those who followed them, the Pontiffs, created archbishops in the provinces, and that bishops are monarchs in their own dioceses. {f} "All ecclesiastical government," he says, "is monarchical; the bishops of the dioceses rule their dioceses; therefore it is monarchical." See Morin's acuteness, since he flatters not only the Roman Pope but also the other bishops. But, these and many other things of the same kind having been dismissed, it will be enough to note that Morin afterwards repented of so foolish a work and often thought of correcting it. It is nevertheless remarkable how eagerly it was received by the Paris theologians,

units.la: {e} Lib.1.Exercit.1,
units.tr: {e} Book 1, Exercise 1.

units.la: {f} Exercit.19.
units.tr: {f} Exercise 19.

units.la: {g} Exercit.12. fuerit,præsertim à junioribus, qui illud, præeuntibus sibi Magistris suis, Scholarum exercitationib9 utilissimum judicarunt ; ita ut post Morini obitum secunda illius editio prodierit, cui cùm obstitisset ejusdem Morini amicus, lepidum à bibliopola editionis istius autore tulit responsum ; scilicet bibliopolas diversum plane de Libris judicium ferre à virorum eruditorum judicio ; bonum illis videri librum, cujus citò exemplaria divenduntur ; se quidem scire, opus dePatriarcharum & Primatum origine Morino non parum displicuisse, sed non tam de Morini fama sollicitum se esse, quàm de pecunia, quam in editione novissima exercitationum illius biblicarum profuderat ; se cogitare de ratione aliqva[?],qva opus illud de rebus biblicis & Rabbinicis,quod marsupium suum evacuaverat, Theologis præsertim Parisiensibus etiam invitis,divenderet : Res ista bibliopolæ, uti meditatus fuerat, feliciter successit, opus enim illud secundo editum in eadem forma,atque exercitationes biblicæ, quæ à nemine legebantur, & in eodem cum his volumine compactum, in fronte illius voluminis præmisit. Qua arte plerosque Theologos delusit, opus de origine Patriarcharum seorsim divendere renuens. Adeo verum est, Parisiis rerum biblicarum studium frigere, maximè apud Theologos, qui scholarum nugis toti incumbunt: Verùm ad Morinum nostra redeat Oratio.
units.tr: {g} Exercise 12. especially by the younger men, who, with their masters going before them, judged it most useful for their school exercises. So after Morin's death a second edition appeared. When a friend of Morin opposed it, the bookseller who published this edition gave him a witty answer: that booksellers form a quite different judgement of books from that of learned men; a book seems good to them when copies of it sell quickly; he knew indeed that the work on the origin of the patriarchs and primates had not greatly pleased Morin, but he was not so much concerned about Morin's reputation as about the money he had spent on the latest edition of Morin's biblical exercises; he was thinking of some way to sell off that work on biblical and rabbinic matters, which had emptied his purse, especially to the Paris theologians, even against their will. This plan succeeded for the bookseller as he had devised it: for he had the work, printed a second time in the same format as the biblical exercises, which no one was reading, bound in the same volume with them, and put it at the front of that volume. By this trick he deceived most of the theologians, who refused to buy the work on the origin of the patriarchs separately. So true it is that the study of biblical matters grows cold at Paris, especially among theologians, who devote themselves wholly to the trifles of the schools. But let our discourse return to Morin.

units.la: ILLE ne in otio cum plerisque Congregationis suæ sociis languere videretur, novam septuaginta Interpretum versionis editionem juxta exemplar Vaticanum meditatus est. Romæ prodierant Græcè illi Interpretes ex codice admodum vetusto & bonæ notæ, si perpauca excipias, quæ in eo desiderabantur, Anno 1587. Jussu & autoritate Sixti quinti Pontificis Maximi: Et anno sequenti Nobilius vir eruditissimus ibidem publicaverat antiquam versionis illius Græcæ translationem, tot seculis intermortuam, quæ olim in occidentali Ecclesia le-gebatur, quamquè si non integram, sal-[?] tem qva potuit industria & labore improbo luci restituit. Utramqve Morinus cùm Græcam tum Latinam in unum corpus redactam notatis versuum distinctionibus Parisiis edi curavit, Anno 1628, opus sane Theologis, qvi sacras Literas tractant, percommodum. Huic autem ne qvid deesset, præfationem, in qva de antiqvis scripturæ sacræ translationibus prolixè. disserit, atqve imprimis de Septuaginta Interpretum autoritate, tàm ex Patrum, qvàm Judæorum sententia, præmisit. Præcipuas etiam in illa præsatione ingentis, qvod Græcos inter & Hebræos codices reperitur, discriminis causas attingit, de his detrahit, ut illos extollat. Romanæ editionis præstantiam & sinceritatem mirè prædicat. Ho-[?] diernis contextus Hebræi exemplaribus, qvibus vitia non pauca inesse existimat, nec non iis, qvi toti à Masorethicis illis codicibus dependent, infensissimum se ostendit. Et ut majorem invidiam Judæis, eorumqve seqvacibus concitet, profert autoritatem Pentateuchi HebræoSamaritani, cujus exemplar ex oriente Parisios asportatum, in Bibliotheca Oratorii Parisiensis asservabatur, eaque inprimis loca animadversit, quibus Samaritani à Judæis discrepantes cum Græcis consentiebant. Jam ex eo tempore Hebraicæ veritatis assertores tàm ex Catholicorum, quàm Protestantium grege manifesto deprehenderunt, quid de sacris bibliorum codicibus Morinus sentiret, quoque animo Samaritanorum Græcorumque exemplaria tantis ornaret laudibus. Berullo præfatio illa, quod vulgaribus Protestantium placitis adversaretur, minimè displicuit. Non enim egregius iste novæ spiritualitatis Magister, Mysticæ Theologiæ, cui Congregationis suæ viros assuefaciebat, ita erat addictus, quin ad Theologiæ libros, quos vulgò Controversiarum appellant, animum attenderet[?] quare autor fuit Morino, ut Pentateuchum Hebræo-Samaritanum in publicum ederet, pertractarer-que dedita opera illud argumentum de rebus biblicis. Jussa Berulli promptus excipit Morinus, ae lætissimus tam eximio Operum suorum approbatore, prius cogitat de publicando libro aliquo, quem Cardinalis Berulli opera Regi offerre posset, tunc scilicet rationem meditatus, quâ studiorum suorum beneficiô ad dignitatem aliquam Ecclesiasticam, cui dudum inhiabat, promoveri posset.
units.tr: Lest he seem to languish in idleness with most of his fellow members of the Congregation, Morinus set about a new edition of the Septuagint according to the Vatican manuscript. The Greek Interpreters had already been published at Rome in 1587, by order and authority of Pope Sixtus V, from a very old and well-regarded codex, lacking only a few passages that were missing from it. In the following year the most learned Nobilius had published there the old Greek translation of that version, which had lain dead for many centuries and had once been read in the Western Church. Though he restored it, if not in full, at least as far as his diligence and tireless labour allowed. Morinus had both the Greek and the Latin, brought together into one volume with the verse divisions marked, published at Paris in In the year 1628. It is a work highly useful to theologians who study the sacred Letters. To make it complete, he prefixed a preface, in which he discusses at length the ancient translations of Holy Scripture, and above all the authority of the Seventy Interpreters, both from the opinion of the Fathers and of the Jews. In that preface he also touches on the main causes of the great difference found between the Greek and Hebrew codices, and draws conclusions from them in order to exalt the former. He praises the excellence and purity of the Roman edition in remarkable terms. He shows himself most hostile to the present Hebrew texts of the Scriptures, which he thinks contain not a few faults, and likewise to those who depend entirely on those Masoretic codices. And to stir up greater odium against the Jews and their followers, he brings forward the authority of the Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch, a copy of which had been carried from the East to Paris and was kept in the library of the Paris Oratory. He especially noted those passages in which the Samaritans, differing from the Jews, agreed with the Greeks. From that time onward, the defenders of Hebrew truth, from the flock of Catholics as well as Protestants, clearly perceived what Morinus thought of the sacred codices of the Bible, and with what spirit he lavished such praise on the Samaritan and Greek copies. That preface did not at all displease Berullus, though it ran counter to the common opinions of the Protestants. For this outstanding master of the new spirituality, whom he trained the men of his Congregation to follow in Mystical Theology, was not so devoted to that discipline that he did not turn his attention to the books of theology commonly called controversial. Therefore he advised Morinus to publish the Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch and to treat that subject of biblical matters with dedicated effort. Morinus readily accepted Berullus's instructions and, delighted by such an excellent approver of his works, first thought of publishing some book which Cardinal Berullus could present to the King. He was evidently planning by this means to win, through the favour of his studies, some ecclesiastical dignity to which he had long aspired.

units.la: ITAQUE Morinus sub finem Anni 1629. Historiam edidit Gallico sermone conscriptam, cui nomen fecit, Historia liberatæ Ecclesiæ ex Constantino Imperatore, ac supremæ summorum Pontificum in rebus temporalibus potestatis, quam à Christianissimis Franciæ Regibus acceperunt. ({b}) Sed res longè aliter, quàm Morinus sibi persvaserat, accidit, quippe moritur Berullus, dum operis illius editio absolvitur, adeoque nec illud, nec scriptoris nomen & eruditionem Regi, cui dicatum erat, commenda-
units.tr: Accordingly, towards the end of the year 1629, Morinus published a history written in the French language, which he called The History of the Church's Deliverance from the Emperor Constantine, and of the supreme power over temporal affairs which the Roman Pontiffs received from the most Christian Kings of France. ({b}) But things turned out very differently from what Morinus had persuaded himself. For Berullus died while the printing of that work was being completed, so that he could not commend it, nor the author's name and learning, to the King to whom it was dedicated.

units.la: {b} Histoire de la delivrance de l'eglise par l'Empereur Constant. & de la grandeur & souveraineté temporelle donné à l'Eglise Rom.: par les Roys de France, Imprim. à Paris in sol. 1630. re potuit. Interea Romani Aulici ipseque Pontifex Maximus graviter offensi fuére tam Inscriptione illius Historiæ, quâm rebus nonnullis in ea contentis, quas in Romanæ Ecclesiæ dedecus verti posse existimabant.
units.tr: {b} History of the deliverance of the Church by the Emperor Constantine, and of the greatness and temporal sovereignty given to the Roman Church by the Kings of France. Printed at Paris, folio, 1630.

units.la: Ferre non potuit Urbanus VIII. quæ ex una parte in prima fronte libri conspicitur, Caroli Magni effigiem, qui ensem manu tenens dexterâ, præsentat sinistrâ Pontifici imaginem, quæ Romam, Ravennam & Neapolim exhibet, sicque illum affatur, Italos parere jubebo; ex altera verò parte extat Papæ Effigies ita respondentis, tu mihi quodcunque hoc Regni. Carolum Magnum adversus Longobardos tantùm bella movisse objiciebant Romani Francos summis Pontificibus reddidisse potius, quæ suæ antea [illegible, ~4 letters]ditionis erant, quàm dedisse; Morinum non tam Francis, quàm Germanis favere, cùm Imperator fuerit Carolus Magnus. Morino præterea sto-machabatur Urbanus VIII. quod de Baptismo Constantini agens, in eorum sententiam propenderet, qui negant, Romæ illum baptizatum ; scilicet opponebat Imperatoris illius baptisterium, quod in Basilica Lateranensi visitur. Ob ista & alia ejusdem naturæ, quæ prætereo, Franciscus Barberinus tunc Cardinalis Nepos, uti loquuntur, seu Patronus, bibliothecæ custodi revisionem Historiæ illius commisit. Is erat Josephus Maria Suaresius, qui postea factus est Episcopus Vasionensis in Comitatu Avenionensi : Et ut erat vir modestissimus, pacisqve amantissimus, ita ab aulicorum Romanorum ingenio, qui de Morini opere apud summum Pontificem detraxerant, valde alienus fuit. Suaresii amicitiam sibi conciliaverat Morinus beneficio Presbyterorum Congregationis suæ, qui Romæ degebant, variasqve ad eum dedit literas, quæ illi pergratæ fuerunt. Scripsit qvoqve operis sui apologeticam Epistolam ad Cardinalem Franciscum Barperinum, cujus animum a se alienatum senserat. In hac pluribus comprobat, se fuisse semper sedis Apostolicæ studiosissimum, meminitqve officio-ficio ficiorum,quæ jam antea huic sedi præstiterit. Verùm Apologia ista non effecit, ut in Cardinalis gratiam rediret: Suaresius enim postea Historiæ illius loca, quæ castigatione egerent, quæque illu-strationis causa addenda essent, ex man-dato Cardinalis, imò & summi Pontificis, indicavit Morino, qui ea omnia in nova operis sui editione, quam paraturus erat, ad mentem aulæ Romanæ se reformaturum libenter pollicitus est; etsi promissis suis minimè steterit: Nunquam enim visa est secunda libri illius editio. Cæterum tunc etiam Romæ non defuere viri Illustrissimi, atque inprimis Cardinalis Bagnius, qui contra summi Pontificis & Cardinalis Barberini sententiam Morini Librum suffragiis suis approbarent. Halloixius Jesuita Duacensis, Morino rescribere veritus non est, se nunquam adduci potuisse, ut crederet, Constantini baptismum aliàs fuisse quàm Nicomediæ, in extrema ejus vita, lætari-que se à Morino in sua sententia fuisse confirmatum.
units.tr: Urban VIII could not bear what is seen on the first page of one side of the book: an image of Charlemagne, holding a sword in his right hand and presenting in his left hand to the Pope an image showing Rome, Ravenna and Naples, and addressing him thus: I will order the Italians to obey. On the other side is the figure of the Pope responding: you, whatever this kingdom is, to me. The Romans objected that Charlemagne had waged war against the Lombards only so that he could return to the supreme Pontiffs what had formerly been theirs, rather than give them anything new. They also said that Morinus favoured the Franks less than the Germans, since Charlemagne was an Emperor. Urban VIII was further offended with Morinus because, in discussing the baptism of Constantine, he leaned towards the opinion of those who deny that he was baptised at Rome, namely by pointing to the baptistery of that Emperor which is seen in the Lateran Basilica. On account of these and other matters of the same kind, which I pass over, Francis Barberini, then Cardinal Nephew, or as they say, patron, entrusted the revision of that History to the librarian. This was Joseph Maria Suarez, who was later made Bishop of Vaison in the County of Avignon. As he was a most modest man and a lover of peace, he was quite far from the temper of the Roman courtiers who had disparaged Morinus's work before the supreme Pontiff. Morinus had won Suarez's friendship through the good offices of the priests of his Congregation who lived in Rome, and he sent him various letters, which were very welcome to him. He also wrote an apologetic letter for his work to Cardinal Francis Barberini, whose feelings towards him he had perceived to be alienated. In it he proves at length that he had always been most devoted to the Apostolic See, and he recalls the services he had previously rendered to that see. But this apology did not bring him back into the Cardinal's favour. For Suarez afterwards indicated to Morinus, by the Cardinal's command, and indeed by that of the supreme Pontiff, the passages of the History that needed correction and those that ought to be added for clarification. Morinus willingly promised that in the new edition of his work, which he was preparing, he would reform all of these to the mind of the Roman court, though he did not keep his promises: a second edition of that book was never seen. Meanwhile, even at Rome there were not wanting most distinguished men, and above all Cardinal Bagni, who, against the opinion of the supreme Pontiff and of Cardinal Barberini, approved Morinus's book with their votes. The Jesuit Halloix of Douai did not hesitate to write back to Morinus that he could never be brought to believe that Constantine's baptism had taken place anywhere other than at Nicomedia at the end of his life, and he said he rejoiced that he had been confirmed in his opinion by Morinus.

units.la: VERUM ut libere dicam, quid sentiam de hac Historia Gallico sermone conscripta; Morinus tunc de unius Regis Christianissimi, cui illam consecrabat, & de Francici nominis gloria cogitans, ad Germanos & Italos parum attendisse videtur, adeoque mirum non est, quòd ab Italis paulò delicatioribus, cùm agitur de honore sedis Apostolicæ potestateque summi Pontificis, quam ad coelum usque extollunt, illi nonnulla objecta fuerint, quasi severius dicta in gentem Italam ac Germanam. In hoc opere nomen Francorum passim reperias, etiam cum nondum illorum nomen in ea Galliæ parte, quæ postea ab illis dicta est Francia, cognosceretur. Ita Morinus Constantinum in Francia, & opera Episcoporum Franciæ ad Christum conversum fuisse asserit: Et quasi Francorum gloria non aliunde, quàm ex Impostoris testimonio peti posset, famosum profert vaticinium de Francorum Rege, qui universum terrarum orbem sub ditione sua tenere[?] debeat, quiqve regum omnium mundi novissimus, demum in urbe Jerusalem ad montem Oliveti sceptrum coronamque suam depositurus sit. Imo hanc communem olim fuisse doctissimorum virorum sententiam, affirmare non dubitat. Alia ejusdem rationis bene multa praetermitto ; neque invideo Joanni Morino, qui elogio Imperatoris Constantini,quod è Graeco Eusebii fecit Gallicum,longè plurima ex aliis scriptoribus addidit: quandoquidem ob praeclara facinora dignus fuit his laudibus Invictissimus ille Imperator,qui supra omnem fidem de ReligioneChristiana bene meritus est. Liceat tamen suspicari, Eusebium exemplo Xenophontis in Cyro-paedia & QvintiCurtii in vita Alexandri Herois ideam sibi effinxisse. Morinus in postrema Historiae suae parte in qua disserit de Constantini donatione,de ingentibus beneficiis à Franciae Regibus Ecclesiae Romanae collatis, de reportatis à gente Normana in Apulia & Calabria, & adversus Saracenos in Sicilia,victoriis, & eorundem Normanorum erga summos Pontificès meritis, longe accuratio-rem se ostendit, quæ pars sola Historiæ suæ digna lectu videtur. In universo autem opere Morinus Gallici sermonis non modo imperitum se demonstrat, sed & scribendi artem penitus ignorasse, adeo ineptum in hac arte ubique se præbet.
units.tr: But to speak frankly what I think of this History written in the French language: Morinus, thinking then of the one Most Christian King to whom he consecrated it, and of the glory of the French name, seems to have paid little attention to the Germans and Italians. So it is no wonder that some objections were raised against him by Italians who are a little more sensitive, when the honour of the Apostolic See and the authority of the supreme Pontiff, which they extol to heaven, is at stake, as though things had been said too severely against the Italian and German nations. In this work you will find the name of the Franks everywhere, even at a time when that name was not yet known in that part of Gaul which was afterwards called France. Thus Morinus asserts that Constantine was converted to Christ in France, and by the work of the bishops of France. And as though the glory of the Franks could be sought from no source other than the testimony of an impostor, he brings forward a notorious prophecy about the King of the Franks, who is to hold the whole orb of the earth under his rule, and who, the last of all the kings of the world, is at last to lay down his sceptre and crown in the city of Jerusalem on the Mount of Olives. He does not hesitate to assert that this was once the common opinion of the most learned men. I pass over many other things of the same kind, nor do I grudge John Morinus, who turned into French the eulogy of the Emperor Constantine taken from Eusebius's Greek, and added very many things from other writers; for that most unconquered Emperor, who deserved beyond all belief well of the Christian religion, was worthy of these praises on account of his famous deeds. Yet one may suspect that Eusebius formed his ideal after the example of Xenophon in the Cyropaedia and of Quintus Curtius in the life of Alexander the Hero. In the last part of his History, in which he discusses Constantine's donation, the enormous benefits conferred by the Kings of France on the Roman Church, the victories gained against the Saracens in Sicily and from the Norman people in Apulia and Calabria, and the merits of those same Normans towards the supreme Pontiffs, Morinus shows himself far more careful, and this part alone seems worth reading. In the whole work, however, Morinus shows himself not only unskilled in the French language but also to have been utterly ignorant of the art of writing, so inept does he show himself in this art everywhere.

units.la: VIX in publicum Morinus ediderat Historiam Ecclesiæ Liberatæ à Constantino, cùm[?] exercitationes Ecclesiasticas in Pentateuchum Samaritanum, cujus editionem jam à duobus annis meditatus fuerat, publicare in animo habuis[?], ad id operis respiciens, coluerat per literas amicitiam Hieronymi Alexandri, viri literarum & literatorum amantissimi, à quo non pauca didicit tam de Samaritanorum siclis[?], quàm[?] de illorum codicibus, & aliis ejusdem gentis rebus, quæ magna ex parte exercitationibus suis postea inseruit.
units.tr: Morinus had scarcely published his History of the Church freed from Constantine when he meant to publish ecclesiastical exercitations on the Samaritan Pentateuch, whose edition he had been planning for two years. With that work in view, he had cultivated by letter a friendship with Jerome Alexander, a man most devoted to letters and to learned men. From him he learned not a few things about the Samaritan shekels, about their codices, and about other matters of that people, much of which he later inserted into his exercitations.

units.la: Alexander patria Romanus scribit Morino, Romæ duo Pentateuchi Samaritani exemplaria reperiri; de primo, quod in Bibliotheca Vaticana asservabatur, non admodum sollicitus fuisse videvidetur Morinus, quòd esset Hebræo-Samaritanum, lingua videlicet Hebræa, charactere duntaxat Samaritano descriptum, & ab Oratoriano Codice non discrepans; alterum vero quod non modo charactere Samaritano exaratum, sed & Lingua scriptum Samaritana, & Pentateuchi Hebræo-Samaritani in dialectum Samaritanam Translatio, perficiendæ Pentateuchi Samaritani editioni apprime necessarium judicavit. Hoc exemplar asservabatur in musæo viri nobilis Petri à Valle, qui annos duodecim in orientalibus regionibus consumpserat. Ejusdemque quoque Petri à Valle opera Harlæus Sanctius, tunc Regis Christianissimi apud Turcarum Imperatorem Orator, nactus fuerat codicem Hebræo-Samaritanum, quò Bibliothecam Oratorii Parisiensis ditaverat, quique postea à Morino editus fuit. Alexander Petro à Valle auctor fuit, ut versionis suæ Samaritanæ editionem pateretur. Jam de illa Romæ edenda Vallæus cogitaverat, verùm de obtinenda à superioribus libri illius permissiomissione desperans, si in aliquibus ab Interprete Latino seu vulgata discreparet, mittit exemplar suum Parisios ad Morinum, ut illud edi curaret, nihil ad se referre judicans, liber an Parisiis an Romæ excuderetur, primo quidem sibi propofuerat[?] apographum duntaxat mittere, sed quia nemo Romæ tunc erat, qui dialectum Samaritanam calleret, adeoque ab homine tantum posset exarari, qui literas absque ulla intelligentia delinearet, misit ipsummet autographum, ad id imprimis adductus precibus Clarissimi Perescii, optans tamen, ut suus codex, quem plurimi faciebat, diligentissime asservatus, nullo pacto ab impressoribus, ut mos est, dissolveretur aut deturparetur. Morinus qui jam ex aliquo specimine versionis illius Samaritanæ, quod acceperat à Vallæo, hanc accuratissimam esse, & fere de verbo ad verbum Pentateuchi Hebræo-Samaritani translationem, cognoverat, dialectumque Samaritanam in paucis à Chaldaica differre, tunc volumen integrum habens præ manibus, non aliud de versione illa Samaritana judicium tulit quàm antea. Interea Petrus à Valle scribit Morino,qvi sit gentis Samaritanæ in oriente status. Samaritanos scilicet hodiernis temporibus numero paucissimos esse,se aliqvot reperisse Cairi in Ægypto,Gazæ, Hierosolymis, Damasci & in civitate Sichem, à Turcis Naplus sive Neapolis nuncupata,qvæ nunc Samariæ Metropolis, eorum Synagogas extra civitatem inter hortos amœnissimos positas,qvæ viles qvidem extrinsecus appareant, intus autem picturis & auro haud indecore ornatus esse,variisq; inscriptionibus Lingua Samaritana insignitas. Miratus est Morinus,gentem Samaritanam in tam contemnenda paucitate legis Mosaciæ exemplar, patrios mores,ritusq; suos conservare potuisse, de ista iterum qværit nonnulla ex Vallæo, qvæ rescire cupiebat; sed hæc penitus se ignorare liberè agnoscit Vallæus, qvippe qvi nihil omnino Lingvarum Orientalium se scivisse profiteatur,cùm ad Samaritanos adiit. Non pauca tamen
units.tr: Alexander, a Roman by birth, wrote to Morinus that two copies of the Samaritan Pentateuch could be found at Rome. Morinus did not seem very concerned about the first, which was kept in the Vatican Library, since it was a Hebrew-Samaritan text: that is, in the Hebrew language, written only in Samaritan characters, and not differing from the Oratory codex. The other copy, however, which was written not only in Samaritan characters but also in the Samaritan language, containing a translation of the Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch into the Samaritan dialect, he judged to be especially necessary for producing an edition of the Samaritan Pentateuch. This copy was kept in the museum of the noble Pietro della Valle, who had spent twelve years in the eastern regions. Through the same Pietro della Valle's efforts, Harlaeus Sanctius, then ambassador of the Most Christian King to the Emperor of the Turks, had obtained a Hebrew-Samaritan codex, which he had enriched the library of the Paris Oratory with, and which was later edited by Morinus. Alexander advised Pietro della Valle to allow an edition of his Samaritan version to be published. Della Valle had already considered publishing it at Rome, but, despairing of obtaining the permission of his superiors for that book, in case it differed in some places from the Latin translator, or the Vulgate, he sent his copy to Morinus at Paris so that he might arrange for its publication, judging that it made no difference to him whether the book was printed at Paris or at Rome. At first he had intended to send only a copy, but since there was then no one at Rome who understood the Samaritan dialect, and so it could be written out only by someone who traced the letters without any understanding, he sent the autograph itself, being moved above all by the entreaties of the most distinguished Peiresc. Yet he wished that his manuscript, which he valued very highly, should be kept with the greatest care and on no account be taken apart or defaced by the printers, as is the custom. Morinus, who had already learned from some specimen of that Samaritan version, which he had received from Della Valle, that it was a most accurate translation, and nearly word for word of the Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch, and that the Samaritan dialect differed from the Chaldee in few points, and who now had the complete volume in hand, formed no different judgment of that Samaritan version than he had before. Meanwhile Pietro della Valle wrote to Morinus about the state of the Samaritan people in the East. He said that the Samaritans in modern times are very few in number; that he had found some of them at Cairo in Egypt, at Gaza, at Jerusalem, at Damascus, and in the city of Sichem, which the Turks call Nablus or Neapolis, now the metropolis of Samaria; that their synagogues lie outside the city among most pleasant gardens, which look mean on the outside but are decorated inside, not unbecomingly, with paintings and gold, and marked with various inscriptions in the Samaritan language. Morinus was astonished that the Samaritan people, in such a contemptible small number, had been able to preserve a copy of the Mosaic law, their ancestral customs and their rites, and he again asked Della Valle for some further information on these matters, which he wished to learn. But Della Valle frankly admitted that he knew nothing of these things at all, since he professed that he had known nothing whatever of the Oriental languages when he went among the Samaritans. Nevertheless, he did write to Morinus a good deal

units.la: scripsit Morino de Chronologia Muham-medanorum, eaque in primis quæ in Perside à Doctoribus illius gentis de hoc negotio didicerat; accepit etiam à Vallæo Morinus Linguæ Ægyptiacæ Alphabetum & alia nonnulla, quæ ad sermonem Ægyptiacum pertinebant, quorū cognitione ideò Morinus tenebatur, quòd in Bibliothecæ Oratorii Parisiensis foculis hunc[?] delitesceret exemplar quatuor Evangeliorum, scriptum Linguâ Coptica, quò eam donarat Harlæus Sancius.
units.tr: about the chronology of the Muhammadans, especially what he had learned at Persia from the teachers of that people concerning this matter. Morinus also received from Della Valle the alphabet of the Egyptian language and some other things pertaining to the Egyptian tongue. He was obliged to know these things because a copy of the four Gospels, written in the Coptic language, which Harlaeus Sanctius had given, lay hidden in the Paris Oratory library's cupboards.

units.la: PRODEUNT interea Parisiis Morini exercitationes in utrumque Pentateuchum Samaritanorum, ({i}) in quibus de gentis illius Religione, Moribus, illius literis, quas antiquos Hebræorum characteres[?] esse fusius probat, & de illorum siclis, quorum nonnullos profert, variè differit; statim ab initio operis in eo peccat quòd existimet, Samaritanorum Pentateuchum ab antiquis Ecclesiæ Patribus in usum suum Linguâ Græcâ donatum fuisse, cùm longè verisimilius sit ab ipsis
units.tr: MEANWHILE there appeared at Paris Morinus's exercitations on both Samaritan Pentateuchs ({i}), in which he treats at greater length of that people's religion, their customs and their letters, which he proves to be the ancient Hebrew characters, and of their shekels, some of which he produces, and discusses variously. Right at the beginning of the work he errs in thinking that the Samaritan Pentateuch was turned into Greek for its own use by the ancient Fathers of the Church, whereas it is far more probable that

units.la: {i} Edit. Parif, in 4. Anno 1651. Samaritanis, quibus Lingua Græca vernacula erat, Græcè conversum fuisse, ut in eorum Scholis & Synagogis legeretur, exemplò Judæorum Hellenistarum, qui Græcam Septuaginta Interpretum versionem in Synagogas suas introduxerant, ad id potissimum adducti. Verio-ra sunt, quæ habet Morinus in hoc Libro de Codicis Samaritanorum sinceritate, ut probet, illum eundem omninò esse, atque ille, qui ab Eusebio, Hieronymo, & aliis patribus laudatus olim fuerat. Multa & alia adjungit, quæ nuperum non esse exemplar istud, aperte evincunt: sed ex his confici non potest, illud hodierno Hebræorum contextui, quem Judaicum & Masorethicum appellat, in omnibus præferendum esse. Nævos quidem in Judæorum codicibus esse, nemo paulò cordatior diffitebitur; sed forsan longè adhuc plures extant in Samariticis. Mira illa Samaritani exemplaris locis aliquot, quæ alicujus momenti esse videntur, cum Græco Septuaginta seniorum consensio non probat evidenter, uti Morinus existi-mamavit, in his omnibus mancum esse & impurum Judæorum codicem, qvi eadem non repræsentet. Fieri siqvidem potest ut Samaritani exemplar suum, qvod inito perfectè cum Judaico consentiebat, ad Græcum in hisce locis reformaverint, illi præsertim, qvibus Lingua Græca erat domestica ; idqve ex eo etiam probari posset, qvod ibidem Morinus subjungit de Syrorum versione, qvæ cum Græco & Samaritano codicibus concordat : Syriaca enim illa versio, qvam producit Morinus, qvæqve postea edita est in polyglottis Parisiensibus, hac ratione pluribus in locis ad Græcam Septuaginta Interpretum haud dubiè accommodata suit. His accedit, Morinum etiam invitum agnoscere, Samaritanos in describendis suis codicibus parum religiosos fuisse, cùm illi multa his assuerint ex aliis Scripturæ locis petita ; qvæ tamen additamenta, siMorino[?] [?]eredamus, contextum mirè illustrant, & ut loqvitur, ({k}) Textus authentici consimilis illustratio milles à San-
units.tr: {i} Paris edition, in quarto, 1651. it was translated into Greek by the Samaritans themselves, for whom Greek was the vernacular language, so that it might be read in their schools and synagogues, just as the Hellenistic Jews had introduced the Greek version of the Septuagint interpreters into their synagogues, being moved chiefly to do so. More true are the things Morinus has in this book about the sincerity of the Samaritan codex, where he tries to prove that it is altogether the same as the one praised by Eusebius, Jerome and other Fathers long ago. He adds many other things which clearly show that this copy is not recent; but from these it cannot be concluded that it should be preferred in all respects to the present Hebrew text, which he calls Jewish and Masoretic. Blemishes certainly exist in the Jewish codices, as no one of even moderate sense will deny; but perhaps there are far more in the Samaritan ones. As for those wonderful passages of the Samaritan copy in some places which seem to be of some importance, where the agreement of the Greek Septuagint does not clearly prove them, as Morinus thought, in all these cases the Jewish codex is defective and impure for not representing the same readings. For it may well be that the Samaritans, who wrote out their copy so that it agreed perfectly with the Jewish one, altered it to match the Greek in these places, especially where Greek was their native language; and this could also be proved from what Morinus adds there about the Syriac version, which agrees with the Greek and Samaritan codices. For that Syriac version, which Morinus produces, and which was later published in the Paris polyglots, was undoubtedly adapted in many places to the Greek of the Septuagint interpreters in this way. To these points is added that Morinus himself unwillingly admits that the Samaritans were not very scrupulous in copying their codices, since they inserted many things taken from other places of Scripture; yet these additions, if we believe Morinus, wonderfully illuminate the context, and, as he puts it, ({k}) a clearer illustration of the authentic text, similar to a thousand [others], has been made easier by the holy Fathers with the greatest praise of all.

units.la: {k} Mor. in Pentat. Sam. Exercit. 4. cap. 4. à Sanctis patribus maxima cum omnium laude facilitata est. Imò & à patribus non secus atque à Samaritanis in hoc gravissimè erratum, si verum tamen est, Patres, uti Morinus affirmat, complura scripturæ sacræ contextui intulisse, inseruisse[?], implicuisse, & immiscuisse, neque ad rem istam quidquam faciunt exempla, quæ sumit ex Origine & illius hexaplis. Ista enim diversæ sunt omninò rationis. In hoc libro id unum respexisse videtur Morinus, ut Samaritanorum codices Hebræis, quos passim elevat & extenuat, longè anteponendos esse, demonstraret; qua in re de Ecclesia bene mereri se existimat, si palàm de Judæorum codicibus detrahat, quos à fullonibus, sarcinatoribus, institoribus, mangonibus, vitrorum interpolatoribus descriptos fuisse asserit, {l} quasi verò non alia Scripturæ Sacræ exemplaria apud Judæos essent, quàm quæ à plebejis hominibus scripta fuerint, cùm & ipse in hoc eodem opere laudet aliqua optimæ notæ, & à sacerdotibus in usum
units.tr: {k} Morinus, on the Samaritan Pentateuch, Exercitation 4, chapter 4. a clearer illustration of the authentic text, similar to a thousand [others], has been made easier by the holy Fathers with the greatest praise of all. Indeed the Fathers erred in this matter no less than the Samaritans, if it is true, as Morinus affirms, that they introduced, inserted, entangled and mingled many things into the context of Holy Scripture; and the examples he takes from Origen and his Hexapla do nothing to this point, for those are of an altogether different kind. In this book Morinus seems to have had only one aim, to show that the Samaritan codices are far to be preferred to the Hebrew ones, which he disparages and belittles everywhere; in this matter he thinks he deserves well of the Church, if he openly detracts from the Jewish codices, which he asserts were copied by fullers, tailors, pedlars, hucksters and glass-menders, {l} as if there were no other copies of Holy Scripture among the Jews than those written by common people, when he himself in this same work praises some copies of the best quality, and written out very elegantly and accurately for the use of the priests and of men who held the first places among the Jews. Yet Morinus had asserted that those who did not agree with him in this matter were hostile and furious toward the Catholic Church, when he himself rather, in these exercitations, everywhere

units.la: (l) Ibid. cap. 8. virorum., qui primas inter Judæos tenerent, perquam eleganter & accuratè descripta. Eos tamen Morinus qui sibi in hoc negotio non assentiuntur, animo esse in Ecclesiam Catholicam infenso & furioso asseruerat,cùm ipse potius in hisce exercitationibus ubique ferme furere videatur ; adeo sæpe extra propositi sui fines excurrit. Ingentes hic laudes sileo, quas Morinus in operis sui Dedicatione fusius congerit in Theologorum Sorbonensium gratiam, quorum Collegium appellat ({m}) Scientiarum Emporium, instructissimum telorum omnis generis adversus Haereticos & Schismaticos armamentarium, defecatissimum antiquitatis Ecclesiasticae archivum & tutissimum fidei sacrarium. Sed tunc Cardinali Richelio, cui opus suum consecrabat, adulabatur, quòd istud Collegium à fundamentis resectumRegia magnificentia exornavis-set; quid enim de Sorbonensibus aliisque Theologis ascriptitiis , qui vocantur Scholastici, ipse sentiret, tum Romæ tum
units.tr: (l) Ibid. cap. 8. Men who held the first places among the Jews, described most elegantly and accurately. Yet Morinus had asserted that those who do not agree with him in this matter are hostile and furious toward the Catholic Church, when he himself seems to rave almost everywhere in these exercises, so often does he run beyond the limits of his own purpose. I pass over here the great praises which Morinus heaps up more fully in the dedication of his work, for the sake of the Sorbonne theologians, whose college he calls a warehouse of learning, a most fully equipped armoury of weapons of every kind against heretics and schismatics, a most pure archive of ecclesiastical antiquity and a most secure sanctuary of the faith. But he was then flattering Cardinal Richelieu, to whom he dedicated his work, because that college had been rebuilt from its foundations and adorned with royal magnificence. For what he really thought of the Sorbonne and the other theologians called Scholastics, he openly declared at Paris, and at Rome as well.

units.la: {m} In Epist. ad Card. Richel. Parisiis aperte declaravit: Verum de his infra.
units.tr: {m} In a letter to Cardinal Richelieu. Concerning these matters, see below.

units.la: JAM Polyglottorum Parisiensium primum volumen editum fuerat, com-plectens Biblia Graeca, Latina, Chaldaea & Hebraea, quae antea Antverpiae excusa fuerant, novumque testamentum quadri-lingue sub prelo erat, cum Morinus & Gabriel Sionita Syrus è monte Libano parant editionem Pentateuchi Samaritanam, Syriacam & Arabicam; ille Samaritanos codices, hic verò Syriacos & Arabicos una cum Latina Interpretatio-ne: verùm dum nimis urget operis illius editionem Morinus, minus accurati pro-dierunt Samaritani codices. Pentateuchum siquidem Hebraeo-Samaritanum ex uno exemplari Oratoriano, & versionem Samaritanam ex eo tantum, quod à Petro Valle acceperat, edidit; vix autem peracta fuerat illa editio, cum illi super-venerunt à Perescio, viro Clarissimo, gen-tis Samaritanae codices Hebraeo-Samaritani & Arabici; Thomas quoque Com-berus collegii Sanctae Trinitatis apud Cantabrigenses in Anglia Socius, qui de Pentateuchi Samaritani editione, quae Parisiis tunc parabatur, aliquid resciverat, Morinum de exemplari Hebraeo-Samaritano, quod tunc in privata Cottonorum Bibliotheca asservabatur, monuit, misitque ad illum postea diversas Pentateuchi illius Samaritani ab Hebraeo seu Judaico Lectiones. Cui malo ut manum medicam adhiberet Morinus, excusum Pentateuchum Samaritanum relegit, manuscriptos inter se codices & cum sua editione comparavit, variisque annotatis Lectionibus eas cum aliis ejusdem natu-rae animadversionibus, quas jam paraverat, adtexere meditatus fuerat, ad volumen alterum observationum criticarum in omnes Bibliorum editiones, quod ad calcem Bibliorum Parisiensium mox e-dendum erat; sed ob eorum, qui Polyglottis illis praerant, contentiones ac dissidia egregium illud opus ad finem perduci non potuit: unus tandem Morinus longo post tempore criticas illas Animadversiones sub nomine opusculo-rum rum Hebraeo-Samaritanorum seorsim edi curavit.{n} In quo tamen opere ea quæ de hoc Argumento ab illo desiderabantur, non omnino explicuisse visus fuit, iis præsertim, qui callent haisce literas.
units.tr: NOW the first volume of the Paris Polyglot had been published, containing the Greek, Latin, Chaldee and Hebrew Bibles, which had earlier been printed at Antwerp, and the New Testament in four languages was in the press. Morinus and Gabriel Sionita, a Syrian from Mount Lebanon, were preparing an edition of the Samaritan, Syriac and Arabic Pentateuch: Morinus the Samaritan manuscripts, and Sionita the Syriac and Arabic ones, together with a Latin translation. But because Morinus pressed too hard for the completion of that edition, the Samaritan texts came out less accurate. For he published the Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch from a single Oratorian copy, and the Samaritan version only from what he had received from Pietro della Valle. Yet scarcely had that edition been finished when Peiresc, a most distinguished man, sent him Hebrew-Samaritan and Arabic manuscripts of the Samaritan people. Thomas Comber, a fellow of Trinity College at Cambridge in England, who had learned something about the edition of the Samaritan Pentateuch then being prepared at Paris, also warned Morinus about the Hebrew-Samaritan copy then kept in the private library of the Cottons, and afterwards sent him various readings of that Samaritan Pentateuch different from the Hebrew or Jewish text. To remedy this evil, Morinus reread the printed Samaritan Pentateuch, compared the manuscripts with one another and with his own edition, and intended to add the noted variant readings, along with other observations of the same kind which he had already prepared, to the second volume of critical observations on all the editions of the Bible, which was soon to be published at the end of the Paris Bibles. But because of the quarrels and dissensions of those who presided over the Polyglots, that outstanding work could not be carried to completion. At last Morinus alone, after a long time, saw to it that those critical observations were published separately under the title of Hebrew-Samaritan little works. Yet in this work he seemed not to have fully explained the things about this subject that were wanted from him, especially for those who are skilled in these letters.

units.la: PERESCIUS præter memoratos jam supra Samaritanorum codices miserat etiam ad Morinum duas eorundemSamaritanorum ad Josephum Scaligerum Epistolas, quarum prima Synagogæ urbis Sichem nomine scripta; altera vero nomine Samaritanorum in Ægypto commorantium, quæ tamen Epistolæ ad manus Scaligeri nunquam pervenerant, sed Genebrardo redditæ, & ut audio, nunc in Bibliotheca Regis Christianissimi asservantur: utramque Morinus ex autographo in Latinum sermonem[?] convertit, cujus tamen Interpretatio nondum in lucem edita fuit. In his Samaritani Scaligero aperiunt gentis suæ mores ac ritus, & qua in re ipsi a Judæis, quos violatæ legis Mosaicæ reos peragunt, diserepens.
units.tr: Besides the Samaritan manuscripts already mentioned above, Peiresc had also sent to Morinus two letters of the same Samaritans addressed to Joseph Scaliger. The first was written in the name of the synagogue of the city of Shechem; the second in the name of the Samaritans living in Egypt. But these letters never reached Scaliger's hands; they were handed over to Genebrard and, as I hear, are now kept in the library of the Most Christian King. Morinus translated both from the autograph into Latin, but their translation has not yet been published. In these letters the Samaritans set out to Scaliger the customs and rites of their people, and in what respects they differ from the Jews, whom they accuse of violating the Mosaic law.

units.la: {n} Paris in 12. Anno 1657. Sacerdotem magnum sibi esse, cui nomen Eleazar, huncque ex semine Phinées gloriantur, illi quoque filium esse, cui nomen Phinées, qui sacerdotio etiam cùm patre suo fungatur; quippe affirmant, ritus sacrificiorum semper se retinuisse, & adhuc superesse: at vetitum illis, alibi sacrificare, quàm in urbe Sichem, è Regione montis Garizim. Hæc & alia ejusdem rationis plurima de moribus Samaritanorum in illis Epistolis exponuntur, quarum tamen sensum neque Perescius, neque Morinus in omnibus videntur assecuti; quis enim credat Perescio affirmanti in Epistola ad Morinum, {o}Sectam Samaritanorum usus aliquot in Kalendario præsertim, notandisque diebus festis ab Ecclesia Romana accepisse? Haud dubie deceptus fuit[?], legens in autographo Samaritico, vocem illam, quam postea Morinus simili errore interpretatus est Nisan Romani; & hæc extat non longè ab initio Epistolæ, quæ nomine Synagogæ urbis Sichem scripta fuit. Loco au-
units.tr: {n} Paris, in 12mo, 1657. They boast that they have a high priest named Eleazar, and that they trace him from the seed of Phinehas; that he also has a son named Phinehas, who serves the priesthood along with his father. For they affirm that they have always kept, and still keep, the rites of sacrifice, but that it is forbidden them to sacrifice anywhere except in the city of Shechem, opposite Mount Gerizim. These matters and very many others of the same kind about the customs of the Samaritans are set out in those letters, though neither Peiresc nor Morinus seems to have grasped their meaning in every point. For who would believe Peiresc, when he asserts in his letter to Morinus {o} that the sect of the Samaritans had adopted from the Roman Church certain usages, especially in the calendar and in the marking of feast days? He was doubtless deceived in reading in the Samaritan autograph that word which Morinus afterwards, by a similar error, rendered Nisan Romani. This occurs not far from the beginning of the letter written in the name of the synagogue of Shechem. Instead of

units.la: {o} Epist. Peresc. Anno 1631. autem dictionis, Romani, apponendum est, Græci, quippe Græcis junioribus Pω-μᾶϊον[?] idem esse constat, atque Latinè Græcum, à quibus illa dictio postea ad cæteras Regionum Orientalium nationes transiit; quin & alii errores in hisce Epistolis à Morino in Latinum Sermonem conversis deprehendantur, nullius dubito: verùm de his autographa consulere necesse fuerit, dignæ tamen sunt, quæ publici juris fiant, cùm illarum beneficio Samaritanorum religio, mores, ac ritus illustrari possint. Eadem Samaritanorum natio de eodem argumento ad quosdam Ecclesiæ Anglicanæ Theo-logos scripsit Literas, quæ cum iis partem maximam consentiunt; significaverat etiam Perescius[?] in eadem Epistola Morino, exemplar versionisSamaritanæ, quod erat Petri à Valle, quodque in Bibliis Parisiensibus excusum fuit, non esse bonæ notæ, mendisque fœdissimis illud scatere, similiter penes se habere longè pluresSamaritanorum siclos,eosque longè perfectiores, quám qvos in exercitationibus suis inPentateuchum Samaritanum publicaverat Morinus, qui tam Pentateuchum utrumque Samaritanorum, quàm exercitationes illas nimis festinanter edidit. Morinus ob jam editos à se Libros in universa ferme Europa notissimus, in primis ob illam præfationem, quam novæ Septuaginta Interpretum editioni præmiserat, & exercitationes Ec- clesiasticas in Pentateuchum Samaritanum, ad id unum respicit, ut antiquas Ecclesiæ versiones adversus protestantes aliosque veritatis Hebraicæ assertores vindicaret; novum idcirco opus in lucem edit, cui nomen fecit exercitationem Biblicarum de Hebræi Græciqve textus sinceritate (p). Verius profecto inscribi poterat de parum fidis Hebræis, Græcis, nec non Latinis Bibliorum codicibus; dum enim totus incumbit refellendæ Judæorum, eorumque sequacium de Hebræi ex- emplaris integritate Sententiæ, longè adhuc impuriora esse Græca Latinaque exemplaria, etiam non volens manifestè pro-
units.tr: {o} Letter of Peiresc, 1631. the word Roman, one must put Greek, since it is certain that to the younger Greeks Romaion [Ῥωμαῖον] meant the same as Latin Graecum; from them that word afterwards passed to the other nations of the Eastern regions. Nor do I doubt that other errors are to be found in these letters translated into Latin by Morinus. But for these matters it would be necessary to consult the autographs. Yet they are worth publishing, since by their help the religion, customs and rites of the Samaritans can be illustrated. The same Samaritan people wrote letters on the same subject to some theologians of the English Church, and these agree for the most part with them. Peiresc also indicated to Morinus in the same letter that the Samaritan version which belonged to Pietro della Valle, and which was printed in the Paris Bibles, is not of good quality and is full of most foul errors; that he likewise had in his possession far more Samaritan shekels, and much more perfect ones, than those which Morinus had published in his exercises on the Samaritan Pentateuch, since Morinus had published both Samaritan Pentateuchs and those exercises far too hastily. Morinus, known almost throughout Europe for the books he had already published, chiefly for that preface which he had prefixed to the new edition of the Septuagint, and for his ecclesiastical exercises on the Samaritan Pentateuch, aimed at one thing only: to vindicate the ancient versions of the Church against the Protestants and other defenders of Hebrew truth. He therefore brought out a new work, to which he gave the title Exercitation on Biblical Hebrew and Greek Text Sincerity (p). It could truly have been titled better as a work on the little-trusted Hebrew, Greek and also Latin Bible manuscripts. For while he devoted himself entirely to refuting the opinion of the Jews and their followers about the integrity of the Hebrew copy, he showed, even without meaning to, that the Greek and Latin copies are far more corrupt, and openly proved it.

units.la: (p) Exercit. Bibl. Parif, in 4. Anno 1635. probat. Inde jam à principio operis sui contendit, ut de codicibus Hebræis detrahat, Divina Oracula ab Ecclesia & in Ecclesia esset, non verò à Synagoga Christiano nomini infensissima; deinde alia ejusdem generis plurima subjicit, quæ speciem veri dumtaxat præ se ferant, possintque minus cautos in errorem inducere.
units.tr: (p) Exercit. Bibl. Paris, in 4to, 1635. From the very beginning of his work he contends that the divine oracles should be taken from the Church, and within the Church, and not from the synagogue, which is most hostile to the Christian name. Then he adds very many other things of the same kind, which show only the appearance of truth and can lead the less cautious into error.

units.la: Illud omne, quod undequaque tam ex vetustis Ecclesiæ patribus, quàm nu-peris Theologis potuit corradere, in has exercitationes sæpius absque judicio conjecit, ita ut uno veluti ictu tum veteris tum novi Testamenti Librorum auto[?]-ritatem omnem præcidat; dignus tamen est liber iste, qui à viris sacrarum litera-rum studiosis attentius legatur, ob vari-am, quæ in eo relucet, rerum Biblicarum & Judaicarum eruditionem. Morinus eo tantum fine Hebræi contextus auto[?]-ritatem evertit, ut Græcam Septuaginta Interpretum editionem & Latinam Hieronymi in ejus locum substitueret, de quarum authentia disputans nihil præter nugas ex futilibus Theologorum Scholsticorum[?] distinctionibus profert, qvæ haud dubie Morino aliud cogitanti exciderunt :: vix enim umbraticorum ejusmodi doctorum scholas à limine salutaverat ; præclare qvidem interdum sentit de Hieronymi, qvem merito vulgatæ, saltem partem maximam, autorem putat, peritia in Lingua Hebraica ; alias verò illum insectatur velut hominem parum sibi constantem, qviqve sæpius loqvatur ex anteceptis opinionibus, qvàm ex rerum ipsarum veritate.
units.tr: He has thrown into these exercises, often without judgment, everything he could gather from every side, both from the ancient Fathers of the Church and from more recent theologians, so that with one blow, as it were, he cuts off all authority of the books of the Old and New Testaments. Yet this book deserves to be read more carefully by those who study the sacred letters, on account of the varied learning in biblical and Jewish matters that shines through it. Morinus overturned the authority of the Hebrew text for this sole purpose: that he might substitute in its place the Greek edition of the Septuagint and the Latin of Jerome. In disputing their authenticity he offers nothing but trifles drawn from the trivial distinctions of the Scholastic theologians, which doubtless slipped out of him while he was thinking of something else; for he had scarcely greeted the schools of such shadowy teachers from the threshold. He sometimes judges well of Jerome, whom he rightly believes to be the author of the Vulgate, or at least of its greater part, for his skill in the Hebrew language; but elsewhere he attacks him as a man little consistent with himself, who speaks more often from preconceived opinions than from the truth of the matters themselves.

units.la: SED rigidus iste censor, qvi adeo iniqvum de Judæis & eorum codicibus judicium tulerat, illorum, qvorum intere-rat, veritatem Hebraicam asserere maledicta in caput suum attraxit, atqve inprimis eruditissimi viri Simeonis de Muis, tunc literarum Hebraearum apud Parisios Professoris Regii. Is scilicet de arte sua actum judicans, nisi Morini audaciam reprimeret, scripsit paulo iracundior libellum adversus Ecclesiasticas illius exercitationes in Pentateuchum Samaritanum ; scriptum qvoqve accerbissimum contra Morini praefationem quasi junćto umbone ediderunt Taylorus & Bootius, homines è secta Protestantium, quorum ille Anglus, hic verò Batavus; sed illorum omnium conviciis ac maledictis injuriarum plaustra reddit Morinus, {q}adeo[?] vili venerunt convicia ac maledicta apud istam Theologorum gentem furentem saepius ratione. Muisius iterum ad novam adversus Morinum scriptionem se accingit, quâ responsum illius castigat, & castigationis suae initium ducit ab explicatione sententiae libri proverbiorum, quae diversa plane ratione in hoc libro concipitur, nimirum, {r} Ne respondeas stulto juxta stultitiam ejus, ne sibi sapiens esse videatur; & quasi de illa explicanda ageretur, testes profert quosdam Judaeorum Magistros, sed revera tunc alludebat ad Morini nomen, sicut alias Erasmus homo facetissimus celeberrimi illiusMo-rini nomen intuebatur, cum Librum su-um
units.tr: But that stern critic, who had passed so unfair a judgment on the Jews and their manuscripts, drew curses onto his own head by defending the Hebrew truth of those whom he had wronged, above all the most learned Simon de Muis, then Royal Professor of Hebrew letters at Paris. Judging that Muis was meddling in his own field, and that he must check Morinus's boldness, he wrote a rather angry little book against Morinus's Ecclesiastical Exercitations on the Samaritan Pentateuch. Taylor and Boot, men of the Protestant sect, one an Englishman and the other a Dutchman, also published a very bitter writing against Morinus's preface, shoulder to shoulder, as it were. But Morinus returned all their insults and abuse in full measure, so cheap are insults and abuse among that quarrelsome race of theologians, who are often furious without reason. Muis then girded himself for a new writing against Morinus, in which he rebukes the reply and begins his censure with an explanation of a saying in the Book of Proverbs, which in that book is understood in a quite different way: Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes. As if that saying were the subject of his explanation, he adduces certain Jewish masters as witnesses. In truth, he was alluding to the name of Morinus, just as Erasmus, that most witty man, once had the name of the famous Morinus in view when he dedicated his book In Praise of Folly to him.

units.la: {q} Mor. in diatribe Elenctica & Animadv. in censur. edit. in 8. Parif. Anno 1639.
units.tr: Morinus, in the Diatribe Elenctica and the Animadversiones in censuram, octavo edition, Paris, 1639.

units.la: {r} Muif.[?] castig. anim. Parif.[?] in 8. Anno 1639. um de Moria ei dicavit. Laudandus quidem in hoc est Muisius, quòd egregium veritatis Hebraicæ defensorem adversus Morinum se ostendit; sed dum nimis anxiè hodierni codicis Judaici Lectioni adhæsit, illum omnino ab adversarii sui objectionibus non potuit asserere: versantur adhuc in omnium manibus Morini de rebus Biblicis opera, & à multis partem magnam approbantur; à paucissimis vero leguntur, quæ Muisius, similiter Taylorus, Bootius & alii ad versus Morinum scripserunt.
units.tr: Muis, Castigationes Animadversionum, octavo, Paris, 1639. Muis deserves praise for this, that he showed himself an excellent defender of the Hebrew truth against Morinus. But because he clung too anxiously to the reading of the present Jewish codex, he could not altogether defend his side against his adversary's objections. Morinus's works on biblical matters are still in everyone's hands, and many approve a great part of them. Yet very few read what Muis, likewise Taylor, Boot and others, wrote against Morinus.

units.la: In hoc autem Morinus habuit consentientes sibi Theologos Parisienses, quòd Hebræos codices evertens illorum imperitiæ patrocinaretur; scripsit prætera adversus Morini exercitationes in Pentateuchum Samaritanum Joannes Henricus Hottingerus, qui statim à Libri sui limine cujus hæc est inscriptio, Exercitationes anti-Morinianæ de Pentateucho Samaritano ejusque udentica[?] authentica, {f} Morinum appellat Monachum, qui communem Mo-
units.tr: In this matter Morinus had as allies the Parisian theologians, in that, while overturning the Hebrew codices, he defended their ignorance. Besides, John Henry Hottinger also wrote against Morinus's Exercitations on the Samaritan Pentateuch. Right at the threshold of his book, whose title is Exercitationes anti-Morinianae de Pentateucho Samaritano ejusque authentica, he calls Morinus a monk, who surpasses the common lot of monks in

units.la: {f} Edit. Tiguri in 4. Anno 1644. Monachorum sortem superet. Ille de Samaritanis & eorum codicibus disserit, putatque Samaritanos à Judæis Pentateuchi sui exemplar hausisse; sed conjecturis tantum, non autem firmissimis rationibus, ut ita sentiret, adduci potuit; istud minus accuratum esse, probat exemplis aliquot pleonasmorum, vocum vel mutatarum in alias, vel omissarum, similibusque erroribus, quos profert, & ex quibus confici posse arbitratur, non magis credendum esse Samaritanis, Pentateuchum suum jactantibus, quàm Ebionitis, verum & solum Matthæi Evangelium Hebræum venditantibus, qua in re profecto gravissimè hallucinatus est Hottingerus, qui tam venerandæ Antiquitatis Pentateuchum Samaritanum cum adulterato Ebionitarum Evangelio comparare audeat.
units.tr: (footnote) Printed at Zurich, quarto, 1644. ...monks. Hottinger discourses on the Samaritans and their manuscripts, and thinks the Samaritans took their copy of the Pentateuch from the Jews. But he could be led to think so only by conjectures, not by very firm reasons. He proves that this copy is less accurate by several examples of pleonasms, of words changed into others or omitted, and similar errors, which he brings forward, and from which he believes it may be concluded that the Samaritans, boasting of their Pentateuch, deserve no more credit than the Ebionites, who vaunted the Gospel of Matthew in Hebrew as the true and only one. In this matter Hottinger was certainly very much mistaken, for he dares to compare the most venerable antiquity of the Samaritan Pentateuch with the corrupted Gospel of the Ebionites.

units.la: Morinum etiam imperitiæ arguit Hottingerus, quasi Rabbinorum quorundam, quos laudaverat, mentem haud assecutus fuisset; simile quid jam antea in ejusdem Morini exercitationibus animadverterat Muisius: sed longè plura Rabbinorum testimonia Morino in Latinum malè conversa postea observavit Joannes Buxtorfius vir in Ju-dæorum Libris diu multumque volutatus.
