Ille {t}in dissertatione de Literarum Hebraicarum genuina Antiqvitate Morini exercitationes vocat Librum cruda & indigesta materiæ mole infertum & confertum, ubi testimonia autorum Judæorum mutila sæpe adducit; aperit Buxtorfius, quàm multis in locis lapsus fuerit Morinus, quæ inscite & imperitè interpretatus est. In hoc tamen & ipse erravit Buxtorfius, dum totus à Rabbinorum quorundam sententia dependens, contendit pugnaciter contra scriptorum tum veterum tum recentiorum turbam, primas gentis Hebræ[?] literas, in quibus lex antiquitus scripta fuerit, hodiernas esse Hebræas, non verò Samaritanas seu Phœnicias, uti rectè affirmaverat Morinus.
units.tr: Hottinger also accuses Morinus of ignorance, as if he had not grasped the meaning of certain rabbis whom Morinus had cited. Muis had already noticed something similar in Morinus's Exercitations. But John Buxtorf, a man who had long and deeply immersed himself in the Jewish books, later observed far more passages of the rabbis that Morinus had badly rendered into Latin. In his dissertation on the genuine antiquity of Hebrew letters, Buxtorf calls Morinus's Exercitations a book stuffed and crammed with a crude and undigested mass of material, in which he often adduces the mutilated testimonies of Jewish authors. Buxtorf shows in how many places Morinus slipped, and how he clumsily and ignorantly interpreted them. Yet Buxtorf himself also erred in this matter: wholly dependent on the opinion of certain rabbis, he contended stubbornly against the crowd of writers, both ancient and more recent, that the original letters in which the law was written of old are the present Hebrew letters, and not the Samaritan or Phoenician letters, as Morinus had rightly affirmed.

units.la: Nomen autem Morini tunc temporis in plerisque Europæ partibus ita celebra-
units.tr: The name of Morinus had by then become so famous in most parts of Europe that

units.la: {t} In dissert. Philol. Theol. edit. Basil. in 4. Anno 1645. lebratum fuerat, ut Cardinalis Barberi-nus, jubente Pontifice maximo, Romam illum per literas invitaverit, volueritqve, ut Cardinalis Bichii; qvi è Gallia Romam mox rediturus erat, comitatui se ad jun-geret. Hæc autem Romam vocandi il-lius causa fuit. Urbanus VIII, dudum in animo habens, Græcos aliosqve Orientalis Ecclesiæ populos, qvos vulgò Schismaticos appellant, ad fidem Ecclesiæ Romanæ convertere, Nationum illarum libros undiqve conqviri jussit, ac Ro-mam vocari ex omnibus Europæ partibus viros rerum Theologicarum peritissimos. Indicati sunt Urbano ex Gallia Dionysius Petavius, Jesuita doctissimus, & Joannes Morinus, è Congregatione Oratorii Parisiensis. Hic statim in Comitatu Cardinalis Bichii Romam prosi-ciscitur; at ille minus gloriæ cupidus & ex Societatis suæ consensione iter illud detrectat. Morinus à Cardinali Barberino Romæ perhumanè exceptus fuit, atqve ab eo commendatus Lucæ Holstenio & Leoni Allatio, viris doctissimis, quoquorum ille Vaticanæ Bibliothecæ cu-stos erat, hic verò tunc Barberinæ: illi qui dudum urbanis Romanorum moribus assuefacti erant, statim ex Morini conversatione judicârunt, illum minus humanum esse & ingenii agrestis. Morinus verò admirabatur illorum erga se officia, putabatque se in alium quasi orbem delatum. Vaticanam Barberinamque Bibliothecas visitat, simulque earum custodes, qui ei comites dati fuerant, seu potius actionum suarum & studiorum inspectores, sæpius invisit. Contigit autem, ut in familiari colloquio oborta fuerit quæstio aliqua de iis, quæ tunc a Theologis, jussu & auctoritate Pontificis maximi Romæ congregatis, disputabantur, cujus quæstionis explicandæ causa Librum Manuscriptum scriptoris cujusdam e junioribus Græcis consulere necesse fuerit, statim codex manuscriptus Morino legendus offertur, rogaturque, ut suam de scriptoris illius mente sententiam diceret. Verum Holstenio & Allatio minimè satisfecit, iisque visus est Linguæ Græcæ parum peritus ; Souvignius, Congregationis etiam Oratorii Presbyter, vir Græ-cè doctus, qui Romani itineris comitem Morino se junxerat, arrepto ex illius manibus Græco exemplari, totum illud negotium, de quo agebatur, prompte & expeditè declaravit, seque ostendit in Linguæ Græcæ cognitione versandisque Græcis scriptoribus non inferiorem Allatio & Holstenio, qui ex eo tempore de Souvignio longè melius, quàm de Morino senserunt, remque totam, uti probabile est, Cardinali Barberino eo modo, quo peracta fuerat, denunciârunt ; & id in causa fuisse videtur, cur postea Cardinalis vix de Morino cogitaverit, qui ad illam Theologorum Congregationem, quæ tunc Romæ habebatur, vocatus non fuit, nisi post elapsum multum temporis spatium : sed puduit demum Cardinalem è Gallia Romam invitasse hominem, ut ibi otiosus viveret. Iussit itaque, ut ille in istam Congregationem admitteretur, in qua tunc de Nationum Orientalium fide & ritibus Græcorum potissimum disputtabatur. Horum Euchologium expendebantTheologi isti,illudque ad ritualeRomanum referebant, ut ex illa comparatione utriusque differentia internoscere-tur, & quia maxima esse deprehensa est, jam bene multi,ij maximè,qui ex opinionum, quas in Scholis acceperunt, præjudiciis de rebus ab illorum captu longè semotis audeant pronunciare, Græcorum ritus damnabant, utminus probos, nec tolerandos, nisi postquam ad Romanos accommodati fuissent; sed his Lucas Holstenius & Leo Allatius, viri egregie docti & sapientissimi, strenuè ac for-titer restituerunt: Inprimis Holstenius, qui palam asserere veritus non fuit, miserandum illud Schisma, quod occidentalem inter & orientalem Ecclesiam dudum exortum, adhuc continuatur, illis potissimum tribui debere, qui ex disputandi pruritu vocant omnia in controversiam, nulloque erga fratres suos amore tenentur: quos etiam gravissimè arguit, quod veritatis minimè solliciti de rebus parum sibi compertis audacter judijudicium ferrent, nihil interim ex sacris Literis, nihil ex conciliis, nihil ex priscis patribus proferentes, sed vanas dumtaxat invalidasque ratiunculas. Morinus cui iam pridem genus illud Theologorum displicebat, qui plura passim in suis Libris definire ausi sunt, quae extra salutis dispendium ignorari poterant, vel in dubio relinqui, Holstenii sententiam suffragio suo comprobavit, eamque multis & gravissimis argumentis confirmavit; quippe per illud omne tempus, quo Romae otiosus, nec dum in Theologorum Congregationem admissus vixerat, animum suum ad illas applicuerat, quaestiones, quae tunc in his locis illustrabantur. Itaque compluribus ostendit Morinus, de Orientalis Ecclesiae ritibus judicium ferendum non esse ex hodierna Ecclesiae Romanae praxi, neque etiam ex Doctrina Theologorum Scholasticorum, qui minus constantes in iis tractandis, quae ad sacramenta pertinent, nihil omnino habeant inter se con-cordiae: verum ad illa recurrendum esse tempora, quæ Photianum Schisma antecesserant; aliàs fore, ut prisci Orientalis Ecclesiæ Patres damnandi sint, si verum sit, Græcos recentiores in Sacramentorum Administratione cum his ut plurimum consentire.
units.tr: (footnote) In the Dissertationes Philologico-Theologicae, Basel edition, quarto, 1645. ...was celebrated, so that Cardinal Barberini, at the command of the Supreme Pontiff, invited him to Rome by letter, and wished him to join the retinue of Cardinal Bichi, who was about to return from France to Rome. This was the reason for calling him to Rome. Pope Urban VIII, having long intended to convert the Greeks and other peoples of the Eastern Church, whom they commonly call Schismatics, to the faith of the Roman Church, ordered that the books of those nations be sought out everywhere, and that the men most skilled in theological matters be summoned to Rome from every part of Europe. From France, Dionysius Petavius, a most learned Jesuit, and John Morinus, of the Congregation of the Oratory of Paris, were named to Urban. Morinus set out for Rome at once in the retinue of Cardinal Bichi, but Petavius, who was less eager for glory and, by the agreement of his Society, declined that journey. Morinus was received most courteously in Rome by Cardinal Barberini, who recommended him to Lucas Holstenius and Leo Allatius, most learned men, of whom the former was keeper of the Vatican Library and the latter then of the Barberini. Those two, who had long been accustomed to the urbane manners of the Romans, judged at once from Morinus's conversation that he was less courteous and of a rustic disposition. Morinus, however, admired their kindness towards him, and thought he had been carried into another world. He visited the Vatican and Barberini libraries, and often called on their keepers, who had been assigned to him as companions, or rather as overseers of his actions and studies. It happened that in a familiar conversation some question arose about the matters then being debated by the theologians gathered at Rome by the order and authority of the Supreme Pontiff. To explain this question it was necessary to consult a manuscript book by a certain young Greek writer, and at once the manuscript was offered to Morinus to read, with a request that he state his opinion of that writer's meaning. But he did not satisfy Holstenius and Allatius, and seemed to them not very skilled in Greek. Souvigny, a presbyter of the same Congregation of the Oratory, a man learned in Greek, who had joined Morinus as companion on the Roman journey, snatched the Greek copy from his hands and promptly and quickly explained the whole matter under discussion. He showed himself in knowledge of the Greek language, and in handling Greek authors, not inferior to Allatius and Holstenius. From that time on they thought of Souvigny far better than of Morinus, and reported the whole affair to Cardinal Barberini, probably as it had been carried out. This seems to have been the reason why the Cardinal afterwards scarcely thought of Morinus, who was not summoned to that Congregation of theologians then meeting at Rome until a long time had passed. But at last the Cardinal was ashamed to have invited a man from France to Rome to live there idle. So he ordered that Morinus be admitted to that Congregation, in which at that time the faith and rites of the Eastern nations, chiefly of the Greeks, were being discussed. Those theologians were weighing the Greek Euchologion and referring it to the Roman ritual, so that the difference between the two might be discerned from the comparison. And because the difference was found to be very great, many already, and especially those who, prejudiced by the opinions they had learned in the schools about matters far beyond their grasp, dared to pronounce judgment, condemned the rites of the Greeks as less sound and not to be tolerated unless they had first been brought into line with the Roman rites. But Lucas Holstenius and Leo Allatius, men of outstanding learning and wisdom, vigorously and bravely opposed them. Holstenius in particular did not hesitate to assert openly that the pitiable schism which arose long ago between the Western and the Eastern Church, and still continues, ought chiefly to be attributed to those who, from an itch for disputation, call everything into controversy and are held by no love for their brothers. He also rebuked them severely because, being little concerned with the truth, they boldly passed judgment on matters they understood poorly, bringing forward nothing from the holy Scriptures, nothing from the councils, nothing from the ancient Fathers, but only empty and feeble little arguments. Morinus, who had long disliked that kind of theologian, who dared to define in their books many things here and there which could have been left unknown without loss to salvation, or left in doubt, gave his support to Holstenius's opinion and confirmed it with many weighty arguments. Indeed, throughout the whole time when he lived idle at Rome, not yet admitted to the Congregation of theologians, he had applied his mind to those questions which were then being examined in those places. Therefore Morinus showed in many ways that a judgment on the rites of the Eastern Church ought not to be formed from the present practice of the Roman Church, nor from the teaching of the scholastic theologians, who, being inconsistent in treating those matters that pertain to the sacraments, have absolutely no agreement among themselves. Rather, one must go back to the times that preceded the Photian schism; otherwise the ancient Fathers of the Eastern Church would have to be condemned, if it were true that the more recent Greeks mostly agree with them in the administration of the sacraments.

units.la: Viris sapientioribus rerumque Ecclesiasticarum bene peritis placuit illud Morini judicium, summaque illius eruditio laudata fuit etiam à Cardinale Barberino. Mirum tamen est, tunc temporis illam Romæ approbatam fuisse sententiam, quæ fidem prope omnē & autoritatem detraheret Theologis Scholasticis, quos quadrigentos abhinc annos Ecclesia Romana Doctrinæ suæ Magistros acceperat in iis omnibus, quæ de fide & moribus tulit decretis. Illudque adhuc videtur admirabilius, quod præcipui sententiæ illius autores Lucas Holstenius, Joannes Morinus, Leo Allatius, & alii hujus conterranei, vel ex Protestantium, vel ex Græcorum Scholis exissent. Rem tamen ita gestam fuisse, uti eam narravimus, ex ipsius Morini schedulis, quæ in manus meas, pervenerunt, & in qvas illud omne retulit, qvod in Congregatione Theologorum pronun-ciaturus erat, probare non esset arduum nisi de ordinationibus, quod tunc Romae coeptum, Parisiis postea perfectum est, meminisset Congregationis illius, in qua singulae periodi Eucologii Graecorum ad fidei Catholicae canonem examina-bantur. Cum primum, inquit, ({u}) huic Congregationi adscriptus sum. coepta erat in Graecorum ordinationes Inquisitio, varii Theologi varias judicii ferendi rationes inibant; mihi non satis tutum videbatur, ex solis doctorum Scholasticorum dictatis de re tanti momenti pronunciare: experie-bar enim, eos nulla Graecorum morum Scientia tinctos, nulla Linguae Graecae cognitione aspersos, nunquam illis in mentem venisse, ut inquirerent, quae, quot, qualesve essent Graecae ordinationes.
units.tr: Wiser men, well versed in ecclesiastical affairs, approved Morinus's judgment, and Cardinal Barberini also praised his great learning. It is nonetheless remarkable that at that time an opinion was approved in Rome which would strip the scholastic theologians, whom the Roman Church had for four hundred years accepted as the teachers of her doctrine in all the decrees she issued on faith and morals, of almost all their faith and authority. It seems even more remarkable that the chief authors of that opinion, Lucas Holstenius, Johannes Morinus, Leo Allatius and others of their country, had come out of either the Protestant or the Greek schools. That the affair went as we have related, however, is not hard to prove from Morinus's own notes, which have come into my hands and in which he set down everything he was going to say in the meeting of theologians. The only thing he could not have remembered was the meeting concerning ordinations, which began at Rome and was later completed at Paris, in which each section of the Greek Euchologion was examined against the canon of the Catholic faith. As soon as I was, he says, enrolled in this congregation, an inquiry into the Greek ordinations had begun, and the various theologians were adopting various ways of reaching a judgment. It seemed to me not safe enough to pronounce on a matter of such moment from the dictates of the scholastic doctors alone. For I found by experience that they, untouched by any knowledge of Greek customs and not sprinkled with any acquaintance with the Greek language, had never once thought of inquiring what the Greek ordinations were, how many they were, or of what kind.

units.la: Et paulo post. Religio mihi erat, ex solis eorum hominum decretis, qui ne levissima quidem earum rerum cognitione imbuti fuissent, de rebus tan-
units.tr: And a little later: I felt it a scruple to pronounce on such weighty matters from the decrees of men who had not been imbued with even the slightest knowledge of those things.

units.la: {u} Mor. Præf. comm. de ordin. edit. Parif. in sol. Anno 1653. tantis judicium ferre. Opus illud Fran-cisco Cardinali Barberino dedicatum, [?]simo & eminentissimi illius Cardinalis o-perà Romæ edita sunt Lucæ Holstenii post ejus obitum opuscula, in quibus de Doctoribus Scholasticis gravissimè conquestus Holstenius, disidia, quæ inter Ecclesiam Orientalem & Occidentalem extant, illis tribuere non reformidat: hic missa facio ea omnia, quæ passim Leo Allatius in suis operibus adversus ejusmodi Theologos adscriptitios congerit, ut ad Morinum nostrum, unde diverteratOratio, redeam.
units.tr: {u} Morinus, Preface to the commentary on ordinations, Paris edition in folio, year 1653. ...to pass judgment on such weighty matters. That work was dedicated to Cardinal Francis Barberini, and the posthumous little works of Lucas Holstenius were published at Rome by the care of that most eminent cardinal, in which Holstenius, complaining most bitterly of the scholastic doctors, does not hesitate to lay on them the blame for the discord that exists between the Eastern and Western Church. I pass over all the things which Leo Allatius, in his works, heaps up everywhere against theologians of this sort, so that I may return to our Morinus, from whom my speech has digressed.

units.la: Vix Morinus novem mensibus Romæ commoratus est, ({x}) è quibus per menses tantum quatuor Congregationi Theologorum interfuit; postea Parisios à Cardinale Richelio revocatum se suisse testatur, atque ignorare revocationis suæ causas, sed ei parere necesse fuisse et iam dura præscribenti: Verùm non est cur Richelium hic accusat Morinus, su-am ipse potius damnet credulitatem in hoc
units.tr: Morinus scarcely stayed nine months in Rome, of which he attended the meetings of the theologians for only four months. Afterwards he testifies that he was recalled to Paris by Cardinal Richelieu, and that he did not know the reasons for his recall, but that it was necessary for him to obey, even though the command was harsh. But there is no reason for Morinus to accuse Richelieu here; rather he should condemn his own credulity in this matter and his own lightness of mind.

units.la: {x} In cap. Præf. hoc negotio & ingenii sui levitatem Morino Romam proficiscenti Cardinalis Richelius haud contemnendam pecuniæ summam obtulerat in Viaticum, eamque cum gratiarum actione Morinus acceperat, simulque aliam à Cardinale Bichio; aliquo post tempore idem Richelius, qui jam didicerat, Morinum Cardinalis Barberini amicitiam sibi Romæ conciliasse, quæsivit ab Harlæo Sancio, tunc Maclovienfi Episcopo, quid Morinus, ejus amicus Romæ ageret, addiditque, dolere se virum ita eruditum Franciam reliquisse; statim Morino scribit Sancius, ut reditum suum Parisios properaret, Cardinalem Richelium cogitare de illo evehendo ad aliquam dignitatem Ecclesiasticam. Morinus acceptis Sancii literis existimans, absque cunctatione parendum esse Richelio, jamque putans se esse Episcopum, neque amicorum suorum precibus, neque Cardinalis Barberini erga eum officiis Romæ detineri potuit; interim Richelius ubi cognovit, Morinum Roma discessisse, monuit Sancium cium, ne autor esset Morino, ut Romam desereret [?], ubi ejus studia rebus Ecclesiasticis, quae tunc ibi agitabantur, perquàm utilia erant; sed alteras, quas Sancius scripsit literas, Morinus non accepit, qui jam Massiliam appulerat, cum Romam pervenerunt; quare Parisios profectus in domo Oratoriana à suis gregalibus humanè exceptus fuit; rumor erat tunc temporis, Morinum in privatis colloquiis de Cardinale Richelio paulò liberiùs Romæ locutum fuisse, & ob hanc causam Sancii operâ subdole usum Richelium, ut Morinum in Galliam revocaveret. Et rem ita fuisse ex eo suspicari licer, quòd minus quàm antea Cardinalis erga eum beneficus, nullo illum subsidio adjuverit, palamque dixerit, Morinum non alii negotio, quam tractandis libris suis intra privatos parietes, idoneum vi-deri.
units.tr: {x} In the preface... Cardinal Richelieu had offered Morinus, as he set out for Rome, a not contemptible sum of money for his travel expenses, and Morinus had accepted it with thanks, along with another sum from Cardinal Bichi. Some time later Richelieu, who had already learned that Morinus had won the friendship of Cardinal Barberini at Rome, asked Harlaeus de Sancy, then bishop of Saint-Malo, what his friend Morinus was doing at Rome, and added that he regretted that a man so learned had left France. Sancy at once wrote to Morinus that he should hasten his return to Paris, since Cardinal Richelieu was thinking of raising him to some ecclesiastical dignity. Morinus, having received Sancy's letter and believing that he must obey Richelieu without delay, and already thinking himself a bishop, could be detained neither by the entreaties of his friends nor by the kindnesses of Cardinal Barberini at Rome. Meanwhile Richelieu, when he learned that Morinus had left Rome, warned Sancy not to be the instigator of Morinus's abandoning Rome, where his studies were very useful for the ecclesiastical matters then being debated there. But Morinus did not receive the second letter that Sancy wrote; he had already landed at Marseilles when the letters reached Rome. So he went on to Paris, where he was received kindly by his fellow members in the Oratorian house. There was a rumour at that time that Morinus had spoken rather too freely at Rome about Cardinal Richelieu in private conversations, and that for this reason Richelieu, acting craftily through the agency of Sancy, had brought Morinus back to France. One may suspect that this was so from the fact that the Cardinal, who was less kind to him than before, gave him no help of any kind, and openly said that Morinus seemed fit for no business except working on his books within his own four walls.

units.la: REVERSUS Parisios Morinus, {y} eorum omnium, quorum gratiam sibi Romæ conciliaverat, atque inprimis Fran-
units.tr: On returning to Paris, Morinus [cultivated the goodwill] of all those whose favour he had won at Rome, and above all of Fran-

units.la: {y} Anno 1640. Francisci Cardinalis Barberini amicitiam per literas coluit; laetatus est Cardinalis, talem, habere eorum, quae tunc Parisiis agebantur, exploratorem ac monitorem, qui sedis Apostolicae nuncium tunc ibi commorantem saepius inviseret. Contigit autem circa illud tempus, famosum Patris Celloti Jesuitae Librum de Hierarchia & Hierarchis Parisiis in fronte testimonio; de hoc statim Cardinali Barberino scripsit Morinus {z} urgens promptam ac severam sedis Apostolicae in illud opus Animadversionem; monet Cardinalem, aliis opus esse remediis, quam illis, quibus in Patris Boni Libros animadversum fuerit, & haec cum frustra adversus Jesuitas, quibus Cardinalis Richelius favebat, ab Episcopis Galliae aut a Sorbona sperarentur, non aliunde pro ea tempestate expectari posse, quam a Pontifice Maximo. Iterum Morinus per aliam Epistolam, quam ipsi nuncio Romam redeunti dederat, Barberino significat, Celloti librum ab Episcopis Me-dun-
units.tr: {y} In the year 1640 he kept up by letter the friendship of Cardinal Francis Barberini. The Cardinal rejoiced to have in Paris such an informant and adviser on what was then going on there, one who could visit the nuncio of the Apostolic See, who was staying there, quite often. It happened, however, that about that time the notorious book of the Jesuit Father Cellot, on the hierarchy and the hierarchs, appeared at Paris with a title page bearing approval. Morinus at once wrote to Cardinal Barberini about this, urging a prompt and severe censure of that work by the Apostolic See. He warns the Cardinal that this work needed remedies other than those by which the books of Father Bonus had been dealt with, and since in vain the bishops of France or the Sorbonne could be expected to act against the Jesuits, whom Cardinal Richelieu favoured, no help could be looked for in that crisis from anywhere but the Supreme Pontiff. Again, Morinus, in another letter which he gave to the nuncio returning to Rome, informs Barberini that Cellot's book had been censured by the bishops

units.la: {z} Anno 1641. duntæ Carnutum congregatis notatum fuisse censurâ, quæ omnium EpiscoporumChirographis subscripta,&ad Richelium postea delata, intra manus ejus substiterit; his præterea adjungit Morinus, Sorbonicos bene multas libri illius propositiones notâsse, eorumque censuram plusquàm 80 doctorum suffragiis comprobatam, Sorbonæ Registris inscriptam fuisse,quam tamen in publicum edere per supremam autoritatem non licuerit: Cardinalem Richelium Sorbonæ doctores aliquot deputâsse, qui cum Celloto de his propositionibus conferrent; Jesuitas asserere, Cellotum Sorbonicis doctoribus satisfecisse, contra affirmare Sorbonicos, malas propositiones[?] à Celloto male propugnatas: de quaCollatione nihil publicè editum fuerat. Rescripsit Morino {a} Cardinalis Barberinus, etiam nondum lecto Cel'oti opere, intra brevissimum tempus fore, ut suprema Ecclesiæ autoritas ejusmodi scriptorum, qui nihil ad res Ecclesiasticas tractandas.
units.tr: {z} In the year 1641. assembled at Meaux of Chartres. The censure, signed with the handwriting of all the bishops, was afterwards referred to Richelieu and remained in his hands. Morinus further adds that the Sorbonnists had noted a good many propositions of that book, and that their censure, approved by the votes of more than eighty doctors, had been entered in the registers of the Sorbonne, though it was not permitted to publish it by supreme authority. Cardinal Richelieu had appointed some Sorbonne doctors to confer with Cellot about these propositions. The Jesuits affirmed that Cellot had satisfied the Sorbonnists; on the contrary the Sorbonnists affirmed that bad propositions had been badly defended by Cellot. Nothing had been published publicly about this conference. Cardinal Barberini replied to Morinus, even though he had not yet read Cellot's work, that within a very short time the supreme authority of the Church would curb the impudence of such writers, who brought nothing to the handling of ecclesiastical matters except an itch for innovation. But the Jesuits of Paris, secure under the patronage of Cardinal Richelieu, openly mocked Jove threatening with thunderbolts, just as Momus does in Lucian.

units.la: {a} Anno 1640. præter innovandi prurigiem afferebant, proterviam compesceret; verùm Jesuitæ Parisienses subCardinalis Richelii patro-cinio securi, Jovem fulmina minantem non secus atque Momus apud Lucianum palam deridebant. Iterum Morinus scribensCardinali Francisco Barberino,eum longè pressius ac vehementius quam anteà urget,ut curet sedes apostolica promp-to atque efficaci remedio, ne ex Librorum, quos quotidie Parisiis Jesuitæ e-dunt, pernicie, res Christiana damnum capiat; Ausim inquit Morinus in Epistola ad Cardinalem Barberinum, ut id faciat eminentiam vestram exhortari: Nisi enim remedium illud à sede Apostolica exoriatur, nulla spes est ut aliunde proveniat.-Morbus tamen celerrimum effugitat[?] remedium, non enim serpit cancer ille, sed longis passibus graditur, omniaque circumcirca latè vastat & depascitur. De altero Jesuitarum Libro recens edito in hac Epistola loquitur Morinus, illusque au-
units.tr: {a} In the year 1640. Morinus, writing again to Cardinal Francis Barberini, urges him far more pressingly and vehemently than before to see that the Apostolic See applies a prompt and effective remedy, so that the Christian cause does not suffer harm from the ruin caused by the books which the Jesuits publish daily at Paris. I would venture, says Morinus in his letter to Cardinal Barberini, to exhort your eminence to do this: For unless that remedy arises from the Apostolic See, there is no hope that it will come from elsewhere. Yet the disease escapes the remedy very swiftly; for that cancer does not creep but advances with long strides, and lays waste and devours everything round about far and wide. In this letter Morinus speaks of another Jesuit book recently published, and he brands its author, Rabardeau, with the name of rashness and impiety.

units.la: (b) Mor. Epist ad Card. Fr. Barb. de lib. Rebar-dei Jesuitæ edito Par. in 4. Anno 1641. torem, Rabardeum, nomine temeritatis notat atque impietatis. In eo quippe non agebatur de Episcopis, Presbyteris, ac Monachis, ut in Celloti opere de Hietarchia & Hierarchis,sed de ipso summo Pontifice, de eujus suprema autoritate valde diminutum fuisset in Gallia, si res ex illius Jesuitæ voto successissent,qui inter alia opinionum suarum placita contendebat,novum etiam ætate nostra Patriarchatum erigi posse in Patriarchatu Romano, sumebatq; exemplum ex Constantinopolitano Patriarchatu ; prodierat scilicet nuperrime libellus incerto autore ; sub nomine Optati Galli sive de cavendo schismate,quod tunc Galliæ portendebat larvatus ille Gallus. Jam omnia in Schismatis structuram prona esse asserebat,ac personare Patriarchā, seu,ut ille loquitur, Papalis dignitatis in Francorū Regno furem. Mirum est,quâm vehementerCardinalisRichelius ob in epti illius libelli, quiq; contemni poterat, editionem commotus fuerit; quæsivit ex omnibꝰ[?] ordinibus Theologos,qui Optato responresponsum pararent, inter quos repertus est Rabardeus Jesuita, nec non Jurisconsultos, e quorum numero fuêre illustrissimi viri de Marca & Bosquetus, qui postea facti sunt Episcopi. Itaqve Morinus scripsit Cardinali Barberino, Rabardeum Jurisdictionem omnem & immunitatem ab Ecclesia avulsam in Laicos judices transtulisse, primum omnium Catholicorum dixisse, in potestate Laicorum situm esse Matrimonium irritare, ac Principes posse condere leges, quæ Matrimonium dirimant; demum liberorum adultorum conjugia sine parentum consensu nulla esse & irrita. Hæc & alia ejusdem rationis non nulla, tanquam impiè & temerariè à Rabardeo Jesuita asserta, gravissime conquestus est Morinus, quem tamen non tam ex rei veritate in hoc negotio locutum, quam faciendæ invidiæ causa Richelio & Jesuitis, ut credam, his potissimum rationibus adducor:
units.tr: (b) Morinus, letter to Cardinal Francis Barberini concerning the book of the Jesuit Rabardeau, published at Paris in quarto, in the year 1641. For in that book the question was not about bishops, presbyters and monks, as in Cellot's work on the hierarchy and the hierarchs, but about the supreme Pontiff himself, whose supreme authority would have been greatly diminished in France if matters had turned out according to the wish of that Jesuit. Among other propositions of his opinions, he contended that in our own age a new patriarchate could also be erected within the Roman patriarchate, and he took as his example the patriarchate of Constantinople. A little pamphlet by an unknown author had lately appeared under the name of Optatus Gallus, or On avoiding schism, which that masked Frenchman was then threatening to France. He asserted that everything was now prone to the building of a schism, and that the patriarch, or, as he puts it, the thief of papal dignity, was resounding in the kingdom of the French. It is remarkable how vehemently Cardinal Richelieu was stirred by the publication of that foolish pamphlet, which could have been despised. He asked for theologians from every order to prepare a reply to Optatus, and among them was found the Jesuit Rabardeau, and also jurists, of whose number were the most illustrious men de Marca and Bosquet, who afterwards became bishops. And so Morinus wrote to Cardinal Barberini that Rabardeau had transferred all jurisdiction and immunity, torn away from the Church, to lay judges; that he had been the first of all Catholics to say that marriage lies in the power of laymen to annul, and that princes can make laws which dissolve marriage; and finally that the marriages of adult children without the consent of their parents are null and void. Morinus complained most gravely of these and some other assertions of the same kind, made by Rabardeau impiously and rashly. I am led, however, to believe that he spoke in this matter not so much from the truth of the case as for the sake of stirring up odium against Richelieu and the Jesuits, and for this reason above all:

units.la: OPTATUS ille Gallus famosi istius libelli autor, de quo tam anxiè, sed frustra inquisivit Richelius, Gallus reapse fuit, idemque Parisinus Presbiter, cui nomen Hersenius, homo cerebrosus, judicii pauci, vehementissimus concionator, qui quiq; in CongregatioueOratorii Parisiensis vixerat, ac tum etiam probe notus Morino & aliis nonnullis Congregationis istius Presbyteris, cum quibus semper fuit conjunctissimus Hersenius, quos etiam licet paucissimos, propositi sui consiliique suscepti participes fecerat, non secus ac nuncium sedis Apostolicæ, cui obtulit viginti exemplaria libelli sui, cum primùm editus est, quæ Romam mitterentur; oderant præterea plerique Congregationis Oratorii Parisiensis Cardinalem Richeli-um, atque inprimis Joannes Morinus, non ita pridem illius arte delusus: ficta enim & adulatoria, quæ antea scri-pserat idem Morinus {b} de Richelii erga Berullum & Berullistas amore, quasi ille hunc viventem unicè coluerit, ab invidorum allatratibus vindicaverit, mortuum amarissimis lacrymis prosecutus, filio-
units.tr: That Frenchman, the author of that notorious little book, whom Richelieu so anxiously but fruitlessly sought, was in fact a Frenchman, and was the Parisian priest named Hersenius, a hot-headed man of little judgement and a most vehement preacher, who had lived in the Congregation of the Oratory at Paris. He was well known to Morinus and to some other priests of that Congregation, with whom Hersenius was always very close. He had shared his plan and purpose with a very few of them. He also offered twenty copies of his little book, as soon as it was published, to the nuncio of the Apostolic See, to be sent to Rome. Moreover, most members of the Paris Oratory hated Cardinal Richelieu, and above all Jean Morin, who had recently been deceived by his skill. For Morinus had earlier written flattering and fawning things about Richelieu's affection for Bérulle and the Bérullists, as if he had cherished Bérulle alone while he lived, had defended him against the snarling of his envious critics, and had mourned him with the bitterest tears and comforted his sons with the protection of his own authority. Yet everyone knows that Bérulle was defamed by Richelieu and by the writers of that age, at Richelieu's command, as if under the pretext of piety he had done no small harm to the affairs of France.

units.la: {b} Mor. in dedic. exercit. in Pent. Samarit. Anno 1631. filiosq; ejus autoritatis suæ præsidio consolatus sit : notum qvippe est omnibus, Berullū à Richelio & ab ætatis illius scriptoribꝰ diffamatū, jubente Richelio, qvasi ille sub specie pietatis non parvū rebus Franciæ detrimentum attulisset. Novissime qvcqve Richelius Claudium Segvenotum, Congregationis Oratorii Presbyterum, in custodia acris, vulgo dictæ la Bastille Poni Jusserat; & ob hanc potissimuū causam Morinus Celloto & Rabardeo Jesuitis infensissimum se præbuit, qvi in suis operibus Segvenotum miris modis traduxerant : Hic opusculum Beati Augustini de Virginitate èLatino Gallicum fecerat auxeratqve notis, qvas ut scandalosas & communi Ecclesiæ praxi contrarias damnârunt Theologi Parisienses, ad id eos impellente Richelio, qvi Segvenoti ad sobrietatem non sapientis in, genium reformidabat.
units.tr: {b} Morinus, in the dedication of his exercitations on the Samaritan Pentateuch, 1631. Most recently Richelieu had ordered Claude Séguenot, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, to be placed in close custody in the prison commonly called the Bastille. Chiefly for this reason Morinus showed himself most hostile to the Jesuits Cellot and Rabardeau, who had slandered Séguenot in a wonderful manner in their works. Séguenot had translated into French a little work of Blessed Augustine, On Virginity, and had enlarged it with notes, which the Paris theologians condemned as scandalous and contrary to the common practice of the Church, at Richelieu's urging, since Richelieu feared the spirit of Séguenot, who was not sober-minded.

units.la: Segvenotus vir erat magna de se sentiens, judicii non contemnendi, & cum Abbate Sancyrano, cujus doctrinam & mores plurimi facibat, amicitia conjunctus severioris di-sci-
units.tr: Séguenot was a man who thought highly of himself, of no contemptible judgement, and joined in friendship with Abbé Saint-Cyran, whose teaching and morals he greatly esteemed. He was a teacher of a stricter discipline.

units.la: sciplinæ magister, ille quæ à Sancyrano hauserat, vulgata Theologorum Scholasticorum placita de attritione vix ferre poterat, & ob id inprimis apud Richelium male audiit; quia tunc temporis quidam Jesuita, qui erat à Confessione Regis Christianissimi, hanc doctrinam de necessitate contritionis contra vulgus Theologorum & communem societatis suæ sententiam Regi suggerebat, & quia Rex erat ingenio moroso ac difficili, rebus tractandis postea minus commodum illum expertus est Richelius. Itaqve Segvenoti de attritione sententia à Theologis Parisiensibus autore Cardinale Richelio damnata est, at in Jesuitæ illius rigidioris ac minus humani locum, alius Jesuita humanior ac mollior audiendæ Regis Confessioni succederet.
units.tr: He could scarcely bear the common opinions of the scholastic theologians about attrition, which he had absorbed from Saint-Cyran, and for this reason he fared badly, above all with Richelieu. For at that time a certain Jesuit, who was the king's most Christian confessor, was suggesting to the king this doctrine about the necessity of contrition, against the common view of the theologians and the common opinion of his own Society. And because the king was of a moody and difficult temper, Richelieu later found it less convenient in managing affairs. Therefore Séguenot's opinion on attrition was condemned by the Paris theologians, at the instance of Cardinal Richelieu, but in place of that stricter and less humane Jesuit, another Jesuit, more humane and gentle, succeeded in hearing the king's confession.

units.la: Interim Morinus Richelio atqve inprimis Celloto & Rabardeo Jesuitis, qui de Segvenoto palam in libris suis detraxerant, infensissimus nuncium sedis Apostolicæ una cum Bertado ejusdem Congregationis Oratorii Theologo invisit, & gregalem suum à Jesuitarum conviciis conatur asserere ; sed argumentum illud de attritione, rem pro more suo in utramque partem versans,in colloqvio ita implicavit , ut nuncius plus in eo judicii, minus eruditionis desideraverit ; denique Morinum in hoc negotio minus sincerè egisse cum Cardinale Barberino,adversus Rabardeum Jesuitam probat evidentissimè Morini ipsius responsio, qvi sententiam suam de Rabardei libro à Thiersaldo, congregationis Oratorii Presbytero, cùm rogatus fuisset dicere, ejusdem Rabardei opiniones in plerisqve confirmavit,præsertim in causa novi Patriarchatus , qvem in Gallia etiam invito ac reluctante summo Pontifice erigi posse asseverat. Hanc Thiersaldi consultationem habeo præ manibus, in qva ex mente Mo-rini observatur, Jesuitas , licet Pontifici Maximo se addictissimos profiteantur, totos tamen dependere à placitis ac nutibus principum , in qvorum ditionibus vivunt; unde factum fuerit, ut Rabardeus Jesuita in opere suo opiniones sele-gerit, gerit, qvæ principibus favebant, qvod Librum suum in gratiam Regis Christianissimi & Cardinalis Richelii scriberet; perpaucis compertum est, inde, jam à pluribus annis ex communi Jesuitarum omnium consensu statutum fuisse, Librorum, qvi à Societatis hominibus in publicum ederentur, approbationem non amplius, ut antea à patre Generali expectandam, sed à provincialibus cujuslibet Provinciæ, ita ut hodiernis temporibus de aula Romana parum solliciti, eas inter scribendum liberè sequantur opiniones, qvas principibus acceptiores fore prævident.
units.tr: Meanwhile Morinus, most hostile to Richelieu and above all to the Jesuits Cellot and Rabardeau, who had openly disparaged Séguenot in their books, visited the nuncio of the Apostolic See, together with Bertaud, a theologian of the same Congregation of the Oratory, and tried to defend his fellow member against the Jesuits' abuse. But when he dealt with the question of attrition, turning it, as was his way, to both sides, he so entangled himself in the conversation that the nuncio found more judgement in him and less learning. Finally, Morinus's own reply to Cardinal Barberini against Rabardeau the Jesuit proves most clearly that he acted rather insincerely in this affair. When Thiersault, a priest of the Oratory, asked him to give his opinion of Rabardeau's book, he confirmed the same Rabardeau's opinions in most points, especially on the question of a new patriarchate, which he asserts can be set up in France even against the will and resistance of the supreme Pontiff. I have in hand Thiersault's consultation, in which, according to Morinus's own view, it is observed that the Jesuits, although they profess themselves most devoted to the Pope, nevertheless depend entirely on the pleasure and nods of the princes in whose dominions they live. Hence it came about that Rabardeau the Jesuit, in his work, chose opinions that favoured the princes, since he wrote his book to please the King Most Christian and Cardinal Richelieu. It is well known to few that for several years, by the common consensus of all the Jesuits, it had been decided that the approval of books published by members of the Society should no longer be sought from the Father General, as before, but from the provincials of each province. Thus, nowadays, being little concerned about the Roman court, they freely follow in their writing those opinions which they foresee will be more acceptable to princes.

units.la: QUIA his & similibus literis Joannes Morinus Cardinalis Barberini amicitiam sibi comparaverat, seque ostenderat sedi Apostolicæ devotissimum, longè freqventius quàm antea cum eodem Cardinali habuit literarum commercium, ita ut tum res Congregationis suæ, tum amicorum, sæpius illi commendare ausus fuerit. Commendavit{c} Episcopum Carnuten-
units.tr: Because of these and similar letters, Jean Morin had won the friendship of Cardinal Barberini and had shown himself most devoted to the Apostolic See. He now corresponded with that cardinal far more often than before, so that he dared to commend to him, more frequently, both the affairs of his Congregation and those of his friends. He commended the Bishop of Chartres,

units.la: {c} Anno.1642. nutensem, qui ad Archiepiscopatum Rhemensem translatus fuerat, deinde {d} clarissimum virum Dominum deMarca, nuperrimè ad Episcopatum Conseranensiũà Rege Christianissimo designatum, antea in Parlamento Palensi Præsidem, cujus summam eruditionem & ingenium laudans, de illius libro, cui nomen fecerat de Concordia Sacerdotii & Regni ita loquitur : materia ubique fere, sed in Gallia potissimum anceps, lubrica & difficilis, aitqve in confesso esse apud omnes hujus rei peritos, neminem è foro scriptoremabhinc annos 120. Ecclesiasticæ autoritati magis favisse. Interea {e} Cardinalis Barberinus Morini sui haud immemor, eum beneficio Ecclesiastico donare voluit, sed illud acceptare se non posse testatus est Morinus, tam ob residentiæ obligationem quàm quòd in ea Regione, ubi situm erat beneficium istud, bella undiqve circunstreperent. Commendavit etiam {f} Morinus Cardinali Francisco Barberino per literas Feroni-
units.tr: {c} In 1642. who had been transferred to the archbishopric of Reims, and then the most distinguished man, Monsieur de Marca, recently designated by the King Most Christian as bishop of Couserans, formerly president of the Parlement of Pau. Praising his very great learning and talent, Morinus speaks of his book, which he had entitled On the Concord of Priesthood and Kingdom, thus: the subject is everywhere nearly the same, but in France especially doubtful, slippery and difficult. He says it is agreed by all experts in this matter that no writer from the bar in the last 120 years has favoured ecclesiastical authority more. Meanwhile Cardinal Barberini, not forgetful of his Morinus, wished to bestow an ecclesiastical benefice on him, but Morinus testified that he could not accept it, both because of the obligation of residence and because in that region where the benefice was situated, wars were rattling on every side.

units.la: {d} Anno 1643.
{e} Anno 1644.

{f} Anno 1653. um, Ecclesiæ Carnutensis Archidiaconum, & officialem ac Doctorem Sorbonicum, qui nominatus ad Abbatiam sancti Laudomari Blesensis, summi Pontificis diplomata seu bullas optinere non poterat, quòd Romæ male audiret, tanquam eorum, quos Jansenistas vocabant, quia partibus addictus, scilicet Cornelii Jansenii Episcopi Iprensis Librum, cui titulus, Augustinus, suffragio suo comprobaverat; rem ita esse non diffitetur Morinus sed videbat, inquit,
units.tr: {f} In 1653. Morinus also commended by letter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini Feron, archdeacon of the church of Chartres, official and Doctor of the Sorbonne, who, though nominated to the abbey of Saint-Laumer at Blois, could not obtain the papal diplomas or bulls, because at Rome he was ill-regarded as one of those whom they called Jansenists, being committed to that party. For he had by his vote approved the book by Cornelius Jansen, Bishop of Ypres, entitled Augustinus. Morinus does not deny that this is so, but he saw, he says,

units.la: Librū ab Episcopo Catholicæ communionis compositum, cujus autor omnes labores suos Ecclesiæ Romanæ emendandos & expungendos humillime subjicebat, videbat Librum in Belgio à Librorum censoribus examine facto probatum & commendatum, & duplici privilegio Imperatoris & Regis Catholici munitum; videbat Librum à multis viris doctis in Gallia magni fieri, & à nemine tum attentatum. Deinde in laudes Feronii fusius excurrit Morinus, atque eam exciitatis de Jansenimsmo qvæsti. oui-
units.tr: a book composed by a bishop of the Catholic communion, whose author most humbly submitted all his labours to be corrected and expunged by the Church of Rome; he saw the book in Belgium examined by the censors of books, approved and commended, and fortified by a double privilege from the Emperor and the Catholic King; he saw the book held in high esteem by many learned men in France, and attacked by no one at that time. Then Morinus ranges more fully over Feron's praises, and, with the questions about Jansenism stirred up, he says that Feron not only did not favour the Jansenist faction, but also, by the mandate of the bishop of Chartres, whose vicar general he was, promulgated throughout the diocese of Chartres the papal bull on the five impious propositions attributed to Jansen.

units.la: (g) Mor. in Epist. ad Card. Barb. onibus; Jansenistarum factioni non mo-do non favisse, sed & ipsum bullam Pontificiam, de quinque propositionibus impiis Jansenio tributis, editam ex Episcopi Carnutensis mandato, cujus erat vicarius Generalis, per dioecesim Carnutensem promulgasse; plurimi tunc temporis è Congregatione Oratorii non tam ex rerum ipsarum cognitione, quàm ex odio in Jesuitas, Jansenistarū doctrinae favebant, quibus tamen nunquam Morinus assentiri potuit; quia ejusmodi homines rerum Ecclesiasticarum minus peritos noverat, minusque tutum jùdicabat, in rebus fidei ab uno dependere Augustino, qui & ipse in aliquibus novator visus fuerat. Hæc & similia in familiari cum gregalibus suis colloquio Morinus de beato Augustino & ejus discipulis palam asserere non verebatur, simulque deridebat patres Societatis, qui se etiam Augustini discipulos profiterentur, cum debuissent Augustini partes deserere, ac demonstrare, ipsum â recepta temporum suornm fide prifcorumque Ecclesiæ Patrum doctrina recessisse; videbatur, tamen Morinus Jesuitis infensior, quàm Jansenii discipulis: de Arnaldo enim ejus libro de frequenti Communione, non ita male sensisse visus est, cum hæc scribebat Lucæ Holstenio, Anno 1644. Arnaldi Liber 5. Episcoporum & lectissimorum 20. Sorbonæ Doctorum testimoniis commendatus prodiit. Insurgunt tamen Jesuitæ, & in eum publicis prædicationibus, ut in Lutheranum, Calvinianum & quid non, invehuntur. Cum autem ad pontificem provocandum esset, potestates mundi advocant, ut eorum autoritate & Liber & autor & ipsi approbatores, si fieri potuisset, opprimantur.
units.tr: (g) Morinus, in a letter to Cardinal Barberini. At that time many members of the Oratory favoured the teaching of the Jansenists, not so much from knowledge of the matters themselves as from hatred of the Jesuits. Morinus, however, could never assent to them, because he knew such men to be less skilled in ecclesiastical affairs, and he judged it less safe in matters of faith to depend on Augustine alone, who himself had seemed to some to be an innovator. Morinus did not hesitate to say such things openly, and things like them, about Blessed Augustine and his disciples in familiar conversation with his fellow members. At the same time he mocked the Fathers of the Society, who also professed themselves disciples of Augustine, when they ought to have abandoned Augustine's side and shown that he had departed from the faith received in their own times and from the teaching of the ancient Fathers of the Church. Yet Morinus seemed more hostile to the Jesuits than to the disciples of Jansen. For he did not think too badly of Arnauld's book on frequent communion, when he wrote to Lucas Holstenius in 1644: Arnauld's book, commended by five bishops and twenty of the most select doctors of the Sorbonne, has appeared. The Jesuits, however, rise up and attack it in public preaching, as they would a Lutheran, a Calvinist, or anything you like. But since they must appeal to the Pope, they call upon the powers of the world, so that by their authority both the book and its author and even its approvers may, if possible, be crushed.

units.la: SILEO, & alias ejusdem Morini ad Cardinalem Barberinum Epistolas, quia nullius fere sunt momenti, si unam excipias, in qua suam de critica sacra Ludovici Capelli sententiam fusius exponit. Morino scripserat Barberinus, opus istud quod Capelli filius Catholicus & sacerdos ediderat ({h}) disputationibus materiam
units.tr: I pass over the other letters of Morin to Cardinal Barberini, since they are of almost no importance, with one exception, in which he sets out more fully his view of Louis Cappel's sacred criticism. Barberini had written to Morin about the work that Cappel's son, a Catholic and a priest, had published ({h}), which had recently given material for disputation at Rome, concerning the decree of the Council of Trent on the Vulgate edition of the Bible and the judgment of that decree on this criticism.

units.la: ({h}) Anno 1653. am Romæ nuperrimè suppeditasse, ob concili Tridentini de vulgata Bibliorum editione decretum, atque judicium illius de ista critica effl agitaverat; testatur Cardinalis, se jam cum in Gallia commoraretur, de hac non nihil didicisse: Apud me, inquit, alicujus momenti est, quòd cum apud vos agerem, accepisse, diu hæsitatum fuisse circa Libri editionem, nam ab ea deterrebat nimius censoris rigor in textum Hebraicum, ob Historiæ sanctitatem & inviolabile sacramentum, cùm tamen omni studio contenderetur, ideo hoc opus in Lucem edendum esse, quòd perspicuè demonstraret, Hæreticos abusos Hebraico textu; ita ut si publici juris hoc opus fieret, verisimile esset, illos id agre laturos, præsertim homine ejusdem farinæ hæc docente, ut postea evenit. Huic Cardinalis Francisci Barberini Epistolæ respondit Morinus, criticam sacram Capelli per longum temporis spatium Genevæ, Sedani ac Lugduni Batavorum hæsisse manuscriptam[?]; sed ut imprimeretur, obtinere non potuisse, licet Salmasius Lugduni duni editionem urgeret. Ministros ritus Calviniani, statim atque hoc opus e-ditum acceperunt, Capello valde succensuisse, qvi Catholicis arma ministraret, suosqve ad autoritatem Ecclesiæ, ut aliqvid certi de scripturis haberent, recurrere cogeret, ita ut Libri censura Capello gratissima futura sit, simulqve occasio cum suis in gratiam redeundi ; susius in hac Epistola Morinus Capellum ejusqve criticam tuetur, docetqve, qvid utilitatis ex hoc opere in Ecclesiam Catholicam redundet, & qvantum detrimenti Protestantibus afferat : fatetur qvidem, multa Capellum omisisse, qvæ vir Catholicus non reticuisset, verùm nihil omnino in hoc opere critico extare, qvod Religioni Catholicæ sit aperte contrarium ; complures viros doctos, inter qvos Dionysius Petavius Jesuita, & Marinus Mersennus è Minimorum familia, secum hujus libri editioni favisse. Addit nullum Doctorem Catholicum publice suffragio Librum istum probasse aut commendasse, autoris filium, qvi Catholicus est, Impressioni praefuisse, diligenterque cavisse, ne quid atrox in Religionem Catholicam patri elapsum suisset ; deinque quia Barberinus Morino objecerat autoritatem Concilii Tridentini, illiusque de vulgata editione decretum, ille respondit, si hac in parte accusetur Capellus, acculandos quoque doctissimos Ecclesiae tractatores, profertque Bellarmini testimonium, de vulgata ita scribentis Lucae Brugensi, Anno 1603. {i}Scias velim, vulgata à nobis non esse accuratissimè castigata: multa enim de industria iis de caulis[?] pertransivimus, quae correctione indigere videbantur ; variae Lectiones, quae in Bibliis Lovaniensibus habentur, & in quas tu Librum utilissimum scripsisti, mihi videbantur omnino addenda. Atque ibidem hæc Cardinalis Baronii verba {k}de isto negotio proferuntur: Fateor, in Bibliis nonnulla adhuc superesse, quae in melius mutari possunt. Hoc argumentum de ratione, qua in tel-
units.tr: ({h}) In 1653. Cardinal Barberini testifies that, while he was still living in France, he had learned something about this matter: For me, he says, it is of some importance to have heard, while I was working among you, that for a long time there was doubt about the publication of the book, since the excessive severity of the censor toward the Hebrew text deterred them from it, on account of the sanctity of the history and its inviolable sacrament. Yet it was strongly urged that this work should be brought to light, because it clearly demonstrates that the heretics have abused the Hebrew text. So if this work were made public, it would probably be taken very badly by them, especially since a man of the same stripe teaches these things, as later came to pass. Morin replied to this letter of Cardinal Francesco Barberini. He wrote that Cappel's sacred criticism had for a long time lain in manuscript at Geneva, Sedan and Leiden, but could not be obtained for printing, although Salmasius was pressing for an edition at Leiden. He said that the ministers of the Calvinist rite, as soon as they received this work once it was published, were very angry with Cappel, who was supplying weapons to the Catholics and forcing his own people to have recourse to the authority of the Church in order to have anything certain about the Scriptures. So the censure of the book would be most welcome to Cappel, and an opportunity for him to return to favour with his own people. Morin defends Cappel and his criticism at greater length in this letter. He shows what advantage this work brings to the Catholic Church and how much harm it does to the Protestants. He admits indeed that Cappel has omitted many things that a Catholic would not have passed over, but he holds that there is absolutely nothing in this critical work that is openly contrary to the Catholic religion. He adds that several learned men, among them Denis Petau the Jesuit and Marin Mersenne of the order of the Minims, favoured the publication of this book along with him. He adds that no Catholic doctor has publicly approved or recommended the book, and that the author's son, who is a Catholic, supervised the printing and took careful care that nothing atrocious against the Catholic religion had slipped from his father. Finally, since Barberini had objected to Morin the authority of the Council of Trent and its decree on the Vulgate edition, he replied that if Cappel is accused on this point, the most learned doctors of the Church must be accused too. He cites the testimony of Bellarmine, who wrote about the Vulgate to Lucas of Bruges in 1603: I would have you know that the Vulgate has not been corrected by us with the greatest accuracy. For we have deliberately passed over many things in it that seemed to need correction. The variant readings that are found in the Louvain Bible, and on which you wrote a most useful book, seemed to me altogether to be added. And in the same place the cardinal's words about this business are quoted from Baronius: {k}I admit that in the Bible some things still remain which can be changed for the better. The question of how the decree of the Council of Trent is to be understood, which Cardinal Barberini did not seem to grasp, is pursued at greater length here by Morin, following the opinion of the most learned theologians of the Roman Church. Finally, to satisfy Barberini in every respect, he adds to all this that Cappel indeed wished for a new version of the Old Testament made from the Hebrew text, with various readings gathered from all sides and placed in the margin; but he says this does not prejudge the decree of the Council, which only wishes the Latin edition to be preferred to the other translations, and has never forbidden a new translation from the Hebrew or Greek to be made for the illustration of the original text. So far Morin. In everything he shows himself the most vigorous defender of Louis Cappel's sacred criticism. This letter is certainly worth publishing, so that especially the Parisian theologians, most of whom worship the Vulgate and cannot bear those who think of preparing a new translation from the Hebrew or Greek text, may learn from it what the more learned theologians, who are also skilled in critical matters, think about biblical questions. For in this letter Morin sets out his opinion on this subject much more sincerely than in his biblical exercitations, in which he attends only to this, that he might set himself against the Protestants and others who maintain the Hebrew and Greek text of the New Testament.

units.la: {i} Bellarm. Epist. ed. in fine Biblior. Antuerp. Anno 1608.[?]
units.tr: {i} Bellarm. Epist. ed. at the end of the Antwerp Bibles, year 1608.[?]

units.la: {k} Card. Baron. ibidem. ligi debeat Concilii Tridentini decretum, quod non assequi videbatur Cardinalis Barberinus, fusius prosequitur hoc loco Morinus, ex sententia doctissimorum Ecclesiæ Romanæ Theologorum: ac demum his omnibus subjungit, ut Barberino in omnibus satisfaciat, optâsse quidem Capellum, novam fieri veteris testamenti versionem ex Hebraeo contextu, in cujus margine variæ lectiones undiq; selectæ collocarentur, sed hoc non præjudicare Concilii decreto, quod tantum vult, Latinam editionem cæteris translationibus præferri, at novam ex Hebraeo aut Græco Interpretatione ad originarii textus Illustrationem condi, nunquam prohibuit. Hactenus Morinus; qui in omnibus se ostendit Criticæ Sacræ Ludovici Capelli strenuissimum defensorem; dignaque est profecto hæc Epistola, quæ in lucem edatur, ut Theologi præsertim Parisienses, quorum pleriqve vulgarem editionem adorant, eosque ferre non possunt, qui de nova ad contextum Hebræum aut Græcum translatione paranda cogitant, discant ex illa Epistola, quid de rebus Biblicis doctiores Theologi, iidemque rei Criticæ periti sentiant. In hac enim Morinus suam de isto argumento sententiam longè sincerius exponit, quàm in suis exercitationibus Biblicis, in quibus ad id unum attendit, ut protestantibus aliisque contextus Hebraei ac Græci novi Testamenti assertoribus sese opponeret. Cæterum non animadvertit Morinus, à se vel ab aliis expurgatoribus ex autographo Criticæ Capelli integrum fere caput expunctum fuisse, in quo Capellus sententiam illius de Latinis Græcisque codicibus, quos Hebræis longè anteposuerat, prolixius refellit. Objectum scilicet fuit Capello {l} ab homine ejusdem sectæ, communicato de evertendis codicibus Hebraeis consilio cum Morino, ambos novam istam opinionem conjunctim fabricatos fuisse; quàm falsum istud fuerit, & à sua mente alienum, ut ostenderet, in apologia, quam pro criticæ suæ defensione adversus ejuf-
units.tr: {k} Card. Baron. ibidem. Morinus here pursues more fully, on the judgment of the most learned theologians of the Roman Church, the question of how the decree of the Council of Trent is to be understood, a point which Cardinal Barberini did not seem to grasp. Finally, to satisfy Barberini in every respect, he adds that Capellus indeed wished for a new version of the Old Testament made from the Hebrew text, with variant readings gathered from every source placed in its margin, but that this would not prejudice the decree of the Council. That decree only wills that the Latin edition be preferred to other translations, and it has never forbidden a new translation from the Hebrew or Greek to be made for the illustration of the original text. Thus far Morinus, who in every respect shows himself the most vigorous defender of Ludovicus Capellus's Sacred Criticism. And this letter is certainly worth publishing, so that the Parisian theologians, most of whom adore the vulgar edition and cannot bear those who think of preparing a new translation from the Hebrew or Greek text, may learn from it what more learned theologians, and those skilled in critical matters, think about biblical questions. For in this letter Morinus sets out his opinion on the subject far more candidly than in his Biblical exercises, in which he aimed only at opposing the Protestants and others who uphold the Hebrew and Greek text of the New Testament. Moreover, Morinus did not notice that, by himself or by other editors, almost an entire chapter was struck from the autograph of Capellus's Criticism, the chapter in which Capellus refutes at greater length his view of the Latin and Greek codices, which he had preferred far above the Hebrew ones. For it had been objected to Capellus by a man of the same sect, who had shared with Morinus his plan of overthrowing the Hebrew codices, that the two of them had jointly fabricated that new opinion. How false this was, and how far from his own mind, he showed in the apology he wrote in defence of his criticism against such a man.

units.la: {l} Boot. Epist. ad Usser. advers. Crit. Cap. modi hominem scripsit, caput illud, quod ex suo opere expunctum fuisse conquestus fuerat, repraesentavit. In hoc autem capite Morinum mire suggillat, qui mera criminandi intemperantia{m} & carpendi libidine multa Evangelicis objecerit, Facile est inquit Capellus, ({m}Ignaræ plebi fumos vendere, & ad populum phaleras jactare atque ostentare ; at nunquam doctis, ne mediocriter quidem Hebraicè peritis, persuadere poterit Morinus, non potuisse viros, qui post Hieronymum surrexerunt, longe doctissimos quam plurima in ejus translatione observare gravissima σφάλματα atque hallucinationes.
units.tr: {l} Boot. Epist. ad Usser. advers. Crit. Cap. He restored that chapter, the loss of which he had complained of, from his own work. In this chapter he mocks Morinus wonderfully, who, out of pure intemperance in accusing and a lust for carping, has brought many charges against the Evangelical writers. "It is easy," says Capellus, "to sell smoke to the ignorant common people, and to parade and display trappings before the crowd; but Morinus will never persuade learned men, not even those moderately skilled in Hebrew, that men who arose after Jerome, far more learned than he, could not observe in his translation very serious errors [σφάλματα] and hallucinations." {m}Ignaræ plebi fumos vendere

units.la: Multum tamen tribuit idem Capellus veteribus translationibus, ob earum antiquitatem & perpetuum Ecclesiae usum; sed ferre non potest, ut iis locis, ubi manifesto vitiosæ sunt, præponatur earum vitium authentico textui, aut aliis translationibus longè acceuratiori-bus: quare Morinum arguit, ut planè iniquum, qui autoritatem septuaginta Inter-
units.tr: Cappel nevertheless attributes much to the old translations, on account of their antiquity and their constant use in the Church. But he cannot bear that, in places where they are manifestly faulty, their fault should be preferred to the authentic text or to other translations far more accurate. Therefore he argues against Morin, as altogether unfair, that he set the authority of the Seventy interpreters and of Jerome so against the more recent translators that it would be wrong to depart from them even a little.

units.la: {m} Cap. Epist. Apolog. ad Usser. Interpretum & Hieronymi recentioribus Interpretibus ita opposuerit, ut ab illis vel tantillum discedere nefas fuerit. Hæc & alia bene multa ejusdem rationis in illo Capite, quod ex critica sua expunctum fuit, adversus Morini sententiam Capellus animadverterat, quæ manifeste ostendunt, illum cum Morino nullatenus consensisse in evertend.[?] textus Hebræi autoritate, eiqve fubftituenda Græca Septuaginta Interpretum & Latina Hieronymi translatione; fi autem Capellum cum Morino comparare liceat in iis, quæ uterque de rebus Biblicis composuit, in hujus quidem libris plus eruditionis apparet, sed quæ sæpius sit extra rem; at in illo plus Ingenii atque Judicii qui nunquam à scopo aberret, & id quod sibi proposuit, firmissimis rationibus comprobet.
units.tr: {m} Cappel, letter, apology against Ussher. Cappel had pointed out against Morin's opinion these and many other similar things in that chapter which was struck from his criticism, and these plainly show that he did not agree at all with Morin in overthrowing the authority of the Hebrew text and substituting for it the Greek of the Septuagint interpreters and the Latin translation of Jerome. If, however, one may compare Cappel with Morin in what each has written on biblical matters, there appears more learning in the books of the latter, but often learning that is beside the point. In the former there is more talent and judgment: he never strays from his aim, and he confirms what he proposed with the firmest arguments.

units.la: NON solum autem cum Cardinale Barbarino in Italia Morinus habuit literarum commercium, sed & cum Luca Holstenio, Leone Allatio, & Abrahamo Ecchellensi Maronita. Illorum benefico excerpta aliquot ex Libris quibusdam Græcorum recentiorum, qui in Bi-bliothecis Vaticana & Barberina asserva-bantur, obtinuit, quæ postea inservit Commentariis suis de sacramento pœnitentiæ & de ordinationibus. Morino quoque scripsit Leo Allatius, de veteris Ecclesiæ apud Græcos partibus. Abrahamus autem Ecchellensis ad eum misit capita epitomes constitutionum Eccelsiæ Maroniticæ, Arabicè & Latinè descripta, simulque per Literas ei indicavit, quâ ratione pœnitentiæ Sacramentum apud Maronitas administraretur, & quænam esset illorum Ecclesiæ figura : Ecchellensis autem ille est, qui Polyglotta Parisiensia adhuc imperfecta in Syriacis & Arabicis, intra anni unius spatium perfecit.
units.tr: NOT only, however, did Morin have a correspondence with Cardinal Barberini in Italy, but also with Luke Holstein, Leo Allatius and Abraham Ecchellensis the Maronite. Through their kindness he obtained some extracts from certain books of the more recent Greeks, which were kept in the Vatican and Barberini libraries, and these later served his commentaries on the sacrament of penance and on ordinations. Leo Allatius also wrote to Morin about the part played by the old Church among the Greeks. Abraham Ecchellensis sent him sections of an epitome of the constitutions of the Maronite Church, written out in Arabic and Latin, and at the same time he informed him by letter how the sacrament of penance was administered among the Maronites, and what their Church's figure was. This Ecchellensis is the one who, within the space of a single year, completed the Syriac and Arabic parts of the Paris Polyglot, which was still unfinished.

units.la: Romā enim Parisios asportavit Libros Baruch & Estheris Arabicè, qui in illis Polyglottis deerant, exscriptos ex Arabicis Bibliis Cardinalis Francisci Barberini, idemque ex Vaticano exemplari titulos capitum aliquot, quæ desiderabantur in Bibliis Syriacis Morini, supsupplevit. Morini autem nomen non modo in Italiam pervenerat, sed & in Angliam, in Belgium & ad Helvetios. In Anglia Comberi praesertim & Junii virorum doctissimorum amicitiam coluit,& ad utrumq; libere scripsit,quid de vetusto illo codice Graeco Septuaginta Interpretum versionis sentiret,qui ab Æ-gypto in Angliam deportatus fuerat ; maxime in Epistola ad Patricium Junium, cujus opera Liber Iobi Londini editus fuerat ; de codilis illius, quo usus fuerat Junius,vetustate& bonitate fusius disserit, ac de aliis vetustis codicibus Septuaginta Interpretum translationis, simulque de Graecis novi Testamenti exemplaribus Manuscriptis, quae etsi illo autore in numeris in locis a se invicem disideant, vera tamen & germana censentur Exemplaria. Romanam,quae ex codice Vaticano prodiit, Septuaginta Interpretum editionem aliis omnibus editionibus praefert,ita tamen, ut & haec suos etiam naevos habeat, neque à mendis quibuscunque sit libera. In hac autem Epistola relucet in primis ingenium atque eruditio Morini, qui de Græcis Bibliorum editionibus longè sincerius loquitur, quàm in præfatione, quæ Græcis interpretibus, illius cura Parisiis ex codice Vaticano editis, præmittitur, & in exercitationibus Biblicis.
units.tr: For he carried from Rome to Paris the books of Baruch and Esther in Arabic, which were missing from those Polyglots, copied from the Arabic Bible of Cardinal Francesco Barberini. From the Vatican copy he also supplied the titles of several chapters that were lacking in Morinus's Syriac Bible. Morinus's name had reached not only Italy but also England, the Low Countries and the Swiss. In England he cultivated the friendship of the most learned men Combefis and Junius, and wrote to both of them frankly about what he thought of that ancient Greek codex of the Septuagint translation which had been brought from Egypt to England. He discusses this at length, especially in his letter to Patrick Junius, through whose efforts the Book of Job had been published in London: he considers the age and quality of the manuscript Junius had used, and also other old manuscripts of the Septuagint translation, as well as the Greek manuscript copies of the New Testament. Although, by his account, these differ from one another in their numbers and places, they are still considered true and genuine copies. He prefers the Roman edition of the Septuagint, published from the Vatican codex, to all other editions, yet holds that this too has its own blemishes and is not free from any errors. In this letter the talent and learning of Morinus shine forth above all. He speaks of the Greek editions of the Bible far more sincerely here than in the preface which is placed before the Greek translators, edited at Paris from the Vatican codex under his care, and in his Biblical exercises.

units.la: In Belgio Morinus per literas commercium habuit cum Auberto Miræo, Decano Antuerpiensi, viro rerum Ecclesiasticarum peritissimo, ad quem misit exemplar præfationis suæ in Septuaginta Interpretum editionem: Curaverat enim duodecim illius exemplaria seorsim edi, quæ Romam mitterentur. Bruxellis cum Godefrido Vendelino, canonico Candatensi, qui illum per literas consuluerat de rebus Chronologicis, atque inprimis de Libro Rabbi Eliezeris, quem Gamalielis generum, & Pauli condiscipulum existimaverat, deceptus iis, quæ Morinus in exercitationibus suis in Pentateuchum Samaritanorum de antiquitate Libri istius jactanter scripserat: quare idem Morinus Godefrido respondens, longè aliud qvàm antea de isto Eliezere se sentire aperte profitetur, & varie de negotio Chronologico disputat. Notus etiam fuit Morinus Amstelodami Nihusio, & Duaci Petro Halloixio, Jesuitae rerum Ecclesiasticarum haud imperito; apud Helvetios famosissimus erat Morinus, Tiguri praesertim & Basileae, ubi Henricus Hottingerus & Joannes Buxtorfius de eo loquebantur, tanqvam homine opinionem insania laborante & monstrosi dogmatis autore: de Morino enim ita scripsit Muisio Hottingerus, {n}sed Morinus hujusmodi triumviratum despexit, atque post Simeonis de Muis obitum, qui ei inimicos Basileae, Lugduni aliisqve in locis apud Protestantes qvaesierat, venit in amicitiam Joannis Buxtorfii, qvi amico erga eum esse animo per literas illi significavit, ad qvas amicè etiam respondit Morinus {o}Buxtorfii eruditionem plurimi faciens, à qvo etiam in aliqvibus haud immerito reprehensum se fuisse, lubens agnoscit, dum Rabinorum testi-
units.tr: In the Low Countries Morinus had a correspondence by letter with Aubert Miraeus, dean of Antwerp, a man most expert in ecclesiastical affairs, to whom he sent a copy of his preface to the edition of the Septuagint. For he had arranged for twelve copies of it to be printed separately, to be sent to Rome. At Brussels he corresponded with Godefroid Wendelin, canon of Kanten, who had consulted him by letter on chronological matters, and above all on the Book of Rabbi Eliezer, whom he had thought to be the son-in-law of Gamaliel and a fellow pupil of Paul. Wendelin had been misled by what Morinus had boastfully written in his exercises on the Samaritan Pentateuch about the antiquity of that book. Therefore Morinus, replying to Godefroid, openly declares that he now thinks quite differently about that Eliezer from what he had before, and discusses the chronological question in various ways. Morinus was also known at Amsterdam to Nihusius, and at Douai to Pierre Halloix, a Jesuit not unskilled in ecclesiastical history. Among the Swiss Morinus was most notorious, especially at Zurich and Basel, where Johann Heinrich Hottinger and Johann Buxtorf spoke of him as a man labouring under a madness of opinion and the author of a monstrous doctrine. Hottinger wrote thus of Morinus to Muis: {n} but Morinus despised this triumvirate of critics, and after the death of Simeon de Muis, who had sought out enemies for him among the Protestants at Basel, Lyons and elsewhere, he came into friendship with Johann Buxtorf. Buxtorf signified to him by letter a friendly disposition towards him, and Morinus replied to him in a friendly way too. {o} Holding Buxtorf's learning in high regard, Morinus gladly acknowledges that he had been, not undeservedly, rebuked by him on some points, since he had not fully understood the rabbinic testimonies which he had translated into Latin;

units.la: {n} Anno 1645.
units.tr: {n} In the year 1645.

units.la: {o} Anno 1647. testimonia, quæ Latinè fecerat non ex omni parte intellexerit; etsi contendat, in nonnullis male à Buxtorfio castigatum se fuisse. In eadem quoqve Epistola, quæ longè prolixior est, de secta Caraitarum & Judæis Grammaticis disserit, ac demum Buxtorfii sententiam de punctorum vocalium apud eosdem Judæos antiqvitate, plurimis iisdemq; evidentissimis rationibus refellit; de qvibus omnibus postea summatim scripsit Ludovico Capello, {p}eumq; monuit, sectam Caraitarum Masoretas magni æstimare, unde ortum fuisse existimat, ut Judæi Rabbanistæ eos contempserint; qva in re gravissimè hallucinatus est Morinus: verum qvidem est, Judæos Caraitas non secus atqve alios Judæos, qvi vulgo Rabbanistæ appellantur, à punctis, qvorum Masorethæ autores putantur, totos dependere; sed falsum est, Rabbanistas ex illorum odio Masoretharum laborem despectui habuisse, cùm punctuationem istam Caraitæ à Rabbanistis, èqvorum classe
units.tr: {o} In the year 1647. although he maintains that he was wrongly corrected by Buxtorf in some other points. In the same letter, which is much longer, he discusses the sect of the Karaites and the Jewish grammarians, and at last refutes Buxtorf's view on the antiquity of the vowel points among those same Jews, with very many and very evident arguments. Morinus later summarised all of these matters in writing to Louis Cappel, and warned him that the Karaite sect held the Masoretes in high esteem; he thinks this is why the Rabbanite Jews despised them. In this matter Morinus was most gravely mistaken. It is true that the Karaite Jews, no less than the other Jews commonly called Rabbanites, wholly depend on the points whose authors are thought to be the Masoretes. But it is false that the Rabbanites, out of hatred for them, held the labour of the Masoretes in contempt, since the Karaites drew that punctuation from the Rabbanites, from whose class

units.la: {p} (p) An 16[?]4[?] classe fuerunt Masorethæ, hauserint, & utriusque illius sectæ viri eruditiores Masoretharum opus, non ut divinum quidem, sicuti nonnulli Judæorum Rabbanistarum Magistri, sed tanquam utilissimum, & ab hominibus Linguæ Hebraicæ ac rei Criticæ peritissimis, profectum respiciant.
units.tr: {p} (p) In 16[?]4[?]. from whose class the Masoretes were, and the more learned men of both those sects regard the work of the Masoretes not as divine, as some of the Rabbanite masters of the Jews do, but as most useful, and as the product of men most skilled in the Hebrew language and in critical scholarship.

units.la: POENITUIT tandem Morinum, ut etiam non diffitebatur, tantum temporis in rerum Biblicarum studio, atque inprimis in evolvendis Judæorum Libris consumpsisse, quare ingens volumen de Sacramento poenitentiæ ab annis ferme 30[?], inchoatum ac pluries interruptum ob materiæ difficultatem in lucem edidit {q}Liber ille, ut ipse testatur in Epistola, quam scripsit Lucæ Holstenio, antiquam Sacramenti illius praxim complectitur, & quæcunque in illius administratione, per duodecim secula tam in orientis, quam occidentis diversis Regionibus variariata sunt, explicat; opus sane istud dignum est, quod ab omnibus rerum Theologi-
units.tr: MORINUS at last regretted, as he did not deny, that he had spent so much time on Biblical studies, and especially on the reading of Jewish books. Therefore he published, in light, a huge volume on the sacrament of penance, begun about thirty years earlier and interrupted several times because of the difficulty of the subject. As he himself testifies in the letter he wrote to Lucas Holstenius, this book embraces the ancient practice of that sacrament and explains whatever variations in its administration occurred over twelve centuries in the various regions of both East and West. This work is certainly worthy of being read more attentively by all students of theology.

units.la: {q} Edit. Parif. in sol. Anno 1651. logicarum studiosis attentius legatur: qvandoqvidem argumentum illud admodum Theologorum Schola non tractavit Morinus, sed ubiqve Historicum agens, nec contentus, Patrum conciliorumq; testimonia proferre,vetusta ritualia, pontificalia & alios ejusdem naturæ Libros,qvi in Bibliothecarum Italiæ & Galliæ forulis delitescebant, imo & opera veterum Scholasticorum, qvæ nunqvam publici Juris facta sunt, producit, qvorum omnium beneficio aperte ostendit, qvantum in hac materia, etiam in Ecclesia occidentali varitatem fuerit qvamq; diversa sit hodierna Ecclesiæ Romanæ praxis à prisco administrandæ pœnitentiæ ritu. Mirum est profecto,repertos fuisse Parisiis Theologos, qvi Librum illorum placitis ac methodo ita contrarium approbaverint; novi qvidem,Morinum tunc temporis de illis sæpius ac diu conqvestum fuisse,qvòd cum metaphysicis pótius, qvàm cum Theologis sibi agendum esset : Coactus tamen fuit, ne Crabrones istos irritaret, multa retractare,aliqua emollire præfatione,& in fronte operis nonnulla præmonere.
