Ita se Historici tantum partes agere conjecturasq; meras interdum proferre admonet, se de sufficientia attritionis cum Confessione scripsisse,ante decretum Sorbonicum pro eadem sententia latum, quando scripsit, Diaconis olim, imò & Laicis apud Latinos concessum fuisse, Confessiones in extrema necessitate audire,& pœnitentes à peccatis absolvere,illud de absolutione Sacramentali minimè intelligendum,sed de ea solùm, quæ sit Ceremonia & quid Sacramentale,ut excitetur ægrotantis dispositio; verùm hæc & alia ejusmodi complura, quæ Morinus præmonet, à se invito ac reluctante, & ad mentem dumtaxat Theologorum Parisiensium recognita fuisse, manifestè probant ea ipsa, quæ in contextu operis sui habentur: exempli causa, palam astruit, Patrum & veteum Scholasticorum autoritate, contra Sorbonæ decretum, necessitatem contritionis, sententiam Dominici Soto de attritione, quæ in Sacramento fit contritio, sibi duram videri affirmat, atque, cum, qui sibi diceret, se propter Deum non pœnitere, non ausurum absolvere: & hanc Doctrinam etiam Judæorum Testimoniis confirmat, qui in hoc cum prisci s Ecclesiæ Patribus consentiunt, quòd omnes actiones nostras amoris divini causa faciendas existiment, atque inprimis pœnitentiam, aliàs hanc non fore validam.
units.tr: {q} Paris edition in folio, 1651. For Morinus did not treat that subject in the manner of the schools of the theologians. Rather, acting throughout as a historian, and not content with bringing forward the testimonies of the Fathers and councils, he produces ancient ritual books, pontificals, and other books of the same kind which lay hidden in the storerooms of libraries in Italy and France, and even the works of the ancient Scholastics which were never made public. By the help of all of these he clearly shows how great the variety in this matter was, even in the Western Church, and how different the present practice of the Roman Church is from the ancient rite of administering penance. It is indeed remarkable that there were found at Paris theologians who approved a book so contrary to their opinions and method. I know that Morinus at that time often and long complained about them, because he had to deal with metaphysicians rather than with theologians. Nevertheless, lest he provoke those hornets, he was forced to retract many things, to soften some, and to forewarn of certain points at the front of the work. Thus he reminds the reader that he is only playing the part of a historian and sometimes putting forward mere conjectures; that he had written about the sufficiency of attrition together with confession before the Sorbonne decree was issued in the same sense; that when he wrote that deacons once, and even laymen among the Latins, were granted the right to hear confessions in extreme necessity and to absolve penitents from their sins, this should not be understood of sacramental absolution, but only of that which is a ceremony and something sacramental, to stir up the disposition of the sick man. But these and many other things of this kind which Morinus forewarns of, that they were revised by him against his will and reluctantly, and only in accordance with the mind of the Parisian theologians, are clearly proved by those very things which are found in the body of his work. For example, he openly maintains, on the authority of the Fathers and the ancient Scholastics, against the decree of the Sorbonne, the necessity of contrition. He affirms that the opinion of Domingo de Soto on attrition, which becomes contrition in the sacrament, seems harsh to him, and that he would not dare to absolve one who said to him that he did not repent on account of God. He also confirms this doctrine by the testimonies of the Jews, who agree with the ancient Fathers of the Church in this, that they think all our actions must be done for the sake of divine love, and above all repentance, since otherwise it would not be valid.

units.la: Præterea multis iisque evidentissimis Patrum & Conciliorum testimoniis, maximè autoritate Cypriani, probat, diaconos olim in Ecclesia Latina eorum Confessiones, qui in extremo erant vitæ periculo audivisse, & pœnitentes reconciliasse, addit, verba Cypriani eo loco non posse explicari de absolutione ab Excommunicatione ; verùm intelligenda de absolutione à peccatis, quam statim comitabatur Eucharistiæ[?] Communistiæ ; quam etiam absolvendi à peccatis potestatem & Confessiones audiendi ad Laicos extendit eodem modo, quo hodiernis temporibus & ipsi in casu necessitatis infantes ex omnium Theolorum sententia baptizare possunt; id autem ex eo ortum fuisse crediderim, qvòd vera pœnitentia, qvæ à Christo & Apostolis in novo testamento annunciata est,in sola cordis atqve morum ad Deum conversione posita sit,pœnitentia verò illa exterior seu peccatorum Confessio, Jejunia & aliæ Mortificationes, uti loqvuntur,exteriores, signa tantùm esse videantur pœnitentiæ illius interioris seu resipiscentiæ: qvare in hoc etiam à Morino erratum, qvi Confessionem peccatorum Divinæ Institutionis esse arbitretur,qvamqve Ecclesia gravissimis de causis nunqvam abrogare posit. Communis est Doctorum Canonistarum adversus Theologos sententia,Confessionem Juris tantùm esse positivi & Ecclesiastici, nullatenus à Christo, sed ab Ecclesia institutam ; valde autem probabile est, usum Confessionis ac pœnarum, qvibus fontes plectuntur,ex Synagogarum usu,nec non è Philosophorum, maxime Platonicorum,Scholis in Ecclesiam venisse : sed ut ad Morinum nostra redeat oratio, ille non Parisiensibus solùm Theologis, operis sui approbatoribus, placere debuit; sed & Jesuitis, qui insignem adversus Jansenistas victoriam reportaverant. Idcirco ne Sancyrani, Arnaldi, gregalis sui Segvenoti, & aliorum, qui [?]e Augustini discipulos profitebantur, opiniones stabilire videretur, quasi commentaria sua de Sacramento poenitentiae eo dumtaxat fine in publicum edidisset, ut antiqua Ecclesiae praxis in Sacramenti illius Administratione revocaretur in usum, statim ab ingressu operis praefatus asserit, se illud ante annos 27. suscepisse, adeoq; neminem posse suspicari, quòd ob tumultus de poenis peccatis debitis recenter excitatos scripserit; & ut se à discipulis B. Augustini alienum ostenderet, ait, hactenus inauditum in Ecclesia, unius cujusdam Magistri, quantumlibet illustris, Doctrinam esse fidei regulam, in iis praesertim controversiis, in quibus caeteros Magistros sibi suisque discipulis habet contradicentes, eos demum, qui simile Augustino elogium tribuunt. ipsos esse infensiores illi-usus adversarios: præmonet tamen, se, his verbis Augustino & de illius Doctrina detrahere noluisse. Præfatio ista Arnaldo aliisque Augustini discipulis multum displicuit; quia autem nonnullis Theologis visus fuerat Morinus, dum rem istam curiosius ac diligentius tractat, Calvinianis favere, qui existimant, in Ecclesia Romana vix umbram & imaginem antiquæ pœnitentiæ remanere, quia Scholastici Doctores ac summi Pontifices priscam illam veterum Patrum duritiem emendaverant. Addit in eadem præfatione, quatuor potissimum capitum illustrationem in opere suo sibi proposuisse, quorum primum est singulorum peccatorum Confessionem sacerdoti secreto & particulatim edendam esse; secundum, peccata Baptismum præcedentia sine satisfactione, subsequentia vero non sine ipsa remitti. Tertium, satisfactiones peccatis post Baptismum remittendis esse imponendas. Quartum denique, pœnas ac antiquis patribus indictas non solùm Ecclesiæ, sed Deo satisfecisse. Uttrum autem promissa sua Morinus explicuerit, an absoluta operis sui editione hac præfatione doctores Scholasticos deluserit, illi judicent, quorum interest. Sileo etiam tum Seguenotum, & alios nonnullos Congregationis Oratorii Presbyteros, cum negotium istud tractaret Morinus, hodiernam Ecclesiæ Romanæ praxim in Administratione Sacramenti pœnitentiæ, verbis & exemplo suo valde improbasse, neque Concilii Tridentini Episcopis pepercisse, quasi Doctorum Scholasticorum placitis hac in re nimis adhæsissent.HancOratoriani illi Doctrinam hauserant à Sancyrano, sed postea pœnituit Gundramum, tunc Congregationis istius præpositum generalem, cum Sancyrano amicitiam coluisse, monuitque suos gregales, ut ab illo Abbate sibi caverent, qui de Concilii Tridentini Patribus eorumque decretis, quasi à Doctoribus Scholasticis profecta fuissent, male sentiens, omnia ad antiquæ disciplinæ severitatem revocanda esse censebat. Itaque Morinus,ne in ejusmodi suspicionem inciincideret, ab ipso libri sui exordio prositetur se antiquas Ecclesiae in administratione poenitentiae consuetudines ea mente non explicuisse, ut eas ad praxim & usum restitui velit; res enim ista inquit, periculosa, turbulenta, seditionibus obnoxia. Verùm etiam nostra aetate non ita bene audit Morinus ob ejusmodi Librum apud nonnullos è Schola Sorbonae Magistros, eos praesertim, quos Librorum vocant revisores: non ita pridem enim Canonici quidam Regulares Sancti Augustini è domo Sancti Victoris, cùm in animo habuissent, publici juris facere veterum quorundam Scholasticorum opera, quorum Morinus testimonia aliquot in commentaria sua de Sacramento poenitentiae transtulerat, nunquam illorum edendorum facultatem impetrare potuerunt, atque Morini nomen illis potius in hoc negotio obfuit quàm profuit: verùm de his satis superque.
units.tr: Moreover, by many and most evident testimonies of the Fathers and Councils, chiefly the authority of Cyprian, Morinus proves that deacons in the Latin Church formerly heard the confessions of those in danger of death and reconciled penitents. He adds that Cyprian's words in that passage cannot be explained as referring to absolution from excommunication, but must be understood as absolution from sins, which was immediately accompanied by communion in the Eucharist. He extends this power of absolving from sins and of hearing confessions to laymen in the same way that, in our own times, even laymen may baptize infants in cases of necessity, according to the opinion of all theologians. I would believe this arose from the fact that true repentance, which Christ and the Apostles proclaimed in the New Testament, consists solely in the conversion of heart and conduct to God, whereas that outward repentance, the confession of sins, fasting and the other so-called outward mortifications, seem to be only signs of that inward repentance or resipiscence. Wherefore Morinus has erred also in this, in thinking that the confession of sins is of divine institution, though the Church could never abolish it for the gravest reasons. The common view of the canonists, against the theologians, is that confession is only of positive and ecclesiastical right, instituted not by Christ but by the Church. It is, however, very probable that the practice of confession and of the penalties by which sinners are punished came into the Church from the custom of the synagogues and from the schools of the philosophers, especially the Platonists. But to return to Morinus: he ought to have pleased not only the Parisian theologians, who approved his work, but also the Jesuits, who had won a notable victory over the Jansenists. Therefore, lest he seem to establish the opinions of Sancyranus, Arnauld, his fellow Séguenot, and others who professed themselves disciples of Augustine, as if he had published his commentaries on the sacrament of penance solely with the aim of restoring the ancient practice of the Church in administering that sacrament, he asserts at the very beginning of his work that he undertook it twenty-seven years earlier, so that no one could suspect he wrote because of the recent tumults over the penalties due for sins. And to show that he is alien to the disciples of St Augustine, he says that it is hitherto unheard of in the Church for the doctrine of one master, however illustrious, to be the rule of faith, especially in those controversies in which other masters and their disciples contradict him; and that those who grant such praise to Augustine are themselves the most hostile opponents of that practice. He warns, however, that by these words he did not wish to disparage Augustine or his doctrine. This preface greatly displeased Arnauld and the other disciples of Augustine. Some theologians, moreover, thought that Morinus, in treating this matter more carefully and diligently, favoured the Calvinists, who hold that in the Roman Church scarcely a shadow or image of the ancient penance remains, because the Scholastic doctors and the supreme pontiffs had softened that former severity of the ancient Fathers. In the same preface he adds that he proposed to himself the illustration of four main points in his work. The first is that the confession of each sin must be made secretly and individually to a priest. The second is that sins committed before baptism are remitted without satisfaction, but those after baptism are not remitted without satisfaction itself. The third is that satisfactions must be imposed for sins to be remitted after baptism. Fourth, and finally, that the penalties imposed by the ancient Fathers satisfied not only the Church but God. Whether Morinus fulfilled his promises, or whether, having finished the edition of his work, he deceived the Scholastic doctors with this preface, let those judge whom it concerns. I say nothing either of Séguenot and some other presbyters of the Congregation of the Oratory, who, while Morinus was handling this business, strongly condemned by word and example the present practice of the Roman Church in administering the sacrament of penance, and did not spare the bishops of the Council of Trent, as if they had clung too closely to the opinions of the Scholastic doctors in this matter. Those Oratorians had imbibed this doctrine from Sancyranus. Afterwards, however, Gondran, then general superior of that Congregation, regretted having cultivated friendship with Sancyranus, and warned his fellows to beware of that abbot, who, thinking ill of the Fathers of the Council of Trent and their decrees, as though they had proceeded from the Scholastic doctors, held that everything must be restored to the severity of the ancient discipline. Therefore Morinus, lest he fall under such suspicion, professes from the very beginning of his book that he has not set out the ancient customs of the Church in administering penance with the intention of wishing them restored to practice and use; for, he says, that matter is dangerous, turbulent and liable to seditions. Yet even in our own age Morinus is not well regarded because of this book by some teachers of the Sorbonne, especially those whom they call revisers of books. For not long ago certain regular canons of St Augustine of the house of St Victor, when they intended to publish the works of certain older Scholastics, some of whose testimonies Morinus had transferred into his commentaries on the sacrament of penance, could never obtain permission to print them, and the name of Morinus harmed them in this business rather than helped them. But enough, and more than enough, about these matters.

units.la: Doctoribus quidem Scholasticis in libro, quem modo recensuimus infensissimum se praebet Morinus, quòd ad res Theologicas nihil fere præter rationes metaphysicas afferant; sed longe adhuc infensiorem illis se ostendit in commentariis, quæ postea edidit, de sacris Ecclesiæ ordinationibus {r}illos enim ab operis sui exordio traducit tanquam homines imperitos & argumenti quod tractat plane ignaros. Jam illud opus, ut supra observatum fuit, Romæ inchoaverat, cum cuidam Theologorum Congregationi interesset, in qua jussu Urbani VIII,Pontificis Maximi Græcorum Euchologium ad fidei Ecclesiæ Romanæ regulam expendebatur; quid autem à se in hac materia præstitum sit, declarat in Epistola ad Leonem Allatium, cui scripsit, se inquisivisse in sacras Clericorum ordinationes tam Græcas quam Latinas. Inquisitionem illam, inquit, Scholastico more non instituo; id existimo hac in causa & probationibus, quas adhibeo, plane inutile: his enim argumentis cedat universa Scholastica, & illis se accommodet necesse est. Deinde addit, se in lucem edere an-
units.tr: Indeed, in the book just reviewed, Morinus shows himself most hostile to the Scholastic doctors, because they bring almost nothing to theological questions except metaphysical arguments. But he shows himself far more hostile to them in the commentaries he later published on the sacred ordinations of the Church, for from the very beginning of that work he disparages them as men unskilled and wholly ignorant of the subject they treat. Now he had begun that work at Rome, as noted above, when he attended a certain congregation of theologians in which, by order of Urban VIII, the Supreme Pontiff, the Greek Euchologion was being examined by the rule of faith of the Roman Church. What he himself accomplished in this matter he declares in a letter to Leo Allatius, to whom he wrote that he had inquired into the sacred ordinations of clerics, both Greek and Latin. I do not carry out that inquiry in the Scholastic manner, he says; I judge that in this cause, and with the proofs I use, it is completely useless. For all Scholastic theology must yield to these arguments, and it must accommodate itself to them. Then he adds that he is bringing into the light the most an-

units.la: {r} Edit, Paris. infol. Anno 1653. tiquissimos ordinandorum Clericorum ritus Latinos, quorum nonnulli è Codicibus mille annorum & nongentorum ætatem superantibus, multi octingentorum; Græcos septem, qui tamen antiquissimis Latinis ætate sint inferiores, quorum primus ac vetustissimus è Codice Barberino exscriptus fuerat, secundum habuerat ex Monasterio Cryptæ Ferratensis, tertium & quartum è Bibliotheca Vaticana: & animadverit, non omnes in illis ordinationes repræsentari, sed præcipuas tantum; quintum è Codice Sancti Andreæ Vallensis exscriptum fuisse testatur; sextum è Bibliotheca Regia; septimum denique, qui recentior est & omnium amplissimus, ad eum miserat ipsemet Leo Allatius, quæ omnia à Morino Latino sermone donata sunt, & variis Annotationibus illustrata: Ex horum, inqvit, {s} comparatione manifestum est, eodem plane modo ordinationes sacras apud utramque gentem antiquitus factas esse, & quæ nonnulli Scholastici opinantur
units.tr: {r} Paris edition, folio, 1653. tiquissimos ordaining rites of Latin clerics, some of which come from codices more than 1,900 years old, many from codices of 800 years; seven Greek ones, which, however, are younger in age than the most ancient Latin ones. Of these, the first and oldest was copied from the Barberini Codex; the second he had from the Monastery of the Crypt of Grottaferrata; the third and fourth came from the Vatican Library. He observes that not all the ordinations are represented in them, but only the principal ones. He testifies that the fifth was copied from the Codex of St Andrew of Vallombrosa, and the sixth from the Royal Library. The seventh, which is more recent and the fullest of all, Leo Allatius himself had sent to him. Morinus gave all of these in Latin and illustrated them with various annotations. From a comparison of these, he says, {s} it is clear that sacred ordinations were made in exactly the same way among both peoples in antiquity, and those things which some Scholastics think are substantial

units.la: {s} In Epist. ad Leon. Allat. esse substantialia, neutram gentem olim usurpasse. Adeo verum est, illam Scholasticorum Nationem ratione furentem & superbam, quæ dudum in Ecclesia Romana principem locum obtinet rebus Theologicis plus obscuritatis attulisse & detrimenti, quàm lucis & utilitatis. His omnibus ordinationum ritibus adjungi etiam debent Syrorum tum Maronitarum tum Nestorianorum ordinationes, quas sermone Syriaco & Latino operi suo inservit Morinus. Illas describi curaverat ex Codice vetusto, qvi erat Abrahami Ecchellensis natione Maronitæ, has autem è Codice Vaticano; utrasqve in Latinum sermonem à se conversas fuisse, Morinus affirmat, adjutus forsan in hac opera Latina illarum Ordinationum Interpretatione, quæ tunc cùm Romæ degeret asservabatur in Collegio sapientiæ apud Maronitas; Ecchellensem etiam per Literas in iis, quæ non asseqvebatur, sæpius consuluit: pene omiseram Jacobitarum ordinationes, qvas etiam Syriacè & Latinè exhibet.
units.tr: {s} In his letter to Leo Allatius: were not formerly used by either people. So true is it that that Scholastic nation, reasoning madly and proud, which for long has held the chief place in theological matters in the Roman Church, has brought more obscurity and harm to theology than light and usefulness. To all these rites of ordination should also be added the ordinations of the Syrians, both Maronite and Nestorian, which Morinus includes in his work in Syriac and Latin. He had had the former copied from an old codex belonging to Abraham Ecchellensis, a Maronite by nation, and the latter from a Vatican codex. Morinus affirms that he rendered both into Latin, perhaps aided in this Latin version by the interpretation of those ordinations which, while he was living at Rome, was kept in the College of Sapience among the Maronites. He also often consulted Ecchellensis by letter on those points which he did not grasp. I had almost omitted the ordinations of the Jacobites, which he also presents in Syriac and Latin.

units.la: Deniqve opus qvoqve suum locupletavit Morinus Cophitarum seu Ægyptiorum ordinationibus, quas Athanasius Kircherus, Jesuita Clarifsimus [?], è Codice, qui Romam ex Ægypto missus fuerat ad Congregationem, de propaganda fide in Latinam Lingvam transtulerat; ne quid autem operi suo deesse videretur, his omnibus adjecit varias exercitationes, in quibus de ordinatione qualibet tam secundum Scholasticorum quàm veterum scriptorum placita disputat, simulque adnotat, quid novi in antiquos ordinationum ritus maximè in Ecclesia Occidentali invectum fuerit. Inde colliget, inquit, Morinus, immane quantum aberraverint à vero plerique, Scholastici, cùm Græcarum ordinationum & antiquæ Latinorum traditionis incuriosè definire voluerunt, quæ sint in sacris ordinationibus Apostolicæ traditionis, quæ Ecclesiasticæ Institutionis; quæ substantialia, quæ accidentalia. Ad id unum in his exercitationibus respexisse videtur Morinus, ut Doctoribus Scholasticis, quorum diversas de materia & forma Sacramentorum. uti loquuntur, opiniones usque ad nauseam refert, invidiam faceret, eorumque imperitiam palam argueret, multas interim quæstiones gravissimas & majoris momenti, quæ ad id, quod tractabat, argumentum pertinebant, silentio præternittens; eas autem potissimum se-ligit explicandas, quæ videntur magis implicatæ, & de quibus vix aliquid certi affirmari potest, adeo parum constans est de his Doctorum traditio. Interdum tamen Patrum Concilii Tridentini autoritate velut obrutus, ejusmodi quæstiones pro more suo in utramque partem versare non ausus est. Ita de Charactere locu-tus, quem Sacramentis aliquot affigunt Scholastici,hæc habet: ({t}) Assumimus,non probamus,Characterem esse atque à tribus Sacramentis in anima peculiarem imprimi. Noverat tamen Morinus,Cajetanum asserere, novam hanc esse de Charactere sententiam; Hugonem à Sancto Victore, Robertum Pullum & Magistrum sententiarum nullam illius mentionem fe-cisse;
units.tr: Finally, Morinus also enriched his work with the ordinations of the Copts, or Egyptians, which the most distinguished Jesuit Athanasius Kircher had translated into Latin from a manuscript sent from Egypt to the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith. Lest anything seem to be missing from his work, Morinus added to all of this various exercitations, in which he discusses any ordination whatever according to the opinions both of the Scholastics and of the older writers, and at the same time notes what new practices concerning the ancient rites of ordination were introduced, especially in the Western Church. From this, says Morinus, it may be gathered how enormously most of the Scholastics have gone astray from the truth, when they carelessly tried to define, from the Greek ordinations and the ancient tradition of the Latins, what in sacred ordinations belongs to apostolic tradition and what to ecclesiastical institution, what is substantial and what accidental. In these exercitations Morinus seems to have had only one aim: to make the Scholastic doctors, whose varying opinions on the matter and form of the sacraments, as they call them, he recounts to the point of nausea, objects of ill will, and to expose their ignorance openly. Meanwhile he passes over in silence many very weighty questions of greater importance that pertain to the subject he was treating, and he chose above all those to explain which seem more involved and about which hardly anything certain can be affirmed, so little consensus is there among these doctors on them. Yet sometimes, as if overwhelmed by the authority of the Fathers of the Council of Trent, he did not dare to turn such questions over on either side in his usual way. Thus, speaking of the character which the Scholastics ascribe to some sacraments, he has this: ({t}) We assume, we do not prove, that the character is something spiritual and indelible, and is impressed on the soul by three sacraments. Yet Morinus knew that Cajetan asserted this opinion about the character to be new, and that Hugh of Saint Victor, Robert Pullus and the Master of the Sentences made no mention of it at all;

units.la: {t} Exercit. 3. c. 1. cisse; Scotum quidem & Gabrielem illum admisisse, sed ea ratione, ut illum potius destruerent, quàm astruerent: sta-tim enim subjiciunt, illius existentiam neque Scripturæ Sacræ autoritate, neque Patrum testimoniis probari posse. Hæc, inquam, omnia noverat Morinus; tamen asserit, post clarissimam Concilii Tridentini definitionem, statui debere, tanquam principium primum & per se notum, Characterem esse signum spiritale & indelebile virtute Sacramenti animæ impressum. Imo addit, qualitatem esse specialem & indelebilem, quia Doctorum Ecclesiæ maxima pars in eam sententiam inclinare videtur; si autem quæramus, qui sint Doctores illi Ecclesiæ, à quibus hic totus dependet Morinus, iidem sunt, quos paulo antea velut homines imperitos, & rei, quam tractat, prorsus ignaros suggil-lavit: Ita quandoque bonus dormitat Mo-rinus. Iterum expendens quæstionem de iterandis ordinationibus, utrum scilicet aliquando possint iterari, maximè cum agitur de Hæreticis, Schismaticis, depodepositis, de gradatis & excommunica- tis, consensum Scholasticorum ab annis 400. in hac materia plurimi facit. Postquam enim Episcopos Episcopis, Concilia Conciliis, Pontifices Pontificibus, ut ipse loquitur, collisit, & eos Cadmæam pugnam depugnantes ostentavit, in retam dubia & tam incerta, in quam nullum adhuc supervenerat Ecclesiæ decretum, maluit Scholasticorum sententiæ suffragari, quàm rem in dubio relinquere. Tam multorum Doctorum concors, inquit, {u}est[?] tam diuturnus consensus nobis est in- star legis, quam dissensu nostro temerare nec volumus nec debemus. Sciebat Mori- nus, Crabrones istos, uti jam dictum est, irritandos non esse, quare hoc loco veluti tergiversatus hoc Vasquezii, quem Theologiæ Scholasticæ lumen splendidissimum appellat, pronunciatum affert. Turbam Doctorum aliquando amplecti unam opinionem absque delectu, contra quos de- inde alius doctor magnæ autoritatis opinionem aliquam mature excogitatam in Scho-
units.tr: {t} Exercit. 3. c. 1. Scotus indeed, and that Gabriel, admitted it, but in such a way that they rather destroyed it than established it; for they immediately add that its existence can be proved neither by the authority of Holy Scripture nor by the testimonies of the Fathers. All these things, I say, Morinus knew; nevertheless he asserts that, after the most clear definition of the Council of Trent, it must be laid down, as a first and self-evident principle, that the character is a spiritual and indelible sign impressed on the soul by the power of the sacrament. Indeed he adds that it is a special and indelible quality, because the greater part of the teachers of the Church seems to incline to that opinion. But if we ask who those teachers of the Church are, on whom Morinus relies entirely, they are the very men whom a little earlier he had branded as unlearned and utterly ignorant of the matter he is treating. So sometimes good Morinus nods. Again, weighing the question of repeating ordinations, namely whether they can ever be repeated, especially when the case concerns heretics, schismatics, the deposed, those of lower rank and the excommunicated, he sets great store by the consensus of the Scholastics for the last four hundred years on this matter. For after he has set bishops against bishops, councils against councils, popes against popes, as he himself puts it, and has displayed them fighting a Cadmean battle, he preferred to lend his support to the opinion of the Scholastics rather than leave the matter in doubt, in a question so doubtful and uncertain that no decree of the Church had yet come down on it. Such agreement of so many doctors, he says, and such a long-standing consensus, serves us as a law, which we neither wish nor ought to disturb by our dissent. Morinus knew that those hornets, as has already been said, should not be provoked; so here, as it were, evading the issue, he brings forward the pronouncement of Vasquez, whom he calls the most brilliant light of Scholastic theology: A crowd of doctors may at some time embrace one opinion without discrimination, and against them another doctor of great authority may afterwards introduce into the schools some opinion carefully thought out.

units.la: {u} Exert. 5. c. 8. [?]las introducere potest. Licet istud Vasqvezii pronunciatum multo æstimet, non ausus tamen est, à turba Doctorum in hoc negotio recedere; sequi malumus, inquit, quam anteire: deinde asserit, multas quæstiones primis Ecclesiæ temporibus dubias & in utramque partem diu disputatas, postea indubitatas fuisse; in cujus rei exemplum profert Concilii Tridentini Episcopos, qui longe plurimas definierunt, quæ antea in utramque partem probabiliter agitabantur. Hoc quoque in causa ordinationum iterandarum accidisse, auctor est. Scilicet quæstionem hanc dubiam olim[?], nunc & ab annis quadringentis, unanimi Doctorum consensu esse resolutam & definitam. Iterum hic dormitat Morinus, dum fidem suam è Scholæ placitis, quæ annos quadringentos non superarent, vult dependere; verùm cum Doctoribus istis umbraticis, quos gravissimè læserat, reconciliari voluit. Quare auctor fuerim, ut in toto ordinationum Libro non tam Morini verba ponderentur, quàm illius rationes: debuit enim ad vulgata Theologorum placita se accommodare, ut Cardinalis Francisci Barberini, cui opus suum consecrabat, desiderium expleret, ab eo jam monitus per Literas, ne eos imitaretur, qui in suis operibus nihil præter philautiam & innovandi studium afferunt. Mirum itaque nemini videatur, si Morinus interdum in hoc Libro Doctoribus Scholasticis plus æquo tribuat, quos tamen noverat rem Theologicam graviter non tractare ; satis enim erat, illum ab operis sui principio palam asseruisse, nulla eos fide dignos in hac materia sibi videri.
units.tr: {u} Exert. 5. c. 8. Although he values this pronouncement of Vasquez highly, he did not dare to depart from the crowd of doctors in this matter; we prefer to follow, he says, rather than to go before. Then he asserts that many questions which were doubtful in the earliest times of the Church and long disputed on either side were afterwards regarded as beyond doubt; as an example of this he cites the bishops of the Council of Trent, who defined a great many things which had previously been debated on both sides with some probability. He also declares that this happened in the matter of repeating ordinations. Namely, he says, this question, once doubtful, has now been resolved and defined, by the unanimous consent of the doctors, for four hundred years. Once more Morinus nods, while he wishes to make his faith depend on the opinions of the Schools, which have not lasted more than four hundred years; yet he wanted to be reconciled with those shadowy doctors, whom he had gravely wronged. Hence, I would advise that in the whole book on ordinations we weigh not so much Morinus's words as his reasons. For he had to accommodate himself to the commonly accepted opinions of the theologians, so as to fulfil the wish of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, to whom he dedicated his work, and who had already warned him by letter not to imitate those who in their works bring nothing but self-love and a passion for innovation. It should therefore seem no marvel to anyone if Morinus in this book sometimes grants the Scholastic doctors more than is fair, though he knew they did not handle theology seriously; for it was enough that at the very beginning of his work he had openly declared that in this matter they seemed to him worthy of no trust.

units.la: Inde jam à pluribus annis Morinus alteram exercitationum Biblicarum partem, cujus editi fuerant indices, ad calcem prioris partis promiserat ; sed variis negotiis impeditus, & aliorum Librorum editione retardatus, demum ut promissis suis se exolveret de posteriori illa parte exercitationum, quæ jam ab Anno 1637. ad umbilicum redacta fuerat, ut ipse testatur, scribens Cardinali, Francisco Barberino, in publicum edenda ferio cogitavit, Anno 1657. quid autem hac in re à se præstitum fuerit, declarat his verbis in Epistola ad eundem Cardinalem, {x} Potissimum illo opere mihi propositum fuit, quidquid unquam Judæi antiqui & recentiores, ante vel post Talmud compositum, ad hæc usque tempora in gratiam & illustrationem textus Hebrei præstiterunt, eorumdem de istius textus castigatione & dispositione diversas admodum & pugnantes sententias, varias ejusdem textus lectiones, plusquam mille locis adnotatas, aliaque id genus ex correctissimis ipsorum Biblicis Codicibus, ex ipsorum tantum archivis & Commentariis antiquis & recentioribus eruere & Christianis omnibus propalam dare conspicienda. Hinc enim luce meridiana clarius est, nihil Judæos in gratiam sui textus nunquam tentasse, quod sit ingentibus Ecclesiæ laboribus in sacri textus conservatione exantlatis comparandum, & Hæreticos, etiam nobis tacentibus, ea quæ prorsus ignorabant, in immensum temere laudasse;
units.tr: For several years now Morinus had promised, at the end of the first part, the second part of his Biblical exercitations, the indexes of which had been published; but hindered by various business, and delayed by the publication of other books, at last, to fulfil his promises, he seriously set about publishing the latter part of the exercitations, which, as he himself testifies, had already been brought to completion in 1637; he wrote to Cardinal Francesco Barberini about it. In 1657 he thought about what he had done in this matter, and he declares it in these words in a letter to the same Cardinal: The main purpose I had in that work was to bring out of the archives and ancient and more recent commentaries of the Jews alone, and to show openly to all Christians to examine, whatever the ancient and more recent Jews, both before and after the Talmud was compiled, have produced up to these times for the sake of the illustration and explanation of the Hebrew text; and likewise their very diverse and conflicting opinions on the correction and arrangement of that text, the various readings of the same text, noted in more than a thousand places, and other things of that kind taken from their most correct Biblical manuscripts. For it is clearer than the noonday sun that the Jews never attempted, for the sake of their text, anything that could be compared with the immense labours the Church has undergone in preserving the sacred text; and that the heretics, even when we are silent, have rashly praised beyond measure those things of which they were utterly ignorant;

units.la: {x} Mor. Epist. ad Card. Franc. Barb. Anno 1637. vulgatamque editionem, adversus quam furore potius quàm ratione debacchabatur, fontibus Hebraicis multo puriorem ac limpidiorem fluere. Hæc scribebat Morinus Anno 1637. Sed,
units.tr: {x} Morinus, letter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini, 1637. and that the printed edition, against which he raged rather with fury than with reason, flows far purer and clearer from Hebrew sources. Morinus wrote this in 1637. But,

units.la: Quid dignum tanto feret hic promisso, hiatu[?]?
units.tr: What worthy of so great a promise will this man bring forth from such a gaping mouth?

units.la: INGENS ille variantium Lectionum numerus, quem verbis suis adeo exaggerat Morinus, ad paucissimas easque nullius fere momenti revocari potest, quæque jam ab ipsismet Judæis sub nomine diversarum Lectionum Orientalium & Occidentalium Judæorum, annotatæ sunt ad calcem Bibliorum Venetorum, unde à Drusio postea exscriptæ; & ab ipso etiam Buxtorfio, Codicis Hebraici acerrimo defensore, variantes omnes illæ lectiones Bibliorum suorum editioni adjectæ sunt: similiter Judæi alia diversarum lectionum exempla, quæ vulgo appellantur Keri & Cetib, quas etiam refert Morinus, ad oram Bibliorum suorum retulerunt, quas nec diffitentur Protestantes, quibus hic invidiam facere conatur Morinus: longe satius erat, novas & ineditas lectiones ex vetustis Bi-bliorum Codicibus producere, quàm eas, quæ jam in omnium manibus versabantur, iterum in lucem edere.
units.tr: That huge number of variant readings, which Morinus so greatly magnifies in his words, can be reduced to very few, and those of almost no importance. These were already noted by the Jews themselves, under the name of various readings of the Eastern and Western Jews, at the foot of the Venice Bible, and were afterwards copied from there by Drusius; and by Buxtorf himself, the most zealous defender of the Hebrew manuscript, all those variant readings were added to his own edition of the Bible. Likewise the Jews also recorded in the margins of their Bibles the other examples of various readings commonly called Keri and Cetib, which Morinus also mentions, and which the Protestants do not deny; and it is on these that Morinus here tries to bring odium upon them. It would have been far better to produce new and unpublished readings from ancient Bible manuscripts than to bring out again into the light those which were already in everyone's hands.

units.la: Magnam quidem opus illud Morini præfert eruditionem, in eoq; se ostendit, in libris Judæorum diu multumque volutatum; sed pars maxima ejusmodi Literaturæ ad rem, quam sibi proposuit, nihil aut parum conferre videtur; totus enim est, ut demonstret, nullum apud Judæos esse antiquæ Historiæ monumentum, sed omnia esse nova plenaq; Fabularum, Talmud utrumque, Chaldaicas Onkelosi ac Jonathanis paraphrases, Medrascim sive commentarios mysticos in legem & in quinq; Meguillot seu volumina, opera esse longe recentiora, quàm vulgo existiment Judæi; verùm quid ex his omnibus adversus Codicis Hæbrai integritatem confici possit, minimè percipio: non enim minus inter Ecclesiæ Orientalis & Occidentalis Scriptores, quàm apud Judæos, reperiuntur libri supposititii[?], qui magnam præ se ferant antiquitatem; sunt & alii etiam anilibus Fabularum Commentis referti; quis autem paulo cordatior inde sumpserit argumenta adversus Græcos & Latinos Bibliorum Codices? deinde in pluribus etiam, quæ animo Judæis infensiore Morinus asseruit, graviter hallucinatus est, quibus tamen recensendis, ne sim longus, supersedeo. Ea quidem, quæ in eodem Libro de Masora & illius autoribus, de punctorum vocalium apud Judæos novitate, ac de illorum Grammaticis erudite animadvertit, alicujus momenti esse videntur, nec à proposito suo ita aliena; tamen nondum illud, quod sibi in hoc opere proposuisse testatur in Epistola, quam scripsit ad Cardinalem Franciscum Barberinum, omnino conficiunt: ij enim omnes, qui eruditionis habent aliquid ac judicii, cum Catholici tum Protestantes, eadem atq; ille de hoc argumento sentiunt; unt; at non ideo Codices Hebræos accusant. Egregie quidem refellir Morinus in hac postrema operis sui parte Buxdorfium, Muisium, Flavigium & alios, nonnullos, qui Judæorum aliquot superstitiosiorum placitis nimium adhærentes, non satis caute hodiernam Codicis Hebraici lectionem adversus illum, usque ad minimos apices asserverunt. Inde enim factum est, ut illis ipsis Morinus insultaverit gloriabundus, quasi victoriam consecutus, profligatis Hebraistarum & Protestantium copiis seu Hæreticorum, ut ipse loquitur, qui ea, quæ prorsus ignorabant, in immensum laudaverant, ut adversus vulgatam editionem furore potius, quàm ratione debaccharentur; è classe tamen illorum Protestantium erant Drusius, Scaliger, Erpenius, Salmasius, Hugo Grotius, Capellus, Waltonus & alii bene multi, quibus nec linguæ Hebræ cognitio, nec judicium defuit, qui tamen eadem atque Morinus de hodierno Judæorum Exemplari hac in parte sentiunt: quin nec ab ea opinione abhorruerunt Lutherus, Calvinus, & Zvinglius,Secta-rum,quæ nomenReformatarum sibi assu-munt,principes. Adeoque non erat,cur Morinus victoriam abHæreticis reportatam superbe & verbis sesquipedalibus jactaret; non aliam sortem hac in re Lingua Hebræa nancisci potuit, quàm Arabica,Chaldæa & Syriaca : neque in vitiumCodicumHebræorum id trahi potest, quod illis veluti naturale est ac ingenitum,atque etiam commune cum libris Arabicis,Chaldæis, & Syriacis,quippe in illos omnes postea Grammatici , uti norunt ejusmodi Lingvarum periti,punctavocalia invexère, ut illorum Lectio facilior esset ac paratior, etsi initio vocales quoque suas, sicut & cæterae Lingvæ congenitas habuerint , nimirum Aleph, Vau, & Jod & alias, quæ peti possunt ex Beati Hieronymi Libris.
units.tr: Morinus's work certainly displays great learning, and in it he shows that he has long and widely pored over the books of the Jews. But most of this sort of scholarship seems to contribute little or nothing to the matter he set himself. His whole aim is to demonstrate that the Jews possess no monument of ancient history, and that everything is recent and full of fables: both Talmuds, the Chaldee paraphrases of Onkelos and Jonathan, and the Midrashim, or mystical commentaries on the Law and on the five Megillot or volumes, are far more recent works than the Jews commonly suppose. But what can be inferred from all this against the integrity of the Hebrew text, I do not in the least perceive. For spurious books with a great show of antiquity are found no less among the writers of the Eastern and Western Church than among the Jews, and there are others crammed with silly fabulous inventions. Yet what fairly sensible person would draw from this arguments against the Greek and Latin codices of the Bible? Moreover, in many points which Morinus asserted with a mind more hostile to the Jews, he has gravely erred, but I will pass these over rather than list them, lest I grow tedious. Those things which in the same book he learnedly remarks concerning the Masora and its authors, the novelty of the vowel points among the Jews, and their grammarians, seem to be of some weight and not so far from his purpose. Yet they do not at all accomplish what he states in his letter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini that he meant to accomplish in this work. For all those who have some learning and judgement, both Catholic and Protestant, think about this subject just as he does, and yet they do not on that account accuse the Hebrew codices. Morinus refutes admirably, in this last part of his work, Buxtorf, Muis, Flavigny and others, who, clinging too closely to the opinions of certain more superstitious Jews, asserted the present Hebrew text, down to the smallest apices, too incautiously against him. For this reason Morinus exulted over these very men as if he had won a victory, the forces of the Hebraists and Protestants (or heretics, as he himself calls them) having been routed, men who had praised beyond measure things they utterly did not know, so that they raged against the Vulgate edition with fury rather than reason. Yet among those Protestants were Drusius, Scaliger, Erpenius, Salmasius, Hugo Grotius, Capellus, Walton and many others, who lacked neither knowledge of the Hebrew tongue nor judgement, and who nonetheless think about the present Jewish text in this respect exactly as Morinus does. Indeed Luther, Calvin and Zwingli, the leaders of the sects that call themselves Reformed, did not shrink from this opinion either. And so there was no reason for Morinus to boast haughtily, and in high-sounding words, of a victory won against heretics. The Hebrew language could not have obtained any other lot in this matter than Arabic, Chaldee and Syriac did. Nor can it be charged as a fault against the Hebrew codices that this feature is, as it were, natural and innate to them, and common also to Arabic, Chaldean and Syriac books. For later grammarians, as those skilled in such languages know, introduced vowel points into all of them so that reading them would be easier and quicker. Yet at first they too had their own vowels, inherent in the language, namely Aleph, Vau, Yod and others, which can be sought in the books of Saint Jerome.

units.la: Didici à viris probis & Morini amicis[?],illum non semel suscepti consilii de edendis in publicum exercitationibus Biblicis pœnituisse, non solum quòd in hoc studii genere, quod illi minus placebat, nimium temporis consumpsisset, sed etiam quod dum illas aggressus fuit, rem criticam non satis calleret: verum quia apud Berullistas Bibliothecam invenererat Judaeorum Libris instructissimam, & haec studia tunc Parisiis ob Bibliorum Polyglottorum Clarissimi Domini le Jay editionem celebrabantur, non potuit, quin ad illa animum suum applicaret, quae tamen, ut scribit, ad Cardinalem Barberinum, Consiliis suis su-ére tantum accessoria & παρέργα[?]; ista enim, inquit, {y}materies, quae antiquam Ecclesiae vel disciplinam vel Historiam spectat, meam esse cupio, huic cognoscendae ab adolescentia tempus otiumque meum potissimum dicavi. Utinam Morinus in tractanda Ecclesiae disciplina & Historia omnem operam suam collocasset, neque illi agendum fuisset cum Tayloris, Booti-is, Hottingeris, Muisiis, Flavigniis & aliis ejusmodi hominibus, qui illius, ut erat paulo iracundior ac difficilior, bilem commoverant: Habuεremus enim maxi-mam
units.tr: I learned from upright men who were friends of Morinus that he more than once repented of his plan to publish biblical exercises. This was not only because he had spent too much time on this kind of study, which pleased him less, but also because when he undertook them he was not sufficiently skilled in textual criticism. Yet because he had found in the library of the Berulle fathers a collection very well stocked with Jewish books, and because these studies were then being cultivated at Paris on account of the edition of the Polyglot Bible of the most illustrious Monsieur Le Jay, he could not help applying his mind to them. Yet, as he writes to Cardinal Barberini, these were only accessory and by-works to his plans (παρέργα); for, he says, {y} the subject which concerns the ancient discipline or history of the Church is what I wish to be mine; to learning this I have devoted my time and leisure from youth. Would that Morinus had devoted all his effort to treating the discipline and history of the Church, and had not had to deal with Taylor, Boot, Hottinger, Muis, Flavigny and other men of that kind, who stirred his bile, for he was somewhat too irascible and difficult. For we would have had the greatest

units.la: {y} Mor. in Epist. ad C. Fr. Barb, imam Theologiæ partem ab eo gravissimè tractatam, & non ex more Scholasticorum, qvi temere & sine judicio de rebus magni ponderis sententiam ferunt, nihilqve edunt in Theologiam præter sophismata & argutias, qvæ viros doctos ad risum & contemptum incitent: Hacte-nus de iis, qvæ Morinus publici juris fecit, judicium tulimns.
units.tr: {y} Morinus, in his letter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini: the deepest part of theology, handled by him very gravely, and not in the manner of the Scholastics, who rashly and without judgement pronounce opinions on matters of great weight and produce nothing for theology but sophisms and quibbles, which move learned men to laughter and contempt. Thus far we have passed judgement on those things which Morinus made public.

units.la: VERUM liqvet ex illius Epistolis, complures alios in lucem edere libros sibi propositum fuisse, & cùm hæc scribebam, accepi indicem opusculorum qvorundam Morini, qvæ nondum edita sunt; & qvia index ille {z} difficilè reperitur, huc integrum referre non pigebit.
units.tr: INDEED it is clear from his letters that he intended several other books to be brought to light. While I was writing these things I received a list of some small works of Morinus that have not yet been published, and since that list {z} is hard to find, it will not be tedious to give it here in full.

units.la: Opusculorum Joannis Morini, Blesensis, Oratorii Presbyteri Index.
units.tr: Index of the Works of John Morin of Blois, Presbyter of the Oratory.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: DE Basilicis Christianorum singulisque earum partibus: opus exquisita eruditione refertum capitibus 47. pagi-nisque 335. contentum.
units.tr: Concerning the basilicas of the Christians and each of their parts: a work full of exquisite learning, comprising 47 chapters and 335 pages.

units.la: {z} Index opusc. posthum. Mor. Edit, Anno 1675.
units.tr: {z} Index of the posthumous works of Morin, edition of 1675.

units.la: 2. De iisdem Basilicis alterum brevius opusculum centum fere paginarum, aliqua continens, quae in priori desiderantur, puta de oblatione olim in Basilicis fieri solita.
units.tr: 2. A second, shorter work on the same basilicas, of about a hundred pages, containing some things missing from the first, for example on the offering formerly made in the basilicas.

units.la: 3. De Graecorum Ecclesiis ad Leonem Allatium Epistola prolixa cum earumdem delineatione.
units.tr: 3. A lengthy letter to Leo Allatius on the churches of the Greeks, with a drawing of them.

units.la: 4. Altera de materia eadem Epistola, quam secutum est Allatii responsum, in Lucem nuper editum à R.P. Richardo Simone nostrae Congregationis Presbytero.
units.tr: 4. Another letter on the same subject, which was followed by Allatius's reply, recently published by the Reverend Father Richard Simon, a presbyter of our Congregation.

units.la: 5. De Paschate, seu de vetustissimis [?] Christianorum Paschalis exercitatio Ec-clesiastica, quam olim à se edendam promiserat Morinus ipse in Praefatione Exertitationum Ecclesiasticarum.
units.tr: 5. On Easter, or the most ancient Paschal observance of the Christians [?], an ecclesiastical exercise, which Morin himself had promised in the preface to his Ecclesiastical Exercitations that he would publish.

units.la: 6. De Sacramento Confirmationis dissertatio, in qua praesertim celebres de ejus materia & Ministro quaestiones ventilantur.
units.tr: 6. A dissertation on the Sacrament of Confirmation, in which the well-known questions about its matter and its minister are especially debated.

units.la: 7. De Disciplina à Patribus observata in expiatione Catechumenorum, & eorum ad Baptismi susceptionem praeparatione, tractatus ducentarum fere paginarum.
units.tr: 7. On the discipline observed by the Fathers in the expiation of catechumens and their preparation for receiving baptism, a treatise of nearly two hundred pages.

units.la: 8. Christiani Lupi Augustiniani, Epistola ad Joannem Morinum de aliquot circa antiquam pœnitentiæ administrati-onem difficultatibus.
units.tr: 8. Christian Lupus, Augustinian: a letter to John Morin on some difficulties concerning the ancient administration of penance.

units.la: 9. Ad eundem Morini Epistolica re-sponsio.
units.tr: 9. Morin's epistolary reply to the same.

units.la: 10. Consultatio, an Canonici jura Episcopalia & exemptionem à Jurisdicti-one Episcoporum, præscriptiones possint ac-quirere.
units.tr: 10. A consultation on whether canons can acquire episcopal rights and exemption from the jurisdiction of bishops by prescription.

units.la: 11. Joannis Morini ad Bartholdum Nihusium Epistola de loco Tertuliani, de Ligno Crucis scribentis cap. 12. lib. ad Na-tiones & de aliis.
units.tr: 11. John Morin's letter to Bartholdus Nihusius on the passage of Tertullian, who writes in chapter 12 of the book To the Nations about the Wood of the Cross, and on other matters.

units.la: 12. Epistola altera de explicatione vo-cis confirmari in ordine Romano de Com-municantibus Christi Sanguini agente.
units.tr: 12. A second letter on the explanation of the word "confirmari" in the Roman Order, where it treats of those communicating of Christ's blood.

units.la: 13. Epistola tertia de autoritate Libri Maimonidæ & eorum, quos sequitur, & an Pontifex veteris Testamenti vel solus vel cum concilio sacerdotum inferior esset synedrio magno ejusque Principe.
units.tr: 13. A third letter on the authority of the book of Maimonides and of those whom he follows, and on whether the high priest of the Old Testament, either alone or with the council of priests, was inferior to the Great Sanhedrin and its prince.

units.la: 14. Consultation si une terre donnée à ferme à longues années perd l' exemption des decimes.
units.tr: 14. A consultation on whether land leased for many years loses its exemption from tithes.

units.la: 15. Animadversiones in scriptum quoddam Ms. de translatione Episcopi CarnuCarnutensis ad Archiepiscopatum Remensem.
units.tr: 15. Animadversions on a certain manuscript writing concerning the translation of the Bishop of Chartres to the Archbishopric of Reims.

units.la: 16. Discours sur le nombre & sur la qualitè des fautes remarquées dans le texte Hebreu & Caldaique de la grande bible de Monsieur le Jay.
units.tr: 16. Discourse on the number and quality of the errors noted in the Hebrew and Chaldee text of Monsieur Le Jay's great Bible.

units.la: 17. Avis à Monsieur de Chartres sur le mesme sujet sur la consultation faite parordre de Monsieur le Cardinal de Richelieu.
units.tr: 17. Advice to Monsieur de Chartres on the same subject, concerning the consultation made by order of Monsieur the Cardinal de Richelieu.

units.la: 18. Scriptum Joannis Morini de Dictionario Philippi Aquintais[?] vocum Hebraicarum Chaldaicarum Talmudicarum.
units.tr: 18. Morin's writing on the dictionary of Philip Aquinas [?] of Hebrew, Chaldee and Talmudic words.

units.la: His omnibus adjungi possent complures aliæ Epistolæ , quas mihi communicavit vir pietate & eruditione conspicuus Dionysius Amelotus, Congregationis Oratorii Presbyter , & ex quibus non pauca in hanc Morini vitam transtuli ; sed juvat etiam, mox recensita opuscula illustrare : Haud dubiè Morinus in animo habuerat tractatum de Basilicis & earum partibus edere ad Calcem Libri sui de ordinationibus , ut ipsemet testatur in Epistola ad Cardinalem Franciscum Barberinum in qua etiam opusculi illius rationem explicat his verbis{a}: Existimabā necessarium, hu-ic operi (de ordinationibus) nonnulla inferere de Ecclesiarum antiquarum figura & forma interiori, ut commodius Episcopi inSancto Sanctorū Tribunal, Presbyterorū & Diaconorum ad altare aut circū ædes, aliorum inferiorum Ministrorum in Choro seu Sanctuario Confessus, fidelium tam virorum quam mulierum extra chorum distincti ordines, variaqve pœnitentium post ambonem stationes explicarentur. Cum autem interior illa figura & structura non parum illustrari possit templi Hierosolymitani, quale erat Jesu Christi & Apostolorum secuto, comparatione; multa enim ad illius exemplar instituerunt primi Ecclesiæ fundatores, nonnulla etiam de illius delineatione cogitaveram : verum quod pauculis Capitulis me posse conficere sperabam, fœcunditate materiæ in molem excrevit, ideo separato libello hæc edere constitui. Hujus quoque opusculi de
units.tr: Several other letters could be added to all these, which were communicated to me by Dionysius Amelot, a man distinguished for piety and learning, presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, and from which I have transferred not a few into this Life of Morin. But it is also worth illustrating the works just listed. Morin had doubtless intended to publish a treatise on the basilicas and their parts at the end of his book on ordinations, as he himself attests in his letter to Cardinal Francesco Barberini, in which he also explains the plan of that work in these words: I thought it necessary to insert into this work (on ordinations) some remarks on the inner figure and form of the ancient churches, so that the position of the bishop in the Holy of Holies, the tribunal, of the presbyters and deacons around the altar or the apse, of the other lesser ministers in the choir or sanctuary, the separate ranks of the faithful, men and women alike, outside the choir, and the various stations of penitents behind the ambo, might be explained more conveniently. Since that interior figure and structure can be not a little illuminated by comparison with the Temple of Jerusalem, such as it was in the time of Jesus Christ and the Apostles, for the first founders of the Church established many things after its pattern, and I had also thought about some things concerning its plan; but what I hoped I could complete in a few chapters grew into a bulk through the abundance of its material, so I resolved to publish these things in a separate little book. Of this little work too, concerning

units.la: {a} Mor. Epist, ad Card, Fr. Barb. Basilicis meminit in aliis Epistolis Morinus; scripsit enim Lucæ Holstenio (b), hac in re non parum adjutum fuisse Leonis Allatii monitis & lucubratiunculis aliquot, in iis potissimum, quæ hodiernas Græcorum Ecclesias spectant. De Pa-schatis autem scripsit nonnulla Morinus, tam ex Judæorum quàm Christianorum sententia, ad Godofridum Vendelinum, de quo jam supra; quibus autem rationibus ad scribendum de Sacramento Confirmationis adductus fuerit, ex hisce[?] Epistolis cognoscere non potui; liceat tamē suspicari, jā inde ab eo tempore, quo Romæ commorabatur, de illa scriptione cogitasse: nam video, opusculum Lucæ Holstenii de hoc argumento post ejus obitum à Cardinale Francisco Barberino Romæ editum fuisse, in quo Holstenius Ecclesiæ Orientalis ritus, quo in hoc negotio contrarii erant Ecclesiæ occidentalis moribus, strenuè vindicat. Simulq; Theologorum Scholasticorum imperitiam & disputandi de rebus omnibus
units.tr: {a} Morin's letter to Card. Fr. Barb. Morin mentions the basilicas in other letters too; for he wrote to Lucas Holstenius that in this matter he had been not a little helped by the advice and some short essays of Leo Allatius, especially those concerning the present churches of the Greeks. Morin also wrote several things on the Passovers, both from the Jewish and from the Christian point of view, to Gottfried Wendelin, of whom above. By what reasons he was led to write on the Sacrament of Confirmation I could not learn from these letters; yet I may suspect that from the time he was living in Rome he had been thinking of that writing. For I see that the little work of Lucas Holstenius on this subject was published at Rome by Cardinal Francesco Barberini after Holstenius's death, in which Holstenius vigorously defends the rites of the Eastern Church, which in this matter were contrary to the customs of the Western Church. At the same time he sharply censures the inexperience of the Scholastic theologians and their itch to dispute about all things.

units.la: (b) Mor, Epist, ad Luc, Holst. pruriginem vehementer coarguit ; quibus etiam accedit, gravissimas tunc temporis de Sacramento confirmationis disputationes in Gallia extitisse inter Petrum Aurelium seu Sancyranum, & Sirmondum Jesuitam doctissimum; fortan ægretulit Morinus, Aurelii sententiam, cui nihil inerat probabilitatis, ab omnibus fere Theologis approbari: Sirmondum vero, qui argumentum illud diligenter tractaverat, partes executus Theologi rei Criticæ peritissimi a plerisque despectum fuisse. Tractatus autem ille, cui titulus; de disciplina à Patribus[?] observata inexpiatione catechumenorum, primam ejus commentariorum de Sacramento pœnitentiæ partem occupare debebat, ut etiam ex Bibliopola didici, qui illum à Morino acceperat cum reliquo opere, ut ederetur; sed à Theologis Parisiensibus rejectus fuit, qui Morino opposuerunt tractatu isto receptam Ecclesiæ traditionem de Sacramento pœnitentiæ; atque in primis Doctrinam Confessionis Sacramentalis penitus everti. Morinum à Nihusio consultum fuisse de voce confirmari in ordine Romano ubi agitur de Communicantibus Christi sangvini, patet ex ejusdē Nihusii ad illū Epistola. Liber Maimonidæ, de cujus autoritate inqvisivit Morinus, videtur esse ille, qvi inscribitur jad ha zaca [?] seu manus fortis, & est absolutissimum Doctrinæ Talmudicæ compendium, qvod hodie māgni fit à Judæis ; etsi initio Doctrina Judæi illius á sectæ suæ magistris severius reprehensa fuerit, qvod veluti paternarum traditionum desertor Philosophiæ Peripaticæ Sophismata in Judaicam Religionem invexisset, maximè in opere cui nomen fecit, more nevo-kim seu Doctor perplexorum. Qvid à Morino observatum fuerit de erroribus jam annotatis in contextu Hebræo & Chaldæo Polyglottorum Parisiensium, nescio ; at notum est omnibus, Flavignium Doctorem Sorbonicum & Regium in Academia Parisiensi Linguæ Hebrææ profesorem gravissime ea de re conquestum fuisse, magnaqve disidia inter eos, qvi huic editioni præerant, coorta,qvæ in causa fuerunt, ut hodie nihil omnino habeamus prolegomenôn & annotationum, qvæ ad calcem ingentis illius operis adjiciendæ erant; demum Philippus Aqvinas Gallicè d' Aqvin, de cujus Dictionario Hebraeo-Rabbinico extat Morini dissertatio manuscripta, fuerat ante è Judæorum secta qvi postqvam Ecclesiæ nomen dedit, cum Berullo & Morino,aliisqve Oratorii Parisiensis Presbyteris amicitia conjunctus fuit, verùm qvia erat Gramatices Hebraeæ ignarus, ut à viris fide dignis accepi, & Lingvam Hebraeam pro more Judæorum usu potius didicerat, qvàm ex Grammaticorum præceptionibus, Morini etiam animum ab ejusmodi præceptionibus avertit; ita ut Judæorum Libros, qvi vulgo absqve punctorum vocalium notis exarantur, nunqvam emendatè legere sciverit Morinus, qvem tamen in evolvendis & explicandis Rabbinorum operibus non parum adjuvit ille Aqvinas; similiter & alius Judæus, Bolonia oriundus, qvi studio Masorae se applicuerat, contra Judæorum fere omnium consvetudinem, bene multa de Maforetharum arte ei indicavit, quæ videbantur abstrusissima & à paucissimis etiam Judæis intellecta, sed non est, cur diutius his detinear, cum Indicis illius opuscula edenda sint in lucem à Presbyteris Congregationis Oratorii Parisiensis: qvi Catalogum illum publici juris secerunt. Miratus sum profecto, & ab his adjunctas non fuisse huic Indici Epistolas, qvas mihi benignè communicavit ejusdem Societatis Presbyter Clarissimus Amelotut; sed ut audio, in varias partes scissi sunt Congregationis illius homines, ibiqve reperitur discordia trà santi offici è messi. His etiam adjici potuissent varia constitutionum genera ad qvas respondisse fertur Morinus, multaqve illarum exemplaria penes Amelorum extant & in musæo illius asservantur; ferunt etiam, Morinum scripsisse de Baptismo & de Matrimonio, virqve è primariis illius Congregationis certiorem me fecit, se vidisse intra manus ejusdem Morini Librum de Baptismo ex omni parte absolutum, de quo tamen in Indice mox allato nulla fit mentio.
units.tr: (b) Morin's letter to Lucas Holstenius. He vehemently rebukes that itch. To this may be added that there were very serious disputes in France at that time about the Sacrament of Confirmation between Peter Aurelius, or Sancyranus, and Sirmond, the very learned Jesuit. Perhaps Morin was displeased that the opinion of Aurelius, which had no probability in it, was approved by almost all theologians, while Sirmond, who had treated the subject diligently and taken up its cause, was despised by most, although he was a theologian most skilled in critical matters. That treatise, entitled "On the discipline observed by the Fathers in the expiation of catechumens", ought to have occupied the first part of his commentaries on the Sacrament of Penance, as I also learned from the bookseller who received it from Morin along with the rest of the work to be published. But it was rejected by the Parisian theologians, who opposed to Morin in that treatise the received tradition of the Church on the Sacrament of Penance, and above all overturned the doctrine of sacramental confession. That Morin was consulted by Nihusius on the word "confirmari" in the Roman Order, where it deals with those communicating of Christ's blood, is clear from Nihusius's letter to him. The book of Maimonides, on whose authority Morin inquired, seems to be the one entitled Yad ha-chazaka, or "strong hand", which is a most complete compendium of Talmudic doctrine and is greatly esteemed by the Jews today; although at first that Jewish author was rather severely criticised by the masters of his sect, because, as a deserter of the paternal traditions, he had introduced the sophisms of Peripatetic philosophy into the Jewish religion, especially in the work he called more nevokim, or Guide of the Perplexed. What Morin observed about the errors already noted in the Hebrew and Chaldee text of the Parisian Polyglots I do not know; but it is known to everyone that Flavigny, Doctor of the Sorbonne and royal professor of Hebrew in the University of Paris, complained very gravely about this matter, and that great quarrels arose among those who presided over that edition, which caused us today to have absolutely none of the prolegomena and notes that were to be added at the end of that huge work. Finally, Philip Aquinas, in French d'Aquin, of whose Hebrew-Rabbinic dictionary Morin's manuscript dissertation survives, had earlier belonged to the Jewish sect; after he joined the Church, he was bound in friendship with Bérulle and Morin and other presbyters of the Paris Oratory. But because, as I have learned from trustworthy men, he was ignorant of Hebrew grammar, and had learned the Hebrew language by the practice of the Jews rather than from the rules of the grammarians, he also turned Morin's mind away from such rules. So Morin never learned to read correctly the Jewish books that are commonly printed without the vowel points, although Aquinas did help him not a little in unfolding and explaining the works of the rabbis. Similarly another Jew, a native of Bologna, who had devoted himself to the study of the Masorah, contrary to the custom of almost all Jews, pointed out to him many things about the art of the Masoretes that seemed most abstruse and were understood by very few Jews. But there is no need to detain myself longer with these matters, since the works of that Index are to be brought out by the presbyters of the Paris Oratory Congregation, who made that catalogue public. I was indeed surprised that the letters kindly communicated to me by the most distinguished presbyter of the same society, Amelot, were not added to this Index; but, as I hear, the men of that Congregation have been split into various factions, and there is discord there trà santi offici è messi. To these might also be added the various kinds of constitutions to which Morin is said to have responded, and many copies of them survive with Amelot and are kept in his museum. They also say that Morin wrote on Baptism and on Matrimony; and a man of the first rank in that Congregation informed me that he had seen in the hands of this same Morin a book on Baptism, complete in every part, although no mention of it is made at all in the Index just cited.

units.la: EXTAT & alius Liber à Morino editus, quem tamen antea cum aliis ejusdem operibus recensere nolui, quia pauciffimis cognitus, & adhuc paucioribus visus, omniaqve illius exemplaria, ne in publicum emitterentur, penes se reservavit; scripserat scilicet, ut & olim Joannes Mariana, Jesuita celeberrimus, de Societatis suae morbis, illa omnia, quae in ea tolerari non posse indicabat, acerrime reprehendens: at quia notat in hoc Libello Morinus viros Congregationis suae Clarissimos, parco illorum nominibus, ne Societatis, quae aetate nostra non ita male audit, turpitudinem imprudens videar revelare. Invidebant potissimum Francisco Borgoneo, tertio illius Congregationis praeposito Generali, quem in isto opere contendit omnia pro arbitratu suo regere, spretis Ecclesiae legibus, atque inprimis Concilii Tridentini decretis; artes illius & fraudes miris verbis exaggerat, & ut loqui amat, ses fourbes & contraventions estranges contre les Canons & l'usage universel de l'eglise: Verùm simplicioris videtur ingenii fuisse Morinus, qui nesciverit, fraudem potissimùm intra Monasteriorum & sodalitatum domos residere, cujus ef-figiem non malè dudum repræsentavit nugator ille Ariostus his verbis: {c}
units.tr: There is also another book published by Morinus, which I did not want to list earlier with his other works, because it is known to very few, seen by even fewer, and he kept all its copies to himself so that they would not be put before the public. As the famous Jesuit Juan de Mariana once did about the diseases of his own Society, Morinus wrote about the faults of his Congregation, sharply condemning everything he judged intolerable in it. But since in this little book Morinus marks out the most distinguished men of his Congregation, I spare their names, so that I do not seem to reveal, unwisely, the shameful side of the Society, which in our own age does not have such a bad reputation. He especially resented Francis Bourgoin, the third Superior General of that Congregation, whom in this work he accuses of ruling everything according to his own will, scorning the laws of the Church, and above all the decrees of the Council of Trent. He magnifies Bourgoin's arts and frauds in striking words and, as he loves to say, ses fourbes & contraventions estranges contre les Canons & l'usage universel de l'eglise: his tricks and strange contraventions against the Canons and the universal practice of the Church. But Morinus seems to have been of rather simple mind, not knowing that fraud resides chiefly within the houses of monasteries and fraternities. The trifler Ariosto long ago portrayed its likeness well in these words: {c}

units.la: Havea piacevol, viso [?] habito honesto, Hin' umil volger d' occhi, un andar grave, In parlar sì benigno, è sì modesto, Che parea Gabriel, che dicesse, ave, Eva brutta, è diforme in tutto il resto; Mà nascondea queste fatte[?]zze prave Con lungo habito, è largo, & sotto quello Attossicato havea sempre il Coltello.
units.tr: She had a pleasing face and an honest bearing, a humble lowering of the eyes, a grave walk, a speech so kind and modest that she seemed Gabriel saying "Ave"; yet Eve was ugly and misshapen in all the rest. But she hid these wicked defects under a long, wide habit, and beneath it she always kept a poisoned knife.

units.la: Non debebat profectò Morinus homines liberos & nullius voti obligatione obstrictos, Romanæ curiæ legibus subjicere, cùm ipsi palàm profiteantur, se non esse monachos neque Religiosos. In hoc quoque à Borgoneo gravissimè erratum
units.tr: Morinus certainly ought not to have subjected free men, bound by no vow, to the laws of the Roman curia, since they openly profess that they are neither monks nor religious. In this too Bourgoin had gravely erred

units.la: {c} Cant. 14. erratum fuerat,qui primus dignitatis suæ præpositi Generalis confirmationem per literas quaesierat à summo Pontifice, à quo tamen Berullistæ minimè dependeant ex institutionis suæ regulis, sed ab Episcopis & Ecclesiarum rectoribus locorum, in quibus commorantur,uti testatus est ipsemet institutor Berullus in Declaratione sua ad senatum Normaniæ anno 1616, verba declarationis istius, quia Episcopis & Ecclesiarum rectoribus non cognita fuisse videntur, imò nec plerisque Oratorianis, proferre non crit intempestivum. {d} Ils declarent[?] premierement à la Cour, qu'ils ne sont point Religieux, mais seulement prestres associez ensemble, suivant la Coutume ancienne & premiere institution sous l'obeissance volontaire d'un superieur, qui est Monsieur de Berulle; secondement ils assurent la cour, qu'ils n'ont point d'exemption de l'Ordinaire, & qu'ils n'en pretendent aucune:
units.tr: {c} Cant. 14. erratum fuerat, who was the first to seek, by letter from the supreme Pontiff, confirmation of his dignity as Superior General. Yet the Berullians by the rules of their institution do not depend on the Pope at all, but on the bishops and rectors of the churches in the places where they live, as the founder Bérulle himself attested in his Declaration to the Parliament of Normandy in the year 1616. It will not be out of place to set out the words of that declaration, since they seem to be unknown to bishops and church rectors, and indeed to most Oratorians as well. They declare first to the Court that they are not religious, but only priests associated together, according to the ancient custom and first institution, under the voluntary obedience of a superior, who is Monsieur de Bérulle; secondly, they assure the Court that they have no exemption from the Ordinary, and claim none:

units.la: {d} Declaration des pp. de l'Oratorie de Paris au Parlement de Norm. à l'occasion d'un procez avec les Curés de Rouen, qui s'opposerent à leur reception, Anno 1616[?], aucune: mais ils sont immediatement dependans des Evéques des lieux là, où la Congregation est establie. Ce qui fera juger par leur soumission aux prelats, ne travaillant que par eux, que sous eux & pour eux, & par consequent ils ne sont extraordinaires, ains en l'ordre de la Hierarchie de l'eglise, accomplissans tout ce que les Curez requereront d'eux, comme confesser, administrer les saintes sacremens aux paroisses sous eux, & par leur autorité, & non autrement comme les Chappelains de leurs paroisses. Hæc Oratorii Congregatio quantum mutata[?] es ab illa! Judicent nunc Episcopi & rectores Ecclesiarum, quorum interest, de illa Presbyterorum Oratorii declaratione, cui subscripserunt ipse Petrus Berullus. Guillelmus Gibieuf, Theologus Parisiensis & Presbyter Oratorii, & Claudius Boinon, ejusdem Congregationis Presbyter. Berullistas à prima sua institutione degeneres à monachismo potius revocare debuerat Morinus, quam illis monachismi ingenium & mores ingerere; totus quippe est in hoc libello ut monachorum Religiosorumque regulas consvetudinibus Oratorianis opponat; ne autem dominationem suam in Berullistas Borgoneus tueri vellet exemplo praepositi Generalis Jesuitarum, qui Societatis suae Dominus est & Monarcha,fusius inquirit Morinus in supremam illius potestatem & rationes, quibus illa intra limites coërceatur. Haec & similia in hoc libello fusius tractatMorinus, & ut eadem saepius etiam in familiari Colloquio cum Societatis suae hominibus inculcabat, contigit, ut in frequenti gregalium suorum concilio, nescio quid arguens ex regulis Juris Canonici, à Senaldo, Presbytero Societatis illius clarissimo, & postea ejusdem praepositο Generali dignissimo, verbis hisce Festi ad Paulum increpitus fuerit, Insanis Morine,multae te literae ad insaniam convertunt; quae illum ita punxere, ut jam ab illo tempore cogitaverit, Librum edere, quo sodalibus suis ostenderet, se veritatis & sobrietatis verba loqui, uti revera ab ipso postea praestitum fuit: egregium enim hunc libellum,&Marino dignum, qui Casparis Meturas, bibliopolæ Parisiensis cura à Varennio editus fuerat, misit ad Congregationis suæ Presbyteros in solennibus comitiis suis tunc congregatos. Mirati sunt plerique Morini libertatem: immò eum laudaverunt, sed longe aliud tulit judicium Borgoneus de hoc Morini libello, in quo se adeo turpiter diffamatum noverat. Illum publicè retractare coactus est Morinus, veniamque precatus didicit, diis non esse detrahendum. Interim semper postea obganniit, de Oratorianis consuetudinibus intra privatos parietes & cum amicis suis detrahens; solent gregales sui post prandium & à coena interse confabulari, & id vocant conversationem, cui ab eo tempore raro admodum interfuit Morinus ad studia sua se totum applicans; sed tandem his veluti obrutus, apoplexia laborans mortuus est anno ætatis suæ 68, nondum confectus senio, sed duris victus laboribus: ita non sensit graves senectutis molestias, quæ plerisque senibus odiosæ sunt. Huic extremo vitæ Morini actui interfuêre sodalium suorum non pauci, & cum aliis adfuit Harlæus, frater Harlæi Sancii Congregationis etiam Oratorii Presbyter, homo mortalium omnium facetissimus, qui Morinum intuitus anhelum & vix dimidiata verba pronunciantem, ita sodales suos affatus est, mehercle Morinus noster Samaritice loquitur, quibus auditis omnes in risum effusi sunt; & hic fuit extremus Morini vitæ actus; tunc temporis sub prælo erat nova editio exercitationum illius Bibli-carum, nondumque ad partem alteram, quam primæ adjungebat, pervenerat, cùm inter evolvendum Rabbinorum Libros obiit, & quia tunc nemo inter gregales suos repertus est, qui excudendo re-liqvo operi manum admovere posset, quòd omnes ob Rabbinologiam ab hoc onere suscipiendo deterriti fuissent, Pater Fronto ex ordine illorum qui vulgo appellantur Canonici Regulares Sancti Augustini, Cancellarius Universitatis Parisiensis illud aggressus est, & ut erat Rabbinologiæ parum peritus, secundam illam partem Biblicarum exercitationum Morini non ita bene castigatam in lucem emisit. {e} Hæc sunt, vir clarissime, quæ de vita, moribus, & ingenio Joannis Morini, sumpta partim ex illius Epistolis & operibus, partim accepta ex consuetudine doctissimorum Congregationis Oratorii Presbyterorum, Laurentii, Souvignii, Broglii, Ameloti, Cointi, & aliorum quorundam rescire potui.
units.tr: {d} Declaration of the priests of the Oratory of Paris to the Parliament of Normandy, on the occasion of a lawsuit with the curés of Rouen, who opposed their admission, year 1616[?]. None; but they are immediately dependent on the bishops of the places where the Congregation is established. From this it will be judged, by their submission to the prelates, working only through them, under them and for them, that they are not extraordinary, but stand in the order of the hierarchy of the Church, performing all that the curés require of them, such as hearing confessions and administering the holy sacraments in the parishes under them and by their authority, and not otherwise, like the chaplains of their parishes. How much this Congregation of the Oratory has changed from what it was! Let the bishops and rectors of churches, whom it concerns, now judge that declaration of the Oratorian priests, to which Pierre de Bérulle himself subscribed, together with Guillaume Gibieuf, theologian of Paris and priest of the Oratory, and Claude Boinon, priest of the same Congregation. Morinus ought rather to have called the Berullians back to monasticism, from which they had degenerated from their first institution, than to force on them the spirit and manners of monks. Indeed his whole aim in this little book is to set the rules of monks and religious against Oratorian customs. But lest Bourgoin wish to defend his domination over the Berullians by the example of the Superior General of the Jesuits, who is the Lord and Monarch of his Society, Morinus inquires at greater length into that supreme power and the reasons by which it is restrained within limits. Morinus treats these and similar matters at greater length in this book. As he often impressed the same things also in friendly conversation with men of his Society, it happened that at a frequent meeting of his fellows, when he was arguing something from the rules of Canon Law, he was rebuked by Senault, a most distinguished priest of that Society and later a most worthy Superior General, in these words of Festus to Paul: Morinus, you are mad; much learning turns you to madness.
