units.la: Hier. Alexander Jo. Morino de aliis siclis Samarit.
units.tr: Hieronymus Alexander to Johannes Morinus, on the other shekels of the Samaritans

units.la: Doctissimo viro Joh. Morino Hier. Alexan-der.
units.tr: To the most learned man Johannes Morinus, from Hieronymus Alexander.

units.la: Post tuas illas litteras, quibus significacabas, priores, quas ad te miseram, siclorum delineationis istuc pervenisse, nihil abs te praeterea literarum accepi, quamquam binis alteris alias itidem siclorum delineationes ad te subinde perferendas curaverim, nunc duos etiam siclos descriptos in schedulis, quas hisce literis habebis: quorum alterum Venetiis à Nicolao Crasso, alterum Patavio à Laurentio Pignorio nuper accepi,quamquam postremum hunc, in quo Hebraici recentiores, non prisci illi, seu Samaritani characteres leguntur, illi similem esse omnino credo, quem alias tibi misi. Quidquid sit, tu nostrum in te studium saltem notabis, neque quod te vehementer rogo,amare perges.
units.tr: After your letter, in which you indicated that the earlier drawings of shekels which I had sent to you had arrived there, I have received nothing further from you, although I have from time to time arranged for other drawings of shekels to be conveyed to you in two further letters. Now I have also enclosed two shekels described on the slips which you will have with this letter: one of which I lately received at Venice from Nicolaus Crassus, the other from Padua from Laurentius Pignorius. Although I believe that this latter one, on which the more recent Hebrew characters, not those ancient or Samaritan ones, are read, is entirely similar to the one I sent you before, nevertheless, you will at least note our goodwill towards you, and you will continue, as I earnestly ask, to love me.

units.la: Vale. Romæ. die XX. Septembr.
units.tr: Farewell. From Rome, 20th September.

units.tr: Jo. Morinus to Hier. Aleandro. Some Remarks on the Pentateuch in the Samaritan and Hebrew Texts, and in the Jewish Hebrew

units.la: Clarissimo & Doctissimo viro Hier. Aleandro, Jo. Morinus S. D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and learned man Hier. Aleandro, Jo. Morinus sends greetings.

units.la: POstremas litteras tuas die 20. Septemb. datos paulo tardius accepi, quòd Parisiis alio diverteram ; cum iis schedulas duas, in quibus sicli duo delineati habebantur, unus veteri Samaritanorum charactere, alter Hebraico recentiore ; benevolentiam erga me tuam hisce donis sane cumulâsti, studium tuum in re præstanda quam tibi commendaveram non amo & laudo tantũ, sed admiror, quas habeã tibi gratias, opere ipso demonstrare etiã atq; velim animi mei gratitudinem tibi, etiam verba enim, quibus testatum faciam, vix mihi suppetunt. Rescripserã tibi de transcribendo geneseos libro ex Samaritano vulgari, quam penes te habet vir nobilis Petrus à Valle; sed cùm ille se difficilem præbeat consilio meo, sufficient 4 auts capita, ta, codicem enim illum edere, nunquam mihi proposui. An cum Hebraico-Sama-ritano ad amussim consentiat, & verbum de verbo sit redditum, scire tantùm avebam, quod ex 4 aut 5 capitibus facile de-prehenditur ; officiosæ tuæ amicitiæ quod rependam;quamquam res nihili præ manibus jam versabam : me liberius te-cum colloquentem tantisper sustine, Ex-odi 3[?] ver. 15 Hoc nomen mihi est in æter-num, Hebr. scribitur לעלם cum defectu Vau, adesse enim ex Mosse deberet, ut ibi notant Masorethæ. R. S. Jarki in istum locum & cæteri Hebræi hinc colligunt, nomen יהוה aliter legi, aliter scribi o-portere, eò quòd עלם abscondere signifi-cet, ideoque nomen istud à Deo datum ut abscondatur ; sed codex Samaritanus habet plene & perfecte לעולם. In sequenti mysterio vix risum continere possis, Ge-nef. 1. ver. 14. fiant luminaria . מארת[?], Vau similiter rationem reddit Jarki, quia eo die, qui est quartus, infantibus an-gina quædam contingere solet, atque i-deo jejunium quartæ feriæ institutum esse. Base. Baal Naturim subtilius philosophatur, ut scilicet doceatur, solem tunc ad illuminandum datum esse: sed codex Samaritanus perfecte scribit מאורות mysteriaq; omnia ista in ventos diffundit. Plurima sunt magni momenti, in quibus codex ille ab Hebræo differt, & cum LXX. consentit, sed de his alias. Vale vir clariss. & quod mihi exoptatissimum est, me amare perge.
units.tr: I received your last letter, dated 20 September, a little late, because I had gone off elsewhere in Paris. With it came two small sheets on which were drawn two shekels, one in the old Samaritan script and the other in the more recent Hebrew script. You have certainly heaped kindness upon me with these gifts. I not only love and praise your zeal for the task I had commended to you, but I marvel at it, and I would like to show by my actions how much thanks I owe you and how grateful my mind is; indeed, words to declare it barely come to me. I wrote back to you about copying the book of Genesis from the common Samaritan text, which the nobleman Pietro della Valle has in his possession. But since he proves difficult to my suggestion, four or five chapters will suffice, for I never intended to publish that codex. I was only eager to know whether it agrees exactly with the Samaritan-Hebrew text and whether the words are rendered word for word, which is easily judged from four or five chapters. As for repaying your dutiful friendship, although I was already handling trivial matters at hand, bear with me a little longer while I talk more freely with you. Exod. 3, ver. 15: "This is my name for ever." In Hebrew it is written [לעלם] with the Vav missing, though it ought to be there from Moses, as the Masoretes note on that passage. Rabbi Solomon Jarchi and the other Hebrews on this passage infer from it that the name יהוה is to be read one way and written another, because עלם means to hide, and so that name was given by God to be hidden. But the Samaritan codex has it full and complete, [לעולם]. In the following mystery you can hardly keep from laughing: Gen. 1, ver. 14, "let there be lights" [מאורות]. Jarchi likewise gives the reason for the Vav: on that day, the fourth, a certain quinsy usually attacks infants, and so a fast was instituted on the fourth day of the week. Baal Naturim philosophises more subtly, namely to teach that the sun was then given for illumination. But the Samaritan codex writes [מאורות] fully, and all those mysteries are scattered to the winds. There are very many matters of great importance in which that codex differs from the Hebrew and agrees with the Septuagint, but of these I will speak another time. Farewell, most distinguished sir, and continue, which is my most ardent wish, to love me.

units.la: Aubertus Miræus Jo. Morino gratias agit de Libro Exertitationum Ecclesiasticarum, quo eum donaverat Morinus.
units.tr: Aubertus Miræus thanks Jo. Morinus for the book of Exercitationes Ecclesiasticae, which Morinus had given him.

units.la: Reverendo admodum Patri J. Morino Aub. Miræus, S. D.
units.tr: To the most reverend Father J. Morinus, Aub. Miræus, sends greetings.

units.la: Reverende admodum in Christo Pater,
units.tr: Most reverend Father in Christ,

units.la: EXercitationum Ecclesiasticarum Libros duos eruditionis variæ plenos antea mihi non visos, ut primum accepi, avide mox percurri; gratiam habeo pro munere, & hortor, ut tertium, qvartum & cæteros, quorum in Præfatione ad Le-ctorem meminisi[?], luce publica brevi dones : & verò placent mihi inprimis id genus scriptiones, partim Historicæ partim Theologicæ, utpote quæ fructum ingentem adferunt Ecclesiæ ac Reip. Christianæ, & faciunt quam maxime ad Hæreticos confundendos, atque Orthodoxos in Religione, veteri rectiores. Perge itaque, vir eruditissime, in Antiquit. Ecclesiasticis illustrandis ; & quoniam nunc aliud mihi nihil ad manum , habe pro munere nostras Donationes pias & diplomata Belgica , quorum tomus unus atque alter , si Deus vitam dederit , brevi sequetur. Illustrissimo ac Reverendissimo D. Cardinali Berullo, si apud vos est, obsequia omnia ac salutem defero,& Deum rogo, ut ipsum atque universos Oratorii Patres quam diutissime servet, ac donis spiritualibus augeat, quorum me studiosissimum libentissime profiteor;raptim Bruxellis V. idus Julias MDCXXVII. Reverendæ admodum dominationis vestræ studiosissimus Aubertus Miræus Decanus Antverp. indignus.
units.tr: I have eagerly run through at once the two books of Ecclesiastical Exercitations, full of varied learning, which I had not seen before, as soon as I received them. I am grateful for the gift, and I urge you to publish soon, as a public work, the third, fourth and the others you mentioned in your Preface to the Reader. Indeed, I am especially pleased with writings of this kind, partly historical and partly theological, since they bring great benefit to the Church and the Christian commonwealth, and they greatly serve to confound the heretics and to make Orthodox believers more upright in religion. Go on, then, most learned man, in illustrating the ecclesiastical antiquities; and since I have nothing else at hand just now, accept in return our pious donations and Belgian diplomas, of which one or two volumes will follow shortly, God willing. To the most illustrious and most reverend Lord Cardinal Berulle, if he is with you, I offer all respects and greetings, and I pray God to keep him and all the Fathers of the Oratory in good health for as long as possible and to increase them with spiritual gifts; I gladly declare myself their most devoted servant. Hastily written at Brussels, 11 July 1627. Of your most reverend lordship the most devoted, Aubertus Miræus, Dean of Antwerp, unworthy.

units.tr: John Morinus likewise thanks Aubertus Miraeus for the books with which Miraeus had presented him.

units.la: Joh. Morinus, Aub. Miræo S. D.
units.tr: John Morinus to Aubertus Miraeus, greeting.

units.la: Cum primum Lugduno Lutetiam veni, redditæ mihi sunt literæ tuæ, quibus Exercitiones meas Ecclesiasticas, te accepisse cognovi, sed literæ, quas ad te miseram, serius in manus tuas pervenerunt, tibi tamen postea datas esse nihil ambigo. Plurimum mihi gratulor, quod tibi viro in omni scientiarum genere versatissimo placent exercitationes meæ; ea enim es eruditione, & apud omnes eruditos æstimatione, ut nulli aut pauci improbaturi sint, quæ tuo calculo comprobas. Itaq; ut alia atque etiam majora tentare audeam in hoc scriptionis genere, tua cohortatione facis, addisque ut ajunt, calcaria currenti, præsertim cum videam in ea te esse sententia quæ mentem meam jam olim occupavit, ejus-modi rerum Ecclesiasticarum tractatio-nes, etiamsi ab omni cum Hæreticis con-tentione abhorrere videantur, ad controversias tamen dirimendas plurimum posse. Pro donationibus piis & diplo[?]atibus Belgicis, quæ ad me misisti, habeo tibi gratias, pleraque in iis quamvis ab itenere vix quieverim, avide percurri, nam ejusmodi antiquitatem quæ utram-que Historiam Politicam & Ecclesiasticam illustrant, sum studiosissimus; quæ vero legi ita me afficiunt, ut cætera quam primum per lecturus sim, interea munusculum quod tibi offero, boni velim, consulas: Editionem 70. Interpretum Græcam & Latinam quæ Sixti V. summi Pon-tificis auspiciis Romæ edita est, Parisiis iterum edendam curavi; inter cætera quæ editioni accesserunt, Præfationem præ-posui, cujus exemplaria pauca supernumerum Bibliopolis consuetum, mihi cusa sunt, quæ amicis aliquot communicarem,unum adhuc mihi superesse animadvertens, cui illud consecrem, potiorem te neminem habeo: quæstiones magni exagitatPræfatio ista, qua industria judex esto vir docte, sententiam tuam qvæcunqve futura sit, lubens amplectar; qvā-qvam[?] opusculum istud rebus aliis implicitum sit, Bibliaqve ipsa in Belgium aut jā pervenerint, aut brevi perventura sint, illud tamen offerre tibi solitarium minime erubesco: ut possim munus tuum hoc qvalicunqve gratitudinis meæ testimonio remunerari, bene volentiamqve tuam mihi nostraqve Congregationi promereri.
units.tr: When I first came to Paris from Lyon, I was handed your letter, in which I learned that you had received my Ecclesiastical Exercitations. The letter I had sent you reached your hands later, but I do not doubt that it was given to you afterwards. I rejoice greatly that my exercitations please you, who are most versed in every branch of learning. They are of such erudition, and so esteemed by all the learned, that few or none will disapprove of what you approve with your judgment. So, as you urge me to attempt other and even greater things in this kind of writing, adding (as they say) spurs to a running horse, especially since I see you hold that opinion which long ago occupied my own mind: that treatises on ecclesiastical matters of this kind, even if they seem to shun all contention with heretics, nevertheless have great power to settle controversies. I thank you for the pious gifts and the Belgian diplomas you sent me. Although I had scarcely rested from my journey, I have eagerly run through most of them, for I am most devoted to such antiquities as illustrate both political and ecclesiastical history. What I have read affects me so much that I shall read the rest as soon as possible. Meanwhile, I hope you will kindly accept the little gift I offer you. I have had reprinted at Paris the Greek and Latin edition of the Seventy Interpreters, which was published at Rome under the auspices of Pope Sixtus V. Among the other things added to the edition I have prefixed a Preface, of which a few copies have been printed for me beyond the usual number for the booksellers, so that I could share them with some friends. Noticing that one copy still remains to me, to which I might dedicate it, I know of no one more worthy than you. The questions of great controversy debated in this Preface, learned sir, judge with whatever diligence you can; whatever your opinion may be, I shall gladly embrace it. Although this little work is entangled with other matters, and the Bibles themselves have either already reached Belgium or will arrive shortly, I am not at all ashamed to offer this to you alone. In this way I may repay your gift with this token of my gratitude, and earn your goodwill toward me and our Congregation.

units.la: Joh. Morinus, Nob. viro Petro à Valle de Alphabeto Linguæ Ægyptiacæ, simulqve de exemplari M. S. Evange- liorum Lingua Coptica; de Samari- tanorum Pentateucho eorumqve Lin- gua.
units.tr: Johannes Morinus to the noble Peter à Valle, concerning the alphabet of the Egyptian language, and at the same time concerning a manuscript copy of the Gospels in the Coptic language; and concerning the Samaritan Pentateuch and the language of the Samaritans.

units.la: Nobilissimo & Perillustri viro Petro à Valle
units.tr: To the most noble and most distinguished man Peter à Valle

units.la: Joannes Morinus S. D.
units.tr: Johannes Morinus sends greetings.

units.la: MEnses aliquot jam elapsi sunt, cùm R. Pater Bertinus Alphabetum Ægyptiacum ad me misit, quod delineaveras; donum mihi fuit gratissimum & exoptatissimum, gratias habui tibi, atqve nunc habeo maximas, utinam referre possem, divitias enim multas rebus ejusmodi, quæ ad sacræ scripturæ cognitionem conducunt, longe postpono: ab eo tempore huc usque huic studio mihi vacare non licuit, nunc cum licet, beneficii accepti gratias ago, & simul importunus esse tibi cogor, sed importunitate-m meam ab humanitate tua superatum iri confido; sunt in Bibliotheca nostra quatuor Evangelia Lingua Coptica eleganter atq: ab antiquo descripta, quæ R. Pater de Sancy Constantinopoli Lutetiam attulit. Græcus est character, propter literas tamen additicias paucissimas voces perfectæ legere poteram. Sed Alphabeti tui ope adjutus nihil amplius me à literarum cognitione & syllabarum comcompositione retardat. Verum scribendi morem sequitur gens illa antiquitus Græcis usitatum: voces enim à se invicem non separat, literas omnes lineæ unius velut dictionem unicam conjungit, dictiones autem se jungere & dividere laboriosum. Hoc nonnunquam animi causa præstiti variorum locorum, in quibus dictiones illæ usurpantur, collatione & fortasse non infelici; sed in isto negotio plurimum me juvare poteris, optimeque de me mereberis, si ex Grammatica tua Coptica, pronominum, præpositionum, conjunctionum & adverbiorum quorumdam breviculum exscribere, & ad me mittere curavenis, præterea, an nomina declinentur, ut apud Latinos & Græcos, an vero differat tantum singularis à plurali, ut Hebræis, Syris,Chaldæis aliisque Orientalibus solenne est, qui vero terminatio pluralis à singulari differat, quomodo ut plurimum verborum tempora formentur, atque à se invicem distinguntur, hæc enim si semel assequor, facile patebit mihi ad Linguam istam aditus; facile autem me illa assecuturum spero, si conatibus meis favere importunum tibi non fuerit, hæc equidem forte solus eruere possem, sed maximo cum labore: si quid in ejusmodi studio profeccero, totum illud tibi acceptum referam.
units.tr: Several months have now passed since Reverend Father Bertin sent me the Egyptian alphabet that you had drawn up. It was a most welcome and most desired gift, and I thanked you then and I thank you most warmly now. I wish I could repay you, for I put far below many riches the materials of this kind that help toward knowledge of Holy Scripture. Since that time I have not been free to give myself to this study, but now that I am free, I give thanks for the kindness I have received. At the same time I am forced to be a nuisance to you, but I trust that your courtesy will overcome my importunity. In our library there are the four Gospels in the Coptic language, elegantly written and of ancient date, which Reverend Father de Sancy brought from Constantinople to Paris. The script is Greek, yet, apart from a few additional letters, I was able to read the words perfectly. With the help of your alphabet, nothing further hinders me from recognising the letters and putting syllables together. But that people follows the manner of writing once common among the Greeks: it does not separate words from one another, but joins all the letters of a line as if they were one single word, and it is laborious to join and divide the words. I have sometimes done this for my own amusement, by comparing various passages in which these words occur, and perhaps not without some success. But you could help me greatly in this business, and you would deserve very well of me, if you would be so kind as to copy out for me a short summary from your Coptic grammar of the pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions and certain adverbs. Further, I would like to know whether nouns are declined as among the Latins and Greeks, or whether the plural differs only from the singular, as is customary among the Hebrews, Syrians, Chaldeans and other Orientals; and how the plural ending differs from the singular; and how the tenses of verbs are for the most part formed and distinguished from one another. For once I grasp these things, a way into that language will readily lie open to me. I hope I shall easily attain it, if you do not think it too troublesome to favour my efforts. Indeed, I might perhaps work out these things alone, but with very great labour. If I make any progress in this kind of study, I will credit the whole of it to you.

units.la: Istius Linguæ addiscendæ non parvo desiderio teneor, cum enim Ægyptii antiquissimi sint Christiani, versionem antiquissimam illos habere mihi persvadeo, secus de Arabibus & Æ-thiopibus judicarem: si preces meas non aversatus fueris, desiderium meum facile me expleturum, nescio an temere, mihi tamen persvadeo; accepi præterea ab eodem R.P. Bertino specimen Pentateuchi tui charactere & Lingua Samaritani: Statim illud intellexi, Samaritana enim dialectus, quantum ex specimine tuo conjicere possum:, paucissimis à Chaldaica differt aut Syriaca; contuli deinde specimen istud cum Samaritano-Hebræo, qui penes me est, deprehendi codicem tuum versionem esse exactissimam Pentateuchi Samaritano-Hebræi, verba enim verbis numero & sensu respondent, interpres enim ille omni paraphrasi abstinet, neque tantum sensum sensui reddit, verum etiam dictiones numerat, ita ut versioni suae plures non inserat dictiones, quàm in prototypo reperiantur, atque ubique nomina nominibus, verba verbis, conjunctiones conjunctionibus, &c. interpretatur, quo sane interpreta-tionis genere nullum est exactius. Tam accurata interpretandi Religio Talmudistarum sententiam confirmat, qui Samaritanos, quos Butaeos vocant τοῖς קרא[?] adnumerant, hoc est, Haereticis quibusdam, qui traditiones nullas admittunt, aridaeque literae mordicus adhaerent; quaedam suberant errata in schedula tua, quae facile correxi, prius excerptum ex primo cap. Geneseos duas voces in unam miscebat, & in fine tres posterius ex initio 15. cap. Exodi semel resch habebat: scriptum pro beth & rursum resch pro dalet; si fragmentum aliud ex Pentateucho tuo vulgari Samari-tano ad me iterum mittas[?], securius de comcomparatione ista judicabo: non refert è qua parte Pentateuchi illud extrahas, neque opus est, ut in notando capite labores; facile unde evulsum sit conjiciam, atque iterum illud cum Pentateucho meo conferam, & comparationis sententiam ad te rescribam; spero plane, vir Nobilissime atque literarum sacrarum amantissime, te precibus mei aliquid concessurum, beneficiumque, quo me jam devinctum habes novo beneficio cumulaturum. Vale atque ut me plurimum ames, etiam atque etiam velim.
units.tr: I am held by no small desire to learn this language. For since the Egyptians are very ancient Christians, I am persuaded that they have a very ancient version; I would judge otherwise of the Arabs and the Ethiopians. If you do not turn away from my prayers, I trust, though perhaps rashly, that you will easily satisfy my desire. Moreover, I have received from the same Reverend Father Bertin a specimen of your Pentateuch in the Samaritan character and language. I understood it at once. As far as I can judge from your specimen, the Samaritan dialect differs from the Chaldean or Syriac by very few points. I then compared that specimen with the Samaritan-Hebrew text that I have in my possession, and I found that your manuscript is a most exact version of the Samaritan-Hebrew Pentateuch. For the words correspond to the words in number and in sense. The translator abstains from all paraphrase; he does not merely render sense for sense but also counts the words, so that he inserts into his version no more words than are found in the original, and everywhere he translates nouns by nouns, verbs by verbs, conjunctions by conjunctions, and so on. Truly no kind of translation is more exact than this. Such a scrupulous religion of translating confirms the opinion of the Talmudists, who reckon the Samaritans, whom they call Butaeans, among the Karaites [τοῖς קרא], that is, among certain heretics who admit no traditions and cling stubbornly to the dead letter. There were some errors in your schedule, which I have easily corrected. In the first excerpt from the first chapter of Genesis, you ran two words into one, and at the end you wrote three words in a row; from the beginning of the fifteenth chapter of Exodus you once had resch where it should be beth, and again resch for daleth. If you send me another fragment from your common Samaritan Pentateuch, I will judge this comparison more securely. It does not matter from which part of the Pentateuch you take it, nor is there any need for you to trouble yourself in marking the chapter. I shall easily guess where it has been torn from, compare it again with my Pentateuch, and write back to you my judgement of the comparison. I hope, most noble sir and lover of the sacred letters, that you will grant me something of what I ask, and so heap a new kindness upon the kindness by which you already hold me bound. Farewell, and please, I beg you again and again, love me very much.

units.la: Parif. 18. Kal. Octob. An Christi, 1629.
units.tr: Paris, 18th day before the Kalends of October, in the year of Christ 1629.

units.la: EPIST. XIV.
units.tr: LETTER XIV.

units.la: Petrus à Valle Peregrinus de suo exemplari M.S. Pentateuchi Samaritani, quid de Samaritanorum & Carraim sectis in Asia didicerit, fusius declarat.
units.tr: Peter of the Valley, the Pilgrim, sets out more fully what he learned in Asia about the Samaritan and Karaite sects, together with an account of his own manuscript copy of the Samaritan Pentateuch.

units.la: Rev. Patri atque eruditissimo Domino meo Patri Joanni Morino, Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero Petrus à Valle Peregrinus S. P. D[?].
units.tr: To the Reverend Father and most learned Lord, my Father John Morinus, Presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, Peter of the Valley, the Pilgrim, sends his greetings.

units.la: ERubescendum sane mihi est, vir doctissime, cum abhinc tot diebus humanissimæ literæ tuæ, à R. Patre Bertino mihi redditæ fuerint, & usque adhuc nullum, uti debebam, dederim responsum: Plura certe, & quidem vera possem afferre, quæ huic negligentiæ meæ causam dederunt: verùm tamen brevitatis gratia omnia illa omittens, satis esse arbitrabor, si apud benignitatem tuam me deliquisse confitear, & ab illa, uti ex tuis similibus sperare licet, veniam [illegible, ~3 letters]urus expectem. Sed ut ad nostra veniamus; Pentateuchum Samaritanum, qui apud me est, cum primum in Syria reperi, semper ea sui mente, ut publicæ utilitati in lucem emitterem; pretiosum enim aliquid arcanum in arca reservare, nihil facio: sed quidquid habeo boni, tantum id æstimo, quantum aliis omnibus, & præsertim bonis impertire possim. Volvebam igitur animo dare operam, ut characteres isti Samaritani effformarentur, occasione cujusdam Germani, hujus artis peritissimi, qui modo Romæ commoratur, nec procul aberam ab impressione libri omni[?] conatu aggredienda, quandoquidem alius adest nobis ad hæc aptissimus vir, Stephanus Paulinus, alumnus olim eruditissimi viri Joannis Baptistæ Raimundi, qui Orientales litteras, & præsertim Arabicas, in Europa semidemortuas, suscitavit, illasque elegantissime imprimendi modum primus adinvenit, sed ab his omnibus ea me detinuit cogitatio ; quia Pentateuchum Samaritanum absque versione typis mandare[?] infructuosum putavi. Illum vero Latine qui reddere, Romæ non erat ; & si fuisset, uti sibi persvadebat optimus amicus noster, sacrarumque litterarum studiosissimus, Hieronymus Alexander, qui ex hac migrans vita, magnum sui nobis desiderium reliquit, Romæ fortassis non facile futurum erat, ut hujusmodi Liber imprimi à superioribus impetraretur, præcipuè si textus iste à vulgata editione in aliquo tantisper discordaret ; hæc omnia præstiterunt, ut ad hanc usque diem nihil amplius sim molitus, præterquam quod sacræ de propoganda fide Congregationi libenter concessi, ut excerpto ab exemplari meo literarum specimine, ad ejus usum Germanus ille characteres hosce Samaritanos, in quo nunc laborat, excudat. Attamen mirum in modum lætatus fui, quando R. Pater Bertinus una cum Aleandro, nec non amantissimus ille bonarum literarum de iisque optime meritus Dominus de Peiresc, me de R. Paternitate tua admonuerant, virum nempe LingvarumOrientalium studiosissimum æque ac peritissimum esse, & propterea ad id onus suscipiendum Pentateuchi Samaritani tum fideliter interpretandi tum eximia diligentia inprimendi, ante alios omnes longe idoneum itemque paratissimum fore. Persvadentibus idcirco, ut ad te librum in Gallias amandarem, facile assensi; dummodo enim publico consulatur commodo, nihil ad me refert, an liber Parisiis, an Romæ sit excusus: & quia hic nullum habebamus, qui Samaritani idiomatis, nec prima quidem limina attingeret, & ab homine linguæ ignaro, qui literas tantum instar pictoris absque ulla intelligentia delineare poterat, si transumptum fieret, parum feliciter res eveniret, libenter etiam in hanc sententiam descendi, ut ipsummet originale ad te mitteram; hoc demum promisi me facturum Domino de Peiresc, cui de hac re jampridem scripsi, sed ob exortas, ut puto, belli & pestis, in suis regionibus turbulentias, nihil adrespondit: hoc idem R. Patri Bertino, & tibi ipsi, quem ob egregia merita tua mirifice colo, nunc denuo promitto. Verum enim vero, quemadmodum & Patri Bertino, & Domino de Peiresc significavi, tria in hoc negotio desidero, quae ab humanitate tua certo scio non fore mihi deneganda; primum quidem, ut librum ad te quam tutissime mittere possim, cum enim nullum aliud exemplar, quam istud Pentateuchi Samaritani in Europa habeamus, & ex Asia adducere difficillimum sit, ne dicam fere impossibile, illud in itinere alicui periculo objicere, impudentis[?] esset; alterum quod cupio, est ut codex iste meus diligenter adseruetur nec ab impressoribus ut illis mos est dissolvatur, nec ullo pacto aut laceretur aut deturpetur, nam, etsi plura exemplaria typographiae ac diligentiae tuae beneficio in lucem sint proditura, nihilominus ad illorum fidem magis confirmandam; hoc manuscriptum Musæi[?] nostri, quantulumcunque illud sit, insigne ornamentum, perpetuo adservare Plurimii[?] facimus. Postremo deinque[?] oprandum[?] mihi est, & a benignitate tua me facile impetraturum confido, ut in perquirendo hoc libro non mediocris in Asia atque in Ægypto adhibitæ diligentiæ, atque in illo per tot tantaque itinera Romam usque feliciter, ut Deo placuit, deferendo laboris insumpti non leve mihi præmium, in illius impressione aliqua mentio fiat mei, qui totum hoc præstiti in Ecclesiæ Catholicæ obsequium atque literatorum oblectamentum; & quomodo illud habuearim, ubi, & quando ac de omnibus circumstantiis ad hoc pertinentibus, cum opus fuerit, te certiorem facere non pigebit. Interim accipe R. Pater hoc aliud specimen præfati Pentateuchi, quod huic Epistolæ adjunctum mitto : confer il-lud, uti placet, cum aliis codicibus, nihil enim dubtio, quin omnia quam facillime assequaris. Et quia in Epistola tua quædam attingis de opinione Talmudistarum circa Samaritanos, quid de illis in Asia com-perèrim coramque sim assecutus, silentio non præteream. Τὰς[?] Quarraim à Samaritanis Religione longe diversos esse e-xistimo, itidem Chutæos & Samaritanos non eosdem esse puto ; nam Cuthæus, seu Cuthi à Cuthe civitate, quæ ignoro ubi-nam sit, Samaritanus vero à Samaria Samri ubicunque vivat, appellatur. Porro Samaritani oriundi sunt ab Assyriis illis, quos Sennacherib sive Salmanassar si be-ne memini, ex Assyria Samariam in co-loniam adduxit, translato Israele in Assy-rios, cum vero à leonibus infestarentur, & ob alia incommoda ibi vivere non possent, responso accepto ab oraculis, mo-niti sunt, ut servirent Deo terræ. Quapropter Assyriorum rex misit ad eos nonnul-los Aaronitas, seu Levitas antistites, qui MosaiMosaicis illos ritibus initiarunt; attamen eum ab Idololatris essent orti. Hebraicas ceremonias nunquam perfecte arripuerunt, sed aliquid semper antiquae gentili-tatis retinuerunt; & praesertim columbae, sub cujus figura ab Assyriis Semiramis, ni fallor, colebatur, nescio quid honoris aut cultus exhibebant: unde à Judaeis omni tempore, usque ab aevo Servatoris nostri pro haereticis sunt habiti. Sacrarum autem scripturarum quod tunc extabat, cum primum in Samariae regionem sunt ingresi, ab initio receperunt, Pentateuchum nempe, & nescio num aliud aliquid: Prophetas vero, & alios libros, qui postea prodierunt, cum tunc temporis non extarent, nec hodie inter sacros adnumerant. Contra oi [?] Qvaraim, ni decipior, libros omnes sacros Hebraeorum recipiunt: sed literalem tantum sensum observant, nulla admissa interpretatione neque traditione majorum; exempli gratia eum dicatur in lege, Die S. bbati nihil esse operandum, neque lucernas noctu incendendas, sed alii Hebraei lucernas die Veneris accendant, præparentqve, ad lumen illius nocte sequenti ministrandum, οἱ[?] Qvarraim ut mandatum custodiant. nimis scrupulosè lucernas nullo pacto incendunt, & nocte Sabbati penitus in tenebris morantur. Chutæi, num Samaritanis adhæreant, num τοῖς Qvarraim, num diverso ab aliis vivant ritu, incertum mihi est, cum ex illis nullos, ex istis vero aliis omnibus plures sæpe in Asia viderim. Samaritani quidem hodie perpauci sunt, ex his aliquot reperi in Ægypto, Cairi, & Gazæ, quosdam alios in Palæstina, in civitate Sichem, à Turcis Naplus nuncupata, quæ nunc Samariæ regionis Metropolis est, Samaria, sive Sebastia civitate funditus diruta, atque etiam Hierosolymis; alios denique Damasci in Syria Cairi erant circiter septem familiæ eorum, inter quos unus erat, quem vidi, Antistes sacrorum de progenie Levi, quod ab illis pro certissimo habetur; nam hujusmodi dignitas hæreditaria semper fuit in progenie Levitarum, qui cum aliis nec matrimonio se unquam miscuerunt, cum ipsi ex Levitis, populi verò, quos docent, ex gentibus originem deducant. Cacæ,Hierosolymis, ac in urbe Sichem similiter Pauci erant, ut Cairi, Damasci profecto aliquantulo plures, at non multo. Ibi domus eorum & Synagogas inspexi, quæ sunt extra civitatem, inter hortos amænissimos; extrinsecus quidem pauperum more, ob metum Turcarum, qui divitiis admodū inhiant, intus verò elegantes, præsertim ædes illis sacræ, picturis & auro decenter cohonestatæ, pluribusque in locis inscriptionibus Samaritano charactere insignitæ. Sed de his hactenus. Quod ad libros Ægyptiacos, plures hic habemus; in Bibliotheca Vaticana nonnulli sunt: in Typographia Congregationis de fide propaganda aliquot alii: apud me verò Psalterium, Evangelium Joannis, & quædam alia ex Evangeliis omnibus, ex Epistolis Canonicis, & præsertim Epistola Jacobi, quæ, ni fallor, ab Hæreticis recentioribus impugnatur: & nescio, quæ alia Ecclesiastici usus, omnia Arabice, optima atque antiqua versione ab illis populis recepta, interpretata; sed quod pluris aestimo, Di-ctionarium habeo non certe amplissi-mum, sed satis sufficiens, ad sex fere millia vocum complectens, illas nimi-rum, quae magis necessariae sunt, praeser-tim ad sacrarum litterarum intelligenti-am, materiarum ordine digestas, & Ara-bice ad amussim interpretatas, unde illarum omnium sensum assequi mihi parum difficile. Insuper habeo huic vocabula-rio adjunctos authores aliquot, qui Arabico sermone Ægyptii idiomatis gram-maticen, si non copiose ad pompam, ex-acte tamen ad utilitatem quam brevissi-me pertractant. Haec omnia modo, Di-ctionarium scilicet, & Grammaticos, Latinitate donandi sibi onus assumpsit R.P. frater Thomas à Novaria, ordinis Sancti Francisci, Arabicae Linguae peritissimus, & in regionibus Orientis diu versatus; & jam elapsi sunt dies, à quo feliciter in hoc operam navat. Cum primum absolverit, ea omnia typis tradentur, characteres enim Ægyptiaci superius memoratæ Congregationis jussu, jam sunt efformati; & tunc curabo diligenter, ut illis quam primum perfruaris. Cæterum te R. Pater etiam atque etiam rogo, ut me, sicut facis diligas, meque tibi devinctissimum, ac tui semper observantissimum fore pro certo habeas.
units.tr: I must indeed blush, most learned sir, that your most courteous letter, delivered to me by the Reverend Father Bertin many days ago, has until now received no reply, as it ought to have. I could certainly offer many true reasons that have caused this negligence of mine, but to be brief I shall omit them all, and think it enough to confess to your kindness that I have done wrong, and to await, as one may hope from men like you, your pardon for it. But let us come to our business. The Samaritan Pentateuch that I have, I resolved from the moment I found it in Syria to bring out into the light for the public good, for I do not keep any precious thing locked away in a chest; whatever good I have, I value only so far as I can share it with everyone else, and especially with good men. I therefore intended to have those Samaritan characters cut, through the help of a German, a most skilled craftsman in this art, who is now staying in Rome; and I was not far from beginning the printing of the book with every effort. There is also another man most suited to this task, Stephen Paulinus, once a pupil of the most learned Giovanni Battista Raimondi, who revived Oriental letters, especially Arabic, which were half-dead in Europe, and was the first to discover the most elegant method of printing them. But a single consideration held me back from all these plans: I thought it fruitless to print the Samaritan Pentateuch without a translation. Yet there was no one in Rome who could render it into Latin. And even if there had been, as our excellent friend, a most devoted student of sacred letters, Girolamo Alessandro, who, departing this life, left us a great longing for himself, persuaded me, it would perhaps not easily have been possible in Rome to obtain from the superiors permission to print such a book, especially if this text differed at all somewhat from the Vulgate edition. All these things have meant that until this day I have undertaken nothing further, except that I gladly granted to the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith that, from a specimen of letters excerpted from my copy, that German might cut these Samaritan characters, on which he is now working, for its use. Nevertheless I rejoiced greatly when the Reverend Father Bertin, together with Aleandro, and that most kind lover of good letters, the Lord de Peiresc, who has deserved very well of them, reminded me of your Paternity, that you are a man most diligent and equally skilled in Oriental languages, and therefore, before all others, by far the most suitable and most ready to take on the burden of faithfully translating the Samaritan Pentateuch and of printing it with outstanding care. Persuaded by them, I readily agreed to send the book to you in France; for so long as the public good is served, it makes no difference to me whether the book is printed in Paris or in Rome. And since we here have no one who even touches the first threshold of the Samaritan language, and a copy made by a man ignorant of the language, who could only trace the letters like a painter without any understanding, would turn out badly, I also willingly came round to this view, that I should send you the original itself. This at last I promised the Lord de Peiresc, to whom I had written about this matter long ago, but he has not replied, owing, I think, to the disturbances of war and plague in his region; the same promise I now renew to the Reverend Father Bertin and to yourself, whom I greatly esteem for your outstanding merits. However, as I have indicated to Father Bertin and to the Lord de Peiresc, there are three things I desire in this business, which I know for certain your kindness will not deny me. The first is that I may send the book to you as safely as possible; for since we have no other copy of the Samaritan Pentateuch in Europe than this one, and it is most difficult, not to say almost impossible, to obtain another from Asia, it would be shameless to expose it to any danger on the journey. The second thing I wish is that this my codex be carefully preserved, and not taken apart by the printers, as is their custom, nor in any way torn or defaced; for although several copies are going to be brought to light by the help of your press and diligence, nevertheless, to strengthen their authority further, we hold this manuscript, however small it may be, as a distinguished ornament of our museum, and we intend to keep it always. Lastly, and I must add this, I trust that your kindness will readily grant me that, in the printing of this book, some mention be made of me, who, for the search for this book, have expended no small diligence in Asia and Egypt, and who, through so many and such great journeys, have brought it safely to Rome, as God has been pleased, and who have done all this for the service of the Catholic Church and the delight of scholars; this labour is not a slight reward for me. Should it be needed, I will not hesitate to inform you more fully of how I obtained it, where and when, and of all the circumstances pertaining to this. Meanwhile, Reverend Father, accept this other specimen of the aforesaid Pentateuch, which I send attached to this letter. Compare it, as you please, with other codices, for I have no doubt that you will grasp everything most easily. And since in your letter you touch on some points concerning the opinion of the Talmudists about the Samaritans, I shall not pass over in silence what I have learned about them in Asia and what I was able to ascertain. I think the Karaites [Τὰς] are far different from the Samaritans in religion; likewise I do not think the Cuthaeans and the Samaritans are the same. For the Cuthaean, or Cuthi, is so called from the city of Cuth, whose location I do not know, but the Samaritan is so called from Samaria, Shomron, wherever he may live. Furthermore, the Samaritans are descended from those Assyrians whom Sennacherib, or Shalmaneser, if I remember rightly, brought from Assyria into Samaria as colonists, when Israel had been carried away into Assyria. But when they were troubled by lions and could not live there because of other troubles, having received an answer from the oracles they were advised to worship the God of the land. Therefore the king of the Assyrians sent to them some of the Aaronites, or Levite priests, who initiated them into Mosaic rites; yet since they had sprung from idolaters, they never fully adopted the Hebrew ceremonies, but always retained something of their old paganism; and especially toward the dove, under whose figure Semiramis, if I am not mistaken, was worshipped by the Assyrians, they showed some kind of honour or worship. Hence they have been held as heretics by the Jews at all times, even from the age of our Saviour. As for the sacred Scriptures that existed at the time when they first entered the region of Samaria, they received from the beginning the Pentateuch, and I know not whether anything else besides. The Prophets and the other books, which appeared later, since they did not yet exist at that time, they do not count among the sacred books even today. On the other hand, unless I am mistaken, the Karaites receive all the sacred books of the Hebrews; but they observe only the literal sense, admitting no interpretation nor tradition of the elders. For example, when it is said in the law, that on the Sabbath day nothing is to be done, and no lamps are to be lit at night, the other Hebrews light lamps on Friday and prepare them to give light on the following night, but the Karaites, that they may keep the command, do not light lamps at all, and they spend the night of the Sabbath in complete darkness, being overly scrupulous. Whether the Cuthaeans adhere to the Samaritans, or to the Karaites [τοῖς Qvarraim], or live in a different rite from the others, is uncertain to me, since I have seen few or none of them, but often more of the others in Asia. Today the Samaritans are very few indeed. Of these I found some few in Egypt, at Cairo and Gaza, and some others in Palestine, in the city of Shechem, which the Turks call Nablus, which is now the metropolis of the region of Samaria, Samaria or Sebaste having been utterly destroyed, and also at Jerusalem. Others, finally, in Syria at Damascus; there were about seven families of them at Cairo, among whom was one whom I saw, a chief priest of the sacred rites from the line of Levi, which is held by them as most certain; for this dignity has always been hereditary in the line of the Levites, who never intermarried with the others, since they themselves derive their origin from the Levites, but the people whom they teach derive theirs from the nations. At Cacae, at Jerusalem, and in the city of Shechem, they were likewise few, as at Cairo; at Damascus, certainly, somewhat more, but not many more. There I inspected their houses and synagogues, which lie outside the city among most pleasant gardens; outwardly, in the manner of poor people, for fear of the Turks, who are very greedy for riches, but inside elegant, especially their sacred buildings, decently adorned with paintings and gold, and marked in many places with inscriptions in the Samaritan character. But so much for these matters. As for Egyptian books, we have many here: some are in the Vatican Library, some others in the press of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith; and in my own possession a Psalter, the Gospel of John, and some other passages from all the Gospels, from the Catholic Epistles, and especially the Epistle of James, which, unless I am mistaken, is attacked by recent heretics; and I know not what other things of ecclesiastical use, all translated into Arabic in the excellent and ancient version received by those peoples. But what I value more, I have a dictionary, not indeed very large, but quite sufficient, containing some six thousand words, namely those that are most necessary, especially for understanding the sacred letters, arranged in order of subjects and rendered into Arabic exactly; so that it is not very difficult for me to grasp the sense of all of them. Moreover, I have with this vocabulary some authors who treat the grammar of the Egyptian idiom in Arabic, if not copiously for display, yet accurately and as briefly as possible for use. All these things, namely the dictionary and the grammarians, Brother Thomas of Novara, of the Order of Saint Francis, a most skilled master of the Arabic language, who has long lived in the regions of the East, has taken upon himself the task of translating into Latin; and already some days have passed since he has happily been engaged in this work. As soon as he has finished it, all these things will be handed over to the press, for the Egyptian characters have already been cut by order of the aforesaid Congregation; and then I will take care diligently that you may enjoy them as soon as possible. For the rest, Reverend Father, I ask you again and again to love me as you do, and to hold for certain that I shall be most devoted to you and always most observant of you.

units.la: Vale Romæ. Duodecimo Kalend. Aprilis [?], Anno Domini MDCXXX.
units.tr: Farewell from Rome, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord 1630.

units.la: Joh. Morinus Petro à Valle Exemplaris M. S. versionis Samaritanæ, quod erat Petri à Valle judiciis à viro de Samar- itanorum Judæorumque Codicibus Annotata.
units.tr: Johannes Morinus to Pietro della Valle, concerning a copy of the manuscript Samaritan version, which bore Pietro della Valle's judgments, annotated by a man learned in the Samaritan and Jewish codices.

units.la: Nobilissimo & perillustri viro Petro à Valle, Joannes Morinus S. D.
units.tr: To the most noble and illustrious man Pietro della Valle, Johannes Morinus sends greetings.

units.la: NUdiusfertius literas tuas accepi, quæ multis nominibus mihi fuerunt gratissimæ. Plurima enim, quæ à te rescire exoptabam, mihi aperuerunt, in nonnullis etiam desiderium meum humanitas tua prævenit. Sed eo præsertim nomine mine mihi gratissimæ fuerunt, quod a-micitiæ tuæ, quæ mihi honorificentissi-ma est, conciliationem nuntiaverunt, qua me prosequi, & ornare, ut semper velis, etiam atque etiam rogo. Primùm autem habeo tibi gratias maximas, quòd exscribere curasti, & mitti mihi speci-men aliquod Pentateuchi tui Samarita-ni; literæ, ut ipse notasti, minus exacte efformatæ erant, sed hoc incommodum nihil me moratum est, cùm figuras istas jam longa consuetudine mihi familiares effecerim, negotium aliquod facesserunt dictiones aliquæ perperam in duas divi-sæ, una aut altera plus media sui parte trunca, duæ aut tres Chaldæis & Syris admodum insolentes, hæc tamen non obstiterunt, quò minus pauculo tempo-re speciminis sensum caperem, atque ex sensu, de quo Pentateuchi loco expres-sum esset, assequerer. Primum igitur specimen in duas sectiones divisum, ex capite 12. Deuteronomii desumptum est à versu 27. ad finem usque capitis: secun-dum continet primum Geneseos ver-sum, sum, sed non integrum, cui statim subjunctus est versus nonus ejusdem primi capitis, cum quo finiunt pagina & specimen.
units.tr: Three days ago I received your letter, which was most welcome to me for many reasons. It revealed much that I was eager to learn from you, and in some matters your kindness anticipated my wish. It was especially welcome for this reason: it announced the forming of your friendship, which I count a great honour, and I ask you again and again to continue to regard and honour me as you always have. First, I give you my heartfelt thanks for having had a copy made and sending me a specimen of your Samaritan Pentateuch. The letters, as you yourself noted, were not very exactly formed, but this inconvenience did not hold me up, since I have long been familiar with those shapes. Some words caused a little trouble: some were wrongly divided into two, one or other truncated by more than half its part, and two or three were quite unusual even for Chaldeans and Syrians. Yet none of this prevented me from grasping the sense of the specimen in a short time, and from working out from that sense which passage of the Pentateuch was being rendered. The first specimen, divided into two sections, is taken from Deuteronomy 12, from verse 27 to the end of the chapter. The second contains the first verse of Genesis, but not in full, and is immediately followed by verse 9 of the same first chapter, with which the page and the specimen end.

units.la: Quæ amanuensis incuria male scripta sunt, nihil attinet castigare; hæc tantum illustrem Dominationem tuam monebo: comparavi Pentateuchi tui Samaritani specimen cum eodem loco Pentateuchi nostri Samaritano-Hebraei; tuus versio est Samaritana, verbum verbo ad amussim respondens, nostro Samaritano-Hebraeo versio exactior & rigidior fingi non potest. Interpres ille longe pertinacius ipso Onkelo, Paraphraste Chaldaeo, textui Hebraeo adhaeret; exactam istam translationem, ex alio brevissimo specimine, quod ad me antea nomine tuo missum fuerat, jam conjeceram, conjectura ista ex præsenti periclitatione confirmata est.
units.tr: It is pointless to correct what was badly written through the scribe's carelessness. I will only advise your illustrious Lordship of this: I have compared the specimen of your Samaritan Pentateuch with the same passage in our Samaritan-Hebrew Pentateuch. Your version is Samaritan, rendering word for word with exact precision, and no more exact and rigid version than our Samaritan-Hebrew one can be imagined. That translator adheres to the Hebrew text far more stubbornly than Onkelos the Chaldee paraphrast himself. I had already conjectured this exact translation from another very brief specimen previously sent to me in your name, and that conjecture has now been confirmed by the present test.

units.la: Cum Samaritanum tuū [?] cum Hebraeo tam Samaritanorum, quam Judeorum conferrem, deprehendi in paucis versibus ad me missis, utrumque Samaritanum in nonnullis cum 70. interp. editionis Romanæ consentire, & ab Hebræo Judaico dissentire v. 28.cap. 12. Deut. ita legunt 70. Φυλαξον ἡ ἀκουε ἡ ποιήσεις, &c. in Hebræo abest ἡ ποιήσεις; sed illud repræsentant uterque Samaritanus. In fine ejusdem versus LXX. τὸ ἀρεστὸν ἡ τὸ καλὸν Hebræi legunt ordine inverso [illegible, ~5 letters] καλὸν ἡ ἀρεστὸν uterq; Samaritanus bonum & placitum, Ver. 32. Hebræi legunt præcipio vobis, uterque Samaritanus præcipio hodie, 70. verò utramque lectionem jungunt, ἐντέλλομαί ὑμῖν σήμερον, hæc tantum ex schedula tua observata sunto: nam plurima ejusdem generis, ex continua Pentateuchi istius lectione mihi præsto sunt, quæ Epistolii modum longè excedunt; plurima denique ex eodem codice, quæ masoreticas censuras, λεπτολογίας, superstitiosa & ridicula mysteria plane evertunt. Avide legi, quæ de Samaritanis scripsisti; non existimabam, gentem illam ad tantam paucitatem redactam esse: miror quomodo in tam contemnenda paucitate librum legis, & cæremonias suas conservare potuerunt. Cum ea, quæ de sacerdote eorum scribis ad me, legebam, innovatum est desiderium, quo sæpius affectus sum, cognoscere videlicet, an Samaritani cum Judæis in vocum Hebraicarum pronuntiatione conveniant; vocales seu puncta, quibus juvetur lectio, certum est eos non adscribere, literarum magnarum & minimarum certis in locis efformandarum, dictionum plenarum & defectivarum aliarumque ejusmodi nugarum rationem nullam habere, rursus manifestum est ex ipsorum codicibus, in quibus ejusmodi περιεργιῶν[?] nulla apparent vestigia: nescio quomodo sciri posset, quo sono pronuntient voces Hebræas, video enim non tantum 70, sed etiam Josephum, Philonem & ipsum S. Hieronymum his multo recentiorem à neotericis Judæis in vocum ejusmodi pronuntiatione sæpe dissidere, multo magis, ut suspicor, Samaritani dissidebunt. Dissidium istud in hypothesi confirmat Theodoretus, qui ait, Samaritas nomen tetragrammaton Jave pronuntiare; quo sono nomen istud sit efferendum, se nunc ignorare omnes fatentur Judæi; illius pronunciationem ab antiquissimis temporibus vulgo fuisse interdictam, testes sunt Josephus, & Philo, Eusebius, Theodoretus aliique Patres; Judæorum superstitiones hac in er missas[?] facio, interdictionem istam neoterici Judæi concludunt ex cap. 3. ver. 15. Exodi, ubi dicitur, nomen meum est לעלם in æternum, notant enim vocem istam defective scribi atque cum hoc defectu, explicari posse abscondere, Deum igitur dixisse nomen meum est ad abscondendum: hanc glossam præter cæteros tradit R. S. Jarki in hunc locum; sed codex meus Samaritanus vocem istam plene repræsentet לעולם quo mysterii istius radix avellitur, neque præterea est insolens apud Hebræos, ut dictio ista defective scribatur, notant enim masorethæ ad hunc locum, octodecies sic in Bibliis scribi & loca in masora magna super Psal. 75. enumerantur. Quæ illustris Dominatio tua doctissime scribit de Samaritanorum eorumque religiogionis origine, vera esse existimo, Samaritanos quoque ubique ita appellari, si Judæos excipias, qui eos Chutheos semper appellant à Chutheis, qui in Israelitidum regionem à Salmanasero rege coloni transmissi sunt, ut constat ex 4 Reg. c. 17. sed videndus Josephus antiquit. Judaic. I. 9. c 14. & præterea lib. 11. cap 7. quæ enarrare urgente tabellario non vacat. Quæ exigit illustris dominatio tua in codicis sui commodatione, justissima sunt, res ipsa hoc postulat, sincere igitur & Christianæ me illa præstiturum, si libri tui commodatione me beaveris, ego polliceor. Parisiis pridie nonas Maij 1630.
units.tr: When I compared your Samaritan text with the Hebrew of both the Samaritans and the Jews, I found in the few verses sent to me that both Samaritan texts agree in some places with the Seventy in the Roman edition, and differ from the Jewish Hebrew. Verse 28 of Deuteronomy 12 is read by the Seventy as "Keep, or hear, or do" [Φυλαξον ἡ ἀκουε ἡ ποιήσεις], and so on; in the Hebrew the words "or do" are absent, but both Samaritan texts represent them. At the end of the same verse the Seventy have "what is pleasing or good" [τὸ ἀρεστὸν ἡ τὸ καλὸν]; the Hebrews read the terms in reverse order, "good or pleasing" [καλὸν ἡ ἀρεστὸν], while both Samaritans read "good and pleasing." In verse 32 the Hebrews read "I command you," both Samaritans read "I command today," but the Seventy join both readings: "I command you today" [ἐντέλλομαί ὑμῖν σήμερον]. These observations are taken only from your note, for I have at hand very many of the same kind from my continuous reading of this Pentateuch, which would far exceed the limits of a letter; indeed, many from the same codex entirely overturn the Masoretic censures, the subtleties [λεπτολογίας], and the superstitious and ridiculous mysteries. I read eagerly what you wrote about the Samaritans. I did not think that the people had been reduced to so small a number, and I wonder how, in such a contemptible smallness, they have been able to keep their book of the law and their ceremonies. As I read what you write to me about their priest, the long-standing desire I have often felt was renewed: namely, to know whether the Samaritans agree with the Jews in the pronunciation of Hebrew words. It is certain that they do not add the vowels or points that aid reading, and that they take no account of the rules for writing the great and small letters in certain places, of full and defective spellings, and of other such trifles. Again, it is clear from their codices, which show no trace of such curiosities, that they do not. I do not know how one could discover the sound with which they pronounce the Hebrew words. For I see that not only the Seventy, but also Josephus, Philo, and St Jerome himself, who are much earlier than the modern Jews, often differ from them in pronouncing such words. Much more, I suspect, will the Samaritans differ. This disagreement is confirmed in principle by Theodoret, who says that the Samaritans pronounce the tetragrammaton Jave. All Jews admit that they do not now know in what sound that name is to be uttered, and that its pronunciation was commonly forbidden from the most ancient times. Witnesses are Josephus, Philo, Eusebius, Theodoret and other Fathers. I set aside the Jewish superstitions in this matter. Modern Jews infer this prohibition from Exodus 3:15, where it is said, "my name is for ever" [לעלם]. They note that this word is written defectively, and that with this defect it can be explained as "to hide," so that God said, "my name is for hiding." Of the others, R. S. Jarchi alone hands down this gloss on the passage. But my Samaritan codex gives this word in full, as לעולם, by which the root of that mystery is pulled away. Nor is it unusual among the Hebrews for this word to be spelled defectively; the Masoretes note on this passage that it is written so eighteen times in the Bibles, and the places are listed in the Great Masorah on Psalm 75. What your illustrious Lordship writes so learnedly about the Samaritans and the origin of their religion, I think true. The Samaritans are also called so everywhere, except by the Jews, who always call them Cuthites, from the Cuthites who were sent as colonists into the land of the Israelites by King Shalmaneser, as is clear from 4 Kings 17. But Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, book 9, chapter 14, and also book 11, chapter 7, should be consulted; there is no time to recount these matters now, since the courier is pressing. The conditions your illustrious Lordship asks for in lending me your codex are most just, and the matter itself demands them. I therefore promise to observe them sincerely and in a Christian manner, if you will oblige me by lending me your book. Paris, the day before the Nones of May, 1630.

units.la: EX literis tuis, qvas R.P. Bertinus mihi reddidit, non minus humanitate, qvam eruditione refertis, qvam percepe-rim jucunditatem, verbis haud facile ex-plicare possem; non mediocrem enim benevolentiam, qva me, licet immeritum, proseqveris, mirifice testantur: & eximii semper aliquid afferunt, unde multa addiscere mihi usu venit; qva-propter ut illis aliquando, cum vacat, me recreare non pigeat, te etiam atqve etiam rogo. De eo, qvod scribis, in spe-cimine jam missō Pentateuchi Samarita-ni aliqvas te reperisse dictiones, perpe-ram in duas divisas, unam aut alteram plus media sui parte truncam, duasqve aut tres Chaldæis & Syris admodum in-solentes, si modo recte erant scriptæ, ni-hil certi affirmare audeo, cum specimen illud non à me, sed ab alio fuerit transcriptum, lingvæ penitus ignaro, & qvi pictoris more characteres effingebat, absqve qvod illos dignoscereret, ex qvo non mirum, si aliqva commisisset errata, nec eam ipse adhibuerim diligentiam, ut accuaccurata [?]inspicerem, num dictiones illæ absqve mendis essent exaratæ. Verùm cum alioqvin homo ille sit solers atqve in his rebus admodum versatus, facile in suspicionem incidi, ne forte dictiones illæ nullum hujusmodi patiantur defectum, sed peculiari qvodam modo Samaritani idiomatis ita se habeant; Lin-gvam enim Samaritanam, etsi ex Hebraica & Chaldaica ortum ducit, mixtione tamen, & proprio ipsius Samaritanismo, in tertium qvid ab ambobus diversum, degenerasse arbitror. Dictiones vero Chaldæis & Syris tantopere insolentes, non absurde suspicari licet, Arabicas esse: nam ab Arabismis non puto Samaritanos abhorrere, qvippe qvi hodie Arabico sermone pro vulgari utuntur. Si voces istas ad me transmisisses, & loca, un-de excerpta erant adnotasses, facile in textu meo Samaritano, qvomodo se ha-beant, comperissem. Versiculum 15. tertii capitis Exodi, ubi de nomine ineffabili verba habentur, in codice meo Samaritano reperi qvidem, aliqvo tamen labore, cum capita capitibus Latini textus, nec numero, nec principiis, sæpe respondeant, verbaque illa ibi sic extant [illegible, ~10 letters] hos characte-res pessime delineatos esse non dubito, cùm huic scriptioni nunquam antea operam dederim, nihil tamen in ipsis magis aut minus quàm in originali inesse, pro certissimo habeas. Valde delectatus sum, te mihi aperuisse Samaritanos & Cuthæos eosdem esse, & unde Samaritanis Cuthæorum nomen apud Hebræos derivetur; num verò in vocum pronuntiatione, atque in vocalibus, Samaritani cum Hebræis conveniant penitus ignoro: eo enim tempore, quo Samaritanos adivi, harum Lingvarum notitia nulla mihi erat, ut hæc & similia percipere possem; quinimo eandem ob causam plures etiam mihi oblatos tunc despexi libros, quibus poteram ditari, quod incassum modo me fecisse, acerrime doleo. Hoc mihi compertum est, Hebræos, qui Romæ & alibi in Europa versantur, in pronuntiatione quorumdam consonantium, non parum ab Orientalibus Hebræis differre, qui eos eodem ef- ferunt sono, quo Arabes, Chaldæi cæteriqve omnes Orientales, genuino quodam modo, & antiquissimo; contra verò nostrates Hebræi, & Europæi omnes, qui Hebraicas, Syriacas, Chaldaicas, sive Arabicas literas addiscunt; inter quos nullos fere reperi, qui recte pronuntiare noverint literas quaedam, uti præcipue sunt קגערנכטחה [?] & ח [?] sed præsertim literas ח & ע mirum est, quam diverso & quam ridiculo apud Orientales sono nostrates enuncient; quæ sit genuina harum literarum pronuntiatio, calamo non facile describi potest, voce fortassis non infeliciter ostenderem, cum diu jam Orientalium pronunciationi assueverim. Literæ ע genuinum sonum Georgius Amira Chaldaicæ Grammatices auctor, inter omnes meo judicio præstantissimus, optime docuit, similitudine mugitus vitulorum. Litera ח quomodo sit recte efferenda, similitudine cuiusvis [?] in oriente me docuerunt. Diffe- rentirentiam inter [?]⊃ & [?]P optime norit, qui K. Græcorum à Q. Latinorum non ignoravit distinguere; sed hæc, & alia hujusmodi omitto, quæ R P tuæ longe magis quam mihi comperta esse existimo. Hoc tantum reliquum est, ut me tui studiosissimum omni opere futurum fore commemorem, & abste, ut me diligas, & si quid valeo, mihi imperes, toto corde exposcam. Valde vir charissime, & ne desinas de literis bene mereri.
units.tr: I could hardly put into words the delight I took in your letter, which Reverend Father Bertinus handed to me, filled as much with courtesy as with learning. It clearly attests the no small goodwill with which you embrace me, though I do not deserve it, and it always brings something outstanding from which I learn much. Therefore I ask you again and again not to be reluctant to refresh me with such letters whenever you have leisure. As to what you write, that in the specimen of the Samaritan Pentateuch already sent you have found some words wrongly divided, one or other cut short by more than half, and two or three very unusual for Chaldeans and Syrians, if indeed they were written correctly: I dare affirm nothing certain. That specimen was not copied by me but by another man, wholly ignorant of the language, who formed the characters like a painter without distinguishing them. It is no wonder, then, that he made some mistakes, and I myself did not apply such care as to examine carefully whether those words were written without errors. But since that man is otherwise skilful and very experienced in these matters, I easily came to suspect that those words perhaps suffer no defect of this kind, but stand thus by a peculiar feature of the Samaritan idiom. For I think the Samaritan language, though it derives from Hebrew and Chaldean, has degenerated by mixture and by its own Samaritan character into a third thing, different from both. The words, however, so very unusual for Chaldeans and Syrians, one may not unreasonably suspect to be Arabic, for I do not think the Samaritans shrink from Arabisms, since today they use Arabic as their everyday speech. If you had sent me those words, and noted the places from which they were taken, I would easily have found in my Samaritan text how they stand. I did find verse 15 of the third chapter of Exodus, where the ineffable name is spoken of, in my Samaritan codex, though with some labour, since the chapters often correspond to the chapters of the Latin text neither in number nor in beginnings. The words stand there thus: [illegible, ~10 letters]. I do not doubt that these characters are very badly drawn, since I had never before applied myself to this script; yet you may hold as quite certain that nothing in them is greater or less than in the original. I was very delighted that you revealed to me that the Samaritans and the Cuthaeans are the same, and whence the Cuthaean name is derived among the Hebrews. Whether the Samaritans agree wholly with the Hebrews in the pronunciation of words and in the vowels, I entirely do not know, for when I visited the Samaritans I had no knowledge of these languages, so as to perceive these and similar things. Indeed, for that very reason I then despised several books offered to me, by which I might have been enriched, and I now bitterly regret having done so to no purpose. This I have learned: that the Hebrews who live at Rome and elsewhere in Europe differ not a little from the Eastern Hebrews in the pronunciation of certain consonants. The Eastern Hebrews utter them with the same sound as the Arabs, Chaldeans and all other Orientals, in a genuine and most ancient manner. On the contrary, our Hebrews, and all Europeans who learn the Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldean or Arabic letters, among whom I have found almost none who knew how to pronounce correctly certain letters, such as qof, gimel, ayin, resh, nun, kaf, tet and het. Especially remarkable is how differently and how ridiculously our people utter the letters het and ayin compared with the Orientals. What the genuine pronunciation of these letters is cannot easily be described with the pen; perhaps I could show it by voice, not unsuccessfully, since I have long been accustomed to the pronunciation of the Orientals. The genuine sound of the letter ayin Giorgio Amira, author of a Chaldean grammar and in my judgment the most outstanding of all, taught very well by the likeness of the lowing of calves. How the letter het is to be rightly uttered, they taught me in the East by the likeness of a certain sound. The difference between kaph and pe he will know very well who did not fail to distinguish the Greek K from the Latin Q. But these and other things of this kind I omit, which I think are known to your Reverence far better than to me. This only remains: that I call to mind that I shall be most devoted to you in every endeavour, and I ask with my whole heart that you love me and, if I am of any worth, that you command me. Most dear sir, do not cease to deserve well of learning.

units.la: Literas tuas avide accepi, Pentateuchum Samaritanum, quem nobis polliceris, avidius accepturus, gratiam istam ab humanitate & studio, quo erga sacras literas incenderis, non modo speramus [?], sed etiam expectamus; promissis tuis standi ut occasionem cito nanciscaris, Deum Opt. Max. & ego efflagito, & omnes literati deprecantur; quæ aberrata fuerunt in ἀπογράφῳ[?] Samaritano, quod mihi misisti, quoniam ita desiderasti, lubens transmitto: ista exscripta fuerunt ex cap. 12. Deuter. à v. 27. ad finem cap. facile autem hæc reperies, si sectiones libri tui sectionibus libri mei respondeant. Dividunt Samaritani singulos libros Mosis in varias sectiones, quas קצין[?] vocant, quæ parasc his[?] Judæis longe breviores sunt; librum quintum, qui nobis est Deuteronomium in 166. Katsin distinguntur, quarum 71. ab initio versus 29. atque ab his verbis incipit אני עקריהוה[?] initio igitur, ver. 27. ואדמה sanguinem [?]irrepsit, dicendum enim רם[?] ut paulo post, vel רמה[?] Nomen illud, ut scriptum est, terram significat vel rubedinem; fieri tamen potest, ut Aleph sit hæmanticum in eo nomine, ut aliquando Chaldæis, in fine vers. 28. באות[?] ponitur pro Hebræo-Samaritano בעיני[?] in oculis, suspicor scriptum esse, בהאות[?] in præ-sentia, sentia, nisi sit error, explicandum est, in desiderio, scilicet Domini. Sed hæc levia : versu 29. ad finem ותרוב [?] ultima litera debet esse Resch non Bet, רור [?] enim habitare significat, versu 30. בארין [?] post eos, loco Aleph reponendum ית [?] versi, 31. לי אלהך [?] Domino Deo tuo, pro לי [?] scribendum לרהוה [?] eodem versu רס בא [?] delendum punctum, quo in duas dictiones fit separatio & continuo legendum רסבא [?] qve[illegible, ~3 letters]dit ; eodem versu יקרון [?] delendum punctum ne fiant duæ voces, combusserunt ; comparatione textus Hebræo-Samaritani facile fuit ista corrigere, sed de quo loco ista eruta essent, nescienti negotium facessere potuerunt, voces insolentes Syris & Chaldæis istæ videntur צריוח [?], qua significatur צרים [?] gentes רער [?] quæ pro Hebræo נקש [?] ista-queare מלמס [?] creavit, quæ vox est secunda Pentateuchi ; quæ dixi de superstitione Judaica circa nomen Tetragrammaton, quam ex v. 16. c. 3. Exodi eliciunt, vera sunt tantum sicut cætera ejusmodi omnia de textu biblico, tantum enim circa textum illum λεπτολογῶσι : itaque ad versiones & Paraphrases, qualis est Illustris Dominationis tuæ Pentateuchus, ista non sunt transferenda. Recte igitur versio tua habet לעלם quamquam in Hebræo Samaritano sit לעולם. Si Linguæ naturam spectemus, alia omnino ratio est, in tuo codice scribi non debuit, ut in Hebræo Samaritani עלם seculum: non pronuntiant hholam cum Vau, sed cum A seu camets; Syrita עלם hhalam, sic Samaritani ut ex literis apparet: Chaldæi vero addunt Aleph in fine עלמא hhalma. Hebræi vero cum Vau efferunt עולם hholam, atque vel Vau scribendum vel subaudiendum; si in versione tua haberetur עולם perperam scriptum esset: Vau enim nunquam quiescit in camets, neque camets seu A supplet literam Vau, sed Aleph, quæ aliquando exprimitur cum camets, unde fit ut,ut nonnunquam in scriptura legatur םנכ[?] pro םע, & similia. Itaque ex natura Linguæ Syriacæ & Chaldaicæ tolerabilius esset, scribere עולם qvam עולם ad significandam æternitatem. Quæ de pronuntiatione scripseram de literis non intellexi, sed de vocalibus seu punctis, & de nomine tetragrammato, circa quæ non existimo Samaritanos Judæorum instar minute Philosophari.
units.tr: I received your letter eagerly, and I will receive the Samaritan Pentateuch you promise us even more eagerly. We not only hope for this favour, but expect it, from the kindness and the zeal for sacred letters that you have shown. As for keeping your promises, which I and all scholars pray God Almighty to grant, you should seize an opportunity soon. I am gladly sending you the passages that were mistaken in the Samaritan copy you sent me, since you asked for them. These are taken from Deuteronomy 12 from verse 27 to the end of the chapter. You will find them easily if the divisions of your book match the divisions of mine. The Samaritans divide each book of Moses into various sections, which they call qatsin, and these are much shorter than the Jewish ones. The fifth book, which for us is Deuteronomy, is divided into 166 katsin. The 71st of these begins at verse 29 and starts with the words ani aqarihweh. So at the beginning, in verse 27, waadamah [and the ground] has crept in as sanguinem [blood]. For it should read dam, as shortly after, or damah. That word, as written, means earth or redness. Still, it may be that Aleph is a hamantic letter in that word, as it sometimes is in Chaldee. At the end of verse 28, ba-ot is put for the Hebrew-Samaritan be-ene, "in the eyes." I suspect that b-ha-ot was written, meaning "in the presence." Unless it is an error, it must be explained as "in the desire," namely of the Lord. But these are small matters. In verse 29 to the end, wtrwb: the last letter should be Resh, not Bet, since rwr means to dwell. In verse 30, b-arin "after them": instead of Aleph, Yod-Tav should be put in place of the verse. In verse 31, li elhk, "to the Lord your God," should be written l-yhwh instead of li. In the same verse the point between rsb' should be deleted, which divides it into two words, and it should be read continuously as rsb', "[illegible] dit." In the same verse the point in yqrwn should be deleted so that it does not form two words, "they burned." By comparing the Hebrew-Samaritan text these things were easy to correct. But those who did not know where these passages were taken from could find it troublesome. The words seem strange to Syrians and Chaldeans, such as tsrywh, by which tsrym, "nations," is meant, and rwr, which for the Hebrew nqsh [?], "iste queare" [?], and mlms, "he created," which is the second word of the Pentateuch. What they say about the Jewish superstition concerning the name Tetragrammaton, which they derive from verse 16 of chapter 3 of Exodus, is true only as far as all such things about the biblical text are true, for they are over-precise about that text alone. So such things should not be carried over to versions and paraphrases, such as your Lordship's Pentateuch. Your version rightly has l'olam, although the Samaritan Hebrew has le-olam. If we look at the nature of the language, the case is entirely different. It should not have been written in your manuscript as the Samaritan Hebrew writes 'lm, "age." They do not pronounce holam with Vav, but with Alef or qamets. The Syriac has 'lm, halam, and the Samaritans do the same, as appears from the letters. The Chaldeans, however, add Aleph at the end, 'lm', halma. The Hebrews pronounce 'wlm with Vav, holam, and either Vav must be written or understood. If 'wlm were found in your version, it would be written wrongly. For Vav never rests in qamets, nor does qamets or Alef supply the letter Vav. Instead Aleph, which is sometimes pronounced with qamets, is used. Hence it is that sometimes 'nkm is read in Scripture for 'm, and similar cases. So, from the nature of the Syriac and Chaldee language, it would be more tolerable to write 'wlm than 'lm to signify eternity. What I wrote about pronunciation I did not understand concerning the letters, but concerning the vowels or points, and about the Tetragrammaton, in which I do not think the Samaritans philosophise in minute detail as the Jews do.

units.la: Benjaminus in itinerario scribit, Chutæos has tres literas non habere החע[?] legemque Mosis his tribus literis exceptis agnoscere, inqve harum literarum vicem Aleph substituere. Sed ista Judæorum calumniæ sunt, sicut id, quod Aben Ezra in primum cap. Esth. scribit, Cuthæos initio Geneseos pro בראשית ברא אלהים reposuisse initio creavit Asima, Idolum scilicet suum omnia creasse.
units.tr: Benjamin, in his itinerary, writes that the Cuthaeans do not have these three letters heth, ayin, he [החע], and that, apart from these three letters, they acknowledge the law of Moses, substituting aleph in place of these letters. But these are the calumnies of the Jews, as is also what Aben Ezra writes on the first chapter of Esther, that the Cuthaeans in the beginning of Genesis replaced bereshit bara elohim [בראשית ברא אלהים] with "in the beginning Asima created", meaning that their idol Asima created all things.

units.la: Notat præterea idem Benjaminus, id quod nuper ad me scripseras, Samaritanorum sacerdotes ab Aarone genus ducere, & cum suæ superstitionis hominibus connubia non miscere, atque ideo ab suis Aaronitas vulgo dici; sed de hisce satis.
units.tr: Benjamin further notes what you wrote to me recently, that the Samaritan priests trace their descent from Aaron and do not intermarry with men of their superstition, and that for this reason they are commonly called Aaronites by their own people. But enough on these matters.

units.la: Recenter legi magna cum animi oblectatione libellum, quem edidisti, delle conditioni di Abbas Re di PerPersia: velim quae tanti Regni Politiam & Geographiam spectant, descripsisses; hactenus enim admodum obscura sunt hujus regni interiora. Hoc te facturum spero in compendio Historiae Persicae, quod publico spospondisti, fidemque tuam sic praestiturum; finem tandem scribendi faciam, si prius, ut plurimum me ames, Illustrissimam Dominationem tuam instantissime rogaverim; nihil tua amicitia & suavius & honorificentius mihi contingere posse existimo. Vale iterum dico & me ama.
units.tr: I have recently read with great pleasure the little book you published, delle conditioni di Abbas Re di Persia. I would wish that you had described the polity and geography of so great a kingdom, for hitherto the interior of this realm has been very obscure. I hope you will do this in the summary of Persian history that you promised the public, and so keep your word. I will finally end my writing, but first I earnestly ask your Most Illustrious Lordship, since you love me so much, for something. I think nothing can come to me from your friendship that is sweeter or more honourable. Farewell, I say again, and love me.
