units.la: Reverendo Patri atque eruditissimo Domino meo Patri Joanni Morino Congregagationis Oratorii Presbytero, Petrus à Valle Peregrinis S.P.D.
units.tr: To the reverend Father and most learned lord, my Father Jean Morin, presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, Peter à Valle Peregrinis sends very many greetings.

units.la: REverende mi Pater ad calcem Pentateuchi, disjunctè [?] tamen, & diversa ab aliis magnitudine exaratos versiculos aliquot reperies, verba scriptoris, quibus ut Orientalibus mos est, nomen suum, tempus, quo volumen hoc scripsit, & alia multa explicantur, quæ non bene assequi potui, cum non extense, sed compendiariis notis sint scripta. Pergratum mihi erit, si ea, cum optime percepers, ad amussim quomodo se habeant, & eorum sensum quis sit, ad me rescripseris. Valei-terum & mei memor vive.
units.tr: Reverend Father, at the end of the Pentateuch you will find some short verses, set apart from the rest and written in larger letters. In them, as is the custom with Orientals, the writer explains his name, the time when he wrote this volume, and many other things. I could not follow these well, since they are written not in full but in abbreviated notes. It would give me great pleasure if, once you have understood them thoroughly, you would write back to me how they stand exactly and what their sense is. Farewell, and remember me.

units.la: In fronte libri, quæ duabus in paginis à tergo Arabica extant scripta, syngrapha sunt quorundam Doctorum ex Samaritanis, qui variis temporibus volumen legisse, illudque correctum esse testantur.
units.tr: On the front of the book, the signatures written in Arabic on the two pages at the back belong to certain Samaritan teachers, who testify that at various times they read the volume and that it had been corrected.

units.la: Inter interpretandum, quod Paternita-ti tuæ parvo labori futurum esse existimo, rem summopere gratam mihi facies, si hujusce mei textus in margine, ut illius usus nostris eo magis facilis reddatur, numeros capitum, versiculorumque Pentateuchi Latini, suis locis, opportune, ac non ineleganti aliquo modo, signaveris; nec non alia in margine, è regione, vel ubi melius videbitur, numeros etiam sectionum juxta Samaritanos: quæ quidem
units.tr: While you are interpreting it, which I think will be a small labour for your Paternity, you would do me a very welcome favour if, in the margin of my text, so that it may be more easily used by our people, you mark in their proper places, appropriately and in some tasteful way, the numbers of the chapters and verses of the Latin Pentateuch; and also, in another margin opposite, or wherever it seems better, the numbers of the sections according to the Samaritans, which indeed

units.la: etsi scriptura sint distinctæ, numeros tamen nullos habent. Hoc ipse non præstiti, qvia absqve errore uti apparebat, illud agere non considebam.
units.tr: although they are written as separate sections, have no numbers. I did not do this myself, because I did not think it worth undertaking, since it seemed it could be done without error.

units.la: Nudistertius R. P. Fr. Thomam á Novaria invisi, & ipse libellum mihi Samaritanum ostendit, preces illius gentis, ut opinor, continentem; ibiqve nonnulli erant versus, qvorum primæ dictiones incipiunt à literis Alphabeti ordine digestis, veluti Lamentationes Jeremiæ; atq; ex manifeste comprehendi, me hujusqve in Alphabeto Samaritano samec pro sade, & è contra sade pro samec, perperam usurpasse, nescio qva deceptum conjectura. Putabam enim literam samec esse, & sade; at in eo libro contrarium nempe ab una qvintum decimum in Alphabeto locum, ab altera vero decimum octavum occupari vidi, tibi significari necessarium duxi, & de eo, qvid ipse sentias me certiorem facias velim.
units.tr: The day before yesterday I visited Father Fr. Thomas à Novaria, and he himself showed me a little Samaritan book, containing, I believe, the prayers of that people. In it there were some verses whose first words begin with the letters of the alphabet in order, as in the Lamentations of Jeremiah. From these it is plainly clear that I had wrongly used samec for sade and sade for samec in the Samaritan alphabet, misled by I know not what conjecture. For I had thought that samec and sade were the same letter, or at least that they held the same place; but in that book I saw the opposite, namely that the one occupies the fifteenth place in the alphabet and the other the eighteenth. I thought it necessary to point this out to you, and I would like you to inform me what you think of it.

units.la: Idem Pater à Novaria præ manibus habet Interpretationem Grammaticæs, qvam ei tradidi, Ægyptio.Arabicæ, nec non vocabularii ; ipsiusmet diligentiæ calcaria adjungere non desinam : vereor tamen, ne obmulta quæ illum præmunt negotia, eam tam cito, uti desideramus, ad finem perducat. Nec plura, ac tertio
units.tr: The same Father of Novara has in his hands the grammatical interpretation, Egyptian-Arabic, which I gave him, as well as a vocabulary. I shall not cease to add spurs to his own diligence, but I fear that, because of the many affairs that press upon him, he may not bring it to an end as quickly as we would wish. Nothing more at present, and once again, farewell.

units.la: Vale.
units.tr: Farewell.

units.la: EPIST. XIX.
units.tr: EPIST. XIX.

units.la: Pet·à Valle J. Morino. Responsio ad præcedentem de Lingua & Libris Samaritanorum.
units.tr: Pietro della Valle to Giovanni Morino. Reply to the preceding letter on the Language and Books of the Samaritans.

units.la: R. Patri, atque eruditissimo Domino meo Patri Joanni Morino Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero Petrus à Valle Peregrinus S.P.D.
units.tr: To the Reverend Father, and my most learned lord, Father Giovanni Morino, Presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, from Pietro della Valle, the Pilgrim, with greetings.

units.la: NOn mediocrē mihi lætitiam attulere vir eruditissime,& literæ tuæ, quas nuper accepi;& optima, quæ nunc sese offert, occasio mittendi ad te tantopere optatum Samaritanum Pentateuchum. Reverendus Pater Bertinus, nostri amantissimus, una cum Nuncio Pontificis ad Regem delegato, iter in Gallias brevi est aggressurus: mari quidem usque, in Provinciam, quam vocant Galliæ, seu Narbonensem oram, sed triremibus, quibus quam tutissime navigari solet; ac inde Lutetiam usque, pedestri itinere, facillime ut opinor, atque expeditissime ad te perveniet, quod jam expectas feliciter, ni fallor, allaturus, illud namque in clusum capsula, & adversus pluvias, aliosque hujusmodi sinistros casus optime munitum, illi tradidi; non laborabo de Pentateuchi locis, quæcumque enim extant in hoc textu, animadversione digna, tibimet proprlis oculis intueri licebit; tantum dicā, ea omnia errata, quæ in ἀπογραφῷ [?] jam missō adnotasti, in hoc exemplari meo ita prorsus se habere, me reperisse, sicut tu corrigenda esse prudenter existimaveras. De pronunciatione vocalium apud Samaritanos nihil ausim [?] dicere, cum neque eorum Linguam intelligam, neque illos legentes unquam audiverim; illud tantum observavi, hujusce exemplaris mei scriptorem, in quibusdam dictionibus, quas evolvendo libro facile reperies, super aliquas literas virgulas quasdam, seu lineolas apposuisse, vel jacentes, vel dextrorsum aliquantulum e-[?] rectas, in star accentus acuti Græcorum: quod præstitisse procul dubio opinor, ad tollendam lectori omnem de earum pronunciatione ambiguitatem. Verùm, si lineolæ, illæ in hac scriptura eandem, quā in Arabica, vim habeant, quod non inverisimile mihi videtur, cum Samaritani Arabica Lingua hodè pro vulgari utan-tur, & ad Arabici scribendi ritus exemplum, qui illis familiaris est, in propriis etiam characteribus distinctionis ergo, lineolas illas efformasse posibile sit, dum hujusmodi signa ad distinguendum vocales ipsi non habent, nihil aliud profecto, quam A vocalem, hisce lineolis ab iisdem repræsentari existimo; nam apud Arabes hujusmodi signum- seu motio, ut ipsi dicunt, quam Jathha appellant, valet A Latinorum, sive E. clarum ad A. declinantem, vel medium quidem sonum inter A. & E. clarum. Cæterum Masoretas illos, & alios recentiorum, qui fuerunt, tam apud Hebræos, quam apud Chaldæos, vocalium inventores, in eo quod ad pronunciationem spectat, multa innovasse, non abs resure suspicor. Nam Arabes, qui priscarum consuetudinum teneatiores fuerunt, & quorum cum Lingua. Hebraicam atque Chaldaicam maximam affinitatem habere, nemo non fatetur, tres tantum vocales agnoscunt, A.nempe, V. & I. tribus literis quiescentibus, Aliph, Vau, & Je respondentes; quae tamen variis in locis, plus vel minus clare prolatae, virtualiter ( ut Scholasticorum votibus utar) nostrarum quinque vocalium sonum, eorumq; brevitatem ac longitudinem, quodammodo referunt; cum revera plures tribus, nec sint, nec esse possint, quandoquidem tres tantummodo existunt quiescentes & earum sonum, ubi opus est, appositae, accentu quodam magis producere debent; quod Hebraeis etiam & Chaldaeis antiquitus commune fuisse, & Genebrardus mecum sentit, & ipsamet scribendi atque legendi ratio manifeste ostendere, mihi videtur: neque in hac tantum parte novatores illos posteris imposuisse arbitror, sed in alia quoque, vocales nimirum immutando, & aliam pro alia sæpe usurpando in quamplurimis dictio-nibus sive corruptela Linguæ, sive di-versitate τῆς διαλεκτῶ[?], sive temeritate, sive alio quovis casu. Ad hoc credendum me persuadet illud argumentum; priscam scilicet, rectam genuinamque pronunciationem complurium vocum earum Linguarum, quæ corruptelas passæ sunt, apud exteros potius, quam apud propriæ gentis homines, reperiri; si quidem exteri dictionum sibi peregrinarum pronunciationem fere semper eandem retinent, quam ab initio ab iis, quibus Linguæ illæ propriæ erant, audivêre, nulla adhuc in eorum idiomata corruptione illapsa: contra vero cujuscunque nationis homines priscas proprii sermonis voces, non nisi corrupte, pronunciare solent, immutata admodum annorum cursu, non minus sermonis, quam vestium, aliarumque rerum omnium consuetudine. Quod in Italia accidisse videmus, non modo mutata Lingua Latina in Italicam, verùm etiam adeo mutata ut hodie in vocabulis, quæ cum Latinis tinis tum Italis communia sunt, si Hetrusce loqvamur,hoc est, majori qvi nu-do[?] possumus elegantia regula sit, ut a Latinorum pronunciatione qvanimax-[?] me fieri potest, aberremus. Hanc eamdem corruptionem sermonis, licet non[?] tantam, ipsamet Græcia experitur: Armenia verò,ut de aliis regionibus tacea-m, tantopere majorem, ut qui hoc sæculo vivunt Armeni priscorum suorum Lingvam, nisi illam addiscant, multo minus qvam Itali, Latinam intelligunt. Qvod autem dixi,apud extraneos multarum vocum cujuscunqve Linguæ priscam, rectamqve pronunciationem reperiri, non paucis exemplis comprobare possem,sed hic nobis satis erit nomen, Cæsar, qvod ab Arabibus, à Persis, & ab Orientalibus fere qvibuscunqve ad hanc usqve diem antiqvo more apud nos penitus abolito, Caisar efferri consvevit. Idem de vocibus Hebraicis evenire, ut hac scilicet tempestate nonnullæ earum minus recte ab Hebræis, qvam ab aliis extraneis, pronuncientur, qvid dubium corrupta jam inter Hebræos Lin-gva, vel temporis injuria, vel Maforeta-[illegible, ~40 letters] rum, aliorumqve recentiorum temeraria innovatione? Plures reperiuntur dictiones, tam Hebræis & Chaldæis, qvam Arabibus communes, qvæ qvidem ab utrisqve iisdem prorsus litteris scribuntur, diverse tamen pronuntiari solent ob diversam illarum gentium vocales illis affigendi consvetudinem; sed pace recentiorum Masoretarum dixerim, Arabum pronuntiatio mihi magis arridet, magisqve antiqvorum usui consentanea videtur. Exempli gratia dictio היכל qvæ juxta Genebrardum in Epistola ad lectorem in Commentariis Psalmorum, ab Hebræis Hecal pronunciatur, & significat armarium illud in Synagoga Hebræorum, ubi volumen legis adversari solet, ab Arabibus iisdem qvatuor literis exaratur, diversa tamen vocalium adhibita ratione Hikel effertur, & recte qvidem; qvomodo enim Hecal dici potest, si secunda hujus dictionis litera est ה qviescens, qvæ cum motione, seu vocali[?] caret,nihil aliud legenti, quam tempus aliquantulo diuturnius præcedentis vocalis,si modo sit J. longa, sibi natum respondens innuere potest: sin alia ex vocalibus præcesserit, soni ipsiusmet literæ Je contractiorem in syllabam antecedentem,ita ut si non Hikel,saltem Heikel,vel Haikel per diphtongum, ut more nostro loquar, sit legendum; Hecal vero absque ulla literæ J. expressione, nullo pacto.
units.tr: Your most learned letter, which I lately received, has brought me no small joy, most learned sir, and so has the excellent opportunity now offered of sending you the Samaritan Pentateuch, which you have so eagerly desired. Reverend Father Bertin, who is most fond of us, is about to set out shortly for France together with the Nuncio of the Pope, who has been sent to the King. They will travel by sea as far as the province called Gaul, or the Narbonese coast, but in galleys, in which one usually sails as safely as possible; and from there to Paris they will travel on foot, which I think is very easy and most expeditious. He will bring it to you there, as you are already happily expecting, unless I am mistaken; for I have handed it over to him, enclosed in a box and well protected against rain and other such mishaps. I will not labour over the passages of the Pentateuch; whatever in this text is worth noting you will be able to see for yourself with your own eyes. I will only say that all those errors which you noted in the copy [ἀπογραφῷ] already sent, I have found in this copy of mine exactly as you wisely judged they needed correcting. I would not venture to say anything about the pronunciation of the vowels among the Samaritans, since I neither understand their language nor have ever heard them reading. I have only observed that the writer of this copy of mine, in certain words which you will easily find on leafing through the book, placed some little strokes or lines over some letters, either lying flat or leaning slightly to the right, like the acute accent of the Greeks; which he certainly did, I believe, to remove all ambiguity about their pronunciation for the reader. But if these little lines have the same force in this script as in Arabic, which does not seem to me unlikely, since the Samaritans today use Arabic as their everyday language, and it is possible that, following the example of Arabic writing, which is familiar to them, they formed those little lines in their own characters for the sake of distinction, since they have no such signs for marking vowels, I certainly think those little lines represent nothing other than the vowel A. For among the Arabs such a sign, or vowel mark, which they call fatha, has the value of the Latin A, or of a clear E inclining towards A, or indeed a sound midway between A and clear E. Moreover, I suspect that those Masoretes, and the other more recent men who were the inventors of the vowels both among the Hebrews and among the Chaldeans, introduced many innovations as far as pronunciation is concerned. For the Arabs, who have kept more tenaciously to ancient customs, and whose language nobody denies has the greatest affinity with Hebrew and Chaldean, acknowledge only three vowels, namely A, U and I, corresponding to the three quiescent letters Aleph, Waw and Yod. Yet these, pronounced in various places more or less clearly, virtually (to use the words of the Schoolmen) represent in some way the sound of our five vowels, and their shortness and length; whereas in fact there are, and can be, no more than three, since there exist only three quiescent letters, and where necessary they must be lengthened by a certain accent when the vowel signs are added to them. That this was from ancient times common also to the Hebrews and Chaldeans, Genebrardus agrees with me, and the very method of writing and reading seems to me to show it plainly. Nor do I think those innovators imposed errors on posterity only in this part, but also in another, namely by changing vowels and often using one for another in very many words, whether through corruption of the language, or through difference of dialect, or through rashness, or by some other chance. What persuades me to believe this is the following argument: that the ancient, correct and genuine pronunciation of many words of those languages which have undergone corruption is found among foreigners rather than among the people of the nation itself. For foreigners retain almost always the same pronunciation of foreign words which they heard at first from those to whom those languages were native, no corruption having yet crept into their own idioms. On the contrary, men of any nation are accustomed to pronounce their own ancient words only corruptly, their customs of speech changing considerably over the course of years, no less than their dress and all other things. We see this has happened in Italy, where the Latin language was not only changed into Italian, but so changed that today, in words which are common to both Latin and Italian, if we speak Tuscan, that is, with greater elegance, we can hardly avoid deviating from the Latin pronunciation. Greece itself experiences the same corruption of speech, though not to so great an extent; but the Armenians, not to speak of other regions, have changed so much more that the Armenians who live in this century, unless they learn it, understand their ancient language far less than the Italians understand Latin. But that I said that the ancient and correct pronunciation of many words of any language is found among foreigners, I could prove by not a few examples; here, however, the name Caesar will be enough for us, which by Arabs, Persians, and almost all Orientals, down to this day, is customarily pronounced Caisar, the ancient manner having been utterly abolished among us. That the same thing happens with Hebrew words, so that at present some of them are pronounced less correctly by Hebrews than by other foreigners, what doubt can there be, since the Hebrew language has now been corrupted, either by the injury of time or by the rash innovation of the Masoretes and other more recent men? Many words are found, common to Hebrew and Chaldean as well as Arabic, which are indeed written in exactly the same letters by all, but are usually pronounced differently because of the different custom of those peoples in attaching vowels to them. But with due respect to the more recent Masoretes, I must say, the Arabic pronunciation pleases me more, and seems more in keeping with the usage of the ancients. For example, the word היכל [hekhal], which according to Genebrardus, in his letter to the reader in his commentaries on the Psalms, is pronounced by the Hebrews Hecal, and signifies that cupboard in the synagogue of the Hebrews where the volume of the Law is usually kept, is written by the Arabs with the same four letters, but with a different arrangement of vowels is pronounced Hikel, and rightly so. For how can it be called Hecal, if the second letter of this word is a quiescent ה, which, lacking any vowel sign or movement, can signify to the reader nothing more than a somewhat longer duration of the preceding vowel, which, if it is a long I, can properly answer to it? But if another vowel has preceded it, the sound of the letter Yod itself must contract into the preceding syllable, so that, if not Hikel, at least Heikel or Haikel should be read, through a diphthong, to speak in our manner. But Hecal, without any expression of the letter I, is in no way possible.

units.la: Diversitate autem vocalis A. vel E. in postrema hujus dictionis syllaba nihil dico, cum id parum intersit ,& motio Phatha utramque pariter possit denotare; sed de his hactenus: garrula quippe jam nimis loquacitate, ineptis his meis nugis purgatissimis auribus tuis, importuna cornix, obstrepui, quod præ tua humanitate, ut mihi ignoscas,ardenter efflagito. Libellum meum de Rege Persarum te legisse, atque fuisse delectatum, valde lætor, quid enim jucundius scribenti accidere potest, quam ab erudito viro, tui simili, sua scripta comprobari? attamen ipse, nequid arrogem, fateor, in eo libro nil a-liud esse boni, præter veritatem, cuius semper studiosissimus fui, & diligentiam, qua rerum scripturarum notitiam assequi, exactissime curavi. Quod desideras de Geographia Persici Imperii, non quidem Mathematici, sed potius Historici, ac Politici more, si ea nomina mihi fas usurpare, jam in promptu est: sed Romæ difficilis admodum librorum promulgatio experitur, ob nimium scrupulosas superiorum censuras: longe autem à me parum feliciter hæc typis traderentur, tum ob innumeros voces barbaras, in quarum orthographia si error irreperet, omnia profecto corrumperet, tum etiam quia nomina barbarra locorum, non parva cum utilitate eruditorum legentium, Romæ Persicis etiam characteribns in margine facile possent exarari, quod alibi impossibile futurum existimo, chalcographiæ defectu; verumtamen nihilominus fortasse aliquando illud etiam tibi mittam, ut de eo quod libuerit facias; obscura quæ ad hanc ætatem nobis fuere de regionibus illis, non despero futurum, ut hoc meo opusculo aliquantulum illustrentur, sed certe multo magis epistolis meis, si unquam prodierint vernacula lingua, ad amicum quondam conscriptis, in quibus universae peregrinationis meae narratio diffuse continetur.
units.tr: I say nothing about the difference between the vowel A and E in the final syllable of this word, since it matters little, and the sign Patah can denote either equally. But enough of these matters: indeed, having already become far too garrulous, an importunate crow, I have clamoured with these silly trifles of mine at your most refined ears, which, in view of your kindness, I earnestly beg you to pardon. I am very glad that you have read my little book on the King of Persia and been pleased with it, for what can happen that is more agreeable to a writer than to have his writings approved by a learned man like yourself? Yet, lest I claim too much, I confess that there is nothing good in that book besides the truth, which I have always most eagerly pursued, and the diligence with which I have taken the greatest care to attain knowledge of the matters of Scripture. As to what you wish for concerning the geography of the Persian Empire, written not in the manner of a mathematician but rather of a historian and a political writer, if I may use those terms, it is already at hand. But at Rome the publication of books is very difficult, owing to the overly scrupulous censorship of the superiors. Moreover, it would go very badly for me to have these printed far away, partly because of the countless barbarous words, in whose spelling if any error crept in it would surely corrupt everything, and partly because the barbarous names of places could easily be written out in the margin at Rome, even in Persian characters, to the no small benefit of learned readers, which I think would be impossible elsewhere for lack of engraving facilities. Nevertheless, perhaps at some time I will send you that too, so that you may do with it as you please. I do not despair that the obscure matters about those regions, which up to this age have been unknown to us, will be somewhat illuminated by this little work of mine; but certainly much more by my letters, if ever they are published in the vernacular, which I wrote to a former friend, in which the whole account of my entire journey is set out at length.

units.la: Has ut publico conceedam, eadem me remorantur difficultates, & insuper non parum laboris ac temporis, quod in illis rescribendis expoliendisque, operae pretium foret insumere. Nihil aliud reliquum est, Vir doctissime, nisi ut te rogem, curiosae cuidam exercitationi meae satisfaciendi gratia, ut ad me, cum primum rescripseris, mittas Hebraico inprimis sermone, mox & Samaritano atque unoquoque eorum propriis utriusque Linguae Characteribus, separatim, correctequae[?] scripta, eademque Latinis etiam literis, ut sonus vocalium cuiuslibet dictionis melius à me percipi possit, verba illa, quae ab ecclesia Catholica in signo sanctae crucis, necnon in Baptismate, recitari solent, videlicet, In nomine Patris, & Filii, & Spiritus San-cti ; quæ sane quamquam & ipse effor-mavi, ne forte in aliquo erraverim, abs te nihilominus magis emendata acci-pere, summopere cupio. Interim vale, & me tui observantissimum, sicut jam soles ama.
units.tr: Since I am held back by the same difficulties from making these public, and besides by no small amount of labour and time, which it would be worth spending on rewriting and polishing them, nothing remains, most learned sir, but to ask you, to satisfy a certain curious exercise of mine, to send me, as soon as you have written back, the words in Hebrew first and then in Samaritan, each in its own proper characters of the two languages, separately, corrected and written out; and the same also in Latin letters, so that I may better perceive the sound of the vowels of each word. These are the words which the Catholic Church is accustomed to recite in the sign of the holy cross, and also in Baptism, namely, "In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." Although I have formed them myself, lest perhaps I have made some error in them, I nonetheless very much desire to receive them from you in a more emended form. Meanwhile farewell, and love me, your most devoted admirer, as you already are wont to do.

units.la: Romae idibus Sept. Anno salutis MDCXXX,
units.tr: Rome, on the Ides of September, in the year of salvation 1630.

units.la: EPIST. XX.
units.tr: EPIST. XX.

units.la: Jo. Morinus Leoni Allatio. de Libris quos edidit ipse J. Morinus, de Ad-ministratione Sacramenti poenitentiae, & de antiquissimis ordinando-rum Clericorum ritibus, &c.
units.tr: Jo. Morinus to Leo Allatius, concerning the books he has published himself, on the Administration of the Sacrament of Penance, on the most ancient rites of ordaining clergy, etc.

units.la: Leoni Ablatio J. Morinus,
units.tr: To Leo Allatius from J. Morinus,

units.la: Ita officiose mecum semper egisti, quoties auxilium aliquod literarum, aut consilium à te poposci, ut semper crediderim, mihi facilem fore ad te aditum, quoties occasione sese offerente id repo-scerem; ea spe fretus te preces meas admis-furum[?] furum[?] facile confido, nec multa præfari benevolentiæ tuæ conciliandæ causa mihi necessum esse existimo : quapropter ab ipsa prece exponenda exordiar, sed prius de precis causa nonnihil mihi dicendum arbitror. Ante paucos menses copiosum volumen de administratione Sacramenti pœnitentiæ in lucem edidi, administrationem istam per duodecim secula tam in oriente quàm in occidente deduxi, varietatesq; prope omnes, quæ in eo contigerunt, enarravi; nunc fert animus, in sacras Clericorum ordinationes tam Græcas quam Latinas inquirere, & quæ deprehendi, publici juris facere; inquisitionem illam Scholastico more non instituo; id existimo hac in causa, & probationibus, quas adhibeo, plane inutile, his enim argumentis cedat universa Scholastica, & illis sese accommodet omnino necesse est, hujusmodi est totius operis ordo & ratiocinatio, in lucem edo antiquissimos ordinandorum Clericorum ritus Latinos, quorum nonnulli è codicibus mille annorum & nongentorum ætatem superantibus, multi octingentorum eruti sunt; sunt etiam posteriores. Græcos edo septem, sed antiquissimis Latinis posteriores; vetustissimus è Barberino codice exscriptus est, secundus ab eo è Cryptæ Ferratensis monasterio; tertius & quartus è Bibliotheca Vaticana, sed omnes ordinationes in illis non exhibentur, præcipuas tamen repræsentant; quintus è codice S. Andreæ Vallensis exscriptus: textus è Bibliotheca Regia; ultimus & recentior, sed omnium amplissimus Allatianus est, cujus ectypum jam ante multos annos ad me misisti; his addo librum de Sacramento ordinis Symeonis Thessalonicensis, quem Romæ è Bibliotheca Vaticana descripsi, tandem quæ de ordine scripsit Gabriel Philadelphensis, Metropolita; hæc omnia prelo matura sunt, latinitate donata, & variis adnotationibus illustrata, quibus, quæ Latinis obscura esse possunt, breviter explicantur. Ex horum comparatione manifestum est, eodem[?] plane modo ordinationes sa-[?] cras apud utramque gentem antiquitus factas esse & quæ nonnulli Scholastici opinantur esse substantialia, neutram gentem olim usurpasse. His præpono dissertationem, qua demonstratur, Ecclesiam Romanam Græcas ordinationes ante schisma, & post schisma semper & continue in hunc usque diem admisisse, & probasse; Græcos Schismaticos ad Ecclesiam conversos nunquam ordinasse, sed non modo in ea ordinatione, quam apud suos acceperant admisisse, verùm etiam ut à Græcis Catholicis more Græco, si quas ordinationes non accepissent, ordinarentur, permisisse atque etiam procurasse.
units.tr: You have always treated me so obligingly whenever I have asked you for some help or advice, by letter or in person, that I have always believed access to you would be easy for me whenever an opportunity offered itself to ask for it. Relying on that hope, I confidently expect that you will admit my requests, and I think it unnecessary to say much by way of preface to win your goodwill. I will therefore begin with the request itself, but first I think I should say something about the reason for it. A few months ago I published a large volume on the administration of the Sacrament of Penance, in which I traced that administration through twelve centuries, in both East and West, and described almost all the variations that occurred in it. Now I am inclined to inquire into the sacred ordinations of clergy, both Greek and Latin, and to make public what I have discovered. I am not conducting that inquiry in the scholastic manner. I think that approach is entirely useless for this purpose and for the proofs I am using, since all scholastic theology must yield to these arguments and must wholly adapt itself to them. Such is the order and reasoning of the whole work. I am publishing the most ancient Latin rites of ordaining clergy, some of which have been drawn from manuscripts more than 1,900 years old, and many from manuscripts of 800 years. There are also later ones. I am publishing seven Greek rites, but they are later than the most ancient Latin ones. The oldest was copied from the Barberini codex, the second from the Ferrata monastery of the Crypt, the third and fourth from the Vatican Library. These do not contain all the ordinations, but they present the principal ones. The fifth was copied from the codex of St Andrew of Vallombrosa. The text is from the Royal Library. The last and most recent, but the fullest of all, is the Allatian, of which you sent me a copy many years ago. To these I add the book on the Sacrament of Orders by Symeon of Thessalonica, which I copied in Rome from the Vatican Library, and finally what Gabriel of Philadelphia, the Metropolitan, wrote about orders. All these are ready for the press, translated into Latin and illustrated with various notes, which briefly explain whatever may be obscure to Latin readers. From comparing these it is clear that sacred ordinations were performed in antiquity in exactly the same way among both peoples, and that neither people ever used what some scholastics think are essential. I preface this with a dissertation which shows that the Roman Church has always and continually admitted and approved Greek ordinations, both before and after the schism, up to the present day. It also shows that Greek schismatics who were converted to the Church never received ordination again, but that the Church not only allowed them to keep the ordination they had received among their own people, but also permitted and even arranged that, if any of them had not received ordination, they should be ordained by Greek Catholics in the Greek manner.

units.la: His de scopo & opere meo delibatis, quid à solita in me humanitate & benevolentia tua impetrare velim, breviter expono: Cùm Romæ essem, & hæc quæstio de ordinatione Græcorum acriter agitaretur, è tomo Symeonis Archiepiscopi Thessalonicensis de Sacramentis qui in Bibliotheca Vaticana asservatur, excerpsi librum sive tractatum de Sacramento ordinis, sive sacerdotii; verum cum non liceat, ut probe scis, in ea Bibliotheca quantum libuerit immorari, brevitate temporis coactus nonnulla passim praetermisi, quæ scopo meo videbantur mihi minus[?] prodesse, ea nunc operâ & ductu tuo resarcire & complere vellem, ut illius libri editio, quam meditor, perfectior, sit & cumulatior. R. Pater Anthonius Petit, qui has literas tibi tradidit, quæcunque erunt necessaria, & jusseris Amanuensi, persolvet.
units.tr: Having briefly touched on the aim and work I have in hand, I now set out briefly what I wish to obtain from your customary kindness and goodwill. When I was in Rome, and this question about the ordination of the Greeks was being hotly debated, I excerpted from the volume on the Sacraments by Symeon, Archbishop of Thessalonica, which is kept in the Vatican Library, the book or treatise on the Sacrament of Orders or of priesthood. But since, as you well know, one is not permitted to linger as long as one likes in that library, I was forced by lack of time to omit here and there some things which seemed to me of less use for my purpose. Now I would like, with your help and guidance, to make good and complete these omissions, so that the edition of that book which I am planning may be more perfect and fuller. Father Antonio Petit, who delivers this letter to you, will pay whatever costs are necessary, and whatever you direct your scribe to charge.

units.la: Rogo tantum, ut autoritate tua descriptionis jus obtineas, Amanuensemque, qui scribere sciat Græce, eligas atque quæ scribenda sunt, prærnonstres; ut hoc commode & minimo cum labore fieri possit: quæ excripsi & quæ prætermisi in tabella huic Epistolæ conjuncta, adnoto & velut depingo: hoc insuper te rogo, ut considerato scopo & opere meo, si qua in re illud juvare potes, cum in commodum Græcorum, quorum mores sacros illustrare laboro, mihi non deneges, jam multorum debitor sum, plurium esse spero, pluribus apud te non agam, quem toties beneficum, & amicorum desideriis & commodis desudantem expertus sum.
units.tr: I ask only that, by your authority, you secure the right to make the copy, that you choose a scribe who knows how to write Greek, and that you show him what is to be written. I want this to be done conveniently and with the least possible labour. In a table enclosed with this letter I note, and as it were outline, what I have excerpted and what I have omitted. I also ask you this: if, having considered my aim and work, you can help in any way, please do not refuse me, since it is for the benefit of the Greeks, whose sacred customs I am labouring to illustrate. I am already deeply in your debt, and I hope to become more indebted, but I will not press further upon you, since I have so often found you generous and tireless in serving the wishes and interests of your friends.

units.la: EPIST. XXI.
units.tr: Letter XXI.

units.la: J. Morinus P. à Valle de libris & Lingua Samaritanorum.
units.tr: J. Morinus to P. à Valle, on the books and the Samaritan language.

units.la: Perillustri viro, Petro à Valle Romano Patricio Domino meo admodum colendo Jo. Morinus S. D.
units.tr: To the most illustrious man, Pietro della Valle, Roman patrician, my most esteemed lord: J. Morinus sends greetings.

units.la: Jure mihi succensere potuisti, quòd literis tuis respondere tamdiu distulerim. Videri enim potui parum gratus memoriamque beneficii accepti admodum subito ex animo excussisse: id tamen vitii quod à me longissime semper abfuit, diuturni mei silentii minime causa fuit, scribendi tarditatem alia pepererunt. R. P. Bertinus, qui literas tuas mihi reddidit, temporis in itinere suo plurimum consumpsit, multo verò magis supellex ipsius, quæ cum Illustrissimi Nũntii[?] supellectile vehebatur. Nudius tertius tantùm Pentateuchum tuum sanum, integrum, nulla sui parte laceratum, contortum aut maculatum accepi, ante autem libri tui felicem vectionem, ad te scribere nolebam, ne de literis tuis sine libro acceptis nuntio adveniente libri in periculum adducti scrupulum injicerem, admodum autem oportunus advenit; nam folium postremum sub prælo erat Exercitationum Ecclesiasticarum, quas in Samaritanorum Pentateuchum elaboravi, specimina autem Pentateuchi ad calcem libri exhibere statui. Itaque cum tuum nactus sim, utriusque conjunctim exhibiturus sum. Initio Exercitationum Pentateuchum tuum describo, & ex speciminibus quæ olim ad me misisti, judicium facio, nunc autem quæ sperabam beneficio & diligentia tua me consecutum scripsi; quacunque data occasione Exercitationum istarum te participem faciam: Proponebam mihi primùm tria aut quatuor foliola, non plura in Samaritani Pentateuchi illustrationem typis committere, sed discendi studio in justi libelli mensuram sub prelo creverunt : Verùm his præteritis ad librum tuum redeo.
units.tr: You could justly be angry with me for putting off my reply to your letter for so long. I may have seemed ungrateful and to have all but forgotten the kindness I received so suddenly. Yet that fault, from which I have always been far removed, was in no way the cause of my long silence; other things produced the delay in writing. Reverend Father Bertinus, who handed me your letter, spent a great deal of time on his journey, and his baggage even more so, since it was carried along with the baggage of the most illustrious Nuncio. Only three days ago I received your Pentateuch, safe, whole, and in no part torn, twisted or stained. Before the book's happy arrival I did not want to write to you, lest news of your letter arriving without the book should cast doubt on the book's safety. It came at a very opportune moment, for the last sheet of my Ecclesiastical Exercises, which I have worked out on the Samaritan Pentateuch, was already at the press, and I had resolved to give specimens of the Pentateuch at the end of the book. So, since I now have yours, I shall present both together. At the beginning of the Exercises I describe your Pentateuch and form a judgment of it from the specimens you once sent me; now I have written what I hoped to gain through your kindness and diligence. On whatever occasion offers, I will make you a sharer in these Exercises. At first I planned to commit to print only three or four leaves to illustrate the Samaritan Pentateuch, but out of eagerness to learn, they grew under the press to the size of a fair-sized booklet. Setting these aside, I return to your book.

units.la: Cùm primùm illum accepi, nonnulla contuli cum nostro ; nostri, id est, Hebræi interpretationem deprehendi literæ adeo mordicus adhærentem, ut hac in parte omnes interpretes superare mihi videatur, duo quidem verba offendi, quæ periphrasi vertebantur, non illa multiplicante verba, sed sensum unius verbi altero verbo reddente : scribæ etiam hallucinationem semel aut iterum, Aleph pro Tau scribentis ; legi præterea, quæ in fine à scriba addita sunt ; illa sunt Hebraica ut constat ex prima linea, & nonnullis aliis dictionibus, quæ integrè scribuntur, cætera quæ plurima compendia sunt dictionum, quæ imperfecte scribuntur, illa autem pleraque nihil a-liud sunt, quàm Rabinorum, de quibus mentio fit, honorificæ appellationes, quales in nostro Pentateucho plures integrè describuntur : sensus autem additamenti istius hic esse mihi videtur, scrip-sit hanc legem sanctam servus, &c. & tradidit eam Josepho filio Justitiæ, filio Josephi sacerdotis in Damasco, & correxit eam Abraham de filiis Matar anno nongentesimo & vicesimo regni Ismaelitarum decima mensis Elul, itaqve anno Christi, 1542. scriptus est, character & papyrus alteram ætatem non videntur arguere; dicam præterea sectiones istius codicis sectionibus nostri omnino pares esse, unoqve & eodem nomine קציץ appellari in fine Geneseos 250. adnotantur; in fine Exodi 200, in fine Levit. 130. totidem in nostro iisdem locis numerantur, ad finem Numerorum & Deuter. in tuo omissæ sunt: sed æqvalitatem ubiqve esse non ambigo.
units.tr: As soon as I received it, I compared some passages with our text. I found that the Hebrew, that is, our own version, clings so closely to the letter that in this respect it seems to me to surpass all the translators. I did come across two words that are rendered by a periphrasis, not by multiplying words, but by giving the sense of one word with another word. I also noticed once or twice a slip of the scribe, who wrote Aleph for Tau. I have read, moreover, the things that the scribe added at the end. They are in Hebrew, as is clear from the first line and from some other words written in full; most of the rest are abbreviations of words written incompletely, and these are mostly nothing other than the honorific titles of the rabbis mentioned, of which many are written out in full in our Pentateuch. The sense of this addition seems to me to be: This holy law was written by the servant, etc., and handed down to Joseph, son of Justice, son of Joseph the priest, in Damascus, and Abraham of the sons of Matar corrected it in the nine hundred and twentieth year of the kingdom of the Ishmaelites, on the tenth day of the month Elul, and so it was written in the year of Christ 1542. The script and the paper do not seem to indicate an older age. I will add that the sections of this codex are altogether equal to the sections of ours. In both they are called by the same name, qatsatz [קציץ]: at the end of Genesis 250 are noted, at the end of Exodus 200, at the end of Leviticus 130, and as many are counted in ours in the same places. At the end of Numbers and Deuteronomy they are omitted in yours. But I do not doubt that the equality holds everywhere.

units.la: Petis à me expressionem istorum verborum, in nomine Patris & Filii & Spiritus sancti, Hebraice & Samaritice; sic Hebraice efferri debent beschem abuben veruach haqvodesch, בשם אב ובן ורוח הקדש Samaritani ita efferent[?]: [illegible, ~8 letters] qvomodo pronuntient ista Samaritani, hoc est, ut Judæorum more loqvar, qvibus punctis loqvendo illa afficerent, divinare licet, non demonstrare ; hoc disci non potest, nisi ex Grammatica, aut ex ipsorum Samaritanorum pronuntiantium auditu. Ego sic pronunciarem Bescham Ab ubar veriach quadesch, quod ad virgulas, quas dictionum quibusdam literis imminentes animadvertisti, multo frequentiores sunt in nostro codice, qvàm in tuo; usu autem didici, illis significare, verbum in usitatiori significatione esse sumendum, vel verbum passivè intelligendum, vel contra formam scribi vel quid simile.
units.tr: You ask me for the expression of these words, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, in Hebrew and Samaritan. In Hebrew they should be pronounced beschem abuben veruach haqvodesch [בשם אב ובן ורוח הקדש]. How the Samaritans would pronounce it, I will put it: [illegible], and how they would pronounce these words, that is, to speak in the manner of the Jews, with what vowel points they would mark them in speaking, one may guess but not show. This cannot be learned except from grammar or from hearing the Samaritans themselves pronounce it. I would pronounce it thus: Bescham Ab ubar veriach quadesch. As for the little strokes that you noticed above certain letters of some words, they are much more frequent in our codex than in yours. I have learned from use that they signify that the word is to be taken in its more common meaning, or that the word is to be understood passively, or, on the contrary, that the form is to be written otherwise, or something of the sort.

units.la: De Hebraicarum dictionum pronunciatione plane tibi assentior, multisqve argumentis demonstrare possem antiqvissimos Judæos multa aliter pronuntiasse, qvam jubeant Masorethicæ censuræ, ut ineptissimas lectionis eorum argutiolas præterea.
units.tr: I entirely agree with you about the pronunciation of Hebrew words. I could show by many arguments that the most ancient Jews pronounced many things differently from what the Masoretic rules require, and I could add their most foolish little subtleties of reading.

units.la: Cum desideres Sectionum, capitum & versuum tuo codici adnotationem, hoc sedulò & terse inter legendum præstabo.
units.tr: Since you desire a notation of the sections, chapters and verses for your codex, I will carry this out carefully and neatly while I read.

units.la: Qvæ de Persici imperii Historica & Politica Geographia scripsisti, sive literis ad amicos, sive libri, in hanc rem de industria compositis, si mihi commiseris, curabo, ut quàm emendatè hic typis mandentur; cura tantum, ut correctè describantur; cæterorum vadem me tibi sisto. Clarissimus vir D. Ie Jay, qui Bibliorum magnorum editionem suscepit, & propriis sumptibus præstat, gratias mirùm quàm maximas agit commodati Pentateuchi. Vale Domine mihi omnibusque literarum alumnis colendissime, & me ama 3o. Jan. 1631,
units.tr: As for what you have written on the historical and political geography of the Persian empire, whether in letters to friends or in a book composed for this purpose, if you entrust it to me I will see to it that it is printed here as correctly as possible. Only take care that it is copied correctly; I will answer for the rest. The most distinguished man, Mr. Le Jay, who has undertaken the edition of the great Bible at his own expense, gives you very great thanks for the lent Pentateuch. Farewell, Sir, most esteemed by me and by all the students of letters, and love me. 30 January 1631.

units.la: EPIST. XXII.
units.tr: LETTER XXII.

units.la: P. à Valle J. Morino, de Chronologia Mahumadanorum quid à Persa rerum Mathematicarum peritissimo didicerit, explicat.
units.tr: Pietro della Valle to Giovanni Morino, explaining what he learned from a Persian most skilled in mathematics about the Muslim chronology.

units.la: Reverendo Patri atque eruditissimo Domino meo Patri Joanni Morino Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero Petrus à Valle Peregrinus S. P. D.
units.tr: To the reverend Father and most learned Lord, my Father Giovanni Morino, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory: Pietro della Valle the Pilgrim sends greetings.

units.la: NUdius tertius accepi, vir clarissime humanissimas literas tuas, quibus mihi significasti adventum R. Patris Bertini, teque ab eo Pentateuchum optimè custocustoditum, uti optabam, recepisse. Id mihi pergratum fuit; namque multis abhinc diebus pervenisse istuc Pontificis nuncium, apud nos fama vulgaverat, & cum mihil abs te de Patre Bertino, nec de libro audirem, incipiebam quidem in aliquam incidere suspicionem, ne quid forte sinistri in itinere illis accidisset. Imprimis summopere jucundum mihi fuit, Pentateuchum ad te fuisse delatum, antequam Exercitationes tuæ Ecclesiasticæ prodirent, ut in illis perficiendis, si quid opus erit, tibi præsto sit. Easdem ipse Exercitationes, quibus me ditare promittis, non mediocri cum desiderio expecto, novi enim, quanta eruditione resertæ sint futuræ; verba illa, quæ Hebraice ac Samaritice à te reddita misisti, perquam grata mihi evenere, innumeras de illis tibi gratias ago, nec non de eo quod scribis, te operam daturum, ut lucubrationum mearum si aliquid ad te mittam, typis istic emendate mandetur, id mihi summi beneficii loco futurum esse non dubites, quo ut quam primum perfruar, brevi aliqvam earum ad te mitere non desinam, qvam exactissime exaratam. De Anno Christi, nempe 1542. si recte qvod scripsisti legi, vel 1592. penultima namqve hujus numeri figura non satis bene mihi perspicua fuit, licet priori potius modo qvam secundo exaratam fuisse exi-stimem, qvo qvidem anno tibi persvades Pentateuchum meum fuisse scriptum, annotaverit scriba se id præstitisse anno nongentesimo & vigesimo regni Ismaëlitarum, non facile tibi assentior: hoc e-nim mihi certo constat, annum servatoris nostri 1622. qvo ipse in Perside eram, anno Ismaëlitarum 1031. majori ex parte respondisse, qvemadmodum etiam, ut ex literis ad me Constantinopoli da-tis postqvam Romam reversus fui, col-legi, ejusdem servatoris annum 1627. Muhammedanorum Hegiræ anno 1027. fere prorsus respondere: qvod si accurate perpendamus, nec non Ismaëlitarum annum lunarem esse undecim circiter diebus minorem nostro, qvi solaris est, transactos annos retrorsum supputando, certo tamen considerato utriusque anni iterum numero, facile reperies, annum Ismaëlitarum nongentesimum & vigesimum in Annum Christi 1514. vel certe 1515. circiter incidere., Memini Davidem Origanum in altera suarum Ephemeridum parte eorundem annorum, nostri scilicet ac Saracenici, collationem facere; liber iste apud me non est modo: tu illum consulere poteris, attamen quod dixi de annis nostræ salutis 1622.& 1627. eos nimirum respondere annis Muhamedanorum 1031[?]. & 1036. pro certissimo habeas, quidquid in hanc sententiam Origanus adferat, vel alii quicunque[?]; hoc enim ipse, inter Mahumedanos diu versatus, in eorum scriptis atque libris sæ-pe ac sæpius observatum, oculatus testis omnibus dubio procul affirmo; & ne quid in hoc arg[illegible, ~2 letters]mento desideres, si forte hujus rei certitudinem assequi cupies, ut in interpretatione Pentateuchi,de illius scriptionis tempore differendo ab omni erroris offensione magis securus incedas, tria hic subjungere non pigebit. Primum quidem, unde cimam[?] diem mensis Aprilis anni Redemptionis nostræ 1586. qua ipse die natus sum, à doctissimo quodam Persa Mathematicarumque Exerciotatinum[?] peritissimo viro, mihi familiaritate conjuncto, qui meæ genituræ cœlestem, ut moris est, figuram, quam apud me habeo, erigere voluit, annorum supputatione sedulo facta, vigesimam secundam diem mensis Rabia etthani, hoc est Rabia secundi (qui mensis in anno quartus est ordine) anni Mahumedicæ Hegiræ 994. Persice scriptam fuisse, secundo vero vigesimam primam diem Martii, qua sol primum punctum Arietis ingredi solet, unde anni solaris initium exactissime Astrologorum more Persæ assumunt, Anno Christi 1622. me, ut dixi, in Perside apud eos-dem Astrologos commorante, uti notatum est in Ephemeride Persica illius an-ni, quæ duplex apud me extat, à duobus nempe Mathematicis separatim elaborata in octavam diem mensis Gemadhiel ouvcl[?], hoc est, Gemadhi prioris, qui mensis qvintus est illis ordine, anni qvidem Hegiræ Muhamedicæ 1031, incidisse. Tertio deniqve, vigesimam sextam diem Junii, Anni Domini 1627, à Turcis Constantinopoli duodecimam mensis, Sceuval, qvi decimus est ordine, anni eorum Hegiræ 1036, fuisse numeratam, hæc autem sunt nomina mensium Arabicorum, qvibus Muhammedani fere omnes in describendis fastis, ut ita dicam, utuntur; 1. Muharrem. 2. Sefer. 3. Rabia eleuvel vel primus. 4. Rabia etthani sive secundus. 5. Gemadhi eleuvel. 6. Gemadhi etthani. 7. Regeb. 8. Scioaban, 9. Ramadhan. 10. Sceuval. 11. Dhilcaade. 12. Dhilhagge; & hi omnes sunt lunares, sex [?]30. diebus, sex vero 29. alternatim constantes, nisi aliqva intercalatio-ad adæqvandas novilunia cum mensium principiis occurat, qvæ triginta qvolibet, sive viginti novem, ni fallor annorum spatio, undecies certo ordine apponi solet ad calcem postremi mensis, qvi tunc addita intercalari die, & ipse 30. diebus terminatur. Persæ alios habent menses solares, & aliam solarium annorum supputationem, quam docti non ignorant, & æram Gelalinem appellant, à Rege quodam Gelal nomine, qui illam instituit; sed & ipsi ut plurimum in scriptis & in usu quotidiano, sicut & Turcæ, non alia prorsus quam Arabicâ à me superius memorata æra utuntur, utpote quæ religionis est, nihil enim est aliud Hegira Muhammedis, nisi ejusdem Muhammedis fuga, sive exilium ab urbe Meka voluntarium, necessariumque religionis causa, quando ob ineptias suæ legis, quas promulgare inceperat, resistentibus populis, illumq; ut par erat, dignis poenis afficere volentibus, patria illi cedere necessum fuit: sed jam nimis hisce nugis te defatigavi.
units.tr: The day before yesterday I received your most courteous letter, most distinguished sir, in which you informed me of the arrival of the reverend Father Bertini, and that you had received the Pentateuch from him, well preserved, as I had hoped. This pleased me greatly. For the rumour here had long since spread that the papal messenger had reached you, and since I heard nothing from you about Father Bertini or the book, I began to suspect that some misfortune had perhaps befallen them on the journey. Above all, it was most welcome to me that the Pentateuch reached you before your Ecclesiastical Exercitations appear, so that it may be at hand for completing them, if anything is needed. I myself await those same Exercitations, which you promise to send me, with no small longing, for I know how full of learning they will be. The words that you sent me, rendered by you in Hebrew and Samaritan, have been most pleasing to me, and I give you countless thanks for them, as well as for your statement that you will take care to have anything of my writings that I send you printed there correctly. Do not doubt that this will be counted by me as a very great kindness. In order to enjoy this as soon as possible, I will not cease to send you shortly some of them, written out as exactly as possible. Concerning the year of Christ, namely 1542 (or 1592, if I have read correctly what you wrote; the penultimate figure of this number was not clear enough to me), though I think it was written in the former way rather than the latter, in which year you persuade yourself that my Pentateuch was written: I do not readily agree that the scribe noted that he had done this in the nine hundred and twentieth year of the reign of the Ishmaelites. For this I hold as certain: the year of our Saviour 1622, in which I myself was in Persia, corresponded for the most part to the year 1031 of the Ishmaelites. Likewise, as I have gathered from letters dated to me at Constantinople after I returned to Rome, the year 1627 of the same Saviour almost exactly corresponds to the year 1027 of the Hegira of Muhammad. If we weigh this carefully, and also count back the years elapsed, taking into account that the Ishmaelite year, being lunar, is about eleven days shorter than ours, which is solar, yet after again considering the number of each year, you will easily find that the nine hundred and twentieth year of the Ishmaelites falls about the year 1514 or certainly 1515 of Christ. I remember that David Origanus, in the second part of his Ephemerides, compares these years, namely ours and the Saracen. That book is not with me now; you may consult it. Yet, whatever Origanus or anyone else may bring forward to the contrary, you may hold for certain that the years 1622 and 1627 of our salvation correspond to the years 1031 and 1036 of the Muslims. For I, having lived for a long time among the Muslims, affirm this without doubt as an eyewitness, having observed it again and again in their writings and books. And so that you may lack nothing in this matter, should you wish to attain certainty of this fact, so that you may proceed more safely, free from any offence of error, in interpreting the Pentateuch and in deciding the time of its writing, I will not hesitate to add three points here. First, the twenty-second day of the month of Rabi' al-Thani, that is, of the second Rabi' (which is the fourth month in order of the year), in the year 994 of the Muslim Hegira, was the day on which, by the careful calculation of years, a certain very learned Persian, a man skilled in mathematics and joined to me in friendship, drew up (as is customary) the celestial figure of my nativity, which I have, and wrote it in Persian. That day was the twenty-sixth of April in the year of our Redemption 1586, on which I myself was born. Second, the twenty-first day of March, on which the sun is accustomed to enter the first point of Aries, from which the Persians, following the practice of the astrologers most exactly, take the beginning of the solar year, in the year of Christ 1622, when I, as I said, was staying in Persia with these same astrologers, fell on the eighth day of the month Jumada al-Ula, that is, of the first Jumada (which is the fifth month in their order), in the year 1031 of the Muslim Hegira, as is noted in the Persian Ephemeris of that year, of which I have two copies, separately prepared by two mathematicians. Third and last, the twenty-sixth day of June, in the year of the Lord 1627, was counted by the Turks at Constantinople as the twelfth day of the month Shawwal, which is the tenth in order, in their year 1036 of the Hegira. These are the names of the Arabic months, which nearly all Muslims use in drawing up their calendars, so to speak: 1. Muharram. 2. Safar. 3. Rabi' al-Awwal or the first. 4. Rabi' al-Thani or the second. 5. Jumada al-Ula. 6. Jumada al-Thaniya. 7. Rajab. 8. Sha'ban. 9. Ramadan. 10. Shawwal. 11. Dhu al-Qa'da. 12. Dhu al-Hijja. All of these are lunar, alternately consisting of thirty and twenty-nine days, unless an intercalation occurs in order to bring the new moons into agreement with the beginnings of the months. This is usually inserted eleven times in a cycle of years, I believe, at the end of the last month, which, with the intercalary day added, then ends on its thirtieth day. The Persians have other solar months and another reckoning of solar years, which the learned do not ignore, and which they call the Jalali era, after a certain king named Jalal, who instituted it. But they too, for the most part, in their writings and daily use, like the Turks, use no other era than the Arabic one I mentioned above, since it belongs to their religion. For the Hegira of Muhammad is nothing other than the flight of Muhammad himself, or his voluntary and necessary exile from the city of Mecca for the sake of religion. When the people resisted him, because of the absurdities of his law which he had begun to promulgate, and wished to inflict on him the punishments he deserved, he was obliged to withdraw from his homeland. But I have already wearied you too much with these trifles.

units.la: Ob diligentiam, qua polliceris, te in Pentateucho inter legendum capitum & versuum numeros adnotaturum, maxime tibi sum devinctus, eodemque tui beneficio multo perfectior evadet. Clarissimo Domino le Jay meo nomine salutem dicas rogo; & ut viro de bonis literis optime merito, me quoque illi una cum orbe universo plurimum debere, fac quæso certiorem; si apud me aliquid aliud reperiri compererit, quod ad publicam utilitatem desideret, paratus sum, omnibus quæ possideo, & ipsi, & literatorum reipublicæ inservire. Tu interim vale, amantissime Pater mihiqve semper & bonis omnibus merito apprimeqve Reverende, & mei memor vive tui observantissimi.
units.tr: I am very much indebted to you for your diligence, which you promise, in reading through the Pentateuch, to note the numbers of the chapters and verses, and through your kindness it will become much more complete. Please give my greetings to the most distinguished Monsieur Le Jay on my behalf, and, since he has deserved very well of good letters, please let him know that I too, together with the whole world, owe him very much. If he discovers that I have anything else that he needs for the public benefit, I am ready to serve him and the republic of letters with all that I possess. Meanwhile, farewell, most loving Father, always dear to me and, deservedly, most reverend in every way, and remember me as your most devoted servant.

units.la: Romæ, Idibus Martii partæ salutis Anno MDCXXXI.
units.tr: At Rome, on the Ides of March, in the year of the saved one, 1631.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo Patri, atque eruditissimo Domino suo, Patri J. Morino Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero, Petrus à Valle Peregrinus S.P.D.
units.tr: To the most reverend Father and most learned Lord, Father Jean Morin, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, from Peter della Valle the Pilgrim, with greetings.

units.la: NUnquam molestè tuli, mirificè, cultè atque amantissime mi Pater,
units.tr: I have never been troubled, most admirable, courteous and dearest Father,

units.la: Jo. Morino's name and the Latin salutation are printed in italic; the dateline is set in italic roman. Samaritanorum Pentateuchum, quem transactis mensibus, ut typis mandaretur, ad te miseram, adhuc mihi non fuisse remissum; consulto enim putabam id fieri, nempe ut is, usque ad extremum operis absolutionem tibi inservire posset, tantum hortantibus amicis, ut alia quaedam, in eundem finem in Gallias allegarem, respondi, me, priusquam alia mitterem, velle inspicere, procuratæ antea Pentateuchi impressionis diu expectatum exitum: qva nimirum sui, merqve[?] felicitate liber iste prodiret, atque ex illius fato de reliquis postea decreturum. Nam de futuro ad votum hujus libri eventu non de festinata exemplaris restitutione, me summopere sollicitum fuisse, & qvousqve id intuear, mirum in modum continuo futurum, sincere fateor. Amplissimus vir nostriqve studiosissimus Dominus Perescius, qvi mittendi olim ad te Pentateuchi primus certe mihi auctor extitit, optime novit, qvis sit meus hac super re sensus: qvanto scilicet ardeam desiderio vulgationis hujus Pentateuch à te Latine redditi, ut publico bono con-sulatur; & quo denique pacto publicæ istius utilitatis curam ac diligentiam quoque meam, quà fieri potest, participem fore enixe cupiam. Ille idcirco te de his, atque de aliis, ut exopto, certio-rem facere non desinet, ac præsertim de summa animi mei erga te propensione: teque, ut illi in omnibus indubitatam, quam meretur, fidem exhibeas, etiam atque etiam rogo: atque illud præcipue, amicitiam tuam me tanti facere, ut nemo pluris virtutes, quibus es præditus, quam qui maxime venerari; nihilque de-mum magis in votis habere, quam occa-sionem nancisci, ut tibi ex animi sententia inservire, atque aliquod observantiæ in te meæ non vulgare argumentum o-stendere valeam. Vale Vir Doctissime, & me amare perge, ut soles. Romæ.
units.tr: that the Samaritan Pentateuch, which I sent you some months ago to be printed, has not yet been returned to me. For I deliberately thought this was being done so that the copy could serve you right up to the final completion of the work. When friends urged me to send some other books to France for the same purpose, I replied that before sending others I wished to see the long-awaited outcome of the earlier printing of the Pentateuch, so that this book might come out under its own good fortune, and that I would decide about the rest afterwards according to its fate. For I sincerely confess that I have not been anxious about a speedy return of the copy, but about how this book will turn out as we wish; and so far as I can see, it will prove wonderfully successful in the long run. That most distinguished man and our most devoted Lord Peiresc, who was certainly the first to advise me to send you the Pentateuch, knows very well what my feeling is on this matter: how eagerly I desire the publication of this Pentateuch translated into Latin by you, for the public good, and how earnestly I wish my own care and diligence, as far as possible, to share in that public usefulness. He will therefore not cease to keep you informed about these matters and others, as I wish, and especially about the great inclination of my mind towards you. And I ask you again and again to give him the full trust he deserves in all things. Above all, I value your friendship so highly that no one venerates the virtues with which you are endowed more than I do; and finally I have nothing more at heart than to find an opportunity to serve you as I wish and to show a considerable token of my respect for you. Farewell, most learned man, and go on loving me as you are wont. Rome.

units.la: Doctissimæ Exercitationes, qvas à te nuper elaboratas, dilecte mi Pater, semperqve observande Morine, uti pollicitus fueras, ad me misisti, à R. R. Patribus Congregationis tuæ mihi redditæ fuerunt; earum lectione mirum in modum sum delectatus: nec prius ad te re-scribere volui, qvam illas, ut feci, à principio ad finem avidissime evolverem. Omnia reperi, sicut jam mente conceperam, non minus doctrina qvam curiosa novitate, & summa demum eruditione referta, qvæ præcipue, de Cabbala ex-plicasti, mihi perjucunda fuere: diue-nim aliqvid certi rescire concupiveram de reconditis istis Judæorum mysteriolis; non tamen ab ipsis, qvos in omni scientia vanissimos esse jampridem com-pereram. De Cabbalisticis hisce inter-pretationibus, ex Arabum, Persarumq; ac Turcarum Monumentis, à Talmudi-stis, stis, ut puto, mutuatis aliquid jam & ipse delibaveram; sed certe primis tantum labiis, qvippe qvi res illas tanqvam levissimi ponderis contempseram; qvinimo primis, qvæ inspexeram, illius artis fundamentis, ipse etiam proprio Marte nonnulla alia philosophando adstruxeram, qvæ num Hebræis sint usitata, ex te cognoscere mihi pergratum erit: videlicet, non modo ex literarum numeris, seu simplicibus seu qvadratis, iisqve excerptis, vel ex literis simpliciter vel ex literarum nominibus expansis in qvalibet dictione, aut nomine, vel si mavis sententia, aliqvam reconditi sensus interpretationem Gmetrice, ut loqvuntur, elici posse; verum etiam, eodem numero denuo in literas commutato, ex significatione dictionis, qvæ ex resultantibus literis emergit; exempli gratia; ex venerabili nomine Jesu, qvod ab Arabibus scribitur Isua ישוע[?] si literarum numeros supputemus, colligentur 146. qvo numero iterum in literas resoluto exorietur dictio Caʋin משיח[?], qvæ Arabice sonat Inservire. Recte igitur dicetur de Domino Nostro Jesu Christo, qui, ut iniquitates nostras ipse portaret, servi formam induit, uti scriptum est; attamen hujus-modi interpretationes fallacissimas esse, ac persæpe ineptissimas, bifariam demonstratur; primo quidem, ut in exer-citationibus prudentissime notasti, quia licet aliquando forte fortuito hac inter-pretandi ratione, sensus valde appositi ex di-ctionibus eliciantur, nihilominus sæpe ac sæpius aut nulli deducuntur aut insulsissimi, & quod pejus est, non semel impii: secundo vero, quia sensus isti di-ctionibus, unde eruuntur, sunt nimis communes; nec verisimile est, eidem dictioni vel nomini, vel sententiæ, ubi-cunque collocatæ, eosdem prorsus sen-sus omni tempore adaptari posse. Sexcenti reperiuntur Johannes, & Pauli, & horum alii viri optimi existent, alii pessimi, singulique ob morum conditionisque varietatem inter se valde diversi; quis igitur existimabit, his omnibus, & unicuique eorum eosdem sensus apposite applicari posse, quos ex consimili nominum interpretatione extrahere licebit? quod ad Notaricum attinet, Arabes, Turcæ ac Persæ eo passim utuntur, brevitatis causa, in describendis tabulis Astronomicis, Ephemeridibus, Fastis, & quæ sunt his similia, ita ut absque illius notitia ejusmodi libros quis intelligere non possit. Ego autem illud parvi facio, licet penitus non ignorare necessarium duxerim, quia genus est scribendi erroribus quam maxime obnoxium, cum propter notarum inter se similitudinem, aliam pro alia usurpari, tum ab inerudi-tis amanuensibus tum à lectoribus non satis expertis, facillimum sit. Sed de his hactenus; tantum cupio, ut me quoque certiorem reddas, quibus notis apud Hebræos designentur millenaria & centenaria supra 400. nam Arabibus ad millenarium usque designandum propriæ ac peculiares sunt literæ, cum eorum Alphabetum sex literis plusquam Hebraicum abundet; illæque sunt, quæ respon-dent [illegible, ~7 letters], quando molles pronuntiantur, ut apud Chaldæos in usu est, præsertim in dictionibus Arabicis describendis: quod tamen ignoro, an Hebræis etiam sit commune, an potius, pro mil-lenariis designandis, primas literas, simplicium numerorum significativas, usur-pent, quæ ante notas centenariorum col-locatæ apud Arabes etiam aliquando millenaria designant. Sed missis his, quæ forsitan plus, quàm par erat, tibi tæ-dii attulere, modo reliquum est, ut gratias quas referre non possum, tibi saltem innumeras agam, non modo de libro transmisso, verùm etiam quod plurimi faciendum est, de multiplici honore, quo me in illo prosecutus es, tot tantisque laudibus me supra quam mereor, ex-tollendo. Erubui sane quoties in illas incidi: at blandientis sibi animi titilla-tionem quis compescet? mei profecto imbecillitatem ut fatear necesse est: non possum his laudibus licet immeritis sum-mopere non oblectari, quippe quæ, tui beneficio, laudatissimi viri nomen meum tam honorifice immortalitati commendant, ex quo quantum tibi debeam, verbis exprimi posse non duco: manebit tamen dum vixero, alta mente repostum. Duo supersunt, quae ab humanitate tua abstinere non possum, quin enixe efflagitem; primum quidem, ut in impressione Samaritani nostri Pentateuchi versione Latina illum minime defraudes: nam, etsi versio Latina Hebræo Samaritani Samaritano etiam, ut ostendis, est communis, cum iste illius sit exactissima translatio, lectori tamen permolestum erit, Samaritani sententiae quomodo Latine efferantur, longe alibi inquirere, & dubii semper aliquid apud ipsum remanebit, num verba ubique singula singulis bene respondeant: at e contra versionem Latinam, licet prorsus eamdem utrique[?] suis in locis apponere quid erit impendii? Alterum, quod expecto, est, ut quamvis codex iste Samaritanus magnis illis Bi-bliis adjunctus prodirumus[?] sit, non desinas tamen curare, ut seorsim etiam cum propria illius versione Latina imprimatur, quo facilius omnibus illo perfrui li-ceat; ceat; quod publicæ utilitati quam maxime conducturum existimo, nam magna illa biblia, quæ immania sunt volumina, & magni pretii, cuilibet præsto esse non facile poterunt. Pluribus non est cur te defatigem: tantum vale, & me tibi devinctissimum vivere pro certo habeas.
units.tr: I received through the Reverend Fathers of your Congregation the most learned Exercitationes, dear Father and ever to be honoured Morin, which you recently finished and, as you promised, sent to me. I was wonderfully delighted by reading them, and I did not wish to write back until I had read them eagerly from beginning to end, as I did. I found everything just as I had already imagined: full of learning, of curious novelty and of the highest erudition. What you have explained about the Cabbala gave me the greatest pleasure, for I had long wanted to learn something certain about those hidden little mysteries of the Jews, though not from the Jews themselves, whom I had long since found to be most vain in every kind of learning. About these Cabbalistic interpretations, drawn from the Arab, Persian and Turkish monuments and borrowed, I think, from the Talmudists, I had already tasted something myself, but only with the tip of my lips, since I had despised those things as being of the lightest weight. Indeed, on the first principles of that art which I had looked into, I had myself, by my own effort, built up some other philosophical points. It will be most welcome to me to learn from you whether these are customary among the Hebrews: namely, that by the numbers of the letters, whether simple or square, and by those excerpted from them, or from the letters taken singly, or from the expanded names of the letters in any word or name, or if you prefer, sentence, some hidden sense can be drawn out Gematrice, as they say; and further, that by the same number turned back again into letters, from the meaning of the word that emerges from the resulting letters, something can be derived. For example, from the venerable name of Jesus, which the Arabs write Isua [ישוע], if we count the numerical values of the letters, we get 146. Turning this number back into letters again, there arises the word Caʋin [משיח], which in Arabic means Inservire, that is, to serve. So it will rightly be said of our Lord Jesus Christ that, in order to bear our iniquities himself, he took the form of a servant, as it is written. Yet it is shown in two ways that interpretations of this kind are most deceptive and very often most absurd. First, as you very prudently noted in the Exercitationes, although sometimes by chance, through this method of interpreting, senses quite apt may be drawn out of words, nevertheless again and again either none are drawn out or they are most silly and, what is worse, not once impious. Second, because those senses are too common to the words from which they are drawn. Nor is it likely that the same senses can always be fitted to the same word or name, or sentence, wherever it is placed. There are countless Johns and Pauls, and of these some are most excellent men, others most wicked, and each is very different from the others because of the variety of their characters and conditions. Who, then, will think that the same senses which may be extracted from a similar interpretation of names can be aptly applied to all of them and to each one of them? As for the Notaricon, the Arabs, Turks and Persians use it everywhere, for the sake of brevity, in describing astronomical tables, ephemerides, calendars and things similar to these, so that no one can understand such books without knowing it. I, however, make little of it, although I have thought it necessary not to be wholly ignorant of it, since it is a kind of writing most liable to error, both because of the similarity of the signs to one another, so that one is taken for another, and because it is very easy for unlearned copyists and for readers not sufficiently experienced to go wrong. But so much for this. I only wish you would also let me know by what signs the Hebrews designate thousands and hundreds above 400. For the Arabs have particular and peculiar letters for designating up to the thousands, since their alphabet has six more letters than the Hebrew. These are the letters that correspond to [illegible] when they are pronounced softly, as is the custom among the Chaldeans, especially in writing Arabic words. I do not know, however, whether this is also common to the Hebrews, or whether, for designating thousands, they use the first letters, which signify the simple numbers, and which, placed before the signs for hundreds, sometimes also designate thousands among the Arabs. But setting aside these matters, which have perhaps wearied you more than was fitting, it remains only that I should thank you, at least in countless words, for the gifts I cannot repay: not only for the book sent to me, but also, which is of the greatest importance, for the manifold honour with which you have treated me in it, extolling me with so many and such great praises beyond what I deserve. I blushed indeed each time I came across them, but who can check the tickling of a mind that flatters itself? I must confess my own weakness: I cannot help being greatly pleased by these praises, however undeserved, since, through your kindness, the name of a most praiseworthy man commends mine to immortality so honourably. I do not think I can express in words how much I owe you for this; it will remain, however, laid up deep in my mind as long as I live. Two things remain which I cannot refrain from earnestly asking of your kindness. The first is that in the printing of the Latin version of our Samaritan Pentateuch you should by no means cheat it. For although the Latin version is common to the Hebrew and the Samaritan text, as you show, since that is the most exact translation of it, nevertheless it will be very troublesome for the reader to seek elsewhere how the sense of the Samaritan is rendered in Latin, and there will always remain some doubt whether the individual words everywhere correspond well to the individual words. But on the other hand, what expense would it be to place the Latin version, quite the same, in each of their places? The second thing I look for is this: although that Samaritan codex has been published attached to those great Bibles, please do not cease to take care that it is also printed separately with its own Latin version, so that it may be easier for all to enjoy it. I think this would greatly serve the public good, for those great Bibles, which are huge volumes and of great price, will not easily be available to everyone. There is no need to weary you further. Farewell, and be certain that I live as your most devoted.

units.la: Romæ, quarto Nonas Julii MDCXXXI
units.tr: Rome, 4 July 1631.

units.la: EPistolam tuam quam ad me una cum libro, misisti non accepi: Pater qui detulit, dixit, se illam perdidisse, ubi quotquot forinsecus literæ importantur, ob pestis suspicionem, igne purgari solent. Si quid forte continebat, quod me non latere cuperes, rescribas quaso, ne aliorum incuria mandatis tuis, quæ vehementer exopto, gratissimisque nunciis me defraudet. Vale iterum & me ama.
units.tr: I did not receive the letter you sent me together with the book. The Father who brought it said he had lost it, since all letters that are brought in from abroad are usually purged by fire because of suspicion of plague. If it contained anything you would not want me to miss, please write back, I beg you, lest the carelessness of others deprive me of your commands, which I earnestly desire, and of your most welcome news. Farewell again, and love me.

units.tr: On the Chronology of the Mahummedans.

units.la: Nobilissimo & Perillustri Viro Petro à Valle Johann Morinus
units.tr: To the most noble and most illustrious man Pietro della Valle, from Johann Morinus.

units.la: PRimas Litteras à te accepi, quibus me respondisse non memini. Prioribus difficultatem non immeritò mones, quod Annum Arabum 920. cum Anno Chri-sti 1542, commiserim; ais enim, te certissimum esse annum verae Salutis 1622. cum Mahummedico[?] 1031. majori ex parte concurrisse, & 1627. cum 1036, unde-cimum praeterea Aprilis anni 1599. cum anno Hegirae 994, & die 22. mensis Ra-bie secundi. De hisce exemplis nihil ambigo, alia addam, quae tua nobiliter confirmant. Refert Gordonus in Chro-nologia sua ad annum 621, in Edictopacis[?] Caroli V. Imperatoris, cum Afro, Rege, annum Hegirae, 942, cum anno Christi 1535, copulatum fuisse: In Literis verò Solimani ad Ferdinandum, annum consimiliter ab Epocha Mahommedis 954, cum Christiano 1547, conjunctum. Refert quoque Mulerus in Tabulis Astro-nomicis, Turcarum Imperatorem litteras ad Belgarum Ordines anno 1610, rescrip-sisse, ad quarum calcem æra notabatur 119. Ista sane contradicere nobis videntur, annum Arabum 920, cum Christia-no 1542, maritavimus. Nodum istum, qui multis perplexus videri potest, paucis e-nodabimus: Aliud est annos ab Epocha Arabica juxta Arabes & Turcas putare, aliud eosdem annos juxta Christianos a-liosve populos. Arabes annis utuntur mere Lunaribus dierum 354, nec illos curant ullis embolismis cum solaribus exæquare, abrogata prorsus annorum solarium consuetudine, Embolismo-rum quidem speciem quandam usurpant, sed à nostris prorsus dissimilem, cum e-nim annus lunaris juxta Astronomorum antiquorum & recentiorum epilogismos dierum sit 354. hor. 8 m. 48. ad finem cu-juslibet anni 354. dierum residui sunt hor. 8, m 48, quæ ad finem anni tertii collectæ diem præstant, horasque duas & 24 min. Tertio itaque anno diem intercalant, quo annus ille dierum constituitur 355, supersuntque Epactae horae duae & 24. min. quibus anno quarto horas 8 denuo addunt, & 48 min, & sic continuant donec compleatur annus trigesimus. Tum enim undecim embolismis unius diei peractis, nullae prorsus supersunt Epactae, idemque embolismorum & epactarum redit ordo, qui prius effluxerat, quod manifestum & palpabile fit, multiplicatis horis 8. & 48. min. per 30, consurgunt enim horae 264, ex quibus undecim dies exactissime, nullo superfluo, componuntur. Hæc est illa triacontaeteris, seu periodus Arabica triginta annorum, qua anni Arabici exacte satis juxta lunares motus, nulla solarium habita ratione,definiuntur,Non incassum hæc præmissa sunt: Si quis enim me roget, quotus annus hægirae juxta annos Arabum supputetur hoc mense Septembri æræ Christianæ 1631, respondebo 1041. Si autem me roget, quotus vero juxta annos Julianos, qui Christiani sunt ? respondebo 1010.
