Annorum 31. est discri-men, hoc est à fuga Mahumedis anni Arabici effluxerunt 1039, & aliquot dies; anni vero Christiani 1009, sed ista exa-ctissime subducamus: hujus enim rei i-gnoratio Genebrardo, Gordono aliisque Chronologis persvasit, Arabes Afros Epochen Hegirae ab anno Christi 591, aut 592. initium ducere. Verùm praestantissimi quique Chronologi, istiqve Arabes consentiunt, Hegirae Epochen decimo sexto Julii anni Christi 622. coe-pisse. Pluribus id probare non opus est; facile enim ex dicendis colligetur. Ab eo tempore usque ad mensis Julii 16 diem anni praesentis, effluxerunt anni Arabici 1340. Annus ille ut dicimus, dierum est 354, hor. 8. m. 48. Annus vero solaris juxta Alphonsum, & fere juxta Ticho Brahen, est 365. dierum, 5. hor. m. 46. Excessus igitur Anni Solaris supra Lunarem Arabicum est 10. dierum, 21. hor. m. 1. Cum igitur 1009 anni solares praeterierint, ducantur decem dies, 21 hor. 1. m. in 1009, summa erit 10973 dierum, 13. 13 hor. m. 49. Tot igitur diebus 1009 anni solares superant 1009. Arabicos, sed 10973[?], dies, 13. hor. m. 49, divisi per dies 342, 8. hor. 48 m. annum Arabicum, annos nobis præstant. Arabicos 30, dies insuper 342. hor. 13. m. 49. itaque anno Christi 1631, 15 Julii præterierunt anni Arabici ab Hegira 1339, & præterea dies 342, hor. 13. m. 49, ergo annus 1040. Arabicus seu Neomenia Muharram cœperat octavo Augusti anni 1630. Ab octavo enim Augusti mensis anni 1630; ad 15 Julii 1631, dies 342 numerantur. Præterquam quod Epilogismus iste rectus, huic assentiuntur Tabulæ Astronomicæ; Neomeniam enim ex Alphonsinis Tabulis collegi anno 1630 factam fuisse juxta medios & æquabiles motus, octava die Augusti, hora ante meridiem 9. & 3. m. in Romano meridiano. Nunc si 342. diebus, addantur 12, (existimarem enim annum illum esse ὑπερήμερον[?] & intercalarem; etenim triacontateridis Arabicæ vigesimus) finietur annus 1040 Hegiræ, Julii die 28. inibitque Neomenia nia Muharram anni Arabici 1041, Julii die 29. Neomeni a media juxta Tabulas Alphonsinas accidit Romæ 28. Jul. hora post meridiem 7. m. 51. sec. 17. paulo post occasum: itaqve hodie annus supputa-tur Hegirae 1041, & 21. mensis Sepher, Christi vero & nostri, 1631, & 16. Cal. Septembris, misi forte propter Arabica-rum Neomeniarum πρόσπτωσιν[?], de qva mox, coeperit Muharram 31. Julii, quo casu incidit hoc anno 16. Septemb. in 19. mensis Sepher. Ut ex annis solaribus datis, Arabicos collegimus, ita & con-trario modo ex Arabicis facile est solares colligere. Hoc in numeris tuis pericli-tabimur, aliqvid enim continent qvod animadversione dignum videtur. Ais igitur Aprilis undecimum diem anni 1586, concurrere cum 22 die Rabie po-sterioris anni Hegirae 994. qvia anni Arabici numero superant Christianos in eadem dierum collectione, excessus an-norum solarium simul collecti, & ex an-nis Arabicis lunaribus exempti, anno-rum solarium numerum exhibent. De-sectus sectus anni lunaris Arabici à solaris est 10. dier. 21. hor. 1. m. Defectus ille uniuscujusqve anni in annis 993. integris consurgit in summam diem 10799, h. 13. m. 33. Anni vero 29. solares dies conficiunt 10592. min. 41. horas, & minuta ista securi nunc negligimus. Dies igitur 10592, tolle ex 10799, sive annos 29. à 993, residui erunt anni Christiani 964, & dies 207. rursus eximendi, nam omnes dies defectus lunaris sunt exemptiles. Denuo itaque ab annis Christianis 964, tol-le dies 237, annos assequeris 963, dies 158. Dico igitur annos Hegirae 993. completos æqvari annis solaribus 963, diebus 158. Hinc facile est, postremum diem Anni Arabici 993[?]. oruere[?], & Neomeniam Muharram anni Arabici 994. Annus solaris Hegirae semper finitur 15. Julii, & incipit 16. ejusdem mensis, à quo die si numeres 158. dies, terminabitur annus ille 20. Decemb. inibitque 993. annus Hegirae Decemb. 21. qvi duravit per universum fere annum Christianum 1586. Si igitur ab annis 1585, cum qvibus concurrebat annus Hegiræ 993, tollas annos solares 963, relinquentur 622. Christiâ decima sexta Julii, pro initio & radice supputationis Hegirae, cui Epochæ omnes celebres Chronologi consentiunt, quæque, ut vides ex ipsissimis Arabum Epilogismis, Astronomicè putatis, colligitur. Sed ex iis, quæ addis, difficultas oritur. Ais enim ex Astronomorum Persarum exacta supputatione, undecimum diem Aprilis anni 1586, concurrere cum 22. die Rabie posterioris anni Hegirae 994. nam concursus ille attribuendus videtur April. 9, aut saltem 10, uno die citius, menses enim tres priores Arabici cum quarti 22. diebus, dies componunt 110, atqui dies 110. à vicesimo primo Decembris exclusive supputati, decimo Aprilis terminantur. Difficultatem augent Tabulae Alphonsinæ, ex quibus colligo Neomeniam mediam factam fuisse anno 1585, Decembris 21. die, hora post meridiem secunda in Meridiano Babylonico, eo prorsus modo, quo ex annorum solarium & lunarium epilogismis adnotavi. Astronomi autem tui lapsum non esse ex aliis, quæ affers, exemplis manifestum est. Refers in Ephemeride Persico, 21. diem Martii anni Christi 1622, in octavum diem Gemadi, prioris anni Hegirae 1031. adnotatum fuisse: idem brevissime quod in priori exemplo præstitemus. Anni 1030 completi superant 993 completos, annis 137, defectus anni lunaris à solari 16 d. 21 h. 1 m. ducatur in 37, emergent 402 dies, quibus junge 207, residuum superius adnotatum, dies fient 609; hoc est annus solaris & 244 d. quæ juncta annis 29, efficient anni 30, & 244 dies, quo annorum & dierum numero anni Hegirae 1030 completi superant numerum annorum solarium ejusdem Hegirae. Demantur igitur à 1030, anni 30, restabunt mille anni solares: ab his iterum deme dies 244, residui erunt 999 anni, dies 121, prorsus æquales 1030 annis Hegirae completis. Anni autem 999 solares finiti sunt die 15. Julii an. 1621, duravit Hegirae annus præterea diebus 121; finiit ergo die Nov. 13, ac proinde annus 1031 Hegirae cœpit die 14. Nov. anno Christi 621. Eo die ex Tabulis Astronomicis colligo commissum fuisse Novilunium Babylone hora quarta matutina. A Neomenia autem Muhar-ran ad octavum Gemadi prioris inclusi-ve 126 dies effluxerunt [?]; sed à decimo quarto Novembris, ad 21 Martii 128 [?]. Tertium uno expediam; 26 dies Junii anni 1627, concurrit cum duodecima mensis Sceval anni Hegirae 1036. A Neomenia Muharan ad duodecimum diem Sceval dies 227, totidem retro numerati à 22 Jun. incipiunt à 23 Septemb. quo juxta id, quod scribis, cœpit Neomenia Muharran. Sed Tabulæ Astronomicæ exhibent Novilunium Babylone die 21 Sept. paulo post, aut circa mediam noctem. Ex his exemplis constat, cœlestes Neomenias duobus diebus Arabicas nunc anticipare, Lunamque primam eorum pronuntiare, cùm est tertia, cujus rei causam à te scire velim: nam quod Neomeniam, ut Judæi, stante Templo, non à Luminarium Synodo, sed à Visione [?] cœlecelebrent? Num Cycli ipsorum vitio, ut olim Christiani ante Gregorii correctionem, Luna prima dicebatur, cùm erat quarta: tantus tandem apparuerat enneadecaeteridis inemendate defectus, aut quavis alia de causa. Ista nunc introspicere, urgentibus aliis negotiis, non vocat, alias forte non ex tempore ut nunc, sed consulto de hisce differendi dabitur occasio. Quamquam verbosâ scripturâ meâ importunus nimium tibi fuerim, id, quod rei à te animadversæ caput est, non omittam. Samaritanos aio, non secus ac Judæos annis uti solaribus, non lunaribus, ut Arabes. Hujus rei multa sunt Argumenta, Lex Mosis, quam profitentur, cujus Festa solari & lunari motui addicta sunt, unde fit, ut ipsis & Judæis solemne, lunares menses per Embolismos dierum triginta, annuo Solis motui accommodare, atque adeo quamvis eorum menses sint lunares sicut Arabici, nusquam tamen cum illis conveniunt. Præterea hujus rei testes habeo Mosem Ægyptium & Abenezram, ut à Commenatore Libri Cozri[?] citatur, in-super Scaligerum cum Calendario Sama-ritano, quod in lucem edidit, deniqve ipsum librum tuum & meum; nam in Libro tuo cum supputatio annorum ini-tur à regno Ismaelitarum, additur men-sis Elul, in meo vero mensis Marthusan, qvi menses Judaici sunt, & cum annis lunaribus Arabum accommodari non possunt, nisi qvis scrupulosam Astronomorum supputationem advocet. Igitur fa-ciunt Samaritani, qvod nos in eadem causa faceremus. Siqvis enim me rogaret, qvot hodie 1631, & Sept. die 16, anni elapsi sunt ab Hegira seu fuga Maho-metis? non responderem per annos Ara-bicos, sed solares vulgares, annos scili-cet praeteriisse 1000, anni vero 1010 diem 63 fluere: nec aliter supputant Chronologi Christiani aut Judaei, sicut vice ver-sa Arabes, qvae apud nos fiunt, annis He-giræ suae applicant. Latine versa est Hi-storia Sarracenica ab Arabe docto & Chronologo exactissimo, Lugduni Ba-tavorum, anno 1625 edita: innumeris in locis historias Christianorum recensens Hegiræ annos semper usurpat. Sed de hisce hactenus.
units.tr: I have received your first letter, though I do not remember having replied to it. You rightly warn me of a difficulty in your earlier letter, where I matched the Arabs' year 920 with the year of Christ 1542. You say you are quite certain that the year of true salvation 1622 coincided for the most part with the Muhammadan year 1031, and 1627 with 1036; and moreover that the eleventh of April 1599 fell in the year Hegira 994, on the 22nd day of the month Rabi II. I have no doubt about these examples, and I will add others that nobly confirm yours. Gordon, in his Chronology at the year 621, reports that in the edict of peace of Emperor Charles V with the king of Afro, the year Hegira 942 was joined to the year of Christ 1535. In the letters of Suleiman to Ferdinand, likewise, the year 954 from the epoch of Muhammad was joined to the Christian year 1547. Muler also reports, in his Astronomical Tables, that the Turkish Emperor wrote back to the States of the Netherlands in 1610, and that at the foot of the letter the era 119 was noted. These things certainly seem to contradict us, since we matched the Arab year 920 with the Christian 1542. We shall untie this knot, which may seem tangled to many, in a few words. It is one thing to reckon years from the Arabic epoch according to the Arabs and Turks, and another to reckon the same years according to Christians or other peoples. The Arabs use purely lunar years of 354 days, and do not bother to equate them with solar years by any intercalations; they have quite abandoned the custom of solar years. They do use a certain kind of intercalation, but one quite unlike ours. For since, according to the calculations of ancient and modern astronomers, the lunar year is 354 days, 8 hours and 48 minutes, the remainder at the end of each year is 8 hours 48 minutes. Collected at the end of the third year, these make a day and 2 hours 24 minutes. So in the third year they intercalate a day, making that year 355 days, and there remain epacts of 2 hours 24 minutes. To these, in the fourth year, they again add 8 hours 48 minutes, and so they continue until the thirtieth year is complete. Then, with eleven intercalary days carried out, no epacts remain at all, and the same order of intercalations and epacts returns that had passed before. This becomes manifest and palpable when 8 hours 48 minutes is multiplied by 30: the hours come to 264, from which eleven days are made up exactly, with nothing left over. This is that thirty-year cycle, the Arabic period of thirty years, by which Arabic years are defined quite exactly according to the lunar motions, with no account taken of solar years. These things were not premised in vain. If someone asks me what year of the Hegira, by the years of the Arabs, is reckoned in this month of September of the Christian era 1631, I will answer 1041. If, however, he asks what year it is by the Julian years, which are the Christian ones, I will answer 1010. The difference is 31 years: since the flight of Muhammad, Arabic years have run out to 1039 and some days, but Christian years to 1009. But let us reckon these things most exactly, for ignorance of this matter persuaded Genebrard, Gordon and other chronologers that the African Arabs began the epoch of the Hegira from the year of Christ 591 or 592. Truly, the most distinguished chronologers, and those Arabs too, agree that the epoch of the Hegira began on the sixteenth of July in the year of Christ 622. To prove this at length is unnecessary, for it will easily be gathered from what follows. From that time until the 16th day of July of the present year, Arabic years have run out to 1340. That year, as we said, is 354 days, 8 hours and 48 minutes. The solar year, according to Alphonsus, and nearly according to Tycho Brahe, is 365 days, 5 hours and 46 minutes. The excess of the solar year over the Arabic lunar year is therefore 10 days, 21 hours and 1 minute. Since 1009 solar years have passed, let 10 days, 21 hours and 1 minute be multiplied by 1009: the sum will be 10,973 days, 13 hours and 49 minutes. So by so many days the 1009 solar years exceed 1009 Arabic years; but the 10,973 days, 13 hours and 49 minutes, divided by 342 days, 8 hours and 48 minutes (the Arabic year), give us 30 Arabic years and, besides, 342 days, 13 hours and 49 minutes. Thus on 15 July of the year of Christ 1631, Arabic years from the Hegira have run out to 1339, and in addition 342 days, 13 hours and 49 minutes. Therefore the Arabic year 1040, or Muharram's new moon, had begun on 8 August of the year 1630. For from 8 August 1630 to 15 July 1631, 342 days are counted. Besides the fact that this reckoning is correct, the Astronomical Tables agree with it. For I gathered from the Alphonsine Tables that the mean new moon in 1630 fell on 8 August, at 9 hours and 3 minutes before noon on the Roman meridian, according to mean and equable motions. Now, if 12 days are added to these 342 days (for I suppose that year to be hyperemeron [ὑπερήμερον] and intercalary, since it is the twentieth of the thirty-year cycle), the year 1040 of the Hegira will end on 28 July, and the new moon of Muharram of the Arabic year 1041 will begin on 29 July. According to the Alphonsine Tables, the mean new moon fell at Rome on 28 July, at 7 hours, 51 minutes and 17 seconds after noon, shortly after sunset. So today the year is reckoned as the Hegira 1041, the 21st day of the month Safar, and of Christ and of our era 1631, the 16th before the Kalends of September. Unless, by chance, because of the anticipation [πρόσπτωσιν] of the Arabic new moons, of which I shall speak shortly, Muharram began on 31 July; in which case this year 16 September falls on the 19th day of the month Safar. Just as from given solar years we have gathered Arabic ones, so conversely it is easy to gather solar years from Arabic ones. Let us test this on your numbers, for they contain something that seems worth noting. You say, then, that the eleventh day of April in the year 1586 coincided with the 22nd day of the second Rabi of the Hegira 994, since Arabic years, by the number of days, exceed Christian ones in the same collection of days; the excess of solar years, collected together and subtracted from the lunar Arabic years, gives the number of solar years. The deficiency of the Arabic lunar year from the solar year is 10 days, 21 hours and 1 minute. The sum of this deficiency for each year over 993 complete years comes to 10,799 days and 13 hours and 33 minutes. Twenty-nine solar years make 10,592 days, 41 minutes and some hours, and these minutes we now safely neglect. Take 10,592 days from 10,799 days, or 29 years from 993, and there remain 964 Christian years and 207 days, which are to be subtracted again, since all the days of the lunar deficiency are removable. So, taking 207 days from the 964 Christian years, you will arrive at 963 years and 158 days. I say, therefore, that 993 complete Hegira years equal 963 solar years and 158 days. From this it is easy to see that the last day of the Arabic year 993 falls on, and the new moon of Muharram of the Arabic year 994 begins on, 16 July, from which day, if you count 158 days, that year will end on 20 December, and the Hegira year 993 will begin on 21 December, and it lasted through almost the whole Christian year 1586. If then from the years 1585, with which the Hegira year 993 coincided, you subtract the solar years 963, there remain 622, the sixteenth of July of the year of Christ, which is the starting point and root of the Hegira reckoning, on which all the famous chronologers agree, and which, as you see, is gathered from the very calculations of the Arabs, reckoned astronomically. But a difficulty arises from what you add. For you say that, by the exact calculation of the Persian astronomers, the eleventh day of April in the year 1586 coincided with the 22nd day of the second Rabi of the Hegira 994. For that coincidence seems to be assigned to 9 April, or at least to 10 April, one day earlier; for the first three Arabic months, together with the 22 days of the fourth, make 110 days, and 110 days counted from 21 December, exclusive, end on 10 April. The difficulty is increased by the Alphonsine Tables, from which I gather that the mean new moon fell in the year 1585, on 21 December, at 2 hours after noon on the Babylonian meridian, exactly in the way I noted from the calculations of the solar and lunar years. Your astronomers' error is clearly not shown by the other examples you bring. You say that in the Persian Ephemeris, the 21st day of March in the year of Christ 1622 was noted as the eighth day of Jumada, in the earlier year of the Hegira 1031. This we can do very briefly, as in the earlier example. The completed years 1030 exceed the completed 993 by 37 years. The deficiency of the lunar year from the solar year, 10 days, 21 hours and 1 minute, multiplied by 37, gives 402 days; add to these the 207 days noted above, and there result 609 days, that is, one solar year and 244 days. This, added to 29 years, makes 30 years and 244 days, by which number of years and days the completed Hegira years 1030 exceed the number of solar years of the same Hegira. Take 30 years from 1030, and there remain 1000 solar years; from these again take 244 days, and there remain 999 years and 121 days, exactly equal to the 1030 completed Hegira years. The 999 solar years ended on 15 July in the year 1621, and the Hegira year lasted 121 days beyond that. It therefore ended on 13 November, and so the Hegira year 1031 began on 14 November in the year of Christ 1621. On that day, from the Astronomical Tables, I gather that the new moon occurred at Babylon at 4 o'clock in the morning. From the new moon of Muharram to the eighth day of the earlier Jumada, inclusive, 126 days ran out; but from the 14th of November to 21 March, 128. I shall dispatch the third example in one go: the 26th day of June in the year 1627 coincided with the twelfth day of the month Shawwal of the Hegira year 1036. From the new moon of Muharram to the twelfth day of Shawwal there are 227 days; counted back the same number of days from 22 June, they begin on 23 September, when, according to what you write, the new moon of Muharram began. But the Astronomical Tables show the new moon at Babylon on 21 September, shortly after, or about, midnight. From these examples it is established that the heavenly new moons are now anticipated by two days in the Arabic reckoning, and that they proclaim as the first moon what is the third. I should like you to tell me the cause of this; for why do they, like the Jews while the Temple stood, celebrate the new moon not from the conjunction of the luminaries but from the sighting? Is it through a fault in their cycle, as Christians once did before Gregory's correction, when the first moon was called the first though it was the fourth? Had so great a defect of the uncorrected nineteen-year cycle appeared at last, or is it for some other reason? Other business presses on me now, and I am not free to examine these matters. Perhaps on another occasion, not hastily as now but deliberately, there will be a chance to discuss them. Although I have been too tedious to you with my wordy writing, I will not omit the chief point of what you have noticed. I say that the Samaritans, no less than the Jews, use solar years, not lunar ones like the Arabs. There are many arguments for this. There is the Law of Moses, which they profess, whose feasts are bound to both the solar and the lunar motion; whence it is customary for them and the Jews to adjust the lunar months to the annual motion of the sun by intercalary months of thirty days. So, although their months are lunar, like the Arabic ones, they never agree with them. Moreover I have witnesses to this: Moses the Egyptian and Abenezra, as cited by the commentator on the Book of the Kuzari; besides Scaliger, with the Samaritan calendar which he published; and finally your book and mine. For in your book, when the reckoning of years begins from the kingdom of the Ishmaelites, the month Elul is added, and in mine the month Marheshvan is added; these are Jewish months, and cannot be fitted to the lunar years of the Arabs, unless one calls in the scrupulous calculation of the astronomers. So the Samaritans do what we would do in the same case. For if someone asked me how many years have elapsed since the Hegira, or flight of Muhammad, as of today, 16 September 1631, I would not answer in Arabic years, but in ordinary solar years: that is, 1009 years have passed, and 1010 years and 63 days are running. Nor do Christian or Jewish chronologers reckon otherwise, just as, conversely, the Arabs apply to their own Hegira years what is done among us. The Saracen history was translated into Latin by a learned Arab and most exact chronologer, and published at Leiden in 1625; in countless places, when recounting Christian histories, it always uses the years of the Hegira. But so much for these matters.

units.la: Posteriores Litteræ tuæ mihi lecto decumbenti redditæ sunt, sed tui nominis jucunda recordatione animum recrea-runt, febrisque ardorem elevarunt. Quæris à me, eruditissime Domine, num per Judæorum Cabbalisticam Gematriam, numeri ex dictionis resolutione manantes, soleant iterum in dictionem coalescere, qua Mysterium aliquod significetur; exemplo tuo quæstionis sensum aperiam. ישוע[?] Jesus, Arabice componit 146, numero illo iterum in litteras resoluto exoritur dictio [illegible, ~3 letters], quæ Arabice inservire sonat, recte de Domino nostro dicitur, qui formam Servi induit, &c. Respondeo, Gematriæ Cabbalisticæ genium esse, dictionis unius sensum aut mysterium, ex alia per numeros expiscari, atque ad id tantum Gematriam inventam esse, hincque sæpius mysteria emergere. Huic conformia quod ex Arabica Lingua adnotasti, verbi gratia dictio מצותי, Præcepta mea, in numerum 546 resolvitur. Idem numerus in lit-teras iterum resolvitur שמר [?] dictionem componentes, quæ custodi significat; quo Mysterio, Mandata Dei sedulo ser-vanda esse, demonstratur. Huc tendit omne negotium Gematricum, nisi Judæi barbaris nominibus sæpius oblectarentur; verbi gratia, nominis barbari Mitatron, ממטרון[?], apud eos maxima est reverentia; sicque Angelum qui primum cœlum movet, vocari fabulantur, eo quod literæ istæ 314 conficiant; qui numerus in dictionem שדי Schaddai iterum resolvitur; quæ unum est ex maximis Dei nominibus. Alterum est, quod quærit de Numeris Judæorum supra quadringentesimum: duobus modis illos solent exprimere, ope scilicet quinque litterarum finalium; ץ. ף. ן. ם. ך[?] 500, 600, 700, 800, 900, vel alias litteras conjungendo; ut 500, hoc modo, ךק[?], 600, תר[?], &c. Pro millenariis autem, litteris iterum utuntur, ut ברלך[?], 2234 cum ponunt litteras finales illas semper ad finem nem relegant ; verbi caufa , fumma Verfuum à Maforetis in Pfalmis fic adnota- tur, אאכוך[?], 2527, natura duce fic fcribi- debuiffet, אאכן, alias pro duobus א uterentur ב. Saepe millenarios omittunt, & inferiores tantum numeros adfcribunt, qvod faepiffime faciunt, cùm annos Epochae mundi numerant, fed tum faepius addunt פק. hoc eft, פרט קשון, juxta Numerum minorem. Exempli caufa, aliud hoc anno accidiffe dicerent, שנח שעא[?], anno 391, juxta Numerum minorem , hoc eft , anno mundi juxta ipforum Numeros, השעא[?], ʒ391. Sed de hifce hactenus. Pentateu- chi 17 caput Leviitici fub praelo eft. Pen- tateuchum tuum integrum cum Hebraeo Samaritano contuli ; tam exacta eft, & verbis adhaerens verfio , ut Latina dupli- ci minime fit opus, unaqve verfio utri- qve textui ad amuffim refpondeat ; alteram verfionem condere, prorfus esta- ctum agere. Ita autem Samaritanus uterqve codex in editione difponitur, ut La- tina verfio utriqve textui ex aequo respondeat, nullaque versio cum archety-po facilius ista comparari possit. Hæc habui, perillustris & mihi observantis-sime Domine, quæ doctissimis Litteris tuis rescriberem, me ut magis ac magis a-mes etiam atque etiam rogo.
units.tr: Your later letter was delivered to me while I lay in bed. Its pleasant reminder of your name refreshed my spirit and eased the heat of my fever. You ask, most learned Sir, whether the numbers that arise from resolving a word by Jewish Cabbalistic Gematria are usually recombined into a word that signifies some mystery. I will make the sense of your question clear by your own example. The Hebrew ישוע [Yeshua], Jesus, makes 146 in Arabic. Resolving that number again into letters gives a word [illegible, about three letters], which in Arabic means to serve, and which is rightly said of our Lord, who took the form of a servant, and so on. I reply that the nature of Cabbalistic Gematria is to draw out the sense or mystery of one word from another by means of numbers. Gematria was invented for this purpose alone, and so mysteries often emerge from it. Conformable to this is what you noted from the Arabic language: for example, the word מצותי [mitzvotai], my precepts, resolves into the number 546. The same number is resolved again into the letters שמר [shamar], which make the word custodi [keep!]. By this mystery it is shown that God's commandments are to be diligently kept. All Gematric practice tends toward this, except that the Jews also often delight in barbarous names. For example, the barbarous name Mitatron, מטטרון, is held in the greatest reverence among them, and so they fable that the angel who moves the first heaven is called by this name, because its letters make 314. That number is resolved again into the word שדי Schaddai, which is one of the greatest names of God. As for your other question, about the Hebrew numerals above four hundred: they usually express them in two ways, namely by means of the five final letters, ץ, ף, ן, ם, ך, standing for 500, 600, 700, 800 and 900, or by combining other letters, so that 500 is written in this way, ךק, 600 as תר, and so on. For thousands, they use the letters again, as in ברלך, which is 2234. When they put those final letters, they always send them back to the end of the number. For instance, the sum of the verses in the Psalms is noted by the Masoretes in this way, אאכוך, which is 2527. Nature would have dictated that it be written thus, אאכן, otherwise the letter ב would be used for two א's. They often omit the thousands and write only the lower numbers, which they do most often when they count the years of the epoch of the world. But then they add פק, that is, פרט קשון, according to the smaller number. For example, they would say that something else happened this year, שנח שעא [the year 391], according to the smaller number, that is, in the year of the world by their own reckoning, השעא, 3391. But enough of these matters for now. The seventeenth chapter of Leviticus is under the press. I have collated your complete Pentateuch with the Samaritan Hebrew text. The version is so exact and so faithful to the words that there is no need for a second Latin translation, and one version corresponds exactly to each text. To make another version would be to do what has already been done. Both Samaritan codices are arranged in the edition so that the Latin version answers equally to each text, and no version could be more easily compared with the original. These are the things I have to write back in reply to your most learned letter, most distinguished Sir, and most respected by me. I ask you again and again to love me more and more.

units.la: EPIST. XXVI.
units.tr: LETTER XXVI.

units.la: Responsio ad præcedentem Epistolam Ephemerides Persicæ ac Turcicæ, quas penes se asservabat Auctor Tabularum Astronomicarum, quibus nunc Persæ utuntur, & de his judicium. Diagramma Triacontaeteridis Arabicæ, quam ab Astronomo Persa habuerat.
units.tr: Reply to the preceding letter. Persian and Turkish ephemerides, which the author of the astronomical tables now used by the Persians kept in his possession, and a judgement on them. A diagram of the Arabic thirty-year cycle, which he had from a Persian astronomer.

units.la: Reverendo Patri atque Eruditissimo Domino meo, Patri Joanni Morino, Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero, Petrus à Valle Peregrinus, S. P. D.
units.tr: To the Reverend Father and most learned Lord of mine, Father John Morin, presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, Peter à Valle the Pilgrim, sends greetings.

units.la: Vale.
units.tr: Farewell.

units.la: Romæ postremæ Decembris die exa-cti jam Anni 1631.
units.tr: Rome, on the last day of December, in the year 1631 now completed.

units.la: Plurimum doleo, te febri tam graviter fuisse vexatum: spero, tamen fore, ut hæc Epistola reperiat te jam optima fruentem valetudine; quod ut Deus faxit, toto corde exopto.
units.tr: I am very sorry that you were so severely troubled by fever. Still, I hope this letter finds you enjoying excellent health now, and I wholeheartedly pray that God grants it.

units.la: Mitto etiam ad te hic inferius descriptum Diagramma Triacontaeteridis Arabicæ, quod habui ab eodem Astronomo amico meo, Mulla Zareddin Larita, de quo supra memini. Illudque mitto Italice scriptum, sicuti extat in chartulis meis eodem modo quo tunc ab ore dictitantis excepti, ne forte Latine vertendo, aliquid ei detraherem, qua de causa hoc itidem observavi in folio Patris Thome à Novaria, de antiquissimis litteris in deserto Montis Sinai repertis. Periodus verò intercalationis Arabicæ, num viginti novem annis constet, num triginta ignoro; nihil enim de hoc reperi in chartulis meis, nihilq; me ab Astronomo Persa nec audisse ne quæsivisse memini.
units.tr: I am also sending you, written out below, a diagram of the Arabic thirty-year cycle, which I had from the same astronomer, my friend Mulla Zareddin Larita, whom I mentioned above. I am sending it written in Italian, just as it stands in my notes, taken down in the same way as he dictated it, so that I might not spoil anything by translating it into Latin. For the same reason I have kept to this practice in the paper of Father Thomas of Novara about the very ancient letters found in the desert of Mount Sinai. As for whether the Arabic intercalation period consists of twenty-nine years or thirty, I do not know. I found nothing about this in my notes, and I do not recall ever hearing or asking about it from the Persian astronomer.

units.la: L'anno lunare de gli Arabi non ha giorna, mese alcuno intercalcare per pareggiarsi con Panno solare, ma si ben ha di quando in quando alcum giorno intercalare, per pareggiar la differenza de' mesi lunari, che corre traun novilunio e Paltro. E perche nell' anno Arabico sei mesi sono di trenta giorni, e sei di ventinove, il terzo di trenta, il quarto di ventinve e cosi semper per ordine, ne gli anni, ne'qvali si aggiunge il giorno intercalare, si aggiunde all' ultimo mese, che dovendo esser di ventionove giorni, nell' anno intercalare è ditrenta. Hora gli anni, ne qvali si aggiunge il giorno intercalare sono i seqventi; il secondo, il qvinto, il settimo, il ventesimo primo, il ven-tesimo qvarto, il ventesimo sesto, il ventesimo nono, e cosi sempre vico minciando da capo co'l medesimo ordine L'anno presente, secondo l'Era de gli Arabi 1031 della Hegira, mà secondo noi 1622 di no-stro Seigre, è l'anno primo di qvesto conto; onde l'anno segvente, che sara il secondo, sarà intercalcare. E qvesto l'houto d'al Mulla Zeinnenddin Astrologo Larita amico mio,
units.tr: The Arabs' lunar year has no intercalary month to match it with the solar year, but it does have an intercalary day now and then, to make up the difference between the lunar months, which runs between one new moon and the next. And because in the Arabic year six months have thirty days and six have twenty-nine (the third has thirty, the fourth twenty-nine, and so on in order), in the years in which the intercalary day is added, it is added to the last month, which should have twenty-nine days but in the intercalary year has thirty. Now the years in which the intercalary day is added are these: the second, the fifth, the seventh, the twenty-first, the twenty-fourth, the twenty-sixth, the twenty-ninth, and so it always begins again from the start in the same order. The present year, by the Arabic era, is 1031 of the Hegira, but by our reckoning 1622 of our Lord, and is the first year of this cycle; so the following year, which will be the second, is intercalary. I had this from my friend Mulla Zeinnenddin, the astrologer Larita.

units.la: Hucusqve in chatula mea, cui postea hic Romæ non multos ante dies qvod se-qvitur subjunxi.
units.tr: So far in my notebook; after that, here in Rome, a few days ago, I added what follows.

units.la: Differisce poco de qvesto la diatrive di Nicolo Mulerio nello Chronologia di Ubbone Emmio, che secondo le tavole Alfonsine si à incercalari, in vece de gli-anni 15. e 17, gli anni 16, e 18, & fa tuito l'periodo di anni 30.
units.tr: The treatise of Nicolaus Mulerius in the Chronology of Ubbo Emmius differs little from this. According to the Alfonsine tables, it intercalates in the years 16 and 18 instead of the years 15 and 17, and makes the whole period thirty years.

units.la: EPIST. XXVII.
units.tr: EPIST. XXVII.

units.la: J. Morinus Illustrissimo Cardinali Barberino scribit Apologiam Libri, cui Nomen fecerat De la Grandeur & Souveraineté temporelle Donnée al' Eglise Romaine, ob cuius Editionem male audiebat Morinus apud Aulicos Urbis.
units.tr: J. Morinus writes to the most illustrious Cardinal Barberini an apology for the book he had titled De la Grandeur & Souveraineté temporelle Donnée al' Eglise Romaine, on account of whose publication Morinus was ill spoken of among the courtiers of the City.

units.la: Illust.& Rever. Card. Barberino, J. Morinus.
units.tr: To the Most Illustrious and Reverend Cardinal Barberini, from J. Morinus.

units.la: ACcepi à R. Patre Bertino, sinistra non-nulla Galliâ Romam perlata esse de libro, quem vernacula lingua nuper in lucem edidit, Ista ut audivi, contempsi, quàmquam enim cogitarem, vulnus à calumniatoribus inflictum vix ita obduci posse, quin cicatrix semper emineret, me tamen à calumnia cum de Sedis Apostolicæ honore & auctoritate agebatur, tur, lædi posse non existimabam. Tantam fiduciam pariebant in animo meo conscientia primum mea, consilium deinde meum in libro illo scribendo, testimonium deniqve illorum, qui ante divulgationem, manuscriptum examinarunt, & qui post divulgationem, perlegerant. Conscientia mea, cui nihil antiquius, nihil charius unquam fuit, quàm Sedis Apostolicæ autoritatem publice, & in privatis congressibus quacunque occasione data defendere, qui adolescens aliquot annos in Illustrissimi Card. Perronii comitatu vixi, qui postea in Reverendi Episcopi Lingonensis familiam, cum primum Episcopus creatus est, adscitus sum, qui inde Congregationi Presbyterorum Oratorii nomen dedi, atque ab eo fere tempore à latere Caroli Mironii Andegavensis Episcopi, qui à summo Pontifice, Lug-dunensis Archiepiscopus & primas electus & constitutus est, eo postulante & ultra modum urgen-te, ad mortem usque indivulsus fui. Si nunc vita illi superstes esset, negotii propter quod catholice & feliciter gestum Brevia duo Apostolica in gratiarum actionem accepit, me illi impulsorem fuisse, ne quid amplius dicam, non diffiteretur. Si illustrissimum Card. Spadam coram nunc aloquerer?, ea de isto negotio proderem, quibus facile cognosceret, Archiepiscopum Lugdunensem nihil ea in re me inconsulto tentasse, nedum egisse. Strenue & catholice se praebuit in ista causa R. Episcopus Lingonensis, quae egit aut dixit, me cum ille communicavit. Tum temporis in libro illo componendo & elaborando totus versabar. Num ego cum periculo clam adstruere conabar, quod publice destruere meditabar? Calumniae atrocitas me imprudenter aperire coegit, quod aeternum latuisse desideravi. Itaque ne immodestius de me verba facere pergam, scriptionis meae consilium Illustrissimae Reverentiae tuae exponam ex Historia Ecclesiastica, cui ab incunte aetate praecipue incubui, dedicisse mihi videor ante Fran-co. [?]orum Reges Pipinum & Carolum, summos Pontifices continua fere tum Imperatorum, tum Longobardorum tyrannide vexatos fuisse, ab ea tandem Francorum armis vindicatos. In hujus libertatis assertione Libri mei pars tertia tota versatur, cujus scopus unus est, demonstrare Francorum peculiare esse pro libertate Sedis Apostolicae vitam profundere, Ecclesiam Romanam provinciis maximis ditare, honore & gloria cumulare, contra omnes tam Christianorum, quàm Infidelium insultus & furores protegere, à nongentis annis magna animi fortitudine&pietate protectionem istam conservasse, hanc spartam nactos esse, hanc illis ornandam. Unde tacita complexione popularibus meis colligendum relinquo, non modo Religionis, sed etiam Majestatis Franciae perduelliones esse, quotquot à Sede Apostolica schisma machinantur. Haec autem ex Post facto non dici testatur EPistola ad Regem, testantur prima & ultima tertiae partis capita Testantur innumeri loci, quibus hanc veritatem quacunque data occasione,propono,inculco ; mitto nunc Francorum donationes ex antiquis monumentis erutas quibus demonstratur, provincias Sancti Petri vix tertiam partem donationum Francorum nunc æquare, quæ diffuse tractantur ejusdem partis capite 16. c. 20, 22. quæ adversus Italos & Germanos Historicos disputo, c. 23. Nullam Francos in provincias illas supremæ potestatis jurisdictionem sibi reservasse, neque Carolum Magnum aut ejus Successores Francorum Reges authoritatem confirmandi Pontifices electos Græcorum more sibi usurpasse ; quæ præterea adversus Monarchiam Siculam, c. 30. & indirecte sæpius capitibus præce-dentibus.
units.tr: I have received word from the Reverend Father Bertin that some unfavourable things have been carried from France to Rome about the book which I recently published in the vernacular. As I have heard, I have despised these things. For although I thought that a wound inflicted by slanderers could hardly be healed without a scar always showing, I did not think I could be harmed by calumny when the honour and authority of the Apostolic See were under discussion. Four things produced such confidence in my mind: first my conscience, then my purpose in writing that book, and finally the testimony of those who examined the manuscript before publication and read it through after publication. My conscience, than which nothing has ever been dearer or more important to me, has always been to defend the authority of the Apostolic See publicly and in private conversation whenever any occasion offered. As a young man I lived for some years in the household of the most illustrious Cardinal Perron. Afterwards, when the Reverend Bishop of Langres was first made bishop, I was taken into his household, and from there I gave my name to the Congregation of the Priests of the Oratory. From about that time, at the side of Charles Miron, Bishop of Angers, who was chosen and appointed by the supreme Pontiff as Archbishop and Primate of Lyon, I was inseparable from him until his death, at his request and under pressure beyond measure. If he were still alive, he would not deny, to say nothing more, that I was the instigator of his receiving two Apostolic Briefs in thanksgiving for an affair conducted in a Catholic and fortunate manner. If I were now speaking before the most illustrious Cardinal Spada, I would tell him things about that affair by which he could easily recognise that the Archbishop of Lyon had attempted nothing in that matter without my knowledge, let alone carried it out. The Reverend Bishop of Langres showed himself vigorous and Catholic in that cause, and whatever he did or said, he communicated to me. At that time I was wholly occupied in composing and elaborating that book. Was I trying secretly to establish, at risk, what I was planning to overthrow publicly? The enormity of the calumny has forced me imprudently to reveal what I wished to remain hidden for ever. So that I may not go on speaking too immodestly about myself, I will set out for Your Illustrious Reverence the purpose of my writing, drawn from ecclesiastical history, to which I devoted myself especially from early youth. I seem to have learned that before the Frankish kings Pippin and Charles, the supreme Pontiffs were harassed almost continually by the tyranny of emperors and Lombards, and were at last vindicated by the arms of the Franks. The whole third part of my book is devoted to asserting this liberty, and its one aim is to demonstrate that it is peculiar to the Franks to lay down their lives for the liberty of the Apostolic See, to enrich the Roman Church with very great provinces, to load it with honour and glory, and to protect it against every assault and fury of Christians and unbelievers alike; that for nine hundred years they have maintained this protection with great courage and piety; and that this distinction is theirs to keep. Hence I leave it to my countrymen to gather by tacit inference that all who plot schism against the Apostolic See are guilty of treason not only against religion but also against the majesty of France. These things are not said after the event: the Epistle to the King attests it, the first and last chapters of the third part attest it, and countless passages attest it, in which I set forth and inculcate this truth on whatever occasion offers. I now pass over the donations of the Franks, dug out of ancient records, by which it is shown that the provinces of St. Peter now scarcely equal a third part of the Frankish donations. These are treated at length in chapters 16, 20 and 22 of the same part; in chapter 23 I dispute against the Italian and German historians; and I argue that the Franks reserved to themselves no jurisdiction of supreme power over those provinces, nor did Charlemagne or his successors, the Frankish kings, usurp for themselves, in the manner of the Greeks, the right of confirming elected Pontiffs. In addition, this is argued against the Sicilian Monarchy in chapter 30, and indirectly, quite often, in the preceding chapters.

units.la: Vera quidem hæc sunt, opponetur forte mihi, sed hoc agens multà passim inseruisti, quæ in Sedis Apostolicæ dedecus vel incommodum vergere possunt. Tria sunt præcipua capita Illustrissime Card. quæ de potestate Pontificis disputari solent.
units.tr: "These things are true," it may perhaps be objected to me, "but in doing this you have often inserted here and there many things which may tend to the dishonour or disadvantage of the Apostolic See." There are three principal heads, most illustrious Cardinal, which are customarily disputed concerning the power of the Pontiff.

units.la: Primum est de Fide, Pontifici Religionis Christianorumque omnium á Christo curam esse commissam. Hanc Doctrinam quam quam in Libro isto purum putum historicum me profitear, fuse nonnunquam instituta digressione confirmavi, ut 2 part. c. antepenultimo, & 3. part.c.3.brevius sæpissime quotiescunque scilicet vel tenuissima occasio id ferre potuit.
units.tr: The first concerns faith: that the care of religion and of all Christians has been committed to the Pontiff by Christ. Although I profess in this book to be a purely historical writer, I have confirmed this doctrine at length, sometimes by an extended digression, as in part 2, chapter next to last, and in part 3, chapter 3; and more briefly, very often, whenever even the slightest occasion could bear it.

units.la: Secundum est ex Ecclesiastica illa potestate, temporalem indirecte sequi, quâ Pontifex, reges & principes, si Ecclesiam eversum eant, deponendi jus habet, quæ sententia omnium ferme est Theologorum; illam tamen Card. Perronius toto applaudente Episcoporum Francicorum cœtu, problematicam scripsit, contrariamque ab Ecclesia tolerari.
units.tr: The second concerns the temporal power which follows indirectly from that ecclesiastical power, by which the Pontiff has the right to depose kings and princes if they go about to overthrow the Church. This opinion is held by almost all theologians. Yet Cardinal Perron, with the whole assembly of French bishops applauding, wrote that it is problematic and that the Church tolerates the contrary view.

units.la: Tertium est Canonistarum, qui Pontificem totius orbis Dominum directum à Deo datum esse contendunt. Sententia ista, ab omnibus fere Theologis exploditur; in ea refutanda plurimum laborat Card. Bellarminus. Nunc autem tissime Cardinalis, reus ego sim, pœnam non deprecor, si vel litterulam scripsi, quâ non secuuda sententia, sed tertia, cui tamen Romæ liberrime contradicitur, vel levissime convellatur. Tanto studio à me præcautum & provisum est, quod quilibet Sedi Apostolicæ asserit, verbis meis vel tantillum lædderetur.
units.tr: The third concerns the Canonists, who contend that the Pontiff has been given by God as direct lord of the whole world. This opinion is rejected by almost all theologians, and Cardinal Bellarmine labours greatly in refuting it. Now, most illustrious Cardinal, if I am guilty, I do not beg for punishment, provided I have written even a single little letter by which the second opinion, or rather the third, which nevertheless is freely contradicted at Rome, is slightly shaken. Such care and foresight have been taken by me that whatever anyone asserts for the Apostolic See would not be injured even a little by my words.

units.la: Tertium Fiduciæ meæ adversus calumniam argumentum fuit eorum, qui ante & post Libri divulgationem illum recensuerunt, AnteLibri divulgationem, Doctores Sorbonici quatuor, quorum duo regulares fuerunt, nominibus subscriptis non modo approbarunt, sed e-tiam laudarunt, De præcipuis Capitibus Illustrissimum Card. Berullium consulueram, illo consilium meum approbante, & Editionem urgente, Typis mandatus, & ad umbilicum perductus est, atqve si Deus illi corporis sanitatem dies octo prorogâsset, ipsemet Regi Librum obtulisset. Anteqvàm enim morbo premeretur, traditus fuerat Bibliopolæ com-pingendus.
units.tr: The third ground of my confidence against calumny was the judgement of those who reviewed the book before and after its publication. Before publication, four Doctors of the Sorbonne, two of whom were regulars, not only approved it with their names subscribed but also praised it. I had consulted the most illustrious Cardinal Bérulle about the principal heads; he approved my plan and urged publication. It was given to the printer and brought to completion, and if God had granted him eight more days of bodily health, he himself would have presented the book to the King. For before he was overcome by illness, it had been handed to the bookseller to be bound.

units.la: Post divulgationem, innumeri homines, Episcopi, Doctores, Clerici, Monachi, omniumque Ordinum Laici, diverso quisque consilio atque in congregationem nostram affectu legerunt. Nemo tamen vel syllabam notavit, quâ Apostolicæ Sedi præjudicium aliquod fieret; quæ publice mihi privatim in operis laudem dicta fuerunt, praetermitto. Illustrissimus Card. à Rupe Fulcadio postquam oculis Librum lustravit, consilium meum statim præsenti, atque non tantum laudavit, verùm etiam mihi dixit, se diu desiderâsse, ut quid simile adversus Schismaticos publicaretur; ipse præterea præ cæteris tum adstante Reverendo Archiepiscopo Senonensi, Librum meque ipsum cum honoris præsatione Regi commendávit. Cui credibile fiet, ut acerrimi Sedis Apostolicæ defensores, qui Episcopis & Archiepiscopis netantillum peperceruunt[?] homuncionis operibus non modo perceisse, sed etiam famam procurasse
units.tr: After publication, countless people (bishops, doctors, clergy, monks, and laymen of every order) read it, each with a different purpose and with a different attitude toward our congregation. Yet no one has noted a single syllable by which any prejudice would be done to the Apostolic See. I pass over what was said to me, publicly and privately, in praise of the work. The most illustrious Cardinal de la Rochefoucauld, after he had looked over the book himself, immediately praised my plan to my face, and not only that: he also told me that he had long desired something of the kind to be published against the schismatics. Moreover, he himself, before the others, with the Reverend Archbishop of Sens standing by, commended the book and me personally to the King with a preface of honour. Who will believe that the keenest defenders of the Apostolic See, who have spared not even a little the bishops and archbishops, have not only perused the works of a humble man but have even procured his fame?

units.la: His ego fretus Argumentis, Illustrissime Card. sinistros rumores animi securus primum contempsi; verùm cum se-cundis litteris ad aures usque tuas perla-tas esse didici, animumque tuum abs me nonnihil alienasse, quamquam nullius criminis conscius, graviter tamen commotus sum: ægerrime enim tuli Illustr. Rever. tuam,quam omnium maxime obsequio[?] meo mihi conciliatam velim, de crimine me suspectum habere, ad quod semper exhorrui, & ad quod propellendum studia omnia collimo. Sed præter conscientiam, quæ à scopo non aberrasse tot augustis testimoniis confirmatur, dolorem meum solatur æquitas tua, quæ librum, cujus auctor, ut de Apostolica Sede bene mereretur, diu noctuque desudavi, non lectum & examinatum nunquam condemnabit, Si in historia mea aliquid non dicam contra Theologos, sed contra Canonistas protuli; si testem necessitate materiæ coactus citavi, qui contra Sedem Apostolicam iniquius loqueretur, quem statim adhibito antidoto non correxerim; si Regis aut Imp. actionem[?] enarravi, quæ Pontificibus injuriam intulerit, quam Tyrannidis execrandæ non accusaverim. Addam & hoc, si occasionem ullam probabilem de Sede Apostolica granditer & magnifice dicendi præterierim, reus esse volo, nec pœnam deprecor. Historiam ita scripsi, Illustrissime Card. & in Francia hoc tempore scripsi. Quid calumniatores mei confidentius ausuri fuissent, novit Deus, hoc unum novi, qua in re Sedem Apostolicam læserim, hactenus eorum neminem notasse. Scripsisse mihi[?] notatum est, Avenionem Pontificibus à Francorum Regibus dono datam fuisse. Quid criminis in homine Franco? Verum qui hoc asseruit præter Capitis Titulum, de meo libro, nihil legit. Scripsit Sciaconus Avenionem à Clemente sexto triginta Florenorum millibus emptam, ego vero octoginta[?] millium pretium fuisse demonstro. Scripsi equidem, Avenionem Pontifici à Sancto Ludovico donatam, Archivorum Tolosanorum, triumque Historicorum, qui tum vivebant, authoritate[?] fultus: sed decimo qvinto post donationem anno ab Innocentio IV. restitutam fuisse Comiti Raimundo, eadem authoritate probavi, quæ quoniam ibidem luculenter narrantur, importunus essem otioque tuo abuterer, illustrissime Card. si huc ista repeterem. Quidquid sit, judicio tuo cadere aut stare volo. Antequam tamen scribendi finem faciam, Illustr. Reverentiam tuam etiam atque etiam rogo, ut me Symbolum meum, æra scilicet minuta duo in Domini gazophylacio conferentem, pilosq; caprarum in ædificium portantem favore & patrocinio tuo protegas; præjudicium enim quod concepisti facile obliteratum iri non dubito. Te Deus quam diutissime Ecclesiæ suæ conservet. Parisiis sexto Kal. Augusti, 1630.
units.tr: Relying on these arguments, most illustrious Cardinal, I at first despised the unfavourable rumours with an untroubled mind. But when I learned from further letters that they had reached even your ears, and that your mind had been somewhat estranged from me, I was gravely moved, although I am conscious of no crime. For I took it very ill that Your Illustrious Reverence, whom I would above all wish to have won to me by my obedience, should hold me under suspicion of a crime which I have always abhorred and to avoid which I direct all my efforts. But apart from my conscience, which so many august testimonies confirm has not strayed from its aim, my grief is consoled by your fairness, which will never condemn a book, the author of which has sweated night and day to deserve well of the Apostolic See, without having read and examined it. If in my history I have put forward something not against the theologians but against the canonists; if, compelled by the necessity of the material, I have cited a witness who spoke more unfairly against the Apostolic See, and I did not immediately correct him by applying the antidote; if I have narrated an action of a king or emperor which did injury to the Pontiffs, and did not denounce it as accursed tyranny: I will add this too, that if I have passed over any probable occasion of speaking greatly and magnificently of the Apostolic See, I am willing to be held guilty, and I do not beg for punishment. I wrote the history thus, most illustrious Cardinal, and I wrote it in France at this time. God knows what my calumniators would have dared more boldly. This one thing I know: in what matter I have injured the Apostolic See, none of them has so far noted. It has been noticed that I wrote that Avignon was given as a gift to the Pontiffs by the Kings of France. What crime is there in a Frenchman? But he who asserted this read nothing in my book except the title of the chapter. Sciaconus wrote that Avignon was bought by Clement VI for thirty thousand florins; I, however, demonstrate that the price was eighty thousand. I indeed wrote that Avignon was given to the Pontiff as a gift by St. Louis, supported by the authority of the Toulouse archives and of three historians who were living at that time; but I proved by the same authority that in the fifteenth year after the donation it was restored by Innocent IV to Count Raymond. Since these things are narrated lucidly there, I would be tiresome and abuse your leisure, most illustrious Cardinal, if I repeated them here. Whatever the case, I am willing to stand or fall by your judgement. Before I make an end of writing, however, I earnestly beg Your Illustrious Reverence to protect with your favour and patronage me and my contribution, which is two small coins cast into the Lord's treasury and goats' hair carried to the building; for I do not doubt that the prejudice you have conceived will easily be effaced. May God preserve you for his Church for as long as possible. Paris, sixth day before the Kalends of August, 1630.

units.la: EPIST. XXVIII.
units.tr: Letter XXVIII.

units.la: Renatus Geraldus J. Morino, De iis quæ Romani Aulici in ejus Libro notaverunt.
units.tr: Renatus Geraldus to J. Morinus, concerning those things which the Roman courtiers noted in his book.

units.la: Au Reverend Pere le Pere Morin Prestre de la Congregation de Jesus.
units.tr: To the Reverend Father, Father Morin, Priest of the Congregation of Jesus.

units.la: MOn Reverend Pere, la grace de Jesus pour jamais. Au retour de la Cour qui a esté aux champs tout le mois passé, j'ay fuit, comme je vous avois fait dire par le P. benin faure, un extrait de la lettre, qv' escrivis au Bertin touchant vostre livre, & la communiqua á un Gentilhomme du Card. Barbarin, grand amy du P. Bertin, leqvel me convia de la bailler au plutost àMr. Suarez, leqvel enfin je trouvai à la bibliothèqve du Card. Barbarin, duqvel il est le bibliotheqvaire, qvi le receut de bon cœur & le voulut conserver, & me témoigna grande affection, & envers vous & vostre livre, qv'il loüe & estime. & le lit par ordre du Card. & est arrivé seulement au 3 me livre & dit, qv'il ne presse pas la lecture pour Aous favorifer d'aventage, & qv'en belle matiere il est beaucoup meilleur de retrarder[?], qve le Card. ni pense peut-estre pas à present, & qv'il ne l' en veut pas faire souvenir, & qve lors qv'il luy reddemandera fe livre, alors ille luy portera, & luy fera fon rapport fidellement & le plus favorablement, qv'il pourra pour vous, & comme il voudroit, qv'on le traittât en unc femblable occafion, & qv'apres cela si on veut luy permettre, if traittera avec vous dar lettres, & qv'il y a divers poincts, qvi fe penvent accommmoder facilement en faisant une autre imprefsion, & appofant qvelqves marges eu certains poincts ; Je l'ay voulu convier de vous efcrire, & vous marqver les poincts, mais il dit qv'il n'eft bon qu'il vous efcrive à present, parce qu'il fe rendroit suspect, attendu qv'il eft commis par le Card. pour voir; & examiner le dit livre ; mais qv'apres avoir fait son raport il le pourra faire avec permission, il dit qve ce frontifpice a donné peine au Card. voyant unCharlemagne avec ces mots Italos parere subebo, qve les Italiens disent qve Charlemagne n'a eu guerre, si non avec les Lombards. Il estime cela peu, il nous a recommandè de ne laisfer voir Pautre exemplaire si non à perbien affectionnées, parceque d'autres parleroient & aigriroient Passaire, il P estonne un peu pour[?] le baptesme desConstantin, & dit qv'on aura de la peine à passer ici ce point attendre la tradition ancienne de St. Jean de Latran, il dit qve tous les Autheurs, qve parlent contre ce Baptesme, ne sont approuvèx en tous leurs escrits, il s'estonne qve n'avès'veu un livre, qv'il estime beau par excellence, tout de ce Baptesme de Constantin, fait par un nommè Paulus. Il dit, que le Card. a receu bien vostre lettre, qv,illa luy fit lire devant luy, & le Card. la leut encore apres luy mesme, & qve le Card vous affectionne;mais je vois bien, qv'il faudra vous accommoder, & leur donner ici contentement accommodant, expliqvant & changeant qvelqve chose. Pour cette affaire de Mad. la Rocheguion, Mr Marchand a receu les lettres, mais il y a des oppositions à ce, qve cette affaire ne passe point sous l'Invocation du St, Sacrement, mais sous telle auautre, qu'on voudra, parce qu'il y a déja un autre Monastere du St. Sacrement corrigé à Paris: pour les frais il seront peut estre de 150, ou 160, ou 180 escus, on ne peut pas asseurer au vray, il m'a dit, que c'est Monsieur Joisel banquier, qui luy a commis cette affaire, tellement que c'est au Sieur Joisel, à qui il faudroit payer l'argent, vous aures maintenant le P. Bertin, par de là qui vous niformera[?] de tout ce que je vous pourray servir. Je vous prie de commender librement à celuy qui est pour jamais en nostre Seigneur, & en sa tres sainte Mere, apres vous avoir presenté non tres humbles recommendations de tous à vos SS. Prieres & Sacrifices,
units.tr: My Reverend Father, the grace of Jesus be with you forever. On my return from the Court, which had been in the country the whole of last month, I made, as I had told you through Father Benin Faure, an extract of the letter I wrote to Bertin concerning your book, and I gave it to a gentleman of Cardinal Barberini's household, a great friend of Father Bertin. He urged me to hand it over as soon as possible to Mr. Suarez, whom I at last found in the Cardinal's library, where he is the librarian. He received it gladly and wished to keep it, and he showed me great goodwill both towards you and towards your book, which he praises and esteems. He reads it by order of the Cardinal, and has only reached the third book. He says he will not hurry the reading, in order to favour you the more, and that in a weighty matter it is much better to delay, since the Cardinal perhaps is not thinking of it at present and he does not wish to remind him of it. When the Cardinal asks for the book back, Suarez will then carry it to him and give his report faithfully, and as favourably to you as he can, and as he would wish to be treated himself on a similar occasion. After that, if they are willing to allow it, he will deal with you by letter. He says there are various points which can be easily adjusted by making another impression and adding some marginal notes at certain places. I wished to urge him to write to you and to note down the points, but he says it is not good for him to write to you at present, because he would make himself suspect, since he has been commissioned by the Cardinal to see and examine the said book. But after he has made his report he will be able to do so with permission. He says that the frontispiece has caused the Cardinal some trouble, seeing a Charlemagne with the words "I will make the Italians obey", since the Italians say that Charlemagne waged war only against the Lombards. He thinks little of this. He has advised us to show the other copy only to well-disposed persons, because others would talk and embitter the matter. He is somewhat astonished at the baptism of Constantine, and says that it will be difficult to get this point passed here, given the ancient tradition of St. John Lateran. He says that all the authors who speak against this baptism are not approved in all their writings. He is astonished that you have not seen a book, which he considers excellent beyond all others, entirely on this baptism of Constantine, written by a man named Paulus. He says that the Cardinal received your letter well; he had it read to him in his presence, and the Cardinal read it again himself afterwards, and that the Cardinal is well disposed towards you. But I see clearly that you will have to accommodate yourself and give them satisfaction here, by making concessions, explaining, and changing something. As for the affair of Madame de la Rocheguion, Mr. Marchand has received the letters, but there are objections to it: this affair cannot pass under the invocation of the Holy Sacrament, but under some other invocation, whichever one is chosen, since there is already another monastery of the Holy Sacrament reformed in Paris. The costs will perhaps be 150, 160 or 180 écus; one cannot be sure of the exact figure. He told me that it is Monsieur Joisel, the banker, who has been entrusted with this affair, so that the money would have to be paid to Sieur Joisel. You will now have Father Bertin over there, who will inform you of whatever I can do to serve you. I beg you to command freely him who is forever in our Lord and in his most holy Mother, after I have presented to your holy prayers and sacrifices the very humble recommendations of all of us.

units.la: Mon Reverend Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: A Rome, ce Vostre tres humble & tres affectionné Serviteur 9. Sept. 1630. Ren. Gezauld. Prestre de l'Oratoire de Jesus.
units.tr: At Rome, 9 September 1630. Your most humble and affectionate servant, Ren. Gerauld, Priest of the Oratory of Jesus.

units.la: EPIST. XXIX.
units.tr: EPISTLE XXIX.

units.la: Joh. Morinus Dom. Soari, cui impositum fuerat onus à Cardinale Barbarino in Opus illud inquirendi.
units.tr: Joh. Morinus to Dom. Soari, on whom Cardinal Barberini had laid the burden of that inquiry.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo Domino, Domino Soari, Juris utriusque Doctori Eruditissimo, Joh. Morinus.
units.tr: To the Most Reverend Sir, Lord Soari, most learned Doctor of both laws, from Joh. Morinus.

units.la: Retulit mihi R. P. Bertinus, & qui Romæ est, scripsit Goezellus noster, quam in me sis propenso & amico animo. Lætatus sum plurimum, & congratulatus mihimetipsi, amari me à Viro, dignitate & doctrina & virtute celebri: nihil amicitia tua mihi optatius contingere poterat, aut laude tua honorificentius. Quapropter non possum[?] non amare illorum maledicentiam cuius occasione, & tibi innotui. & benevolentia tua mihi conciliata est. Fœlicíter accidit, quod est in proverbio, ἀ-μύνει ἡ πάγη[?]. Nam eorum diligentiâ factum est, ut liber, quem, si ita loqui licet, personato & fucato titulo præsertim adversus schismaticos & sanctæ Sedis Apostolicæ occultos hostes vernacule & popularibus tantum meis scripseram, Italiam penetraret, & ad manus usque tuas perveniret, neque odium, quod desiderabant, sed mihi desideratissimam amicitiam tuam pareret: itaque unum votis contendendum superest, ut qua amicitia me immerentem ornare coepisti, merentem in posterum tandem prosequaris. Hoc ab humanitate tua spero, & studio quo tu litteratissimus in litteras incenderis, me consecuturum confido. R. P. Bertinus mecum te plurimum salutat. Vale. Atque ut pergas amare me, etiam atque etiam rogo.
units.tr: Father Bertinus has told me, and our friend Goezellus, who is in Rome, has written, how well disposed and friendly your feelings are towards me. I was very glad and congratulated myself that a man so renowned for rank, learning and virtue loves me. Nothing could have come to me more welcome than your friendship, or more honourable than your praise. For this reason I cannot but be grateful for the malice of those men, through whose occasion I became known to you and won your goodwill. It has turned out fortunately, as the proverb has it, that the snare defends itself [ἀ-μύνει ἡ πάγη]. For through their diligence it came about that the book, which I had written in the vernacular and only for my own people, under a mask and a false title, chiefly against schismatics and the hidden enemies of the Holy Apostolic See, has penetrated Italy and reached your hands. It has not produced the hatred they wanted, but has won me your friendship, which I most desired. So only one thing remains to be wished for: that you who have begun to honour me with friendship, though I do not deserve it, will at last continue it towards me now that I have deserved it. I hope for this from your kindness, and I trust I shall obtain it through the zeal for letters with which you, most learned as you are, have kindled yourself. Father Bertinus sends you his warm greetings. Farewell. And I ask you again and again to go on loving me.

units.la: Datum Parisiis prid. Kal. Febr. 1631.
units.tr: Given at Paris, the day before the Kalends of February 1631.

units.la: EPIST. XXX.
units.tr: EPIST. XXX.

units.la: Idem Eidem, Soarem sibi devincire conatur Morinus.
units.tr: The same to the same: Morinus seeks to bind Soarius to himself.

units.la: Perillustri & admodum Reverendo Domino, Domino Soario, eruditissimo Juris utriusque Doctori.
units.tr: To the most illustrious and very reverend Lord, Lord Soarius, most learned Doctor of both laws.

units.la: TAntam benevolentiae erga me tuae fiduciam verba Reverendi P. Bertini dederunt, ut te familiariter uti jam parum verear. Amicitiae enim beneficio, si quid audeam parum modesteè, te excusaturum spero. Exercitationes ecclesiasticas in utramque Samaritanorum Pentateuchum in lucem jamjam edidi, Pentateuchum utrumque brevi editurus. Si Romam Librum deferendi occasio sese nunc præberet, in amicitiæ, qua me colis, μνημόσυνον[?], merito lubensque mitterem Lucubrationes meas à te Viro eruditissimo sive probari, sive emendari magni facio, occasionem ideo quamlibet occupabo, qua ad manus usq; tuas pervenire possint. Interea indicem capitum, quæ toto Libro tractantur, amicitia tua familiariter abutens, ad te mitto. Hæc boni consule, quæso, atque ex iis, velut ex ungve leonem, non tantùm de Libro judica, sed etiam propensissimum in te obsequium meum, velim existimes. Nunc istam officii erga te mei demonstrandi occasionem nactus sum, ut opportunior sese exhibeat, vehementer desidero. Litteras ad te scripsi Kal. Febr. quibus benevolentiæ, quâ me incognitum prævenisti, gratias egi, meque beneficii à te accepti non esse immemorem testatus sum: illas te accepisse non dubito. Unum itaque mihi superest, ut enixissime te deprecer, benevolentiam, qua me colere coepisti, conserves, & indies augeas.
units.tr: The words of the Reverend Father Bertin have given me such confidence in your goodwill that I now hardly fear to use your friendship freely. I hope that, by the favour of our friendship, you will excuse me if I venture anything somewhat immodestly. I have just now published my ecclesiastical exercitations on both Samaritan Pentateuchs, and I shall shortly publish both Pentateuchs. If the opportunity of carrying the book to Rome were offered to me now, I would gladly and deservedly send my labours to you, as a memorial of the friendship with which you cherish me; I greatly value that my studies should be approved or corrected by you, a most learned man. I shall therefore seize any opportunity by which they may reach your hands. Meanwhile, presuming on your friendship, I send you an index of the chapters treated throughout the book. Please take these things in good part, and from them, as one judges the lion from its claw, I would have you judge not only of the book but also of my most devoted obsequiousness towards you. I have now found an occasion of showing my duty towards you; I earnestly desire that a more opportune one may present itself. I wrote to you on the first of February, thanking you for the goodwill with which you anticipated me, though I was unknown to you, and declaring that I am not unmindful of the kindness I have received from you. I do not doubt that you have received that letter. There remains for me, therefore, only this: that I most earnestly beg you to preserve the goodwill with which you began to regard me, and to increase it from day to day.

units.la: Datum Parisiis 8. Idus Martii.
units.tr: Given at Paris, the 8th of the Ides of March.

units.la: EPIST. XXXI.
units.tr: LETTER XXXI.

units.la: Josephus Maria Suaresius Joh. Morino, Nævos quos ex ipsius Libro eximen- dos notaverat, aperit,
units.tr: Josephus Maria Suaresius explains the blemishes he had marked for removal from John Morin's book.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo Patri J. Morino, Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero, Viro Erudituissimo, Josephus Maria Suaresius, S. P. D.
units.tr: To the Most Reverend Father J. Morin, presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory, a man most learned, Josephus Maria Suaresius sends greetings.

units.la: Gratias habeo non vulgares R.P. Bertino, quod meum erga te propensum & obsequiosum animum patefecerit, neque minores egi Goezello, qui perscipsit. Ardebam jamdudum foedus tecum inire immortalis amicitiae, quam officiis excolerem, atque litterario commercio sancirem, quod optanti, Divum promittere nemo auderet, volvenda dies en attulit ultro. Conqueror tamen, quod infestus tibi casus mihi festus fuerit, sed, ut ominor, utrique faustus erit; etenim si te novi ex litteris, quanta tua est doctrina, tanta inest tibi pietas, perlegi volumen eruditione refertum, & eloquentiæ Gallicæ luminibus & Pigmentis respersum atque illustratum omnibus, paucos, veniam dabis amico candido, & libertate Gallica tecum agenti, nævos eximendos reperi, & adnotavi, pressique, & premo me penes, mox in sinum effusurus tuum, nam internos ex formula fiduciæ cuncta geri, & inter bonos bene agier oporteret: interim gratias habeo ingentes pro indice Ecclesiasticarum exercitationum ad Samaritanum Pentateuchum, qui tui in me benevoli animi & ingenii in sacris historiis, librisque versatissimi fidissimus, & certissimus index est, mox relaturus pro ipsis Exercitationibus, quas Goezellus à te missus pollicitus est, eas ego jam legi apud eminentissimum Cardinalem Mecœnatem meum, & collaudavi uti decebat. Sed vidist in[?] illud Tertuliani fragmentum cum Donationis charta, quæ typis etiam Lutetiæ fuêre mandata? cum à me prius Roma fuissent in lucem edita, tuam ego de his sententiam rogo; verùm priusquam feras, abs te peto, ut ab Illustr. V. Rigaltio epistolæ meæ nuperrimæ acceptum exemplum perlegas, Oratiunculas has æqui boniqve consulas, & si ad ambas quibus me antevertisti, litteras datas prid. Kal. Febr. & 8 Idus Martias serius rescribam, mihi quæ tua est humanitas, indulgeas. Vale-
units.tr: I am very grateful to the Reverend Father Bertin for showing me his well-disposed and obliging spirit toward you, and I am scarcely less grateful to Goezel, who wrote to me about it. I have long been eager to enter into a covenant of lasting friendship with you, one to be cultivated by mutual services and confirmed by a correspondence of letters. This is something no one would have dared to promise to one who wished for it, yet the turning days have brought it of their own accord. I do complain that the misfortune which befell you has been a happy event for me, but, as I hope, it will be fortunate for us both. For if I know you from your letters to be as pious as you are learned, I have read through your volume, which is full of learning and has been sprinkled and adorned with all the graces of French eloquence. I have found a few blemishes that ought to be removed, and I have noted them. Since you will allow a candid friend, who deals with you in French frankness, to say so, I have marked them and am keeping them by me, and I will soon send them into your bosom. For all things should be done on the basis of mutual trust, and good men ought to deal well with good men. Meanwhile I give you my heartfelt thanks for the index to your Ecclesiastical Exercises on the Samaritan Pentateuch. It is a most faithful and certain sign of your benevolent feeling toward me and of your skill in sacred history and in books. I shall soon send back a reply concerning the Exercises themselves, which Goezel, sent by you, promised. I have already read them at the house of my most eminent patron, Cardinal Mecaenas, and I praised them as was fitting. But have you seen that fragment of Tertullian together with the charter of the donation, which has also been printed at Paris? I had first published it at Rome, and I ask your opinion on these matters. Before you give it, I ask you to read through the copy of my most recent letter received from the Illustrious Rigaltius, and to take these short orations in good part and with fairness. If I reply late to the two letters you sent before me, dated the day before the Kalends of February and the eighth day before the Ides of March, please grant me the indulgence that your kindness is accustomed to show. Farewell.

units.la: Roma, Prid. Idus Junias MDCXXXI.
units.tr: Rome, the day before the Ides of June, 1631.

units.la: EPIST. XXXII.
units.tr: Letter XXXII.

units.la: Joh. Morinus Suaresio, suum de frag-mento quodam Tertuliani nuper e-dito, judicium interp[?]nit, similiter de excepto quodam ex Epistola S. Maximi ad Monachos Siculos.
units.tr: Jean Morin gives to Suárez his judgment on a certain fragment of Tertullian recently published, and likewise on an excerpt from a letter of St. Maximus to the Sicilian monks.

units.la: Clarissimo Viro Dom. Suaresio.
units.tr: To the most distinguished Mr. Suarez.

units.la: Litteras tuas accepi, simulque Orationes duas, quas coram summo Pontifice habuisti. Utramque statim avide legi, nobilissimamque materiam eloquentia tua exæquante, avidius relegi. Dignissimæ Sedis Apostolicæ Bibliothecario orationes, dignissima maximi ingenii & ad summa qvæq; nati ἐγχειρήματα. Quantus assurgere author cum libuerit qvam, graviter, vehementer, granditer dicere possit, ex hoc specime non conjicere, sed asserere licet. Itaque duplici nomine mihi fuit hoc munus gratissimum, & qvod amicitiæ erga me tuæ μνημοσυνον honorificum, & qvod eloqventiæ nitidissimæ & ornatissimæ, quâ maxime oblector, insigne sit monumentum, tuis præterea litteris admonitus, clarissimum virum Rigaltium adii. qvi eruditissimam Epistolam, qvam Paulo ante illi rescripseras, mihi legendam mutuo dedit. Tertuliani fragmentum istud ostenderat mihi Reverendissimus Aurelianensis Episcopus, cùm primùm Parisios Roma allatum est; te autem minime cælabo, qvid mihi tunc dictaverit animus, suppositum Tertuliano fœtum existimabam, ita etiam censebat doctissimus ille Episcopus, sed in charta Donationis nihil adulterini suspicabar. Verùm causa ista recens à me retractata, cumque tuis animadversionibus diligenter comparata, adeo probabilis mihi visa est sententia tua, ut ab ipso livore laudari debeat, αὐτῷ[?] τε τῷ μώμῳ[?] ἀρέσκειν. Rationes enim, quae fœtum istum, vel ut dubium, vel ut plane rejiculum à Tertulliani sobole abigere videntur, consimilium ex ipso Tertuliano exemplorum redhibitione tanta arte elevas, ut iis consideratis hæc & illa ævo prognata esse eodem, nemini non fiat probabile. Legi quoque ἀπο-τυπωμάτιον tuum, ex Epistola S. Maximi, ad Monachos Siculos, manifeste demonstratur, Maximnm, cum ad Pyrrhum scribens, laudibus eum ornavit, id talionis reciprocatione, atque optimo fine præstitisse, ne scilicet animum jam ægrum exasperaret, sed blandis sermonibus ad orthodoxam fidem revocaret; cuiv[?] s[?] enim parum erat credibile, tantum Christi Athletam in Monothelitarum impietatem quoque modo deflexisse, ex cuius disputatione contra Pyrrhum, tot egregia argumenta in Honorii Papæ defensionem jamdiu collegerant doctissimi & celeberrimi Cardinales, Bellarminus & Baroni-us. us. Qvod ad Librum meum attinet, qvem præ manibus habes, à te laudari viro laudatissimo, mihi erat votis omnibus exoptandum. Aliorum judicia, si qva sunt, minus æqvata approbante despiciam securus: merito enim tu mihi es, Vir Erud, πάντων ἀντάξιον[?] ἄλλων. Nævos esse non dubito, si nulli notarentur, hoc amicitiæ condonarem, diligentiæ meæ non vendicarem. Verùm qvicunqve illi sint, summo beneficio me afficies, horum me admonueris, illos statim cara, ut aiunt, obedientia abstergam, obliterabo, delebo, avellam; judicium enim tuum retractare nefas existimo, longissimeqve absum ab eorum sententia, qui nævos suos lumina credunt. Hoc unum antequam dicendi fi-nem faciam, à te vehementissime flagito & spero, ut me plurimum ames. Litte-ris tuis maturius respondissem, nisi lenta febris & continuis me his diebus canicularibus integris detinuisset. Vale
units.tr: I have received your letter, together with the two orations you delivered before the Supreme Pontiff. I read both at once with eagerness, and then read them again with even greater eagerness, since your eloquence matches so noble a subject. These are orations worthy of the Librarian of the most worthy Apostolic See, and undertakings worthy of a great genius born for the highest things [enchEirēmata]. From this specimen one may not conjecture, but may rightly affirm, how lofty, weighty, vehement and grand the author can be whenever he chooses. I therefore received this gift with a double pleasure: it is an honourable memorial [mnēmosynon] of your friendship towards me, and a distinguished monument of that most elegant and polished eloquence in which I especially delight. Moreover, prompted by your letter, I went to the most famous Rigault, who lent me to read the most learned letter you had written to him a little before. The Most Reverend Bishop of Orléans had shown me that fragment of Tertullian as soon as it was brought from Rome to Paris. I will not hide from you what my own feeling was at the time: I thought it a spurious offspring, not Tertullian's, and the bishop, that most learned man, thought so too; but I suspected nothing spurious in the deed of donation. Yet now that I have taken up the question again and carefully compared it with your remarks, your view seems to me so probable that even envy itself must praise it, and "to please even by blame" [autō te tō mōmō areskein]. For you so skilfully recall similar examples from Tertullian himself, and so remove the reasons which seem to banish that offspring from Tertullian's family, either as doubtful or as plainly ridiculous, that once these are considered it becomes probable to anyone that both this and that were born in the same age.
