I have also read your little work [apotypōmation] on the excerpt from the letter of St. Maximus to the Sicilian monks, in which it is clearly shown that Maximus, when writing to Pyrrhus, praised him with compliments, doing so by way of retaliation and with an excellent purpose: namely, so as not to exasperate a mind already sick, but to call him back to the orthodox faith by gentle words. For it seemed scarcely credible to you that so great an athlete of Christ had in any way turned aside into the impiety of the Monothelites; and from his disputation against Pyrrhus the most learned and renowned Cardinals Bellarmine and Baronius had long since gathered so many excellent arguments in defence of Pope Honorius. As for my book, which you have before you, that you, a man most highly praised, should praise it was for me the thing above all to be desired. The judgments of others, if there are any, I will disregard calmly, since they are less balanced; for you, learned sir, are to me worth [antaxion] all others [pantōn antaxion allōn]. I do not doubt there are blemishes; if no one pointed them out I would pardon them to friendship but not claim them for my own diligence. But whoever they are, you will confer on me the greatest kindness if you point them out to me; I will at once wipe them away, erase them, delete them, tear them out, with what they call dear obedience. For I think it wrong to call your judgment in question, and I stand far from the opinion of those who think their blemishes are lights. One thing more, before I make an end of speaking: I most earnestly demand and hope from you that you will love me very much. I would have answered your letter sooner, but a lingering fever has kept me entirely occupied these past canicular days. Farewell.

units.la: Parisiis, 1631. Sept. 16.
units.tr: Paris, 1631, September 16.

units.la: EPIST. XXXIII.
units.tr: LETTER XXXIII.

units.la: Petrus Hal- loix J. Morino. Laudat illius de Baptismo Constantini sententiam, quam suam quoque esse libere profite- tur.
units.tr: Peter Halloix to J. Morinus. He praises the opinion of Constantine on Baptism, which he freely professes as his own too.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo Patri P. J. Morino, Congregationis Oratorii Iesu Christi Presbytero, P. Halloix.
units.tr: To the Most Reverend Father P. J. Morinus, Presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus Christ, from P. Halloix.

units.la: Admodum R. Presbyter, Pax Christi.
units.tr: Most Reverend Presbyter, peace of Christ.

units.la: LItteras tuas longe gratissimas, & una doctissimum illud ἔντυπον[?] de Sancto Hyppolito, nuper recepi, pro quo ingentes tibi gratias ex corde ago. Valde enim gavisus sum intelligere, quidnam super difficili & intricata quæstione sentires, atque adeo quibus de causis ad id sentiendum movereris.
units.tr: I have recently received your very welcome letter, and with it that most learned printed work [ἔντυπον] on St Hippolytus, for which I give you my heartfelt thanks. I was very glad to learn what you think about this difficult and intricate question, and for what reasons you were moved to think so.

units.la: Equidem nihil dum video, quid illis valide opponi possit, si quid post occurrerit, scribam. Nunc enim sum in opere, quod quo propius lucem est, magis me distringit. De Baptismo Constantini magni, quem nemo unquam mihi persuadere potuit, aliàs fuisse quam in extrema ejus vita, lætor ita esse à te pertractatum, ut in mea confirmatus sim sententia. Nam ejus nomine Baptisterium in urbe Roma non alia de causa sic est appellatum, quam quia ipse, ut alia multa, liberali ære con-didit. Tuas ad Pentateuchum Samaritanum exercitationes oppido doctas legi & probavi, laudo studium, & annos plurimos ad ea, quæ supersunt, apprecor, & quem nunc decurrimus, ita opto felicem, ut feliciores ac feliciores succedant. Si quid mihi esset in manu, quô tuos promovere aut sublevare labores possem, id neque exposci, neque expectari pate-rer, sed ultro & cito mitterem. Verum est enim, ad eundem tendentes finem fratres fratribus manum dare. Vitas Scriptorum Græciæ Ecclesiasticorum ordine ætatis stilo meo, compositas meditor edere, & scripta eorundem illustrare, ac defendere eâ fere formâ, quam in S. Justini Philosophi ac Martyris ante annos aliquot expresi. Hinc & ipsorum fragmenta, si qua usquam lateant aut alibi, quàm in propriis operibus laudata extent, perquiro. Aliud in præfentia mihi R. P. nihil occurrit, quod addam, nisi vota super vota pro tua incolumitate animi & corporis ad utiles ecclesiæ labores. Ita bene vale mei in SS, precibus memor,
units.tr: For my part, I do not yet see anything that can be validly set against these views. If anything occurs to me later, I will write. At present I am busy with a work which, the nearer it comes to publication, the more it distracts me. I am glad that you have treated the baptism of Constantine the Great so thoroughly, since no one has ever been able to persuade me that it took place at any time other than at the very end of his life, and your treatment has confirmed me in my opinion. The baptistery in the city of Rome was named after him for no other reason than that he built it, along with many other things, at his own generous expense. I have read and approved your exercises on the Samaritan Pentateuch, which are very learned indeed. I commend your zeal, pray for many years of life for you to complete what remains, and wish the work you are now pursuing such good fortune that it succeeds more and more happily. If I had anything at hand by which I could advance or lighten your labours, I would not wait to be asked or expected, but would send it of my own accord and promptly, for it is right that brothers should lend a hand to brothers who aim at the same end. I am thinking of publishing Lives of the Greek ecclesiastical writers, arranged in order of their age and written in my own style, and of illustrating and defending their works in much the same form as I set out some years ago for St Justin the Philosopher and Martyr. For this reason I am also searching for their fragments, wherever they may lie hidden, or wherever they survive other than as quoted in their own works. Nothing else occurs to me at present to add, except prayers upon prayers for your well-being in soul and body, and for your useful labours for the Church. So farewell, and remember me in your holy prayers.

units.la: Mihi rure redeundi, redditus est Libellus tuus Heroico Poemate conscriptus, quem Musarum Solatium inscribis. Opus quamprimum accepi non legi, sed oculis hausi, autoris jamdudum admiratione captus, & operis gratissima, æque ac difficillima novitate pellectus. Restinctâ curiositatis ardentissima siti, non feci fateor, & culpam deprecor, id quod oraculo facere jubentur Crotoniatae δῶ-ρον δ᾽ ὅτι δῶ τις ἐπαινεῖ, qvodqve plebeio fertur adagio, qvid plebeium voco, qvo usus est S. Hieronymus, noli dentes equi donati inspicere, introspexi enim & attente legi & consideravi ingeniosissimum illud & eloqventissimum Poëma, nihilqve spem meam fefellit, aut admirationem praeceptam minuit. Idem mihi accidit, qvod splendida palatia, aut ingentes montes prospicientibus. Eminus palatiorum mirantur lata moenia, minaces turres, sublimia tecta, totiusq; operis molem & splendorem, cominus vero murorum compages, vestibula, porticus, tabulata laqvearia, universamqve architectonicen stupent: montium qvoqve magnitudo qvo propius accedimus, eo procerior & altior apparet; ita mihi Poëma tuum minutim consideranti, & ad singula verba mentem advertenti, qvae prius ἐν πλάτει, ut ita dicam, & in fasce elegantia, erudita, & ingeniose elaborata judicaveram, admirationi fuêre, meqve tenuis & jejunae laudis poeni-tuit. tuit. Qvis in rei impeditissimæ descriptione, qvam versus horret, perspicuitatem non miretur? Qvis hortorum ambages, undarum mæandros magnificentissimi ædificii, ut cætera præteream, triumphales statuas graphicè effictas non suspiciat? Ad istorum spectaculum Academicos frustra invitas, visendi studium hospitibus nam reddis inane, cognita sic facili carmine cuncta patent, ut non minus acute qvam eleganter de Poëmate tuo cecinit, qvi hæc spectat eruditus N. Scalopier. Qvis sententiarum lumina, schematum varietatem, verborum majestatem, poetici deniqve promptuarii ornamenta omnia deprompta, & juxta uniuscujusqve rei indolem, decusqve nativum collocari non stupeat? nullibi autem Pygmæorum, ut ajunt, acrothinia colosso adaptari, sed grandia granditer dici mediocria temperate, humilia terse, omnia copiose & ornate. Itaqve duplici nomine gratias habeo tibi maximas, qvod incomparabili poëtices specimine me beasti, & qvod mei memoriam ex a- nimo
units.tr: On my return to town I received your little book written in heroic verse, which you entitle The Muses' Consolation. I did not read the work as soon as I had it; I devoured it with my eyes, having long been captivated by admiration for its author and drawn on by the most welcome yet most difficult novelty of the work. I confess that, with my desire to know burning fiercely, I did not do what the Crotoniates are commanded by the oracle to do, δῶρον δ᾽ ὅτι δῶ τις ἐπαινεῖ [a gift, because someone praises it], and what the common proverb says, which I call common because Saint Jerome used it: do not look into the teeth of a gifted horse. I beg your pardon for this fault. For I did look into it, read it attentively and considered that most ingenious and eloquent poem, and it has not disappointed my hope or lessened the admiration I had conceived beforehand. What happened to me is what happens to people who look at splendid palaces or huge mountains. From a distance they admire the wide walls, the threatening towers, the lofty roofs and the whole mass and splendour of the work; but close up they marvel at the joinery of the walls, the vestibules, the porticoes, the panelled ceilings and the whole architecture. Likewise, the greatness of mountains appears taller and loftier the closer we approach. So it was with your poem: as I studied it bit by bit and attended to each word, the things I had earlier judged, so to speak, in breadth and at a glance to be elegant, learned and ingeniously wrought, became objects of admiration, and I was sorry for my meagre and paltry praise. Who would not marvel at the clarity in your description of a most difficult subject, which verse shrinks from? Who would not gaze in awe at the windings of the gardens, the meanderings of the waters of that magnificent building, and, to pass over the rest, at the triumphal statues vividly portrayed? By inviting the scholars of the Academy to view those things you make the desire to see them empty for your guests, since everything is so plainly set out in easy verse, as the learned N. Scalopier, who has looked at these things, has sung no less shrewdly than elegantly about your poem. Who would not be amazed that the lights of your sentences, the variety of your figures, the majesty of your words and all the ornaments of your poetic storehouse have been drawn out and placed each according to the nature and native dignity of its subject? Nowhere are the little heads of the pygmies, as they say, fitted onto a colossus; rather great things are said greatly, middling things moderately, humble things neatly, and all things copiously and elegantly. Therefore I am grateful to you on two counts: because you have blessed me with an incomparable specimen of poetry, and because you have kept my memory in your heart...

units.la: ACcepi Opusculum tuum de Sacro Eucharistiae mysterio juxta S. Augustini sententiam explicato. Cùm autem negotiisquibusdam literariis eodem tempore impeditus essem, attentam illius lectionem quatuor aut quinque dies distuli, donec aliis curis expedito huic uni incumbere liceret. Neque enim pro tua in me benevolentia tibi gratias agere, proque merito tuo tam doctam lucubratiunculam digne gratulari me posse existimavi, nedum quanto ornamenio hæc una appellatus decorata sit Ecclesia Catholica, tenuiter describere, nisi prius tam pretiosi thesauri reclusis adytis singula illius γυμνάλια[?] lustrassem. Legi itaque, & perlegi libellum tuum, miratusque sum eum, cujus scripta varia legeram, alia adversus hæreticos, non loquentia latine autorantia, sed fulguranti a & tonantia. Alia poetice ludentia, & in asper materia pegasæum melos resonantia, tam repente vernaculam linguam adeo emendate eloqui, ut nihil elegantius, adeo eloquenter, ut nihil splendidius. Arnobium, ut recte notasti, castigat S. Hieronymus, ut inæqualem, & nimium, & absque operis partitione confusum. At vero quamcunque in partem tua verto & inverto, te tibi semper æqualem deprehendo, sive Latina Latinis comparem, Gallica Gallicis, sive hæc χιασμῶς[?] permisceam, sermo nusquam tumidus, nusquam jejunus, nusquam redundans, nusquam exanguis, sed ubique sanus & vividus, rationibus pressus, sensu sublimis, figuris efflorescens, affectibus concitatus, salibus passim intertextis jucundus, nunquam dissolutus. Quid partitionis lumen prædicem, cum adeo fulgeat, ut vel cæcum oculare possit & Myopem excæcare. Ausim itaque adulatione explosa, veritate suadente, quod ex S. Hieronymo de S Hilario animadvertisti, hac in causa usurpare, Galli cano cothurno attolleris & cum Græciæ floribus adorneris, non longis interdum periodis ut Hilarius involveris, sed ubique compositis, numerosis, teretibus, limpidissime fluis. Sane naturæ videtur hoc adagium, non omnis fert omnia tellus: unde merito Hectorem monet Æneas apud Euripidem,
units.tr: I have received your little work explaining the sacred mystery of the Eucharist according to the opinion of St Augustine. Since I was at the same time hindered by certain literary business, I put off a careful reading of it for four or five days, until I could be free of other cares and give myself to this alone. For I did not think I could thank you enough for your goodwill towards me, or congratulate you worthily on your merit in producing so learned a little work, still less describe in any detail with what ornament this one work has adorned the Catholic Church, unless I had first gone through each part of this precious treasure, with its inner sanctuaries unlocked, and examined its exercises [γυμνάσια]. So I read, and read through, your little book, and I was amazed at the man whose various writings I had read: some against the heretics, not speaking Latin but thundering and flashing like lightning; others playing poetically and sounding a Pegasean song on a rough subject. That he should so suddenly speak his native tongue so correctly, nothing more elegant, and so eloquently, nothing more brilliant! St Jerome, as you rightly note, reproves Arnobius as uneven, excessive, and confused, without any division of the work. But whichever way I turn and overturn your work, I find you always consistent with yourself, whether I set Latin beside Latin and French beside French, or mix them crosswise [χιασμῶς]. Your style is nowhere bombastic, nowhere dry, nowhere redundant, nowhere bloodless, but everywhere sound and lively, compact in its arguments, lofty in its sense, flowering with figures, stirred with feeling, delightful with wit woven in here and there, and never loose. Why should I praise the light of your division, when it shines so brightly that it could give sight to the blind and blind the myope? So, with flattery set aside and truth urging me, I venture to say that what you observed from St Jerome about St Hilary applies to you in this matter: you rise on the Gallic buskin and are adorned with the flowers of Greece. You do not, as Hilary sometimes does, wrap yourself in long periods, but everywhere you are composed, measured, polished, and flow most limpidly. Surely this is the saying of nature: not every land bears everything. Therefore Aeneas rightly advises Hector, in Euripides,

units.la: 'Αλλ' οὐ γὰρ αὐτὸς[?] πάντ' ἐπίστασθαι[?] βροτῶν πέφυκεν, ἄλλῳ δ' ἄλλο προσκεῖσθαι γέρας.
units.tr: But it is not in the nature of mortals to know everything; each has his own gift assigned to him. [Ἀλλ' οὐ γὰρ αὐτὸς πάντ' ἐπίστασθαι βροτῶν πέφυκεν, ἄλλῳ δ' ἄλλο προσκεῖσθαι γέρας.]

units.la: idem iis sacris donis evenire multis docet gentium eloquentissimus Apostolus, 1. Cor.12. Divisiones Gratiarum sunt, &c. Ideo poëticen tentasse Demosthenem nunquam legimus, id fecit Cicero, sed infeliciter ; neuter eloqventiæ vernaculæ limites egressus est. Quædam Cicero adolescens græce periclitatus est, sed umbratilem exercitationem potius prolusit, quam serio dixit ; quapropter ipse omnia ejusmodi obliteravit, nec unquam ab umbra in aprieum eduxit. Absolutam perfectionem mortalibus invidisse natura videtur, ut cùm divinæ & humanæ naturæ participes sint, divinam ita cogitent, ut humanæ non sint immemores. Verùm quidquid tibi libuerit, natura insolenter indulgens tibi concedit, omnia quæ ferre jubet contra morem felicissime unam & eamdem tellurem; cui igitur potius gratuler, anceps sum, tibi an S. Augustino, an Ecclesiæ Catholicæ ; tibi, qui fortissimum civem ex hostium manibus fortissime ereptum, reipublicæ Catholicæ reddidisti : S. Augustino, quod calumniæ, quibus sanctissima ipsius doctrina ab hæreticis appetitur ac obtenebratur, eloquentiæ tuæ fulmine tactæ qenitus[?] evanuerint: Ecclesiæ, quæ celeberrimum doctorem suum, hostium contumetumeliis laniatum corpore toto, & lacerum crudeliter ora Æsculapii Rothomagensis studio & opera, sanum & integrum recepit. Sed his omnibus simul vehementissime gratulari nos oportet, immo Augustinus, immo Ecclesia tibi summopere gratulantur: Augustinus enim Civicæ Coronæ ob sui salutem tibi reus est. Ecclesia verò Catholica ob victoriam de hæreticis reportatam, triumphalis & aureæ: Conatibus, quos quotidie pro Ecclesia capessis ingentes, faveat Deus, faxitque ut ex iis frugem boni omnes colligant quam opimam.
units.tr: The most eloquent of the Gentiles, the Apostle, teaches that the same holds of these sacred gifts for many people: 1 Cor. 12. There are diversities of gifts, and so on. Hence we never read that Demosthenes tried poetry; Cicero did, but unsuccessfully. Neither went beyond the limits of native eloquence. As a young man Cicero made some trial in Greek, but he practised it as a shadowy exercise rather than speaking in earnest; for that reason he himself blotted out all such things and never brought them from the shade into the open. Nature seems to have begrudged mortals absolute perfection, so that, though they share in both divine and human nature, they conceive of the divine in such a way as not to forget the human. But whatever you have wished for, nature, indulging you beyond its usual custom, grants you most happily, bidding all things to be borne upon one and the same earth. To whom, then, I should rather offer my congratulations I am uncertain: to you, or to St Augustine, or to the Catholic Church. To you, who restored a most valiant citizen, seized most valiantly from the hands of enemies, to the Catholic commonwealth; to St Augustine, because the calumnies by which his most holy teaching is assailed and obscured by the heretics have vanished, struck by the thunderbolt of your eloquence; to the Church, which has received back, sound and whole, its most celebrated teacher, torn in every part of his body by the insults of enemies and cruelly mangled, through the zeal and labour of the Rouen Aesculapius. But we must congratulate you most heartily on all these things together. Indeed, Augustine and the Church itself congratulate you most warmly: Augustine owes you a civic crown for his safety, and the Catholic Church, for the victory won over the heretics, owes you a triumphal and golden one. May God favour the great efforts you make daily on behalf of the Church, and grant that all good men may gather from them a most abundant harvest.

units.la: J'Ay porté avec un extreme regret le retardement du voyage de celuy, qvis'estoit chargé de porter à Paris mes Pentateuqves Samaritains, & autres livres & papiers venus de Levant, qve vous eussiez receus bien long temps ya, si mes vœus eussent peu sortir à effect ; mais ils ont esté traversés tantost par l'interruption du commerce, que la peste de Lyon, & de ces pays de déca renouvellée à diverses reprises avoit causée, tantost par les desordres publics, donc cette pauvre ville a esté affligée pendant quelqves temps, & tantost par des maladies, qvi nous ont assa illi par plusieurs fois, tant le Fr. Prieur de Roumoules, qvi en devoit estre le porteur comme moy dont nous n'avons gueres eu de relache, ni l'un ni l'autre durant la plus part de ce temps là, outre ceqve Monsieur de la Poterie Maistre des Reqvestes, intendant de la justice en cette Province, m'avoit tenu qvelqves mois dans l'esperance, qv[?] il les feroit porter avec ses hardes, n'aiant pas cru que le Roy l'arrestast si long temps comme il a fait par deca : c'est pourquoy j'estime, que quand vous prendres la peine d'en vouloir scavoir la verité, vous me trouverés plus excusable, qu'on ne se scauroit possible imaginé : attendu mesme, que comme du commencement on m'avoit mandé, que Mr. le Jay ne pretendoit pas se prevaloir du Pentateuque Samaritain en l'edition 'de[?] sa grande Bible, que pout en faire enricher des notes sur son texte Hebraique aux endrois ou les diverses lecons pourroint estre plus considerables. Lorsque par aprés il se fut resolu d'imprimer le texte Hebreu des Samaritains, nous eusmes quasi aussitost l'advis qu'il estoit sous la presse deja grandement avancé comme celuy de sa resolution de l'imprimer ; de sorte que nous avions sujet de croire, qu'il avoit tout ce qui luy pouvoit estre utile à ce dessein, & qu'il n'avoit gueres affaire de nos livres. Toutefois ajant sceu depuis qu'il y avoit quelque regret, & que vous desiries de les voir, j'ay esté bien aise de les vous faire communiquer estant, tresveritable que je ne suis nullement jaloux de ce que j'ay, & que le principal but de toutes mes recherches ne tend qu à en aider le public, ou à en faire part à ceux, qui en peuvent estre curieux, & qui en peuvent mieux faire leur profit, que moy dans les infirmités, qui me suivent depuis quelque temps; tant est que j'estime que le dit Fr. Prieur de Roumoules soit à ses heures à Paris avec ma caisse de livres, & que Mr. du Puy vous aura mis en main tout ce qui s'y sera rencontre de vostre goust, estant bien marri de n'avoir peu contribuer à vos doctes labeurs des pieces plus dignes de vous, & qu'elles ne soient moins defectueufes que ce qu'elles sont, mais en matieres de vieux livres, qui vinnent de si loin, & dont il faut aller faire la conqueste parmi des peuples si barbares, il se faut con enter de ce qu'on en peut arracher de vive force, & s'en prevaloir ou moins mal que faire se peut. Vous y trouveres trois volumes, & par consequent trois divers, exemplaires, du Pentateuque Hebraique des Samaritains, dont le plus ancien, qui est in quarto, est defectueux de plusieurs cajers, tant du commencement de la fin, & le plus recens (qui est en plus grande forme in folio, & qui n'est pas de guere plus de soixante & dix ou deuze ans d'antiquite) n'est imparfait que d'un seule page de son commencement ; mais l'autre, qui estoit le plus important de tous, & qui comme des tritaples est escrit par triples colomnes en chaque page (qui contient non seulement le texte Hebraique primitif, mais aussi l'ancienne version Arabique, & une troisieme vulgaire, que vous aimes mieux appeller Samaritaine que Syriaque) est imparfait en tant de divers endroit, qu'il y'a bien dequoy deploror qu'un si digne piece soit passée par de si indignes mains, & qu'elle en soit demeurée mutilée ainsi de la sorte, dont je regrette principalement le commencement{a} a cause de la conformité des nombres des années[?], de l'age de ces anciens Patriarches, qui eut esté bonno à exa-miner en ces deux versions,aussibien qvau texte Hebraiqve, & le livre sembloit estre de si bonne marqve, selon ceqvi se trouve cotté tant à la fin de l'Exode, qve toute la fin du volume depuis plus de qvatre cents ans de l'autre, qvi meritoit bien d'estre tenu en plus grande consideration qve beaucoup d'autres. Vo-us y aures par mesme moyen une petit Lexicon des Samaritains pour les mesmes trois langves,* qvi est pareillement imparfait de plusieurs feuilles à mon grand regret pour Pamour de vous; mais encore en vaut il mieux, si je ne me trompe, avoir ces fragmens qve nous en aurez, qve de n'en avoir point,& toujours n'est il point si moderne qv'il ne soit de plus de cent cinqvante ans. Vous y aurez encore en teste du plus moderne Pentateuqve, un fevillet d'un plus vieux Pentateuqve où il n'y avoit, qve la version Arabiqve é regione de l'Hebraiqve avec qvoy on avoit pense suppléer la defectuosite de cet exemplaire, où c'est qve ce petit supplement est possible plus considerable qve tout reste du volume: mais dans les grands tritaples vous verrez avec qvelle simplicitè un bon homme, de qvi on les a re couvrés ,avoit pense suppleer les defectuosités en faisant transcrire en characteres Syriaqves tous les cajers; qve vous y trouverés au commencement du texte Hebraiqve, & en dechirant un autre vieux Pentateuqve Hebraiqve, escrit en papier de damas, escrit pres de cent qvatrevingt ans, ya pour en entrelasser qvelqves caiers & qvelqves fevillets auxendroits ou l'on en avoit arrache aucuns dans cet exemplaire des tritaples Samaritains. Vous aurez en outre divers petits cajers, ou fevillets volants, qvi ne lont [?] qve fragmens de diverses pieces, ou autres escritures des Samarirains, qvæ j'ay fait assembler en un petit volume, non obstant leues imperfections, pour ne rieu negliger de tout ce qvi peut se retirer de leuers mains, où c'est qvjil y aura possible qvelqve petite chose à profiter qvand ce ne seroit, qv'en la comparaison de qvelqves petits escrtis [?] Arabiqves, avec une autre langve, qvi femble assez differente de la troisiesme colomne des tritapies, que nous avons prises pour qvelqve plus particulier jargon des Samaritains, qve le commun Syriaqve, dont vous ferez je m'assure meilleur juge qve nous. Finalement vous y ares deux autographes originaux de lettres escrites à feu Monsieur Joseph della Scala, tant par la Synagogve des Samaritans au lieu de Sichem, Iesqvelles lettres missives ne soni jamais tombeés es mains dudit Sr. Scaliger,qvi eut esté infiniment alse d'y apprendre la responfe de tout plein de qvestions,qv'illeurs avoit faites, dont il pretendoit se prevaloir urai semblablement en ses estudes Chronologiqves, & dont je m'assure aussi qve vous pourres tirer beaucoup de fruit, si vous daignes prendre la peine de les examiner. Je ne scay, comment elles estoient tombées entre les mains de feu Monsieur de Genebrard, qvi eut pris plaisir sans donte d'en voir le contenu, s'il se fut denne la[?] peine de les traduire comme me il le pouvoit; car il y a de tres belles curiosítez pour les usages & observances de cette secte là, qvi emprunte des usages de l'Eglise{†} Romaines, les reglemens de leurs festes mobiles, & de leurs computations plus importantes. Aureste je croy bien, qve vous aures fait faire instance en Hollande pour avoir la communication du Pentateuqve du Sr. Golius, puisqve c'est urai-semblablement le texte de la version, contenu en la troisieme colomne des tritaples Samaritains, qve vous voules faire jo indre à leur texte Hebraiqve en vostre edition; car il importe de ne la point publier qve bien correcte & bien complete, ce qve vous ne scauriès faire avec l' exemplaire du Sr. Pietro della Valle, non plus qv avec le mien, puisqve le mien est imparfait en tans de divers endroits, d' autant qve celuy du Sr. Pietro della Valle est si mal correct, qv en aiant seulement voulu conferer les deux versets du Deuterono-me,
units.tr: I have felt most keenly the delay in the journey of the man who undertook to carry to Paris my Samaritan Pentateuchs and the other books and papers that came from the Levant, which you would have received long ago if my wishes had been able to take effect. But they have been thwarted, sometimes by the interruption of commerce caused by the plague, renewed at various times, in Lyon and in these parts on this side; sometimes by the public disorders that afflicted this poor city for some time; and sometimes by illnesses that have attacked us several times, both Brother Prior of Roumoules, who was to be the bearer, and myself, so that for most of that period neither of us had any respite. Besides this, Monsieur de la Poterie, Master of Requests and intendant of justice in this Province, kept me for some months in the hope that he would have them carried along with his own baggage, not having thought that the King would detain him so long here as he has done. That is why I think that, when you take the trouble to learn the truth of the matter, you will find me more excusable than you could possibly have imagined; especially since, as I was told at the beginning, Monsieur Le Jay did not intend to make use of the Samaritan Pentateuch in the edition of his great Bible, but only to enrich his Hebrew text with notes at those places where the variant readings might be more important. When afterwards he resolved to print the Hebrew text of the Samaritans, we were almost immediately informed that the work was already far advanced at the press, as was his resolution to print it; so that we had reason to believe he had everything that could be useful for this purpose and had little need of our books. Nevertheless, having since learned that there was some regret and that you wished to see them, I was very glad to have them communicated to you. It is most true that I am not at all jealous of what I possess, and that the principal aim of all my researches is only to help the public, or to share them with those who may be curious about them and who can make better use of them than I can, given the infirmities that have followed me for some time. So I suppose that the said Brother Prior of Roumoules is at Paris from time to time with my chest of books, and that Monsieur du Puy will have put into your hands whatever in it has been to your taste. I am very sorry not to have been able to contribute to your learned labours pieces more worthy of you, and less defective than they are; but in matters of old books that come from so far away, and whose conquest must be made among such barbarous peoples, one must be content with what one can wrest from them by force, and make the best use of it that one can. You will find there three volumes, and therefore three different copies, of the Hebrew Pentateuch of the Samaritans. The oldest, which is in quarto, is defective in several quires, both at the beginning and at the end. The most recent (which is in a larger format, in folio, and is not much more than seventy or seventy-two years old) is imperfect only in one page at its beginning. But the other, which was the most important of all, and which is written like a triple text, in three columns on each page (containing not only the original Hebrew text, but also the old Arabic version and a third, vernacular one, which you prefer to call Samaritan rather than Syriac), is imperfect in so many different places that there is good reason to lament that so worthy a piece should have passed into such unworthy hands, and remained thus mutilated. I especially regret its beginning, because of the agreement of the numbers of years in the ages of those ancient Patriarchs, which would have been good to examine in these two versions as well as in the Hebrew text. The book seemed to be of very good quality, according to what is marked both at the end of Exodus and at the end of the volume, dating from more than four hundred years earlier than the other, and it deserved to be held in much greater esteem than many others. You will also find there, at the same time, a small Lexicon of the Samaritans in the same three languages, which is likewise imperfect in several leaves, to my great regret for your sake; but still, if I am not mistaken, it is better to have these fragments than to have nothing at all, and in any case it is not so modern that it is less than a hundred and fifty years old. You will also find at the front of the most recent Pentateuch a leaf of an older Pentateuch, which contained only the Arabic version set against the Hebrew, by which they had thought to supply the defect of this copy; and this little supplement is perhaps more valuable than any other remaining part of the volume. But in the large triple texts you will see with what simplicity a good man, from whom they were recovered, had thought to supply the defects, by having all the quires transcribed in Syriac characters; you will find this at the beginning of the Hebrew text, and by tearing apart another old Hebrew Pentateuch, written on damask paper and about a hundred and eighty years old, he has inserted some quires and some leaves in the places where some had been torn out of this copy of the Samaritan triple text. You will also have various small quires or loose leaves, which are only fragments of various pieces or other Samaritan writings. I have had these gathered into a small volume, despite their imperfections, so as not to neglect anything at all that can be recovered from their hands; there may perhaps be something of small profit in them, if only in comparing some short Arabic writings with another language, which seems rather different from the third column of the triple text, which we have taken to be some more particular jargon of the Samaritans rather than the common Syriac. About this you will, I am sure, be a better judge than we are. Finally, you will have two original autographs of letters written to the late Monsieur Joseph Scaliger, both from the Samaritan synagogue at the place of Shechem. These letters never came into the hands of the said Monsieur Scaliger, who would have been infinitely glad to learn there the answers to a great many questions which he had put to them, and which he intended to use, as is likely, in his chronological studies; and I am also sure that you will draw much profit from them, if you deign to take the trouble to examine them. I do not know how they came into the hands of the late Monsieur de Genebrard, who would doubtless have taken pleasure in seeing their contents, had he given himself the trouble of translating them as he could have done; for there are very fine curiosities concerning the customs and observances of that sect, which borrows from the usages of the Roman Church the rules for its movable feasts and its more important computations. Moreover, I believe well that you will have asked in Holland for the loan of the Pentateuch of Monsieur Golius, since it is probably the text of the version contained in the third column of the Samaritan triple text which you wish to add to their Hebrew text in your edition; for it matters that it should be published only when it is very correct and very complete, which you could not manage with the copy of Monsieur Pietro della Valle, any more than with mine, since mine is imperfect in many places, and because that of Monsieur Pietro della Valle is so badly corrected that when I wished only to compare the two verses of Deuteronomy,

units.la: {†} Id verum non est; Consule Vitam Jo. Mo-rini, qvæ his Epistolis præfixa est, me, dont m'aves ci devant envoié copie, qui sont le 27 & le 28 du 12 chapitre, nous y avons trouvez plus de huict ou dix paroles, où l'on avoit obmis, ou changé, ou transpose des lettres, essentielle qui en alteroient grandement le vray sens, & en d autres y avoit des lettres redoublées, ou surabondantes, qui agrifsoient[?] un peu la douceur du langvage Syriaqve, les distinctions mesmes y estoient si fautives, (comme vous l'aviez remarqve, les) qu'en un endroit on l'voit mis apres la premiere parole d'un nouveau verset, & possible n'estre qve pour telles incorrections ou barbarismes. Qve vous aviéz fait difficulté de prendre ce langvage pour vray Syriaqva, comme vous aviez fait, pour raison de qvoy je me rapporterai toujours volontiers à vos bons advis. Or je ne trouverois pas estrange qve l'exemplaire dudit Sr. Pietro della Valle fusse plus negligement escrit qve les autres, puis qu'il n'est qu'en papier, & non parchemin, & par consequent qu'il n'estoit fait qve pour servir à l'usage de quelq; personne particuliere, là où les copies faites en parchemin pouvoiét servir à l'usage public des Synagogues, pour lequel vrai semblablement il faloit qu'on y regardast de plus prés. Je regrette beacoup plus la perte des cajers, qui manquent en mon exemplaire Tritaple pour la version Arabique, que pour les autres deux textes, lesquels sont beaucoup plus conformes l'un à l'autre que l'Arabique, à cause que dans l'Arabique il y a certaines petites diversités de paroles capables de fournir de tres belles conceptions à ceux qui y voudroient mediter, & rechercher l'energie des unes & des autres; mais je ne scay, s'il se trouvera jamais de moien de perfectioner & suppléer les deffauts de mon Exemplaire, pour le texte de cette version Arabique. Celuy qui me la fait recouvrer en la ville de Damas y est retourné pour l'amour de moy, & usera de toutes les diligences possibles pour en venir à bout, & pour fouiller le plus avant, qu'il lui fera possible tans toutes ces familles des Samaritains, tains, qui restent non seulement en la Sy-rie, mais aussi dans le Cayre, où il veut aller repasser une seconde fois devant que s'en revenir en Chrestienté. S'il recouvre quelque chose, que je juge vous estre [?]duisable ou à Monsieur le Jay, vous pouvez vous assurer, que je vous en feray telle part que vous voudrés, & que je voudrois bien avoir peu contribuer quelque chose pour faciliter l'Edition si parfaite & accomplie de ces Pentateuques Samaritaint, qu'il n'y eusse rien à desirer pour l'importance de la publication d'un si rare monument de la plus haute antiquité, lequel nous avoit fourni un entretien des plus agreables, que nous eussions jamais [?]favouré en matiere de livres. Des la premiere ouverture, que nous fismes de ce volume tritaple, où nous rencontrasmes par hazard ou premier mot, que nous voulusmes dechifrer le mon de Benjamin, avec une M. finale au lieu de l'N. finale du texte Hebreu des Juifs, dont l'Etymologie avoit donné tant de vexation aux SS. Peres, qui ne s'y fussent pas tant tourtourmentés, s'ils y eussent veu cette lettre, qui rapporte l'Etymologie à la vraye qualité de la naissance de cet enfant aux jours de la vieillesse de son pere : ce qui nous mit en tel goust, & en telle impatience, que nous ne nous peusmes pas retenir d'entreprendre & achever dans le moins de temps, qu'il nous fut possible la collation de tout ce que nous avions de ce texte, avec celuy des Juifs, & avec les Septante, ou nous admirasmes bien comme vous la rencontre de tant de grands & importans supplemens, qui s'en pouvoient tirer, & que vous aves si dignement remarqves, dont je donneray incontinent un mor[?] d'advis à Mss du Huy, qui ne tarda pas d'estre suivi de l'escantillon, qu'il vous en firent voir. J'ay appris que dans le Vatican, il a este mis depuis peu un exemplaire bien entier d'un Pentateque des Samaritains, aiant fait voir ce que c'estoit, on m'a assuré que ce n'estoit que le simple texte Hebraique ; j'ay appris aussi qu'il y en avoit un autre dans la Biblioteque de l'Empereur à Vienne, dont le Bibliothecaire avoit promis un eschantillon, que je luy en avois fait demander par le Sr. Lucas Holsten, afin de voir si laversion Arabique se pouvoit suppleer, mais je pense que ces grandes du Roy de Svede nous ont oste le moien d en avoir la response, neanmonis j'ay creu vons en deir tenir adverti, cas que vostre curiosité vous portast à vous en enquerir par autre voye. Il me reste à vous dire sur le sujet de vostre livre des exercitations, que vous je suis trop redvable de l'honneur, que vous m'aves voulu faire, & je suis bien marri de me rendre si indigne comme je suis, de la bonne opinion, que vous aves voulu prendre de moy, & de me sentir les reins si foibles, comme ils sont ponr'y pouvoir respondre, ainsi qu'il seroit requis; mais comme c'est de la seul bonté de vostre naturel, que vous vous estes porté à me faire sentir de tels effets de vostre bonté, & de vos bons offices, il faut que vostre mesme courtoisité & honnestete supplee mes defectuosites, & vous en face admettre les excuses, qui ne seroient pas recevables sans cela, en attendant que Dieu m'ouvre de meilleurs moiens de vous témoigner l'estime, que je faits de nostre vertu nonpareille, & à combien grande faveur je recois l'honneur de vostre bienvueillance, & de pouvoir Passer pour l'unde vos tres-humbles Serviteurs.
units.tr: {†} That is not true. Consult the Life of Jo. Morinus, which is prefixed to these Epistles. As for the copy you sent me earlier, of verses 27 and 28 of chapter 12, we found in it more than eight or ten words where letters had been omitted, changed or transposed, essential letters that greatly altered the true sense. In other places there were doubled or superfluous letters, which somewhat spoil the smoothness of the Syriac language. The word divisions were themselves so faulty (as you had remarked) that in one place a word was placed after the first word of a new verse, and this may perhaps be due only to such incorrections or barbarisms. You hesitated to take this language for true Syriac, as you had done, and on that account I shall always willingly defer to your good judgement. Now I would not be surprised that the copy of the said Sr. Pietro della Valle is more carelessly written than the others, since it is on paper and not parchment, and consequently was made only for the use of some private individual, whereas copies made on parchment could serve the public use of the synagogues, for which it was probably necessary to look more closely. I regret the loss of the quires missing from my Tritaple copy for the Arabic version much more than the loss for the other two texts, which agree far more closely with one another than the Arabic does. In the Arabic there are certain small differences of wording capable of furnishing very fine insights for those who wish to meditate on them and seek out the force of each of the others. But I do not know whether there will ever be a means of perfecting and supplying the defects of my copy for the text of this Arabic version. The man who got it for me in the city of Damascus has returned there for my sake, and will use every possible diligence to succeed, and to search as deeply as he can among all those families of Samaritans who remain not only in Syria but also in Cairo, whither he intends to go a second time before returning to Christendom. If he recovers anything which I judge you could make use of, or which could be of use to Monsieur le Jay, you may be assured that I will give you whatever share you wish of it. I would very much like to have been able to contribute something toward facilitating the so perfect and accomplished edition of these Samaritan Pentateuchs, so that nothing would be left to desire, given the importance of publishing so rare a monument of the highest antiquity, which has afforded us the most agreeable entertainment in matters of books that we have ever enjoyed. From the very first opening of this Tritaple volume, where by chance we came upon the first word we wished to decipher, the name Benjamin with a final M in place of the final N of the Hebrew text of the Jews, whose etymology had caused such vexation to the Holy Fathers, who would not have tormented themselves so much had they seen this letter, which refers the etymology to the true circumstance of the child's birth in his father's old age, we were so taken and so impatient that we could not restrain ourselves from undertaking and completing, in the shortest time possible, the collation of everything we had of this text with that of the Jews and with the Seventy. There we marvelled, as you did, at the discovery of so many great and important supplements that could be drawn from it, which you have so worthily remarked upon. I shall shortly send a brief notice of this to Messrs du Hui, which was soon followed by the sample they showed you. I have learned that a very complete copy of a Samaritan Pentateuch has recently been placed in the Vatican; having seen what it was, I was assured that it was only the plain Hebrew text. I have also learned that there is another in the Imperial Library at Vienna, whose librarian had promised a sample, which I had asked Mr. Lucas Holsten to request for me, so as to see whether the Arabic version could be supplied from it. But I think that the great affairs of the King of Sweden have taken away the means of obtaining a reply. Nevertheless I thought I should inform you of this, in case your curiosity led you to inquire by another route. It remains for me to say, on the subject of your book of exercitations, that I am far too much indebted to you for the honour you wished to do me, and I am very sorry to show myself so unworthy of the good opinion you have chosen to form of me, and to feel my strength so weak that I cannot reply as would be required. But since it is only from the goodness of your nature that you have been moved to show me such effects of your kindness and good offices, your own courtesy and honesty must supply my shortcomings and make you admit my excuses, which would not otherwise be acceptable, until God opens to me better means of showing you the esteem I hold for your unparalleled virtue, and how great a favour I count the honour of your goodwill, and of being permitted to pass for one of your most humble servants.

units.la: J'ay veu ce que vous escrivez des cicles anciens, & crois binn, que je pourrois fournir à vostre curiosite quelque chose de plus que ce qui vous en est tombe en main, car j en ay plus de trente pieces differentes, & de differente proportion tant d argent que de cuivre, entr autres le de mi Sicle avec toute son inscription bien entiere, & plusieurs pieces, qui pertent le non de Syon, que vostre Rabi Moses Alascarin avoit remarque de son temps, dont l'un me fut dones des l'annee 1606. de la main de feu Mr. della Scala, qui n' avoit pas pris la deine de la voloit lire & de schifrer, & qui volut absolument, que je l'emportasse aussitost que je luy en eu dit mon avis: j'ay encore Plusieurs pieces battües dans la Judée sous les Rois Herodes & autres Princes,qui peuvent bien aider ce qui est de l'histoire sainte , mais cen'est pas matiere en un mot , qui puisse estre avidable par des simples lettres missives , si vous faisies quelque voyage à Rome, je prendrois grand plaisir de vous gouverner— quelque journée en passant. J'ay mesme bonne quantité de medailles en lettres Phoeniciennes &Puniques,&à recouvray ces jours passes du coste d' Afriq;, une assez grande inscription tirée d'un Mausolée d'importance,qui est pareillement en Caracteres Puniques, dont les figures meritent bien d' estre examinées curieusement, principalement celles, qui peuvent avoir quelque rapport avec la figura de quelques uns des Caracteres Hebraiques anciens , ou modernes Sa-maritains, dont il importe bien de donner l'Alphabet en son ancienne purité; car il est bien vray, que la longue suitte de tant de sicles, a fait que les Samaritains y ont alteré beaucoup de choses affez considerables, principalement en la lettre Tau, comme vous l'aves tres doctement observe; & si vos presses ne fussent allées si viste, il y auroit possible eu moien de rendre vos matieres, ou caracteres, un peu plus gentils sans s'esloigner de la vraye morme de ces caracteres Samaritains, qui se trouvent dans les livres plus anciens, & de meilleure marque, principalement en ce ou le caractere moderne se trouvoit avoir retenu sa forme plus approchante de l'antique, & particulierement pour la lettre Vau : je n'aurois pas voulu laisser la concurrence du plus grand nombre des MSS pour en suivre un tout seul, mais il estime qu'il seroit trop tard pour y apporter aucun remede, puisque j'entens que l'edition de tous vos textes est deja si avancée. Je ne voudrois insister principalement qu'à faire agir toute sorte d'honnestes & lici[?]tes moiens d'obtenir des Estats de Hollande, ou du Sr. Golius la communication de l'exemplaire, que feu Mr. della Scala avoit des livres de Josüe, des Samaritains, qui meriteroent possible d'estre imprimes à la suite de vostre grande Bible, ou pour le moins de passer par vos mains, ou de quelque autre, qui possedast bien la langue Arabique, & qui vous peust donner quelque petit abregé de toutes leurs Chronologies, ce n'estoit que pour parvenir à ce dessein là que Mr. della Scala avoit fait tant d'instance pour avoir le Pentateuque des Samaritains, & principalement la version qu'ils en avoient en Arabe, pour apprendre le moyen d'interpreter plus certainement selon leurs sens les dits livres de Josüé, à quoy je vous prie de songer à bon escient, & de me commander librement en tout ce qve me jugeres propre à vostre service, comme celuy qui veut estre à jamais sous vostre bon plaisir.
units.tr: I have seen what you write about the ancient shekels, and I believe I can supply your curiosity with something more than what has come into your hands. I have more than thirty different pieces, of differing weight, in silver as well as in bronze, among them the half-shekel with its whole inscription intact, and several pieces bearing the name of Zion, which your rabbi Moses Alascarin remarked in his time. One of these was given to me in 1606 by the late Mr. della Scala, who had not taken the trouble to read or decipher it, and who insisted absolutely that I carry it away as soon as I had given him my opinion of it. I also have several pieces struck in Judea under the kings Herod and other princes, which may well help with sacred history. But this is not a matter, in a word, that can be settled by ordinary letters. If you make some journey to Rome, I would take great pleasure in showing you some of these things for a day as you pass through. I also have a good number of medals with Phoenician and Punic letters, and these past days I received from the coast of Africa a fairly large inscription, taken from an important mausoleum, which is likewise in Punic characters. Its figures deserve to be examined carefully, especially those which may have some relation to the form of some of the ancient Hebrew characters, or of the modern Samaritan ones. It matters greatly to set out the alphabet in its ancient purity, for it is indeed true that the long course of so many centuries has caused the Samaritans to alter many quite considerable things, chiefly in the letter Tau, as you have very learnedly observed. And if your presses had not gone so quickly, it might perhaps have been possible to make your material, or type, a little more graceful without departing from the true form of these Samaritan characters, as found in the older and better-marked books, especially where the modern character had kept a form closer to the ancient one, particularly for the letter Vau. I would not have wished to abandon the agreement of the greater number of manuscripts in order to follow a single one. But I think it would now be too late to apply any remedy, since I hear that the edition of all your texts is already so far advanced. My chief wish is only to urge every honest and lawful means of obtaining, from the States of Holland or from Mr. Golius, the loan of the copy which the late Mr. della Scala had of the Samaritan book of Joshua. It might perhaps deserve to be printed after your great Bible, or at least to pass through your hands or those of some other who knows the Arabic language well and who could give you some short summary of all their chronologies. It was only to reach this goal that Mr. della Scala made such insistent requests for the Samaritan Pentateuch, and especially the Arabic version they had of it, in order to learn the means of interpreting the said book of Joshua more surely according to their meaning. I beg you to consider this seriously, and to command me freely in anything you judge useful to your service, as one who wishes to be forever at your good pleasure.

units.la: Reverende admodum D. Vir Clarissime Doctissimeque.
units.tr: Most reverend Sir, most distinguished and most learned.

units.la: CUm rescissem partim ex fama, ad nos per librarios perlata, partim ex praeviis quibusdam lucubrationibus tuis, editionem Bibliorum SS. instructissimam, & caeteris omnibus locupletiorem Parisiis à vobis adornari, avide sane aures animumque adverti, maxime verò praeter additamenta, ornamentaque caetera, Samaritanam quoq; supellectilem nobis Europaeis hactenus per secula complura incognitam, & à paucis aliquot desiderari jam coeptam eidem accessuram esse, equidem serio gaudebam. Dabit ea res cùm utilitatem, quod tu affatim doces, multiplicem ; tum etiam voluptatem è re veteri pariter & nova emersuram. Neque vero ab Ecclesia alienum, quidquid ad Scripturæ nomen pertineat, existimandum est, nedum Samaritarum hoc insigne Κεμμήλιον[?], ubicunque tandem locorum illud abditum, vel quibuscunque hominibus creditum delituerit, quod à custodibus suis jam profugum in Ecclesiæ sinum se recipit. Τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πάντα συνᾴδει[?], inquit Philosophus, idque usu ipso ita esse comperimus, in veritatis scilicet choro cuncta concinere, & vel discrepando erroris sui indicium, vel consensu harmonicam dare. Sapientiæ quoque divinæ illud ingens argumentum habemus, quæ multa cum diu tanquam femina occultaverit, suo tempore in usum proferre novit. Sed hujus rei fructum uberiorem cum ipsa voluminum editione expectamus, quibus coëmendis & pretium seponimus. Nunc quid hoc officii sit, quô te homines ignoti longeque dissiti interpellamus, si placet, paucis accipe.
units.tr: Having learned, partly from report carried to us by booksellers and partly from some earlier writings of yours, that a most fully equipped edition of the Holy Bible, richer than all others, is being prepared by you at Paris, I have listened eagerly and with real joy. I was especially glad that, besides the additions and other ornaments, it will also include a Samaritan apparatus, hitherto unknown to us Europeans for many centuries and only lately desired by a few. This will bring, as you clearly show, a manifold usefulness, and also a pleasure arising from what is old and new alike. Nor should anything that pertains to the name of Scripture be thought foreign to the Church, much less this remarkable Samaritan heirloom [κειμήλιον], wherever in the world it has lain hidden or in whatever hands it has been entrusted, which now, fleeing from its keepers, takes refuge in the bosom of the Church. "All things agree with the truth" [Τῇ ἀληθείᾳ πάντα συνᾴδει], says the Philosopher, and we find by experience that it is so: that in the chorus of truth everything harmonises, and that whatever disagrees gives evidence of its own error, while what agrees gives a harmonious witness. We also have in this a great proof of divine wisdom, which, though it has long hidden many things like a woman, knows how to bring them forth for use at the proper time. But we look for the richer fruit of this matter together with the publication of the volumes themselves, and we are setting aside money to buy them. Now, if you please, hear briefly what service it is for which we, unknown men and far distant, trouble you.

units.la: Editionis hujus novæ non parum in-teresse teresse[?] scimus, ut ea plurimorum collatione codicum confirmata li[?] lucem exeat, sed hanc copiam optare his locis, quam sperare promptius. Cùm igitur penes nos id genus quiddam haberemus, quod ad rem vestram facere videretur, hocque vobis oblatum haud displicuisse intelligamus, id juris vestri, promissi fidem evolventes jam facimus. Quod si forte hæc unde aut qualia sint, requiritis, hoc etiam candoris est nostri ostendere.
units.tr: We know that this new edition will not a little gain in value if it is confirmed and brought to light by the collation of many manuscripts; but to wish for this abundance in these places is easier than to hope for it. Since, then, we had among us a manuscript of this sort, which seemed to bear on your work, and since we understand that the offer was not unwelcome to you, we now make it available to you, fulfilling our promise of your right. And if perhaps you ask where it comes from or what it is like, it is also a matter of our candour to show this.

units.la: Exemplar Samaritanum sat pulchrum, Hebræà lingvâ, charactere Samaritico, sibi ex Oriente comparaverat R. Archiepiscopus Armachanus J. Usherius Hibernus. Is cùm apud nos aliquot mensibus ageret, re cum studiosis quibusdam communicatâ, factaqve Codicis sui copiâ, differentias conferendo annotari, &in usum quoqve nostrum describi non ægre pro humanitate sua concessit. Liber ipse fere in forma Folii, vel Quarti majore, ita fuit exaratus, ut non versibus usitatis, sed periodis, vel pericopis potius longioribus, pars quædam comprehenderetur, & relicto spatio distin-gueretur. singulæ fere paginæ tribus sorte ejusmodi, vel pluribus pericopis. Quæ res annotari, nisi totum describendo, non poterat; voces item singulæ, interposito puncto, distinctæ.
units.tr: The Samaritan copy, fairly handsome, in the Hebrew language and in Samaritan characters, had been acquired for himself from the East by the Most Reverend Archbishop of Armagh, J. Usher, the Irishman. When he was staying with us for some months, after he had shared the matter with certain scholars and had made a copy of his manuscript available, he kindly and courteously allowed its differences to be noted by comparison and also to be copied out for our use. The book itself, in roughly folio or large quarto form, was written in such a way that a certain part was contained not in the usual verse-lines but in periods, or rather in longer sections, and was separated by leaving a space. Each page had about three such sections, or more. This arrangement could not be noted except by transcribing the whole; the individual words were likewise separated by a point placed between them.

units.la: Litterarum quarundum inter se non eadem hic similitudo apparet, quæ in Hebraicis, ex qua re infinita pene judicandi materia suboritur. Quæ à clarissimo Viro J. Selde-no nostro citata memoras ea, ne forte plura exemplaria suspicamini, ab eodem fonte esse sat scimus, & ipse præfatione ad marmora sua testatur. Codicem iplum si quid inspici sit opus, in bibliotheca Oxoniensi jam servari accepimus.
units.tr: The likeness of certain letters to one another is not the same here as in the Hebrew, and from this arises an almost endless matter for judgement. As for the things you mention as cited by our most distinguished J. Selden, lest you suspect there are several copies, we know well that they come from the same source, and he himself attests this in the preface to his marbles. As for the codex itself, if anything needs to be inspected, we have heard that it is now kept in the Oxford library.

units.la: Unum forte audire non pigebit. Venerat tum temporis ad nos Judæus quidam Italus non incelebris, is inspecto libro, hic liber, inquit, si in manus incideret nostras, esset comburendus, neque enim fas nostris, alia litterarum forma, quam usitata, scripturam edere, nec vero alia lingua, ad verbum, sed tantum paraphrastice eam interpretari. Hæc ille ex Judæorum sensu. Nostros quod attinet, præsertim vero eos, qvi Hebræo Judæorum textui addictiores sunt, licet sufficere etiam versiones non inficientur, hoc unum forte dabit solicitos, qvo numero & loco, qvo honore & gradu Samaritana hæc, eodem scilicet & pari, an etiam priori qvam Hebræa, sint habenda. Qvibus enim ajunt concredita sunt eloqvia Dei? Qvæ ab Esdra sunt, potiora dicis, an qvæ à Dositheo & Zacharia? Sed de his plura & meliora vobis sub prælo esse non dubitamus. Vestrum jam erit Vir Rev. qvod candide offerimus, æqvi boniqve consulere: Prolixitati etiam huic nostræ in qvam nec opini incidimus amice ignoscere. Jam enim vobis studiisqve vestris bene precati epistolam claudimus. Vale V.R. meqve vicissim tibi commendatissimum habe.
units.tr: One thing perhaps it will not be a trouble to hear. At that time a certain Italian Jew, not unknown, had come to us; having looked at the book, he said: "If this book fell into our hands it would have to be burned, for it is not lawful for us to publish Scripture in a script other than the usual one, nor indeed to translate it in another language word for word, but only to paraphrase it." So he spoke, out of the Jewish understanding. As for our own people, especially those more attached to the Hebrew text of the Jews, they do not deny that even versions may suffice; this alone will perhaps trouble them, by what number, place, honour and rank this Samaritan text is to be held: whether equal to the Hebrew, or perhaps even earlier than it. "To whom indeed were the oracles of God entrusted?" (Rom. 3.) Are those things which came from Ezra the more important, or those from Dositheus and Zacharias? But we do not doubt that more and better things on these matters are in press for you. It will now be for you, most reverend sir, to receive kindly what we offer candidly; and to forgive this length of ours, into which we did not fall without intention. For now, having wished you well in you and your studies, we close the letter. Farewell, most reverend sir, and hold me in return as most commended to you.

units.la: Quod seriùs hæc ad te veniant, incausa quidam fuit, qui duorum Librorum annotata ita detinebat, & adhuc detinet, ut ea retrahere nullo modo possumus. Quæ tamen si expetantur, operam dabimus, ut postea mitti possint.
units.tr: That these things reach you later was due to a certain person who kept, and still keeps, the notes on the two books, so that we cannot in any way get them back. If, however, they are wanted, we will take care that they may be sent afterwards.

units.la: EPIST. XXXVIII.
units.tr: Epistle 38.

units.la: J. Morinus Tho. Combero gratias agit ob missas ad se ab eo Codicis Samaritani cum Indice Hebraei collati varias lectiones exemplariorum quatuor M. SS. Pentateuchi Samar. formam transcribit Morinus, cum variis in illud Argumentum Animadversioni-bus.
units.tr: J. Morinus thanks Thomas Comber for the variant readings, collated with the Hebrew text, of four manuscript copies of the Samaritan Pentateuch that Comber sent him from the Samaritan codex. Morinus sets out the Samaritan form, with various remarks on that subject.

units.la: Thomæ Combero Carlilensi Decano.
units.tr: To Thomas Comber, Dean of Carlisle.

units.la: Amplissime & Erud. Dom.
units.tr: Most distinguished and learned Sir,

units.la: ACcepi litteras tuas, quæ mihi non potuerunt non esse gratissimæ, cùm amicitiam tuam quamplurimi facio, quamque diligenter excolendam mihi propono, non modo ultro offerant, verùm etiam facto comprobent teqve de-monmonstrent, ἀγλωσσῃ[?] Φίλον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐγγῳ[?] Simul enim cum humanissimis tuis literis accepi codicis Samaritani, qvi penes vos est Judaico textu varietates. Rem mihi perjucundam fecisti, & magnorum Bibliorum apparatui instruendo perutilem, alias,non ego tantum habeo tibi gratias, sed habebit publica rei Christianæ utilitas. Triumtantum LibrorumMosaicorum cum textu Hebræo collationem ad me misisti, duorum,qvi supersunt collationem eadem animi tui benevolentia fretus, te missurum spero, atqve cùm occasio sese obtulerit, ut mittas impensissime rogo. Paucis, Vir amplissime, qvoniam res ipse id mecum qvodammodo expostulat, & tu ansam præbes, de Samaritanis codicibus disseram: paucis, inqvam, nam temporis brevitate plurimum urgeor, nec præsentissimum tabellarii discessum negligere debeo, ne officii mei longiori comperendinatione, beneficii tui immemor, vel tantisper exîstimer. Sunt mihi qvatuor exemplaria manuscripta codicis Hebræo-Samarita-ni, tum est integrum, priori folio excepto quod alio inserto resartitum est, sed recenter scriptum ante annos circiter 70. eleganti & magno charactere. Qvintum Exemplar, Vir clarissime, tuum erit. Excudi praeter ea, curavimus istius Pentateuchi versionem Dialecto Samaritano factam,cujus exemplar integrum Romae nacti sumus, praeter illud, quod in columnato nostro codice habemus. Haec sunt, quibus utimur, exemplaria. Illa versuum distinctio,quam describis, est omnibus exemplaribus communis, atque exacte & rigide ab iis observatur; vocant distinctiones istas - פסוקים[?] Lectiones, Periodorum vero distinctio apud eos, fere ut apud nos est arbitraria; de his plura in Exercitat. nostris ad Samarit. Pentateuchum. Horum omnium exemplarium maxima est conformitas, si dictiones spectes, non autem si litteras: in duplici enim hypothesi illa comparanti nonnunquam deprehenditur. Prior est, cum litterae א[?], qvas Judaei matres pronunciationis vocant, sub audiuntur apud Hebraeos braeos, tum nonnunquam unum exemplar illas exprimit, alterum supprimit, verbi gratia, Gen.50,25. Judæi codices legunt וישבע, sic etiam duo ex meis alia duo cum tuo addunt Jod וישבריע. Hinc colligitur Samaritanos ibi pronunciare ויושבע non ויושבע; pronunciatio enim Vajasbia, seu litteræ Jod scriptori occasionem dedit illam inserendi, sic v. 15. ejusdem cap. tuum, & duo ex meis scribunt הושב; alia duo inserunt Jod. Ratio hujusce rei est, quod dicunt Judæorum Grammatici post motionem longam, sub audiendam unam ex matribus lectionibus scilicet post Chirec & Tzere, Jod; Post. Kamets, Aleph; post Cholem & Schurek, Vau. Nonnunquam Textus Hebræus illas exprimit nonnunquā reticet. Itaq; sæpe transcriptores in hoc variant; istaqve Variatio apud Judæos ante Masoretas creberrima erat, atqve etiam nunc in ipsis Israëliticis numismatis conspicitur, post Masoretas longe minus freqvens; multa tamen post illud tempus, illius ostenduntur exempla, sed qvidqvidqvid sit, variationes ejusmodi distinctionis significationem non variant, sed pronunciationis adjuvandae causa tantum contingunt. Multo rarius in littera Aleph varietas contingit. Posterior hypothesis est permutatio Litterarum Gutturalium אהחע ; non omnino sine causa dixit R. Benjamin, Samaritanos tres litteras ע.ח.ה. non habere ; omnes enim Gutturales, ut א pronunciant, atque ideo in versione saepissime videas in una pagina eamdem dictionem modo per ע. modo per ח modo per ה, scriptam, Ain saepe pro Aleph & pro ה licet apud eos nulla sit litterarum istarum similitudo ; nos innumera ejusmodi observavimus, observando defesi sumus. Hinc in textu sacro, licet rarissime, aliquando tamen in hac re hallucinati deprehenduntur Amanuenses, ut Gen. c. 3. v. 24 codex tuus habet להט[?] ; sic & unus ex meis ; ad vetustus meus לחמ[?], ut Judaicus. Jam Epistolii modulum excessimus, unius tamen te monitum velim ; quatuor mea exemplaria, Gen. c. 50. v. 19, constanter habent אנ התחתאלהים[?]; sic etiam ambæ versiones Samaritanæ, Judaica acdunt כי[?], differentiam ibi nullam notas, qvasi tuum exhiberet כי[?]. Una versio ve- rit אנה[?] דחול אלח[?] Timens Deum ego sum: Cui consentit Onkelos & Jonathan Chaldæi interpretes, & antiqva Pentateuchi Samaritani versio Græca, cujus vestigia nonnulla deprehenduntur in Scholiis, qvæ citantur in Editione 70 interpretum Sixtiana, ἡ γὰρ Φοβού- μένῳ Θεὸν εἰμὶ ἐγώ[?]. Si in tuo exem- plari revera est כי[?] videtur sic legisse interpres Græcus. Sed interptetes illi,& Samarita & Græcus, in textu Hebræo Samaritano,&Chaldæi in Hebræo Judaico dictionis התחת[?] litteras sic permutatas legerunt התחת[?]. Altera Samaritana versio qvam edidimus החלופת[?] אלהים אנה[?] Numqvid vice Dei ego sum? ut legunt & interpretantur Judæi, & antiqvitus legerunt Symmachus & Aqvila 70 non legerunt ה[?], sed sic, כיתחת אלהים אנ[?], ut ex versione manifestum est. Præterea ejusdem 50. cap. v. 23. omnia mea exemplaria constanter habent בִּסְרִי יוֹסֵף. Sic etiam ambo interpretes Samaritani, adnotas tamen in tuo בִּסְרִי scriptum esse, sed עַיִן ut in Hebraeo non praecedere, facile ibi hallucinationem existimarem. Cap. 3. v. 24. Exempla tuum habet תְּמִימָה בְּנַי error est, duo mea integra scribunt, ut apud Judaeos, הַמְמִהְפְּכִים, & interpres Samaritanus eandem vocem in dialecto sua retinet, הַמְּמִיהָ הַבַּי, haec de multis pauca lecta sunto. Quod scribit de illo Judaeo Italo, nugae sunt, istarum rerum ignarus haec effutivit. Nulli enim Judaei docti Samaritanos Characteres negant apud Judaeos olim in usu fuisse, licet nonnulli librum Legis, quo in Synagoga utuntur, eo charactere describere illicitum affirmant. De hac re multis ex Rabbinorum sententia in exercitationibus nostris disseruimus. Verum quidem est, eos tanto in Samaritanos odio agitari, ut librum Legis non modo Samaritano Charactere, sed etiam Assyriaco seu Judaico a Samaritano scri-ptum ptum prophanum censeant, juxta illud Mosis Ægyptii exioma tractat. Thephill. sect. 1. n. 11. כל דבר שצריך מעשה לשמו [illegible, ~3 letters] שהן הכותי פכול Quidquid necesse est fieri nomine tuo, si illud faciat Cutheus, prophanum est; sed hoc personæ, non characteris odio. Consimiliter falsum Judæis ne-fas esse legem κατὰ λέξιν in aliam lin-gvam transferre. Ipsi Talmudistæ Lin-gvam Græcam excipiunt, omnesque Judæi uno R. Azaria excepto Legem à 72. Interpretibus ex Hebræo textu verbum è verbo translatam fuisse testantur. Hic Azarias solus è Libris Chaldaicis Characterè Samaritano descriptis translationem factam fuisse opinatur. Prætere-a R. Saadias apud Judæos celeberrimus, ante sexcentos & quinquaginta annos Legem κατὰ λέξιν transtulit, quæ Thessalonicæ ab ipsis Judæis charactere Hebraeo excusa est, cujus exemplar penes nos est, estque Parisi. ejusdem translationis exemplar Arabicis Characteribus manuscriptum. Cæterùm Judaicos co{*}dices cæteris paribus esse Samaritanis qvibuscunqve præferendos, nemo est opinor, qvi dubitet. Samaritanas tuas Lecti-ones, cum primum usus fuero, remit-tam. Interim communicati mecum laboris tui gratias ago iterum atque ite-rum. Magno sane munere, cum rem ipsum[?] considero[?], me affecisti; sed cum animi tui benevolentiam maximo, ξενίων δὲ τε θυμὸς ἀρίςτῳ[?], hunc ut mihi conserves perpetuo, etiam atque etiam rogo. Vale, Vir amplissime, & me tui observantissimum amare perge.
units.tr: I received your letter, which could not fail to give me the greatest pleasure, since I value your friendship very highly and propose to cultivate it with care. Your letter not only offers it unprompted but also proves it by deed, showing you to be a friend not in word but in deed [ἀγλώσσῳ φίλον, ἀλλ' ἐγγύς]. Along with your most kind letter I received the variant readings between the Samaritan codex in your possession and the Jewish text. You have given me great delight, and a great help in equipping the large Bible apparatus. I therefore owe you thanks, and the public good of the Christian cause will owe you thanks too. You have sent me the collation of only three books of Moses with the Hebrew text. Relying on the same kindness of mind, I hope you will send the collation of the remaining two, and I earnestly ask you to send it when an opportunity arises. Briefly, most distinguished Sir, since the matter itself to some extent calls for it and you give me the occasion, I shall say a few words about the Samaritan codices. Briefly, I say, for I am pressed for time, and I must not neglect the present departure of the courier, lest I seem, through a longer delay of my duty, to have forgotten your kindness. I have four manuscript copies of the Hebrew-Samaritan codex. One is complete, except that the first leaf has been replaced by an inserted one, but it was written recently, about seventy years ago, in a fine large script. The fifth copy, most distinguished Sir, will be yours. Besides these, we have had printed a version of this Pentateuch made in the Samaritan dialect, of which we obtained a complete copy in Rome, apart from the one we have in our columned codex. These are the copies we use. The division into verses, which you describe, is common to all copies, and they observe it exactly and strictly. They call these divisions Lectiones (פסוקים). The division into periods among them is almost as arbitrary as among us. I say more about these in our exercises on the Samaritan Pentateuch. All these copies agree very closely if you look at the words, but not if you look at the letters. The comparison shows discrepancies in two ways. The first concerns the letters א, which the Jews call mothers of pronunciation and which are heard unwritten among the Hebrews. Sometimes one copy writes them and another omits them. For example, at Gen.50,25 the Jewish codices read וישבע, and two of my copies, as well as yours, add a Jod: וישבריע. From this it is inferred that the Samaritans there pronounce ויושבע, not ויושבע. The pronunciation Vajasbia, that is, the letter Jod, gave the scribe the occasion of inserting it. Likewise at v. 15 of the same chapter your copy and two of mine write הושב, while two others insert a Jod. The reason for this is that the Jewish grammarians say that after a long vowel one of the mother letters is to be heard unwritten: after Chirec and Tzere, Jod; after Kamets, Aleph; after Cholem and Shureq, Vau. Sometimes the Hebrew text expresses them and sometimes it leaves them out, so copyists often vary in this. This variation among the Jews was very frequent before the Masoretes, and it is still seen even on the Israelite coins. After the Masoretes it was much less frequent, although many examples of it are shown from that later time. Whatever the case, variations of this kind do not change the meaning of the distinction; they arise only to aid the pronunciation. Variation in the letter Aleph occurs much more rarely. The second discrepancy is the interchange of the guttural letters א ה ח ע. It was not without cause that R. Benjamin said the Samaritans do not have the three letters ע, ח, ה, for they pronounce all gutturals as א. So in their version you will very often see in a single page the same word written now with ע, now with ח, now with ה. Ain is often written for Aleph, and for ה, although among them there is no resemblance between these letters. We have observed countless instances of this kind, and we have grown weary of observing them. Hence in the sacred text, although very rarely, the copyists are sometimes found to have erred in this matter. For example, your codex at Gen. c. 3, v. 24 has להט; one of mine does likewise, while my older copy has לחמ, as the Jewish text does. I have already exceeded the bounds of a short letter, but I want to draw your attention to one point. My four copies at Gen. c. 50, v. 19 constantly have אנ התחתאלהים; the two Samaritan versions likewise, while the Jewish ones have כי. You note no difference there, as if your copy showed כי. One version renders אנה דחול אלח Fearing God I am, and this agrees with Onkelos, the Chaldee paraphrasts Jonathan, and the ancient Greek version of the Samaritan Pentateuch, some traces of which are found in the scholia cited in the Sixtine edition of the Seventy: ἡ γὰρ Φοβούμενῳ Θεὸν εἰμὶ ἐγώ. If your copy really has כי, the Greek interpreter seems to have read it so. But those interpreters, both the Samaritan and the Greek, in the Samaritan Hebrew text, and the Chaldeans in the Jewish Hebrew text, read the words התחת with their letters so interchanged, reading התחת. The other Samaritan version, which we have published, has החלופת אלהים אנה Am I in the place of God?, as the Jews read and interpret it. Symmachus and Aquila read it so in antiquity; the Seventy did not read ה but read כיתחת אלהים אנ, as is clear from their version. Moreover, at the same chapter, v. 23, all my copies constantly have בִּסְרִי יוֹסֵף. The two Samaritan interpreters do likewise. I note, however, that in your copy בִּסְרִי is written, but עַיִן does not precede it as in the Hebrew. I would there easily suppose a mistake. At chapter 3, v. 24, your copy has תְּמִימָה בְּנַי, which is an error. My two complete copies write, as among the Jews, הַמְמִהְפְּכִים, and the Samaritan interpreter retains the same word in his dialect as הַמְּמִיהָ הַבַּי. Let these few words suffice from among many. As for what you write about that Italian Jew, it is nonsense; he who knows nothing of these matters has uttered it. For no learned Jews deny that the Samaritan characters were once in use among the Jews, although some assert that it is unlawful to write the book of the Law, which they use in the synagogue, in that script. I have discussed this matter at length in our exercises, following the opinion of the rabbis. It is true that the Jews are so filled with hatred of the Samaritans that they consider a book of the Law written not only in the Samaritan character, but even in the Assyrian or Jewish character by a Samaritan, to be profane. This accords with the saying of Moses the Egyptian in the treatise Tephillah, section 1, number 11: כל דבר שצריך מעשה לשמו [illegible] שהן הכותי פכול Whatever must be done in your name, if a Cuthean does it, is profane. This, however, arises from hatred of the person, not of the character. It is similarly false that the Jews consider it unlawful to translate the Law word for word into another language. The Talmudists themselves except the Greek language, and all Jews, with the single exception of R. Azariah, testify that the Law was translated word for word from the Hebrew text by the Seventy interpreters. Azariah alone thinks that the translation was made from Chaldean books written in the Samaritan character. Moreover, R. Saadia, most famous among the Jews, translated the Law κατὰ λέξιν six hundred and fifty years ago. It was printed at Thessalonica in Hebrew characters by the Jews themselves, and a copy of it is in our possession, and there is one in Paris. A copy of the same translation, written in Arabic characters, is also there. Furthermore, I suppose no one doubts that, other things being equal, Jewish codices are to be preferred to any Samaritan ones whatever. I shall send back your Samaritan readings as soon as I have made use of them. In the meantime I thank you again and again for sharing your labour with me. Truly, when I consider the matter itself, you have bestowed on me a great gift. But I ask you again and again to keep for me, forever, the great goodwill of your mind, ξενίων δὲ τε θυμὸς ἀρίςτῳ. Farewell, most distinguished Sir, and continue to love me, who am most devoted to you.

units.la: Parisiis, viij Kal. Junii 1633.
units.tr: Paris, 8 days before the Kalends of June, 1633.

units.la: EPIS T XXXIX.
units.tr: EPISTLE XXXIX.

units.la: Joh. Morinus Soario Vasionensi Episcopo, ob illius in Episcopatum assumptionem congratulatur,
units.tr: Joh. Morinus congratulates Soarius, Bishop of Vaison, on his assumption to the episcopate.

units.la: Illustriss.
units.tr: Most Illustrious Sir,

units.la: {*} Videtur tamen Morinus in operibus suis Samaritanos Codices Judaicis seu Hebra-icis anteposuisse.
units.tr: {*} Yet Morinus seems, in his works, to have preferred the Samaritan codices to the Jewish or Hebrew ones.

units.la: Illustrissimo & Reverendissimo D. D. Soa- rio Vasionensi Episcopo, Jo. Morinus Congreg. Orat. Presbyter, S. D.
units.tr: To the most illustrious and most reverend Lord Soarius, Bishop of Vaison, from Jean Morin, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, greetings.

units.la: Reverendissime Præsul,
units.tr: Most reverend Prelate,

units.la: CUm primum ad me fastigii tui Epi-scopalis nuntia pervenerunt, tanta animi voluptate perfusus sum, ut ab ea superatus mihi silentium indicere non potuerim: itaque Epistolam importunam, sed gaudii mei nuntiam scribere non reformidavi, mihique indulgere malui, quam negotiosissimæ dignitatis tuæ rationem habere. Dignitatemne tibi gratuler Episcopalem Apostolicæ supparem?
