Gratulor sane, at non tibi, verum Episcopali Ordini, Ecclesiæ, sacrisque Musis omnibus; non tibi, cui onus impositum est Angelicis humeris formidabile: sed Episcopali Ordini, qui tanti Viri doctrina & pietate decorabitur: sed Ecclesiæ, quæ vigilantissimo Pastore donata, inter hostium cuneos secura quiescet: sed Musis omnibus, quarum Alumnus es, Dux & Præses. Gloriosum tibi, à sanctissimo & eruditissimo Pontifice in Episcoporum collegium cooptari. Verùm hoc tibi cum multis aliis commune: Cooptasse sane Pontifici gloriosius. Eximium enim Virum, eruditione & pietate celeberrimum è cæterorum corona exemisse, atqve ad Sacerdotii apicem evexisse, quid laudabilius ? Soarium ab Urbano VIII. summo Pontifice Episcopatu donatum, non inter postremas Urbani laudes posteritas, præteritarum actionum antiquissima judex, recensebit, & prædicabit. Ego præterea in hac tecum honoris communicatione eminentissimi Card. Barberini erga eruditos benevolentiam suspicio, atqve in iis promovendis vigilantiam & prudentiam, justa animi gratitudine colo, qui te, hoc est, gratias & musas, à comitatu suo indivulsum esse voluit, qui te ut penitus & domi inspectum summo Pontifici studiosè commendavit, atqve in Provincia, in qua Apostolicam habet potestatem Episcopalem, nanscisceris [?], procuravit, ut licet diæcesi obnoxius evaderis, ab eo tamen non divelleris; ita illius animo sedet immotus verus hic & praeclarus versiculus, καλλιςόν ἐςι χρῆμα παι-δείας βροτοῖς. Verum Epistolii modus illius laudibus finem imponere cogit, qvi de litteris, litteratisqve omnibus be-ne merendi finem nunquam facit. Unum mihi superest, ut qva sum in te observantia & obseqvio, in haec vota precesqve non cessem; te, tuamqve dignitatem ad Ecclesiae salutem, Deus Opt. Max. & conservet diutissime, & meritis honoribus augeat, cumuletqve qvam citisime. Vale, Reverendisime Praesul, & me tui observantissimum amare perge.
units.tr: When the news of your episcopal elevation first reached me, I was so overcome with joy that I could not keep silent. So I did not shrink from writing a troublesome letter, though it is only a messenger of my delight, and I preferred to indulge myself rather than take account of your most busy dignity. Shall I congratulate you on an episcopal dignity equal to the apostolic one? I do congratulate, certainly, but not you alone: rather the episcopal order, the Church, and all the sacred Muses. Not you, on whom a burden has been laid that would frighten angelic shoulders; but the episcopal order, which will be adorned by the learning and piety of so great a man; the Church, which, given a most vigilant pastor, will rest secure among the ranks of her enemies; and all the Muses, whose foster-son and leader and president you are. It is a glorious thing for you to be co-opted by the most holy and learned Pontiff into the college of bishops. But this is common to you with many others. To have co-opted him, however, is more glorious for the Pontiff: to have taken out of the crowd of the rest a man of rare learning and famed for piety, and raised him to the summit of the priesthood, what could be more praiseworthy? Posterity will not count among the last of Urban's praises that he bestowed the episcopate on Soarius, and it will recount and proclaim this, as the most ancient judge of past deeds. Moreover, in this sharing of honour with you I recognise the goodwill of the most eminent Cardinal Barberini towards learned men, and I honour with due gratitude his vigilance and prudence in promoting them. He wished you, that is, your gifts and the Muses, not to be separated from his company; he commended you to the supreme Pontiff with close care, having examined you thoroughly and at home; and he took care that, although you should become bound to a diocese in the province where you hold episcopal authority under the Apostolic See, you should not be torn away from him. So that verse, true and famous, καλλιστόν ἐστι χρῆμα παιδείας βροτοῖς [learning is the finest possession for mortals], remains fixed in his mind. But the limit of a letter compels me to end his praises, though he never ceases to deserve well of letters and of all men of letters. One thing remains for me: as I am bound to you by respect and devotion, I will not cease to pray that God, the best and greatest, may keep you and your dignity for the salvation of the Church for a very long time, may increase you with deserved honours, and may heap them upon you as quickly as possible. Farewell, most reverend Prelate, and continue to love me, who am most devoted to you.

units.la: Datum Parisiis, Idibus Septemb.
units.tr: Given at Paris, on the Ides of September.

units.la: Anno Christo 1633.
units.tr: In the year of Christ 1633.

units.la: EPIST. XL.
units.tr: EPISTLE XL.

units.la: R. Goesaldus J. Morino, quod praeter al- lata notent Romani Aulici in ejus Libro De la Grandeur, &c. scribit.
units.tr: R. Goesaldus to J. Morinus, that the Roman courtiers, besides what has been alleged, remark in his book De la Grandeur, etc., he writes.

units.la: Mon Revevend Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: LA Grace de Jesus pour jamais. J'ay donné vostre lettre à Monseigneur Suarez, qu'il a eüe tres agreable. Je l'ay veu encore depuis pour autre affaire, & m[?]a dit, qu'il vous preparoit une belle réponse, & qu'il vous envoieroit un memoire tant pour ce qu'il juge, que devez changer en vostre livre des Grandeurs de l'Eglise, que de diverses choses, qui seroient bonnes a y adjouster, & me par le souvent de ce livre, sans que je luy en parle; cela vient & commence toujours de luy, & il demeure toujours en cette pensée, que devez faire nouvelle impression, & s'accommoder dextrement comme seroit dire redonné au lieu de donné, & autres qu'il vous doit escrire amplement: autrement il craint, que le Pape & le Cardinal Barberin demeurent toujours dans leur mescontentement pour ce sujet, & m'a dit, qu'il y a quelq; temps qu'un certain chambrier fut en France, & pour faire le bon Valet en apporta un au Pape, qui témoigna beaucoup de mescontentement de ce livre à ce qu'il dit; il dit deplus que pensant faire pour le Francois, vous faites pour les Allemans, que Charlemagne estoit Empereur, & que les Empereurs Allemans peuvent s'attribuer tout ce que vous attribué[?] à Charlemagne, & ainsi vous prejudies au Pape, & à la France. En tout ceci & beaucoup d'autres, je ne suis qu'escoutant, afin que vous ne croyez que je di-spute du livre. Je n'ay jamais peu avoir nouvelle de ce Mr.Ecchius Medecin Flaman. Il fera peut estre mort en quelque lieu d'Italie, vous vous aviez promis quelque exemplaire de vostre dernier livre, que nous presentasmes ya deux à Monseigneur le Cardinal Barberin. Il ne m'en demeura aucun, je finis par nos tres humbles recommendations de tous à vos SS. Prieres & Sacrifices, & de nous de la maison, & demeure pour jamais en Jesus & Marie.
units.tr: The grace of Jesus be with you forever. I gave your letter to Monseigneur Suarez, who received it with great pleasure. I have seen him again since, on another matter, and he told me that he is preparing a fine reply for you, and that he will send you a memorandum, both on what he judges you ought to change in your book des Grandeurs de l'Eglise, and on various things that would be good to add to it. He often brings up this book with me without my mentioning it; the subject always starts with him, and he keeps returning to the idea that you should make a new impression and adjust certain expressions adroitly, such as saying redonné instead of donné, and others, which he says he will write to you about at length. Otherwise he fears that the Pope and Cardinal Barberini will remain dissatisfied on this account. He told me that some time ago a certain chamberlain went to France and, to play the good servant, brought one copy to the Pope, who showed great displeasure at this book, so he says. He adds that, thinking to do a service to the French, you have done it for the Germans: Charlemagne was an Emperor, and the German Emperors may claim for themselves everything you attribute to Charlemagne, and so you prejudice the Pope and France. In all this and much else I only listen, so that you will not think I am disputing about the book. I have never been able to get news of this Mr. Ecchius, the Flemish physician; perhaps he has died somewhere in Italy. You had promised us some copies of your latest book. We have already presented two to Monseigneur Cardinal Barberini, and none remained for me. I end by sending our most humble greetings from all of us to your holy prayers and sacrifices, and from us of the house, and I remain forever in Jesus and Mary.

units.la: Mon Reverend Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: A Rome,22.Oct. 1633.
units.tr: At Rome, 22 October 1633.

units.la: Vostre tres humble & affectionné Serviteur René Goez. Presb. de l'Oratoire de Jesus,
units.tr: Your most humble and affectionate servant René Goez, Priest of the Oratory of Jesus,

units.la: Le Cardinal Capucin frere du Pape est fait grand Penitencier par la mort du Card. Borghese, qui a laisse de grands benefices,,dont le Card. Barberin n'en veut rien prendre si non l'Archiprestré de St. Pierre.
units.tr: The Capuchin Cardinal, brother of the Pope, has been made Grand Penitentiary by the death of Cardinal Borghese, who left great benefices, none of which Cardinal Barberini will take except the archpriesthood of St. Peter's.

units.la: EPIST. XLI.
units.tr: EPIST. XLI.

units.la: Godofredus Vendelinus Joh. Morino. Quærit, quis sit Rabbi Eliezer, & de ejus Libro, Antiqua & Nova Judæo-rum Chronologia, ac supputandi Ra-tio.
units.tr: Godfrey Vendelin to John Morin. He asks who Rabbi Eliezer is and about his book; on the ancient and modern Jewish chronology and the method of calculation.

units.la: Viro undequaque Eruditissimo J. Morino, C.O. Presb. Godofr. Vendelinus, S.P.
units.tr: To the man most learned in every respect, J. Morin, priest of the Oratory; Godfrey Vendelin, greetings.

units.la: DUdum est, Eruditissime Morine, cùm pervagata terrarum orbem prolixa tua in rem litterariam merita, & amorem apud omnes doctos excitarunt tui, & post illos admiratione defixum me sic attinuerunt hactenus, ut quamquam visendi tui desiderio incredibilem in modū ardeam, pudore tamen magis retinear, quàm ipso jam quadrimestri morbo, curisque aliis, & inter hæc Pastoralibus. Itaque quoniam פירקי[?] affari tenendum datur, quod reliquum est, quodque Timotheus Hojus noster audere suadet, adscriptionem istam confugio, sed cujusmodi tu à me possis expectare, cujusmodi ego sola venia scio placituram, & discendi, quæ ignoro, studio, responsum quoque eliciturum. Hoc erit primum Argumentum & auspicale nobis, omissis officiorum istis languidis ostentationibus, quibus tot passim bonæ horæ prætereunt, bonæ chartæ pereunt.
units.tr: It has been a long time, most learned Morin, since your extensive merits in literature, which have spread across the whole world, aroused the love of all scholars for you. After them, I, struck with admiration, have been held back so far that, although I burn with an incredible desire to see you, I am restrained more by shame than by the illness that has now lasted four months, by other cares, and among these by my pastoral duties. Therefore, since it is granted to me to speak at last, and since our Timothy Hoyoj urges me to dare, I take refuge in this letter. It will be of a kind that you may expect from me, and that I know will please you only through indulgence; it will also, I hope, draw from you an answer, given my eagerness to learn what I do not know. This will be our first subject and a good beginning, with those languid displays of courtesy set aside, by which so many good hours pass everywhere and so much good paper is wasted.

units.la: Ante omnia ergo à te scire velim, ecquid Rabbi Eliezer Gamalielis ille gener (forsan & Pauli nostri condiscipulus) manuscriptus tantum extet, an vero etiam editus? & ubi? Nam in Bibliotheca Rabbinica Buxtorfii non comparet. Horum alterum te sui admonet, ne diutius latere patiaris; alterum infœlicitatem accusat meam, qui sicut omnibus aliis, sic etiam isto careo, quo vel unico beatus sim in eo, quod mihi sub manu est. Postquam enim dudum ætatem temporum saxum volvo, & multa mecum de antiquo Hebræorum anno reputo: quem nescio — qui Catoblepæ non vident etiam Solomonis temporibus mere fuisse lunarem, vocariqve non semel יבח Mensem, & addi mox חורש [?] ne non satis ἰσοφικῶς [?] exprimatur historia, sedere cœpit apud me jampridem sententia, nihil minus in illa gente solemne fuisse, quam ut Pascha sequeretur æquinoctium, imo enim vero interdum tenuisse vel octiduum totum ante istum cardinem.
units.tr: Above all, then, I want to know from you whether Rabbi Eliezer, that son-in-law of Gamaliel (perhaps also a fellow student of our Paul), survives only in manuscript or has also been published; and if so, where? For he does not appear in Buxtorf's Rabbinic Library. The first question reminds you not to let him remain hidden any longer; the second accuses my misfortune, since I lack him, as I lack all the others, and I would be fortunate even in this one book, if I had it at hand. For I have long been rolling the stone of the ages and reflecting much on the ancient Hebrew year, which, I do not know why those who do not see the Catoblepae think, was purely lunar even in the times of Solomon. The word for "month" was used more than once, and the phrase "to add" soon followed, lest the history be insufficiently expressed. A view has long been forming in my mind that nothing was less customary among that people than for the Passover to follow the equinox; indeed, they sometimes kept it even a whole eight days before that turning point.

units.la: Quasi dicas novilunium quodcunque Martii Gregoriani primum retulisse Nisan: quando neque Mathematicus ullus unquam olim æquinoctii cardinem vel somniarat.
units.tr: It is as if you were to say that whatever new moon fell first in Gregorian March gave the month of Nisan; when no mathematician of old ever even dreamed of the pivot of the equinox.

units.la: Sane sol observationes omnes ante Hipparchum desumptæ sunt à solstitiis, primusque mortalium Hipparchus æquinoctiorum τήρησιν [?] instituit.
units.tr: Indeed, all observations made before Hipparchus were taken from the solstices, and Hipparchus was the first of mortals to institute the observation of the equinoxes.

units.la: Nam quod Tecuphas garriunt, rideo: qui in sacris nihil invenio quam תקופת השנה ותשובת השנה tempestatis istas duas hinc de-clivis clivis, inde acclivis anni; solstitium inqvam, divergentis, & brumam convergentis Solis. Posterius factum intelligo, ut הקופת[?]----etiam brumæ communicaretur. Favit mihi luculenter ille tuus Eliezer. Etenim si Tecupha demum Brumæ admoneret Hebræos intercalationis; si, inqvam dies 19 Tebeth inci-dens in Brumam potuit (nisi qvid aliud accideret annum ducere communem) vides profecto Nisani proximi diem 22 sic tunc debuisse repræsentare æqvinoctium Vernum (Solis Apogæo finem Arietis nondum egresso) ut ne momento qvidem posterior sentiretur: ac proin toto ante æqvinoctium octiduo Paschatis ritum fuisse legitimum Luculentus est iste locus Eliezeris, atqve auro supra mihi carus, qvi tantum jam temporis hoc ipsum testimonium unde comparandum anhelavi. Eliezerum ergo per eruditionem tuam istam ut edas rogo, aut si editus est, ubinam, & qvanti præstat, indi-ces.
units.tr: As for what the Tecuphas babble, I laugh at it. In the sacred books I find nothing but the "turning of the year" and the "return of the year", the two seasons: on one side the descending, on the other the ascending, year; I mean the solstice of the diverging sun and the winter solstice of the converging sun. I understand that the latter was made so that the Tecupha of winter would also be shared with the Hebrews. That famous Eliezer of yours favours me clearly. For if the Tecupha only warned the Hebrews of intercalation at the winter solstice, then, if the nineteenth day of Tebeth fell on the winter solstice (unless something else happened to make the year common), you certainly see that the twenty-second day of the next Nisan must then have represented the vernal equinox (with the sun not yet having left the end of Aries at its apogee), so that not even a moment later would it be noticed. And therefore the rite of the Passover eight days before the equinox was lawful. That passage of Eliezer is brilliant and dearer to me than gold, since I have long longed to find this very testimony from which to obtain such a time-frame. I therefore ask you, through your learning, to publish Eliezer, or, if he is already published, to tell me where and at what price.

units.la: Hic si frustra sum, alterum meum erit αἴτημα, ut eodem ex authore mihi perscribas, ecquot annos numeret ab orbe condito ad Mosen, & ab hoc, ad Templi calum, unde arcessat Siclos illos suos 84; itemque 19 aureum, à quo die Juliano Clavum moveat.
units.tr: If I am wrong in this, my second request will be this: that you write out for me from the same author how many years he counts from the creation of the world to Moses, and from him to the destruction of the Temple, from which he derives those seventy-four shekels of his; and likewise the golden number 19, from which day he moves the Julian cycle.

units.la: Videre mihi videor ex tuis Scriptis attemperament esse illum majorem ad Sabbaticos annos, ut Moses Ægypto excesserit ineunte nova Semitta, quamquam una cum Juliano anno primo existimem primulum excogitatum ab otiosis Mathematicastris; neq; tamen unquam in usum civilem introductum, antequam à Christianis quibusdam probari coeperit, atq; hic illic usurpari: ut operose nihil egerit Bucherius cum suo anno Judaico ad hanc 84. annorum periodum expanso, quo Christi passionem nobis infulciret anno Vulgaris Epochae 31. decimo septimo Tiberii, quae revera debetur anno nostro 33. dieiq; 3. Aprilanno Tiberii 19. quo Eclipsin illam stupendam ex Plegonte disertis verbis protulit Philoponus. Sed quia scilicet primum Pascha Apostolicum celebratum tum est novo ritu die 25. Martii anni 34 nostri, qui fuit Tiberii 22. Hinc obhaesit Ecclesiis (Romanum ac Solarem annum jam sequentibus postquam Mulier amicta Sole, cum sua Synagoga Lunam calcavit sub pedibus suis) bihorium quoque passionem eumdem in diem incidisse. Plane ut quae traditio sane Apostolica (sed ex die 25 Martii, anno 34 orsa) confessa ignoratione omnium hactenus ingenia fatigavit, mihi cesserit in argumentum deprehensae veritatis, quampluribus ac luculenter breviter adstructam dabo. Sane hinc conficio, etiam ævo Christi menses Judaicos fuisse lunares, & quidem ἀπὸ Φάσεως —derivatos sanctificatosque. Super his quid sentias scire perquam aveo.
units.tr: I seem to see from your writings that there is a greater proportion to the sabbatical years, so that Moses left Egypt at the beginning of the new Semitta; although I think that, together with the Julian year, this first year was devised by idle mathematicians, and was never introduced into civil use until certain Christians began to approve it and it was used here and there. So Bucherius labored to no purpose with his Jewish year, expanded to this period of eighty-four years, by which he would thrust Christ's passion upon us in the year 31 of the common era, the seventeenth of Tiberius; but in truth that is due to our year 33, on the third day of April, in the nineteenth year of Tiberius, when Philoponus expressly reported that stupendous eclipse from Phlegon. But because the first Apostolic Passover was then celebrated, in the new rite, on the twenty-fifth of March in the year 34 of our era, which was the twenty-second of Tiberius, from this it came about that the Churches (following the Roman and solar year, since the "woman clothed with the sun" with her synagogue trampled the moon "under her feet") also held that the passion fell on the same day, being a second-hand matter. Clearly, this tradition, certainly Apostolic but starting from the twenty-fifth of March in the year 34, has so far wearied the minds of all in the confessed ignorance of everyone; for me it will serve as an argument for the truth discovered, which I shall give briefly, but set forth more fully and clearly. Surely I conclude from this that even in the age of Christ the Jewish months were lunar, and indeed derived and sanctified from the first appearance of the moon. I am very eager to know what you think of these things.

units.la: Tertium quod à te discere cupiebam, an nihil dum Chronicorum Samaritanorum nactus sis, tum quid censeas de illorum Epochis, imo de conjectura mea, qui existimo, numerare illos ad Christianam nostram æram annos 4306. ac menses 3. ante diluvium scilicet 1327, inde ad natum Abrahamum, 940. ut sint omnes 2267. hinc ad mortem Mosis, Calendarium eorum exhibet 565. & summam colligit 2832. Sunt ergo ex hoc ἐπιλογισμῷ anni 2792, ad Exodum, 2712, ad Natum Mosen, pleni omnes ac completi, ut Exodus quadret in 2793. Venerintque Israelitæ in fines divisionum, hoc est, ad confinia Idumææ anno 2794, pro eo ac citat Scaliger. Jam vero à Nato Mose(ad hunc enim modum capio, quod illic legitur de succinctione Ephod verbis implicatissimis) in fanaticum (Mahometum) exerte habent 2215; quotidem ferme Eusebius & Cyrillus darent. Sunt ergo secundum istos ab Adamo ad Hegiram Mahometis anni 4927. fortean & menses aliquot. Hinc aufer annos 62, & menses 6, vides relinqui ab exordio mundi Samaritano, ad Christum, 4306, sicut dicebam. Fidem facio plenius; Calendarium illorum, quod Scaliger putavit esse anni 1584, longe alterius est, ac forte existimet quispiam, & neque contemptum per novilunia. Imo enim vero nihil aliud repræsentat quam plenilunia ; plenilunia, inquam, vera (non media) anni nostri 893, & 894, scrupulosissime computata ad meridianum Arastæ, non Samariæ. Provoco ad Tabulas, & quidem, si extant uspiam, Albategnianas. Jam vero Calendarium istud profitetur Calendarium Samaritanum annuum
units.tr: The third thing I wished to learn from you is whether you have obtained any Samaritan chronicles, and what you think of their epochs; indeed, what you think of my conjecture. I hold that they count to our Christian era 4306 years and 3 months: namely 1327 years before the Flood, then 940 to the birth of Abraham, making all 2267; from there to the death of Moses their calendar gives 565, and it totals 2832. From this reckoning there are therefore 2792 years to the Exodus, 2712 to the birth of Moses, all of them full and complete, so that the Exodus falls in 2793. And the Israelites came to the boundaries of the divisions, that is, to the borders of Idumea, in the year 2794, as Scaliger cites. Now from the birth of Moses (for in this way I understand what is read there about the girding of the ephod, in very tangled words) to the fanatic (Muhammad) they reckon 2215 years, which Eusebius and Cyril nearly give as well. According to them, then, from Adam to the Hegira of Muhammad there are 4927 years, perhaps also some months. Take away from this 62 years and 6 months, and you see that from the beginning of the world, by the Samaritan reckoning, to Christ there are 4306, as I was saying. I make the matter fuller: their calendar, which Scaliger thought was of the year 1584, is quite different from what someone might suppose, and it is not to be despised on account of the new moons. Indeed it represents nothing else than full moons: true full moons (not mean ones) of our year 893 and 894, computed most scrupulously for the meridian of Aras, not of Samaria. I appeal to the tables, and to the Albategnian tables, if they exist anywhere. Now that calendar professes to be the annual Samaritan calendar.

units.la: Millenarium qvintum ducentesimum & qvartum (sic enim mecum spero leges, non 210 cum Scaligero) qvasi anteriores cogitet Christo 4310 annos, solo qvadriennii discrimine. Sed vereor, ne qvaternarii nota redundet, errore hinc nato, qvòd idem annus fuit Seleucidarum 1204. Nam alioqvin Samaritani, isti anni sic digesti sunt à computistis illorum, ut septimus qvique iniens sit Sabbaticus, & affectatum ut Moses exierit Ægypto anno 2793, jam labante Sabbatico 399, Jubilæo eodem 57. Qvoniam vero annus Calendarii vocatur sextus Semittæ, necesse est, annum intelligi 5200, non 5204, ac videsis hoc qvoqve annum nostrum 893, vocat sextum Semittæ, sed in Succoth jam inchoat Semittam, quæ Judæis anno 894 demum in Succoth iniit. Ergo ne Samaritani à Judæis anno solido dissident ac prævertunt? minime gen-tium: Memorabilis est locus Maimonidæ, quem Cunæus citat, Sabbaticos ac Semittam inire exeunte anno Jubilæos ineunte, nimirum anno nostro 887, in Septembri & festo כפורים publicatus fuerit Jubilæus, quo eodem momento & quinquagesimus numeratus fuerit, & mox post quatriduum à סכות Succoth Jubilaici jam systematis inchoati primus; certe anno 888 inierit annus à Jubilæo secundus, sed γεωργίας primus; anno 889, inierit Jubilæi tertius, γεωργίας secundus. Sic anno 890, & iv & 3. anno 891, quintus & iv. anno 892. sextus & v. anno 893, septimus in Semitta post annum celebranda, idemque revera sextus γεωργίας, atque ad eum modum deinceps donec annus 936, in Septembri daret quinquagesimum inclusive, & Jubilaicum omnino simulq; Semittam, hoc est, quadragesimum nonum à desito postremo Jubilaico anno completo.
units.tr: It contemplates the five hundred and fourth millennium (for so, I hope, you will read it with me, not 210 with Scaliger), as if reckoning 4310 years before Christ, differing only by a four-year interval. But I fear the mark of the four may be redundant, through an error arising from this, that the same year was the 1204th of the Seleucids. For otherwise the Samaritans arranged those years, according to their computists, so that every seventh year begins a sabbatical year; and it is pursued so that Moses left Egypt in 2793, with the sabbatical 399 already failing, and the same jubilee 57. But since the year of the calendar is called the sixth of the Semitta, it is necessary to understand the year as 5200, not 5204; and note that this year of ours, 893, they call the sixth of the Semitta, but the Semitta now begins at Succoth, which the Jews only entered in the year 894 at Succoth. Therefore do the Samaritans differ from the Jews by a full year and anticipate them? Not at all: the passage of Maimonides, which Cunaeus cites, is memorable, that the sabbaticals and the Semitta begin at the end of the year in which the jubilees begin. Namely, in our year 887, in September, on the feast of the Atonement, the Jubilee was proclaimed, and at the same moment the fiftieth was counted, and four days later, at Succoth, the first of the now begun jubilee system. Certainly in the year 888 the second year from the Jubilee began, but the first of the agricultural cycle; in the year 889 the third year of the Jubilee began, the second of the agricultural cycle. So in 890 the fourth and third, in 891 the fifth and fourth, in 892 the sixth and fifth, in 893 the seventh of the Semitta, to be celebrated after the year, and this is truly the sixth of the agricultural cycle; and so on in this manner until the year 936, when in September the fiftieth year, inclusive, would fall, and at once the Jubilee and the Semitta together, that is, the forty-ninth year complete since the last jubilee year had ended.

units.la: Poteram aliunde quoq; atqve 'abunde adstruere,annos Jubilæos in Epocha nostra ineuntes Septembri anno 5. 54. 103. 152. 201. 250. 299. 348. 397. 446. 495. 544. 593. 642. 691. 740. 789. 838. 887. 936. 985. 1034. 1083. 1132. 1181. 1230. 2279. 1328. 1377. 1426. 1475. 1524. 1573, qviqve postremus fuit nostro ævo 1622, eritqve posterorum 1671. Sed ut aliud hic tu me qvoq; juves, si qvid apud Eliezerum aut alios antiqvos (nam recentiores Rabinos nihil moror) ejusmodi indiciorum comperisti, hoc vero sine te exorem; in qva prece finio, & me tibi profiteor
units.tr: I could also show this at length from other sources: the Jubilee years beginning in our Epoch fall in September of the years 5, 54, 103, 152, 201, 250, 299, 348, 397, 446, 495, 544, 593, 642, 691, 740, 789, 838, 887, 936, 985, 1034, 1083, 1132, 1181, 1230, 1279, 1328, 1377, 1426, 1475, 1524, 1573, the last of which was in our age 1622, and there will be one in posterity in 1671. But so that you too may help me in this, if you have found anything of this kind in Eliezer or other ancient writers (I do not concern myself with the more recent rabbis), I cannot obtain this without you. With this prayer I finish, and I declare myself yours.

units.la: Bruxella, Idius Decemb. Anno Christi nati 1637. qui est Epochae vulgatae 1633.
units.tr: Brussels, the Ides of December, in the year of Christ's birth 1637, which is 1633 of the common Epoch.

units.la: Addictum in Christo per omnia obsequiorum & communicatorum votorum momenta Godefr. Vendel. hactenus Pastorem Bethasiorum, nunc Hercanum sed Canonicum Gandavensem designatum.
units.tr: Devoted in Christ in all the moments of mutual service and shared vows, Godefridus Vendelius, hitherto pastor of Bethasii, now designated canon of Ghent at Hercanum.

units.la: EPIST. XLII.
units.tr: LETTER XLII.

units.la: J. Morinus Godofredo Vendelino. Responsio prolixa ad praecedentem Epistolam, varias quae apud diversas gentes diversis temporibus fuere supputandi Rationes, fusius declarat de Samaritanis Corraitis, ex eorum MSS. nonnulla.
units.tr: J. Morinus to Godefroy Vendelin. A lengthy reply to the preceding letter, which sets out more fully the various methods of reckoning that different peoples used at different times, and includes some passages from the manuscripts of the Samaritan Corrais.

units.la: Viro Clarissimo & Eruditissimo Godefrido Vendelino, Jo. Morinus.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and most learned Godefroy Vendelin, Jo. Morinus.

units.la: ACcepi, Vir eruditissime, Litteras tu-as varia & insigni admodum eruditione refertas. Gratulatus sum mihi plurimum, non solum me tibi cognitum, & amicitia tua cohonestatum esse, sed etiam scripta mea tibi probari. Cum enim Viro eruditissimo, atque eorum, quae scripsi, scientissimo placuerint, a caeteris qui istud eruditionis genus vel a limine salutaverint, non omnino negli-genda fore confido. Quam mihi amicitiam offers ultro, hanc avide & gratulabundus amplector, mutuisque officiis coli & conservari cupio, velimque maxi-mopere impraesentiarum propensum erga te animi mei studium, aliquo argumento demonstrare; ideo ægerrime fero, desiderio tuo me plane satisfacere non posse: huc enim missus sum omnibus Rabbinicorum Librorum præsidiis destitutus, iisque præterea negotiis vacaturus, quæ animum meum ab omni pene litterarum studio avertunt. Quod hoc tempore mihi potissimum contigit, quo festa solemnia celebrata sunt, iisque celebratis, iter aliquot dierum mihi suscipiendum fuit. Itaque hoc Epistolium non horis subcessivis, sed tumultuariis scriptum ubique incœpit, ubique desiit. Quantulumcunque igitur illud sit, quod tibi ad quæsita tua respondebo, & excuses, & boni consulas etiam atque etiam rogo. Benevolentiæ ergo & facilitatis tuæ securus, rem licet vix adumbratam dimissurus aggredior.
units.tr: I have received your letter, most learned sir, filled with a variety of material and with remarkable learning. I am greatly pleased that you not only know me and count me among your friends, but also approve of my writings. Since they have pleased a man of such learning, and one so well versed in what I have written, I trust they will not be wholly disregarded by others who have merely greeted this kind of learning from the threshold. I eagerly and gladly accept the friendship you offer so freely, and I wish it to be cherished and kept up by mutual services. I would very much like to show you, by some proof, the warm devotion of my heart toward you at present. So I am extremely sorry that I cannot fully satisfy your wish. I have been sent here without any of the resources of the Rabbinic books, and I am also occupied with business that draws my mind away from almost all literary study. This has fallen on me especially at this time, when the festive solemnities have been celebrated, and after these I had to undertake a journey of several days. So this little letter was begun wherever I could, in spare moments snatched amid the bustle, and it has been broken off wherever I had to stop. Whatever this reply is worth, I beg you again and again to excuse it and take it kindly. Trusting in your goodwill and kindness, I venture to send you a matter only barely sketched out.

units.la: Quæris primum, Vir doctissime, & mihi plurimum colende, an Liber capitulorum Eliezeris editus in lucem ali-quando fuerit? Ita est: edito usus sum; Editio, ni fallor, Veneta est, Charactere quadrato, & oculis grato, folio bis complicato, quod vocant in octavo. Hujus Libri meminit in Bibliotheca sua Buxtorfius, ubi de Zohar agit, atque etiam, ut puto, alibi in eodem Libello, sed male scripsit, Librum esse Historicum; nihil enim minus quam Historiam enarrat. Miscellaneorum est Liber, in quo variae Judaeorum traditiones nulla rerum consequentia edisseruntur. Sæpius in similes scopulos impingit Buxtorfius, cum eos Libros ut plurimum recenseat, quos nunquam legit. Ejusdem Libri meminit Drusius, Serrariumque reprehendit, quo cum Libello de capitulis Patrum illum confuderit. Nunc autem istorum Librorum non est mihi copia.
units.tr: First, most learned sir, and most worthy of my great regard, you ask whether the Book of the Chapters of Eliezer has ever been published. It has: I have used an edition, which, unless I am mistaken, is the Venetian one, in square type, pleasant to the eye, in folio folded twice, which they call octavo. Buxtorf mentions this book in his Bibliotheca, where he treats of the Zohar, and perhaps elsewhere in the same little work; but he wrongly writes that it is a historical book, for it recounts history least of all. It is a miscellany, in which various Jewish traditions are set out without any connected sequence of matters. Buxtorf often runs upon such rocks, since he lists books that he never read. Drusius also mentions this book and rebukes Serrarius, who perhaps confused it with the little book on the chapters of the Fathers. Now, however, I do not have these books at hand.

units.la: Quæris secundo, quot annos Eliezer ille ab orbe condito numeret ad Mosen, atque à Mose ad Templi casum; unde arcessat Cyclos suos annorum 84; itemque suam ἐννεαδεκαέτηρίδα[?] annorum ab orbe condito epilogismum, apud Elie-zerum non memini me legisse, neque ad[?] Mosen usque, neque ab hoc ad Templi casum. Res autem illa est ejusmodi, quam non praeterissem si animadvertissem; non semel legi istius Libri quatuor aut quinque priora capita, quibus integris de rebus Astrologicis, anni intercalatione, & computo Paschali pro Judæorum captu disserit; sed quosquæ-ris Epilogismos, non deprehendi. Cum primum Parisios rediero, quod spero vere proximo, Authorem istum iterum e-volvam, & quicquid de hac materia scribit, in tui gratiam exscribam, atque ad te mittam, ut ipse judices. A qua Epoche Cyclos suos ducat consimiliter non exprimit; aliquid tamen addit, quod in Exercit, nostris notavimus, e quo quid simile colligi potest, Deum in Ægypto Mosi & Aaroni apparuisse in principio mensis Nisan, cum annus ageretur Cycli magni 25, & Cycli Embolismalis 17. atque huic & deinceps numerum illis professisse[?] plura in hanc sententiam non puto continere.
units.tr: Second, you ask how many years that Eliezer reckons from the creation of the world to Moses, and from Moses to the fall of the Temple, whence he derives his cycles of 84 years; likewise, you ask for his summary of years from the creation of the world, his nineteen-year cycle [ἐννεαδεκαέτηρίς]. I do not remember having read these in Eliezer, neither from the creation to Moses nor from Moses to the fall of the Temple. This is the sort of thing I would not have passed over had I noticed it. I have read the first four or five chapters of this book more than once, in which, in full, he discusses astrological matters, the intercalation of the year, and the Paschal computation according to the grasp of the Jews; but I have not come upon the summaries you ask about. As soon as I return to Paris, which I hope will be next spring, I will go through this author again, copy out for your benefit whatever he writes on this subject, and send it to you so that you may judge for yourself. He does not likewise state from what epoch he derives his cycles; yet he adds something which we noted in our Exercitationes, and from which something similar can be gathered: that God appeared to Moses and Aaron in Egypt at the beginning of the month of Nisan, when the year of the great cycle was 25 and of the embolismic cycle 17, and that from then on he professed the number to them. I do not think more than this is contained in that sense.

units.la: Antequam ulterius respondendo per-gam gam[?] monebo te diu Eliezeris Lectioni me diligentius incumbentem sententiam de istius Libri antiqvitate mutasse, multa enim interlegendum mihi deprehendisse videor, qvæ tantam antiqvitatem minime sapiunt; qvidqvid Judæi jactitent, atqve ille potissimum Rabbinus, qvi Librum excudendum curavit. Exempli causa nonnullorum Rabbinorum mentionem facit, qvi post verum Eliezerem Hircani filium diu vixerunt, qva ratione fretus, scripsit author Libri Ju-chasin, Librum istum ab Eliezeris discipulis suis compositum. Fabulæ insuper Talmudicæ passim intertextæ, loca Scripturæ subtili qvodam, vel potius sutili acumine ad rem subjectam detorta, ut Historiolæ explicandis locis Scripturæ difficilibus Talmudico more derepente confictis, longum temp9[?] a Templi ruina, demonstrare mihi videntur, v. g. initio capitis sexti Talmudica ista fabula refertur, qvæ etiam extat in Beresith Rabba, narraturqve à Rabbi Salomone 'in pri-mum caput Genef, velut qvid maxmieno[?] tandum, Lunam Solemqve æqvali magnitudine, forma & & lumine creata suisse; inter verò Solem & Lunam ortis de magnitudine rixis Deum altero alterum minorem reddidisse, cui fabellæ duos aptat Scripturæ versus. Alibi fabulam apud Judæos vulgatam confirmat, Ephraimitarum ducenta millia tempus Exodi perperam supputantia ex Ægypto annis ante Mosem triginta egressa esse, atque à Philistæis cæsa, & ideo dictum esse Exod. 13.v. 17. Non eos duxit Deus per viam terræ Philistiim, qvæ vicina est, &c. cap. 35. Regni Persici durationem annorum putat 52, qvod est Talmudicorum, & recentiorum Judæorum portentum. cap. 28. Bis regnum Ismaeliticum commemorat, atque inter mundi imperia collocat. Horum te admonitum esse gratum tibi fore confido.
units.tr: Before I go on with my reply, I must warn you that, while I have been devoting myself more closely to reading Eliezer for some time, I have changed my view about the antiquity of this book. For I seem to have found many things in the course of reading which hardly savour of such great antiquity, whatever the Jews boast, and especially that Rabbi who had the book printed. For example, he mentions some rabbis who lived for a long time after the true Eliezer, son of Hyrcanus; and on what grounds the author of the book Juchasin wrote that this book was composed by Eliezer's disciples, I do not know. Besides, Talmudic fables are woven through it everywhere, and passages of Scripture are twisted to the matter in hand by a certain subtle, or rather cobbling, cleverness, like little stories suddenly made up in the Talmudic manner to explain difficult passages of Scripture. These seem to me to show that it was written long after the ruin of the Temple. For instance, at the beginning of chapter six this Talmudic fable is related, which is also found in Beresith Rabba, and which Rabbi Solomon tells on the first chapter of Genesis, as if it were the greatest of matters: that the moon and the sun were created of equal size, form and light; and that, after the sun and moon quarrelled over their size, God made the one smaller than the other. To this fable he adapts two verses of Scripture. Elsewhere he confirms a fable common among the Jews: that two hundred thousand Ephraimites, wrongly reckoning the time of the Exodus, went out of Egypt thirty years before Moses and were cut down by the Philistines; and that is why it is said (Exod. 13.17): "God did not lead them by the way of the land of the Philistines, which is near," and so on. In chapter 35 he puts the duration of the Persian kingdom at 52 years, which is a monstrosity of the Talmudists and of more recent Jews. In chapter 28 he twice mentions the Ishmaelite kingdom and places it among the empires of the world. I trust it will be welcome to you to be warned of these things.

units.la: Sententiam tuam de Æqvinoctio in Paschali festo à Judæis antiqvis non observato facile amplector. Græci omnes ante Hypparchum, in solstitiorum propter ludos Olympicos observatione desu-darunt, darunt, ita Cleostratus, Harpalus, Meto, Eudoxus, & Calippus; quam vero in motuum cœlestium observatione infantes fuerint, Ægyptii, Chaldæique omnes, nemo in his rebus mediocriter versatus ignorare potest; cui Græcorum ante Hipparchum infantia perspecta fuerit. Tum enim Græci Ægyptiorum & Chaldæorum adyta omnia penetraverant & Iustraverant, licetque ex Græcorum ignoratione Ægyptios & Chaldæos ignorantiæ convincere. En quam motuum Cœlestium periti, stellarum in occidentem motum-non deprehenderant; ideo octavam sphæram primum mobile opinabantur, Solem Planetasque cæteros in eccentricis moveri nesciebant. Hinc ab uno æquinoctio ad alterum spatium æquale definiebant, idque non ex speciali observatione, sed ex solstitiorum comparatione. Sol tamen deprehensus est ab Hipparcho à verno Æquinoctio ad Autumnale octidui, & aliquot horarum spatium amplius, quam in sequenti conversione consumere. Quid de eorum circaÆquinoctiorum in anteriora retrocelsionem, ignorantia dicam, cum ea fuerit omnibus antiquis Christianis incognita ? Existimarunt omnes 21 Martii æquinoctium vernum alligatum esse. Quid de Beda, qui tam operose de computo Paschali scripsit ? Opinatur ille æquinoctium vernum 21 Martii contingere, ut in Concilio Nicæno animadversum fuerat, & sic credit sese observasse[?], at suo tempore 17, non subsequebatur, neque exactius edoctus fuerat à Victorino & Dionysio Exiguo summis computorum magistris, licet eorum al[?]ter Græcæ eruditionis esset peritissimu.
units.tr: I readily accept your view that the ancient Jews did not observe the equinox in the Paschal feast. All the Greeks before Hipparchus laboured over the observation of the solstices, for the sake of the Olympic games; so did Cleostratus, Harpalus, Meton, Eudoxus and Callippus. How much infants the Egyptians and all the Chaldeans were in the observation of celestial motions, no one moderately versed in these matters can fail to know, provided he has seen clearly how the Greeks before Hipparchus were still in infancy. For then the Greeks had penetrated and explored all the sanctuaries of the Egyptians and Chaldeans, and one may convict the Egyptians and Chaldeans of ignorance from the ignorance of the Greeks. See how skilled they were in celestial motions: they had not detected the motion of the stars toward the west; therefore they thought the eighth sphere was the primum mobile, and they did not know that the sun and the other planets move in eccentric orbits. Hence they defined the space from one equinox to the next as equal, and this not from a special observation but from comparing the solstices. Yet Hipparchus detected that the sun takes eight days and some hours more to pass from the vernal equinox to the autumnal than it takes in the following half of the revolution. And what shall I say of their ignorance about the backward movement of the equinoxes? It was unknown to all the ancient Christians. All of them supposed that the vernal equinox was fixed to 21 March. What of Bede, who wrote so laboriously on the Paschal computation? He holds that the vernal equinox falls on 21 March, as had been noted at the Council of Nicaea, and so he believes he has observed it; yet in his own time it was on the 17th, and he had not been more accurately informed by Victorinus and Dionysius Exiguus, the greatest masters of computation, although one of them was most skilled in Greek learning.

units.la: Solaris motus cum Lunari concordiam non tentabant fœlicius antiqui Græci. Testes sunt octaeteris Cleostrati, & Harpali à vero propius abfuit ; Meto cum sua enneadecaeteride, sed quàm crasse illam delineavit & pinguiter ? exactius paulo Calippus & Eudoxus illam interpolarunt : si certiora docuissent ægyptii & Babylonii, Græcos illos, veri scientissimos[?], non latuissent. Rudia Scientiarum[?] principia Chaldæi & Ægyptii tradiderunt, ea expolierunt Græci, & innumera, quæ illi ignorabant, addiderunt. Sed quid de Christianis, post Hipprachum & Ptolomæum dicendum, Lunæ cum Sole concordiam per octaëterida venantibus? Id præstitit Dionysius Alexandr. Hippolytus verò per heccædecäeterida; quam hæc ad Rhombum? Nec vitium, qui hæc refert, Eusebius animadvertit. Tandem Anatolius primus Christianorum ad enneadecaëterida confugit, quam amplexi sunt Concilii Nicæni Patres, & retexuit Eusebius. Credebant omnes Lunæ ad Solem hac Periodo. absolutissimam ἀποκατάστασιν[?] fieri; credidit hoc Beda, atque annorum mille spatio creditum est, donec erroris evidentia omnium oculos configente tandem rem aliter se habere persuasum est.
units.tr: The ancient Greeks did not attempt the agreement of the solar and lunar motions with better success. The octaeteris of Cleostratus and Harpalus is witness to this; it was not far from the truth, but how coarse and crude was Meton's nineteen-year cycle? Callippus and Eudoxus refined it somewhat more exactly. If the Egyptians and Babylonians had taught more certain things, those Greeks, most skilled in truth, would not have been ignorant of them. The Chaldeans and Egyptians handed down the rough beginnings of the sciences; the Greeks polished them and added countless things which the others did not know. But what must be said of the Christians after Hipparchus and Ptolemy, who sought the agreement of the moon with the sun through the octaeteris? Dionysius of Alexandria accomplished this; Hippolytus did so through the sixteen-year cycle. How far from the mark is this! Eusebius, who reports these things, did not notice the error. At last Anatolius, the first of the Christians, took refuge in the nineteen-year cycle, which the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea embraced, and which Eusebius set forth again. All believed that the moon returned to the sun in this period in a perfectly complete restoration; Bede believed it too, and it was believed for a span of a thousand years, until at last the plain evidence of the error struck everyone's eyes and it was made clear that the matter stood otherwise.

units.la: Ne autem aliquis objiciat, Græcos, Ægypticos, Chaldæos & Christianos antiquos hæc ignorasse, sed Judæis hæc cognita fuisse, quidquid Judæi de his rebus loqvuntur, ab Hipparcho & Ptolemæo desumptum est, ut cuivis conferenti patet. Qvæ antiqviores Judæi cognoverunt, à Græcis Hipparcho prioribus derivata sunt, qvod ex Eliezere manifestum est, vel ex ipsis Signorum nominibus, qvæ Græcis nominibus Hebraice translatis effert. טלה· שור· האומים סרטן· אריה· בתולה· מאזנים· עקרוב קשת· נרי· דלי· דנים Eadem nomina refert Epiphan. hær. 17. sed in Planetarum nominibus dissentit. Sic Eliezer ut Neoterici omnes Judæi, כוכב· לבנה· שבתאי· צרקי· מאדים· חמה נוגה Mercurius, Luna, Saturnus, Jupiter, Mars, Sol, Venus, Græcorum nomina deserit. Qvomodo æqvinoctii rationem habuissent antiqvi Judæi in tanta rerum Astrologicarum ignoratione? Thecupharum artificium, ut recte animadvertis, prorsus ignorabant, nec erat illis ullum dignoscendarum subsidium. De his Judæi in terra Israëlis non cogitabant; Neomenias enim ἀπὸ τῆς Φά-σεως sanctificabant, Paschatis verò tempus ex spicarum virore & maturitate dijudicabant, nulla æqvinoctii ratione habita. Intercalationis igitur sola causa erat frugum maturitas.
units.tr: Lest anyone object that the Greeks, Egyptians, Chaldeans and early Christians knew nothing of these things, and that the Jews alone knew them, I reply: whatever the Jews say about these matters is taken from Hipparchus and Ptolemy, as anyone who compares them will see. What the older Jews knew was derived from the Greeks earlier than Hipparchus, as is clear from Eliezer, and from the names of the signs themselves, which he gives as Hebrew translations of the Greek names: the Ram [טלה], the Bull [שור], the Twins [האומים], the Crab [סרטן], the Lion [אריה], the Virgin [בתולה], the Scales [מאזנים], the Scorpion [עקרוב], the Archer [קשת], the Goat [נרי], the Water-carrier [דלי], the Fishes [דנים]. Epiphanius, heresy 17, gives the same names, but differs in the names of the planets. Eliezer, like all the modern Jews, abandons the Greek names of the planets: Mercury [כוכב], Moon [לבנה], Saturn [שבתאי], Jupiter [צרקי], Mars [מאדים], Sun [חמה], Venus [נוגה]. How could the ancient Jews have taken account of the equinox, given such ignorance of astrological matters? They were entirely ignorant of the art of the tekufot, as you rightly observe, and had no means of distinguishing them. The Jews in the land of Israel did not think about these things at all; they sanctified the new moons from the sighting [ἀπὸ τῆς φάσεως], and judged the time of the Passover from the greenness and ripeness of the ears of grain, with no reckoning of the equinox at all. The sole reason for intercalation, therefore, was the ripeness of the crops.

units.la: Paucis referam, qvod aliqvando legi in Commentario Karaitæ cujusdam, ante 3oo[?] annos, manuscripto in Legem. Ait Karaitas terræ Israelis incolas annos intercalare pro sola ratione mensis Abibh, seu spicarum, ridetqve Gamalielis in Talmud pronunciatum propter tria annum intercalari, propter Spicas, propter Tecuphas,& propter Fructus arborum, אין בן כי האכיב היא לברו נזכר alias Rabban. causas ridet, annos nondum grandes, &c. וידע כי בהמטא האכיב אי אפשר שאין הכל מתוקנים ירלמה נוסיף ער דברי אלהים [illegible, ~4 letters] Notum enim est, inqvit, qvod cum spica reperitur, impossibile est omnia non esse præparata. Ideo mensis primus dicitur אביב; Exod. 13.4. Paulo post idem Autor הנה מורה תויית שי [illegible, ~6 letters] חרשינו בראיר הלבנה ואמר עיר משור
units.tr: I will briefly report what I once read in a manuscript commentary on the Law, written about three hundred years ago by a certain Karaite. The Karaite says that the inhabitants of the land of Israel intercalated the year solely by reckoning the month of Abib, that is, the month of the ears of grain, and he mocks the saying of Gamaliel in the Talmud that the year is intercalated for three reasons: because of the ears, because of the tekufot, and because of the fruits of the trees. He mocks these reasons, saying that the years are not yet ripe, and so on: "for he knows that when the ear [of grain] is found, it is impossible that all things are not prepared" [וידע כי בהמטא האכיב אי אפשר שאין הכל מתוקנים]. Hence the first month is called Abib [Exod. 13.4]. A little later the same author says: "Behold, the Lawgiver established our months by the sight of the moon [ראיה הלבנה], and said, 'Keep still the month of the ears,' and from this we intercalate the year." In the same place he says that his companions outside the land of Israel follow the intercalations of the Rabbanites and their cycle of nineteen years; but he mocks their superstitious observations of the Adu, Badu, and so on. (Some words in this passage are illegible in the scan.)

units.la: שמור חדש האביב ומזה אנחנו[?] Ecce Legislator instituit menses nostros ad visionem Lunæ, dixitque, Adhuc custodi mensem Spicarum, hinc nos intercalamus annum. Ibidem ait, sodales suos extra terram Israëlitæ[?]... Rabbanistarum intercalationes sequi, & cyclum novemdecim annorum: verùm ridet superstitiosas illorum τῶ[?] Adu, Badu, &c. observationes.
units.tr: "Behold, the Lawgiver appointed our months by the sight of the moon, and said, 'Still keep the month of the ears,' and from this we intercalate the year" [Ecce Legislator instituit menses nostros ad visionem Lunae, dixitque, Adhuc custodi mensem Spicarum, hinc nos intercalamus annum]. In the same place he says that the Israelites outside the land follow the intercalations of the Rabbanites and the nineteen-year cycle; but he mocks their superstitious observations, the Adu, Badu, and so on.

units.la: Sic existimo Judæos, stante Tempio, Pascha observâsse, primumque mensem instituisse, nec Deus in celebratione Paschatis ullam aliam rationem, quàm maturitatis spicarum jussit haberi, eo quod cùm Israëlitæ ex Ægypto exierunt, maturuerant. Judæi quoque Rabbanistæ & Talmudistæ licet alia admitterent, ut adnotavimus, hanc tamen paternarum traditionum non omnino obliti nunquam omittebant. Itaque saepe Tecupham Pascha subsequebatur, nonnunquam praecedebat. Interrogabor forsan, num Judæi cyclis in Paschatis supputatione ante Christum uterentur. Brevi distinctione sententiam meam explico, Judæi aut habitabant in terra Israëlis, aut in dispersione gentium. Priores nullos habebant Cyclos Paschales, nec ullam æquinoctii rationem ducebant, sed tantum אביב[?] & Lunæ Φεγγαρίς ; posteriores Cyclis utebantur, sed Brumæ, non Æquinoctii Cynosuram in iis componendis attendebant, ut ex Eliezere demonstratur. Hujus Epochæ seu clavis Paschalis instituendæ causa jam indicata est. Judæi dispersionis à Græcis hæc mutuati sunt. Græcis autem Alexandro regnante, nondum cordi erant æquinoctiales observationes, sed quæ tum maxime vigebat, periodus erat Calippica, quæ Brumæ insita & inoculata erat. Hinc Judæi ante Christum, Calippi Brumam & Enneadecaeterida secuti sunt, eamque Epiphanii tempore secuti videntur, ut ex Judiacæ periodi, quam enarrat, cum Eliezerea comparatione fortasse liquebit. Istis autem Epilogismis Judaicis initium factum est regnantibus Alexandri Successoribus. Longo post Christum tempore, R. Samuel Babylone & R. R. adda, & eum secutus Hilel in Palestina, antiquum computum reformarunt, ut perhibent Judæi Talmudistæ; illi autem non Calippi pingves numeros, sed Hipparchicos & Ptolemaicos amplexi sunt, quorum præsertim postremum Judæi omnes sequuntur, seque ad Messiam usque secuturos profitentur; cum autem ab Hipparcho & Ptolomæo æquinoctia essent observata, Paschatis clavem à vicesima Thebeth, in decimam sextam τῶν Nisan transtulerunt, ut Paschati viciniorem, & ad illud supputandum commodiorem.
units.tr: I think that while the Temple stood the Jews observed the Passover in this way and fixed the first month accordingly, and that God, in the celebration of the Passover, commanded no other reckoning than the ripeness of the ears of grain, since the Israelites had found them ripe when they went out of Egypt. The Rabbanites and Talmudists too, though they admitted other rules, as we have noted, never wholly forgot the traditions of their fathers and never omitted this one. So the Passover often followed the tekufah, and sometimes preceded it. Perhaps I shall be asked whether the Jews used cycles in computing the Passover before Christ. I will explain my view in a short distinction. The Jews either lived in the land of Israel or were dispersed among the nations. The former had no Paschal cycles and took no account of the equinox, but only the Abib and the phase of the moon [Φεγγαρίς]; the latter used cycles, but in composing them they attended to the winter solstice, not to the equinox, as is shown from Eliezer. The reason for establishing this epoch, or Paschal key, has already been indicated. The dispersed Jews borrowed these things from the Greeks. Under Alexander, however, the Greeks had not yet taken to heart the equinoctial observations; the period then most in vogue was the Callippic period, which was implanted and grafted into the winter solstice. Hence before Christ the Jews followed Callippus's winter solstice and the nineteen-year cycle, and they seem to have followed it still in Epiphanius's time, as perhaps will become clear from a comparison of the Jewish period he describes with Eliezer's. These Jewish calculations began under the successors of Alexander. Long after Christ, Rabbi Samuel at Babylon, and Rabbi Rabbi Adda, and Hillel after them in Palestine, reformed the old computation, as the Talmudist Jews relate; but they embraced not the rough numbers of Callippus but those of Hipparchus and Ptolemy, of whom the Jews all follow the last, and profess that they will go on following him until the Messiah comes. Since the equinoxes had been observed by Hipparchus and Ptolemy, they moved the Paschal key from the twentieth of Tishri to the sixteenth of Nisan, to bring it closer to the Passover and make it more convenient for calculating it.

units.la: Verùm hanc amplexus sententiam, quæ mihi admodum probabilis videtur, cogita quid respondendum sit Eusebio & Anatolio, testimoniis Philonis, Josephi, Musæi & Agathobulorum, contendentibus, antiquos Judæos ex majorum decreto post æquinoctium Pascha celebrasse. Si causa cum causa, res cum re, ratio cum ratione, certet, vicisti: sin verò authoritas decretoria est, causa videris cecidisse. Sane si Eusebii verba cap. ultimo, l. 7. historiae perpendantur, A-natolii verba non intellexit Eusebius, aut ipsissima si retulit, neuter, quae scri-bebat, intellexit. Omnia enim ab iis ἀπολογουμένα[?] sunt ἄσυντα[?], vel cer-te Oedipo, qui haec conciliet, opus est. Hoc tamen manifeste sibi volunt, post aequinoctium antiquos Judaeos Pascha semper celebrasse. His plura non fert Epistolii modulus; in tuae sententiae gra-viam nonnulla addam, quae mihi obser-vasse videor.
units.tr: But, embracing this opinion, which seems to me quite probable, consider what must be answered to Eusebius and Anatolius, who contend, on the testimony of Philo, Josephus, Musaeus and the Agathobuli, that the ancient Jews celebrated the Passover after the equinox by the decree of their ancestors. If cause is weighed against cause, fact against fact, reason against reason, you have won; but if the authority of decree is decisive, your cause seems to have fallen. Indeed, if the words of Eusebius in the last chapter of book 7 of his History are weighed carefully, either Eusebius did not understand the words of Anatolius, or, if he reported them exactly, neither understood what they wrote. For all their explanations are inconsistent, or certainly one would need an Oedipus to reconcile them. Yet they clearly intend this: that the ancient Jews always celebrated the Passover after the equinox. The compass of a letter does not allow me to say more about this; I will add a few things which I seem to have observed, to strengthen your opinion.

units.la: Primum, Asiaticos tempore Judaico Pascha observasse, nullam tamen cum iis de aequinoctio quaestionem habitam, sed hac de causa solum, quod diem Domini-cum non morarentur.
units.tr: First, the Asians observed the Passover in the Jewish manner, yet there was no dispute with them about the equinox; they differed from the others only in that they would not defer it to the Lord's Day.

units.la: Secundo, Christianos primos nullis Cyclis in ea observatione usos, sed ex visione Lunae primum mensem supputasse.
units.tr: Second, the first Christians used no cycles in that observance, but reckoned the first month from the sighting of the moon.

units.la: Tertio, Dionysium Alexandrinum primum Cyclos esse architectatum, atque hujus rei occasione Lunae visione deserta aequinoctialem Epochen velut Cy[?]cli sui polum non sine gravi causa amplexum esse. Primus enim Judaeorum mensis, ut recte Liber Henoch, semper circa aequinoctium versabatur.
units.tr: Third, Dionysius of Alexandria was the first to construct cycles, and on this occasion, abandoning the sighting of the moon, he embraced the equinoctial epoch as the pole of his cycle, not without a serious reason. For the first month of the Jews, as the Book of Enoch rightly says, always fell around the equinox.

units.la: Quarto, Post illud tempus de aequinoctii anticipatione cum Judaeis altercatum, non antea, ipsisque exprobrari coeptum, bis eodem anno pascha nonunquā celebrasse, cui incommodo medelam posteriores adhibuerunt clave Paschatis à 20 Thebeth, in 16 Nisan translata. Hinc enim in aequinoctio primum illis Paschā[?] contingit. Haec Sententiae tuae subjecta sunto.
units.tr: Fourth, after that time the anticipation of the equinox began to be disputed with the Jews, and not before; and it began to be thrown in their faces that they had sometimes celebrated the Passover twice in the same year. The later writers applied a remedy to this inconvenience by moving the Paschal key from the twentieth of Tishri to the sixteenth of Nisan. For by this means the Passover first falls on the equinox. These points are to be added to your opinion.

units.la: Tertium postulatum est de Samaritanorum Chronicis. Sunt mihi quinque Pentateuchi codicesSamaritani, dictionarium parvulum, non integrum, & Libellus precum, nihil praeterea. Itaque de illorum Epilogismis Post Mosen, nihil mihi cognitum est, praeter illa, quae Scaliger edidit: ad usque vero Mosen omnibus cogniti sunt tam ex iis, quae nos edidimus, quàm ex Scaligeriano temporum thesauro. Sunt quidem illius gengentis Chronica, quæ Arabice conversa habuit Scaliger; ex illius gentis Chronicis Hebraicis longum fragmentum refertur in fine Libri Juchasin, de magnis quibusdamRegibus trans Euphratem bellum adversum Josuam præparantibus, sed nihil Chronologiæ memini in eo me legisse. Quæ apud Scaligerum post Mosis mortem, ab iis adduntur, sic explicari possunt, à Mose ad reditum Sacerdotum gestantium Ephod, qui ministrant in Tabernaculo 2215 anni, summæ series erit 5047. ad diem ingressus Fanatici. Samaritani litteras gutturales sæpissime permutant; hoc fit ex perversa eorum pronunciatione, qui nullas aspirant, ideo חור & עור pronunciantes אור sæpe scriberent. Hoc Pentateuchum ipsorum Lingua & Charactere Samaritanum legens, millies expertus sum, in Pentateucho Linguâ Hebraicâ studiose evitant, id tamen ipsis nonnunquam excidere animadverti. Itaque in hoc computo singulare quoddam factum, à quâ Epochen ducunt, quodque circa Mahumetis initium contigit, respicere videntur. Nescio quamobrem Scaliger הבריה inexplicatum reliquit, cum nihil aliud sit quam חבריאה: praeterea mihi omnino jungendi videntur anni Mosis summae sequenti, ita ut à Mose sit, à morte Mosis ad reditum Sacerdotum, &c. Quare enim illos subtraheret cum prius addiderit, perpetuaque sit Epilogismorum additio? deinde summa ab iis subducta 5047, aliter constare non potest.
units.tr: The third claim concerns the Samaritan chronicles. I have five Samaritan codices of the Pentateuch, a small dictionary, not complete, and a little book of prayers, and nothing more. So I know nothing of their computations after Moses, apart from those which Scaliger published; but up to Moses they are known to all, both from what we have published and from Scaliger's Thesaurus of Times. There are indeed chronicles of that nation, which Scaliger had in an Arabic translation; a long fragment of the Hebrew chronicles of that nation is cited at the end of the book Juchasin, about certain great kings beyond the Euphrates preparing war against Joshua, but I do not remember reading anything of chronology in it. What they add after the death of Moses, as given by Scaliger, can be explained thus: "From Moses to the return of the priests bearing the Ephod, who minister in the Tabernacle, 2215 years; the sum of the series will be 5047 to the day of the entry of the Fanatic" [à Mose ad reditum Sacerdotum gestantium Ephod, qui ministrant in Tabernaculo 2215 anni, summae series erit 5047, ad diem ingressus Fanatici]. The Samaritans very often interchange the guttural letters; this comes from their faulty pronunciation, since they do not sound any aspirates, and so, pronouncing חור and עור, they often wrote אור. I have tested this a thousand times, reading their Pentateuch in its Samaritan language and character; in the Pentateuch they carefully avoid the Hebrew language, yet I have noticed that this sometimes slips out. So in this computation they seem to have regard to some singular event from which they date the epoch, which occurred around the beginning of Muhammad. I do not know why Scaliger left הבריה unexplained, since it is nothing other than חבריאה. Moreover, the years seem to me to belong entirely with the following sum, so that "from Moses" goes with the death of Moses to the return of the priests, and so on. For why would they subtract them after having first added them, and the addition of the computations is continuous? Then the sum 5047 which they deduce from these cannot be made to agree in any other way.

units.la: Litterae illae ἐπιγραφῆς computi Samaritani אהרן non dubito quin sint ראשי תיבות, quibus Samaritani non secus ac Judæi utuntur. Singulae litterae dictionem aliquam significant, cujus prima tantum littera describitur. Quae autem sic scribunt, vulgata sunt apud eos, & solemnia quaedam rei, de qua agitur, Epitheta. Quid autem haec significent, à Samaritanis tantum divinari potest. Multa conjici possunt, sed cum in infinitum variari possit, quis praeter eos verum secernere poterit? Sumi non posse pro numero 210, ut conjicit Scaliger, hinc manifestum mihi videtur,qvod nec Judæi, nec Samaritani numeros suos unqvam sic disponant, nec Arithmeticesillorum hoc patitur, scribendum suisset יה [?] non aliter. Non ignoro per ipsorum Cabbalistarum Ghematriam è dictionibus numeros sic exprimi, ut mysteria sua expiscentur. Verùm hæc sunt longe diversissima. Scriberent enim אהרך [?] facere יה [?], qvod est verissimum, deinde dictionem illam cum alia ejusdem numeri potente compararent, ut ex Ghematrica illa æqvalitate mysterium aliqvod emergeret; deniqve in utroqve Scripturæ loco idem significasse; sed huic computi loco id aptari non potest. Præterea id faciunt tantum in dictionibus aliqvid significantibus,ut ex mutuo sensu aliqvid eliciant, at אהרך [?] nihil significat. Notarica autem sine רשיא [?] תיבות ut plurimum nihil significare possunt. Deniqve ista Cabbalistica Samaritani plane ignorant. Ejusmodi Ghematria Judæi sæpissime utuntur in librolibrorum excusorum primo folio vel postremo, cum annum mundi, qvo Librum ediderunt, notant. Locum Scripturæ, qvæ Deus operi benedicat, vel Israëlem exaltet, ita eligunt, ut illius loci una dictio Ghematrice sumpta annum mundi præcise contineat. Neqve etiam significare posse mihi videtur §204, expungendus enim esset Aleph, hoc modo, הרך [?], littera ה præcedens notam ducentesimi numeri, millenarios repræsentant, nec aliud fert ipsorum Arithmetica.
units.tr: I do not doubt that those letters of the Samaritan inscription of the computation, אהרן [Aharon], are initial letters (ראשי תיבות [rashei tevot]), which the Samaritans use just as the Jews do. Each letter stands for some word, and only the first letter of that word is written. Those who write in this way use certain set epithets for the matter in question, which are well known among them. What these letters mean, however, can be guessed only by the Samaritans themselves. Many meanings can be conjectured, but since the possibilities are endless, who besides them can pick out the true one? That they cannot be taken as the number 210, as Scaliger conjectures, seems clear to me for this reason: neither the Jews nor the Samaritans ever write their numbers in this way, and their arithmetic does not allow it. It would have had to be written יה [?], and in no other way. I am aware that by the Ghematria of the Cabbalists themselves, numbers are drawn out of words so that they may fish out their mysteries. But those practices are very different. For they would write אהרך [?] to make יה [?], which is quite correct; then they would compare that word with another word of the same numerical value, so that some mystery might emerge from that Ghematric equality; and finally they would have meant the same thing in both places of Scripture. But this cannot be fitted to the present computation. Moreover, they do this only with words that have some meaning, so that some sense may be drawn from their mutual meaning; but אהרך [?] means nothing. Notarica, moreover, without initials (ראשי תיבות) can for the most part mean nothing. Finally, the Samaritans altogether ignore these Cabbalistic arts. Jews very often use this kind of Ghematria on the first or last page of printed books, when they note the year of the world in which they published the book. They choose a passage of Scripture that speaks of God blessing the work, or of Israel being exalted, in such a way that one word of that passage, taken by Ghematria, gives exactly the year of the world. Nor does it seem to me that it can mean §204, for the Aleph would have to be removed, in this way: הרך [?]; the letter ה, which precedes, represents the thousands, and their arithmetic does not allow anything else, as it marks the number 200.

units.la: His incommodis subtilis tua de annis Samaritanorum Sabbaticis dissertatio afficí videtur. Nihil dum de ejusmodi annis apud antiquos Rabbinos notavi, qvia his animum nunqvam applicui. Qvid autem illi hac de re scribant, horum Librorum ope hic destitutus nunc inqvirere non possum, qvam primum potero, id me facturum in tui gratiam spondeo. Qvod Scaliger retulit de Samaritanis, eorum Calendarium non videtur, nec ulla potest esse periodus, sed mensium Arabicorum tantum illo anno cum Samaritanis solaribus, licet Hebraica sint mensium vocabula, conjunctio & alligatio longe scrupulosior, quam civilem deceat administrationem. Mirum est, quod ais, istos epilogismos secundum plenilunia vera anni 893 & 894 esse confectos. Unde hæc tam antiqua eruere potuit gens Samaritana, ut ad Scaligerum mitteret, qui horum nihil petebat? Deinde scriptum illud Samaritanum diserte [?]ראש חדש שביעיinitium mensium anni septimi. Ipsa dictio [?]צמח eorum dialecto, ut & Chaldaice sonat Conjunxit, Congregavit, sæpius in Pentateucho hanc significationem animad-verti.
units.tr: Your subtle dissertation on the Sabbatical years of the Samaritans seems to be troubled by these difficulties. I have not yet noted anything about such years among the ancient Rabbis, because I have never applied my mind to these matters. What they write about this subject I cannot now investigate here, since I lack those books; as soon as I can, I promise to do so for your sake. What Scaliger reported about the Samaritans does not seem to be their calendar, nor can there be any cycle of that kind; rather, the link and connection of the Arabic months with the Samaritan solar year in that year (although the names of the months are Hebrew) is far too scrupulous for civil administration to tolerate. It is remarkable, as you say, that these computations were made according to the true full moons of the years 893 and 894. How could the Samaritan people have dug up such ancient facts to send to Scaliger, who was asking for none of them? Then there is that Samaritan writing, which plainly says the beginning of the months of the seventh year [ראש חדש שביעי]. The word itself, [צמח], in their dialect, as also in Chaldee, means he joined, he gathered; I have often noticed this meaning in the Pentateuch.

units.la: Mirum est pleniluniis visis in Arad meridiano omnia convenire. Fortasse hæc noviluniis veris in anno 1584, aut 1583, in meridiano Sichem, aut Cairi exacte conveniunt.
units.tr: It is remarkable that everything agrees with the full moons seen at Arad at noon. Perhaps these agree exactly with the true new moons of the year 1584 or 1583, as seen at noon at Shechem or Cairo.

units.la: Hæc supputandi nec otium mihi nunc, nec si esset, libri suppetunt: id non tentavit Scaliger; rerum istarum pro captu Critici admodum erat peritus, pro captu vero Astrologi plane ignarus.
units.tr: I have now neither the leisure for such calculations, nor, even if I had, the books that would be needed. Scaliger did not attempt this; he was very skilled in such matters as far as a critic's grasp went, but as far as an astrologer's grasp went, he was entirely ignorant of them.

units.la: Hæc inerudita, Vir eruditissime, boni consule. Jam anni multi præterierunt, cum à Paschalibus & Mathematicis computis animum prorsus averti, nec admodum facile est domesticorum negotiorum diverticulis continenter appetitum iterum ad ea sese convertere. Finiam igitur nimium longam & inanem Epistolam, modo prius sententiam tuam de Epocha Christiana laudavero. Annis quatuor integris à vulgata differs, ideo videris Kepleri & aliorum quorum-dam sententiam amplecti. Legi aliquando Kepleri Viri doctissimi luculen-tam hac de re dissertationem, quæ mihi plurimum probabilitatis semper habere visa est. Iisdem existimo te principiis & Josephi autoritate niti, quam Eusebius & alii non perpendentes annis quatuor aut quinque eam anticiparunt. Neoterici verò plerique eam cognitam incassum meo judicio traduxerunt. Ad hæc imparatus accedens, nihil præter illa, quæ Keplerus adnotavit quæque mihi admodum placent, nunc dicendum habeo. Vale.
units.tr: Most learned sir, take these unpolished remarks in good part. Many years have passed since I turned my mind completely away from Paschal and mathematical computations, and it is not at all easy, when domestic affairs keep pulling one aside, to turn one's desire back to them again. I will therefore end this overly long and empty letter, but first I will praise your opinion on the Christian Epoch. You differ from the Vulgate by four full years, so you appear to embrace the opinion of Kepler and certain others. Some time ago I read the very learned Kepler's excellent dissertation on this subject, which has always seemed to me to have the greatest probability. I think you rely on the same principles and on the authority of Josephus, whom Eusebius and others, not weighing it carefully, anticipated by four or five years. Most modern writers, in my judgment, have pointlessly set it aside once it was known. Coming to these matters unprepared, I have nothing to add now beyond what Kepler has noted, which I like very much. Farewell.

units.la: EPIST. XLIII.
units.tr: LETTER XLIII.

units.la: Jo. Morinus Tho. Combero. Gratias agit ob missas ad se iterum diversitates Lectionum Codicis Samaritani à Judæo Hebraico. Suum de Exemplari, Alexandrino 70. interpretum affert judicium.
units.tr: John Morinus to Thomas Comber. He thanks him for again sending the variant readings of the Samaritan codex from the Hebrew text, and gives his judgment on the Alexandrian copy of the Seventy interpreters.

units.la: Clarissimo Viro Thomæ Combero Anglo, Joannes Morinus S.P.D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man Thomas Comber, an Englishman, John Morinus sends greetings.

units.la: Accepi, Vir Doctissime, Pentateuchi Samaritani ab Hebræo varietates, quas ad me misisti. Multis nominibus tibi devinctus sum, parqve pari, si sors tulerit, referendi reus. Neqve mihi tantum & humanitati & diligentiæ tuæ agendæ sunt gratiæ, verùm universæ eruditorum virorum coronæ id oneris incumbit. Opus enim, quod molior, publicum & non privatum. Tanta autem sedulitate, id quod postulaveram, præstitisti, ut bis quæ in Levitico occurunt variæ lectiones excripseris. Bis maluisti eundem laborem desudare, quàm semel promissum non exsolvere. Fieri poterit, ut ipso Archetypo fruamur, ea quam indigitas via. Textuum tamen comparatione, qvam instituisti, laborqve mihi subeundus fuisset, plurimum levatus est. Uno enim, ut ita dicam, intuitu qvid inter utrumqve codicem interfit. Hebræum inter & Samaritanum demonstras. Qvod ad antiqvum 70 Interpretum codicem attinet, ab Ægypto in Angliam deportatum, illiq qvædam specimina legi, qvæ Vir eruditissimus & clarissimus Junius, cum R. Patre Philippo communicanda descripsit. Textus ille non est 70 Interpretum purus & sincerus textus, sed quantum ex paucis schedulis judicare licet, duobus vitiis laborat; habet admixtas plerasqve sententias περιχοτίας [?] ex Hebræo textu, juxta Theodotionem versó repetitas, qvæ à puro 70 Interpretum textu semper abfuerunt, qvasqve ideo sub Asterisco Bibliis suis inseruerat Origenes. Fortasse etiam nonnulla ab illo sincero textu amputata sunt, qvæ Bibliis suis sub Obelo notaverat idem Origenes; verùm ex schedulis hoc judicare non potui. De istorum Asteriscorum & Obelorum ratione, deque methodo sincerum 70 Interpretum textum ab impuro secernendi, multa disseruimus in Exercitat. nostris Biblicis. Habet praeterea multa, sed minoris momenti, quæ à sincero 70 Interpretum textu nonnihil deflectunt, nec cum Hebræo textu ut plurimum conveniunt, quibus conjicere est, editionem illam esse Hesychianam, ab Hesychio scilicet recensitam, vel certe demonstratur, textum illum Ægyptium admodum esse impurum, utpote ab hexaplis Origenis plurimum differentem. Id quod conjicio, facile dijudicabit, qui textum illum cum Græco textu Esaiæ apud Procopium, & editione textus Josuæ apud Masium contulerit, modo quid sibi velint Origenis Obeli & Asterisci, prius didicerit. Quid autem sibi velint, eorum, quos legimus, solus Masius vidit, nec videre non poterat Vir Græce, Hebraice & Chaldaice eruditissimus, qui codicem Bibliorum Syrum de hexaplis OriOrigenis ante mille annos versum cum adnotatis Asteriscis, Obelis, Lemniscis & Hypolemniscis penes se habebat. Quod autem fama est, codicem illum à Sancta Thecla descriptum fuisse, nugae sunt; circa Concilii Nicaeni tempora, itâ à quadam Matrona Ægyptia, Thecla nuncupata, factum esse auguratur ipse Junius; habet codex ille ut ἐκ τῶν ὑπομνηστικῶν [?] colligo, quod singulari animadversione dignum est.
units.tr: I have received, most learned sir, the variants of the Samaritan Pentateuch from the Hebrew text that you sent me. I am bound to you by many obligations, and if fortune allows, I will repay you in kind. Yet I owe thanks not only for your kindness and diligence but the whole company of learned men shares this debt, for the work I am preparing is public, not private. You have performed with such care what I asked, that you copied out the variant readings occurring in Leviticus. You preferred to labour twice over rather than fail once to keep your promise. It may be that we shall enjoy the archetype itself by the way you point out. Still, the comparison of the texts that you undertook has greatly lightened the labour I would otherwise have had to bear. For at a single glance, so to speak, I can see what lies between the two codices, the Hebrew and the Samaritan, which you have demonstrated. As for the ancient codex of the Seventy interpreters, which was carried from Egypt into England, I have read some specimens of it, which the most learned and distinguished Junius copied out to be communicated to Father Philip. That text is not the pure and sincere text of the Seventy interpreters. As far as one may judge from a few slips, it suffers from two faults. It contains mixed in many passages (pericopes [περικοπάς]) from the Hebrew text, repeated according to Theodotion's version, which were never part of the pure text of the Seventy, and which Origen therefore marked with an asterisk in his Bibles. Perhaps some things also were cut out of that pure text, which Origen had marked with an obelus in his Bibles; but I could not judge this from the slips. We have discussed at length the meaning of these asterisks and obeli, and the method of separating the pure text of the Seventy from the impure, in our Biblical Exercitations. Besides, it contains many things, of lesser importance, that depart somewhat from the pure text of the Seventy and mostly do not agree with the Hebrew text. From these one may conjecture that this edition is the Hesychian, that is, revised by Hesychius, or at least it is clear that that Egyptian text is very impure, as it differs greatly from the Hexapla of Origen.
