Anyone who compares that text with the Greek text of Isaiah in Procopius, and with the edition of the text of Joshua in Masius, will easily judge what I conjecture, provided he has first learned what Origen's obeli and asterisks signify. Of what they signify, only Masius, of those we read, saw clearly, and the man most learned in Greek, Hebrew and Chaldee, who had in his possession a Syriac Bible translated from the Hexapla of Origen a thousand years ago with its asterisks, obeli, lemniscus and hypolemniscus noted, could not fail to see it. As for the report that this codex was written by Saint Thecla, it is nonsense; Junius himself conjectures that it was made around the time of the Council of Nicaea by a certain Egyptian matron named Thecla. As I gather, that codex has something [ἐκ τῶν ὑπομνηστικῶν] that is deserving of singular notice.

units.la: Vulgatum est apud omnes doctos, Mathusalem juxta 70 Interpret. numeros annis quatuordecim vixisse. Antiquissima quaestio, quae antiquorum Patrum ingenia varie torsit. Notat Eusebius in fragmentis Graecis apud Scaligerum in Thesauro Temporum p. 4. Nonnulla Exemplaria ita legere, ut sex annis Mathusalae mors Diluvium praecesserit.
units.tr: It is commonly known among all the learned that Methuselah, according to the numbers of the Seventy interpreters, lived fourteen years... [Note: see correction below.] It is a very ancient question, which has variously exercised the minds of the early Fathers. Eusebius, in the Greek fragments in Scaliger's Thesaurus Temporum, p. 4, notes that some copies read it so that Methuselah's death came six years before the Flood.

units.la: EPIST. XLIV.
units.tr: EPISTLE XLIV.

units.la: Tho. Comberus J. Morino alias mittit in Pentateuchum Annotationes ex Anglicano Exemplari Pentateuchi Samaritani.
units.tr: Thomas Comber, D.D., sends to Morinus, otherwise called (Jean Morin), annotations on the Pentateuch taken from the English copy of the Samaritan Pentateuch.

units.la: Reverendo admodum Eruditissimoque Vi-ro D. Joanni Morino, Ordinis Orato- rii Presbytero.
units.tr: To the most reverend and most learned man, Mr. John Morinus, Presbyter of the Oratory.

units.la: Reverende admodum Pater, Vir Doctis-sime.
units.tr: Most reverend Father, most learned sir.

units.la: ET opportunum satis ad vos, & gratum pervenisse illud primum officii mei specimen, quod vobis pridem mittendum duxeram, mihi Epistolâ tuâ perhumaniter ad me scriptâ innotuisse, jucundum inprimis fuit, neque hoc pacto amicitiæ benevolentiæque tuæ titulo atque tessera donatum, immo insignitum serio equidem gaudeo. Quod autem porro in eadem postulare te memini, nam mihi respondere volenti jam ad manum Epistola ipsa non erat, ut quod reliquum fuerat annotationum istarum adjiceretur, id quia serum jam putabam, cum in procinctu esse emittendi à vobis Libri viderentur, pene consilium scribendi omiseram, nisi eas adhuc quoque expectari admonitus à quodam nuper essem. En igitur, Vir doctissime, jam tandem posteriorum quoque Pentateuchi Librorum annotationes ab hominibus eisdem excerptas, qvarum tarditatem si in culpa esse videtur, vel nimiae qvorundam, à qvibus detinebantur, pertinaciae, vel longinqvae meae ab his locis per aliqvot retro menses absentiae velim attribuas; neqve enim immemor interea temporis promissi fui. Utinam verò qvod in votis erat, ipsum etiam exemplar Samaritícum transmittere potuissem, qvo labori atqve industriæ tuae perspicacissimæ materia non deesset uberior. Neqve enim intentatum vel illud qvoqve reliqvi. Delitescit autem jam qvidem liber iste, qvod certius intelligo non in Oxoniensi, sed in privata Cottonorum Bibliotheca apud D. Roberti Cottoni filium & hæredem paterni animi ac studii tenacissimum juvenem, cujus é manibus tale aliqvid extrahere nisi probe ei cautum de restituendo sit, nonnisi frustra tentaveris. Ego qvidem qvi dis-sitis ab eo locis habito, scribendo nihil proficio. Qvod si autem operæ pretium ducas, impetratis, qvod facile erit, Re-ginæ ginæ serenissimæ litteris, aliquid effici[?] posse existimem, nam & Frontoni Ducæo factam olim ab hujus parente librorum copiam audivi. Qui de his tuo nomine mecum egerunt, cum in Aula Regia versentur, celerius ista conficere possent. De qua re ad D. Massonium hujus negotii conscium perscribam. Sed detineo te, & pecco in occupationes tuas; hoc unum abs te vicissim peto, ubi ad umbilicum perducti Libri erunt, uti eorum exemplaria duo, si commodo fieri potest, mihi transmittenda cures, desi-gnato, cui pretium persolvam, Mercatore, ne librariis scilicet nostris nimium avaris simus prædæ. Ego signa in re tibi commodare possum. Habes devinctissimum paratissimumque, quite ex animo colit amatque. Vale.
units.tr: It was very welcome to me to learn from your letter that my first sample of duty, which I had earlier thought should be sent to you, has reached you at a suitable time and pleasingly. I am truly glad that this has not merely given me a token and pledge of your friendship and goodwill, but has in fact marked me with it. As for the other matter you asked me to address in the same letter: since the letter itself was not at hand when I wanted to reply, and since I thought it too late to send the rest of those notes when the books seemed about to be published by you, I had almost given up the idea of writing, unless someone recently reminded me that they were still awaited. So here, learned sir, at last are the notes on the remaining books of the Pentateuch, taken from the same men. If you think the delay is to be blamed, attribute it either to the excessive obstinacy of certain persons who held them back, or to my absence from these places for some months past; for in the meantime I have not forgotten my promise. I only wish I could have sent the Samaritan manuscript itself, so that your most keen labour and diligence would not lack a richer material. Indeed, I have not left even that untried. The book is now hidden, as I understand more certainly, not in the Oxford library but in the private Cotton library, held by the son and heir of Sir Robert Cotton, a young man very tenacious of his father's spirit and zeal. Unless you have taken proper precautions for its return, you will try in vain to draw anything of that kind from his hands. As for me, since I live far from that place, I achieve nothing by writing. But if you think it worth the effort, I believe something could be done if letters from the most serene Queen were obtained, which will be easy; for I heard that a supply of books was once made to Fronto Ducaeus by this man's father. Those who have dealt with me on your behalf in this matter, since they live at the Royal Court, could complete these things more quickly. I shall write about this to Mr. Masson, who knows of this business. But I am keeping you, and I am trespassing upon your occupations. I ask only this one thing in return: when the books have reached their end, please arrange, if it can conveniently be done, for two copies to be sent to me, and name a bookseller to whom I may pay the price, so that we do not give too much prey to our too greedy booksellers. I can lend you signatures in this matter. Farewell; I remain your most bound and most ready servant, who honours and loves you from the heart.

units.la: Scriptis his etiam complicandis literis reddita est tandem conspectui meo Epistola tua, ad quam tamen ne pluribus respondeam, non mea qu[illegible, ~2 letters]em, neque Tabellarii nostri, sed vestra potius, quam considerare debeo, in opere accelerando festinatio in causa est. Cæterùm cum literis & observationibus tuis mihi gratissimis, Vir Reverende, unius tantum Libri ex tribus, tot enim numeras, nempe Exodi tantum, mihi annotationes remisisti, cæteras, ubi videbitur, remittes. Quoniam verò existimaveram ego, duorum solummodo me Librorum, Geneseos scilicet & Exodi collationes prius dedisse, ideo nunc reliquorum trium, Levitici, Numerorum, Deuteronomii, inclusas addo; ne per errorem forte aliquem, de exemplaris nostri integritate tibi quicquam desideretur. Erat autem in codice hoc nostro, quod ferme tuais[?] de tuo, non solum annus scriptionis, sed etiam nomen ipsum scriptoris, & summi q[illegible, ~3 letters]qve illorum Pontificis adscriptum in fine, sive hoc honoris causa fieret, sive etiam numeris, quo exemplaria examinare & recensere sacerdotes deberent, propter Judæos diversa lectione utentes: cùm & ipsi quoque Judæi pro officio suo religione & fide non minori sibi tradita custodirent. Adeo illis ἀεὶ Φίλον ἀντιπράτηεθαι[?] ἀλλήλοις. De sinceritate textuum tibi editum scriptum adhuc non vidi, aveo videre. Faciet ad eam rem LXX Interpretum praeclara editio, quam D. Patricii, Yongi, sive Junii in manibus esse audio. De Exemplari Regio pervetusto,quod primum ex Alexandria comparatum, Sanctæ Theclæ, (ut credi volunt, nam eleganter scriptum) Patriarcha Cyrillus serenissimo Regi nostro Carolo, per Oratorem suum D. Roëum Constantinopoli nuper transmisit. Hujus specimen jam editum est. Sancti Clementis quæ præfixa erat illa nobilis Epistola jamdiu desiderata olim Ecclesiis legi solita, ad Corinthios; Navigavit olim ex Ægypto Rabbi Moses Narbonum ad consulendum exemplar probatissimum, quod ibi haberi intellexerat; nos ad hoc ex Ægypto perlatum nunc oculos intendimus. Dabunt ista ad meditandum & inquirendum mate-riam & segetem ampliorem. Sed iterum pecco, dum immodicus fio; Te optamus in Domino feliciter vivere ac valere.
units.tr: Even as I was folding up these letters, your letter finally came into my sight. I shall not reply to it at length, for the haste in speeding the work is the cause, not my own, nor that of our courier, but rather yours, which I ought to consider. Moreover, with your letter and observations, most welcome to me, Reverend sir, you have sent me the notes on only one of the three books, since you count three, namely of Exodus alone. The rest you will send when it seems fit. But since I had thought that I had given you only the collations of two books, Genesis and Exodus, I now add those of the remaining three, Leviticus, Numbers and Deuteronomy, enclosed, lest through some error anything be found wanting to you concerning the integrity of our copy. In this codex of ours, which is nearly yours in its character, there was written at the end not only the year of writing but also the name of the scribe, and of the chief priest of those people, whether this was done out of honour or also for the sake of numbers, by which priests were to examine and revise the copies, because the Jews used a different reading; for the Jews themselves also guarded their office with no less religious care and faith handed down to them. So indeed "it is always dear to them to contend with one another" [ἀεὶ φίλον ἀντιπράτηεθαι ἀλλήλοις]. I have not yet seen the printed writing on the integrity of the texts that you mention; I long to see it. The splendid edition of the Septuagint, which I hear is in the hands of Mr. Patrick, Young, or Junius, will help for this purpose. Concerning the very ancient Royal Codex, which was first obtained from Alexandria and is said (for it is elegantly written) to have belonged to Saint Thecla, the Patriarch Cyril lately sent it to our most serene King Charles through his envoy Mr. Roe at Constantinople. A specimen of it has already been published. As for that noble epistle of Saint Clement, once prefixed to it, long desired, which was once customarily read in the churches, the letter to the Corinthians: Rabbi Moses once sailed from Egypt to Narbonne to consult a most approved copy that he had learned was kept there; we now turn our eyes to this copy brought from Egypt. These things will supply a richer matter and harvest for meditation and inquiry. But again I am trespassing, while I become immoderate. We wish you to live and fare well in the Lord.

units.la: Stepniæ, 3. Cal. Octob. stylo quo utimur, A. Sal. M. DC. XXXIV.
units.tr: Stepney, 3 days before the Kalends of October, in the style we use, in the year of salvation 1634.

units.la: Reverentiæ tuæ Studiosissimus,
units.tr: Your Reverence's most devoted,

units.la: EPIST. XLV.
units.tr: Letter XLV.

units.la: Philippus J. Morino mittit, quas à Patricio Junio petierat Morinus, Notas ex MS. Exemplari 70 Interpretum.
units.tr: Philip J. sends Morinus the notes from the manuscript copy of the Seventy that Morinus had asked Patrick Young for.

units.la: Au R. Pere Morin, Prestre de l'Oratoire de Jesus.
units.tr: To the Reverend Father Morin, Priest of the Oratory of Jesus.

units.la: Mon Reverend Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: LA Grace de nostre Seigneur Jesus Christ soit avec vous à jamais. Enfin j'ay receu de Mr. Young ce que vous avez demandé il y a long temps du MS. de 70, & plus que vous n'avez demandé pour recompenser le long delay. Il se recommande fort à vous, & m'a escrit, que le Doyen de Carlile luy a promis de vous envoier les differences des deux der-niers niers livres de Moyse, si vous les desires, parquoy il semble que ledit Doyen n'apas receu la vostre, que je luy ay envoyée l'année passée. C'est pourquoy il seroit à propos de luy escrire encore un mot pour montrer vostre desir, lequel je luy feray servir par M. Young. Ledit M. Y. nous supplie très instamment de faire transcrire pour luy de la Catene Grecque sur les Pseaumes colligée par Nicolas, que le R. P. de Sancy apporta de Constantinople ; & est gardée en vostre Bibliotheque de Paris, l'Exposition sur le Pseaume cɛ[?] qui commence ainsi : πεντα-χῆ τε[?]μημ[?]ῆς τῆς τῶν ψαλμῶν πραγ-ματείας, &c. & sur le Pseuma oγ[?], jusqu'ves au commencement du oδ[?], qui est ainsi : ἐξηγηταί γ[?] ἐτ[?] ὁ ψαλμὸς ἐν πεσσωπα τῶν ἐν Βαβυλῶνι δορυαλωτῶν, &c. Parce que ces deux Pseaumes avec leur explication manquent à la copie MS. qu'il a ici. S'il y a quelque chose, que vous desirés de la Bibliotheque du Roy, il vous promet le mesme plaisir. Toute la Cour part d'ici pour aller au progrés dans cinq semaines au plus tard, & ainsi si vos lettres arrivent ici apres ce temps là, elles seront en danger d'estre perdues. Je suis à jamais
units.tr: May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you for ever. At last I have received from Mr Young what you asked for a long time ago from the manuscript of the Seventy, and more than you asked, to make up for the long delay. He commends himself warmly to you and has written that the Dean of Carlisle has promised to send you the variants of the last two books of Moses, if you want them. So it seems that the Dean has not received your letter, which I sent him last year. It would therefore be well to write him another line to show your wish, and I will have it delivered through Mr Young. The said Mr Y. also begs us very earnestly to have transcribed for him the Greek catena on the Psalms compiled by Nicolas, which Father de Sancy brought from Constantinople and which is kept in your library in Paris: the exposition of Psalm 1xx [?] beginning thus: πενταχῆ τεμημένης τῆς τῶν ψαλμῶν πραγματείας, &c., and on the psalm [?], up to the beginning of [?], which reads thus: ἐξηγηταί ... ὁ ψαλμὸς ἐν πρόσωπα τῶν ἐν Βαβυλῶνι αἰχμαλώτων, &c. These two psalms with their explanation are missing from the manuscript copy he has here. If there is anything you want from the Royal Library, he promises you the same favour. The whole Court leaves here for the journey in five weeks at the latest, so if your letters arrive here after that time, they will be in danger of being lost. I am for ever

units.la: Mon Pere,
units.tr: My Father,

units.la: De Greenwich, 5. de Juin, 1634.
units.tr: From Greenwich, 5 June 1634.

units.tr: EPIST. XLVI.

units.la: Philippus J. Morino. Quærit, utrum ve-rum sit, Canones Concilii Tridenti-ni, qui de Fide tractant, non recipi à Doctoribus Sorbonicis.
units.tr: Philippus J. Morino. He asks whether it is true that the canons of the Council of Trent which deal with faith are not received by the Sorbonne doctors.

units.la: Au R. P. Morin, Prestre de l'Oratoire de Jesus.
units.tr: To the Reverend Father Morin, priest of the Oratory of Jesus.

units.la: Mon R. Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: LA Grace de nostre Seigneur Jesus Christ soit avec vous pour jamais. Mr. Comber vous envoie le reste de ses lectiones sur le Pentateuche[?]. Il a fort recommandé qve ce pacqvet vous foit ren-du seulement , c'eft pourqvoy je vous fupplie de nous mander, qvand vous l'aurés receu & d' escrire un mot à luy mesme. Il a long temps, qve je vous ay envoié les diversités entre les exemples des 70, qve vous aviez demandé escrites par Mr. Junius mesme. Mais je n'ay pas receu voftre reponse, ni seulement qve vous les avés receues. Je vous supplie' de nous faire scavoir maintenant la re-cepte de toutes deux, & ensemble de no-us mander qvelqve chose touchant vo-ftre Assemblée generale. Je suis à jamais
units.tr: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you for ever. Mr. Comber sends you the rest of his lectures on the Pentateuch[?]. He has strongly asked that this packet be delivered to you alone, so I beg you to let us know when you receive it, and to write a word to him yourself. It is a long time since I sent you the differences between the examples of the Seventy, which you had asked for, written out by Mr. Junius himself. But I have not received your reply, nor even learned whether you have received them. I beg you now to let us know the receipt of both, and at the same time to tell us something about your general assembly. I am, for ever,

units.la: Mon R. Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: Hampton-Court, 16. Octob. 1634.
units.tr: Hampton Court, 16 October 1634.

units.la: Voftre tres humble Serviteur R.Phi-lippe P. de l'Or-de Jesus.

units.tr: J. Morinus to Francis Harlay, Archbishop of Rouen; he runs on in praise of him.

units.la: Illustrissimo D. Francisco Harlæo, Erudi-tissimo Rothomag. Archiepisc. & Nor- manniæ Primati J. Morinus Congre- gat. Orator. Presb.
units.tr: To the most illustrious Lord Francis Harlay, most learned Archbishop of Rouen and Primate of Normandy J. Morinus, Presbyter and Orator of the Congregation

units.la: CUm primum longæ peregrinationis tædio, simul ac delectioni finem imposui, domumque me recepi, eh[?] otium tuum occupatissimum abrumpo. Alicui forsan audaculus videar, qvi Episcoporum principem male interpellem ὦ λαυί[?] τ' ἀπιτετραφάταυ[?] ἢ τόσα μέμνηλε[?], qvi vel dormiens Achillis clypeo incumbit. Sed hoc probrum ego, qvi te domestice novi, nihili facio, tibi enim negotia obsequuntur, non tu negotiis; tibi homines inserviunt, non tu hominibus; tu libris, studiis, universæqve literariæ supellectili dominaris, non ista tibi. Ludens hæc omnia, qvæcunqve lubet, agis; duces trahis, nec unqvam de sede sua & statu mens tua dimovetur. Aëris procellas, furentesqve nimborum tempestates, qvæ hæc infima perturbant, hucqve & illuc agunt, ferunt non modo salutis securi, sed & qvietis dispectant superi. Paris fortitudinis atque etiam capacitatis mihi ¡cognitus est animus tuus, ut mare, in quod influunt innumera flumina, nec tamen diffluit; sic mens tua. Itaque licet pro dignitate tua variis & multiplicibus negotiis expositus fis, attamen nullus vel levissimus animum meum timor incessit, ne hoc Epistolium lubens legas & boni consulas: ab eo præterea mittitur, qui dignitati tuæ non assentatur, sed qui tanta in dignitate tuam virtutem & doctrinam supra dignitatem assurgentem amat, colit & admiratur; ab eo mittitur, quem amicitia tua arctissime complexus es, quem multis benevolentiæ testimoniis decorasti. Non igitur spe lætor[?] inani, Φιλέεις Φιλεοῦς[?], ἀγεῖς ἄγοντα ὧς φρονῶς[?], ut verbis utar Pindari. Hanc benevolentiam ut mihi perpetuã conserves, etiam atq; etiam rogo; sic me beneficio maximo afficis, spemque meam pari gaudio cumulabis. Vale.
units.tr: When I had at last put an end to the weariness of a long journey, and to my delay abroad, and had returned home, I interrupt your very busy leisure. Perhaps I may seem too bold to some, to trouble so great a prince of bishops, "O ... ἢ τόσα μέμνηλε" [ὦ λαυί[?] τ' ἀπιτετραφάταυ[?] ἢ τόσα μέμνηλε[?]], who even while sleeping leans upon the shield of Achilles. But I, who know you intimately, make nothing of this reproach. For business obeys you, and you do not obey business; men serve you, and you do not serve men; you rule over books, studies, and all the furniture of literature, and these things do not rule you. You do all these things playfully, whatever you please, and you lead them as you will; your mind is never moved from its seat and condition. The storms of the air and the raging tempests of the clouds, which disturb these lower regions and drive them hither and thither, the heavenly powers look down upon not only free from danger but also in peaceful calm. Your spirit has been known to me as equal in courage and in capacity, like the sea into which countless rivers flow yet which is not overflowed; so is your mind. Therefore, although you are beset by various and manifold affairs befitting your dignity, no slightest fear has crept into my mind that you might read this little letter gladly and take it in good part. Moreover, it is sent by one who does not flatter your dignity, but who loves, reveres and admires your virtue and learning, which rise above your dignity; it is sent by one whom you have embraced in the closest friendship and honoured with many proofs of goodwill. So I do not rejoice in empty hope, "you love the one who loves you, you lead the one who leads you wisely" [Φιλέεις Φιλεοῦς, ἀγεῖς ἄγοντα ὡς φρονῶς], to use Pindar's words. I beg you again and again to keep this goodwill toward me unbroken for ever; you bestow the greatest kindness upon me in this way, and you will fill my hope with an equal joy. Farewell.

units.la: Datum Parisiis xj. Kal. Nov. Anno MDCXXXVI.
units.tr: Given at Paris, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the year 1636.

units.la: EPIST. XLVIII.
units.tr: EPIST. XLVIII.

units.la: R. Goezaldus J. Morino. Quo in pretio sunt Romae ejus Libri etiam apud Cardinales, scribit.
units.tr: R. Goezaldus to J. Morinus. He writes how highly his books are valued at Rome, even among the Cardinals.

units.la: Au.[?] R. Pere Jean Morin assistant du R. P. General de la Congreg. de l'Orat. de Je-sus.
units.tr: To the Reverend Father Jean Morin, assistant to the Reverend Father General of the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus.

units.la: Mon R. Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: LA Grace de Jesus pour jamais. La presente est pour vous donner avis, que partant y a bien 3 semaines de quelq; affaire à Monseigneur le Cardinal Barbe-rin, il me demanda fort de vos nouvelles, où vous estiés, & que faisiez à present, si vous ne composiés plus rien de nouve-au, Je luy dis, que je n'avois pas ouy, qu'essiés rien fait[?] imprimer depuis le der-nier que luy envoiastes, il y a trois ans ce me semble. Il ne me vint pas en pensée de vous excuser sur l'impression de cette grande Bible à quoy je crois qu'aurez employé un grand temps. Il me commanda de vous escrire de sa part, qu'il vous prie & convie de ne demeurer pas oisif, ains de continuër a composer toujours quelque chose. Il me semble, que ce dernier de vos livres, qu'il a veu, c'est prior pars Exercitationum Biblicarum de Hebræi Græcique textus sinceritate, &c. Et vous en promettiés la partie à posterieure, & me semble, qu'à la fin vous mettiés la table des Chapitres, qui devoient estre contenus en cette posterieure partie : si vous l'avez fait imprimer, je vous supplie de nous en envoier pour en presenter à mon dit Seigneur le Cardinal Barberin, & envoier au Cardinal Spada, & au Cardinal de Bagni, auquel j'en dois presenter deux dans peu de jours des vostres, qui luy manquent, scavoir vostre premier, De Origine Patriarcharum, & l'autre, Exercitationes Ecclesiasticæ in utrumq; Samaritanorum Pentateuchum. Je les fais bien relier à ce dessein, il a Monsieur Noudé pour Bibliothecaire, homme docte, & qui fait estat de vos livres ; il m'a assaré, que mon dit Seigneur le Cardinal Bagni n'a que deux de vos li-vres, vres, scavoir les susdits Exercitationes Biblicæ de Hebræi Græcique Textus sinceritate, & le Francois, De la Grandeur de l'Eglise par les Francois, qve mon dit Seigneur le Card. estime. C'est pourqvoy je luy veux donner les deux autres, & celuy De Ara singulari du R. P. Berthauld, duqvel j'en ay receu deux depuis peu de jours. Je voulois donner l'autre au Cardinal Barberin, mais par hazard j'ay sceu, qu'il en avoit deja un, je ne scay, si c'est le dit Pere, qui le luy a envoié, il m'eust fait plaisir de m'en advertir. Vous aurez appris nos brouilleries suscitées par le P. Vacher, & par un ou deux des Chappelains, qui le soutenoient en sa rebellion, de laquelle mesme il ne nous donnoit pas advis, promettant toujours de s'en aller, & sous main par qvantité d'impostures sollicitoient à me renvoier moy-mesme hors de ceans, mais Mr. l'Ambassadeur ne l'a pas permis, par la grace de nostre Seigneur leur procedé estoit injurieux à nostre congregation. Je croy, qv'aurez eu communication des longeus informations, que j'en ay escrites à nostre R. P. General. C'est pourquoy je finis par nos tres-humbles recommandations de tous à vos SS. Prieres, & de tous de la maison, demeurant en J. & M.
units.tr: The grace of Jesus be with you for ever. This letter is to let you know that about three weeks ago, when I had some business with Monseigneur the Cardinal Barberini, he asked me eagerly for news of you: where you were, what you were doing now, and whether you were composing anything new. I told him that I had not heard that you had printed anything since the last book you sent him, three years ago I think. It did not occur to me to excuse you on the ground of the printing of that great Bible, on which I believe you have spent a great deal of time. He commanded me to write to you on his behalf, asking and urging you not to remain idle but always to go on composing something. It seems to me that the last of your books which he has seen is the first part of the Biblical Exercitations on the integrity of the Hebrew and Greek text, etc. You promised the second part, and I think that at the end you set out a table of the chapters that were to be contained in that second part. If you have had it printed, I beg you to send us some copies to present to the said Lord Cardinal Barberini, and to send to Cardinal Spada and to Cardinal de Bagni, to whom I am to present two of yours in a few days, namely your first book, On the Origin of the Patriarchs, and the other, Ecclesiastical Exercitations on both Samaritan Pentateuchs. I am having them bound well for this purpose. He has Monsieur Noudé as his librarian, a learned man who values your books. He has assured me that the said Lord Cardinal Bagni has only two of your books, namely the aforementioned Biblical Exercitations on the integrity of the Hebrew and Greek text, and the French one, On the Greatness of the Church through the French, which the said Lord Cardinal esteems. That is why I want to give him the other two, and that one, On the Single Altar, by Reverend Father Berthauld, of which I received two a few days ago. I wanted to give the other to Cardinal Barberini, but by chance I learned that he already has one. I do not know whether it was the said Father who sent it to him; he would have done me a favour by telling me. You will have heard of the disturbances stirred up by Father Vacher and by one or two of the chaplains, who supported him in his rebellion, of which he himself gave us no notice, always promising to leave, while secretly, through a multitude of lies, they tried to have me sent back out of here myself. But the Ambassador would not allow it, and by the grace of our Lord their conduct was injurious to our congregation. I believe you will have been told of the lengthy reports that I have written on this to our Reverend Father General. So I close with the most humble greetings of all of us to your holy prayers, and of all in the house, remaining in Jesus and Mary.

units.la: Mon R. Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: A Rome, 7. Jan. 1637.
units.tr: At Rome, 7 January 1637.

units.la: Vostre tres humble & tresobeissant Servi-teur Rene Goezald R. de l'Or. de Jesus.
units.tr: Your very humble and most obedient servant, René Goezald, of the Oratory of Jesus.

units.la: EPIST. XLIX.
units.tr: LETTER XLIX.

units.la: J. Morinus Eminentissimo Cardinali Barberino. Studiorum suorum, Li- brorumque tam à se editorum, quam edendorum rationem reddit.
units.tr: J. Morinus to the Most Eminent Cardinal Barberini. He gives an account of his studies, and of the books both published by him and still to be published.

units.la: Eminentissime Card.
units.tr: Most Eminent Cardinal,

units.la: SCripsit ad me Goezaldus noster, eminentiam tuam solùm mei non esse immemorem, verùm etiā de me, studiisq; me is ab ipso multa percontatum esse. Ad hujus rei nuntium, gratias egi Deo opt. max. cujus Ecclesiae labores meos ab adolescentia consecravi, quod eorū recordetur&ad novos incipiendos me hortetur ille, qui summo Ecclesiae Pastore tam arcto sanguinis vinculo cohaeret; qui in Ecelesia regenda non modo à natura, sed potissimum à Iesu Christo Domino nostro Consiliarius summo Pastori datus est & administer. Non est frustrata spes mea, nec, ut ait Sapiens, in ventum me laborasse experior; est enim, quod doctis omnibus placere confidam, quae tibi non displicuere, & frugem in Ecclesia Dei datura, quae non infrugiferafore iudicasti, Plantonem auditorem unicum nactus, Orator operae orationi navatae se non poenitere testatus est. Amico rescribebat Philosophus, eum solum amplum satis esse sibi theatrum. Quid lucubrationū mearum me poeniteat, cum earum non modo approbatorem, sed etiam suasorem & impulsorem nactus sim, qui summa sua autoritate iis potest per universum orbem nomen conciliare, & exquisitissima doctrina existimationem? Quidni igitur audeam Eminentiam tuam hac Epistola studiorum meorum ratioilli redditura trantisper interpellare,maximis licet negotiis quotidie vacantem: Cum præ fulgore Eminentissimæ Purpuræ tuæ pudibundũ & resistante ipsamet ad id me invitet & excuset? Abhinc igitur triennium licet variis negotiis propter congregatione, cui me dedidi, implicitq; fuerim, quæ supererant posteriori parti Biblicarũ Exercitationũ pro qua edenda fidé meâ publice obligaverã, licet priore materiæ necessitate cōpellente, multorū soliorū molę superatura sit, fere ad umbilicum duxi, & Deo cœptis favente, ante mensem Majum nihil ei defuturum spero, quod ab ipsius adornationem, aut conferre possim, aut conferendum existi-mem. Fidem meam illorum editione jam liberassem, nisi me bellorum immanitas, quæ fere per universam Europam grassantur, me retardasset. Qua de re agatur toto illo opere, longum esset hic enarrare, ad finem prioris partis editi Indices χ[?] πόδα id indicant. Attamen hoc unum Eminentiam tuam non celabo, potissimum illo opere mihi propositum fuisse, quidquid unquam Judæi antiqui & recentiores ante vel post Talmund compositum, ad hæc usque tempora, in gratiam & illustrationem TextusHebraei[?] præstiterunt ; eorundem de istius Textus castigatione & dispositione, diversas admodum & pugnantes sententias, varias ejusdem Textus leētiones plus quam bis mille locis adnotatas, aliaque id genus, ex ipsorum Biblicis codicibus, ex ipsorum tantum Archivis , & commentariis antiqui & recentioribus eruere, & Christianis omnibus propalam dare conspicienda : hinc enim luce meridiana clarius est,nihil Judæos in gratiam sui Textus nunquam tentasse, quod sit ingentibus Ecclesiæ laboribus in sacri textus conservatione exantlatis comparandum ; & hæriticos etiam, nobis tacentibus, ea quæ prorsus ignorabant, in immensum temere laudasse, vulgatamque Editionem ,adversus quam, furore potius ,quam ratione debacchantur, fontibus Hebraicis multo puriorem & limpidiorem fluere.Ante quadriennium excudi curavi in corpore magnorum Bibliorum duplicem Pentateuchum Samaritanum cum Latina versione,Hebræo-Samaritanum, & ejusdem in Linguam Samaritanam versionem; utrumque excusum hac hyeme relegi & recensui, & quæ à Typographo errata fuerant, adnotavi, Hebraeo - Samaritanum verò excusum cum quatuor antiquis Manuscriptis comparavi,& varias lectiones exscripsi; Samaritican autem versionem,quæ Judæorum Chaldaicæ respondet, permultis sed brevissimis adnotationibus illustravi. Est mihi præ manibus aliud opus, de antiquo scilicet poenitentiæ ritu, & confessionis necessitate,cui jam sæpius animum applicui , sed aliis sæpe datis scribendi occasionibus manum applicatam è tabula subducere invitus sæpe subduxi. Ista enim scribendi materies, quæ antiquam Ecclesiæ vel disciplinam vel historiam spectat, meam esse cupio, huic cognoscendæ ab adolescentia tempus, otiumq; meum potissimum dicavi; cætera consiliis meis fuere accessaria & πάρεργα. Ita-
units.tr: Our Goezald wrote to me that your Eminence not only remembers me but has also asked him many questions about me and my studies. On hearing this news I gave thanks to God, best and greatest, to whose Church I have dedicated my labours since youth, that the one who is bound by so close a blood tie to the supreme Shepherd of the Church remembers them and urges me to begin new ones. He has been given to the supreme Shepherd as counsellor and minister in governing the Church, not only by nature but above all by our Lord Jesus Christ. My hope has not been disappointed, and, as the wise man says, I find that I have not laboured in vain. For there is something which I trust will please all learned men, since it has not displeased you, and which will yield fruit in the Church of God, since you judged it would not be fruitless. Having found a single hearer in Plato, the orator declared that he did not regret the effort of his speech. The philosopher wrote back to a friend that one man alone was a large enough theatre for him. Why should I regret my labours, since I have found not only an approver but also a promoter and spur of them, who by his supreme authority can win their name throughout the whole world, and by his most exquisite learning, their esteem? Why then should I not dare to trouble your Eminence with this letter, to give an account of my method of studies, although you are occupied every day with the greatest affairs, since the very brightness of your Eminent Purple, which makes me shy and hesitant, itself invites me to do so and excuses me? For three years now, although I have been entangled in various affairs because of the congregation to which I have devoted myself, I have brought the remaining parts of the second part of the Biblical Exercitations almost to completion (to the navel), for whose publication I have publicly pledged my faith. Although the necessity of the first part compelled me, and the mass of many labours is bound to be overcome, God favouring my undertakings, I hope that before May nothing will be lacking in it that I can contribute to its adornment or think should be contributed. I would already have discharged my pledge by its publication, had not the savagery of the wars which rage through almost all of Europe delayed me. It would be long to explain here what the whole of that work is about; the indices at the end of the first published part indicate it. Yet this one thing I will not conceal from your Eminence: the principal aim I set myself in that work was to bring together whatever the ancient and more recent Jews have written, before or after the Talmud, down to these times, in favour and illustration of the Hebrew text. From their own biblical codices, and from their own archives and commentaries alone, both ancient and recent, I have dug out their very diverse and conflicting opinions on the correction and arrangement of this text, the various readings of the same text, noted in more than two thousand places, and other things of that kind, and I have set them openly before all Christians to behold. For it is clearer than midday light that the Jews never attempted for the sake of their text anything that could be compared with the immense labours the Church has undergone in preserving the sacred text. Likewise the heretics, while we keep silent, have rashly praised beyond measure things they utterly did not know, and they rage against the Vulgate edition with fury rather than reason, although it flows from Hebrew sources far purer and clearer. Four years ago I had printed, in the body of the large Bibles, a double Samaritan Pentateuch: the Hebrew-Samaritan text with a Latin version, and a version of the same into the Samaritan language. Having had both printed, I reread and revised them this winter, and noted the errors made by the typographer. The printed Hebrew-Samaritan text I compared with four ancient manuscripts, and I copied out the various readings. The Samaritan version, which corresponds to the Chaldee of the Jews, I illustrated with very many but very brief notes. I have at hand another work, namely on the ancient rite of repentance and the necessity of confession, to which I have often already applied my mind; but when other occasions for writing were often given, I unwillingly often drew my hand back from the tablet once applied. For this subject of writing, which concerns the ancient discipline or history of the Church, I wish to be my own; to learning it I have devoted my time and, above all, my leisure from youth, while the rest were incidental and by-works in my plans.

units.la: que his intra paucos menses expeditis & dimissis, ad antiquam Ecclesiae disciplinam & historiam, velut rure domum revertar. Diutius æquo te interpello & distineo, eruditissime Cardinalis, sed igno-sce quæso confidentiæ meæ. Principes, quotquot animi dotes opibus prætulerunt, hoc est, quotquot Deo, cujus vivere est intelligere, similes esse studuerunt, viris litteras profitentibus multa semper indulsere; deinde si audaci nimium confidentia peccavi, ipse in culpa es, qui summa tua humanitate, & singulari in me benevolentiaEminentiam tuam adeundi, & ei negotiola mea familiariter exponendi confidentiam excitasti. Ecclesiae suae Jesus Christus Dominus noster, te, Cardinalis Eminentissime, valentem & incolumem quam diutissime conservet. Iterum vale, meque Eminentiae tuae ob-sequentissimum, ut amare pergas, impensissime rogo.
units.tr: So, once these few months are finished and dispatched, I shall return home, as from the country, to the ancient discipline and history of the Church. I have troubled and detained you longer than is fitting, most learned Cardinal, but I beg you to forgive my boldness. Princes, all who have preferred gifts of the mind to riches, that is, all who have striven to be like God, whose living is understanding, have always shown great indulgence to men who profess letters. And if I have sinned by too bold a confidence, you yourself are to blame, who by your supreme kindness and singular goodwill towards me have encouraged me to approach your Eminence and to set out my small affairs to you familiarly. May Jesus Christ our Lord, the Church's own, keep you, Most Eminent Cardinal, in health and safety for as long as possible. Farewell again; and I most earnestly ask you to continue to love me, your most obedient servant.

units.la: L y a quelque remps que le fils de Mr. Vitray m'apporta une letre,noftre,contenant certaines reliqves de monumens Puniqves,dont vous me faisiés l'honneur de me demander la communication,que je seray tres aise de vous despartir,n'aiant rien que ne soit à vostre service, & à vostre disposition. La queftion estoit de trouver tems & le loisir de foviller parmi mes layetes pour entirer ce qvi pouvoit vous estre duisable, ce que j'en ay encore pû rencontrer à mon grand regret, & m' attendois à nos prochaines vacations pour tascher de vous pouvoir satisfaire en cela & en toute autre chose, que je jugeray pouvoir tomber dans vostre goust. Mais ayant appris que vous aviés rendu à MSS. du Puy 4. volumes Samaritains de ceux, que j'avois envois de par dela pour de vous, & voyant que vous aures vray-semblablement songe en mesme tems de rendre au Sieur Pietro della Vallé son volume Samaritain, dont il estoit en peine assez long tems ya, j'av cru d'estre obligé de vout supplier,que je scache l'il vous plaist ce que vous en aurez fait, attendu les lettres, que j'avois escrites audit Sieur della Vallé pout le vous faire tober [?] en main. Et ce qu'il m'en avoit fait scavoir principalement depuis que le temps commensoit a luy derer, d'en voir l'edition, qu'on luy avoit fait esperer, & la restitution de son volume, dont je m'estois rendu garent en son endroit. Il ya deplus un autre subject de m'en mettre en soin sur ce qu'on m'a dit, ce me semble, que vous vous estes contenté de faire imprimer seulement le texte Hebraiqve [?] des Samaritains sur l'exemplaire de Mr. l'Evesque de St.Malo, avec quelques diverses leçons ou expositions de certains mots de la version Syriaque ou Samaritaine, sur l'exemplaire dudit Sr. Pie-tro della Vallé. Un autre m'aiant voulu asseurer, que c'est la version entiere de ce volume dudit Sr. Pietra della Vallé, que vous avez fait imprimer, & que du texte Hebraique des Samaritains vous n'en avez marqué si non les diverses leçons de quelques mots plus considerables, auquel cas cette appition nous pourroit suffire à suppléer les imperfections & defectuosités de mon Pentateuque Tritaple. Mais à l'autre premier cas j'aurois grand regret, que ce volume fut sorti de ce Roy-aume sans y avoir fait transcrire les suppléents entiers de ce qui manq; en la troisiesme colomne de mon volume, comme la se conde colomne se suppléer d'un autre volume, que j'ay de la version Arabique des Samaritains, lequel j'avois envoié à Paris, pour vostre usage; mais je me doute, que vostre absence en aura empesché l'effet, outre que possible n'avez vous pas jugé, que la chose peusse[?] meriter de s'en mettre en peine, & toutefois il pouroit bien advenir un jour, q'onqv'og desirast en me illeure soison[?] d'en faire une edition avec toutes les autres langues avec leur Version Latine pour exercer les plus Curieux. C'est pourqvoy je serois bien aise d'envoier deqvoy sournir tout ce qvi peut estre reqvis, & serois volontiers la depense d'un Gepiste, s'il y en a là d'assez entendus pour cela, qvi prist la peine de suppléer & transcrire dans mon volume les cajers & sevillets qvi y manqvet, & d'en prendre le texte ou la version sur les 3 volumes, qvi y peuvent suffire, mais principalement pour la troisieme colomne sur celuy de Sieur Pietro della Valle. Mr. de St. Sauveur ou mon fre-re feront fournir[?] les frais necessaires, je ne seray pas marri de faire cette petite avance pour l'intesest du public, attendant un tems plus calme & plus propre à telles enterprises. Je vous supplie donc de m'y aider, & de disposer à cela celuy, qve vous pouvez avoir emploié à la transcription ou correction de voftre texte, & de voftre edition en characteres Samaritains, & faites estat de moy en revanche com-me.
units.tr: Some time ago the son of Monsieur Vitray brought me a letter from you, containing certain remains of Punic monuments, whose communication you did me the honour of asking for. I shall be very glad to send them to you, since I have nothing that is not at your service and at your disposal. The difficulty was to find the time and leisure to search among my papers for what might be useful to you. I have so far been able to find only part of it, to my great regret, and I had been waiting for our next vacations to try to satisfy you in this and in anything else that I judge might suit your taste. But having learned that you had returned to the Monastery of Puy four Samaritan volumes out of those I had sent over from abroad for you, and seeing that you have probably also meant to return to Signor Pietro della Valle his Samaritan volume, which he has long been anxious about, I felt obliged to beg you to let me know what you have done with it, given the letters I had written to the said Signor della Valle to have it placed in your hands. He had informed me, above all since the time began to hang heavily on him, that he was waiting to see the edition which he had been led to expect, and the return of his volume, for which I had made myself guarantor. There is also another matter that makes me anxious. I have been told, as I recall, that you have been content to print only the Hebrew text of the Samaritans from the copy belonging to the Bishop of Saint-Malo, with some variant readings or explanations of certain words of the Syriac or Samaritan version from the copy of the said Signor Pietro della Valle. Another person, however, has assured me that it is the complete version of that volume of the said Signor Pietro della Valle that you have had printed, and that from the Hebrew text of the Samaritans you have marked only the variant readings of a few of the more important words. In that case this edition might suffice to supply the imperfections and defects of my Triple Pentateuch. But in the first case I would greatly regret that this volume should have left this kingdom without a full copy having been made of the supplements for what is missing in the third column of my volume, just as the second column is to be supplied from another volume I have of the Arabic version of the Samaritans, which I had sent to Paris for your use. I suspect, however, that your absence has prevented this from taking effect. Perhaps you also did not think the matter worth the trouble. Yet it could well happen one day that someone, in a better season, might wish to produce an edition of all the other languages together with their Latin version, for the benefit of the most curious. That is why I should be very glad to send from here whatever may be required, and I would willingly bear the expense of a copyist, if there is one there sufficiently skilled for this, who would take the trouble to supply and copy into my volume the quires and leaves that are missing, taking the text or version from the three volumes which can suffice for this, but chiefly for the third column from that of Signor Pietro della Valle. Monsieur de Saint-Sauveur or my brother will have the necessary costs met. I shall not be sorry to make this small advance in the interest of the public, while waiting for a calmer time more suited to such undertakings. I therefore beg you to help me in this, and to dispose towards it the person whom you may have employed in transcribing or correcting your text and your edition in Samaritan characters, and count on my gratitude in return, as

units.la: Perillustri D. D. Petro à Valle Joannes Morinus S.P.D.
units.tr: To the most illustrious Lord Pietro della Valle John Morin sends greetings (S.P.D.).

units.la: Suspicari non abs re potuisti, perillustris Domine, me tui beneficii, quod à te accepi, immemorem esse, cùm jam annus alter effluxerit, aut etiam amplius, ex quo de me deque tuo Manuscripto Samaritano nihil prorsus acceperis, aut etiam forte audieris. Rescripsera abhinc tres menses R. Patri Goezaldo, ut te meo nomine salutaret, & si Romæ commorabaris, me certiorem faceret, ut ad te scriberem, rationemque editionis Pentateuchi tui tibi redderem, nec non te monerem, nihil aliud nunc me quærere, quam codicis tui restitutionem. Sed Goezaldus ad me scripsit, jam annum integrum elapsum esse, cum Cajetam divertisti, nec te Romæ ante autumnum à tuis expectari. Licet Romam non sis rediturus statim, moras tamen omnes rumpere mihi visum est, & animum tuum anxietate liberare. Paucis igitur habe & editionis Samaritanæ, & retardatæ codicis tui restitutionis rationem. Annus jam quartus agitur si bene memini, cum utriusque Pentateuchi, & Hebræo Samaritani & Dialecto-Samaritani editio cum Latina versione peracta supervenerunt mihi ab amplissimo Domino PerescioMSS. Codices tres, quorum unus trilingvis erat, Hebræo-Samaritanus, Arabicus & Samaritanus, sed à tuo non sensu, sed verbis admodum diversus, ita ut si non alia versio videretur, tota esset interpolata. Verùm Codex ille variis in locis, fere qvinta sui parte mutilatus erat. Cùm codices illos accepi, illorum comparationem cum editione mea facere instituì; deinde adnotiunculis Asteriscorum qvorundam, qvos sæpiusculè textui Samaritano inscripsi, rationem reddere; qvadruplici de causa potissimum Asteriscos inscripseram.
units.tr: You may not unreasonably suspect, most illustrious Sir, that I have forgotten the kindness you showed me, since a second year has now passed, or even more, since you have had no word from me about myself or about your Samaritan manuscript, and perhaps have not even heard anything of me. Three months ago I wrote to the reverend Father Goezaldus, asking him to greet you on my behalf and, if you were still in Rome, to let me know, so that I might write to you, give you an account of the progress of the edition of your Pentateuch, and also tell you that I now seek nothing else than the return of your codex. But Goezaldus wrote back to me that a full year has already elapsed since you went off to Gaeta, and that your people do not expect you in Rome before autumn. Although you may not return to Rome at once, I thought it right to break through all these delays and free your mind from anxiety. Please, then, let me briefly explain both the edition of the Samaritan text and the reason for the delay in returning your codex. If I remember rightly, it is now the fourth year since the edition of both Pentateuchs, the Hebrew-Samaritan and the Samaritan dialect, together with the Latin version, was completed, when there came to me from the most distinguished Lord Peiresc three manuscript codices. One of them was trilingual, in Hebrew-Samaritan, Arabic and Samaritan; but it differed greatly from your text, not in sense but in wording, so that, if another version did not appear, the whole would seem to be corrupted. However, that codex was mutilated in various places, nearly a fifth of it being missing. When I received those codices, I set about comparing them with my edition, and then I set out the results in short notes, marked with certain asterisks, which I often placed against the Samaritan text. I had marked the asterisks chiefly for four reasons.

units.la: Primo. Ob qvasdam dictiones aliqvot in locis in Codice tuo præteritas, qvarum lectorem admonui, eas, cum licuit, ex alio codice resarcivi.
units.tr: First, because of certain words which were omitted in several places in your codex. I told the reader of these, and where possible I restored them from another codex.

units.la: Secundo, Ob qvædam verba Samaritana rara, & intellectu difficilia, qvæ explicui.
units.tr: Second, because of certain rare Samaritan words that are hard to understand, which I explained.

units.la: Tertio, Cùm interpres versioni suæ aliqvid addidit, qvod in textu HebræoSamaritano non extabat, hoc notavi & interpretatus sum. Sed iste interpres ita presse textui adhæret, ut ab eo rarissime discedat.
units.tr: Third, when the translator added something to his version that was not found in the Hebrew-Samaritan text, I noted this and explained it. But this translator adheres so closely to the text that he very rarely departs from it.

units.la: Denique, Cùm versio mea Latina Hebræosa textûs ab interprete Samaritano variat. Verùm occurrentibus aliquot negotiis litterariis, opus hoc, quod trimestri aut quadrimestri tempore me completurum considebam, differo, donec reliquorum Bibliorum editione Arabica & Syriaca urgerer. Sed editione illa pedetentim progrediente propter illius, qui Syriaca & Arabica Latine vertit, lentum nimium, & in labore remissum animum annus unus, & alter, atque etiam tertius elabuntur, necdum tanto temporis spatio ad exitum festinat editio. Itaque hieme proxime praeterita, eum ab aliis negotiis inducias obtinuissem, editionem Hebræo-Samaritanam cum prototypo, & quatuor aliis exemplaribus comparo, varias lectiones adnoto, occurrentia errata corrigo, Asteriscorum, quas memoravi, rationes explico, Samaritanæ versionis textum recognosco: hisque peractis, ad amplissimum Virum Peresciurn[?] scribo, codices suos, quamprimum sese dederit occasio, me remissurum, idem etiam R. Patri Goezaldo de codice tuo significo, eamque ut de salute tua mihi rescribat rogo. Habes, Vir illustris, & mihi plurimum observande Domine, retardationis meæ sinceras excusationes, jam nihil aliud quæro, quàm codicis tui remittendi occasionem, illum brevi Deo dante recuperabis integrum, Capitum & Versuum perpetua adnotatione auctum, Vale, & me tui observantissimum ut amare pergas, etiam atque etiam rogo.
units.tr: Finally, where my Latin version differs from the Hebrew text as given by the Samaritan translator. But, with several literary business matters arising, I have postponed this work, which I had reckoned I would finish in a term of three or four months, until I was pressed to finish the rest of the Bible edition in Arabic and Syriac. But as that edition has advanced slowly, on account of the excessive slowness of the man who renders the Syriac and Arabic into Latin, and his spirit flagging in the work, one year, then another, and even a third, have slipped by, and the edition still does not hasten to completion. So, last winter, when I had obtained a respite from my other business, I compared the Hebrew-Samaritan edition with the prototype and four other copies, noted the variant readings, corrected the errors I met with, explained the reasons for the asterisks I have mentioned, and revised the text of the Samaritan version. With these things done, I am writing to the most distinguished Lord Peiresc that I will return his codices as soon as an opportunity presents itself. I am also informing Father Goezaldus about your codex, and I ask him to write back to me about your health. You have my sincere apologies, most illustrious Sir and Lord whom I greatly esteem, for my delay. I now seek nothing else than an opportunity to return your codex; God willing, you will soon get it back whole, enriched with a continuous annotation of chapters and verses. Farewell, and I beg you again and again to continue to love me, who am most devoted to you.

units.la: EXimia me jucunditate perfuderunt, amantissime mi Pater, atque observantissime Domine, litteræ tuæ, quas Cajetæ accepi. Verè namque anxius eram, non quidem de restitutione Pentateuchi mei: De hac enim ante annum ad te scripseram, qvod in adjuncto folio inspicies ; licet ex epistola ob repentinum meum ex urbe discessum, ad te tunc transmissa minime fuerit. Sed certe mirum in modum angebar, tum ob valetudinem tuam, de qva qvid esset ignorabam ; tum etiam ob jamdiu expectatam, summisqve votis expetitam Bibliorum editionem, cujus retardationis causas luculenter modo mihi patefecisti. Non miror interpretem illum Syriacae & Arabicae Linguae pedetentim, ut narras procedere ; incredibilis enim, & mea sententia improbi sane laboris est lingvarum externarum interpretatio, cum recte peragitur, nec omnes in hujusmodi lucubrationibus tam indefessi viribus, & animo tam pertinacis patientiae, uti Pater Morinus, esse possunt. Faxit Deus, ut multilingvia Biblia ista prodeant tandem, si sero, exacte saltem compilata ; qvod ad Librum attinet meum, immortales tibi gratias ago de inscriptione Capitum, deqve adnotatione Versiculorum, qvibus illum ornasti. Tot tantisque beneficiis, quibus me perpetuo tibi devinctum fore pro certo habeas, ut unum hoc addas exopto, quando nimirum Pentateuchus Samaritanus cum tua versione Latina impressus, sive Bibliis adjunctus, sive solus publici fuerit juris, ut unico impresso exemplari, in tui memoriam, & in tantæ reipublicæ literariæ utilitatis monumentum apud me, pretioso tanquam thesauro adservando, Musæunculum meum quale quale illud fit, locupletari haud dedigneris. Fgo[?] interim cum Romam rediero, ubi & libros & alia mea omnia reliqvi, externorum voluminum, quæ apud me extant, indicem ad te mittam, ut si quid ex illis tibi, ab aliis jam negotiis vel induciis, vel manumissione impetrata, in novæ studiorum exercitationis occasionem habere placuerit, mihi quamprimum significes; quidquid petieris Parisios usque ad te quam citissime amandaturo. Reliquum vale, & me ama, ut soles.
units.tr: Your letter, which I received at Gaeta, has filled me with exceeding delight, my dearest Father and most respected Lord. I was truly anxious, not indeed about the return of my Pentateuch, for I had written to you about that a year ago, as you will see from the enclosed sheet, although that letter was not sent to you at the time because of my sudden departure from the city. But I was in a remarkable state of distress, first because of your health, of which I did not know the state, and then because of the edition of the Bible, long awaited and most earnestly desired, the causes of whose delay you have now clearly explained to me. I am not surprised that the translator of the Syriac and Arabic languages is making progress slowly, as you report; for the translation of foreign languages is an incredible and, in my judgment, truly laborious task, when it is carried out properly, and not everyone can be so tireless in such labours, or have such stubborn patience of mind, as Father Morinus. May God grant that these polyglot Bibles appear at last, even if late, and at least carefully compiled. As for my book, I give you immeasurable thanks for the titles of the chapters and the marking of the verses with which you have adorned it. Be assured that I shall remain bound to you for ever by so many and so great kindnesses; I desire only this one thing more: that when the Samaritan Pentateuch, printed with your Latin version, whether added to the Bibles or published on its own, has come out, you will not disdain to enrich my little museum, such as it is, with a single printed copy, to be kept by me as a precious treasure in memory of you and as a monument to so great a usefulness to the republic of letters. Meanwhile, when I return to Rome, where I have left my books and all my other possessions, I shall send you a list of the foreign volumes that I have there; so that if any of them please you for a new occasion of study, once other business or delays have been dealt with, or a release has been obtained, you may let me know as soon as possible, and whatever you ask for I shall have sent on to you at Paris as quickly as I can. Farewell for now, and love me as you always do.

units.la: Cajetæ, viij Idus Augusti MDCXXXVII.
units.tr: Cajetae, 6 August 1637.

units.la: EPIST. LIII.
units.tr: Letter LIII.

units.la: R. Goezaldus J. Morino. Aulici Romani urgent, ut novam Libri sui de la Grandeur, &c Editionem procudat cum castigationibus, quas illi præscribunt de Congregatione Oratorii nonnulla.
units.tr: R. Goezaldus to J. Morinus. Roman courtiers urge him to bring out a new edition of his book de la Grandeur, etc., with the corrections they prescribe, concerning some matters of the Congregation of the Oratory.

units.la: Au Reverend Pere Jean Morin, Assistant Reverendissime P. General de la Congregation de l'Oratoire de Jesus Christ nostre Seigneur.
units.tr: To the Reverend Father Jean Morin, Most Reverend Assistant to the Father General of the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus Christ our Lord.

units.la: Mon R. Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: LA Grace de Jesus vous soit donnée pour humble salut. Il y a quelque temps, que je receus la vostre du 16 Juin, avec ce qu'aviez appris de Mr. Mainard, sur ce que je vous prie de scavoir de Berengarius. J'en ay donné copie à cet honneste homme qui me l'avoit demandé, il est fort content, & vous remercie infiniment, & moy aussi tres particulierement, comme aussi nous vous remercions aussi tous tres affectieusement de la décharge des frais des Deputations & Assemblées Generales. J'ay salué de vostre part Monseigneur Suarez Evesqve de Vaison, qvi en a receu contentement, & m'a prié de vous rendre le salut avec multiplication, il m'a encore mis sur vo-stre livre Francois, demandant si vous n'aviey point fait faire cette seconde impression avec ces corrections qv'il vous avoit conse illées, & me reitera ce qv'il m'avoit dit autrefois, comme Monseigneur le Cardinal Barberin luy aiant commande de voir vostre livre mesme pour satisfaire au Pape, qvi en estoit un peu esmeu à cause de son Baptistaire de St. Jean de Latran ; il l'avoit tenu long temps jusqves à ce qve la memoire s'en escoulast, & ainsi le laissa comme cela sans en faire son rapport, sinon qv'il vous escrivoit comme il fit des ce temps là, & fit scavoir vostre reponse à Monseigneur le Cardinal Barberin, comme esties disponsé{a} corriger & changer ce qv'on desiroit, & ainsi on n'y pensa plus. Je l'ay remercie derechef de ce procedé qvi ce semble estoit le meilleur, parce que depuis on n'en a plus parlé. J'envoiay ausfi à Cajette pres de Naples vostre lettre au Seigneur Pietro della Vallé, il ne m'a point encore fait de reponse, il y a 18 mois qv'il est là à une maison qv'il y a, Mr. Golstenius est encore à Malthes avec ce Seigneur Alleman frere du Landgrave de Hesse, qvi s'estoit converti ici, & qve le Pape fit Chevalier & grand Croix de Malthe, & on croit qv'il le veut faire grand Prieur d'Allemagne, Mr. Golstenius avoit contribué à son institution pour la conversion. C'est pourqvoy Mr. le C. Barberin l'envoia avec luy. J'aurois remercié Mr. le C. Barberin de vous avoir escrit & témoigne l'estime que faites de ce bonheur; mais je ne luy ay point parlé depuis, tout le temps pos-sé on a fait fort peu d'affaires à cause de la maladie du Pape, leqvel se porte bien à present, graces à nostre Seigneur, & on croit qv'il paroistra en public le jour de la transfiguration à la Chapelle de sa creation. Il y a 2 jours, qve je receus la voftre du 29 du mefme Juin (noftre Courrier a tardé de huit jours à caufe des bruits de Contagion de Lyon, les Genevoisnes ne l'aiant pas voulu laiffer paffer, & a esté contraint d'envoier fe valife par un autre Courrier) avec l'ordre pour la nomination des Deputés, & vous dites pour cela que l'affemblée se doit faire le 12 [?] de ce present mois d'Aoust à noftre Dame de Grace, & nos lettres d'ici pour ce pays là ne peuvent partir de Rome, finon le 9 [?] dudit perfent [?] mois par le Courier d'Avignon, qui emploie d'ordinaire trois semaines à aller en Avignon, d'où on ne trouve pas tous les jours commodité d'envoier à noftre Dame de Graffe, tellement qu'il y faut souvent une autre semaine, au lieu de 4 semaines nous n'aurons qve qvatre jours, neantemoins j'ay affemble nos Peres pour leurs declarer voftre volonté, outre l'excufe de nommer fur l'impossibilité d'en envoier les billets à temps. Ils vous prient tous de ne nous comprendre pas mefme en ces chofes, veu que cela eft inutile, disent ils ; quand mesme on auroit receu les ordres y a cinq semaines: ce qui estoit necessaire pour faire tenir à temps les billets ; car nous ne connoissons pas les sujets de delà, & ne pourrions faire aucunement nomination raisonnable sinon par hazard. Il y a trois ans, que nous n'avions personne qui connust ceux de Provence, ausquels vous nous liez, sinonle Pere Mainier, & Mr. Vaché, qui sont deux tresmauvais juges en semblables affaires, & qui feroi-ent toujours estre les plus aucoles[?] comme eux, comme ils faisoient pour ceux, qu'ils desiroient faire venir en cette residence ; ils ajoutent encore, que ceux de cette residence ne peuvent jamais avoit voix passive en ces deputations la, & que les Deputées de Provence ne peuvent point representer en l'Assemblée les besoins de cette residence, & des particuliers d'icelle,&diverses autres choses,qu'ils alleguent. Il y a tois[?] ans,que nous receumes pareillement semblable ordre tout en mesme temps, scavoir le dernier jour de Juillet & nos billets arriverent trois semaines après la deputation faite.
units.tr: May the grace of Jesus be given to you for humble salvation. Some time ago I received yours of 16 June, together with what you had learned from Mr. Mainard about what I asked you to find out from Berengarius. I have given a copy to that honest man who had asked for it. He is very pleased and thanks you infinitely, and so do I, very particularly. We also all thank you most affectionately for the release from the costs of the Deputations and General Assemblies. I greeted Monseigneur Suarez, Bishop of Vaison, on your behalf, and he was pleased by it and asked me to return your greeting with interest. He again put your French book before me and asked whether you had not had this second impression made with the corrections he had suggested to you. He repeated what he had told me before: Monseigneur Cardinal Barberini, having ordered him to examine your book itself in order to satisfy the Pope, who was somewhat disturbed by it because of his Baptistery of St John Lateran, kept it for a long time until the memory of it faded. So he left it as it was, without making his report, except that he wrote to you as he did at that time and let Monseigneur Cardinal Barberini know your reply, that you were ready to correct and change whatever was wanted. And so no one thought about it any more. I thanked him again for this course, which seemed the better one, since no one has spoken of the matter since. I also sent your letter to Signor Pietro della Valle at Gaeta near Naples. He has not yet replied to me; he has been at a house he has there for eighteen months. Mr. Golstenius is still at Malta with that German lord, the brother of the Landgrave of Hesse, who was converted here and whom the Pope made a Knight and Grand Cross of Malta. It is believed the Pope wants to make him Grand Prior of Germany. Mr. Golstenius had contributed to his instruction for the conversion, and that is why Mr. Cardinal Barberini sent him with him. I would have thanked Mr. Cardinal Barberini for having written to you and for showing the esteem you have for this good fortune, but I have not spoken to him since. All this time very little business has been done because of the Pope's illness. He is well now, thanks be to our Lord, and it is believed he will appear in public on the feast of the Transfiguration at the chapel of his creation. Two days ago I received yours of 29 June of the same year. Our courier was delayed eight days by rumours of contagion from Lyon, the Genevans not having allowed it to pass, and he was forced to send his bag by another courier. Yours enclosed the order for the nomination of the Deputies, and you say that the assembly must be held on the 12th [?] of this present month of August at Notre Dame de Grace. Our letters from here for that country cannot leave Rome before the 9th [?] of the said month, by the Avignon courier, who ordinarily takes three weeks to reach Avignon. From there one does not find a convenient way to send to Notre Dame de Grasse every day, so that often another week is needed. Instead of four weeks we will have only four days. Nevertheless I have assembled our Fathers to declare your wish to them, along with the excuse that it is impossible to nominate when the tickets cannot be sent in time. They all beg you not to include us even in these matters, since it is useless, they say, even if the orders had been received five weeks ago, which was necessary for the tickets to arrive in time. For we do not know the men over there, and could make no reasonable nomination except by chance. Three years ago we had no one who knew those of Provence, to whom you tie us, except Father Mainier and Mr. Vaché, who are two very poor judges in such affairs and would always want the most foolish to be chosen, as they did for those they wished to bring to this residence. They add that those of this residence can never have a passive vote in these deputations, that the Deputies of Provence cannot represent in the Assembly the needs of this residence and of its individual members, and various other things they allege. Three years ago we likewise received a similar order all at the same time, namely on the last day of July, and our tickets arrived three weeks after the deputation had been made.

units.la: II suffit que le R. P. General donne charge à un de ses Assistants de pourvoir aux be-soins de cette resid[?]ence, je vous supplie tres humblement de nous y assister, & re-presenter nos affaires en ladite prochai-ne assemblée, & particulierement vous n'oblires pas de supplier pour moy no-stre R. P. General d'envoir un autre Su-perieur pour cente[?] residence, ou en no-mer un autre de ceux, qui sont ici avec nous, si tant est que les affaires de la Con-gregation ne permettent pas, qu'on en envoie un de France pour cela, & qui se-roit neantmoins tres-necessaire pour le bien & honneur de la Congregation, d'avoir ici un homme docte, & ver-tueux, & & exemplaire, & qui peust traiter avec les grands. Croyez moy que le R. P. Bertin y estoit beaucoup plus utile, qu'on ne comprend pas par delà, & une infinité de personnes l'ont regrette & le regrettent encore, & il servoit gradement la Congregation, & un grand nombre de personnes de divers- ses qualitez & ordres, ce qui donnoit grande estime à la Congregation laquelle se trouvez pas vous priver en France du R. P. Bertin, vous en avez d'antres, qui sont doctes, & ne prechent pas, pourrorient[?] ici en faisant les mesmes estudes, qu'ils font en France, servir beaucoup la congregation, nous avons une de nos six places vacantes, mais je ne vous presseray pas beaucoup de la replir, si ce n'est d'un Superieur, ou d'un qui se vouluft stiler à la sollicitation de affaires, car je n'ay secours de personne & neantmoins je fais peu de chose, & vas toujours en affoiblissant, & diminuant de veue, de force, desante, & autres qualitez requises; & ainsi il y a esperance, qu'il faudra bientost suir, ce sera quand il plaira Dieu. Sur tout je vous supplie de faire en sorte, que je sois[?] descharge de la superiorité, dont je ne fais aucunes fonctions, qui emportent le nom en enstant du texte incapable; il est probable encore, que ces Mefsieurs de la Congregation de St. Loüis n'auront pas de crainte & combrage d'un autre, comme ils ont eu de moy, ils croyoient qvelqvefois qve tous les pas qve je faisois chez les Ambassadeurs estoient pour traitter contre leur authorite, & neantmoins je ne fais pas mesme les visites necessaires de complimens, & qvand en six mois une fois il m'en faut faire qvelqv'une, je tremple & n'a y mot àdire, & je ne parle qve qvand j'ay qvelqve affaire à recommander, ou qvelqve lettre à rendre, il me semble[?] qve le P. Loüis Simian seroit le plus propre pour estre Superieur. Il est zelé pour l'observance des reglemens, mais il seroit fort à desirer, qve vous en envoiassitès un de France, qvi fust docte pour correspondre aux occasions & rencontres particulieres, chose qvi nous manqve à tous au prejudice de l'estime, qv'avoit acqvise autrefois la Congregation en cette ville. Je prie Dieu de nous donner ce qvi sera plus à la glorie, & avons tous les contentemens qve vous desire celuy, qvi desire demeurer à jamais en Jesus & Ma-rie apres vous avoir presenté nos hum-bles recommandations de tous à vos SS. Prieres & Sacrifices, & par vostre moyen au R. P. General, & aux R. R. P. P. Bour-going & d'Orron, & à tous de la maison.
units.tr: It is enough that the Reverend Father General commission one of his Assistants to provide for the needs of this residence. I most humbly beg you to assist us there and to represent our affairs at the said next assembly. In particular, do not forget to beg our Reverend Father General for me to send another Superior to this residence, or to name one of those who are here with us, if the affairs of the Congregation do not allow one to be sent from France for this purpose. Yet it would be very necessary for the good and honour of the Congregation to have here a learned, virtuous and exemplary man who can deal with the great. Believe me, Reverend Father Bertin was much more useful here than is understood over there. Countless people have regretted him and still regret him; he served the Congregation greatly, and a large number of persons of various ranks and orders, which gave the Congregation great esteem. Do not deprive yourselves in France of Father Bertin; you have others who are learned and do not preach, and who could serve the Congregation greatly by pursuing here the same studies they pursue in France. We have one of our six places vacant, but I will not press you much to fill it, unless with a Superior, or with someone who would apply himself to the business of affairs, for I have no help from anyone. Yet I do little, and I keep weakening and losing sight, strength, health and the other requisite qualities, so there is hope that I must soon flee, which will be when God pleases. Above all I beg you to see to it that I am discharged from the superiority, in which I perform none of the functions that the name implies, being in the sense of the text incapable. It is also probable that these gentlemen of the Congregation of St. Louis will not have the fear and anxiety of another as they have had of me. They sometimes believed that every step I took among the Ambassadors was to negotiate against their authority, and yet I do not even make the necessary courtesy visits. When once in six months I have to make one, I tremble and have nothing to say, and I speak only when I have some business to recommend or some letter to deliver. It seems to me Father Louis Simian would be the most suitable to be Superior. He is zealous for the observance of the rules, but it would be much to be desired that you send one from France who is learned, to correspond on particular occasions and encounters, something we all lack, to the prejudice of the esteem the Congregation once acquired in this city. I pray God to give us what will be most to His glory, and may you have all the contentment you desire. I, who desire to remain forever in Jesus and Mary, after presenting to your holy prayers and sacrifices our humble recommendations from all of us, and through you to the Reverend Father General, to the Reverend Fathers Bourgoing and d'Orron, and to all of the house.

units.la: Mon R. Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: A Rome, ce pr. d'Aoust 1637.
units.tr: At Rome, the first of August 1637.

units.la: Vostre tres-humble & tres obeissant Servi-teur René Goezald, P. de l'Orat. de Jesu.
units.tr: Your very humble and very obedient servant, René Goezald, priest of the Oratory of Jesus.

units.la: Le R. Pere Esprit, partit d'ici par mer pour Aix des le pr. de Juin, & nous n'a-vons encore aucunes nouvelles, s'il est arrivé ou non, jugés quel temps il faut pour avoir lettres de ce pays là. Nous les avons bien plutost de Paris.
units.tr: The Reverend Father Esprit left here by sea for Aix at the beginning of June, and we still have no news of whether he has arrived or not. Judge how long it takes to get letters from that country. We receive them much sooner from Paris.

units.la: EPIST. LIV.
units.tr: EPIST. LIV.

units.la: J. Morinus Patr. Junio. Exemplaris Græ-ci 7o[?] Interpretum, cujus specimen de-derat Junius, judicium suum affert, simulque Criticen prolixam præci-puapuarum Editionum Græcarum tàm veterum quàm recentiorum.
units.tr: J. Morinus to Junius. Concerning the copy of the Greek Septuagint, of which Junius had sent a specimen, he gives his judgment, and at the same time a lengthy criticism of the principal Greek editions, both older and more recent.

units.la: Clarissimo & Eruditissimo Viro Patr. Junio Ioan. Morinus.
units.tr: To the most illustrious and learned man, Patricius Junius, from Joannes Morinus.

units.la: JAm fere quadrimestre elapsum est, cùm Exemplar Libri Job. Londini Græcè editum accepi à R. Patre Philippo, ad me tuo nomine missum, titulum præ se fert speciosum admodum, & omnibus, ut opinor, divinorum Oraculorum amantibus εὐπαραδέκτον[?], juxta scilicet verum ac germanum 7o Seniorum interpretationem ex venerando Bibliothecæ Regiæ MS. codice & totius orbis antiquissimo; pridie quam longum iter aggrederer, in quo integrum trimestre consumpsi, redditum est mihi exemplar illud cum R. P. Philippi litteris. Itaque temporis angustia oppressus, nullam tum potuì istius editionis comparationem instituere, sed cùm primum Lutetiam redii, mihique per otium licuit, exemplar istud lustravi, & cum Romana Editione, nonnullisque aliis Textibus aliquot in capitulis contuli. Anteqvam id, quod de isto exemplari sentio, tibi aperiam, illius ad me missi gratias agam tibi non leves: rem pergratam sane mihi fecisti, quamque scire & experiri plu-rimum avebam, ideo me tibi non parum devinctum fateor. Si officiis & obse-quiis erga te meis par tibi referre, amicitiamque tuam, quae mihi charissima est, promereri possum, ea praestare quàm libentissime & pro viribus adnitar. Quod ad rem attinet, pedibus manibusque in tuam eo sententiam, Editionem illam veram esse & germanam 70 Interp. interpretationem: An sit totius orbis antiquissimus Codex ille, ex quo Jobi Editio expressa est, definire difficile, ne diem ἀδύνατον[?]. Litterarum figura, quâ Codex ille Regius exaratus est, ut ex earum specimine à te exscripto conjicio, arguit sane venerandam antiquitatem, & annos mille ducentos superantem. Est Parisiis in Bibliotheca Fratrum Puteanorum antiquissimus Epistolarum Sancti Pauli Codex majoribus litteris Graece & Latine descriptus, & Versio & Character Sancti Hieronymi ætatem non potest non æquare; at Character Characteri adeo similis est, ut eadem manu uterqve merito judicari possit exaratus.
units.tr: It is now nearly four months since I received from Father Philip a copy of the Book of Job, published in Greek at London, which was sent to me in your name. Its title is very striking and, I think, readily acceptable to all lovers of the divine oracles: according, that is, to the true and genuine translation of the Seventy Elders, taken from the venerable manuscript of the Royal Library, the most ancient codex in the whole world. On the day before I set out on a long journey, which took me a full three months, that copy was returned to me with a letter from Father Philip. So, pressed for time, I could make no comparison of this edition then. But as soon as I returned to Paris and had some leisure, I examined the copy, compared it with the Roman edition and some other texts in several chapters. Before I tell you what I think of this copy, I must thank you, and not slightly, for sending it. You have done me a most welcome favour, since I was very eager to know and to see it, and I confess I am much indebted to you. If I can repay you with services and attentions of my own, and deserve the friendship that is so dear to me, I will strive to do so as gladly as I can, to the best of my powers. As for the matter itself, I agree with you wholeheartedly that that edition is the true and genuine translation of the Seventy. Whether that codex from which the Job edition was printed is the most ancient in the whole world, it is hard to determine, not to say impossible. The form of the letters in which that royal codex is written, as I gather from the specimen you copied out, certainly argues for a venerable antiquity, exceeding twelve hundred years. In Paris, in the library of the Puteani brothers, there is a very ancient codex of the Epistles of St Paul, written in large letters in Greek and Latin. Its version and script cannot be less old than St Jerome's time, and yet that script is so like this one that both could fairly be judged to have been written by the same hand.

units.la: Sunt forsan tibi alia tam reconditæ antiquitatis argumenta, quæ Characteri juncta, tam admirandæ antiquitatis venerationem augeant & tueantur, quibus ego, te judice, facile assentiar.
units.tr: Perhaps you have other arguments of such recondite antiquity which, joined to the script, increase and support the reverence due to such admirable age. On your judgement I would readily assent to them.
