units.la: Cum autem dixi Editionem illam Jobi veram esse, & germanam 70 Seniorum interpretationem; non statim colligi velim ὁλόκληρον [?] integritatem esse illi tribuendam, ita ut nihil sit in ea παρεγγεγραμμένον [?]: quis adeo istarum rerum rudis est, aut fatuè superstitiosus, ut tam insanam opinionem de quo libuerit Codice Græco, Hebræo, Latino in animum suum inducat? Vera igitur & germana est 70 interpretatio, hoc est, non adulterina ne quidem interpolata, sed ea ipsa quam ex Hebraico Seniores illi transtulerunt.
units.tr: But when I said that that edition of Job is the true and genuine translation of the Seventy Elders, I do not want it to be inferred at once that it must be credited with complete integrity, so that nothing in it is written in the margin. Who is so ignorant of these matters, or so foolishly superstitious, as to form such an insane opinion of any Greek, Hebrew or Latin codex whatever? The Septuagint translation is therefore true and genuine: that is, not counterfeit, not even interpolated, but the very translation those Elders made from the Hebrew.

units.la: Verùm nihil prohibet, in ea nævos esse & mendas illapsas, & ex Scriptoris vitio ,& exemplaris, à quo est olim Codex ille exscriptus. De hac re plurimum conqueritur ipse Origenes Tractatu octavo in Math. Multam, inquit, differentiam inter exemplaria invenimus, sive per negligentiam scribentium, sive ex temeritate quorundam, sive propter eos, qui negligunt emendare Scripturas, vel propter eos, qui quod ipsis videtur in emendationibus, vel adjiciunt, vel subducunt, &c. Quoties hanc querelam ciet Sanctus Hieronymus, & ei for-san nimium indulget; tu ipse judex esto, qui in eo studiorum genere sæpe & diligenter versatus es. Antiqui Novi Testamenti Codices à se invicem sæpe verbis, & nonnunquam sensu discrepant, germani tamen censentur, quidni pronunciabitur idem de veteris Testamenti Codicibus, cùm præsertim etiam nunc id experientia testetur? Antiqui autem istius Codicis sinceritatem non tantum ex Jobi Textu colligo, sed etiam ex aliis, quæ Codex ille genuinus Septuaginta interpr. Editioni habet conformia, ut Exodi Capita 36, 37, 38 & 39. & Hieremiæ Prophetæ à Cap. 25. ad Libri finem: eadem illa sinceritas duobus aliis argumentis, qvæ latissime sese diffundunt, potissimum comprobari potest, si ea scilicet qvæ Asteriscis Origenem antiqvi Patres antiqvæ Editioni addidisse scribunt, ab eo Textu absint; ea verò, qvæ Obelo notavit Procopius; multa qvoqve Sanctus Hieronymus Commentariis in majoresqve & minores Prophetas. Vix ego dubito, qvin ea fere omnia, qvæ Asterisco fuerunt olim notata, absint à codice tuo, adsint autem qvæ Obelo. Hæc periclitantem plurimum adjuvabit Josuæ Editio à Viro Eruditissimo Masio instaurata: antiqvissimum enim Codicem Syrum nactus fuerat ex Græco Hexaplorum Origenis, qvæ Eusebius Cæsariensis manu sua correxerat, verbum è verbo Syre ante annos mille redditum, Asteriscis, Obeliscis, Lemniscis & Hypolemniscis Origenianis instructum. Videbis si ubiqve pura est, ut facile credo, ea fere omnia, qvæ Asterisco apud eum notantur, à Codice tuo abesse ; qvæ vero Obelo, adesse; quo saepius aderunt illa, haec vero aberunt, eo ἀκιβδηλίας[?] frequentiora erunt τεκμήρια: his duobus argumentis tertium accedit, textus cum testimoniis, quae antiquissimi Patres referunt, comparatio. In exercitationibus nostris Biblicis haec & similia de Editionis Romanae textu frequentissime periclitati sumus, fereque semper deprehendimus, quae Asterisco notata sunt, abesse; quae Obelo, adesse; quae textus 70 Seniorum ἀκιβδήλα[?], qualis ante Origenianarum notarum cum textu confusionem in Ecclesia legebatur, certissima sunt argumenta. Non enim arbitror, te ejusmodi comparationis peritum, eorum sententiae accedere, qui illius prorsus rudes 70 Interpretum editionem eo sinceriorem judicant, quo propius abest à textu Judaeorum Neoterico: Codicem enim tuum veram & germanam 70 Interpretum Editionem inscribis, nec immerito, verum à Judaico Neoterico quantis distat parasangis? Nec istae differentiae Neotericae sunt: easdem depre-hendit hendit Origenes; quæ tantæ discordiæ causa fuerit, non est hujus loci disputare. Ex iis, quæ diximus, oritur difficultas, quæ cuidam forsan videbitur non levis. Si meâ sententiâ Romana Editio germana est 70 Interpretum, unde fit, ut à tuo Codice tantopere dissideat? Primum nego tantum esse dissidium, ut ideo jure non possit utraque dici germana; maximum, inquis, dissidium reperitur in libris Judic. & Job. Jobi multa capita, v. g. sex priora, 24, 30 & 36, & tria posteriora, cum Editione Romana contuli. Confer antiquum aliquem N. T. Codicem Græcum cum excuso Textu, & differentias deprehendes plures & majoris momenti; hoc expertus dico. De illo antiquissimo Evangeliorum & Actuum Codice Cantabrigensi verba non facio, immaniter enim ab excuso distat, sed de quovis alio Manuscripto, qui multo propius ad excusum accedat; imo comparentur duo quilibet antiqui Novi Testamenti Manuscripti, & occurrent tibi varietates vix minus numerosiores. Num ideo alteruter aut neuter Manuscriptus erit N. T. germanus textus, Secundo, Dico istius varietatis triplicem esse causam; primam attigit supra Origenes, quæ aliis omnibus Libris communis est, secundam reddit S. Hieronymus præfat. in Paralip. quæ 70 Interpretes potissimum spectat. Triplex fuit 70 Interpretum correctio. Origeniana, Hesychiana, & Luciana; hinc Codicum istius Interp. triplex varietas. Hesychiana videtur tua Editio: Audio enim Alexandriæ olim descriptum fuisse Codicem tuum. Masio Lucianus videtur ille Codex, ex quo Editio Romana expressa est, mihi vero potissimum Origenianus: Lucianus, ut constat ex Eusebio & Suida in verbo Lucianus, interpretationem Ecclesiasticam, ubi vitiatam esse illi constabat, ad Hebræi Textus normam castigavit; Origenes vero purum putum 70 Interpretum textum repræsentare fategit; ubi autem ab Hebræo variabat, id Asteriscis vel Obelis notavi; ubi vero Codices 70 à se invicem, Lemniscis Hypolemniscis: Sæpissime autem deprehendes, ubi Patres & Scholiastæ monent aliquid esse de Textu 70, sic haberi in Editione R. licet ab Hebræo Textus ille dissentiat. De Asteriscis verba non facio, qui sunt notæ verborum & sententiarum ad repræsentandum Textum Hebræum, ubi Editione Ecclesiastica amplior erat de industria additarum. Sæpissime dico, aliquando enim aliter deprehenditur. Hinc fit sæpius, cùm dif-fert in re tantilli momenti ab Editione R. Codex tuus cum Hebræo Textu consentiat. Alia causa, quamobrem Origenianam illam Editionem existimem aut potissimum Origenianam, est quod non tantum Asiæ majoris Ecclesiæ Codices Origenianos ampelxæ sint, sed Græciæ, Constantinopoleωs[?], Asiæ quoque minoris & vicinarum Regionum, Romæ quoque & Italiæ Magnates, & Bibliothecæ celebres Origenis hexapla describi, ut omnium Editionum correctiss-ima, indeque Editionem 70 exscribi magnopere curabant, ut S. Hieronymus testatur, apparetque ex Authorum, qui in illis Regionibus vixerunt, commentariis, qui omnes Origenis hexapla maxime commendant.
units.tr: Nevertheless, nothing prevents blemishes and errors from having slipped into it, through the fault of the writer and of the exemplar from which that codex was once copied. Origen himself complains greatly about this in his eighth Tractate on Matthew: We find a great deal of difference among the copies, whether through the carelessness of the scribes, or the rashness of certain people, or because of those who neglect to correct the Scriptures, or of those who add or remove in their corrections what seems right to them, and so on (Math.). St Jerome raises this complaint often, and perhaps indulges in it too much. You yourself be the judge, since you have often and diligently worked in this field of study. Ancient codices of the New Testament often differ from one another in words and sometimes in sense, yet they are considered genuine. Why should the same not be said of the codices of the Old Testament, especially since experience even now bears witness to it? I infer the sincerity of that ancient codex not only from its text of Job, but also from other places where it agrees with the Septuagint edition, such as chapters 36, 37, 38 and 39 of Exodus, and of the prophet Jeremiah from chapter 25 to the end of the book. That same sincerity can be confirmed especially by two other arguments, which spread very widely: namely, if the things that the ancient Fathers write Origen added to the old edition under asterisks are absent from that text, and if the things Procopius marked with an obelus are present; and St Jerome, in his commentaries on the greater and lesser prophets, marks many things as well. I scarcely doubt that almost all the things once marked with an asterisk are absent from your codex, and those marked with an obelus are present. In this matter the edition of Joshua restored by the very learned Masius will greatly help. For he had obtained a most ancient Syriac codex, made from the Greek Hexapla of Origen, which Eusebius of Caesarea had corrected by his own hand, rendered word for word into Syriac more than a thousand years ago, and furnished with Origen's asterisks, obeli, lemnisci and hypolemnisci. You will see, if it is everywhere pure, as I readily believe, that almost all the things marked with an asterisk in it are absent from your codex, and those marked with an obelus are present. And the more often those are present and these absent, the more frequent will be the proofs of genuineness [ἀκιβδηλίας]. To these two arguments a third is added: the comparison of the text with the testimonies that the most ancient Fathers report. In our Biblical exercises we have very often tested these and similar points against the text of the Roman edition, and we have almost always found that what is marked with an asterisk is absent, and what is marked with an obelus is present. Those things in the text of the Seventy which were read in the Church before the Origenian marks were confused with the text are most certain arguments [ἀκίβδηλα]. For I do not think you, skilled in such comparison, would side with those who, quite ignorant of this, judge the edition of the Seventy Interpreters to be the more sincere the nearer it stands to the present Jewish text. You call your codex the true and genuine edition of the Seventy Interpreters, and not undeservedly. But how many parasangs does it stand from the modern Jewish text? Nor are these differences modern: Origen detected the same ones. What was the cause of such great discord is not for this place to discuss. From what we have said there arises a difficulty which may seem to some not slight. If in my opinion the Roman edition is the genuine edition of the Seventy Interpreters, how does it come about that it differs so much from your codex? First, I deny that the disagreement is so great that for this reason neither can rightly be called genuine. You say the greatest disagreement is found in the books of Judges and Job. I have compared many chapters of Job with the Roman edition: the first six, 24, 30 and 36, and the last three. Compare any ancient Greek codex of the New Testament with the printed text, and you will find more numerous and weightier differences; I say this from experience. I am not speaking of that most ancient Cambridge codex of the Gospels and Acts, for it differs enormously from the printed text, but of any other manuscript that comes much closer to it. Indeed, compare any two ancient manuscripts of the New Testament and you will meet variations scarcely less numerous. Is either manuscript, or neither, therefore not a genuine text of the New Testament? Secondly, I say that this variety has a threefold cause. The first Origen has already touched on, and it is common to all the books. The second St Jerome gives in his preface to Paralipomenon, and it especially concerns the Seventy Interpreters. The translation of the Seventy underwent a threefold correction: Origenian, Hesychian and Lucianic; hence a threefold variety among the codices of this translation. Your edition seems to be Hesychian, for I hear that your codex was once copied at Alexandria. Masius thinks that the codex from which the Roman edition was printed is Lucianic, but to me it seems mainly Origenian. Lucian, as Eusebius and Suidas attest in the entry on Lucian, corrected the ecclesiastical translation, where it was known to be corrupt, to the norm of the Hebrew text. Origen, however, wished to present the pure text of the Seventy Interpreters: where it varied from the Hebrew he marked the difference with asterisks or obeli, and where the codices of the Seventy differed among themselves, with lemnisci and hypolemnisci. I am not speaking of asterisks, which are signs of words and sentences added deliberately to represent the Hebrew text, where things were added on purpose to the ecclesiastical edition, which was fuller. Very often, I say, you will find that where the Fathers and scholiasts note that something stands in the text of the Seventy, it is so given in the Roman edition, although that text differs from the Hebrew. Sometimes, however, it is found otherwise. Hence it often happens that when your codex differs from the Roman edition in a matter of such small weight, it agrees with the Hebrew text. Another reason why I think that Origenian edition, or mainly Origenian, is this: not only did the Origenian codices prevail in the greater churches of Asia, but in Greece, Constantinople, Lesser Asia and the neighbouring regions, and at Rome and in Italy the great men and famous libraries had Origen's Hexapla copied as the most correct of all editions, and they took great care to copy the Seventy from it, as St Jerome testifies. This appears from the commentaries of the authors who lived in those regions, all of whom greatly commend Origen's Hexapla.

units.la: Tertia varietatis causa est, quod multi antiquitus, si quid in Editione Ecclesiastica varium deprehendebant, nescio qua textus Hebraici & o-stentandae πολυμαθείας ξηροκακοζηλία, illud statim ex Aquilæ aut Theodotionis Editione corrigebant, quis enim tum temporis ex Hebræo textu emendationem illam praestare potuisset? Ex his causis fit, ut Codices 70 Interpretum etiam correctissimi inter se nonnihil varient, etiam ubi Amanuensium negligentia aut ignorantia nulla est vel alteratio commissa: Correctissimos dico, ne existimes hic de mixtis illis Editionibus me verba facere, quales sunt Complutensis, Antverpiensis, Francofurtensis, & aliæ. Illæ enim non sunt ullo modo sincerae 70 Editiones, sed farrago quaedam ex Editione 70 Seniorum, & interpretatione Theodotionis collecta.
units.tr: A third cause of variation is this. In former times, whenever they found something varying in the ecclesiastical edition, many people, from a certain dry and ill-tempered zeal for showing off learning [πολυμαθείας ξηροκακοζηλία] and without any knowledge of the Hebrew text, at once corrected it from the edition of Aquila or Theodotion. For who in that age could have made that correction from the Hebrew text? So it happens that even the most correct manuscripts of the Seventy differ somewhat among themselves, even where no mistake or alteration by copyists has been made. I say "most correct" so that you do not think I am speaking here of those mixed editions, such as the Complutensian, the Antwerp, the Frankfurt and others. Those are in no way pure editions of the Seventy, but a hodgepodge collected from the edition of the Seventy Elders and the version of Theodotion.

units.la: Interrogabor forsan hoc dato, utramque illam Editionem germanam 70 Seniorum interpretationem, utra purior, & ab omni menda defæcatior? Romanam præstare ratio sana & experientia suadere videntur. Ratio Romana est ex Origeniana exscripta, quæ semper habita est sincerissima, deinde Vaticani exemplaris, ex quo expressa est Romana, Character, ut eam describunt, qui Editioni præfuerunt, antiquitatem arguere mihi videtur nonnihil reconditiorem quàm quæ tuo possit exemplari convenire.
units.tr: Perhaps, granting this, you will ask me which of those two editions is the genuine translation of the Seventy, and which is purer and freer from every blemish. Reason and experience seem to me to show that the Roman edition is better. The Roman edition is copied from the Origenian text, which has always been regarded as the purest. Moreover, the character of the Vatican exemplar, from which the Roman edition was printed, as those who supervised the edition describe it, seems to me to point to a somewhat more remote antiquity than could agree with your copy.

units.la: Experientia, extat Olympiodori catena in Job. latinitate donata; est etiam apud nos Græcum illius Exemplar, non equidem uncialibus litteris, sed pulcherrime in charta vitulina descriptum.
units.tr: As for experience: there exists the catena of Olympiodorus on Job, given a Latin dress. We also have a Greek copy of it, not indeed in uncial letters, but very beautifully written on calfskin parchment.

units.la: Scriptio quintum aut sextum ante hoc sæculum indigitare videtur.
units.tr: The writing seems to point to the fifth or sixth century before this age.

units.la: Romanæ Editionis textus cum isto fere semper convenit, & fere ubi dissentit, cum tuo convenit; sed ut plurimum dissensionis causa est, quod Textus tuus & catenæ aliquam dictionem sibi ex Hebræo adsciscunt. Idem facile deprehendetur ex Latina istius Catenæ[?] interpretatione. Paucisima sunt, in quibus Textus Jobi, qui in catena ista integer exhibetur, ab utroque exemplari dissentiat. His addi possunt vetusta illa exemplaria, cum quibus collata est Editio Romana; quorum unum vetustissimum illud, majoribusque literis descriptum, cum eo, de quo Editio illa expressa est, per omnia conveniebat. Aldina Editio, ipsa quoque germana 70 Seniorum interpretatio, atque ex antiquis Codicibus exscripta saepius multo (id in nonnullis capitibus periclitatus sum) cum Editione Romana Jobi convenit, quam interpretatio a te edita, licet nonnunquam ab utraque discedat. Utra sincerior ex aliorum Librorum collatione certius dijudicaretur, de quibus plura extant argumenta eorum, quae juxta Septuaginta adesse debent aut abesse. Non praeteribo eorum, quae notat Origenes in [illegible, ~9 letters]-, quod edidisti, haberi in 70 textu, non autem in Hebraico unum abesse ab Editione Romana, tuae vero adesse cum aliqua tamen varietate; hoc scilicet ωἐλθὼν τὴν γῆν [?] ἐμαρτύρησας ἐν αὐτῇ. Sed R. Editioni consentit catena, necnon ipse Origenes in Commentario, ut Aldinam Editionem omittam, cæterosque libros antiqvos, qvorum ope Editio R. adornata est. Forsan variarunt exemplaria, forsan ab aliqvo deleta sunt, eo qvod in Hebraico non legerentur statim, qvæ repetuntur. In fine Jobi notat Origenes, multa legi apud 70; qvæ apud Hebræos non leguntur. Sic est in utraqve Editione ; verum tua versiculos tres superaddit, qvæ omittit Romana. At Romanæ consentiunt Catenæ textus, Origenis Commentarii, Aldina & alii Libri antiqvi, ipsaqve ratio: continet enim additio illa inane & in-sulsum glossema. Discrimen omnium, qvæ deprehendi, maximum legitur c. 5. post v. 21. Ibi Editio tua versiculos duos exhibet qvi nullibi leguntur, nec in vetustis Rom. exemplaribus, nec in Catena Jobi, nec in Hebræo, nec in Ald; In Aldina tamen paucula qvædam verba adjiciuntur, qvæ alibi non extant; iterum ibidem post v. 22. leguntur in Editione tua quatuor versiculi, quæ R. non habet, nec habebant antiqvi R. Codices. Horum versiculorum duos habet Aldina Editio, qvi ex Hebræo depromptisunt, sed alios nec Hebræus textus exhibet, nec ullus alius, nec exhibere debuerunt, cum ejusdem rei eidem loco superfluam contineant repetitionem; itaqve nihil sunt aliud, quàm ejusdem rei ex Theodotione, aut alio interprete germano textui assuta interpretatio. Cæterarum differentiarum, quæ qvidem mihi occurrerunt, nulla est, quæ huic possit comparari; omnes sunt unius aut alterius dictionis pluresqve in primo capite, quàm alibi deprehendi. Sed harum præcipuæ iis, qvi Editioni R. præfuerunt, non fuerunt incognitæ, illas enim ex nonnullis antiqvis Manuscriptis in Scholis suis adnotarunt. At R. Editio præter antiqvos Codices catenam illam habet adversus tuam semper fere consentientem, ut prætereaм commentarios in Jobum, qvi Origeni tribuuntur. Maximi autem facienda est Catenæ autoritas, cum ipsa sit antiqua, & ex plurimis & antiquis patribus collecta: Initio cap. 38 Exodi, quædam verba habet Editio tua, quæ à Romana absunt, ut & ab Aldina, vetustisq; aliis exempl. quæ ex alia interpretatione juxta Hebræam deprompta videntur; ita enim leguntur initio cap. 37. Sunt & alia nonnulla, quæ ex Asteriscis Orig. ut & in Aldina in tuam videntur intrusa.
units.tr: The text of the Roman edition agrees almost always with this one, and where it differs it nearly always agrees with yours. But for the most part the cause of the disagreement is that your text and the catena take over some wording from the Hebrew. The same can easily be detected from the Latin translation of that catena. There are very few places in which the text of Job, which is given whole in that catena, differs from both copies. To these may be added those ancient manuscripts with which the Roman edition was collated: one of the most ancient, written in larger letters, agreed in every respect with the one from which that edition was printed. The Aldine edition, itself also a genuine translation of the Seventy and copied from ancient manuscripts (I have tested this in some chapters), agrees with the Roman edition of Job far more often than with your translation, though it sometimes departs from both. Which is the purer could be judged more certainly by comparing other books, concerning which there are many arguments as to what ought or ought not to be present according to the Seventy. I will not pass over what Origen notes in [illegible, about nine letters], which you have published: that one word is found in the Seventy text but not in the Hebrew, namely that it is absent from the Roman edition but present in yours, though with some variation; this is the Greek ἐλθὼν τὴν γῆν [?] ἐμαρτύρησας ἐν αὐτῇ. But the catena agrees with the Roman edition, and so does Origen himself in his commentary, to say nothing of the Aldine edition and the other ancient books by whose help the Roman edition was prepared. Perhaps the manuscripts varied; perhaps something was deleted by someone because the things repeated were not read at once in the Hebrew. At the end of Job, Origen notes that many things are read in the Seventy which are not read among the Hebrews. So it is in both editions; but yours adds three verses which the Roman edition omits. Yet the text of the Roman catena, Origen's commentary, the Aldine and other ancient books, and reason itself, agree with the Roman edition, for that addition contains an empty and insipid gloss. The greatest difference I have found is read in chapter 5, after verse 21. There your edition gives two verses which are read nowhere, neither in the ancient Roman manuscripts, nor in the catena on Job, nor in the Hebrew, nor in the Aldine; yet in the Aldine a few words are added which appear nowhere else. Again in the same place, after verse 22, four verses are read in your edition which the Roman edition does not have, nor did its ancient manuscripts. The Aldine edition has two of these verses, which are taken from the Hebrew; but the Hebrew text does not give the other two, nor does any other text, nor ought they to have been given, since they contain a superfluous repetition of the same matter in the same place. So they are nothing other than an interpretation of the same thing, taken from Theodotion or another genuine translator and sewn into the text. Of the other differences which have come to my notice, none is comparable to this; they are all differences of wording in one or another phrase, and more of them occur in the first chapter than elsewhere. But the chief of these were not unknown to those who supervised the Roman edition, for they noted them in their scholia from some ancient manuscripts. Moreover, the Roman edition has, besides the ancient manuscripts, that catena, which almost always agrees against your text; and also the commentaries on Job which are attributed to Origen. The authority of the catena, however, is to be valued very highly, since it is itself ancient and was collected from very many and ancient Fathers. At the beginning of chapter 38 of Exodus your edition has some words which are absent from the Roman, as also from the Aldine and other ancient copies, and which seem to have been taken from another translation made according to the Hebrew; for so they are read at the beginning of chapter 37. There are also some other things which, as in the Aldine, seem to have been inserted into your text from the asterisks of Origen.

units.la: Quod ad cap. 12. Judicum, tanta revera est differentia toto capite in verbis, ut omnino videatur alia translatio, ejusdem tamen rei, verbis enim, non sensibus differentia constat, si primum versiculum excipias. Nunc quæritur, utra 70 Seniorum interpretatio sincerior? Non est mihi antiquus Liber aut Commentarius, cujus testimonio hanc litem discernere possim. Verùm notæ R. in hoc caput nonnulla referunt ex antiquo Scholiaste, quæ eodem modo sese habent, quo Editionis tuæ textus; ea quæ refert Scholiastes ille, ex alia quam ex 70 Interpr. Editione: Neque omnino juvat Codicem tuum Aldina Editio, qvæ hoc loco Co-dici tuo fere persimilis est. Certum est enim, in hanc Editionem seu Codices, ex qvibus exscripta est, multa heteroge-nea irrepsisse, cujus irreptionis multa passim occurrunt argumenta ; nolim, Vir eruditiffime, hæc à me dicta existi-mes in tui Codicis præjudicium, multo minus contemptum. Hæc scribo, eo qvod nonnullis argumentis, qvæ brevi-ter attigi, ad id adducor : Nolim qvoq; existimes, me Editionem R. omnis men-dæ puram credere, habet suos næwos[?] hæc Editio ; qvod non diffimularunt & in Scholiis & in Præfatione, qvi eam Ro-mæ curarunt. Exempli causa, Gen. c. 5. v. 25. Ubi de annis Mathusalæ ; sic cap. 11. v. 24. ubi de Nachor, aliisqve in locis eodem capite, in qvibus tua, sicut Aldi-na multo sincerior est : Multis tamen nominibus excusari potest. Codex e-nim ille vetustissimus, ex qvo Editio ista desumpta est, ab initio Genefeωs[?], ad c. 47. plurimum mutilatus erat, ideoqve Editio R. his locis aliorum Codicum ope restituta est. Deinde in Numeris u-biqve varietas maxima est, & potissi-mum his in locis, ut varias Editiones conferenti, & ea legenti, quæ Jos. Scali-ger ex Eusebii & Georgii Syncelli ἀπολο-δαπῆς[?] ἱστορίας[?] excerpsit, manifestum est. Relege, inquit S. Hieronymus ad Vitalem, omnes veteris & novi Testamenti Libros, & tantam verborum dissonan-tiam, & Numerorum inter Judæum & Israel, idest, inter regnum utrumque confusionem, ut hujusmodi hærere quæstionibus non tam studiosi, quàm otiosi hominis esse videatur.
units.tr: As for chapter 12 of Judges, there is indeed so great a difference in the wording throughout the whole chapter that it would seem altogether to be a different translation of the same thing; for the difference consists in words, not in sense, except for the first verse. Now the question is: which of the two translations of the Seventy is the purer? I do not have an ancient book or commentary by whose testimony I could settle this dispute. However, the notes of the Roman edition on this chapter report some things from an ancient scholiast, which stand in the same way as the text of your edition; but those things which that scholiast reports come from a different edition from the Seventy translators. Nor does the Aldine edition, which in this place is almost exactly like your copy, help much. For it is certain that many heterogeneous things have crept into this edition, or into the manuscripts from which it was copied, and many signs of such intrusion occur everywhere. Most learned sir, I do not want you to think that I say these things to the prejudice, much less the contempt, of your copy. I write this because I am led to it by some of the arguments which I have touched on briefly. Nor would I have you think that I believe the Roman edition to be pure from every blemish; this edition has its own blemishes, which those who supervised it at Rome did not conceal, both in the scholia and in the preface. For example, in Genesis chapter 5, verse 25, where the years of Methuselah are concerned; likewise chapter 11, verse 24, where Nahor is concerned, and in other places of the same chapter, in which your edition, as also the Aldine, is far more genuine. Yet these faults can be excused in many ways. For that most ancient codex from which this edition was taken was very much mutilated from the beginning of Genesis to chapter 47; therefore the Roman edition was restored in these places with the help of other copies. Then in Numbers there is the greatest variety everywhere, and especially in these places, as is clear to anyone who compares various editions and reads what Joseph Scaliger excerpted from the chronicle of Eusebius and George Syncellus. Read over, says St. Jerome to Vitalis, all the books of the Old and New Testament, and such a great discord of words, and such a confusion of the Numbers between the Jew and the Israelite, that is, between either kingdom, that it seems to belong not so much to a studious man as to an idle one to get stuck in questions of this kind.

units.la: Deniqve quod ad annos Mathusalæ attinet, sibi consentientes ha-bet Codex Rom. omnes prope Libros Græcos & Latinos ab annis mille trecen-tis, ut hac de re conquerunt Eusebius, Sanctusqve Augustinus: Græci tamen posteriores defendunt hunc errorem, ut ex Georgio Syncello colligitur apud Scaligerum in Thesauro temporum, initio Notarum ad Eusebii παντοδαπὴν historiam. Vix occurrent unqvam ulli Codices, qvi interpretationem illam ab omni additamento, & deliberata mutatione immunem exhibeant, nisi saltem exæquent Origenis ætatem. Ut enim Luciani & Hesychii correctiones missas faciam, statim post Origenem Hexapla per Ecclesias divulgata, non modo quæ addidit sub Asterisco, sed etiam nonnulla alia ex heterogeneis interpretationibus[?] in textum 70, intrudi cœperunt. Felicissimi sunt illi Codices, qui paucioribus ejusmodi irreptionibus scatent. Editio Romana quantum hactenus judicare potui, omnes alias, tuumque Codicem hac felicitate vincere videtur, idque deprehendes si sinceritatis argumenta superius allata de Codice tuo experiaris, [illegible, ~5 letters] est in Codice tuo totus Liber Jobi: ex-cipienda tamen essent duo priora capita, ultimumque caput à v. 7. ad finem, ut docent Hebræi, notavitque S. Hieronymus, resque Hebraice callentibus palam est. Sed universa illa Libri scriptio manifestissime docet, hodiernas versuum Hebraicorum distinctiones Neotericum esse inventum, non modo Codicis tui scriptori, sed etiam Aquilæ, cæterisqve omnibus antiqvis Interpretibus incognitum, qvod tandem ab Europæis abhinc annis paulo minus centum usurpari cœpit. Aliqvot post hoc tempus annis, Novum Testamentum in versus distingvi coepit. Sed versuum distinctionem capitum divisio qvadringentis fere annis antecessit. Christianam capitum divisionem, & Concordantiarum artificium Judæi tandem imitati sunt, utpote Parafchis suis, necnon Sidris Masorethicis multo faciliorem & tractabiliorem. Meam de Codice tuo sententiam libere aperui, eam ut æqvi boniqve consulas plurimum rogo. Tuæ forsan contraria est, sed ab æqvitate & humanitate tua spero te ægre non laturum, si libenter & amice qvod sentio, tibi expofuerim. Fieri potest, ut cum de Codice tuo plura legerim, sententiam mutem; non enim is sum, qvi absolutam sinceritatem, & omnibus suis numeris velut ἀπαρτιλογίᾳ [?] qvâdam constantem Editioni Romanæ tribuam. Si Codex aliquis daretur exacte ut tuus, & magna cum cura descriptus, quiqve Origenis ae-tate non esset inferior, caeteris paribus, illi potius in rebus dubiis crederem, quam Editioni Romanæ: nec nego, multis in locis illam Editionem ex tuo utiliter corrigi posse, vix enim post Origenem Hexapla ullus Codex omnes ἀπλῶς Aste-riscorum & heterogenearum interpreta-tionum irreptiunculas evasit. Epistolæ modum jamdiu excessi: itaque ne moles-tus tibi sim, scribendi finem facio, sed ne me amandi finem facias plurimum opto. Vale, & me tui observantissi-mum ama.
units.tr: Finally, as regards the years of Methuselah, the Roman Codex agrees with almost all the Greek and Latin books in dating them to about 1300 years, as Eusebius and St Augustine complain. Later Greeks nonetheless defend this error, as is gathered from George Syncellus, cited by Scaliger in the Thesaurus temporum, at the beginning of his notes to Eusebius's universal history [παντοδαπὴν ἱστορίαν]. Hardly any manuscripts are ever found that present that translation free of every addition and deliberate alteration, unless they at least match the age of Origen. For, to say nothing of the corrections of Lucian and Hesychius, immediately after Origen's Hexapla was published among the churches, not only the material he added under the asterisk but also several other items drawn from foreign translations began to be inserted into the text of the Seventy. Those manuscripts are most fortunate which abound in fewer such intrusions. So far as I have been able to judge, the Roman edition seems to surpass all others, and your codex too, in this good quality, and you will discover this if you test your codex against the arguments for sincerity set out above. [illegible] In your codex the whole Book of Job is present, though the first two chapters and the last chapter from verse 7 to the end would have to be excepted, as the Hebrews teach and St Jerome has noted, and as is plain to those skilled in Hebrew. But that whole writing of the book shows most clearly that the present division of Hebrew verses is a modern invention, unknown not only to the scribe of your codex but also to Aquila and all the other ancient translators; it began to be used by Europeans only a little less than a hundred years ago. Some years after this time, the New Testament began to be divided into verses. But the division into verses came almost four hundred years after the division into chapters. The Jews have at last imitated the Christian division into chapters and the device of concordances, as they did with their Parashoth, and with their Masoretic Sidrim, which are much easier and more manageable. I have frankly set out my opinion of your codex, and I earnestly ask you to take it in good part and with fairness. Perhaps it is contrary to yours, but I hope that from your fairness and courtesy you will not be displeased if I have set out what I think to you openly and in friendship. It may happen that, once I have read more about your codex, I shall change my view; for I am not the sort of man who would ascribe absolute sincerity to the Roman edition, consistent in all its parts as if it were some perfect whole. If there were some codex exactly like yours, and copied with great care, and not inferior in age to Origen's, I would, other things being equal, trust it rather than the Roman edition in doubtful matters; nor do I deny that in many places that edition could usefully be corrected from yours, for hardly any manuscript after Origen's Hexapla has escaped entirely the small intrusions of the asterisks and of foreign translations. I have long since exceeded the proper length of a letter; so that I may not trouble you further, I bring my writing to an end, but I earnestly hope that you will not bring my friendship to an end. Farewell, and count me your most devoted admirer.

units.la: Parisiis, 7 Kal. Sept. Anno 1638.
units.tr: Parisiis, 7 Kal. Sept. Anno 1638.

units.la: EPIST. LV.
units.tr: EPIST. LV.

units.la: J. Morinus Cardinali Barberino. Unionem Abbatiæ Juliacensis domui Parisiensi oratorii Postulat.
units.tr: J. Morinus to Cardinal Barberini. He asks that the Abbey of Juilly be united with the Paris house of the Oratory.

units.la: Eminentissimo & Reverendissimo Principi Cardinali Barberino, Domino suo Colendissimo Joan. Morinus Cong. Orat. Presb. cum humillimo obsequio S. D.
units.tr: To the most eminent and most reverend Prince, Cardinal Barberini, his most honoured lord, Jean Morin, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, with the humblest obedience, sends greeting.

units.la: Audaculus forsan Eminentiæ tuæ videar, qui gratiam opemque tuam imploraturus, eam rebus maximis gerendis intentam Epistola mea interpellem; verùm duæ res sunt, quæ me hac suspicione si non penitus liberant, eam tamen ambæ plurimum elevare & excusare mihi videntur; hanc enim confidentiam in animum meum induxit tua in me benevolentia, quam non obscuris verbis & mihi privatim, & aliis publicè testatus es: sed eam potissimum confirmavit res ipsa, cujus causa humilis, supplexque nunc consvetam Eminentiæ tuæ benevolentiam imploro. Concessit Rex Christianissimus in favorem Congreg. nostræ, ut Abbatia, vulgo dicta de Julii Ordinis Canonicorum regularium S. Augustini milliaribus 7. ab urbe distans, Domui Parisiensi in perpetuum uniretur, atque ut ita dicam, incorporaretur, ideoque abdicavit Rex jure Nominationis sive electionis in Abbatem; consensit electioni faciendæ Reverendissimus Episcopus Meldensis, in cujus Dioecesi sita est Abbatia illa, cujusque jurisdictioni est obnoxia; resignavit Abbatiam Abbas, eamque S. D. N. Papæ in favorem & commodum unionis deposuit, unionem optant & promovent ipsi Religiosi; his conditionibus, quæ veluti præjudiciales actiones requiri judicantur, magno cedentium consensu paratis & præparatis, superest rei forma animaque autoritate summi Pontificis infundenda & introducenda, Abbatiæ scilicet illius unio & incorporatio cum domo nostra Parisiensi sedis Apostolicæ diplomatis instituenda & stabilienda: ut huic causæ quam æquam iustamque Rex Christianissimus, & omnes quorum interfuit, censuerunt, Summi Pontificis animum gratiamque consilio & autoritate concilies, non ego, (quis enim sum, ut mei ergo Eminentiam tuam exoratum sperem? Sed optimi Cardinalis Be-rallii Parentis & fundatoris nostri, quem ad supremum Cardinalatus dignitatem summus Pontifex Patrinus tuus peramanter evexit, singularia in Ecclesiam Catholicam merita apud eminentiam tuam intercedunt; intercedit quoque, & quam humili potest cum obsequio, hoc beneficium efflagitat pedibus tuis, mecum provoluta congregatio nostra, quæ immatura parentis sui morte, pupilla patronoque orba, & rerum inops in sinum tuum confugit, benevolentiæque tuæ asilum invocat, vere enim & sincere dicam, Congreg. nostra domus præsertim Parisiensis à Parente suo pietatem, humilitatem, animumque in Ecclesiæ Catholicæ ministerium propensissimum, & in sedem Apostolicam devinctissimum hausit & expressit; sed opes, quibus sustentaretur, & ad scopum, in quem collimat, assequendum juvaretur, parcissime accepit: ideo licet Abbatia illa paucorum reditum sit Sacerdotium, potissimam tamen fundationis partem unita componet; itaque si unionem istam commendatione tua, quam nobis benevolam vehementissimé exoptamus, obtinere nos contingit, non modo tanto beneficio Congreg. nostram devinctissimam tenebis, verum etiam illi fundator alter qui genitam amplexus fueris, teneram foveris, debilem & nutantem sustinueris & confirmaveris. Sicut enim à primo Parente cum vita brachia, manusque accepit; sic, ut ea explicari & movere possit Eminentiæ tuæ beneficio consequetur.
units.tr: Perhaps I shall seem too bold to Your Eminence, since I am about to beg your favour and help and interrupt you with this letter while you are occupied with the greatest affairs. Yet there are two things which, if they do not wholly free me from that suspicion, seem at least to raise and excuse me greatly. The first is your goodwill towards me, which you have declared, not in obscure terms, both to me in private and to others in public. This goodwill gave me the confidence. But the matter itself, for whose sake I now humbly and as a suppliant ask for Your Eminence's accustomed kindness, has confirmed it above all. The Most Christian King has granted, in favour of our Congregation, that the Abbey commonly called of Juilly, of the Order of Regular Canons of St Augustine, seven miles from the city, be united with the Paris house in perpetuity and, as I may say, incorporated with it. For this purpose the King has renounced his right of nomination or election of the abbot. The Most Reverend Bishop of Meaux, in whose diocese that abbey lies and to whose jurisdiction it is subject, has consented to the election to be made. The abbot has resigned the abbey and laid it down in favour of, and for the advantage of, the union, and the religious themselves desire and promote the union. These conditions, which are judged to be preliminary acts, have been agreed and arranged with the great consent of those giving way. What remains is that the form and soul of the matter be infused and introduced by the authority of the Supreme Pontiff: namely, that the union and incorporation of that abbey with our Paris house be established and confirmed by an Apostolic brief. So that you may, by your counsel and authority, win over the mind and favour of the Supreme Pontiff for this cause, which the King and all those concerned have judged as fair and just, I do not make the request myself. For who am I, that I should hope to win Your Eminence's favour on my own account? But the singular merits of the most excellent Cardinal Bérulle, our father and founder, whom your godfather the Supreme Pontiff most lovingly raised to the supreme dignity of the Cardinalate, intercede with Your Eminence on the Catholic Church's behalf. Our congregation also intercedes, and as humbly as it can, with prostrate body at your feet it begs for this benefit. Orphaned by the untimely death of its father, deprived of its protector and lacking resources, it takes refuge in your bosom and invokes the asylum of your goodwill. For I say truly and sincerely that our Congregation, and especially the Paris house, has drawn from its father piety, humility and a readiness for the ministry of the Catholic Church, and a devotion bound to the Apostolic See. Yet the resources by which it might be sustained and helped to reach the goal at which it aims it has received very sparingly. Therefore, although that abbey's income is that of a few priests, its main endowment will furnish the union with its support. If we are granted this union through your recommendation, which we most earnestly desire to be favourable to us, you will not only bind our Congregation to you by so great a benefit, but you will also be, as it were, a second founder to it. As you have embraced it when newborn, cherished it when tender, and sustained and strengthened it when weak and tottering, so it will receive from your kindness the arms and hands with which it can stretch and move, just as it received life and limbs from its first father.

units.la: Consilia coeptaque tua Deus prosperet, teque incolumen Ecclesiæ suæ quam diutissimè conservet: Vale, Eminentissime & Eruditissime Cardinalis, & me tui observantissimum amarę ne desinas.
units.tr: May God prosper your counsels and undertakings, and may he keep you safe for his Church for as long as possible. Farewell, most eminent and learned Cardinal, and do not cease to love me, who am most devoted to you.

units.la: Parisiis xij Kal. Nov. Anno Salutis MDCXXXVIII.
units.tr: Paris, the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the year of salvation 1638.

units.la: EPIST. LVI.
units.tr: EPISTLE LVI.

units.la: J. Morinus Cardinali Barberino Ipsum Romam vocanti se iterum spondet.
units.tr: J. Morinus to Cardinal Barberini, who invites him to Rome, promises again to come.

units.la: Eminentissimo & Reverendissimo Principi Francisco Cardinali Barberino J. Mo-rinus Congreg. Orat. Presb. summa cum observantia S. D. P.
units.tr: To the most eminent and most reverend Prince Francis Cardinal Barberini, J. Morinus of the Congregation of the Oratory of Priests, with the greatest respect, sends greeting.

units.la: Eminentissime Cardinalis,
units.tr: Most eminent Cardinal,

units.la: Literas Eminentiae tuae reddidit mihi Eminentissimus Cardinalis Bichius, quas legens faciem sensi saepius pudore suffundi, singulis enim fere periodis animo recursabat, quae scriptis meis laudes deferrentur, quisve deferret. Me equidem in tenui laborem non impendisse, neque ut dicitur, ἐπὶ τῇ Φακῇ μωΐεγν [?] effudisse, & facile credebam, & res ipsa suadebat; verùm tenuitatis ingenii mei bene conscius, quod difficilia tentaverim à nemine improbatum iri spectavi tantum; difficilis coepti persecutionem aliquantulum laudis promerituram vix conjiciebam; at ab Eminentia tua non approbationem modo, sed laudes, easq; adeo honorificas reportaturam non speravi, non conjeci, non cogitavi: quidquid de illo honore dicam, quo me tam benevolè cumulat Eminentia tua, quae literis suis non minori eruditione qvàm suavitate conditis, me Romam cùm jubere posset, peramanter invitat, idqve iterari mihi per Eminentissimum Cardinalem Bichium procuravit, qvi me ab Eminentia tua studiosè commendatum humanissimè dicam & officiosissimè ex-cepit, itinerisqve sui comitem esse voluit. Ista me obseqvio tuo non devinciunt, Eminentissime Cardinalis, qvip-pe qvi benevolentiae tuae demonstratione me tibi devinctum jamdudum habes, sed animum gratum & obseqviosum testandi, qvanqvam maxime velim, o-mnem occasionem spemqve praeripiunt; non abs re ausim hac in causa usurpare S. Patriarchae Jacobi responsum, Patri, de prospero & tam prompto venationis successu, interroganti datum, voluntas Dei fuit, ut cito occurreret mihi, qvod volebam. Licet enim de me scriptisqve meis tam fausta conjicere, aut etiam cogitare non auderem, effecit Deus, cujus χρειῶν νόῳ [illegible, ~5 letters] ἀνδρῶν, ut cito oc-curreret mihi, qvod volebam, audenter-qve que desiderassem, & conquisiissem, nisi consueta amantibus animi impotentia somnia fingere mihi ipsi visus fuissem: his accedit rei, cui illustrandæ labores meos destinas, nobilitas, utilitas, sanctitas, quæ me ad tua jussa capessenda mea voluntate currentem vehementer incitant. Christianarum enim musarum hoc est, Sacri textus, historiæque & disciplinæ Ecclesiasticæ semper mihi visa sunt dulcissima studia, de his ausim jactare, quod Poëta de suis Musis;
units.tr: The most eminent Cardinal Bichi delivered to me your Eminence's letter. As I read it, I often felt my face flush with shame, for almost every sentence brought back to my mind how much praise was heaped on my writings, and by whom. I readily believed, and the matter itself suggested, that I had not spent much labour on a slight work, and had poured out my effort on a lentil stew, as the saying goes [ἐπὶ τῇ Φακῇ]. Yet, well aware of the slenderness of my talent, I expected only that my attempts at difficult subjects would not be condemned by anyone. I hardly guessed that the pursuit of a difficult undertaking would earn some praise. But from your Eminence I did not expect, did not conjecture, did not even think, that I would receive not only approval but praise, and such honourable praise at that. Whatever I say of the honour with which your Eminence so kindly loads me, you who could have ordered me to Rome, yet invite me most warmly, and have arranged for this invitation to be repeated through the most eminent Cardinal Bichi, who received me, having been earnestly recommended by your Eminence, most courteously and most dutifully, and wished me to be the companion of his journey. These things do not bind me to your favour, most eminent Cardinal, for you already hold me bound to you by the proof of your goodwill. Yet although I would very much like to attest a grateful and obedient mind, these things take away every opportunity and hope of doing so. I would not be out of place in venturing to use in this case the answer which the holy Patriarch Jacob gave to his father when he asked about the lucky and so prompt success of his hunting: It was the will of God that what I wanted should quickly come to meet me. For although I would not dare to conjecture or even think such fortunate things about myself and my writings, God, whose [illegible] of men [χρειῶν νόῳ ἀνδρῶν], has brought about that what I wanted quickly came to meet me. I would not have dared to desire and seek it, unless I had seemed to myself to be inventing the dreams that lovers are wont to have. To this is added the nobility, usefulness and holiness of the matter which you direct my labours to clarify, and these powerfully urge me, of my own will, to run eagerly to obey your commands. For the sacred texts, history and ecclesiastical discipline, the studies of the Christian Muses, have always seemed to me the sweetest pursuits. Concerning these I may venture to boast what the poet said of his Muses:

units.la: Harum sacra fero ingenti perculsus amore, Me igitur illæ ante omnia — Accipiant, cœlique vias, & sidera monstrent.
units.tr: I bear their rites, struck by a mighty love; may they first of all receive me, and show me the paths of heaven and the stars.

units.la: Id tum mihi contigisse credam, cum me domi tuæ acceperis suavissima conversatione tua, & eruditissimis colloquiis beaveris.
units.tr: I would believe this has happened to me, since I have been received into your house and blessed with your most pleasant company and most learned conversations.

units.la: Quoniam igitur ita jubes, Eruditissime Cardinalis, & Φίλτροις insuper tam amabilibus allicis, Romano itineri me accingam, Deoqve juvante, ad diem, qvi mihi ab Eminentissimo Cardinale Bichio circa proximum Pascha condicendum est, expeditus ero, ut ipsius comitatui me posim[?] conjungere, præsensqve propensissimam & devotissimam obsequio tuo animi mei voluntatem, qvæ sola mihi gratitudinis demonstrandæ lux affulget, Eminentiæ tuæ consecrare. Deus te incolumem Ecclesiæ suæ, sacrisqve literis conservet qvàm diutisime, Eminentissime Cardinalis, faxit-qve, ut me tibi obsequentissimum amare pergas.
units.tr: Since you thus command, most learned Cardinal, and draw me on besides with such lovely charms [φίλτροις], I shall prepare myself for the Roman journey. God helping, I shall be free by the day which Cardinal Bichi is to appoint for me, about next Easter, so that I may join his company. And I shall dedicate to your Eminence the most ready and most devoted will of my mind, which alone shines before me as a light for showing gratitude. May God keep you safe, most eminent Cardinal, for his Church and for the sacred letters, for as long as possible, and grant that you continue to love me as your most obedient servant.

units.la: Datuu Parisiis Anno Salutis MDCXXXIX, vij id. Feb.
units.tr: Given at Paris in the year of salvation 1639, on the seventh day before the Ides of February.

units.la: EPIST. LVII.
units.tr: EPIST. LVII.

units.la: Lucæ Holstenii Commonitorium J. Mo-rino Romæ exeunti. Commonitorium P. Johanni Morino.
units.tr: Lucas Holstenius's Commonitory to J. Morinus, leaving Rome. Commonitory to Father John Morinus.

units.la: C'L[?], Morine, Lucas Holstenius hoc te abeuntem rogat, ut amici ex animo tibi addictissimi memoriam serves, ut amiamicos in itinere & Parisiis salutes, hosce potissimum, Senis, Gulielmum Sohier, virum perhumanum & doctum, & Illustrissimum Dominum Piccolominaeum Archiepiscopum; Pisii, Paganium Gaudentium, virum multis libris editis clarum, qui tuo congressu vehementer delectabitur; Liburni, Spiridonem, Monachum Graecum Ecclesiae Graecae ibidem praefectum καλλιγεράφος[?], à quo forte aliquid missorum nancisci poteris; Aquisextiis, fratrem Illustrissimi Domini Peiresci, & Cl. Dominum Gassendum; Avenioni, Illustrissimum Dominum Episcopum Vasionensem, cu-jus Praenesten hic edi curo; Parisiis, Pu-teanos Fratres, viros omnibus nominibus optimè de me meritos, quibus me & mea studia diligenter commendes; tum Reverendum P. Sirmondum, Petavium, Vassaeum; & si adsit, Nic. Rigaltium, tum Dominum Cramoisy; roges Patrem Sirmondum, ut Theodoreti Epistolas Manuscriptas ad Eminentissimum Cardinalem nostrum remittat, ubi satis eo exemplari usus fuerit. Domino Cramoisy mitto indicem librorum Græcorum, qvi penes me sunt, qvos tuo arbitratu cum aliis ab ipso editis commutabo: rem totam plenius ex ipsis literis perspicies. Cum Dominis Puteanis velim agas de Vitis Pontificum, qvas paro; & præsertim de Anastasio bibliothecario, cujus exemplar Parisiis extare a-junt, ab edito longe diversum. Reverendissimo P. Sirmendo qvam commendatissima esse cupio studia mea, cui id velim persvadeas, me nomini ipsius esse addictissimum [?]: id qvoqve perqviras, num Anastasii Sinaitæ opera græca Manuscripta meo sumptu atqve ære hic transcripta, Domino Cramoisy tradita fuerint. Nollem enim perire, uti etiam collationes Hoseæ Prophetæ ad antiqvissimum exemplar Barberinæ bibliothecæ à me institutas, qvas P. Philippæo tradendas miseram: plura tempus vetat, tu amantem redama, & rem feliciter gere: sic tibi iter, qvod paras, cæteraqve omnia ex voto tuo meoqve proveniat.
units.tr: Morinus, Lucas Holstenius asks you, as you leave, to keep in mind a friend who is wholly devoted to you, and to greet my friends on your journey and in Paris. Those I most want you to greet are these. At Siena, Guillaume Sohier, a very courteous and learned man, and the most illustrious Lord Piccolomini, the Archbishop. At Pisa, Paganio Gaudenzio, a man famous for many published books, who will be greatly delighted to meet you. At Livorno, Spiridon, a Greek monk who is in charge of the Greek Church there, a calligrapher [καλλιγράφος], from whom you may perhaps obtain something of the things I have sent. At Aix, the brother of the most illustrious Lord Peiresc, and the distinguished Lord Gassendi. At Avignon, the most illustrious Lord Bishop of Vaison, for whom I am having my Praeneste edited here. At Paris, the Puteani brothers, men who in every way have deserved very well of me; commend me and my studies to them diligently. Then the reverend Father Sirmond, Petau, Vasse, and, if he is there, Nicolas Rigault; then Lord Cramoisy. Ask Father Sirmond to send back the manuscript Letters of Theodoret to our most eminent Cardinal, once he has made enough use of that copy. I am sending Lord Cramoisy a list of the Greek books that are in my possession, which I will exchange, as you think best, for others published by him; you will see the whole matter more fully from the letters themselves. I would like you to deal with the Puteani on the subject of the Lives of the Popes, which I am preparing, and especially concerning Anastasius the librarian, whose copy is said to exist in Paris and to be very different from the printed one. Tell the Reverend Father Sirmond how much I want my studies to be commended to him, and assure him that I am wholly devoted to his name. Also make inquiry whether the Greek manuscript works of Anastasius the Sinaite, which were copied here at my expense, have been handed over to Lord Cramoisy. I would not like them to be lost, just as I would not like the collations of the prophet Hosea, made by me against the most ancient copy in the Barberini library, which I had sent to Father Philippeau to be handed on, to be lost. Time forbids more. Love the one who loves you, and may you carry out your affairs successfully; so may your journey, which you are preparing, and all your other concerns turn out according to your wish.

units.la: Romæ 7. Martii 1640.
units.tr: Rome, 7 March 1640.

units.la: Tuus ex animo,
units.tr: Yours from the heart,

units.la: L. Holstenius.
units.tr: L. Holstenius.

units.la: Dissertationes ad Concilium Nicænum ad Illustrissimum Dominum Archiepiscopum Tholosatem mittas, rogo: cui per patrem Bussonem eas jamdudum promisi, iis si commodum erit, adjungas exemplar Demophili mei. Vale.
units.tr: Please send the Dissertations on the Council of Nicaea to the most illustrious Lord Archbishop of Toulouse, to whom I promised them some time ago through Father Busson. If it is convenient, add to them a copy of my Demophilus. Farewell.

units.la: EPIST. LVIII.
units.tr: EPIST. LVIII.

units.la: J. Morinus Abrahamo Ecchellensi Codices quosdam MSS. qui Bibliis Parisiensibus quæ tunc edebantur utilitati ac splendore futuri erant, Parisios secum deferat illum monet.
units.tr: J. Morinus advises Abraham Ecchellensis to bring with him to Paris certain manuscript codices, which were to be of use and ornament to the Paris Bible then being published.

units.la: Joh. Morinus Abrahamo Ecchellensi.
units.tr: Joh. Morinus to Abraham Ecchellensis.

units.la: LItteræ tuæ primo Julii datæ mihi redditæ sunt, quibus nihil mihi potuit contingere jucundius, cùm præsertim ex iis intellexi, te ad iter Parisiense accingere, huc venias, Deum precor, salvus & incolumis; priores tuas literas accepi, iisque respondi. Eminentissimum Cardinalem Barberinum Arabica Biblia concessurum spero, imo confido; aliter si fiat, liber Esther simul cum libro Baruch esset ex isto codice exscribendus.
units.tr: Your letter dated 1 July has been delivered to me. Nothing could have given me greater pleasure, especially since from it I learned that you are preparing for the journey to Paris. I pray God that you come here safe and sound. I have received your earlier letters and replied to them. I hope, indeed I am confident, that the most eminent Cardinal Barberini will grant the Arabic Bibles; otherwise, if that cannot be done, the Book of Esther, together with the Book of Baruch, would have to be copied out from that codex.

units.la: Dictionaria & vocabularia quæcunque habes aut recuperare potes, non erit inutile, in omnem eventum tecum deferre, quod ad varias illas lectiones, quæ apud Cardinalem Pallotum extant, quæ describendi otium tibi aut nullum erit, aut bene admodum commodius est ut tecum deferas, postquàm hic in lucem editæ fuerint, illas Romam rediens tecum referes.
units.tr: Any dictionaries and vocabularies you have or can recover will not be useless to bring with you in any event, for the various readings which are found with Cardinal Pallotta. Either you will have no leisure to copy them, or it will be much more convenient for you to take them with you; after they have been published here, you can bring them back with you when you return to Rome.

units.la: Sanè editæ erunt Bibliis utilitati & splendori, nec hoc opinor, rogatus denegabit Eminentissimus Cardinalis Pallotus, hæc enim unde accepta fuerint declarabitur, & gratiæ commodantibus publicè habebuntur; amplissimum virum D. le Jay tuo nomine saluta-vi, te quàm officiosissimè expectat, continuationem in adventum tuum differt, tibi se esse devinctissimum, ut verum est ubique prædicat. Optatissimus venies; commodissima ut opinor est occasio itineris Eminentissimi Cardinalis Bichii, qui in Galliam revertitur ad Episcopatum suum. R. P. Goezaldus in Galliam reversurus est, ambo comitatui Cardinal. vos adjungere potestis, eliges, quod erit tibi rebusque tuis magis commodum, itineris sumptus, quos judicaveris necessarios, suppeditabit R. P. Goezaldus. Masiliæ præterea & Lugduni, si qua re indigueris, ut ea nostris, qui ibi habitant, abundè suppeditetur, magna cum cura providebo. Titulos quosdam capitum atque etiam librorum, qui in Bibliis Syriacis à me emptis, desunt, ex vaticano describere, quæso ne sis immemor; faxit Deus, ut salvum & incolumen quam cito hic te amplexemur. Vale & me tui observantissimum & amantissimum ama.
units.tr: They will certainly be published for the benefit and splendour of the Bible, and I do not think that the most eminent Cardinal Pallotta, when asked, will refuse this. For the sources from which they were obtained will be declared, and thanks will be given publicly to those who lend them. I greeted the most distinguished man, Lord le Jay, on your behalf. He awaits you as eagerly as possible and has postponed the continuation of his work until your arrival; he proclaims everywhere, as is true, that he is most deeply bound to you. You will come most welcome. The most eminent Cardinal Bichi, who is returning to France to his bishopric, offers, I think, the most convenient opportunity for travel. Reverend Father Goezaldus is also about to return to France; you may join the Cardinal's retinue together with both of them. Choose whatever will be more convenient for you and your affairs. Reverend Father Goezaldus will supply the travelling expenses which you judge necessary. Moreover, at Marseilles and Lyons I will take great care that, if you need anything, it is amply supplied by our people who live there. Please do not forget to copy out from the Vatican some titles of chapters, and even of books, which are missing from the Syriac Bibles I bought. May God grant that we may embrace you safe and sound as soon as possible. Farewell, and love me, who am most respectful and most affectionate towards you.

units.la: Parisiis 3 nonas Aug. tum Arabicum & Syriacum jam à Gabriele Sionita excusum, illiusque Latinas versiones; hæc omnia tam pauculo tempore desudavit.
units.tr: Paris, 3 August. Then the Arabic and Syriac, already printed by Gabriel Sionita, together with his Latin versions; he laboured over all these things in so short a time.

units.la: Eminentissimus Cardinalis Richelius magnis pretiis ut hic subsisteret, invitavit; sed nihil se polliceri posse injussu Eminentissimi Cardinalis Barberini prudenter & modeste respondit; reversurum plurimi sperant & avent, atque ego existimo, de re literaria esse, ut revertatur: quæ enim ad literas spectant, multo commodius Parisiis, quàm Romæ instruuntur & conficiuntur.
units.tr: The most eminent Cardinal Richelieu invited him, with great rewards, to remain here. But he replied prudently and modestly that he could promise nothing without the command of the most eminent Cardinal Barberini. Many hope and long for his return, and I think, in the interests of learning, that he should return. For matters that concern letters are set up and carried out much more conveniently in Paris than in Rome.

units.la: Quidquid futurum sit, hanc te salutandi occasionem, me meaque studia tibi commendandi lubens accipio. Quid enim honorificentius mihi contingere potest, quàm à viro tanto amari & commendari? Vale, Abbas Reverendissime, meque obsequiosê te colentem continuo amore prosequere.
units.tr: Whatever is going to happen, I gladly accept this occasion to greet you and to commend myself and my studies to you. For what could be more honourable for me than to be loved and commended by a man so great? Farewell, most Reverend Abbot, and continue to love with constant affection one who respects you with devotion.

units.la: Parisiis xvj Kal. Jan. 1641.
units.tr: Paris, 17 December 1641.

units.la: EPIST. LX.
units.tr: EPIST. LX.

units.la: J. Morinus Cardinali Barberino. De eodem Argumento.
units.tr: J. Morinus to Cardinal Barberino. On the same subject.

units.la: Eminentissimo Cardinali Barberino.
units.tr: To the Most Eminent Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: Eminentissime Cardinalis.
units.tr: Most Eminent Cardinal,

units.la: REdit in urbem D. Abraham Ecchel-lensis, officio, propter quod huc vocatus fuerat, diligenter & magno cum omnium doctorum applausu defunctus. Abiens vehemens sui desiderium illis re-liquit ; sperant hic cum bona Eminentiæ vestræ venia brevi reversurum, qua de re pluribus aget cum Eminentia vestra ipse Abraham, quem illi maximo cum affectu commendarem, nisi scirem commendatissimum, utpote ab ea & beneevolentia sua & beneficiis cumulatum: admonuit, credo, Eminentiam vestram Illustrissimus Nuntius de libro quodam paucis ante diebus à Jesuita composito, eumque ad eam aut misit aut mittit, necesse prorsus est, ut librum legat Eminentia vestra aut doctoribus legendum committat, & ab iis excerpta videat & diligenter consideret ; ea enim doctrinæ capita continet, quæ si affirmavero contineri, aut quivis alius, nemo nobis est crediturus, cùm in fronte gestet honori-ficum ficum à societate testimonium, quapropter illorum enarratione supersedebo. Videt Eminentia vestra sanctitatem suam, libros P. Boni libris prohibitis inserendo nihil profecisse, sed animadversionem illam de ridiculo habitam; aliis itaque remediis opus est, quae frustra nunc à nostratibus Episcopis aut à Sorbona sperarentur. Cæterùm Eminentiam vestram enixissimè rogo, ut mei nunquam sit immemor. Deus eam quàm diutissimè servet incolumem.
units.tr: Doctor Abraham of Ecchel has returned to the city, having discharged the duty for which he had been called here, and having done so diligently and to the great applause of all the learned. On leaving, he left behind a strong longing for himself among them, and they hope that, with your Eminence's kind permission, he will soon return. About this matter Abraham himself will speak with your Eminence at length. I would commend him to you with the greatest warmth, were I not sure that he is already most highly commended, having been loaded with your Eminence's goodwill and benefits. I believe the Most Illustrious Nuncio has reminded your Eminence of a book composed a few days ago by a Jesuit, which he has either sent to you or is sending. It is absolutely necessary that your Eminence read the book, or entrust it to learned men to read, and that you look over excerpts from it and consider them carefully. For it contains doctrinal points which, if I were to assert that they are there, no one among us would believe, since the book bears on its title page the honourable testimony of the Society. For this reason I will refrain from setting them out. Your Eminence sees that His Holiness, by placing the books of Father Bonus on the index of prohibited books, has achieved nothing, and that the censure was treated as a joke. Other remedies are therefore needed, and these are now vainly hoped for from our bishops or from the Sorbonne. I earnestly beg your Eminence, moreover, never to forget me. May God keep you safe for as long as possible.

units.la: Parisiis xvij Jan. Anno 1641.
units.tr: Paris, 17 January, 1641.

units.la: EPIST. LXI.
units.tr: Letter LXI.

units.la: J. Morinus Cardinali Barberino exponit, quid sinistri acciderit libro Petri Celloti Jesuitæ de hierarchia & hierarchis; Cellotum notat imperitiæ.
units.tr: J. Morinus sets out to Cardinal Barberini what unfortunate things have happened to the book of Peter Cellot, a Jesuit, on the hierarchy and the hierarchs; he marks Cellot down for ignorance.

units.la: Eminentissimo Cardinali Barberino.
units.tr: To the Most Eminent Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: ILlustrissimo Nuntio Apostolico Romam redeunti has literas dedi, ut summam meam erga Eminentiam vestram, observantiam & humillimum obsequium, cùm aliter non possim, hoc qvali-cunqve gratitudinis officio testarer. Haeret enim animo meo æternumqve hærebit, ea qva me domi tuæ complexus es benevolentia, & eam qvibuscunqve obsequiis & ministeriis promereri non desinam; hoc unum ab Eminentia tua impetrare satago, ut mei nunqvam fis immemor.
units.tr: I have entrusted this letter to the most illustrious Apostolic Nuncio on his return to Rome, so that, since I cannot do otherwise, I may bear witness by this small service of gratitude to my deepest regard and most humble obedience toward your Eminence. The kindness with which you embraced me in your household has taken root in my mind and will remain there forever, and I will not cease to deserve it by whatever services and duties I can perform. There is one thing only I am striving to obtain from your Eminence: that you never forget me.

units.la: Romam redit illustrissimus Nuntius, maximum sui desiderium omnibus, qvi cum eo conversati sunt relinqvens, sincerè enim affirmare possum, me neminem vidisse etsi multos viderim, qvi habito cum eo colloqvio ipsius comitatem, candorem, modestiam, & in rebus agendis dexteritatem & minime fucatam prudentiam non amaverit & laudaverit; defert secum ad Eminentiam tuam R. P. Celloti Jesuitæ librum de hierarchia & hierarchis, qvi ab Episcopis nostris Meduntæ Carnutum congregatis abhinc paucis diebus censurâ notatus est. Confecta censura omnium Episcoporum chirographis subscripta & ad Eminentissimum Cardinalem Richelium delata, in ejus manibus hactenus subsistit. Sorbona quoque in hunc librum graviter insurrexit, multiplicesque propositiones notavit. Censura plusquam 80 doctorum suffragiis approbata registris Sorbonicis inscripta est; verùm eam publicè edere per supremam autoritatem hactenus non licuit. Sua Eminentia doctores nonnullos Sorbonicos deputavit, qui cum R. P. Celloto de his propositionibus conferrent; in hunc usque diem de hac collatione nihil publicè editum est, ideo Jesuitæ Cellotum affirmant Sorbonicis satisfecisse, Sorbonici contra malas propositiones malè propugnasse; de hoc libro quid sentiam, aperire non possum, cùm illum evolvere nondum per otium licuerit. Pauca folia percurri, sed prima fronte mihi visus est hic autor multis locis figulinam, ut dicitur, in dolio discere materiamque humeris æquam non elegisse; ideo aliis negotiis occupatus lectione supersedi; mirati sunt multi, hominem Rhetoricarum Exercitationum τρίβωνα, atque ad collegiorum regimen abreptum ad ejusmodi studium repente animum appulisse.
units.tr: The most illustrious Nuncio is returning to Rome, leaving behind a great longing for himself among all who have associated with him. For I can honestly affirm that, though I have seen many people, I have never seen anyone who, after conversing with him, has not loved and praised his courtesy, candour and modesty, and his skill in managing affairs, together with a prudence that is in no way feigned. He is bringing to your Eminence the book of Father Cellot, a Jesuit, on the hierarchy and the hierarchs, which a few days ago was censured by our bishops gathered at Meduntae Carnutum. The censure, completed and signed in the handwriting of all the bishops, was delivered to the most eminent Cardinal Richelieu, and until now it has remained in his hands. The Sorbonne also rose up vigorously against this book and noted many propositions in it. A censure approved by the votes of more than eighty doctors has been entered in the Sorbonne registers, but up to now it has not been permitted by the supreme authority to publish it openly. Your Eminence appointed some Sorbonne doctors to confer with Father Cellot about these propositions. Up to this day nothing has been published publicly about that conference, and so the Jesuits assert that Cellot has satisfied the Sorbonne, while the Sorbonnists claim that they defended the bad propositions badly. What I think of this book I cannot yet reveal, since I have not had the leisure to read through it. I have run over a few leaves, but at first sight this author seemed to me, in many places, to be learning his potter's craft on a jar, as the saying goes, and to have chosen material beyond his shoulders. So, occupied with other business, I put off reading it. Many were surprised that a man so practised in the Rhetorical Exercises [τρίβων], and carried off to the government of colleges, should have suddenly turned his mind to such a study.

units.la: Propositionum à Sorbonicis notatarum pauca exemplaria cudi curarunt, sed sine Sorbonicis notis, quarum exemplar ad Eminentiam vestram mitto, ut & alias manu scriptas, quæ post Sorbonicam Censuram à nonnullis Sorbonicis ex R. P. Celloti libris excerptæ sunt, quarum exemplar quod in manus meas incidere contigit, similiter mitto, ut Eminentia vestra, quid de his pronunciandum sit, decernat; fere enim omnibus male audit hic liber; meritò an immeritò, propositionibus illis in ipso autoris textu consideratis dicernat hanc litem Eminentia Vestra, quam salvam & incolumem Ecclesiæ suæ Deus quam diutissimè conservet.
units.tr: A few copies of the propositions noted by the Sorbonne have been printed, but without the Sorbonne's notes. I am sending your Eminence a copy of these, together with other manuscript extracts from Father Cellot's books, made by some Sorbonne doctors after the Sorbonne censure. A copy of these that happened to come into my hands I am likewise sending, so that your Eminence may decide what ought to be pronounced on these matters. For almost everyone speaks ill of this book, and whether this is deserved or undeserved, your Eminence should judge this dispute, after considering those propositions in the author's own text. May God preserve your Eminence, and the Church entrusted to you, safe and unharmed for as long as possible.

units.la: Dat. Parisiis xj Kal. Junii 1641.
units.tr: Dated at Paris, the eleventh day before the Kalends of June 1641.

units.la: EPIST. LXII.
units.tr: LETTER LXII.

units.la: Cardinalis Barberinus Johanni Morino: De Abrahami Ecchellensis Bibliis Sy- riacis, Deinde Jaudat[?] propositum de scri-
units.tr: The Cardinal Barberini to Johannes Morinus: On the Syriac Bibles of Abraham Ecchellensis; then Jaudat[?]'s proposal for writing on the antiquity of the ecclesiastical rites.

units.la: scribenda sacra rituum Ecclesiasticorum antiquitate.
units.tr: (Continuation of the heading above; see unit 2.)

units.la: Admodum Reverendissimo Patri Johan- ni Morino Cardinalis Barberinus.
units.tr: To the Most Reverend Father Johannes Morinus, Cardinal Barberinus.

units.la: Admodum Reverendissime & Clarissime Pater.
units.tr: Most Reverend and Illustrious Father,

units.la: GRatum fuit, tua quoque testificatione cognoscere, Abrahamum Ecchellensem eam in Bibliis Syriacis recensendis istic praestitisse operam, quam & perspecta ejus eruditio pollicebatur, & tanti moliminis opus requirebat; sed non minus mihi jucundum accidit, quod ille vicissim de tuis studiis, & pristino in nos affectu ea retulerit, quae jam pridem scire avebam; nam in iis pertexendis te nunc versari audio, quae, cum apud nos esses, de sacra rituum Ecclesiasticorum antiquitate meditari coeperas; quod quidem argumentum eo te cautius tractaturum existimo, quod indies largo proventu succrescere videas Scriptores, qui nihil ad res sacras tractandas praeter Philautiam, & innovandi pruriginem asserentes, Ecclesiae agrum periculosis novarum opinionum spinis ita implicant, ut id unum eos agere dicas, qvi cum adversariis Ecclesiæ paria facere videntur: proinde officium, & diligentiam tuam probo, qvod de ejus generis libro nos præmonere volueris, qvem inter Abrahami Ecchellensis sarcinas adhuc delite-scentem, videre nec dum licuit; interim de remedio opportuno cogitare licebit, qvod mature curabitur, utinam eo esse-ctu, ut istorum proterviam suprema Ecclesiæ autoritas compescat. Vale, vir Reverende, & de tuis studiis subinde ad nos scribe.
units.tr: It was welcome to learn from your own report that Abraham Ecchellensis has taken on the work of revising the Syriac Bible there, as his well-known learning promised and so great an undertaking required. But it was no less pleasing that he, in turn, told me about your studies and your former goodwill toward us, which I had long been eager to hear. For I am told that you are now engaged in working out the matters you had begun to think over while you were with us, namely the antiquity of the sacred rites of the Church. I think you will treat this subject all the more carefully because you see writers multiplying daily in great numbers. They claim nothing in handling sacred matters except self-love and an itch for innovation, and they so entangle the field of the Church with the dangerous thorns of new opinions that, as you say, they seem to be doing nothing else than making common cause with the adversaries of the Church. Therefore I commend your duty and diligence in wishing to forewarn us about a book of this kind, which is still lying hidden among Abraham Ecchellensis's baggage and which we have not yet been allowed to see. Meanwhile we may consider a suitable remedy, which will be attended to in good time. I hope its effect will be that the supreme authority of the Church restrains the insolence of these men. Farewell, Reverend Sir, and write to us from time to time about your studies.

units.la: Romæ, Feb. 1642.
units.tr: Rome, February 1642.

units.la: P. Rua,
units.tr: P. Rua,

units.la: Studiosus,
units.tr: Student,
