units.tr: EPISTLE LXIII.

units.la: Johannes Morinus Cardinali Barberino. Libri Celloti prolixa eaqve paulo acri-or critice; qvi sit antiqvus & nupe-rus Curiæ Francicæ Stylus in iis, de qvibus agit Cellotus.
units.tr: Johannes Morinus to Cardinal Barberini, concerning the book of Cellotus, which is lengthy and rather sharp in its criticism; and concerning which style of the Curia of France, ancient and modern, Cellotus treats in those matters.

units.la: Cardinali Barberino.
units.tr: To Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: Eminentissime Domine,
units.tr: Most Eminent Lord,

units.la: ACcepi literas Eminentiæ tuæ, quibus novum benevolentiæ tuæ mihi testimonium dedisti, cum & mei & studiorum meorum adeo memorem sese demonstrat ; confidenter igitur illi aperiam, quibus animum meum detineam. Operi, quod jam Romæ meditari coeperam, quantum alia negotiola literaria non prævidenti passim occurrentia sinunt,sedulus incumbo : spero brevi me coronidem impositurum, nihil enim tota hac æstate aggrediar ; nec amplius ab hoc opere quoad potero me avelli permittam : existimabam[?] necessarium huic operi nonnulla inserere de Ecclesiarum antiqvarum figura & forma interiori, ut commodius Episcopi in Sancto Sanctorum Tribunal,Presbyterorum & Diaconorum & Altare aut circum Altare ædes,aliorum inferiorum ministrorum in choro seu Sanctuario confessus, fidelium tam virorum quàm mulierum extra chorum distincti ordines, variæqve Pœnitentium post ambonem stationes, explicarentur: cùm autem interior illa figura & structura non parum illustrari possit Templi Hierosolymitani, qvale erat Jesu Christi & Apostolorum sæculo, comparatione (multa enim ad illius exemplar instituerunt primi Ecclesiæ fundatores) nonnulla etiam de illius delineatione cogitaveram; verùm qvod pauculis capitulis me conficere posse sperabam, fæcunditate materiæ in molem excrevit: ideo separato libello hæc edere constitui, iisqve illustrationis causa addere, qvæ Judæi de Templi structura commentantur, atqve ut id ordine & di-lucide fiat, R. Mosis Malmonidis[?] de templo sive domo electa tractatum Latinitate donare, qvo abundè Christianis suppeditabitur, qvid hac de re Judæorum traditiones commemorant.
units.tr: I have received the letter of your Eminence, in which you have given me a new proof of your goodwill, since it shows itself mindful both of me and of my studies. I will therefore openly tell you what occupies my mind. I apply myself diligently to the work I had already begun to plan at Rome, as far as the other literary tasks, which crop up everywhere unforeseen, allow. I hope to put the finishing touch to it soon, for I shall undertake nothing else this summer, and I will not allow myself to be drawn away from this work for as long as I can help it. I thought it necessary to insert into this work some remarks on the figure and inner form of the ancient churches, so that it might be explained more conveniently where the bishop's tribunal stands in the Holy of Holies, where the presbyters and deacons have their seats, and where the altar stands or the buildings around the altar; where the other lower ministers were confined to the choir or sanctuary; and what the distinct orders of the faithful, men and women alike, were outside the choir, and the various stations of the penitents behind the ambo. But since that inner figure and structure can be illustrated not a little by comparison with the Temple of Jerusalem, such as it was in the age of Jesus Christ and the Apostles (for the first founders of the Church modelled many things on its pattern), I had also considered something of its layout. But what I had hoped to finish in a few chapters has grown into a considerable mass because of the abundance of the material. So I have decided to publish these things in a separate little book, and to add, for the sake of illustration, what the Jews comment on the structure of the Temple. And so that this may be done in order and clearly, I have resolved to render into Latin the treatise of R. Moses Maimonides on the Temple, or the chosen house, which will amply supply Christians with what the Jewish traditions record on this subject.

units.la: Qvoniam autem Eminentia Vestra de qvibusdam libris Parisiis recens editis ad me scribit, qvos cum Ecclesiæ adversariis paria facere ait, spem facit opportu-no remedio se curaturum, ne ex eorum pernicie res Christiana damnum capiat, ausim ut id faciat eam exhortari : nisi enim remedium illud à sede Apostolica exoriatur, nulla spes est, ut aliunde prc[?]veniat; cùm enim nunc Episcopi Parisiis non conveniant, & eos convenire certis de causis sit difficile, illius libri censuram edere non possunt nisi singuli, at qui probabile fiet Episcopi unius Censuram libri istius authoritati prævalituram, qui à celeberrima Societate testimonium habet publicum & publicam approbationem ? Morbus tamen celerrimum efflagitat remedium, non enim serpit cancer iste, sed longis passibus graditur, omniaque circumcirca late vastat & depascitur; si hæresim prima fronte disseminaret liber ille, parvum hinc aut fere nullum damnum nunc temporis emergeret ; omnes enim Catholici librum hunc libriq; autorem ut aspidem horrerent, venenum intra se contineret, nec in quem illud cum efficacia ejacularetur, offenderet. Vix enim in spatiosissimo regno, Deo, sic providente, multorum an-norum norum decursu Catholicus aliqvis à fidé[?] defecisse auditur. Appositè S.Augustinus hæreses torrentibus comparat, qvi paucis horis in fluvios crescunt. Sed incremento statim capto paulatim deficiunt & tandem arescunt. At liber ille de jurisdictione & immunitate Ecclesiastica tractat, qvam Laici Judices à ducentis & aliqvot annis arrodunt, vellicant, paulatimqve discerpunt, ut in varias partes discerptam facilius in se transferant. Qvid verò liber ille ab ima radice jurisdictionem & immunitatem ab Ecclesia evellit, & in Laicos velut in nativum solum, qvantum in se est, transponit. Præclare tibi videtur distingvere inter actiones religiosas & actiones humanas civilesqve, crimina qvoqve mera Canonica seu Ecclesiastica, qvæ scilicet contra fidem committuntur & sacramentorum administrationem; humanaqve & civilia,qvæ legibus civilibus coërcentur: priora Pontificibus, posteriora Principibus tribuit; verùm ista distinctione[?] immunitas[?] Ecclesiastica funditus exterexterminatur, immunitas & Jurisdictio Ecclesiastica in prius membrum non cadit. Concludit praeterea, Clericos à Laico Judice damnatos nec degradatos, si degradationem noluerit aut etiam neglexerit Episcopus peragere, supremo supplicio puniri tuto posse. Hactenus Judicum Laicorum nullus eo usque temeritatis & impietatis progressus est. Ea quibus id probat Argumenta crassissimam & Juris Canonici & moris nostri ignorantiam arguunt. Forsan non erit E.V. ingratum, antiquum recentemque curiarum stylum hac in causa ob ipsius oculos breviter ponere, sane id plurimum conducet ad autoris istius arguendum malignam ignorantiam; sic se res habuit apud nos ab annis 150. cūm publice in libertatemEcclesiasticam agere coeptum est, ad usque Bella civilia sub Henrico IV. docent antiqui Jurisconsulti nostri, licet de Jure Divino eximantur Clerici à potestate Seculari, Laicum tamen Judicem in nonnullis casibus agere posse in eorum personas criminaliter, in aliis civiliter; in priori membro prorsus cum jure Canonico conveniunt, casus enim illos tantum complectuntur, quibus Clericus aut ante aut post trinam monitionem per Canones & Pontific. decreta omni privilegio Clericali ipso facto excidit.
units.tr: Since your Eminence writes to me about some books recently published at Paris, which you say are on a par with the adversaries of the Church, and you hold out the hope that you will apply a suitable remedy so that the Christian cause does not suffer harm from their ruin, I venture to urge you to do so. For unless that remedy comes from the Apostolic See, there is no hope that it will come from anywhere else. Since the Bishops do not now meet at Paris, and for certain reasons it is difficult for them to meet, they can issue a censure of that book only individually. But how probable is it that the censure of a single Bishop will prevail in authority over a book that has the public testimony and public approval of the most celebrated Society? Yet the disease urgently demands a quick remedy. This cancer does not creep but advances with long strides, and lays waste and devours everything far and wide. If that book spread heresy openly at first sight, little or almost no harm would now be arising from it, for all Catholics would shudder at the book and its author as at an asp. It would contain its poison within itself and would find no one against whom it could be hurled with effect. For in that most extensive kingdom, God so providing, scarcely any Catholic is heard to have defected from the faith in the course of many years. St Augustine aptly compares heresies to torrents, which in a few hours swell into rivers; but once they have begun to grow, they gradually fail and at last dry up. That book, however, treats of ecclesiastical jurisdiction and immunity, which lay judges have for two hundred and some years been gnawing at, plucking at and gradually tearing apart, so that they may more easily transfer to themselves what has been torn in pieces. Indeed, that book tears jurisdiction and immunity from the Church by the very root and, so far as it can, transplants them into the laity as into their native soil. It seems to you to distinguish clearly between religious actions and human civil actions, and likewise between crimes that are purely canonical or ecclesiastical, namely those committed against the faith and the administration of the sacraments, and human and civil crimes, which are restrained by civil laws. It assigns the former to the Pontiffs and the latter to princes. But by this distinction ecclesiastical immunity is utterly exterminated, since immunity and jurisdiction do not fall under the first category. It further concludes that clerics condemned by a lay judge, if they have not been degraded, or if the bishop has refused or even neglected to carry out the degradation, can safely be punished with the supreme penalty. Hitherto no lay judge has advanced so far in rashness and impiety. The arguments by which he proves this show the crassest ignorance both of canon law and of our custom. Perhaps it will not be unwelcome to Your Eminence to set out briefly before your eyes the ancient and recent practice of the courts in this matter; it will certainly greatly help to expose the malicious ignorance of that author. Thus matters stood among us for 150 years, from when the Church's liberty first began to be publicly debated, down to the civil wars under Henry IV, as our ancient jurists teach. Although by divine law clerics are exempt from secular power, a lay judge could nevertheless proceed in some cases against their persons criminally, and in others civilly. In the former category they agree entirely with canon law, for they embrace only those cases in which a cleric, either before or after the third admonition, has by the canons and papal decrees forfeited every clerical privilege by the very fact of the offence.

units.la: Secundi membri casus vocant privilegiatos, ideo ab annis 250. paulo plus minusve celebris in foro fuit criminis, quod ad Clericos attinet, distinctio in privilegiatum & commune; privilegiatum dicebatur illud, cujus cognitionem sibi vendicare poterant Judices Laici, quod privilegiatum dicebant, eo quod jus illud cognitionis Pontificis privilegio se habere jactabant; in illud autem animadvertebant civiliter tantùm, nunquam criminaliter, hoc est propter crimen illud commissum Cleri-cus multa pecuniaria tantum puniebatur, cogebaturque in carceribus [illegible, ~3 letters]iscopalibus subsistere, donec satisfecisset[?], sed in ipsius personam aliquid attentare nefas ducebant; antiquiores pragmatici duos tantùm ejusmodi enumerant, quos barbare vocant portum (portationem) armorum, & salvæ guardiæ regiæ infractionem, hoc est, rei, quæ sub manu & profectione regia posita erat, direptionem: quatuor alios lapsu temporis addiderunt, tum rex actor erat, tum contra litis ordinem Clericus reus regis actoris forum sequi tenebatur, quia, inquiunt, rex non litigat in curia subditi.
units.tr: The cases of the second category they call privileged. Therefore, for some 250 years, more or less, a distinction between privileged and common crime, as far as clerics were concerned, was fairly well known in the courts. That was called privileged of which lay judges could claim cognizance, and they called it privileged because they boasted that they held that right of cognizance by privilege of the Pontiff. For such offences they punished only civilly, never criminally: that is, for such a crime the cleric was punished only with a large fine, and was compelled to remain in the episcopal prisons until he had made satisfaction. But they considered it an outrage to attempt anything against his person. The older practical writers list only two such offences, which they barbarously call portum (portationem) armorum, the carrying of arms, and the infraction of the royal safeguard, that is, the plundering of a thing placed under the royal hand and protection. In the course of time they added four others: when the king was the plaintiff, the cleric as defendant, contrary to the order of the suit, was bound to follow the forum of the royal plaintiff, because, they say, the king does not litigate in the court of a subject.

units.la: 2. Cum Clericus literis sua manu aut sigillo signatis obligatus est, licet actio ista sit mere personalis, vocari potest ad curiam Secularem, & tenebitur respondere literas istas suas esse fateri aut negare.
units.tr: 2. When a cleric has been bound by letters signed with his own hand or sealed with his seal, although that action is purely personal, he can be summoned to the secular court, and he will be obliged to answer whether he confesses or denies that those letters are his.

units.la: 3. Si Judicem Laicum in tribunali seden-tem injuria affecerit.
units.tr: 3. If he has insulted a lay judge sitting on the bench.

units.la: 4. Cùm Clericus prophanæ administrationi sese immiscet, illius administrationis rationem Laico Judici reddere tenetur, cùm tamen Judicem plerique hoc postremum aggredi religione aliqua percussi reformidarent.
units.tr: 4. When a cleric meddles in profane administration, he is bound to render an account of that administration to the lay judge, although most people, struck by some religious scruple, shrank from attacking the judge in this last matter.

units.la: Franciscus I. à Clemente VII. Bullam obtinuit, qua id illi concessum fuit; quæ in Parlamento publicè lecta est & registrata Anno 1531[?]. sic fere se res habuit ad mortem usqve Henrici II. Regis, id est, ad Annum 1559. cùm igitur quis Clericus crimen commiserat v. g. homicidium, furtum, &c. cum turba armata perpetraverat, duplex erat delictum, privilegiatum & commune; privilegiatum armorum portus; commune, furtum, homicidium , &c. prioris cognitio ad Laicum Judicem pertinebat, posteriotis ad Ecclesiasticum. Clericus in carcere Episcopali detinebatur, & ab Episcopo seu officiali de homicidio, furto, &c. examinabatur, curia verò duos consiliares delegebat, qui Clericum de portu armorum interrogarent, si portûs armorum reus peragebatur, pecuniæ summa à Curia multabatur, prohibebatque officiali, ne eum ante multæ solutionem dimitteret; homicidii verò, furti, &c. judicium pænaque officiali integra & illibata relinquebatur.
units.tr: Francis I obtained from Clement VII a bull by which this was granted to him. It was publicly read in Parliament and registered in the year 1531. Matters stood in much this way until the death of King Henry II, that is, until the year 1559. So when a cleric had committed a crime, for example homicide or theft, or had perpetrated it with an armed crowd, the offence was twofold, privileged and common: privileged for the carrying of arms, common for theft, homicide, and so on. Cognizance of the former belonged to the lay judge, of the latter to the ecclesiastical. The cleric was kept in the episcopal prison and examined by the Bishop or his official about the homicide, theft, and so on. The court appointed two counsellors who would question the cleric about carrying arms; if he was proceeded against as guilty of carrying arms, the court fined him a sum of money and forbade the official to release him before the fine was paid. But judgment and penalty for homicide, theft, and so on were left to the official, whole and unimpaired.

units.la: Paulatim civilis ille procedendi modus in criminalem respectu Clericorum minorum mutatus est, si crimen aliquod atrox commisisset, v. g. si patrem aut matrem trem occidissent, si virginem rapuissent & violassent, aut quid aliud non minoris atrocitatis crimen commisissent; cui juris usurpationi occasionem dederunt duæ Bullæ Pontificiæ, prior à Leone X. data, qvi trinæ monitionis Clerico vestem Clericalem deserenti necessitatem tollit, ut omni privilegio Clericali exuatur, necessitatem solum imponit Bullam qvotannis tribus primis qvadragesimæ Dominicis in Ecclesiis Episcopalibus legendi : posterior licentiam dat Regi Clericos in monetæ cusione servientes nulla habita Clericalis privilegii ratione judicandi & puniendi, cujus mentionem faciunt Franciscus I. in constitut. An. 1540. & Henricus II. in constituit. 1549. passim igitur Clericis minoribus à Judice Laico nulla habita ratione Clericalis privilegii, non tantum amplius civiliter, sed etiam criminaliter punitis, paulatim ad Sacratos Clericos deventum est, si crimen aliqvod atrox contra publicam tranqvillitatem perpetrassent, v.g. si cum prædonibus, publicis viis in[?]dentes, hominem occidissent. Judi-ci sacro offerebatur degradandus, qvod se præstiturum negabat eò qvod de more criminis communis homicidii scilicet cognitionem non habuisset, persistente vero Judice Sacro in degradationis de negatione ; Clericus Sacratus non degradatus morte afficiebatur, sed hoc rarissime contingebat, licet jam tum hæreticorum furoribus tumultuaretur Gallia; cùm tamen aliqvoties in atrocissimis criminibus id factum esset, conqvemente Clero, id prohibuit edicto Carolus IX. Anno 1571. non obstante tamen prohibitione ista, paulatim ab atrocissimis criminibus ad vulgaria, homicidia, adulteria, futura, &c. devenerunt, eaqve privilegiata dici voluerunt; tandem ipsi soli horum criminum litis non vocato Officiali instruxerunt, morteqve damnatum Sacerdotem, si degradare recusat Episcopus, qvod semper recusat, qvoties litem non instruxit, non degraad-tum supplicio afficiunt.
units.tr: Gradually that civil mode of proceeding was changed into a criminal one with regard to minor clerics. If such a cleric had committed some atrocious crime, for example had killed his father or mother, had seized and violated a virgin, or had committed some other crime of no less atrocity, the usurpation of this right was occasioned by two Papal Bulls. The first, given by Leo X, removed the requirement of three warnings before a cleric who abandoned clerical dress was stripped of all clerical privilege; it imposed only the requirement that the Bull be read each year on the three first Sundays of Lent in the cathedral churches. The second gave the King licence to judge and punish, without any regard to clerical privilege, the clerics who served in the minting of coin. Francis I, in his constitution of 1540, and Henry II, in his constitution of 1549, make mention of this. Thus, minor clerics were punished by the lay judge, with no regard to clerical privilege, not only civilly but also criminally, and gradually the practice extended to sacred clerics, if they had perpetrated some atrocious crime against public tranquillity, for example by killing a man in the company of robbers while falling upon him on the public roads. The sacred judge offered him to be degraded, but he refused to submit to this, on the ground that by custom he had not been given cognizance of a common crime such as homicide. If the sacred judge persisted in the degradation despite his refusal, the sacred cleric, not degraded, was put to death. This happened very rarely, although France was already then in turmoil from the fury of the heretics. Yet since it had happened several times in the most atrocious crimes, at the request of the clergy Charles IX forbade it by an edict of 1571. Nevertheless, despite this prohibition, they gradually moved from the most atrocious crimes to ordinary ones, homicides, adulteries, thefts, and so on, and wished these to be called privileged. Finally, they themselves alone conducted the trial of these crimes, without summoning the Official, and put to death the priest who had been condemned, if the Bishop refused to degrade him, as he always refused whenever the case had not been conducted by the Bishop; they did not put him to death once degraded.

units.la: Qvamqvam velim, notet hac in causa E. V. primùm Clerum Gallicanum nunquam approbasse Judicum Laicorum usurpationem, qua de Clericis saltem Sacratis criminaliter judicant extra casus in jure aut Bullis privilegiorum dissertissime expressas, famamque privilegio pro privilegio nunquam admisse imo nunquam admisisse eam consvetudinem, qua de iis, ut explicatum est, civiliter judicant; referre possem multos jurisconsultos Gallos, qui in eos gravi-ter invecti sunt, imò scripserunt, eos i-deo excommunicatos[?]. Hactenus hoc nos docet quotidiana praxis, nusquam enim permittunt Episcopi sic condemnatos degradari; at libri autor hæc approbat, ut æqua, justa, & Canonica.
units.tr: Although I would like Your Excellency to note in this matter, first, that the French clergy has never approved the usurpation by which lay judges pass criminal sentence on clerics, at least consecrated clerics, outside the cases expressly stated in law or in papal bulls of privilege. Nor have they ever admitted that a reputation of privilege counts as privilege, or indeed that custom by which, as has been explained, they judge such men in civil matters. I could cite many French jurists who attacked these practices severely, and even wrote that those who took part were for this reason excommunicated[?]. Everyday practice teaches us this much: bishops never allow men so condemned to be degraded. Yet the author of the book approves these things as fair, just and canonical.

units.la: 2. Istorum criminum cognitionem, si ad Episcopos deferatur, aut Episcopi præveniant, non negant Judices Laici ad Episcopos pertinere, nec ipsi hic litibus ab Episcopo occupatis nisi data aliqua sententia provocetur ab abusu, sese immiscent; at libri autor omnem horum criminum cognitionem ut debitam à tribunali Ecclesiastico abjudicat, docetque solos Laicos esse legitimos & competentes criminum Judices. 3. Hactenus si pro actione civili in personam Clerici adeatur Sacer Judex, nullus pragmaticus obtinetur, aut causabitur judicem esse incompetentem; at autor libri vult hoc esse peculiare foro Seculari, & ei legitimè & per se convenire. 4. Vult crimina, quae respiciunt actus humanos, quorum cognitionem habent Episcopi, dicta fuisse privilegiata eò quòd privilegium hoc eis indulserint Reges; hinc colligit jurisdictionem illam à Principibus & eorum judicibus pro libidine limitari, prorogari & abrogari posse; at o-mnium Juris Consultorum & Canonistarum Francicorum testimonio privilegiata crimina sunt, non quae cogno-scunt Episcopi, sed quae cognoscunt Lai-ci, eò quòd eorum cognoscendorum à Pontifice privilegium Reges acceperint; cùm autem antiqui nostri jurisconsulti de hac re disputantes nullum tale privilegium allegare possunt, famam privile-giii gii ad tuendam judicum conscientiam sufficere scripserunt; postea Reges Franciscus I. & Henricus II. in nonnullis causis Bullas, ut dictum est, à Pontificibus obtinerunt; unicus Legulejus ante 20 Annos sic privilegiata crimina interpretatus est, sed nomen libro, quo ridiculam expositionem ante ipsum inauditam enarrat, præponere ausus non est; at libri novi autor nomen & societatis suæ & suum præposuit.
units.tr: 2. If cases of these crimes are referred to bishops, or the bishops get to them first, lay judges do not deny that they belong to the bishops, and they do not interfere in suits already taken up by a bishop unless an appeal is made against abuse after some sentence has been given. The author of the book, however, strips the ecclesiastical tribunal of all cognizance of these crimes and teaches that only laymen are the lawful and competent judges of crimes. 3. Hitherto, when a civil action against the person of a cleric has been brought before an ecclesiastical judge, no pragmatic sanction has been obtained, and no one has pleaded that the judge is incompetent. But the author of the book wants this to be a special right of the secular forum, one that belongs to it lawfully and of its own accord. 4. He holds that crimes which concern human acts, and whose cognizance belongs to bishops, were called privileged because the kings granted this privilege to the bishops. From this he infers that that jurisdiction may be limited, extended and revoked at the whim of the princes and their judges. Yet by the testimony of all the French jurists and canonists, the privileged crimes are not those which bishops cognize, but those which laymen cognize, since the kings received from the Pope the privilege of trying them. Since our older jurists, when discussing this matter, could cite no such privilege, they wrote that the reputation of a privilege was enough to safeguard the judges' conscience. Later, Kings Francis I and Henry II obtained bulls from the popes in some cases, as has been said. Only Legulejus, twenty years ago, interpreted privileged crimes in this way, yet he did not dare to put his name to the book in which he set out this ridiculous explanation, which no one had heard of before. But the author of the new book has put his own name, and that of his society, at the front.

units.la: 5. Quod nemo cogitaret, cujus nullum hactenus est exemplum, & innumera in contrarium Laicos Episcoporum Judices constituit, ita ut in eos ut in Laicos criminaliter procedere possint, morteque eos damnare, quæ nullus Legalejus, nullus pragmaticus scribere ausus fuerat; longè atrociora evidenter innuit; legantur, pag. 30, 31, 36. 37 & seq. res quasque sanctissimas subjicit Laicali sententiæ nulla habita ratione sententiæ Ecclesiastica præcedentis; cujus hac in causa Laicalis esse tantum debet Executrix; sed hæc longum perse-
units.tr: 5. He makes lay judges the judges of bishops, so that they may proceed against them criminally as laymen and condemn them to death. Nobody would think of this, there is no example of it hitherto, and countless instances point the other way. No legal writer, no pragmatic author, had dared to write this; he clearly hints at things far more atrocious. Let them be read at pp. 30, 31, 36, 37 and following. He subjects the most sacred matters to lay sentence, with no regard for a prior ecclesiastical sentence, when in this matter the lay power ought to be only its executor. But to pursue these points at length...

units.la: Quid de Matrimonio dicam[?]hactenus invaluerat istud, Matrimonia regi jure poli, non jure fori, Reges posse condere Leges ad honestatem Matrimonii spe-ctantes, non ad substantiam. Iisdem adhuc respondent omnes antiqui Curia-rum Senatores, Regum Leges & arresta sua ad effectus civiles spectare, hoc est, dotem, haereditatem, paraphernalia, donationes,non ad Matrimonii substan-tialem diruptionem; at ille omnium Catholicorum primus dixit, Laicos Ma-trimonium irritare posse, & Principes Leges Matrimonium dirimentes conde-re; similli temeritate & impietate libero-rum adultorum conjugia sine parentum consensu esse nulla & irrita, haec contra perpetuam in Gallia ut & in aliis locis praxim & Concilii Trident. decreta; quoslibet praeterea Clericos vectigales proPrincipum voluntate facit non secus ac apud nos rustici virique ignobiles; contra Canones nullam scribere audet Pontificis requirendam licentiam, imo ipsius argumenta eo inclinant, ut inconsulto Pontifice, & invitis Clericis capta[?]ri possint; consideret denique E. V. quid sibi velit in isto libro, & hoc potissimum tempore longa illa disputatio qua contendit in Patriarchatu Romano novum Patriarchatum erigi posse, ut olim Patriarchatus C. P. & Hierosolym; denique utrumque Imperatorum favore sustentatum, Pontificibus licet repugnantibus, vim autoritatemque obtinuisse, cui tandem Pontifices consenserint.
units.tr: Fifth, he suggests things far more atrocious, which no one would think of, of which there is no example hitherto, and which countless others contradict: that he makes laymen judges of Bishops, so that they may proceed criminally against them as against laymen and condemn them to death. No Legulejus, no pragmatic writer, has dared to write such things. Let them be read at pages 30, 31, 36, 37 and following. He subjects the most holy things to lay sentence, with no regard to a preceding ecclesiastical sentence, of which in this matter the lay power ought only to be the executor. But I shall not go on at length about these things. What shall I say about marriage? Hitherto this had prevailed: that marriages are governed by political law, not by the law of the forum; that Kings can make laws concerning the honesty of marriage, but not concerning its substance. All the ancient senators of the courts still answer the same, that the laws and decrees of Kings look to civil effects, that is, dowry, inheritance, paraphernalia, and gifts, and not to the substantial dissolution of marriage. But that man, the first of all Catholics, has said that laymen can annul marriage, and that princes can enact laws dissolving marriage. With similar rashness and impiety he says that the marriages of adult children without the consent of their parents are null and void. This is contrary to the perpetual practice in France, as in other places, and to the decrees of the Council of Trent. Moreover, he makes whatever clerics he likes tributary at the will of princes, no differently from our rustics and ignoble men. Contrary to the canons, he dares to write no licence to be sought from the Pope; indeed, his arguments tend towards this, that without consulting the Pope, and against the will of the clerics, they may be seized. Let Your Excellency finally consider what he means in this book, and especially at this time, with that long disputation in which he contends that a new Patriarchate can be erected in the Roman Patriarchate, as once the Patriarchates of Constantinople and Jerusalem were; and that these, supported by the favour of both Emperors, though the Popes resisted, obtained force and authority, to which the Popes at last consented.

units.la: Dat. Paris Id, ib. Maij, 1642.
units.tr: Given at Paris, Id. ib. May, 1642.

units.la: EPIST. LXIV.
units.tr: EPISTLE LXIV.

units.la: Joh. Morinus Cardinali Barberino in favorem Translationis Episcopi Carnu- tensis in Archiepiscopum Rhemen-sem.
units.tr: Jean Morin to Cardinal Barberini, in favour of the translation of the Bishop of Chartres to the Archbishopric of Reims.

units.la: Eminentissimo Cardinali Barberino.
units.tr: To the most eminent Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: Eminentissime Cardinalis,
units.tr: Most eminent Cardinal,

units.la: PAucos ante dies longâ Epistolâ respondi iis, quæ à me rescire desiderabat Eminentia Vestra. Ipsi datam suisse[?]non dubito, qvare eorum narrationem supersedeo; aliud est, cujus causa hâc Epistolâ E. V. supplex oro; Illustrissimus Episcopus Carnutensis ad Archiepiscopatum Rhemensem à Rege Christianissimo electus est, jam humanissimè & benevolè ejus preces audivit E. V. si translationem ipsius ad Archiepiscopatum illum à summo Pontifice obtinuerit, Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ optimè consultum est. Vir est enim longo usu & multa exercitatione negotiorum Ecclesiasticarum peritissimus, doctrinaqve omni, quæ Episcopum decet, celebris; ab Annis 25 nullus Cleri Conventus aut ordinarius aut extraordinarius habitus est, cui non interfuerit, anno proxime elapso cum extraordinarie Ecclesiasticus Conventus haberetur, ipseqve prima vocatione non essetei adscriptus, omnium voto & suffragiis allectus est; itaqve magnum operæ pretium Em. Vestra Ecclesiæ factura est, si à summo Pontifice translationem hanc impetraverit. Tanti viri Panegyricum hic instituere non desideravi, nec eo opus habet, cùm ipsius præclaræ actiones in Gallia sint notissimæ & E. V. latere non possint; illarum tamen eam memorem facere volui, ut officio, qvo & Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ & tam celebris Episcopi virtuti devinctus sum, defungar; confidentiam meam E. V. pro benevolentia, qva me complectitur, boni consulturam spero, eam qvam diutissime Deus Ecclesiæ suæ servet incolumem.
units.tr: A few days ago I answered at length the questions which Your Eminence wished me to explain. I do not doubt that the answers were delivered to him, so I will leave out their account here. The other matter, for which I humbly beg Your Eminence by this letter, is this. The most illustrious Bishop of Chartres has been chosen by the Most Christian King for the Archbishopric of Reims, and Your Eminence has most kindly and graciously heard his petition. If Your Eminence obtains his translation to that archbishopric from the supreme Pontiff, the Gallican Church will be very well served. For he is a man most skilled in ecclesiastical affairs through long experience and much practice, and he is renowned for all the learning that befits a bishop. For 25 years no clerical assembly, ordinary or extraordinary, has been held which he did not attend. When an extraordinary ecclesiastical assembly was held in the year just past, although he had not been included in the first summons, he was chosen by the vote and suffrage of all. Therefore Your Eminence will do the Church a great service if you obtain this translation from the supreme Pontiff. I have not wished to make a panegyric of so great a man here, nor does he need one, since his distinguished actions in France are very well known and cannot be hidden from Your Eminence. Still, I wished to mention them, so that I might discharge the duty by which I am bound both to the Gallican Church and to the virtue of so celebrated a bishop. I hope Your Eminence will take this boldness of mine in good part, in view of the goodwill with which you embrace me, and may God keep the Church safe for as long as possible.

units.la: Parisiis 10. Kal. Junii, 1642.
units.tr: Paris, 10 days before the Kalends of June, 1642.

units.la: EPIST. LXV.
units.tr: LETTER LXV.

units.la: Johannes Morinus Cardinali Barberino scribit in favorem Domini de Marca ad Episcopatum Coseranensem deno- minati.
units.tr: Johannes Morinus writes to Cardinal Barberini in favour of Lord de Marca, nominated to the bishopric of Coserans.

units.la: Cardinali Barberino.
units.tr: To Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: Jamdiu multumqve est, cùm Eminentiam tuam variis ac difficillimis negotiis occupatam literis meis interpellare non sum ausus; nonnihil enim timebam, ne intempestiva mea observantia Eminentiæ tuæ fastidium crearet; verùm nunc occasio mihi datur, & diuturni mei silentii abrumpendi & obseqviosissimè meæ observantiæ hâc Epistolâ innovandæ. Illustrissimus de Marca in Parlamento Palensi Præses, & in Sanctiori Regis Christianissimi Consilo ordinarius Consiliarius ad Episcopatum de Cose-rans designatus est. Vir est apud nos eruditione non modo sæculari, sed etiam Ecclesiastica celeberrimus, Religionis Catholicæ studiosissimus, atque ex illustri familia oriundus, cui hoc laudi datur, quòd ab antiqua Religione nunquam defecerit, licet in regione habitaret, in qua primum hæreseos Palladium in Gallia collocatum est, quamque hæretici annis sexaginta fere integris oppresserunt. Hujus rei testis esse possum, qui abhinc annos circiter duodecim cum eo sæpius familiariter versatus sum, variisque de rebus, quæ Religionem disciplinamque Eccles. spectant, contuli; librum eruditissimum scripsit de Concordia Sacerdotii & Regni, materia ubique que fere, sed in Gallia potissimum anceps, lubrica, & perdifficilis, de cujus Scriptore id Homeri merito usurpari potest ἐπὶ ξυρῷ ἵσταται ἀκμῆς ; de ea tamen ita scripsit Parlamenti præses, ut in confesso sit apud omnes hujus rei peritos, neminem è foro scriptorem abhinc annos centum & viginti Ecclesiasticæ autoritati magis fuisse, viamque ad antiqua ejus πρεσβεῖα [?] recuperanda confidentius aperuisse, ita ut nonnullis in foro viris primariis prævaricationis suspectus haberetur ; ex quo colligere est, quanta animi confidentia & solertia Episcopus factus eandem autoritatem asserturus sit & propugnaturus ; meam de Viro optimo sententiam Eminentiæ tuæ testificari consultum visum est, non tam ei gratificandi causa, quam Ecclesiæ Gallicanæ, cujus clarissimum lumen aliquando futurus est ; cæterùm Eminentissime Cardinalis hoc unice E. T. & oro & exorare velim, ut me benevolentia sua complecti non desinat, humillimumque obsequium meum à multis annis illi consecratum[?], quodque iterum lubentissimè; quantulumcunque est, offero, æqui boniqe, ut sæpius amanter fecit, consulere dignetur. Deus Opt. Max. te Ecclesiæ suæ quam diutissime conservet incolumem.
units.tr: For a long time now, since Your Eminence is occupied with various and very difficult affairs, I have not dared to interrupt you with my letters. I was somewhat afraid that my untimely devotion might cause Your Eminence annoyance. But now an occasion is given me both to break my long silence and to renew my most dutiful devotion by this letter. The most illustrious de Marca, President of the Parliament of Pau and an ordinary councillor in the Most Holy Council of the most Christian King, has been designated to the bishopric of Couserans. Among us he is a man most celebrated, not only for secular learning but also for ecclesiastical learning, most devoted to the Catholic Religion, and sprung from an illustrious family. This is to his credit: he never fell away from the ancient Religion, although he lived in the region where the Palladium of heresy was first set up in France and which the heretics oppressed for almost sixty full years. I can bear witness to this, since for about twelve years I have often been on familiar terms with him and have conferred with him on various matters concerning the religion and discipline of the Church. He wrote a most learned book on the Concord of Priesthood and Kingdom, a subject which is everywhere delicate, but especially in France doubtful, slippery and very difficult. Of its writer one may rightly use that line of Homer: "he stands on the edge of a razor" [ἐπὶ ξυρῷ ἵσταται ἀκμῆς]. Yet the President of Parliament wrote about it in such a way that all experts in the matter agree that no writer from the bar for the past one hundred and twenty years has been a greater champion of ecclesiastical authority, or has more confidently opened the way to recovering its ancient prerogative [πρεσβεῖα], so that he was suspected of prevarication by some leading men at the bar. From this one may gather how much spirit and skill the bishop, once made, will show in asserting and defending that same authority. It seemed right to bear witness to Your Eminence to my opinion of this excellent man, not so much to do him a favour as for the sake of the Gallican Church, of which he will one day be a most clear light. Most eminent Cardinal, this one thing above all I beg and implore of Your Eminence: that you not cease to embrace me with your goodwill, and that you deign, as you have often kindly and fairly done, to take into account my most humble service, consecrated to you for many years, which I again most gladly offer, however small it is. May the best and greatest God keep you safe for his Church for as long as possible.

units.la: FElicissimus ego mortaliūsum[?]. Quamobrem verò ? quia non tam scribere ad me, quàm effundere viscera animi erga nos benevoli, tibi placuit: quo quidem beneficio longe indignissimus homuncio Nihusius. Viderit perquàm Illustris meus D. Turrius, beneficiis istius pro me procurator. Ita enim affectus ego inde, ut ne quidem sciam, quibus verbis gratias agam; ita, inquam, sentio, me obrutum à Sole hujus ævi, Morino. Longe gratissimum profecto est mihi tuum judicium de iis, quæ ad fabricam Dominicæ Crucis pertinent; jam aveo doceri cum tempore, quid observaverint hodie suismet oculis, quibus ejus reliquias videndi copia fuit. Multo gratissimum pariter est, quod suppeditas nobis de Cassandriano illo, (hic enim locorum sic vocari genus istoc hominum cœpit.) unicum est, quo me perplexum reddis: Offers operam tuam, ubi usui esse possit. Si non acceptem, in Deum ingratissimus sim; sin acceptem, fieri possit, ut fiam impudens in petendo: εὕρηκα. Petam exiguum, & eâ quidem lege, ut silentio, quàm responso dignum potius censeas me, si visum fuerit. Quid obsecro causæ est, quod in ordine Romano, & opusculo, quod insertum anno superiore, Bibliothecæ Patrum l. 6. p. 188. qui Sanguinem Domi-ni sumunt, non communicari sed confir-mari mari dicuntur? Cassander ille (qui Coloniae resipuit ante obitum, & indicta sua cupiens, professioni fidei Pii IV. pag.218. subscripsit) saltem occasionem dat explicandi negotium; si tamen id meretur peculiarem operam, inspicerem observationes Sacras Josephi Vicecomitis: verum mon reperiuntur in hisce regionibus: porro unum necessarium est. Magne vir, Deus te conservet Ecclesiæ suæ bono, seu splendori potius, ut conservavit hactenus.
units.tr: I am most fortunate of mortals [text unclear]. Why? Because you were pleased to write to me not so much as to pour out the feelings of your kindly heart toward us. I, Nihusius, am a most unworthy little man to receive this kindness. Let my most illustrious Mr. Turrius see to it, he who procures these benefits for me. I am so moved by it that I do not even know with what words to thank you. I feel, I say, overwhelmed by the Sun of this age, Morinus. Your judgment on the matters concerning the construction of the Lord's Cross is most welcome indeed. I am eager to learn in due time what those who had the chance to see its relics observed with their own eyes today. Equally welcome is what you supply us about that Cassandrian (for this is what people of that sort in these parts have begun to be called). There is one point that leaves me perplexed. You offer your help where it may be of use. If I did not accept, I would be most ungrateful to God; if I did accept, I may become shameless in asking. Eureka! [εὕρηκα] I will ask for a little, and on this condition: that you think me worthy of silence rather than of a reply, if you think fit. What, I beg you, is the reason that in the Roman Order, and in the little work inserted last year in the Bibliotheca Patrum, volume 6, page 188, those who take the Blood of the Lord are said not to be communicated but confirmed? That Cassander (who repented at Cologne before his death, and, wishing to be in good standing, subscribed to the profession of faith of Pius IV, page 218) at least gives an occasion for explaining the matter. If, however, the matter deserves special effort, I would examine the sacred observations of Joseph Vicecomes, but they are not to be found in these regions. Further, one thing is necessary. Great man, may God preserve you for the good, or rather the splendour, of his Church, as he has preserved you until now.

units.la: Est hic locorum vir aliqvis excellens, tui æstimantissimus, qui vocatur Leonardus Marius, is te cupit salvere plurimum, ut ego, si occasio tulerit, Veronium etiam ac Rigaltium; qui nec abjuravi scribere: deinceps quoque, nihil dissimulo, quia gaudio plenus, è literis tuis, Patrone exoptatissime, penitusque optime.
units.tr: There is here in these parts some outstanding man, one of your great admirers, called Leonardus Marius. He wishes you many greetings, as I do; and if the occasion arises, Veronius too and Rigaltius, to whom I have not ceased to write. Henceforth too I conceal nothing: since I am full of joy at your letter, most desired patron, and most heartily well.

units.la: Quod attinet ad Sacramentum poenitentiæ, cujus modum, ceremonias, poenas injunctas confitenti, aliaque hujusmodi scire peroptas, dico, aliquos confiteri stantes, aliquos sedentes, genuflexi aliquos, prout locus & tempus postulant; peccatis secretis secreta injungitur poenitentia, quæ ut plurimum sunt jejunia, genuflexiones, peregrinationes, orationes, eleemosynæ, &c. peccatis publicis publica infligitur poenitentia, quod ut exactioni tuæ faciam satis, referam ea, quæ habentur in capite de forfornicatione : Dixit ille, cui gloria : qvicunqve homo ex filiis Israël, aut illis, qvi veniunt ad me, seminat semen suum in muliere extranea, occidatur homo ille, & obruat illum lapidibus omnis populus; at Pontifices legis Evangelicæ amplexandos esse existimarunt pœnitentes, cùm dicat Altissimus: nolo mortem peccatoris : qvamobrem constituerunt pro his Canones, qvos aliqvi faciliores addiderunt, alii verò magis arduos, prout sibi visum est, & ratio facilioris & ardui operis suadebat, & pœnitentis ferebat constantia, aut remissio, & vires vel animi vel corporis ; & consideraverunt in hoc tempus, & locum, & posfibilitatem: fornicator autem aut est Sacerdos aut Laicus: Si est Sacerdos & cœlebs, jejunet & oret annum integrum, & Ministerio Sacerdotali interdicatur, donec prætereat annus, tum revertatur ad ministerium suum, ut prius: si autem fuerit Laicus, jejunet septem septimanas. Fidelis si coinqvinatus fuerit cum masculo, jejunet & oret qvatuor annos, tum suscipiatur & communioni restituatur: si autem incidet interea in periculum vitæ ante absolutum tempus, detur illi communio, cùm absolutum non sit tempus. Si quinquagenarium is attigit annum & fuerit cælebs, ne plus nimio opprimatur, ne pereat, sed decernat illi confessarius, prout sibi videbitur & illius ferat conditio, ut mereatur misericordiam & propitiationem Christi, &c.
units.tr: As for the Sacrament of penance, whose manner, ceremonies, the penances imposed on the confessing person, and other such things you are eager to know, I say this: some confess standing, some sitting, some kneeling, as place and time require. For secret sins a secret penance is imposed, which for the most part consists of fasts, genuflections, pilgrimages, prayers, almsgivings, and so on. For public sins a public penance is inflicted. To give you full satisfaction on this, I will report what is found in the chapter on fornication. He to whom be glory said: whoever of the sons of Israel, or of those who come to me, sows his seed in a foreign woman, let that man be put to death, and let all the people stone him with stones. But the Pontiffs of the Evangelical law have judged that penitents should be embraced, since the Most High says: I do not desire the death of the sinner. Therefore they set down canons for these cases, some of which added easier ones, others harder ones, as seemed fit to them, and as the reason of an easier or harder work suggested, and as the constancy or leniency of the penitent, and his strength of mind or body, allowed. They also considered the time, the place and the possibility. A fornicator is either a priest or a layman. If he is a priest and celibate, let him fast and pray for a whole year, and let him be forbidden the priestly ministry until the year has passed; then let him return to his ministry as before. If, however, he is a layman, let him fast seven weeks. If a believer has defiled himself with a male, let him fast and pray four years; then let him be received and restored to communion. If in the meantime he falls into danger of life before the time is completed, let communion be given to him, since the time is not completed. If he has reached the age of fifty and is celibate, let him not be overwhelmed beyond measure, lest he perish; rather let his confessor decide for him as he sees fit and as his condition bears, so that he may merit the mercy and propitiation of Christ, and so on.

units.la: De absolutione hic ordo observatur, si peccata ejus sunt qualitatis, ut longam requirant pœnitentiam, eorumque causa interdicitur pœnitenti Sacramentorum usus, tum datur absolutio post exactam pœnitentiam: Si verò levia sunt peccata, statim datur absolutio, cujus formam cum non habeam ad manus, aliàs tibi illam mittam; similiter ea verba, quibus confessarius accedenti pœnitenti benedicit.
units.tr: Regarding absolution, this order is observed: if his sins are of such a kind that they require a long penance, and because of them the use of the Sacraments is forbidden to the penitent, then absolution is given after the penance has been completed. If, however, the sins are light, absolution is given at once. As I do not have its form at hand, I will send it to you otherwise; likewise the words with which the confessor blesses the penitent as he approaches.

units.la: De Ecclesiæ Maronitarum figura.
units.tr: On the figure of the Maronite churches.

units.la: Interior Ecclesiarum figura, & dispo-sitio quod ultimo loco scire optas, hujus-modi modi est. Primò Ecclesia perpetuo ita disponitur, ut janua versus occidentem semper pateat, & Altara orientem versus constituatur, ita ut celebrans orientem aspiciat. Secundo, Ecclesiæ ut plurimum tribus constant navibus, in quarum suprema parte tria sunt Altaria cancellis occlusa, intra quos nemo ingreditur, nisi Sacerdotes & Minores Clerici, jejuni tamen ; Laici verò ac præsertim mulieres perpetuò ab ingressu Sanctuarii arcentur & contactu Altarium: hujusmodi autem cancelli velis obducuntur, dum proferuntur verba consecratoria, & mysteriorum tunc aspectus Laicis interdicitur. In Ecclesiis hujusmodi formæ, & dispositionis, sinistra navis assignatur mulieribus, quæ ingrediuntur & egrediuntur per ejusdem navis Januam, cum unaquæque navis propriam habeat portam ; in Ecclesiis verò, quæ unicâ navi constant, posterior pars destinatur mulieribus, ita tamen ut se recipiant ad utrumque latus januæ, & nullo modo subsistant in medio Ecclesiæ. Finito Sa[?]cro[?], nullus virorum aut egreditur aut post se respicit, priusquàm mulieres egressæ fuerint. Ista separatio mulierum loci à viris fit propter honestatem. De loco, in quo leguntur Epistola & Evangelium non est eadem dispositio ubique: nam in quibusdam Ecclesiis leguntur prope Altare in plano loco, in aliis verò in loco edito ad summitatem cancellorum Sanctuarii, ita ut conspiciatur, qui legit, tam ab iis, qui sunt intra Sanctuarium, quam ab iis, qui sunt extra. Si hæc non sufficiunt, libenti animo alicujus Ecclesiæ adamussim tibi delineationem mittam.
units.tr: The interior figure and arrangement of their churches, which you ask about last, is as follows. First, a church is always laid out so that its door stands open towards the west, and the altars are set towards the east, so that the celebrant faces east. Second, the churches usually have three naves. In the uppermost part of these are three altars enclosed by screens, within which no one enters except priests and minor clerics, and they fast. Laymen, and women especially, are always kept from entering the sanctuary and from touching the altars. These screens are covered with veils while the words of consecration are spoken, and during that time laymen are forbidden to look upon the mysteries. In churches of this form and arrangement, the left nave is assigned to the women, who come and go through the door of that nave, since each nave has its own door. In churches with a single nave, the rear part is set aside for the women, but they must keep to either side of the door and must on no account stand in the middle of the church. When the Sacrifice is finished, no man leaves or looks back until the women have gone out. This separation of women from men is made for the sake of decency. The place where the Epistle and Gospel are read is not arranged the same everywhere. In some churches they are read near the altar, on a level floor; in others, from a raised place at the top of the sanctuary screens, so that the reader can be seen both by those inside the sanctuary and by those outside it. If these details are not enough, I will gladly send you an exact drawing of one of the churches.

units.la: Interea de mora in his describendis veniam posco, affecto enim animum meum (quamvis imparibus viribus) aliquo signo erga te tuaque declarare; quandoquidem is est meus erga Patrem Morinum affectus, ut vix (Deum testor) dici possit.
units.tr: Meanwhile I ask your pardon for the delay in describing these things. For I wish to show my feeling towards you and yours by some sign, though my powers are unequal to it, since my affection for Father Morin is such that (I call God to witness) it can scarcely be put into words.

units.la: Putabam me iterum, ac cito tua suavissima familiaritate coram Lutetiæ fruiturum: sed nescio, quo fato quove malo genio factum est, ut D. le Jay, cæteriqve amici longa mei oblivione capti sint, & nullis officiis meum promoverint negotium: modo scribo ad ipsum Eminentissimum Cardinalem Mazarinum, ut stet promissis, & una ad eundem literas commendationis mitto, uti per literas quoque certiores facio De le Jay & Vitray: interea dum responsum expecto rei hujus, me tuis bea [?] praeceptis.
units.tr: I thought I would enjoy your most pleasant company in Paris again, and soon. But I do not know by what fate or evil genius it has happened that Monsieur Le Jay and my other friends have been caught up in long forgetfulness of me and have done nothing to advance my business. I am now writing to the Most Eminent Cardinal Mazarin himself, that he may keep his promises, and I am sending a letter of recommendation to him with this one. I am also informing Le Jay and Vitray of this by letter. Meanwhile, while I await his reply on this matter, I remain at your blessed commands.

units.la: ERuditissimam Epistolam tuam, in qua de veteris Ecclesiæ partibus plura doctissidoctissimè disseris, & conjectaris, maxima cum voluptate legi ; & reconditiorem Ecclesiasticæ Antiqvitatis doctrinam admiratus, ingenuè fateor, nihil in ea esse clausum, qvod à te apertissimum factum non sit. Si qvid tamen in re ambigua mihi conandum esset, dum Recentiora cum Antiqvioribus, qvæ penitus immutata fuisse nemo diceret, confero, dicerem Tabulatum Bematis ab eo qvod Narthecis erat, qvam longissime abfuisse, non materia, qvæ eadem utriusqve esse potuit, sed mole: Narthecis enim homine depresius erat, Bematis totam Sanctuarii faciem occupabat, adeo ut tantum non omne occluderet, nihilqve reliqvum faceret, qvod apertum Christianorum, qvi officiis intererunt, oculis objiceretur: qvæ enim in Sanctuario fiebant, tanqvam in remota & occulta templi parte præter Sacerdotes non tantum corpore, sed oculis etiam alios adire nefas erat. Ideo omnia Tabulata suis etiam velis contegebantur. Et tantummodo ea pars patebat, qvæ foribus adapertis., sed media potissimum offerebatur, quæ non usque quaque adaperta est, sed velo etiam contracto, parte sui inferiore duabus portulis sese in medio conjungentibus, præter quàm cùm introitus fiant, & Sacerdos egreditur, & remeat, & Christi fidelibus Sacra Mysteria e-largitur, semper occlusa conspicitur.
units.tr: I read with great pleasure your most learned letter, in which you discuss and conjecture at length about the parts of the ancient Church, and I confess frankly that, marvelling at your deep knowledge of ecclesiastical antiquity, I find nothing in it that you have not made perfectly clear. If, however, I had to attempt something in a matter that is open to doubt, while comparing more recent things with more ancient ones, which no one would say were entirely unchanged, I would say that the platform of the bema was as far as possible from what the narthex was, not in material, which could have been the same for both, but in bulk. For the narthex was lower than a man, whereas the bema occupied the whole face of the sanctuary, so that it closed off almost everything and left nothing open to the eyes of the Christians who attended the services. For what was done in the sanctuary, as in a remote and hidden part of the church, it was forbidden for others to approach, not only bodily but even with their eyes, except for the priests. For this reason all the platforms were also covered with their own veils. Only that part was visible which was offered when the doors were opened, and chiefly the middle part, which was not opened on every side but, with the veil drawn back, was always seen closed at its lower part, where two little doors meet in the middle, except when the entrances are made, when the priest goes out and returns, and when he distributes the sacred mysteries to the faithful of Christ.

units.la: In Ecclesiis Plebanis, in quibus unus est Sacerdos, etiam extra dies Dominicos, & Festos, aliis feriis sive ita postulante populo, vel elemosyna data ad id compellente, vel religione etiam propria, Sacerdos si ita libuerit, Liturgiam celebrat. Hinc fit aliquando, ut singulis diebus, nullo intermisso Missa habeatur; & quadragesimali tempore, cùm libuerit Sacerdoti præsanctificata offeruntur, sin minus decantatis Vespe-ris, & aliis officiis absque præsanctificatorum Missa domum regreditur; observavi tamen in Ecclesiis Plebanis plures in quadragesima Præsanctificatorum missas, quam in Monasteriis & bene constitutis Ecclesiis celebrari; in his enim rare Præsanctificatorum Liturgia aliis feriis, semper tamen Liturgia perfecta Sabbatis & Dominicis conficitur. Quare Die Dominico, cùm celebrant, numerant sibi dies, quibus ea hebdomade Præsanctificata offerre constituunt, & tum demum pro dierum numero, æqualesque quoque particulas consecratas reponunt. Estque in his ordo apud illos, ordinem non servare, cùm nullus Præsanctificatorum certus numerus præscribatur, sed omnia ex arbitrio Sacerdotis celebrantis pendent.
units.tr: In parish churches, where there is one priest, the priest celebrates the Liturgy, if he so wishes, even on days other than Sundays and feasts, on weekdays, whether the people so request, or an alms offering urges him to it, or from his own personal devotion. Hence it sometimes happens that Mass is held every day without interruption. And in Lent, when the priest wishes, the presanctified gifts are offered; otherwise, after the Vespers and the other services have been sung, he goes home without the Mass of the presanctified. Yet I have observed that more Masses of the presanctified are celebrated in Lent in parish churches than in monasteries and well-ordered churches; for in these the Liturgy of the presanctified is rarely celebrated on weekdays, but the full Liturgy is always celebrated on Saturdays and Sundays. Therefore, on Sunday, when they celebrate, they count the days on which they have decided to offer presanctified gifts that week, and then at last they set aside consecrated portions equal in number to the days and likewise equal in size. Among them, not to keep this order is itself a custom, since no fixed number of presanctified offerings is prescribed, but everything depends on the discretion of the celebrating priest.

units.la: De forma Ecclesiarum illud etiam observo, non omnes fuisse quadratas oblongas, & tantummodo brachiis in Austrum & Boream protensis Crucis signum expressisse, cujusmodi sunt plerà-que in Italia: cùm illæ, quas σταυρωτὰς, sive σταυροειδεῖς, nuncupant, perfectam omnino crucem quatuor æqualibus partibus in medio coherentibus efficerent, quod hodie manifeste conspicitur in oppido Armoliæ in Chio insula: in eo enim ad hunc diem vetustissima Ecclesia conspicitur immensis sumptibus extru-cta, quaeque ad crucis perfectam similitudinem quatuor brachia in longum æqualiter protensa in media trulla colligat. Hinc mihi autumo formam, quam nomine præferunt, non in fornicibus & arcibus, atque parte sui superiore, sed in-seriore etiam & pavimento, & qua innituntur structura reddidisse. Confessio Græcorum recentiorum in Insula Chio & ferme aliis insulis quomodo conficiatur, exponam: nam de aliis Græcis partibus mihi non liquet, & forte etiam ibi alius modus observatur. Confessionem auditurus in Ecclesia sive etiam domi, appenso Peritrachelio, sedet; Pœnitens sive mulier sive vir in scamnulo penes eundem accumbit, aperto capite, reverens & totus ad pietatem compositus. Post preces à Sacerdote in pœnitentem effusas, & exhortatiunculam ad promptè[?] peccata omnia confitendum, narrat pœnitens, quidquid præter jus fasque admisit. Postmodum & Sacerdos interrogans memoriam vel-licat, licat, è qva si qvid elapsum est, in mentem reducit. Confessione completa, orationes illas ἐπὶ τῶν ἐξομολογουμένων[?] recitat, ἐπιτίμιον[?] imponit, benedicit & dimittit. Poenitens si ἐπιτίμιον[?] illud est, quod ante Communioni Sacrum diem perfici potest, eo absoluto ad Communionem accedit; si plures requirat dies, licet id non exsolverit, communicat tamen, postea reliquum absolvit: nisi à Sacerdote injunctum fuerit, ut non nisi completa poenitentia ad Eucharistiæ Communionem accedat: tunc enim omnino obedit, nec communicat; Quemadmodum & cùm ob aliquod enorme peccatum jussu Sacerdotis à communione prohibetur. Nec alium ipse poenitentiæ usum jam dictis in locis observavi: habent tamen quædam alia minoris momenti, sed his satis interrogationibus Morini occurritur. Curavi, ut tam quæ Simeon Thessalonicensis in[?] Dialogo de Sacramentis, de Poenitentia disserit, quàm quæ Johannes Monachus, qui se Basilii Magni discipulum nuncupat, in opusculo de pænis pœnitentibus infligendis enunciat, ex Codicibus Vaticanis exscriberentur, eaqve ad te deferenda Patri Germano, qvi tuas mihi reddidit litteras, consignavi; ex scriptorum Græcorum inopia sive socordia, qvæ non nisi magno pretio in Vaticanum expellitur, in causa fuit, ut hoc tempus omne, ante qvam voluntati obtemperaretur tuæ, insumeretur, qvod brevissimum fuerit, si tempora expendas, & qvibus hæc nostra Europæ pars urgetur incommoda. Si qvid ergo interim opus est, impera: ero memor & diligens, ut qvæ imperes, compareant. Vale mi Morine, Vale, & tuum Leonem, tui obse-qventissimum, ut facis, ama.
units.tr: Regarding the form of the churches, I also observe that not all were oblong and square, and that they did not merely express the sign of the cross with arms stretched out to the south and north, as most are in Italy. Those that they call stavrotas or staurocidi [σταυρωτὰς, σταυροειδεῖς] made a perfect cross with four equal parts cohering in the middle. This is plainly visible today in the town of Armolia on the island of Chios, for there to this day one sees a very ancient church built at immense expense, which gathers four arms, extended equally in length, into a central dome so as to resemble a perfect cross. Hence I think that the form they bear in name was produced not only in the vaults and arches and their upper part, but also in the lower part, the floor, and the structure on which they rest. I will set out how the confession of the more recent Greeks is made on the island of Chios and in nearly the other islands, for I am not clear about the other Greek regions, and perhaps a different practice is observed there too. The penitent, about to make confession in the church or even at home, sits with the epitrachelion hung on him; the penitent, whether a woman or a man, sits on a small stool beside him, with head bare, reverent and wholly composed to piety. After the prayers poured out over the penitent by the priest, and a short exhortation to confess all sins promptly, the penitent recounts whatever he has committed contrary to right and law. Afterwards the priest also questions him, to jog his memory, so that if anything has slipped away, he brings it back to mind. When the confession is complete, he recites those prayers [ἐπὶ τῶν ἐξομολογουμένων], imposes a penance [ἐπιτίμιον], blesses him and dismisses him. If that penance is one that can be completed before the day of Communion, the penitent, having performed it, approaches Communion; if it requires several days, he communicates even though he has not yet finished it, and afterwards completes the rest, unless the priest has enjoined that he must not approach the Eucharistic Communion until the penance is wholly complete. In that case he obeys completely and does not communicate, just as when, on account of some grave sin, he is forbidden Communion by the priest's command. I have not observed any other practice of penance in the places mentioned; they have some others of lesser importance, but these questions of yours are sufficiently answered by what I have said. I took care that both what Simeon of Thessalonica discusses about penance in his Dialogue on the Sacraments, and what John the Monk, who calls himself a disciple of Basil the Great, sets out in his little work on the punishments to be inflicted on penitents, should be copied from the Vatican manuscripts; and I entrusted them for delivery to you to Father Germanus, who gave me your letters. The shortage or indolence of Greek scribes, who can be driven into the Vatican only at great price, was the reason that all this time was spent before I could comply with your wish; yet it would be very brief if you weigh the times and the troubles by which this part of Europe of ours is pressed. If anything is therefore needed meanwhile, command it: I shall be mindful and diligent that what you command is supplied. Farewell, my Morinus, farewell, and love your Leo, who is most obedient to you, as you do.

units.la: MAxima sane lætitia perfusus sum, cùm mihi redditæ sunt litteræ tuæ: intra illummet fere diem litteras ad te Eminentissimumque Dominum nostrum meditabar. Hoc tempus ante aliquot menses avide exoptabam, pacem scilicet in Italiæ penetralia atque adyta redivivam & confirmatam, quod nunc publicâ famâ omnibus innotuit. Eminentissimum Cardinalem tot negotiis, præter omnium Ecclesiarum solicitudinem, domi militiæque occupatam meis literis interpellare nonnihil subverebar. Verùm nunc moras omnes rumpendi alteram mihi causam præbes, cùm literis tuis mihi significas, optimum Cardinalem me beneficio Ecclesiastico donatum velle; maximas illi gratias habeo, utinam referre possem; licet ab eo acceptando nonnulla deterreant, bella scilicet, quæ regionem illam circumstrepunt, deinde residentiae, quam vocant, obligatio: ejus tamen Eminentiae me divinctissimum fateor, & profiteor: eam enim video & sentio continuam mei curam gerere, nec unquam mihi deesse; sed occasionem. Ad Eminentissimum Cardinalem ideo rescribo, ut non acceptati beneficii rationem reddam, simulque, qua possum observantia animi mei gratitudinem testatam illi faciam. Te verò ut, quod facis, facere pergas, vehementissimè rogo, hoc est, ut mei semper memor sis, saepiusque Eminentissimum Cardinalem mei memorem facias, qui pluris quam ego, te, tuaque studia faciat, qui fortunatiora tibi optet, & voveat, neminem habes.
units.tr: I was overcome with the greatest joy when your letter was delivered to me. I was almost on the very day of its arrival composing a letter to you and to our most eminent Lord. For some months I had eagerly longed for this time, namely for peace to be restored and established again in the inner sanctuaries of Italy, which is now known to everyone through public report. I was somewhat afraid to interrupt the most eminent Cardinal with my letters, since he is occupied at home and in war with so many affairs, apart from his concern for all the Churches. But now you give me another reason to break off all delay, since in your letter you tell me that the excellent Cardinal wishes to bestow an ecclesiastical benefice upon me. I am greatly grateful to him, and I wish I could repay him. Yet some things deter me from accepting it: namely the wars that resound throughout that region, and then the obligation of residence, as they call it. Nevertheless I acknowledge and declare myself most deeply bound to his Eminence. For I see and feel that he continually takes care of me and is never wanting to me, only the opportunity is lacking. I am writing back to the most eminent Cardinal so that I may give the reason for not accepting the benefice, and at the same time so that I may show him my gratitude by whatever respect of mind I can. As for you, I most earnestly ask that you continue to do what you are doing, that is, that you remain mindful of me and often make the most eminent Cardinal mindful of me. He values you and your studies more than I do; he wishes and prays for your fortunes to be better; you have no one who loves you more.

units.la: Quod spectat ad studia mea, de quibus me interrogas, paucis edisseram. Quatuor varia opera prelo fere matura sunt, quae σὺν Θεῷ, hoc ordine sum editurus. Primum antiquam Sacramenti poenitentiae praxim complectitur, quaecunque in ea administranda duodecim seculorum spatio tam in Oriente quàm in Occidente variata sunt, expliexplicat; Opus ab Annis viginti duobus à me inchoatum, cui sæpius adornando incubui, à qvo etiam sæpius materiæ difficultas me deterruit: qvidqvid enim mihi antiqvorum Volumina diligenter versanti in hac causa occurrit, exscribit, & qvo qvæqve res ordine illo seculo & eo climate administrabatur, describit. Ad octo fere mensibus nihil aliud elaboravi, nec nisi coronide impositâ huic operi insudare desinam, spero cum anno finiente finitum iri.
units.tr: As to my studies, about which you ask me, I shall explain briefly. Four different works are almost ready for the press, and with God's help [σὺν Θεῷ] I shall publish them in this order. The first sets out the ancient practice of the sacrament of penance: whatever was varied in its administration over the space of twelve centuries, in the East as well as in the West. I began this work twenty-two years ago. I have often applied myself to finishing it, and often the difficulty of the material has discouraged me. For whatever I have come upon while diligently turning over the ancient volumes on this question, I copy out, and I describe in what order each matter was administered in that century and in that region. For about eight months I have worked on nothing else, and I hope that when the year ends, the work will be finished, and I will stop toiling at it once the crown has been placed upon it.

units.la: Secundum est de Antiqvis Christianorum Ecclesiis, in qvo earum figura delineatur, variæ par-tes narrantur, sedes in eis sacerdotum, Clericorum, Monachorum, Fidelium, Pœnitentium, Virorum, Mulierum demonstrantur, qvid in Ecclesiarum figu-ra, partibus & sedibus ab Apostolorum tempore hactenus tam in Oriente qvàm in-Occidente variatum explicatur. Hoc in opere plurimum me adjuverunt Leonis Allatii viri eruditissimi monita & lucubratiunculæ aliqvot, in iis potissimum, qvæ hodiernas Græcorum Eccle hoc opere si S. Hieronymum excipias„ vix unquam Latini aut Græci colloquuntur ; multa mihi sunt præterea partim collecta, partim polita, quæ spectant ad Jurisdictionis Ecclesiasticæ nostratibus à Laicis usurpationem. Usurpationum origines, occasiones & progressus in hunc usque diem demonstro: quid ab annis paulo minus quadringentis unoquoque tempore additum est, qua ratione lites in iis rebus instruebantur, quousque progrediebantur, ubi subsistebant. Hoc est quadripartitum ; antiquissima usurpatio est actionis possessoriæ, quæ realis est in Ecclesiæ bona, ipsumque Ecclesiasticum titulum. Hanc secuta est actio personalis in Clericos minores, civilis primum deinde criminalis, postea in sacratos quoslibet Clericos„ quæ nondum Episcopos invasit ; licet id sit aliquando tentatum : hanc Usurpationem Pragmatici nostri nomine delicti privilegiati intelligunt. Tertia respicit appellationes ab abusu dictas, quibus judicium Ecclesiasticæ Sententiæ Laico Tribunali subjisubjiciuntur. Quarta actiones, quæ de validitate aut invaliditate Matrimoniorum intenduntur, quarum prima initia emicuerunt ante annos circiter 45. atque à decem annis invaluerunt.
units.tr: The second is on the ancient churches of the Christians. In it their figure is outlined, their various parts are described, and the seats of the priests, clerics, monks, the faithful, penitents, men and women are shown. It explains what has been varied in the figure, parts and seats of the churches from the time of the Apostles until now, in the East as well as in the West. In this work the admonitions and some little essays of the very learned Leo Allatius helped me greatly, especially those concerning the present-day Greeks... (the Greek churches). Apart from St Jerome, Latins and Greeks scarcely ever speak with one another about this work. Besides, I have many materials, partly collected and partly polished, which concern the usurpation of ecclesiastical jurisdiction by laymen in our country. I demonstrate the origins, occasions and progress of these usurpations down to the present day: what was added at each time over the last four hundred years or a little less, by what method lawsuits in these matters were conducted, how far they went, and where they stopped. The matter is divided into four parts. The oldest usurpation is the possessory action, which is real and concerns the goods of the Church and the ecclesiastical title itself. This was followed by a personal action against minor clerics, first civil and then criminal, and afterwards against any consecrated clerics, which has not yet attacked bishops, although this has sometimes been attempted. Our pragmatic lawyers understand this usurpation under the name of privileged crime. The third concerns the appeals called appeals for abuse, by which the judgment of an ecclesiastical sentence is subjected to the lay tribunal. The fourth concerns the actions brought on the validity or invalidity of marriages. The first beginnings of these appeared about forty-five years ago, and they have gained strength for the last ten years.

units.la: Prodiit Arnaldi liber 15. Episcoporum & Lectissimorum 20 Sorbonæ Docto-rum testimoniis commendatus: insur-gunt tamen Jesuitæ, & in eum publicis prædicationibus ut in Lutheranum, Cal-vinianum, & quid non invehuntur: cum autem ad Pontificem provocandum es-set, qui de Autore & approbatoribus judicium ferret, potestates Mundi advo-cant, ut eorum Autoritate & Liber & Autor & ipse Approbatores, si fieri po-tuisset, opprimantur: Verùm ipsis ac-cidit, quod minatur Euripides in Andro-mache, Θυμώμεθ᾽[?] δὲ τάξεταί Θυμωμένων[?].
units.tr: Arnauld's book on the 15 bishops and the testimonies of 20 most select doctors of the Sorbonne, was published, commended by them. Nevertheless the Jesuits rise up and attack him and the book in public sermons as they would a Lutheran or a Calvinist, and whatever else they can. When the matter was to be referred to the Pope, who would pass judgment on the author and the approvers, they summon the powers of the world, so that by their authority both the book and the author, and the approvers themselves, if it could be done, may be crushed. But it has happened to them what Euripides threatens in the Andromache: [θυμώμεθα δὲ τάξεταί θυμωμένων] ("we are angry, and the angry will set the order" / "they will be ordered by their own anger").
