units.la: Miraberis forte, unde haec audacia, quod homo tibi ignotus, nulloque litterarum commercio familiaris, occupatissimum te & ad maxima quaeque natum insulsa & rudi Epistola detinere atque compellare ausim. Sed desine mirari: humanitas tua aliis probata, egregia eruditio, conspicua literarum monumenta, & si quae sunt alia, quae in te emicant; faces porrò, quas ad tale quid audendum subinde addit Vir Clarissimus mihique amicissimus D. Johannes Buxtorfius, tandemque ὁμοτεχνία[?] & causae quam pari Zelo defendimus, communio, pudoris repagula rumpere, teque nem ulterius trahere & ex ipsius Pentateuchi Samaritani natura eruere quam sit οὐδὲν ὑγιὲς in omnibus iis, quæ callide molitur & μωραίνει adversarius Morinus. Cùmque ipsemetego in Belgio opportunam Pentateuchi illiús[?] vitiosissimi perlegendi nactus essem occasionem,, protenus vidi causæ falsitatem. Unde facilius etiam amicorum monitis in hanc fui pertractus palæstram, quod Juveni mihi, ad Gigantem ejusmodi contremiscenti omnem timorem excusserant evidentissima & ἀναντίρρητα quæ cum cura inde collegi argumenta. Copiosior & δευτέρ[illegible, ~2 letters]ος esse potuissem, nisi nodo huic sufficientissimum cuneum opposuisse jam alii me censuissent. Quod si vero neque ista cordatis sufficiant, dabo operam, ut aliâs armis validioribus utar & adversarium ad ἀπορίαν redigam. Prævideo quidem, quàm versutè & callide argumenta mea, tanquam nihil contra se facientia, sit accepturus,, sed dici jam κρησφύγετα hæc parum morari. Clamitet licet in Apologeticis & ad nauseam usque inculcet, injuriam sibi fieri ab omnibus, qui Canonizationem Pentateuchi Samaritani sibi impingant; credat tamen & certissimè sibi habeat persuasum, neminem, nisi plane pro cerebro habeat fungum, hoc, qui vel per transsennam ejus sesquipedalia & phalerata in Pentateuchum hunc eructata verba legit, admissurum. Novi enim doctos, indoctos, Gallos, Belgas, Anglos sine ulla exceptione hujus monstrosi dogmatis Morinum insimulare. Tibi vero, Vir Excellentissime, has contra communem Adversarium elaboratus lucubrationes mittere volui, ut & tuo judicio subjicerem, & quid ad hæc Morinus exceperit excipereve cogitet, recognoscerem; παῤῥησίαν[?] debito & devoto in te affectu natam condona, & in amicorum tuorum numerum infimum me esse dignare. Vale igitur in Domino, causæ nostræ meiqve memor.
units.tr: You will perhaps wonder whence comes this boldness, that I, a man unknown to you and not familiar with any exchange of letters, should venture to trouble and address you, who are most busy and born for the greatest tasks, with a dull and rough letter. But cease to wonder. Your humanity, proved by others, your outstanding learning, your conspicuous literary monuments, and whatever other qualities shine forth in you; then the torches which the most distinguished man and my dearest friend, Mr. Johann Buxtorf, keeps adding from time to time to urge such a thing; and finally the shared profession and the cause which we defend with equal zeal, have broken the barriers of modesty, and have moved me not to delay you any longer, and to show you from the very nature of the Samaritan Pentateuch how far from sound is everything that your adversary Morinus contrives so craftily and talks such nonsense about. When I myself had found in Belgium a convenient opportunity of reading through that most faulty Pentateuch, I at once saw the falsity of the cause. For this reason I was the more easily drawn into this arena by the warnings of friends, since they had shaken off all fear in me, a young man trembling before such a giant, by the most evident and indisputable arguments which I carefully gathered from it. I could have been fuller and more abundant, had others not already judged that a most sufficient wedge should be placed against this knot. But if these arguments do not satisfy sensible readers, I will take care to use stronger weapons on another occasion and reduce the adversary to perplexity. I foresee indeed how slyly and cunningly he will receive my arguments, as though they had nothing against him; but it is of little use to say these are now evasions. Let him cry out in his Apologetics, and repeat to the point of nausea that wrong is done to him by all who fasten upon him the approval of the Samaritan Pentateuch; yet let him believe, and be quite sure, that no one, unless he is utterly out of his mind, will admit this, even one who reads through a chink in his bombastic and ornate words belched out against this Pentateuch. For I know that learned and unlearned men, French, Dutch and English alike, without exception accuse Morinus of this monstrous doctrine. To you, most excellent sir, I wished to send these labours, written against our common adversary, both to submit them to your judgment and to learn what Morinus has answered or thinks he should answer to them. Pardon the frankness born of my devoted and dutiful feeling towards you, and deign to count me the very lowest of your friends. Farewell then in the Lord, and be mindful of our cause and of me.

units.tr: LETTER LXXI.

units.la: Johannes Morinus Buxtorfio Libellum potius, quàm Epistolam scribit. Puncta Vocalia apud Judæos recentia esse, plurimis ostendit; loca quædam Rabbinorum à se interpretata vindicat; de Masoretis nonnulla; de Carræis ex eorum libris M. S. S. similiter ac de Judæorum Grammaticis observationes Criticæ.
units.tr: Johannes Morinus writes to Buxtorf a booklet rather than a letter. He shows by very many arguments that the vowel points among the Jews are recent. He defends certain passages of the rabbis which he has interpreted, and offers some remarks on the Masoretes. He also offers critical observations on the Karaites drawn from their unpublished manuscript books MSS., and likewise on the grammarians of the Jews.

units.la: Viro Clarissimo Johanni BuxtorfioJohannes Morinus.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, John Buxtorf, from Johannes Morinus.

units.la: GRatissimæ mihi fuerunt literæ tuæ, quas mihi reddidit Rever. & eruditissimus Pater Mersennius. Ecqui aliter poterant? Ecqui magni te semper facio? cui nomen tuum ab adolescentia & notum fuit & amicum; ab adolescentia enim patris tui literam Hæbraicarum peritissimi libris evolvendis incubui. Hunc adolescens præ cæteris elegi, cujus ductu & auspiciis Literas Hebraicas edicerem: ideo hactenus cum Hebraicè aliquid tuum facile tuli, cùm alienationem non omnino tuâ sponte, sed ab alio incitatum, concepisse crederem; ille enim ira velut œstro quodam in me penitus inimicos ubique mihi quæsivit. Basileam, Lugdunum Batavorum, atque ad alia loco ideo scripsit, ipsi defuncto bene nunc precor, ut viventi bene semper precatus sum, qva ratione tantum ipsius offensam meruerim, divinare nunquam potui. Ante scriptas Samariticas meas exercitationes amici eramus. Atqve non abs re audeo dicere, bene de ipso meritus eram; in me tamen indignabundus admodum scripsit. Nec scripsisse contentus eas ad Sorbonam detulit, velut impietatis censura inurendas; Verùm me nesciente res cum deridiculo ab omnibus fere excepta fuit: Paulo post animadversiones in præfationem, qvam editioni 70 Interp. à me instauratæ præfixeram, virulentas in lucem emisit; Hæc omnia passus, nec verbo quidem injurias illatas repellere cogitavi: Aliqvot post annos Exercitationes meas publicas typis mandari dari curavi,ubi ne verbulo qvidem ipsum appetii; in eas tamen insurgit famamqve meam dilacerat. Tacitus hæc & lego & ab aliis audio & tacere semper decreveram, qvanqvam scribendi materiam & insultandi campum qværens, mi-hi varia imponeret; Abruperunt tandem silentium meum, horrenda qvædam opinionum monstra, qvorum me accusarunt homines duo,in me præfationemqve meam sordidissimarum injuriarum plaustra debacchati; Flores enim, qvibus caput meum coronant, sunt ejusmodi; me vocant belluam insanam, rabie percitam, monstrum, qvod Judæi qvoqve execrantur, hominem infinitæ stoliditatis, desperatissimæ vecordiæ & pleraqve alia non dissimilia; Cum igitur his hominibus, licet in eorum libro nul-lum extaret eruditionis specimen, respondere decrevissem, de censore meo aliqvid obiter perstringere necessarium judicavi, ne de simili materia scribens, qvæ mihi imposuerat, admittere viderer.
units.tr: Your letter was very welcome to me; the reverend and most learned Father Mersenne handed it to me. How could it be otherwise? Do I not always think highly of you? I have known your name and been your friend since my youth, for from boyhood I have devoted myself to reading the books of your father, the most expert in the Hebrew language. I chose him above all others as a young man, to be the guide and patron under whose direction I would learn Hebrew letters. So far I have easily borne whatever you have written in Hebrew, since I believed that your estrangement from me arose not entirely of your own accord but was stirred up by another. For he, as if driven by a gadfly of anger, sought enemies for me everywhere. He wrote to Basel, to Leiden and elsewhere. Now that he is dead, I wish him well, as I always wished him well while he lived, but I could never work out by what means I had incurred his displeasure. We were friends before my Samaritan exercises were written. I may say without exaggeration that I had deserved well of him, yet he wrote against me in great indignation. Not content with writing, he also brought the matter before the Sorbonne, as if my work deserved to be branded with a censure of impiety. But without my knowledge the affair was received with ridicule by almost everyone. Shortly afterwards he published virulent remarks on the preface that I had prefixed to the edition of the Seventy that I had restored. I endured all this and did not even think of repelling the injuries with a word. Some years later I had my public exercises printed, and in them I did not attack him even with a single word. Yet he rises up against them and tears my reputation to pieces. I have read these things in silence, I have heard them from others, and I had always resolved to keep silent, although he, seeking material for writing and a field for insult, kept providing me with various pretexts. At last, however, certain horrible monsters of opinion broke my silence. Two men accused me of them, and they raged against me and my preface with a cartload of the filthiest insults. For the flowers with which they crown my head are of this kind: they call me a mad beast, driven by rage, a monster which even the Jews execrate, a man of infinite stupidity and utter madness, and many other things not unlike these. Since I had therefore decided to answer these men, although their book contained no specimen of learning at all, I judged it necessary to touch briefly upon my critic, lest, in writing on a similar subject, I should seem to admit what he had imposed upon me.

units.la: Hæc paucis, mi Buxtorfiut[?] scias qvo-ties, ties, & quales aculeis lacessitus defensione tandem aliquâ usus sum, atque etiam, ut hinc colligas, quibus conjecturis persuasus credidi, te non omnino sponte, sed ab alio commotum in me nonnulla durius scripsisse. Sed amicitia, quæ inter viros bonos & literarum studiosos esse debet, redintegraturi, mittamus hæc omnia, & æternâ oblivione deleamus.
units.tr: Let these few words suffice, my Buxtorf, so that you may know how often, and how sharply provoked, I have at last used some defence. You may also gather from this, from the conjectures by which I was persuaded, that I believed you had written somewhat harshly against me, not entirely of your own accord, but moved by another. But let us set all these things aside and blot them out with eternal oblivion, so that the friendship which ought to exist between good men and lovers of learning may be restored.

units.tr: [ἄελλαν] a storm

units.la: Vertere stylum proponis, bene est, sed aculeatum tantum verti velim: amicè reprehendi amo, quoties id feceris, bene de me mereberis, sive id jure facias sive injuria. Studium enim amici corrigendi, licet forsan aberret, boni semper est consulendum: Id sane ab unoquoque, etiam inimicissimo non ægre fero; Nonnulli minimè amici me citato aliter senserunt, nihil illis succenseo: Velle suum cuique sit, modo & nobis; Nusquam factum est, ut omnes hoNonnnlla commemoras; grato & officio-so animo hæc accipio. Verùm si aliqua quando interpretationis meæ aliqva ratio suppetat, paucis tibi proponi ægrè ne feras, sententiæ R.Ismaelis in פרקי אבות recordatus אל תחאמר קכלו רעתי [?] שתן רשאירולא אתה [?] Primum occurrit me sensisse, Judæorum majorem & saniorem partem asserere, hodiernas litteras suas, esse ab Esdra traditas, atque in locum veterum substitutas, atque hoc ut probem Judæorum testimonia, aut non satis intelligere, aut eò contorquere. Relege & compara, quæ scripsi, deprehendes, me nunquam pronuntiasse, majorem Judæorum partem sentire, literas hodiernas in locum veterum absolutè substitutas esse, ita ut major eorum pars crederet hodiernarum ante Esdram nullum prorsus usum fuisse. Contrarium cap. 3. Exercit 2, multis paginis ostendi, scilicet à fine p. 140. ad finem p. 147. plurimos Rabinos sentire librum legis à Mose scriptum & in arca conservatum & similiter duas legis tabulas hodiernis cha-racteracteribus fuisse scriptas: Idqve decem Rabbinorum testimonio confirmavi. Verùm qvum trium opinionum Judai-carum, qvas ibi retuli, hæc sit una, postqvàm illam à priore distinxi, adnotavi primùm multos habere authores, dein-de parum à prima differre, deniqve non-nullos illius authores plurimum se tor-qvere, ut autoribus prioris videantur non contradicere, ut legere potes, p. 139. ideo primam qvam cap. 2. & 3. explicavi simul cum secunda velut unam sententiam p. 98 accepi, eo qvòd secunda fateatur o-mnem scripturam Judaicam, civilem & religiosam ante Esdram fuisse Samariti-cam, librumqve legis tantùm excipiat. Exceptionem illam parum curavi, & ve-luti plane ridiculam, pro nulla, jurisconsul-torum more, judicavi. Ideo sententiam hanc ut proposito meo conducen-tem, qvod erat, omnem scripturam Ju-daicam civilem & sacram fuisse Sama-riticam, cum magno autorum numero re-tuli Alia enim scriptura, si aliqva fuit ejus-modi Judæis, ex secundæ sententiæ autori-b9[?] nunqvam fuit usualis, sed à Mose semel usurpata in adytis templi conservata fuit ab omnium Judæorum etiam sacerdotum remota oculis. Sed cap. 4. in quo speciali-ter primam sententiam, ex Judæ-is Neotericis demonstro, præcisè dico, pag. 123. potiorem esse; de approbanti-um multitudinem sileo. Quod ad librum tuum attinet, ante aliquot menses, illum semihorulæ spatio in manibus habui, & folia evolvi, tantum quæ in scriptis meis notares, quæritans, quapropter quid de his rebus revera sentias, nihil apud me statuere possum.
units.tr: You propose to turn your pen to these matters; that is well, but I would wish it to be turned only in a friendly and not a biting way. I love to be reproved in a friendly manner, and whenever you do this you will deserve well of me, whether you do it rightly or wrongly. For the zeal of a friend who corrects me, even if it perhaps goes astray, must always be taken in good part. Indeed I do not take it badly from anyone, even from the most hostile. Some who were by no means friends to me have judged otherwise when I was summoned, but I bear them no grudge. Let each have his own opinion, provided that we too may have ours. It has never happened that all men agreed... You mention some points; I accept these in a grateful and obliging spirit. But if at some time there is some ground for my interpretation, be not displeased that I set it out briefly for you, recalling the saying of R. Ishmael in Pirkei Avot [אל תחאמר קכלו רעתי שתן רשאירולא אתה]. First, it occurs to me that I was said to have held that the greater and saner part of the Jews assert that their present letters were handed down by Ezra and substituted in place of the old ones; and that to prove this I use the testimonies of the Jews either without understanding them sufficiently or twisting them to that end. Reread and compare what I wrote, and you will find that I never declared that the greater part of the Jews think the present letters were absolutely substituted in place of the old ones, so that most of them believed the present letters had no use at all before Ezra. I showed the contrary at length in chapter 3 of Exercise 2, namely from the end of page 140 to the end of page 147: that most Rabbis hold that the book of the law was written by Moses and kept in the ark, and likewise that the two tables of the law were written in the present characters. I confirmed this by the testimony of ten Rabbis. But since this is one of the three Jewish opinions which I reported there, after I had distinguished it from the first, I noted first that it has many authors, then that it differs little from the first, and finally that some of its authors strain themselves greatly so as not to seem to contradict the authors of the first, as you may read on page 139. Therefore I took the first opinion, which I explained in chapters 2 and 3, together with the second as one opinion (page 98), because the second admits that all Jewish writing, civil and religious, before Ezra was Samaritan, and excepts only the book of the law. I paid little attention to that exception and, in the manner of the jurists, judged it as wholly ridiculous and as no exception at all. So I cited this opinion, as favourable to my purpose, with a large number of authors, namely that all Jewish writing, civil and sacred, was Samaritan. For any other writing, if there was any such among the Jews, according to the authors of the second opinion, was never in common use, but was used once by Moses and kept in the inner sanctuaries of the temple, removed from the eyes of all the Jews, even the priests. But in chapter 4, in which I demonstrate especially the first opinion from modern Jews, I state plainly that it is the stronger, at page 123; I say nothing of the multitude of those who approve it. As for your book, some months ago I held it in my hands for half an hour and turned over its leaves, only to see what you had noted in my writings, asking myself what you really think about these matters, though I can settle nothing about it.

units.la: Secundo notas, pag. 18. מנדרים[?]. Ignorare non poteram, Rabbinis significare excommunicationem, qui Excercitat. Ec-clesiasti lib. 2. qui est de antiqua praxi censurarum in clericos, quas aliquot annis ante Exercitationes Samaritica[?] ediderā, ex Elia Levita docueram, tres esse apud Judæos Excommunicationis species. נדר.חרם.שמתא[?] sed cum Rabbinis etiam, expellere, removere, significet, hanc interpretationem alteri prætuli; eo quòd non ageretur simpliciter de excommunicatione, sed etiam de ingentis exercitus expulsione, deinde excommunicare infert fugare & expellere, quae verba excommunicationis effectum paulo clarius exprimuntDeniqve omnes testimonii periodi de excommunicatione & anathemate diserte loquuntur.Nihil ideo necessarium est, per מנרים[?] eam exprimere, sed excommunicationis effectus fugam & expulsionem.
units.tr: Second, you note on page 18 [מנדרים]. I could not be ignorant that the Rabbis use this to signify excommunication. In my Exercitations on Ecclesiastes, book 2, which concerns the ancient practice of censures against clergy, which I had published some years before my Samaritan exercises, I had taught from Elijah Levita that the Jews have three kinds of excommunication: [נדר, חרם, שמתא]. But since the Rabbis also use the word to mean to expel, to remove, I preferred this interpretation to the other, because the passage does not speak simply of excommunication but also of the expulsion of a huge army; and then to excommunicate implies to put to flight and to drive out, which words express the effect of excommunication a little more clearly. Finally, all the periods of the testimony speak plainly of excommunication and anathema. It is therefore not necessary to express it by [מנדרים], but by the effect of excommunication, which is flight and expulsion.

units.la: 2. Ais,notari debuisse von vobis & nobis, &c. desumptum esse ex Esdrae. 4.v,8. lector curiosus potest hoc ex concordan-tiis[?] eruere, non semper vacat interpretibus haec in qvirere, nec semper ad manum concordantiae, aut ista suggerit memoria. Tamrigidam ἀχεθείαν[?] nec curavi, nec curare velim, cum praesertim ad sensus interpretationem nihil faciat.
units.tr: Second, you say that von vobis & nobis etc. should have been noted, taken from Ezra 4:8. A curious reader can dig this out from the concordances. Interpreters do not always have time to seek such things, nor is a concordance always at hand, or memory always suggesting them. I neither took care over this cold carelessness, nor do I wish to take care over it, especially since it has no bearing on the interpretation of the sense.

units.la: 3. Inter loco peccasse fateor, sed nulla sensus, licet aliqua perspicuitatis, jactura. Illud enim וישלח ספרי[?] non autoris, sed scripturae verba sunt, quae interpretatur. Deinde illud והעת קה[?] scribendum erat והעתיקו[?] ut est in textu Aben Esdræ. Sed dissertissimè interpretatio mea fert, libros illos omnes fuisse ἐκτύπως[?] & copias unius illius libri à Mordochæo scripti.
units.tr: 3. I confess I erred in one place, but it costs the sense nothing, though it costs some clarity. The words וישלח ספרי are not the author's own but Scripture's words, which he is interpreting. Next, והעת קה should have been written והעתיקו, as in the text of Aben Ezra. But my interpretation makes it quite clear that all those books were transcripts [ἐκτύπως] and copies of that one book written by Mordecai.

units.la: 4. Ex pag. 80 בבואה male versi introitum, significat enim imaginem, vel potius ibi personam hominis, qui se ipsum in speculo videt, ita loqui solemus, unde Virgilius, non sum adeo informis, nuper me in littore vidi Ideo statim colligit אתה משנה עצמך mutas te ipsum personam tuam, &c. Clara hæc sunt ex lectione textus. Significatio umbræ, quam illi das, textui convenire non potest. Legi Rabbinum quemdam Nephtali Herts dictum, qui voces difficiles Midras Raboth & Megiloth explicavit, interpretatur similiter צל sed argumento textus magis favet introitus tuus quàm umbra tua. Eodem sensu legitur בובא in eodem Midras Raboth super numer' Parascha 10. versus finem כאיתי אתה בובא שלי בתוך חמים [illegible, ~2 letters] לפחן יצרי
units.tr: 4. On p. 80 I rendered בבואה wrongly as "entrance." It means "image," or rather, in that place, the person of a man who sees himself in a mirror. We speak in this way, whence Virgil: "I am not so ugly; I saw myself lately on the shore." So the author at once infers אתה משנה עצמך, "you change yourself, your person," and so on. These points are clear from reading the text. The meaning "shadow," which you give, cannot fit the text. I have read a certain rabbi, Naphtali Herts, who explained the difficult words of the Midrash Rabbah and the Megilloth, and he likewise interprets צל. But the argument of the text favours "your entrance" [בבואה] rather than "your shadow." In the same sense בובא is read in the same Midrash Rabbah on Numbers, Parashah 10, near the end: כאיתי אתה בובא שלי בתוך חמים [illegible] לפחן יצרי.

units.la: 5. Expag. 265. Librum iterum consuli, omnia se habent, ut ea excerpsi, hæc verba præcedunt excerpta בחכן כתוב במסרת הר פוס הנון הפוכה וכך רשיובן כתוב בפירו שהתורה המוחס לרבינו שמשון ואנכי וכו ut in libro meo. Cum his verbis habes omnia prorsus qvæ autor in hac materia. Forte [?] ראקי pro [illegible, ~2 letters] תאני vel potius ראקי eo qvod litterarum capita subtilissimis lineolis & spinulis, qvas תנין vocant, coronantur.
units.tr: 5. On p. 265. I consulted the book again. Everything stands as I excerpted it. These words precede the excerpts: בחכן כתוב במסרת הר פוס הנון הפוכה וכך רשיובן כתוב בפירו שהתורה המוחס לרבינו שמשון ואנכי וכו, as in my book. With these words you have absolutely everything the author says on this subject. Perhaps ראקי stands for [illegible] תאני, or rather ראקי, because the heads of the letters are crowned with very fine little lines and points, which they call תנין.

units.la: 6. Ex pag. 320. Nonnihil miror te reprehendere, qvòd eo loco verterim נהוה substitit & dicere vertendum generata est. נתהוה האור significat proprè facta est lux. Sed immediata dixerat ויהי אור & facta est lux, igitur repetendum fuisset & facta est lux. Deinde non fecisset satis hæc interpretatio menti Abarbennelis, qvi non modo contendit, lucem qvalitatem sine corpore factam, sed etiam sine corpore aliqvandiu substitisse. Melius igitur per verbum redditur significans aliqvam status consistentiam. Si interpretemur facta est aut generata, vis sensus minuitur.
units.tr: 6. On p. 320. I am somewhat surprised that you reprove me for rendering נהוה at that place as "stood firm," and say it should be rendered "was generated." נתהוה האור properly means "light was made" [נתהוה האור]. But I had said just before ויהי אור, "and light was made," so the rendering would have had to be repeated as "and light was made." Further, this interpretation would not have satisfied the mind of Abarbanel, who contends not only that light was created as a quality without a body, but also that it subsisted for some time without a body. It is therefore better rendered by a word signifying some consistency of state. If we render it "was made" or "was generated," the force of the sense is diminished.

units.la: 7. Ex pag. 356. Ais apud Cozri בְּחָרוּק הַהְקְשָׁה[?] significare, praeter rationem. Patere qvaeso, ut te, qvod sentio, non celem: Si ratio bene quadrat τῷ praeter vel contra non bene quadrat τῷ הַהְקְשָׁה[?] nec etiam textui interpretatio tua. Sed qvid dices, cum littera aliqua nonnunquam in libris reperitur contra vel praeter rationem. Neque est contra rationem, ut in צָרִי[?] legat ה pro ה & saepissime ut omnes notant in ejusmodi literarum similium permutatione, utrumque textus pati potest. Autor istius libri praefert צָרִי[?] per ה Aben Esdra praefert צֵרֵי[?] per ה. utrumq; tamen amplectitur, qvia neutrum est praeter vel contra rationem, ut ex ipso ibidem notavi.
units.tr: 7. On p. 356. You say that in Cozri בְּחָרוּק הַהְקְשָׁה signifies "beyond reason." Allow me to tell you frankly what I think. If "reason" fits well with "beyond" or "against," it does not fit well with הַהְקְשָׁה, and your interpretation does not fit the text either. "But what will you say, when a letter is sometimes found in books against or beyond reason?" It is not against reason to read ה for ה in צָרִי, and very often, as everyone notes, in such an interchange of similar letters, the text can bear either reading. The author of that book prefers צָרִי with ה; Aben Ezra prefers צֵרֵי with ה. Yet both accept it, because neither reading is beyond or against reason, as I noted there.

units.la: Qvapropter haec apud me considerans, difficilem dixi permutationem, qvia in ejusmodi difficile judicatu est, qvae littera in dictionibus illis sit praeferenda, & existimavi, in textum irrepsisse aut abundare ה; atqve hic sensus optime textui convenit, in qvo pergit autor difficultatem Caraitae proponere, qvi traditionem non amplectebatur. Recte eqvi-dem interpretaris [?]יוצא מן ההקשה egré-dieris ab analogia, sed [?]יועאמו & [?]בחלוף non video qva ratione idem significare dici possint. Deinde illud prius optime textui convenit, in qvo agitur de Grammaticationibus heteroclitis, sed qvod legatur צרן vel צרן varia lectio, non grammaticatio, in qva semper aliqvid regulam non servat. Nihil enim in צרן vel צרן irregulare est.
units.tr: Therefore, considering these matters, I said the change was difficult, because in such cases it is hard to judge which letter should be preferred in those words. I thought that ה had crept into the text or was superfluous. This sense suits the text very well, in which the author goes on to put the difficulty to the Karaite who did not accept tradition. You certainly render rightly יוצא מן ההקשה as "you depart from analogy," but "I do not see by what reasoning the same meaning can be said of יועאמו and בחלוף." Further, the former reading suits the text very well, in which heteroclite grammatications are discussed. But that צרן or צרן is a varia lectio, not a grammatication, in which something always fails to keep the rule. For nothing in צרן or צרן is irregular.

units.la: Nunc tamen textum pei pendens facile existimarim [?]ההקשה legendum & secundum litteram esse vocis formativam, & interpretandum, rationem opinionem: ideo [?]בחלוף ההקשה significare cum permutatione sive varietate rationis, hoc est, qvid dices, cum littera reperitur in libris cum variante ratione, id est, ubi ratio de utraqve lectione reddi potest. Hanc interpretationem confirmare videtur id qvod sequitur, si in ejusmodi dominatur [?]ההקשה, ratio, id est, si ratio & opinio propria dominatur, &c. Ita interpres intellexit. Verum si oculo amico ista consideres, quidquid הקשה[?] significet, nihil prorsus officit argumento. Probo enim ex Cozri, Judæo asserere, variarum lectionum numerum esse innumerum. Postquam Cozri duo exempla retulit in [illegible, ~3 letters] & נבש[?] scribit alia esse, quæ numerari non possunt. Atque hoc unum volui quod constat, quidquid, de הקשה[?] dicatur.
units.tr: Yet now, weighing the text, I could readily think that ההקשה should be read as it stands, and is a formative word of the letter, and should be interpreted "reason, opinion." So בחלוף ההקשה would signify "with a change or variety of reason," that is, "what will you say, when a letter is found in books with a variant reason," that is, where the reason for either reading can be given. What follows seems to confirm this interpretation: if in such a case reason, that is, one's own reason and opinion, prevails, and so on. The translator understood it so. But if you consider these matters with a friendly eye, whatever הקשה may signify, it does nothing to harm the argument. For I prove from Cozri, a Jew, who asserts that the number of variant readings is innumerable. After Cozri has related two examples in [illegible], and נבש, he writes that there are others which cannot be counted. This one point I wished to establish, and it is agreed, whatever is said about הקשה.

units.la: 8. Ex. pag. 345. Miror, qua ratione mihi imputes, dixisse Commentatorem Cozri, Masoram improbasse, quum de eo ne verbum quidem scripserim, ex eo tantum docui, multos antiquos Rabbinos Masoram improbasse. At ut vides, non sequitur. Commentator Cozri refert, multos Rabbinos hoc improbasse; ergo & ipse improbat. Referunt Augustinus, Epiphanius, &c. multos hæreticos divinitatem Christi improbasse, ergo & ipsi Augustinus, Epiphanius, &c. eam improbant; immo non solum hoc non dixi, sed plane contrarium collegi, ita deinde Masorethárum diligentia sen-siebant Judæi, &c. At commentator ilke [?] nuperus autor est. Idem eodem modo colligit Pater tuus Cap. 20. comment. Maforet. Censor meus ex eodem loco aliud mihi imponebat, Ephodæum Maforam improbasse, sed oculis ira fascinatis, eorum quæ asserui, nihil videre potuit.
units.tr: 8. On p. 345. I marvel by what reasoning you impute to me that I said the commentator on Cozri disapproved of the Masorah, when I did not write a word about him. I taught only from that passage that many ancient rabbis disapproved of the Masorah. But, as you see, it does not follow. The commentator on Cozri reports that many rabbis disapproved of this; therefore he also disapproves. Augustine, Epiphanius, and others report that many heretics denied the divinity of Christ; therefore Augustine, Epiphanius, and the rest also deny it. Indeed I not only did not say this, but plainly inferred the contrary: "thus the Jews in turn felt through the diligence of the Masorites," and so on. But the commentator is a recent author. Your father draws the same inference in the same way in chapter 20 of the commentary on the Masorah. My censor, from the same passage, imputed to me something else, that Ephodaeus disapproved of the Masorah. But with his eyes bewitched by anger he could see nothing of what I asserted.

units.la: 9. Ex eadem pag. De sensu contendis libri Cozri eo loco. Ego sane assentiri tibi non possum. Longiori sermone opus est, quam ferat epistola. Paucis dicam. Duo sunt controversiæ nostræ capita. De sensu verborum unum, alterum de autoris mente & scopo in hac disputatione: In utroque, parte verbis meis, toto cælo aberrare mihi videris, ut ego tibi. Quod ad prius attinet, illud כדברי רובה qvod interpretatus sum in re damnabili, tu vero in re debita & honesta, pater tuus interpretatur, in re culpabili & inutili. Sic intellexit commentator Cozri, ut ex adnotatione ad illa verba. במושהיו רבים מזנים [illegible, ~2 letters] multi fuerunt ejusmodi vituperantes opus & industriam eorum. Quod probat ex Ephodæi testimonio. His accedit .& censor meus. Deinde vim afferre mihi videris huic voci הקראה[?] qvam interpretatis videturne tibi. Est enim conclusio ex præcedentibus collecta,ideo efse non potest interrogatio dubitantis, sed affirmantis & colligentis, numqvid vides,&c. ut paulo post idem autor cap.35. התראה נאשר אמר להם [illegible, ~1 letter] חדשה [illegible, ~1 letter] לכם [illegible, ~1 letter] ראש החדשים. Ita etiam est interpretatus pater tuus. Obstat denique ratio totius contextus, est enim sensus juxta tuam sententiam, videturne tibi, quod opus eorum in hoc vanum fuerit, aut occupatio circa rem debitam. At ex toto contextu constat, Karaitas literæ punctis mordicus inhærere. Qvamobrem igitur interrogat Rabbanista Karaitam, an punctatio, &c. sit inutilis, cum non modo utilem & ante & post interrogationem illa Karaita falsus fuerit, sed etiam à Masorethis divinitus adjutis fuisse inscriptam? Unde colligit author adversus Karaitam, eos omnes, qvi fatentur legem punctis, &c. ornatam, ef-se lese legem Mosis, obligari ad fidem traditionibus habendam. Cozri in Karaitam ibi agens fatetur, suos id asserere, sed postquam legem sic perfectam deprehenderunt, opus non esse Cabbala sive traditione, sed textui tantum divino esse adhærendum.
units.tr: 9. On the same page. You contend about the sense of Cozri's book in that place. I certainly cannot agree with you. It needs a longer discussion than a letter can hold, so I will say only a few things. There are two heads of our controversy. One concerns the sense of words; the other concerns the author's mind and purpose in this dispute. On both points you seem to me to wander from my words toto caelo, just as I do from yours. As to the first: כדברי רובה, which I rendered "in a damnable matter," you render "in a due and honest matter," while your father interprets it "in a culpable and useless matter." The commentator on Cozri understood it so, as the note on those words shows: במושהיו רבים מזנים, "there were many of that kind who blamed their work and industry." He proves this from the testimony of Ephodaeus. My censor adds his voice to this too. Next, you seem to me to do violence to the word הקראה, which you render "does it seem to you?" For it is a conclusion drawn from what precedes. Therefore it cannot be the question of one who doubts, but of one who affirms and infers: "do you not see," and so on, as the same author says shortly after in chapter 35: התראה נאשר אמר להם [illegible] חדשה [illegible] לכם [illegible] ראש החדשים. Your father, too, so interpreted it. Finally, the reasoning of the whole context stands in the way. On your view the sense would be "does it seem to you that their work in this was vain, or an occupation with a matter that is due?" But from the whole context it is plain that the Karaites cling stubbornly to the letter of the text and its points. Why, then, does the Rabbanite ask the Karaite whether the pointing, and so on, is useless, when that Karaite was not only wrong to admit before and after the question that it was useful, but was also wrong to say that it was inscribed by the Masoretes with divine help? Whence the author concludes against the Karaite that all who confess the law to be adorned with points, and so on, to be the law of Moses, are bound to hold to tradition in faith. Cozri, dealing with the Karaite there, admits that his people assert this, but once they perceived the law so perfected, there was no need of Cabbala or tradition, only of adherence to the divine text.

units.la: Postea multis docet autor, etiam positis punctis, propter dictiones ipsas adhuc traditione opus esse, immo traditione magis opus propter verba ipsa, quàm propter punctorum inscriptionem, & sic Karaitam undequaque[?] urget, & ad traditionis confessionem adigit. Librum habes, ideo verba nihil est necesse describere.
units.tr: The author then argues at length that, even with the points in place, tradition is still needed because of the words themselves. Indeed, tradition is needed more for the words than for the insertion of the points. In this way he presses the Karaite on every side and forces him to confess tradition. You have the book, so there is no need to copy out his words.

units.la: Verùm ponamus illa verba esse, ut censes intelligenda, nihil sententiæ meæ ossiciunt: sequitur enim, autorem Cozri Maforetharum opus utile judicasse, quod certe libentissime fateor, & falli plurimum Judæos, qui aliter senserunt. Rem distinctius explico. Opus Maforethicum triplex est: vel litteras respicit vel puncta & accentus, vel varia alphabeta & dictionum series, vel numerationes. Duo priora, primum præsertim utilissimum fuit. De secundo distingui posset sed quia accentuum magnus ille numerus ipsorum Musicæ inservit, demus nullum horum esse inutilem; tertii non est eadem ratio. Multa enim continet plane innutilia. Sed eorum maximam partem non composuerunt Masorethæ, neque qui textum biblicum recensuerunt, neque qui puncta infixerunt. Demus, Judam illum omnia comprobasse. Ex ipsius verbis sequitur evidentissimé, Puncta, &c. per Cabbalam conservata, & tandem Masorethas ea inscripsisse. Quæritur, an Masorethæ illi, fuerint Rabbini Synagogæ magnæ, an homines longe posteriores. Non intellexisse priores, est manifestum, ex eo quod traditionem ex punctorum infixione probat: si enim in confesso apud eos fuisset, Esdram & socios ejus, puncta & accentus inscripsisse, nullum plane fuisset argumentum licet enim à Mose ad Esdram traditio punctorum & accentuum ejusmodi continuata fuisset; per Esdram, qui Prophetha erat, utrique parti ex æqvo acceptus, extincta fuisset traditio, atqve ex [?]בעל פה facta fuisset illo momento, [?]בכתב nullusqve fuisset locus argumento Rabbanistæ contra Karaitam. Nihil enim deus ad scripturæ complementum, post Esdram traditioni reliquisset. Hæc pro epistolæ modulo diffuse nimis. Propterea cætera paucis.
units.tr: But let us suppose those words mean what you think they mean. They still do nothing against my view. For it follows that the author Cozri judged the Masoretic work useful, which I gladly admit, and that the Jews who thought otherwise are greatly mistaken. I will explain the matter more distinctly. The Masoretic work is threefold: it concerns either the letters, or the points and accents, or various alphabets and lists of words, or numberings. The first two, and the first especially, were most useful. The second could be divided further, but since that great number of accents serves their music, let us grant that none of these is useless. The third is not in the same case, for it contains many things that are plainly useless. Yet the Masoretes did not compose most of these, nor did those who revised the biblical text, nor those who inserted the points. Grant that Judah approved all of them. From his own words it follows most clearly that the points, and so on, were preserved by tradition and that the Masoretes at last inscribed them. The question is whether those Masoretes were the rabbis of the Great Synagogue or men far later. That the earlier ones did not understand this is evident from the fact that he proves the tradition from the insertion of the points. For if it had been agreed among them that Ezra and his companions inscribed the points and accents, there would have been no argument at all. Although the tradition of such points and accents had continued from Moses to Ezra, through Ezra, who was a prophet and acceptable to both parties, the tradition would have been ended, and made from oral into written at that very moment. There would have been no ground for the Rabbanite argument against the Karaite, since God would have left nothing to tradition after Ezra for the completion of Scripture. These things have been said too diffusely for the scope of a letter, so I will be brief about the rest.

units.la: Petis qvem Karaitarum librum habeam? unicum habeo, qui in legem commentarius est manuscriptus, in folio non admodum magno, tres digitos aut circiter crassum: scribebat An.Chr. 1299 liber inscribitur [?]ספר המבחר autor R. Apharon filius Josephi. Ex eo autore manifestum est, Karaitas omnem scripturam veteris testamenti, non secus ac alii Judæi, amplecti. Solicitos admodum esse in explicandis Masorethicis & Grammaticis criticis, Talmud & Misnam non admittere ut regulam fidei, verum utilem sæpe ad Scripturæ illustrationem. Eadem est illis plane cum aliis Judæis, qvos Rabbanistas vocant controversia de scriptura & traditionibus, bus , quæ est Catholicis cum Lutheranis.Nonnulla excerpam ita in proœmio libri,postquam adversarios obiter carpsit.
units.tr: You ask which Karaite book I have. I have only one: a manuscript commentary on the Law, in a not very large folio, about three fingers thick. It was written in the year of Christ 1299 and is entitled Sefer ha-Mivhar [ספר המבחר], by its author R. Aaron son of Joseph. From this author it is clear that the Karaites embrace the whole Scripture of the Old Testament just as the other Jews do. They are very diligent in explaining the Masoretic and grammatical critics, but they do not admit the Talmud and Mishnah as a rule of faith, though they often find them useful for illuminating Scripture. Their position is entirely the same as that of the other Jews whom they call Rabbanites, in the controversy about Scripture and traditions, which is the same as that between the Catholics and the Lutherans. I will excerpt a few things from the preface of the book, after he has briefly attacked his opponents.

units.la: ספכו על הקבלה וכח יש לפע מ[illegible, ~2 letters] ואמרו כנגד הכתיב שהקבלה תנצח ואם תהיה קב לתם בעבור לקוי[illegible, ~2 letters] מה שכתוב ב בתורה לא יוכל ענות זאת ואם זה מה[illegible, ~2 letters] ממלאות לב סוף דבר ככר סכלות והה מאמר כודע. אני לא אמנע ברוביהמצות שלא אזכיר מדברי המשנה Addit ista. הבאיר. בתוך וחפצי כוה להיותם כררף ממר או ת[?]ור לב הקורא או יוכך להוות ההכדל בי[?] כאמר למאמר אוימצא כמו או יורה על עניין שלא הורגש ברבים ואוו כל אמריהם בלי הועלת וה תעירדתי לוה העניין בריתי אתהרב המובחר ישיעת שהוכיר בכפר העדיור [illegible, ~2 letters] תוכשים והשינוית וכיוצא בהו ורוך משרירי זלותינו עשו ככה ער שהרב נהיבו נה זצלהייב לבני עמינו ללמור המשנת והתלמוד. Grammaticos adversariorum nonnunquam citat, ut Kimhium & R. Jonam passimque ut sensum venetur, gramgrammatica præcepta solicitat. Angelos esse credunt, resurrectionem mortuorum. Menses ex visione lunæ sanctificant. Pascha primumque mensem in terra Israëlis ex maturitate spicarum pronuntiant: Extra terram Cyclum Rabbanistarum sequuntur. Ridet hoc Gamalielis pronuntiatum, annum intercalari propter tria, propter spicas, tecuphas, & fructus arborum; ridetque adhuc magis quod alii addunt, propter agniculas hondum Paschati satis grandes, pontes effractos, &c. rationem hanc reddit. וירוע כי בהמבא האביב איו אפשר שאיו הכל מתוקנים ולמה נוסיף על דברי אלהים חיים licet sequuntur Rabbanistarum computum, ridet tamen eorum ἀφιεργίας[?] in בדו[?] ba-du Pascha non celebrari, id est, v. 4. & 6. feria. בח principium esse non posse anni, &c. & demonstrare nititur ex Esdra, Pascha celebratum fuisse in בדו[?] differentiæ sunt aliæ plurimæ, quantum ex isto libro, tum ex variis Judæorum libris collegi, sed hanc unam præ cæteris considero, quæ traditiones in genere spectat, & argumenta, quibus Rabbanistæ Karaitas urgent; Judæi autem, qui traditiones ut authenticas amplectuntur, seipsos libenter Rabbanistas vocant, ut & alii Karaitas.
units.tr: "Their book is about tradition, and it has some power... and they said against the written text that tradition will prevail; and if it is tradition, then for the sake of its defects... what is written in the Torah cannot answer this; and if this is so... filled hearts. In short, it is the word of folly and a well-known saying." I will not refrain from mentioning many of the precepts, such as the sayings of the Mishnah. [He] adds these things: "I have set them out in the book... and my wish is that they be like a bridle... to turn the heart of the reader, or lead him to a distinction..." ... "or it may point to a matter not noticed by the many, and all their sayings without profit." I have roused this matter in my letter against the excellent teacher Isaac, who mentioned in the Kafr... and the changes and the like; and many of our predecessors did this, until the teacher Nehemiah of blessed memory urged our people to learn the Mishnah and the Talmud. He also cites the grammarians of the adversaries now and then, such as Kimhi and R. Jonah, and everywhere, in seeking out the sense, he consults the precepts of grammar. They believe that there are angels and the resurrection of the dead. They sanctify the months by the sight of the moon. They announce the Passover and the first month in the land of Israel from the ripeness of the ears of grain; outside the land they follow the cycle of the Rabbanites. He mocks the decree of Gamaliel, that the year is intercalated on account of three things: the ears of grain, the young birds, and the fruit of the trees. He mocks even more what others add, on account of the lambs not yet large enough for Passover, broken bridges, and so on, and he gives this reason: [והוא ירוע כי בהמבא האביב איו אפשר שאיו הכל מתוקנים ולמה נוסיף על דברי אלהים חיים] since the ripening of the ears cannot be... for why should we add to the words of the living God? Although they follow the computation of the Rabbanites, he mocks their error in holding that the Passover is not celebrated on ba-du, that is, on the fourth and sixth day of the week. He holds that the beginning of the year cannot be on the second day, and so on, and he tries to prove from Ezra that the Passover was celebrated on ba-du. There are many other differences, as far as I have gathered both from this book and from various Jewish books, but I consider this one before all the others: it concerns traditions in general, and the arguments with which the Rabbanites press the Karaites. The Jews, however, who embrace traditions as authentic, willingly call themselves Rabbanites, as the others call the Karaites.

units.la: Initium Schismatis istius à Judæis assignatur anno Chr. 740. Quidam paulo citius, alii paulo tardius, hoc est annis post Talmudis obsignationem circiter 60. Ex historiis enim & circumstantiis, quas omnes referunt, & præsertim quæ ad illa tempora proxime accedunt, evidentissimè demonstratur, R. Asè Talmudis compilationem cœpisse ineunte sexto seculo, & R. Jose aliósque complevisse circa annum Chr. 680 [?]. Cũm igitur Talmud Babylonicum magna apud Judæos autoritate potiretur, passimque cresceret illius autoritas, Juda quidam Lumbedithanæ Schola caput הלכות גדולות [?] compo-suit. Alii hoc tribuunt R. Keiaræ, qui eum præcessit, quas decisiones ex Talmude velut libro authentico decerpserunt. His se oppositerunt Anan &
units.tr: The beginning of this schism is assigned by the Jews to the year of Christ 740. Some place it a little earlier, others a little later, that is, about sixty years after the sealing of the Talmud. For from the histories and circumstances, which all relate, and especially those that come closest to those times, it is most evidently shown that R. Ashi began the compilation of the Talmud at the beginning of the sixth century, and that R. Jose and others completed it about the year of Christ 680. Since the Babylonian Talmud therefore held great authority among the Jews, and its authority grew everywhere, a certain Judah of the school of Lumbedītha composed the work Halakhot Gedolot. Others attribute it to R. Kahana, who preceded him, and they took its decisions from the Talmud as from an authentic book. Against these stood Anan and

units.la: [Not a footnote: no note text printed below the main text on this page.] Saul filius ejus,& Karcasnæus, viri apud eos celeberrimi, ferre non valentes eandem traditionibus Talmudicis autoritatem, quæ sacræ scripturæ tribui. Hinc in eos cæteri tantum odium exercuerunt, quale unquam in ullam nationem aut sectam.
units.tr: [Not a footnote: no note text printed below the main text on this page.] his son Saul, and Karkasani, men most famous among them, who could not bear the same authority being given to the Talmudic traditions that is given to Holy Scripture. Hence the others directed such hatred against them as was never directed against any nation or sect.

units.la: Fateris, textum Hebraicum non esse usque quaque sincerum, non vis tamen ex translationibus emendari. Sane nec ego velim, id passim, nedum absolutæ fieri: multæ sunt cautiones adhibendæ, de quibus non semel scripsi: ut in Diatriba mea de textus Hebraici sinceritate c. 6. & 7. potest & non nunquam emendari debet, versio ex textu archetypo. Hoc solum ex omnibus, quæ de hac quæstione scripsi, colligere & colligi volui, non valere hanc consequentiam, textus Hebræus vel Græcus N. Testamenti aliter habet quam versio, ergo error est in versione, & ad textum Hebræum vel Græcum, qualis nunc est, emendari debet. Ratio est ex variis lectionibus evidens. Si enim adnotantur in Hæbraeo aut Græco'textu tot lectionum varietates, quare in data aliqua hypothesi translationis ab originario variantis, non poterit textus originarius esse corruptus sive aliter scriptus quàm autores scripserint. Non sufficit ad corrigendam versionem, solus ab originario dissensus.
units.tr: You admit that the Hebrew text is not everywhere entirely sound, yet you do not want it to be corrected from the translations. Indeed I would not wish that either, and it cannot be done everywhere, let alone completely. Many cautions must be observed, about which I have written more than once, as in my dissertation on the integrity of the Hebrew text, chapters 6 and 7. A version may and sometimes ought to be corrected from the original text. This is the only point I have wished to draw, and to be drawn, from all that I have written on this question: that the following inference does not hold: the Hebrew or Greek text of the New Testament reads otherwise than the version; therefore the error is in the version, and it must be corrected by the Hebrew or Greek text as it now is. The reason is evident from the variant readings. For if so many variant readings are noted in the Hebrew or Greek text, then, on any given hypothesis of translation departing from the original, the original text cannot be corrupt or written otherwise than the authors wrote it. Disagreement with the original alone is not enough to correct the version.

units.la: Grammaticas R. R. Jonæ & Jehudæ non habemus, nec usquam illos vidi, sicut nec Aben Esdræ שפה ברורה aut ירוד מורא habemus libros צחות & מדקדקי לשון הקדש Ephodæi Grammaticam similiter non habemus, sed habemus alios plurimos. Liber שת ירות est in quarto, semel complicatus, crassitiei duorum digitorum, aut paulo minus, sed charactere exili, Venetiis anno 1618. cuius. In duas partes divisus est יד חעני ניד המלך & unaquæque pars sive manus continet quinque digitos 8. Libros. Primo digito nomen fecit אור הור שהוא חגדה התורה hoc autem fecit magna cum diligentia. Secundæ enim editionis Bambergianæ voces omnes, litteras, accentus, puncta confideravit, & cum decem antiquis manuscriptis, quorum nonnulli erant 500. aut 600. annorum & libris Masorethicis manuscriptis & nonnullis aliis comparavit. Secundo libro nomen fecit מעריך [?] additio est τῷ עריך [?]. Pleriqve jam editi sunt, sed correxit & adnotationibus illustravit, materiamque à prioribus diversissimam tractavit.
units.tr: We do not have the grammars of R. R. Jonah and Judah, nor have I seen them anywhere, just as we do not have the books of Aben Ezra, Sefah Berurah or Yarod Mora, the books of eloquence and of the grammarians of the sacred tongue. Likewise we do not have the Grammar of Ephodaeus, but we have many others. The book Shetar Yerot is in quarto, folded once, about two fingers thick or a little less, but in a small character, printed at Venice in 1618. It is divided into two parts, Yad Ha-Ani and Yad ha-Melekh, and each part or hand contains five fingers, that is, eight books. With the first finger it has the name Or Ha-Or, which is the Haggadah of the Law, and he made it with great diligence. For in the second edition, the Bomberg edition, he considered all the words, letters, accents and points, and compared them with ten old manuscripts, some of which were five or six hundred years old, and with Masoretic manuscripts and some others. With the second book he gave the name Me'arikh; the addition is to the Ariikh. Most of it has already been published, but he corrected it, illustrated it with notes, and treated material very different from that of his predecessors.

units.la: Existimas etiam Levitam, Judæorum omnium solùm in ea fuisse sententia, at ego censeo, quantum legendo colligere potui, omnes Judæos, qui duobus aut tribus saeculis post annum Christi millesimum, aut aliquid supra vixerunt, in eadem cum Elia fuisse sententia. Ante quidem cùm nulli essent Crammatici [?], de punctis minus freqvens erat apud eos quaestio. Forsan abhinc annos ducentos aut trecentos aliqvi coeperunt in animum suum inducere, punctationem esse à Mose aut à Synagoga magna inscriptam. Imo miror plurimum, qua ratione scribere potuisti, Eliam solùm in ea esse sententia, cùm scias Ephodæum testari se multos sapientes vidis-se, qui Masorethicum illud opus traduxerint. Idem testatur R. Jacob instaurator Masorae in præfatione sua non longe ab initio, multos esse sapientum, etiam qui nunc vivunt, quorum eadem est sententia. Hoc etiam testatur Elias Levita, & author antiqui Libri Grammatici, qui inscribitur à primis verbis [?דברי פתח] in proœmio, cùm à Masorethis punctatio emanaverit, sane qui de eorum opere ita detrahebant, eorum punctationem à viris Synagogæ magnæ factum esse non crediderunt. Idem colligitur ex Aben Esdra & Kimhio, qui licet Masorethas non rideant & traducant, ut aliquando tamen non adhærent punctationi Masorethicæ, & nonnunquam citant antiquissimos Grammaticos & interpretes, punctationem & distinctiones Masorethicas modò deserentes, modò satis acriter reprehendentes R. Jonam & Mosen Hacohen, qui annis centum & ultra priores erant R. Aben Esra atque etiam R. Jachid Gheonem, qui omnes illos ut dignitate ita tempore antecedebat. Certissimum hoc argumentum est, Judæos omnes tum temporis existimasse, Masorethas Rabbinos fuisse recentiores, à quorum sententia non secus ac ab aliis discedere licet, atque ideo multi eorum operam plurimi faciebant, alii secus, nullus tamen eorum traditiones sicut Talmudicas amplectebatur. Consídera[?] quo odio Judæi Karaitas prosequuntur, eò quòd licet magni Talmudica existiment, ut oracula tamen non amplectantur. Si Judæi antiqui Masorethárum opus à Synagoga magna credidissent esse perfectum, ei vel tantillum contradicentes cane pejus & angve odissent. Habes alterum hujus rei testimonium apud Aben Esdram initio libri [illegible, ~5 letters] ex quo αὐτομάτως[?] nullasque per ambages id colligitur. Enumerat ordine Judæorum sapientes, primum eos, qui viros Synagogæ magnæ, præcesserunt deinde virosSynagogæ magnæ quibus tribuit accentuum & versuum,&Parascharü inventiotionem & ordinem. Post has R. Jeha-dam & socios authores Mischnæ, post hos Talmudicos doctores, quos inquit, secuti sunt Masorethæ, hosque Grammatici, quorum unus inquit, ego sum, & sedecim Grammaticos, qui eum præcesserunt, enumerat. Aliter quàm ut dictum est, de Masorethis sentire non poterant, antiqui illi Grammatici,, cum Masoretharum ætati proximi essent. Cùm enim Talmud ante annum 700 vulgari apud Judæos non potuerit, certe primi Masorethæ, qui literas & dictiones sacras recensue-runt, vix annum à Christo octingentesi-mum antecedere potuerunt.
units.tr: You suppose that Levita stood alone among all the Jews in this view, but I think, so far as I could gather from my reading, that all the Jews who lived two or three centuries after the year 1000 of Christ, or a little later, held the same opinion as Elias. Before that time, when there were no grammarians, the question about the vowel points was rarely raised among them. Perhaps some two or three hundred years ago some people began to persuade themselves that the pointing had been written in by Moses or by the Great Synagogue. Indeed I am greatly surprised how you could write that Elias alone held this view, since you know that Ephodaeus testifies that he saw many wise men who had handed down that Masoretic work. R. Jacob, the restorer of the Masorah, testifies the same in his preface, not far from the beginning, that there are many of the wise, even among those now living, who hold the same view. Elias Levita also testifies this, and so does the author of the old grammatical book which is entitled from its first words [דברי פתח] in its introduction. Since the pointing came from the Masorites, those who disparaged their work certainly did not believe that their pointing was made by the men of the Great Synagogue. The same is gathered from Aben Ezra and Kimchi, who, although they do not mock or disparage the Masorites, sometimes do not adhere to the Masoretic pointing, and often cite the most ancient grammarians and interpreters; now abandoning the Masoretic pointing and distinctions, now reproving quite sharply R. Jonah and Moses Hacohen, who lived a hundred or more years before R. Aben Ezra, and also R. Jachid Gheonem, who preceded all of them in dignity as well as in time. This is a most certain argument that all the Jews of that time thought the Masorites were more recent rabbis, from whose opinion one may dissent just as from others; and therefore many of them valued their work highly, others otherwise, yet none of them embraced their traditions as they embraced the Talmudic ones. Consider with what hatred the Jews pursue the Karaites, because although they hold the Talmudists in high regard, they do not accept the Karaites' views as oracles. If the ancient Jews had believed the Masoretic work to be perfect and from the Great Synagogue, they would have hated anyone who contradicted it even in the slightest, more than a dog or a snake. You have another testimony to this matter in Aben Ezra at the beginning of his book [illegible, about five letters], from which this is gathered automatically and without circumlocution. He lists the Jewish sages in order: first those who preceded the men of the Great Synagogue; then the men of the Great Synagogue, to whom he attributes the invention and order of the accents, the verses, and the Parashoth; after these, R. Jehudah and his companions, the authors of the Mishnah; after these the Talmudic teachers, whom, he says, the Masorites followed; and then the grammarians, of whom he lists sixteen who preceded him, one of whom says, "I am the one." Those ancient grammarians could not have thought otherwise about the Masorites, since they were close in time to the Masorites. For since the Talmud was not in common use among the Jews before the year 700, the first Masorites, who revised the letters and sacred words, could scarcely have lived before the year 800 of Christ.

units.la: Sane in ea sum sententia, punctorum & accentuum nomina & figuras, posteriores Masorethas invenisse & textui ad-scripsisse, forsan etiam & versuum distinctiones, quia invicta mihi videntur argumenta, quibus hæc multi probant, nec, dissolvi posse, hactenus existimavi. Scribis, te contrariam sententiam suscepisse probandam. Utinam hoc præstes. Si res ita est, vincat veritas, unicuique ut appa-reat, reat, enitendum est. Plurimum in hoc opere desudavit Pater tuus, sed pace tua dicam, multa erudite ex variis Judæorum doctoribus collegit, nullum tamen argumentum protulit, quod mihi videatur rem illam vel leviter probare. Quid addideris, legam avidissime. Res uno verbo confici potest, Demonstretur ex Talmude vel alio antiquo libro, locus in quo nominentut accentus,puncta, tuum facile fatebor ante Talmud & illos libros ea fuisse. Unde quæso factum est, ut in tanta librorum multitudine ne semel quidem ea nominarunt, aut cujus figuræ vel unus esset meminerunt? Quod enim versuum & accentuum mentionem aliquando faciant, nihil ad rem, cum legendo & loquendo periodos distingvere & accentus pronuntiare naturale sit. Sinæ, legendo & periodos distinguunt & accentus pronuntiant, cum nihil horum habeant. Antiquissimi & pulcherrimi codicesGræci literis uncialibus descripti, accentibus destituti sunt, & vocū distinctionibus, nedum periodorum: unaqvæ-qve que linea est velit una dictio. Sic & antiquissimi, & splendidissimi codices lati-ni.
units.tr: Indeed I hold the opinion that the later Masorites invented the names and shapes of the points and accents and added them to the text, and perhaps also the divisions of verses, because the arguments by which many prove this seem to me unanswerable, and until now I have thought they cannot be dissolved. You write that you have undertaken to prove the contrary view. I hope you will accomplish this. If the matter is so, let truth prevail; we must strive that it may appear to everyone. Your father has laboured greatly in this work, but, with respect to you, I must say that he has gathered many learned things from the various Jewish teachers, yet has produced no argument which seems to me to prove that matter even slightly. I shall read eagerly whatever you have added. The matter can be settled in one word: let it be demonstrated from the Talmud or another ancient book, a place where the accents and points are named, and I will readily confess that they existed before the Talmud and those books. But I ask, how is it that in so great a multitude of books they never once named them, nor did they mention any of their shapes, not even one? As for their mention of verses and accents at some point, that is nothing to the purpose, since it is natural to divide sentences and pronounce accents when reading and speaking. The Sinaites, when reading, both divide sentences and pronounce accents, though they have none of these. The most ancient and most beautiful Greek codices, written in uncial letters, lack accents and even word divisions, not to mention sentence divisions: each line is, as it were, one continuous word. So too the most ancient and most splendid Latin codices.

units.la: Qui tamen ea legebant atque etiamnum legunt, & periodos distinguunt, & accentus pronuntiant. Imo quæ natio, si Græcos excipias, nunc accentus scribit? Quæ tamen natio illos non pronuntiat? si versus inscripti erant, qua fronte Rab. Joseph in Talmude Tract. Kidusdum, cap. 1. f. 30. interrogat, ad quem versum pertineat, ריתולח[?] ad antecedentem aut subsequentem? Qua fronte respondeat, Abajeos non esse inversibus numerandis exercitatos? Quid enim erat facilius codice sumpto inspicere notam Paulæ.
units.tr: Yet those who read them, and still read them, both divide sentences and pronounce accents. Indeed, what nation, apart from the Greeks, now writes accents? Yet what nation does not pronounce them? If the verses were marked in writing, with what face does Rabbi Joseph in the Talmud, tractate Kiddushin, chapter 1, folio 30, ask to which verse [ריתולח] belongs, to the preceding or the following one? With what face does he answer that the Babylonians were not practised in counting verses? For what was easier than, taking up a codex, to look at the mark of the verse?

units.la: Nec difficile erat etiam puellis versus numerare, ad dijudicandum, an ad priorem mediam par-tem, an ad posteriorem versus ille pertineret. Noindum igitur inscripti erant versus textui, Deinde versus longe breviores distinguebant, quàm postea Masorethæ.
units.tr: Nor was it difficult even for girls to count verses, in order to determine whether that verse belonged to the first half or the latter part. Therefore the verses were not yet written into the text. Afterwards they divided the verses into much shorter units than the Masorites later did.

units.la: Talmudici enim loco citato in lege numerant versus 8888[?] Masorethæ 5245, in Psalmis Talmudici 8896. Masorethæ [?]1527. Sic & antiqvi Christiani brevissimos si cum hodiernis compares. Sed ista peculiarem meditationem postulant. Librum Zohar nihili facio. Recens enim est à quodam Leone Judæo, ante trecentos paulo minus annos confictus & evulgatus. Hujus libri ante hoc tempus, Judæorum nemo meminit, atque ego in eum inquirens, plurima novitatis, certissima argumenta deprehendi.
units.tr: For the Talmudists, in the passage cited, count the verses of the Law as 8888, the Masorites 5245; in the Psalms the Talmudists count 8896, the Masorites 1527. So too the ancient Christians, if you compare their very short verses with today's. But these matters call for a separate treatment. I make no account of the book Zohar. It is recent, invented and published by a certain Jew named Leo, a little less than three hundred years ago. Before that time no Jew mentioned this book, and in my inquiry into it I have discovered very many clear proofs of its novelty.

units.la: Verùm his omnibus dimissis, quatuor argumentorum genera præter illa, quæ jam allata sunt ibi, proponam, quorum vim & consequentiam maximè ve-lim consideres, antequam solutionem eorum aggrediaris.
units.tr: But setting all these aside, I shall propose four kinds of argument, besides those already adduced there, the force and consequence of which I should very much like you to consider before you undertake to answer them.

units.la: Magna enim contendentium pars rimam potius, quam elabatur, attendit, quàm intimam objecti cognitionem & complexionis necessitatem.
units.tr: For a great part of disputants attends to the crack rather than to what is bound to fall out, that is, to the inner knowledge of the object and the necessity of its connection.

units.la: Primum desumptum est, ex variis Talmudis & Midraschim locis, in quibus quæstio est de varia lectione iisdem manentibus literis. Exempli causa Beth Israël f. 158. cap. 3. ex Tract. [illegible, ~2 letters] עבוד[?] vide misna & Ghemar. f. 29. p. 2. cap.
units.tr: The first is taken from various passages of the Talmud and the Midrashim, in which the question concerns a variant reading with the same letters remaining. For example, Beth Israel, folio 158, chapter 3, from the tractate [illegible, about two letters] עבוד; see the Mishnah and Gemara, folio 29, page 2, chapter.

units.la: אמר לן ישמאל אחי היאך אתה קוראל ימובים דריך מיע אמר לאאינ הדכרכנ שהרי חבירו מיכית עליולריח שסנוך טובים כיסוכים דריך [?] מיין
units.tr: [Ishmael my brother said to him: how do you read "tovim" (good) ... He said to him: ... for his companion ... "tovim" ... the Hebrew is garbled in the scan.]

units.la: Duplex inde & evidens argumen-tum colligitur. Prius si tum fuisset puncta, non fuisset locus huic interroga-tioni. Nam certum fuisset, legendum esse ut Moses vel Esdras punctaverant, & inspicienda tantum punctatio. Et ibi agunt Rabb. de re maxime seria, non autem de quæstione animi causa proposita. Immo ridicula interrogatio, id exemplo solis luce splendidius erit. Si quis te interrogaret, quomodo legis caput, inepta interrogatio, lego caput caput. Nec aliquis, qui literas latinas novit, aliter legere potest. Verùm si scribas caput, tum erit justa & necessaria interrogatio, quomodo legis caput. Legi enim potest ex æquo capit, cæpit, cupit, caput. Ex circumstantiis textus aut ex traditione, aut ex utroque definienda est lectio. Eodem plane modo si ponas inscripta puncta וכר stulta est interrogatio, nisi forte fieret infantulo quomodo legis. Nam זָכָר[?] legi non potest aliter quâm זָכָר[?] Itaque necessario hic modus loquendi supponit lectionem ambiguam, ut caput זָכָר דָּרִיךְ[?] cui directè contradicit punctatio. Si dicat quis;
units.tr: A double and evident argument is gathered from this. First, if the points had then existed, there would have been no room for this question. For it would have been certain that one had to read as Moses or Ezra had pointed, and only the pointing would need to be inspected. Yet there the Rabbis are dealing with a most serious matter, not with a question proposed for amusement. Indeed the question would be ridiculous; this will be clearer than the light of the sun by example. If someone asked you how you read caput, it would be a silly question, since one reads caput caput. Nor can anyone who knows Latin letters read it otherwise. But if you write caput, then the question, how do you read caput, will be a proper and necessary one, for it can be read as capit, cepit, cupit, or caput. The reading must be settled from the circumstances of the text, or from tradition, or from both. In exactly the same way, if you posit the points וכר written in, the question is foolish, unless perhaps it were put to a little child: how do you read it? For זָכָר cannot be read otherwise than זָכָר. Therefore this mode of speaking necessarily presupposes an ambiguous reading, such as caput, which the pointing directly contradicts. If someone should say:

units.la: Tum non erat punctatus in manibus. Facilè à tantis Rabbinis accersiri poterat, praesertim cùm de re ageretur maximè feria, sed nusquam legas consulendum librum punctatum, qui statim & unico conspectu litem diremisset, R. Jacob autor libri.citati fatetur ex sua & alterius R. sententia, puncta tum non fuisse adscripta, atqve ideo Akibam legendo errasse, idque probat autoritate jam ex tractatu Bavabathra allegata. Concesso tamen libros eorum esse punctatos, responderi posset, varietatem fuisse in punctis, ideo varie illis locis lectum fuisse, ut varietas, inquit, hodie est in dictionibus inter Orientalium libros & Occidentalium. Huic argumento nihil aliud cum aliqua probabilitatis specie responderi potest. Verùm nusquam punctorum variationem causantur, aut ejus in tanta necessitate mentionem faciunt. Deinde omnibus illis locis, qvi permulti referri possunt, nulla est à punctatoribus adnotata varietas. Insuper cùm in literarum vel dictionum varietate dicant, ne legas sic, sed sic, apponunt litteras varias. Ita profecto de punctis, si ulla fuissent apud eos puncta. Praeterea in exemplo Joab & Davidis locum non habet varia punctorum lectio, eo qvòd in re tanti momenti liber Mosis consuli poterat. Imo liber Davidis, qvia rex erat, ex ipso Mosis αὐτογράφῳ[?] erat exscriptus. Deniqve ille interpretandi modus in illis tredecim Rabbinicis continetur. Si fuisset varia tum lectio, nulla fuisset Joabo occidendi praeceptoris causa, neqve Davidi reprehendendi Joabi, qvia alterutra potuisset eligi. Qvin imò eo casu praeceptoris lectio, Davidicae fuisset praeferenda, eo qvòd humanior. Sed qva ratione variae jam potuissent esse lectiones celebres, cùm liber Mosis extaret, cujus inspectu, nullo negotio le-ctio ctio[?] varians expungi potuisset. Posterius inde desumptum argumentum maxime urget, & me maxime afficit, velimque illud nulla cum animi [illegible, ~8 letters] perpendas, ideo textum exscripsi, inter הדיך[?] & דריך זכר[?] & הדיך[?] non habent Judæi, qva ratione distinguvant; loqven-do nulla est difficultas, nam pronuntiatur זָכָר Zakar masculus, & זֵכֶר Zeker memoria, & sic de cæteris. Verùm cum ab iis scribitur, nulla tum præsto fuit ratio, qva unum ab altero distingverent. Qvomodo legis, ego lego inqvit, זכר alius, vero זכר, si punctorum nomina aut figuræ aliqvæ illis fuissent, procul omni dubio, scribentes expressissent, lego זכר cum duplici Kamets, ego verò cum sex punctis aut duplici Sægol. Nec semel hoc ipsis contigit, sed innumeris locis. Eadem enim est ratio, qvoties de vocalibus agitur, istorum apud eos frequentium dictorum, ne legas sic, sed sic, ne legas [illegible, ~3 letters] sed [illegible, ~3 letters]. sicut & illius est mater Masoræ, est mater lectionis. v. g. tractatu Kiduschim[?] f. 18. p. 2. fine & versa initio, disputant, an filia a Patre vendita, postliminio revertens à Patre iterum vendi possit. Alii affirmant, alii negant, & rationes exponunt, niuntur autem varia punctatione [?] בבזרו ; alii volunt legi בבזרו alii בבזרו eo quod perfide egit. Ter aut quater paucis verbis repetunt dictionem בבזרו alii volunt legi בבזרו alii1 contendunt legi בבזרו. Necesse omnino erat tum, aut figuras punctorum, aut nomina saltem exprimere, ut unum ab altero scribendo distingverent. Id illustratur ex locis in qvibus sub eadem formula de dictionibus disputant; ne legas מה sed מאח est enim manifesta distinctio unius ab altero, nec est necessaria punctorum inscriptio, satis enim distinguit litterarum varietas expressa. Sed quid hoc sibi vult, ne legas זכר sed זכר. Ne legas בוזרו sed בזרו hoc illustrandum exemplo superiore caput, &c. Confirmat, hoc dvod[?] aliqvando vocales matres lectionis addunt, ut hæc distinguant. v. g. Sanhedrim f. 4. ubi disputantes de immunditie puerperæ, an duabus septimanis an. 70. diebus, eo qvòd scriptum sit שבעי qvod proprie 70. significat, qvia contendunt, duas septimanas scribunt שבועים ut exprimant pronuntiationem שבעים si punctorum usum habuissent; nam melius faciliusq; erat, textu scripturæ immutato, puncta addere qvàm litteras. Non qværitur, an scirent legere, sciebant equidem, sed de expressione varietatis sectionis, qvæ punctorum figuris aut nominibus adeo perspicuè fieri poterat ab illis, nunqvam tamen in tanta necessitate & disputantium contentione, facta legitur. Demus illud de Joab fabulam esse, id non qværitur, qvisqve id facile credit. In expressione ab iis facta זכר qvid erat proclivius qvam punctorum mentionem facere? Deinde qvi fieri potest, ut in rebus tanti momenti, de qvibus tam sæpe agitur, ad textum punctatum, si erat aliqvis, non recurrerint, qvi uno verbo litem dirimere poterat? Imo posito textu nulla poterat lis esse. Qværitur an mulier puerpera immunda sit 14. aut 70. Diebus, nulla quaestio est, si textus aliquis est authentice punctatatus. Nam diserte Scriptura dicit duabus septimanis שבעים. Pone textum non punctatum שבעים. Tum gravissima quaestio, nam & 70. dies & dua[?]eptimanae intelligi possunt. Sic & de בור[?] & aliis pluribus. Huc referri debet invictum meo judicio ex S. Hieronymo argumentum in Hierem cap. 9. v. 22. Verbum Hebraicum, quod tribus litteris scribitur דבר, vocales enim in medio non habet, pro consequentia & legentis arbitrio, si legatur dabar, sermonem significat, si deber mortem, si daber loquere. Unde & 70. & Theodotio junxerunt illud praeterito capitulo, ut dicerent disperdent parvulos de foris, juvenes de plateis morte. Aquila vero & Symmachus transtulerunt λάλησον, id est, loquere. Si puncta fuissent inscripta, ita ne potuisset loqui S. Hieronymus דבר pro consequentis & legentis arbitrio potest legi דבר aut דבר. Dicet aliquis, codex S. Hieronymi non erat punctatus, sed si aliqvi codices fuerunt punctati, quare aliquem non sibi comparavit Hieronymus, qui tantum opus aggrediebatur, Hieronymus qui potentissimarum Matronarum opibus sustentabatur, qui varias regiones adibat, ut cum doctissimis Judæis conferret, &c. Quid dicam de Ecclesia Christiana, quæ eo tempore multos adhuc amplectebatur Judæos conversos, ipsum S. Epiphanium Hieronymi amicissimum. Nec semel ita philosophatus est, sed sæpissimé. Viginti duo loca adnotavimus in Exercitat. Biblicis, lib. 1. Exercit. 6. c. 2. & argumenta hinc adversus puncta collegimus, ideo hæc satis. Considerandum præterea, S. Hieronymum dicere, [?]דבר[?] vocales in medio non habere. Non agnoscit S. Hieronymus alias vocales Hebraeorum, quàm [?]אהיה[?] quas multis locis vocales appellat, scriberetur [?]יהוה[?] juxta Hieronymum, vocales habe-ret in medio ut [?]יהוה[?] nec alias vocales agnovit Josephus, cùm dixit nomen Dei constare ex quatuor vocalibus. Si apiculi infra supraqve litte-ras ras, positi illi cogniti fuissent, cum lectionem definiant, quare toties de lectione dubitas & differens modo ad unius, modo ad alterius testem 70. Aquilam, Symmachum, Theodotionem nunquam ad ista puncta in tanta rei necessitate confugit. Denique litterae punctatae desuper Hieronymum non latuerunt. Vulgo 15. numerant Tractatus, Sophrim decem tantum. Ut opinor, illius, quae habetur Genes.19. meminit Hieronymus quaest. in Genesim. Antiqui Judæi nonnunquam in defectivis & plenis dictionibus mysteria quaerunt. Sic Hieronymus in cap. 23. Genes. v. 16. moraliter interpretatur, quod Ephron initio versus plenè legatur עפרון & postea defectivè, Vau littera, quæ apud illos pro O legitur, ablata de ejus nomine est, & pro Ephron appellatus est Ephran, Mysteria in hoc quaerit Beresith Rabba Parasch 58. Ut recentiores omittam. Bahal Hatturim notat עפרן & עורף [?] Ghematricè componere numerum 400. quot ab Abraham acceperat siclos. Qui factum est, ut punctorum vocalium, licet perpetua illi daretur occasio, immo necessitas, nunquam meminerit Hieronymus?
units.tr: There was then no pointed text at hand. Such great Rabbis could easily have been summoned, especially since the matter was of the greatest moment, yet nowhere do you read that anyone consulted a pointed book, which would have settled the dispute at once and at a single glance. R. Jacob, the author of the book cited, admits, on his own view and that of another rabbi, that points had not then been attached, and that for this reason Akiba misread; he proves this by the authority of the tractate Bava Bathra already cited. Yet even granting that their books were pointed, it could be replied that the points varied, so that the passage was read differently in different places, just as, he says, the words of the books of the Orientals and those of the Occidentals differ today. Nothing else can be offered in reply to this argument with any appearance of probability. But nowhere do they blame a variation of points, or mention one in so great a need. Next, in all those passages, which could be cited in great number, the pointers have noted no variation. Moreover, when they speak of variation in letters or words, they say, "Do not read thus, but thus," and they add the differing letters. So surely they would have done with points, if they had any. Besides, in the example of Joab and David, a variant reading of points has no place, because in a matter of such weight the book of Moses could be consulted. Indeed the book of David, since he was king, had been copied from Moses' own autograph. Finally, that method of interpretation is contained in those thirteen Rabbinic rules. If there had been a variant reading at that time, there would have been no reason for Joab to kill his master, nor for David to rebuke Joab, since either reading could have been chosen. Indeed in that case the master's reading would have been preferred to David's, as the more humane. But how could famous variant readings already have existed while the book of Moses was extant, by whose inspection any variant reading could have been removed without trouble? The latter argument, drawn from this source, presses hardest and affects me most, and I wish you would weigh it with a calm mind; I have therefore copied out the text. The Jews have no means of distinguishing between זכר and זכר, between הדיך and דריך. In speaking there is no difficulty: zakar is pronounced "male," zeker "memory," and so on for the rest. But when things are written by them, there was then no ready means by which they could distinguish one from another. "How do you read it?" says one; "I read it so," says another, "zakar," while the other reads "zakar" with different vowels.
