If the names or some figures of points had existed among them, the writers would without doubt have expressed them: "I read zakar with double kamets, but I with six points or with double segol." Nor did this happen to them once only, but in countless places. The reason is the same whenever vowels are discussed, a phrase frequent among them: "Do not read thus, but thus; do not read ... but ..." as also "is the mother of the Masora," "is the mother of the reading." For example, in the tractate Kiddushin, folio 18, page 2, near the end and at the beginning of the next, they dispute whether a daughter sold by her father, returning by postliminy, may be sold again by her father. Some affirm, others deny, and they set out their reasons, resting however on a varying pointing: some wish it read בבזרו, others בבזרו "because he acted treacherously"; three or four times in a few words they repeat the expression, some wish it read one way, others contend it should be read another. It was altogether necessary then to express either the figures of the points or at least their names, so that they could distinguish one from another in writing. This is illustrated by the passages in which they dispute about words under the same formula: "do not read מה but מאח," for the difference of one from the other is plain, and no inscription of points is needed, since the expressed variety of letters distinguishes sufficiently. But what does this mean: "do not read זכר but זכר," "do not read בוזרו but בזרו"? This is to be illustrated by the example of the chapter above, etc. It is confirmed that they sometimes add the vowels as mothers of reading, to distinguish these words. For example, in Sanhedrin, folio 4, where those disputing about the uncleanness of a woman in childbed ask whether it lasts for two weeks or seventy days, because it is written שבעי, which properly means seventy; for they contend that the word should be written שבועים, to express the pronunciation שבעים, if they had had the use of points; for it was easier and better, with the text of Scripture unchanged, to add points than letters. The question is not whether they knew how to read, for they certainly did know, but about the expression of the variety of reading, which could have been made most plainly by them through the figures or names of the points; yet it is never read that this was done, in so great a need and in the heat of the disputants. Grant that the story of Joab is fiction, which is not the question, and which anyone readily believes. In the reading of זכר that they expressed, what was more obvious than to mention the points? Further, how can it be that in matters of such moment, about which they so often argue, they did not have recourse to a pointed text, if there was one, which could settle the dispute with a single word? Indeed, given such a text, there could be no dispute at all. The question is whether a woman in childbed is unclean for fourteen or for seventy days; there is no question, if some text is authentically pointed. For Scripture expressly says שבעים, "two weeks." Suppose the text unpointed: שבעים. Then the question is most serious, for both seventy days and two weeks can be understood. So too with בור and many others. To this belongs, in my judgment, the unanswerable argument from St. Jerome on Jeremiah 9:22: "The Hebrew word, which is written with three letters, דבר, has no vowels in the middle; by consequence and the reader's choice, if it is read dabar, it means word; if deber, pestilence; if daber, speak. Hence both the Seventy and Theodotion joined it to the preceding chapter, so as to say, 'they will destroy the little ones outside, the youths in the streets by death.' But Aquila and Symmachus translated it λάλησον, that is, speak." If points had been inscribed, St. Jerome could not have said this; דבר can be read דבר or דבר according to the consequence and the reader's choice. Someone will say that St. Jerome's codex was not pointed; but if some codices were pointed, why did Jerome, who was undertaking so great a work, not procure one for himself? Jerome, who was supported by the wealth of the most powerful matrons, who visited various regions to confer with the most learned Jews, and so on? What shall I say of the Christian Church, which at that time still embraced many converted Jews, and St. Epiphanius himself, Jerome's closest friend? He philosophised in this way not once but very often. We have noted twenty-two passages in the Biblical Exercitations, book 1, exercise 6, chapter 2, and gathered arguments from them against the points, so let this suffice. It must further be considered that St. Jerome says that דבר has no vowels in the middle. St. Jerome does not recognise other vowels of the Hebrews than אהיה, which he calls vowels in many places; according to Jerome, יהוה would have vowels in the middle, like יהוה. Nor did Josephus recognise other vowels, when he said that the name of God consists of four vowels. If the little marks above and below the letters had been known, since they define the reading, why do you so often doubt the reading and defer now to the witness of one, now of another, of the Seventy, Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and never in so great a need take refuge in these points? Finally, pointed letters above were not hidden from Jerome. Commonly they count fifteen tractates of Sopherim, but only ten. As I think, Jerome mentions the one found in Genesis 19 in his Questions on Genesis. The ancient Jews sometimes seek mysteries in defective and full spellings. So Jerome, on Genesis 23:16, interprets morally that Ephron, written fully עפרון at the beginning of the verse and afterwards defectively, has had the letter Vav, which among them is read as O, removed from his name, and was called Ephran instead of Ephron. The Beresith Rabba, Parasch 58, seeks mysteries in this too. To omit more recent writers: Bahal Hatturim notes that עפרן and עורף, arranged by gematria, make the number 400, the shekels Abraham had received. How is it that Jerome never mentions the points of the vowels, though a constant occasion, even a necessity, was given him?

units.la: Secundum argumentum ex libro Sophrim, qui post publicatum Talmud compositus est, hoc est intra annum Christi 700 & 800. Quique Talmudis honorificè meminit, totus est in docendo modo scribendi, hæc omnia minuté & scrupulosè admodum. Quo in pergameno, quomodo præparato, ex quibus bestiis confecto,à quibus scribi, quod spatium inter litteras, quot litteræ in linea, quot lineæ in pagina. Quæ malè scripta, eradi possunt, quæ non eradi sine libri profanatione, quæ dictiones dividi, quæ non dividi, quæ super punctari, quæ scribi & non legi, & contrà quæ aliter scribi & aliter legi, & è contra, quæ litteræ scribi debeant majores, & minores, extensiores, & alia permulta, quæ enarrare longum sit, & importunum. At de punctis nusquam apud eum mentio. Quomodo factum est, ut in tam copioso de his rebus sermone, punauctorum[?] nusqvam meminerit, nisi qvod ea Judæis nondum ad juvandum lectionem erant invecta.
units.tr: A second argument comes from the book Sophrim, which was composed after the Talmud was published, that is, between the years 700 and 800 of Christ. Its author speaks honourably of the Talmud, and his whole book is devoted to teaching the manner of writing, and all of it very minutely and scrupulously: on what parchment, how prepared, from what animals it was made, by whom it was to be written, what space to leave between letters, how many letters in a line, how many lines on a page. He says which letters, if badly written, may be erased, and which may not be erased without profaning the book; which words are to be divided and which not; which are to be marked above; which are written but not read; and conversely, which are written one way and read another, and the reverse; which letters are to be written larger or smaller, more extended, and many other things, too long and tedious to recount. But nowhere does he mention points. How is it that in so copious a discourse on these matters he never mentions vowel points, unless because they had not yet been introduced to aid the Jews in reading?

units.la: Tertium argumentum ex Masoretharum distinctione sumitur. Duplices fuere, priores textum recensuerunt; posteriores puncta infixerunt. Priores autorem sive autores libri Sophrim secuti sunt, qvod certissimis argumentis demonstratur. Autor libri Sophrim & Masorethæ in eadem materia versati sunt. Adnotaverunt utriq; τὸ קרי וכתיב, varias Judæorum lectiones. Sed si utrorumqve traditiones comparentur, qvintuplo aut sextuplo plures adnotaverunt Masorethæ, qvàm tractatus ille, & multitudo illa ingens prætermissa, non est minoris momenti, qvàm commemorata. Autor igitur tractatus illius ignoravit,qvod fie-ri non potuisset, si Masorethæ viri tantæ autoritatis & omnibus Judæis noti eum præcessissent, & multo minus si Masore-thæ fuissent Esdræ collegæ; deinde cer-tissimum est in ejusmodi causa, posterio-res prioribus semper addere, qvædam etiam corrigere, quod etiam fecerunt Masorethæ, cùm quædâ à tractatu Sophrim adnotata omiserunt, quia sc. libros-diligenter consulendo, ipsius observationem notare deprehenderunt. Præterea nihil ille tractatus de scribenda in margine vera lectione, & alia in textu vel è contra. Nihil in eo de distinctione scriptionis marginalis & textualis, quæ apud Masorethas adeo celebris est, & totius eorum laboris effectus.
units.tr: The third argument is drawn from the distinction between the Masorites. There were two sorts: the earlier ones settled the text, the later ones inserted the points. The earlier ones followed the author or authors of the book Sophrim, as is demonstrated by the most certain arguments. The author of the book Sophrim and the Masorites were versed in the same subject. Both noted the qere and kethiv, the various readings of the Jews. But if the traditions of each are compared, the Masorites noted five or six times as many as that treatise, and that huge multitude passed over by it is no less important than those it records. The author of that treatise therefore was ignorant of them. This could not have happened if the Masorites, men of such authority and known to all Jews, had preceded him, and still less if the Masorites had been colleagues of Ezra. Then, it is most certain in such a matter that later writers always add to earlier ones and also correct some things; the Masorites did this too, when they omitted some things noted in the treatise Sophrim, because, by diligently consulting the books, they found that its observation was to be noted. Moreover, that treatise says nothing about writing the true reading in the margin and another in the text, or the reverse. It says nothing about the distinction between marginal and textual writing, which is so celebrated among the Masorites and is the whole result of their labour.

units.la: Deniqve quamobrem nusquam citat Masorethas אנשי המסר[?] vel בעלי המסר[?] ut toties, qvi eos secuti sunt.
units.tr: Finally, why does it never cite the "men of the Masora" [אנשי המסרה] or "masters of the Masora" [בעלי המסרה], as the later writers who followed them so often do?

units.la: Præcessit igitur Masorethas autor sive autores istius tractatus, sic nec unquam Talmud Masorethas citat, istud autores Masorae vel Masorethae, est omnibus illis cognitum.
units.tr: The author or authors of that treatise, therefore, preceded the Masorites. Likewise the Talmud never cites the Masorites. That the authors are called Masora or Masorites is known to all of them.

units.la: Nam hoc axioma ישאם למקראישאם למסרה[?] nihil ad rem prorsus facit, qvum Masora ibi significet traditionem, non homines aliqvos, & in illo apud Talmudicos frequenti axiomate, nihil aliud significat, qvam textum legis, Mosê Israëlis traditum, ut Talmudis glossatores interpretantur. Unde manifestum est, Talmudicos constanter censuisse, lectionem à Mose scripto non esse traditam, quàm id, quod scriptum est à Mose, per traditionem à lectione distinguunt. Ita quod refertur Meghill. c. 1. f. 3. Nec unquam Talmudici Maforae contradicunt. Contradictio illa in Talmude nunquàm legitur, sed est in Scripturis recentiorum, Maforam cum Talmude comparantium. Sic dici possunt 70 Interpretes, Hieronymus, Aquila, Symmachus, Onkelos, & Talmudi & Maforae contradicere. Priores Maforethas textū tantum recensuisse, hoc est קְרִי וּכְתִיב [?] plenas, deficientes, & abundantes dictiones, & ejusmodi quae litteras spectant adnotasse, autor est Elias Levita in tertia praefatione, sed non tam ipsum confidero, quàm rationem certissimam ab eo allatam. Maforethae illi erant Occidentales, Judaico more, hoc est in Judaea, & eis Euphraten habitantes, postquam recensionem suam in lucem emiserunt, codicesque à se corre-ctos publicarunt, Orientales sive Baby-lonii lonii in eorum operam inquisiverunt, atque ducentis & aliquot locis ab iis dissenserunt, suosque codices cum Maforetharum in iis locis correctione similiter publicarunt. Sed nullae eorum differentiae puncta spectant & accentus, sed litteras tantum & dictiones, ut notavit Elias, & singula examinanti notum est. Manifestum est igitur, Maforethas illos, qui textum recensuerunt, & varias lectiones, ad marginem adnotarunt, de punctis non cogitasse. Si enim biblia punctassent, num Babylonii, qui tot differentias in rebus multo majoris momenti adnotaverunt, nullas in punctis adnotassent? Si quaeratur aera temporis istorum Maforetharum, ex dictis constat, annum Christi octingentesimum praecedere non potuisse.
units.tr: That axiom [ישאם למקרא ישאם למסרה] has nothing whatever to do with the matter, since Masora there means tradition, not some men. In that frequent Talmudic axiom it signifies nothing other than the text of the law handed down by Moses to Israel, as the glossators of the Talmud explain. Whence it is plain that the Talmudists consistently held that the reading was not handed down from Moses in writing; they distinguish by tradition the reading from what Moses wrote. So it is related in Megillah, ch. 1, f. 3. And the Talmudists never contradict the Masora. That contradiction is never read in the Talmud; it is found in the writings of recent authors who compare the Masora with the Talmud. Thus one may say that the Seventy, Jerome, Aquila, Symmachus and Onkelos contradict both the Talmud and the Masora. Elias Levita is the authority that the earlier Masorites merely settled the text, noting the qere and kethiv, full, defective and excessive words, and things concerning letters. I rely less on the man himself than on the very certain reason he gives. Those Masorites were Western, in the Jewish manner, that is, in Judaea, and those living beyond the Euphrates. After the Western Masorites had published their recension and issued their corrected codices, the Eastern or Babylonian Jews sought out their work and dissented from them in some two hundred places, and likewise published their own codices with the Masorites' correction in those places. But none of their differences concern points and accents; they concern only letters and words, as Elias observed, and as anyone who examines the individual cases knows. It is plain, therefore, that those Masorites who settled the text and noted the various readings in the margin were not thinking about points. For if they had pointed the Bible, would the Babylonians, who noted so many differences in matters of far greater weight, have noted none in the points? If one asks the age of these Masorites, it is clear from what has been said that they cannot have preceded the year 800 of Christ.

units.la: Posteriores Maforethae, cum viderent libros a praecedentibus castigatos, & varias lectiones seu castigationes margini adscriptas, linguamque Chaldaicam & Syriacam, quae ipsis vernacula erat, Arabum mutari, lectionemque biblicam corrumpi, puncta invenerunt, quibus pronuntiatio efformaretur, & quasi pingeretur. Arabum exemplo existimo commotos, qui cum religione sua varias gentes infecissent Alcoranum punctaverunt, ut barbaros religionis suae amantes, sed linguae ignaros in lectione juvarent. Hoc autem & antiquorum autoritate, & evidentibus rationibus demonstrare possum.
units.tr: Later Masorites, seeing that the books had been corrected by their predecessors and that various readings or corrections were written in the margins, and seeing that the Chaldaic and Syriac language, which was their vernacular, was being changed by Arabic, and the biblical reading corrupted, invented points by which pronunciation could be formed and, as it were, painted. I think they were moved by the example of the Arabs, who, when they had infected various nations with their religion, pointed the Koran to help barbarians who loved their religion but were ignorant of its language in reading. I can demonstrate this both by the authority of the ancients and by evident reasons.

units.la: Tiberienses fuisse istos Masorethas, asserunt antiqvi Grammatici; hujus rei optimus testis Aben Esdra, qvi librum compositurus [illegible, ~2 letters] tot evolvit, qvi eum praecesserunt, Grammaticos. Ita in libro צחות [?] capite de Patach minore sive Segol rationem redditurus punctationis insolentis כן מיהג חכמי טב דיא ותם העקר כיטהם היו אנשי המסרה ואגהנו מהם [illegible, ~2 letters] קבלו המגקד ויכתסק לורנהם העקר כי טהם אולי עאי קשלא י חשוב ארם בי שכח [?] clarius id docere non potuit Aben Esdra; à Tiberiensibus igitur omnis punctatio. Tiberienses autem illi numero erant quindecim[?] præcipui, qui libros sacro non modo recensuerunt, secundum dictiones & litteras, ut priores, sed etiam neqvis in illis legendis erratet, puncta, inve-nerunt & textui inscripserunt, ut lectio quæ hactenus fuerat πατροπαράδοτος[?], scripto conservaretur; deinde libros illos publicè exposuerunt, ut Judæi libros suos ad eorum formam scriberent & corrigerent; cùm autem viderent, paucos homines eorum opera uti posse, eo qvòd pauci Judæi Palæstinam sese conferre possent, eorum libros inspecturi & eum suis comparaturi, aliud opus ingens aggressi sunt, libros scilicet continentes; hæc dictio toties cum Patach, his scilicet locis qvæ per initia versuũ designarunt; toties cum Sægol, &c toties reperitur in Scriptura cum hac voce conjuncta, &c. hi libri dicti sunt Masoretici, atqve ab eo tempore Masora sumi cœpit pro libro ista complectente, qvod ante fuerat inauditum; existimarem tamen, priores Masorethas libellos aliqvos ejusmodi ad dictiones & literas spectantes in Judæorum gratiam composuisse; quos posteriores, multis observationibus non modo circa puncta & accentus, sed etiam circa litteras & dictiones auxerunt. Scribæ Judæi hanc Masoram ad Margines Bibliorum transferre, conati sunt, sed abrupte & confuse admodum, ut videre est in Bibliis Manuscriptis; & notarunt Elias Levita, & R. Jacob Chaiim. Biblia ab ipsis Tiberiensibus quindecim correcta, vidit, evolvit & consideravit Aben Esdra ut testatur in 25.[?] v. 31. Exodi, de quibus juraverant, se ter considerasse omnem punct. & defic. & plenas dictiones ; non sequitur autem punctationem inscriptam fuisse v. g. Nunc Misna cuditur Amsterodami cum punctis; quod antea factum non est. Si diceret quis, punctato-res illiter consideraverunt omnem punctationem, non sequitur, ergo Misna antea fuit punctata; tandem ascenditur ad aliquod principium, quo non datur superius, ut, pro Bibliis Tiberienses, pro Misna Amsterodamenses; sequitur quidem, ergo antea punctatio, sive pronuntiatio & lectio fuit, sed non inscriptiq, quæ tum cœpit. Masorethici autem libri etiamnum extant, ut nihil de Maf. excusa loquamur, ut tuipse optimè nósti. His Masoretharum libris posteriores multas addiderunt observationes, & Alphabeta, & paria, & varias dictionum similium & dissimilium, sive literas, sive puncta, sive accentus, sive sensum spectes, series & ordines; ωεσεργίαι[?] enim tam variæ in sacram Scripturam excogitatæ & tam accuratè enumeratæ uno sæculo perfici non potuerunt. Masorethas fuisse Tiberienses illos, jam ex libro מאגכאי[?] probatum evidentissimè: sic eos vocare solent antiquissimi Grammatici. Aben Esdra in libro צחרת[?] non longè ab initio, ubi agit de pronunciatione literæ מ[?] eos testes citatus vocat אנשמטכריא[?], & alibi non semel verba Judæ Chiug primi Grammatici refert, quibus eos Judas appellat אנשירטבר[?] יקראישוא המתנועע וכו[?] ubi multa specialia refert Masorethis consueta, quæ tamen alii non sequuntur, & in libro [?]מאוגל capite הנקראים peculiarem af-fert ex R. Juda lectionem, quam confirmat Judas hoc modo ואמרו כיכן [?] אנשי טבר יא eos Aben Esdra & antiquisimi Grammatici sic vocant, & de iis tanquam de hominibus non adeo antiquis verba faciunt. Ideo sæpius Masoretharum sententiam & punctationem audent rejicere, ut ipse Aben Esdra qui eos magnifacit, in libro [?]צחרת cap. [?]אמר בעל המסרת כי והנחו חשר אלף והם שתימלות המורכבים ולפירעתי שאו צריך רק חתא כומף על הנו מירך זכו addit suæ sententiæ contra Masorethas rationem. Eodem libro in littera ה iterum negar Aleph deficere. אף שאנשי המסר אמרו שהוא חמר objicit sibi quomodo mendacii arguat Masorethas; deinde emollit dictum, recte ex traditione quam habebant, scripsisse [?]יהנדיר & dixisse tantum [?]דרמטבר quod deficiat. Verum in margine adnotarunt [?]יהבהההוא quod est potissimum & legendum; hoc modo liceret omnia Marginalia, quæ sunt τὰ κύρια & legenda, ad opinionem revocare. Quidquid sit in duobus à Masorethicis prudens volensque dissentit, quod Aleph deficit, & quod sint duæ dictiones. Et in litera Vau, durius arguit, & ratio Masorethārum non est ratio; & in Nehemiam c.2.15.ad הבירשרוי scribit unicam esse dictionem, Masorethas vero divisisse ut significarent effractionem murorum Hierusalem; nihilominus ait הראשון בעיני נבק והררך in fine libri dicit, multos explanatores seu commentatores erroris arguere Pausatorem, inter quos Moses Hacohen, & Jachid, quem alibi Gheonem vocat, qui decem versus male distinctos esse contendebat.
units.tr: The ancient grammarians assert that these Masorites were Tiberians. The best witness to this is Aben Ezra, who, when about to compose his book, unrolled so many grammarians who had preceded him. Thus in the book Tzachoth, in the chapter on the minor Patach or Segol, where he gives the reason for an unusual pointing, he says: "So the wise men of Tiberias [כן מיהג חכמי טבריא] practised, and the principle is that they were the men of the Masora [והעיקר כי הם היו אנשי המסרה]..." He could not have taught this more clearly; all pointing, therefore, comes from the Tiberians. Those Tiberians were fifteen chief men who not only settled the sacred books according to words and letters, like the earlier ones, but also, so that no one should err in reading them, found the points and inscribed them in the text, so that the reading handed down from the fathers until then might be preserved in writing. Then they publicly exhibited those books, so that the Jews might write and correct their own books after their form. But when they saw that few men could make use of their work, since few Jews could betake themselves to Palestine to inspect those books and compare their own with them, they undertook another huge work, namely the books containing the Masora: this word occurs so often with Patach, in those places which they marked by the beginnings of verses; so often with Segol, and so on; and it is found so often in Scripture joined with this word. These books were called Masoretic, and from that time the word Masora began to be taken for the book containing all this, which had been unheard of before. I would, however, think that the earlier Masorites composed some little books of this kind concerning words and letters for the benefit of the Jews, and that the later ones enlarged them with many observations, not only about points and accents but also about letters and words. Jewish scribes tried to transfer this Masora to the margins of the Bibles, but abruptly and very confusedly, as can be seen in the manuscript Bibles; Elias Levita and R. Jacob Chaiim have noted this. Aben Ezra saw, unrolled and studied the Bibles corrected by the Tiberians, fifteen in number, as he testifies at Exodus 25, v. 31, where they swore that they had three times considered every pointing and every defective and full word. It does not follow, however, that the pointing was written into the text: v. g. Now the Mishnah is printed at Amsterdam with points, which was not done before. If someone should say that the pointers carefully considered all the pointing, it does not follow that the Mishnah was pointed before. At last one comes to some principle beyond which there is nothing higher, as for the Bibles the Tiberians, for the Mishnah the Amsterdammers. It does follow, indeed, that there was pronunciation and reading before, but not the written inscription, which began at that time. Masoretic books still exist, not to mention the printed Masora, as you yourself know very well. To these Masoretic books later writers added many observations, alphabets, pairs, and various series and orders of similar and dissimilar words, whether one looks at letters, points, accents or sense. Such varied contrivances on Sacred Scripture, so accurately enumerated, could not have been completed in a single century. That the Masorites were those Tiberians has now been most evidently proved from the book [מאגכאי]; ancient grammarians usually call them so. Aben Ezra, in the book Tzachoth not far from the beginning, where he treats of the pronunciation of the letter mem, cites them as witnesses and calls them [אנשמטכריא]. Elsewhere, more than once, he reports the words of Judah Chiug, the first grammarian, by which Judah calls them [אנשי טבריא]. There he reports many special things customary among the Masorites, which others do not follow. In the book [מאוגל], chapter "those called," he brings forward a peculiar reading from R. Judah, which Judah confirms in this way: "and they said thus, the men of Tiberias." Aben Ezra and the most ancient grammarians call them so, and speak of them as men not very ancient. Therefore they often dare to reject the opinion and pointing of the Masorites, as Aben Ezra himself does, although he magnifies them. In the book Tzachoth, chapter "he says," he adds his own opinion against the Masorites, with a reason: The master of the Masora says that aleph is one of the seven compound words, but I am not obliged to follow him, since the rule is clear. In the same book, under the letter he, he again denies that aleph is deficient. Although the men of the Masora said it is superfluous, he objects to himself, how he could charge the Masorites with falsehood; then he softens the statement, saying that they rightly wrote according to the tradition they had, and that they only said it is deficient. But in the margin they noted [...], which is the principal reading and the one to be read; in this way one could call back to opinion all the marginal readings, which are the chief ones and the ones to be read. Whatever the case, he knowingly and deliberately dissents from the Masorites in two points: that aleph is deficient, and that there are two words. On the letter vav he argues more harshly: and the reason of the Masorites is no reason. On Nehemiah 2:15, at the word [הבירשרוי], he writes that it is a single word, although the Masorites divided it to signify the breaching of the walls of Jerusalem. Nevertheless, he says at the end of the book that many expositors or commentators charge the Pausator with error, among them Moses Hacohen and Jachid, whom elsewhere he calls Gaon, who contended that ten verses had been wrongly distinguished.

units.la: Non sane credebant viri illi apud eos maximi, Esdram versuum & Pausarum autorem fuisse. Iis equidem non assentitur Aben Esdra, immo miratur admodum, quod hoc faciant, quia si non est, inquit Esdras, vir tantus, est quantus post ipsum non alius fuit. Existimavit Aben Esdra, Pausatorem esse Tiberiensibꝰ antiqviorem; ex ea Judæorum
units.tr: Certainly those men, the greatest among them, did not believe that Ezra was the author of the verses and the pausal marks. Aben Ezra does not agree with them. He is in fact greatly astonished that they hold this view, because, he says, if Ezra was not so great a man, he was at least one than whom no greater came after him. Aben Ezra thought that the Pausator was older than the Tiberians. This is the opinion of the Jews.

units.la: de Masorethis sententia factum est, ut Rabbini celebres in variis provinciis, libros diligenter pro genio corrigerent: id praestitit R. Ben Asher, quem Moses Bar Maimon Masorethis praetulit, & ad quem relictis Masorethis, librum tuum correxit, ut ipse testatur cap. 8. de libro legis; hac in causa Mosis verba sunt decretoria.
units.tr: Because of this opinion about the Masorets, famous rabbis in various regions diligently corrected books according to their own judgement. R. Ben Asher did this. Moses Maimonides preferred him to the Masorets, and abandoned them in favour of him, when he corrected his book, as Ben Asher himself testifies in chapter 8 on the book of the Law. In this matter the words of Moses are decisive.

units.la: ולפי שראיתי שיבוש גרול ככל [?] המפרם שראיתי [?] בדברי אלו וכן בעלי [?] המשרת שבותבי ומחבכית להיריע [?] הבתו הות והכתומות גחלקו בדברים [?] אילו במחלו קות המפרים [illegible, ~2 letters] שממכיש [?] צלותנ [?]
units.tr: [Garbled in the scan; rendered as far as it can be read:] And since I have seen a great corruption in the commentators, which I have seen in these words, and likewise in the masters of ... that they have ... in the variants of the Pausators ... [ונשם המפרם שראיתי בדברי אלו וכן בעלי המשרת שבותבי ומחבכית להיריע הבתו הות והכתומות גחלקו בדברים אילו במחלו קות המפרים]

units.la: Vides in his, quae sunt apud eos maximi momenti, in quo si error committatur, prophanus est, donec folium illud avellatur, omnes libros, quos vidit Moses, fuisse multum confusos. 2. Masorethas de hac re libros composuisse. 3. Magnam esse apud Masorethas de hac re litem & varietatem propter librorum, quos secuti sunt, differentiam; denique quod statim sequitur, libros illos deseruisse. & secutum in his Paraschis scribendis, & & aliis librum R. Aser accuratissime multis vicibus ab eo correctū, Hierosolymis à multis annis, ut inde libri corrigerentur expositum; & inquit, נעלי לממכת בְּמִפִּי הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי כְּהֲלָכָתוֹ alius erat Hierosolymis, vel forte idem liber Hierosolymitanus, quem antiquissimus Grammaticus R. Jonam sequebatur, ut de eo testantur Kimhi & Elias Levita. Erat in Hispania celeberrimus dictus Hillelianus, de quo Elias. Et habemus hic antiqua Manuscripta Biblia quaedam, qua-dringentorum annorum, in quibus ad marginem saepe citatur; aliis in locis alii fuerunt; testatur Kimhi in proœmio in radices, magnam se invenisse confusionem in punctationibus librorum regionis, in qua vivebat; eam autem in Dictionario suo & Grammatica correxisse, ope librorum correctorum ex Hispania adductorum, atque in hoc nationi suae magnum operae, pretium fecisse. In Europa autem libri Hispanici primas tulerunt, testatur Elias Levita in fractorum tabulis, & ita quoque censet R. Menacham,
units.tr: You see in these matters, which are of the greatest importance to them, that if an error is made, the page is profane until that leaf is torn out; that all the books which Moses saw were much confused. 2. That the Masorets composed books on this subject. 3. That among the Masorets there is great dispute and variety on this subject, because of the difference between the books they followed. Finally, what immediately follows: that they abandoned those books, and followed in writing these Paraschas, and others, the book of R. Aser, corrected by him most carefully many times, which had been set out at Jerusalem for many years so that books could be corrected by it. And he says: [נעלי לממכת במפי התורה שכתבתי כהלכתו] "...". This was another book at Jerusalem, or perhaps the same Jerusalem book which the very ancient grammarian R. Jonah followed, as Kimhi and Elias Levita testify about it. In Spain there was a very famous book called the Hillelian, of which Elias speaks. And here we have some ancient manuscript Bibles, four hundred years old, in which the marginal citations are often given. In other places there were other books. Kimhi testifies in the preface to his Roots that he found great confusion in the vowel-pointing of the books of the region in which he lived. He corrected it in his Dictionary and Grammar with the help of corrected books brought from Spain, and in this he did great service to his nation. In Europe the Spanish books took first place, as Elias Levita testifies in his tables of the (?) and R. Menahem also thinks so.

units.la: הם המוצהירם והכאסכים שראוי [?] לממיר עלירם [?] qvod autoritate duorum antiqvorum Rabbinorum confirmat, R. Abraham Ben Dir & R. Mosis Bar Nachman; præ cæteris celebres, fuerunt in punctatione, Ben Asher & Ben Nephtali, hic orientalis, iste occidentalis; ficut igitur post priores Masorethas, Babylonii eorum opus recensuerunt, & varias differentias adnotarunt; ita postqvam alii Masorethæ puncta inseripserunt, Babylonii punctationem istam examinaverunt, atqve in nonnullis ab ea discesserunt.
units.tr: [Hebrew, garbled:] [הם המוצהירם והכאסכים שראוי לממיר עלירם] They are the ones who make clear and ... that it is fitting to ... over them. This is confirmed by the authority of two ancient rabbis, R. Abraham ben Dior and R. Moses bar Nachman. Beyond all others the famous men in pointing were Ben Asher and Ben Naphtali: the one an Oriental, the other a Westerner. Therefore, just as after the first Masorets the Babylonians reviewed their work and noted various differences, so after other Masorets had inscribed the points, the Babylonians examined that pointing and departed from it in some respects.

units.la: Verùm Ben Asher pro Masorethis stans in nonnullis R. Nephtali Babyloniorum capiti non cessit, hincq; orta est celeberrima apud Judæos de certis punctationibus differentia. Hæc tantum commemoravi, ut appareat, priores Masorethas, qvorum recensitionem habemus, nihil de punctis cogitasse, alioqvin ut postea factum, & rectè adnotavit Elias, aliqvid in eorum punctatione reprehendisse Babylonii, cùm textum ab iis emendatum lustrarunt; ab eo tempore Judæorum libri, punctorum meditationibus, & disquisitionibus pleni fuerunt; antea æternum de illis silentium; hinc sicut in primis Masorethis contigit, ut textu ab iis lustrato Babylonii in multis literis & dictionibus ab iis dissentirent, ita postquam Tiberienses, atque hos secutus Aser, puncta inscripserunt, eorum punctationem lustrantes Babylonii, ab iis quoque in nonnullis discesse-runt, factaque est apud eos dissensio sub nominibus Aser & Nephtali.
units.tr: But Ben Asher, standing with the Masorets, did not yield in some points to R. Naphtali, the head of the Babylonians, and hence arose the most famous difference among the Jews concerning certain pointings. I have mentioned these things only so that it may be clear that the earlier Masorets, whose recension we have, thought nothing about points. Otherwise, as was later done, and as Elias rightly notes, the Babylonians found fault with something in their pointing when they went over the text emended by them. From that time the books of the Jews have been full of meditations and investigations about points; before that there was eternal silence about them. Hence, just as it happened in the case of the first Masorets that the Babylonians, who went over the text they had revised, differed from them in many letters and words, so after the Tiberians, and Aser who followed them, inscribed the points, the Babylonians who examined their pointing also departed from them in some respects, and a dispute arose among them under the names of Aser and Naphtali.

units.la: Si quis roget, quando vixerunt illi Tiberienses; præcisum tempus assignare difficile est; certum tamen est, annum Christi nongentesimum, aut subsecutos esse, aut non multum antecessisse. Ghe-dalias ait R. Aser vixisse ea generatione, quæ computatur ab anno Mundi 4700. ad 4800. hoc est ab anno Christi 940. ad 1040. Tiberiensibus autem proximus fuit: id etiam consonat Aben Esdræ, qui biblia ab iis recensita legit & consuluit. Erat autem Aben Esdra Romæ anno 1146. itaque Masorethis illis posterior fuit annis 220. & forsitan aliquid ex-currebat.
units.tr: If anyone asks when those Tiberians lived, it is difficult to give an exact date. It is certain, however, that they either came after the year of Christ 900, or were not much earlier. Gedalias says that R. Aser lived in that generation which is reckoned from the year of the world 4700 to 4800, that is, from the year of Christ 940 to 1040. He was close to the Tiberians. This also agrees with Aben Ezra, who read and consulted the Bibles revised by them. Aben Ezra was at Rome in the year 1146, so he was about 220 years later than those Masorets, and perhaps a little more.

units.la: Qvarto denique idem demonstratur ex studio Grammaticali ante illud tem-pus Judæis incognito. Aben Esdra, A-braham Levita, Kimchi, Elias Levita, Ghedalias, uno ore ajunt, R. Judam Chiug, Arabem è civitate Fessana oriun-dum primum esse Grammaticum, quem postea permulti, quos enumerant, se-cuti sunt, Judam autem referunt eorum Historiæ juxta annum Christi millesi-mum; quod sane argumentum est e-videntissimum ante tempus à nobis ad-notatum puncta non fuisse scripta; nam sine punctis scribi non potest Gramma-tica, ut recte adnotavit Elias, & res per se clara est; experiatur enim quis, exem-pli causa, conjugationem Kal sine pun-ctis describere, & statim illi aqva hære-bit; multo magis in Piel. Grammatica-lia enim illa sine punctis, ore tantum & sono exprimi & doceri possunt; atq; hinc est, quod statim post inscripta puncta Grammaticorum examen ebullierit.
units.tr: Fourthly, the same thing is shown from the study of grammar, which was unknown to the Jews before that time. Aben Ezra, Abraham Levita, Kimchi, Elias Levita and Gedalias all say with one voice that R. Judah Chiug, an Arab from the city of Fez, was the first grammarian. Many others whom they name followed him afterwards. They place Judah in their histories around the year of Christ 1000. This is surely a most evident argument that the points had not been written before the time we have noted. For grammar cannot be written without points, as Elias rightly observes, and the matter is clear in itself. Let anyone try, for example, to describe the Kal conjugation without points, and at once he will be stuck; much more so the Piel. Those grammatical rules can be expressed and taught without points only by mouth and sound. Hence it is that, immediately after the points were inscribed, an examination of the grammarians broke out.

units.la: Aben Esdra, qui post primam Grammaticam annis ad summum 140. scribebat, sedecim ante se enumerat, qui plurimos libros de Grammatica scripserant.
units.tr: Aben Ezra, who wrote at most 140 years after the first grammar, lists sixteen who before him had written many books on grammar.

units.la: His multa conjungi possunt, punctorum & accentuum nomina Chaldaica esse, nonnulla barbara prorsus quorum nescitur Etymon, quia neque Hebraicum, neque Chaldaicum quæque ut testratur R. Elias c. 2. de accentibus, deprompta sunt ex dialecto Thargum Hierosolymitani.quorum originationem divinare nunquam potuit: hinc manife-stum est, Masorethas illos, isto Thargum non esse priores, & consequenter Arabica dominatione; secundo Tiberienses paucis punctis nomina dederunt; apud eos reperitur tantum Kamets & Patach, nam Chirek, Cholum, Schurek, Kibuts per ipsas vocales exprimunt, [illegible, ~4 letters] Grammatici postea invenerunt iis nomina, nec in iis sunt concordes, ut videre potes in tertia præfatione Eliæ, pag. 24. ex quibus manifestum est, hanc artem ab illis Masorethis initium sumpsisse, atque ut in cæteris artibus moris est, temporis lapsu perfectam; omnes autem & priores & posteriores, qui sive in punctatione sive in litteris & dictionibus varie numerandis & comparandis operam navarunt, Masoretharum nomen tulerunt.
units.tr: To these many things may be added. The names of the points and accents are Chaldean, and some are altogether barbarous, and their etymology is unknown, because they are drawn neither from Hebrew nor from Chaldee, but from the dialect of the Jerusalem Targum, as R. Elias testifies in chapter 2 on accents. They could never guess their origin. Hence it is clear that those Masorets were not earlier than that Targum, and consequently not earlier than the Arabic domination. Second, the Tiberians gave names to few points; among them are found only Kamets and Patach. For Chirek, Cholem, Shureq and Kibbuts they express by the vowels themselves [illegible, about four letters]. Later grammarians devised names for them, and these are not in agreement, as you can see in the third preface of Elias, p. 24. From these things it is clear that this art began with those Masorets and, as is the custom with other arts, was perfected over time. All of them, both earlier and later, who laboured in pointing or in numbering and comparing letters and words in various ways, bore the name of Masorets.

units.la: 3. Idem testatur mos ille constans Ju-dæorum & Karaitarum, non modo librum legis Synagogicum, sed etiam Mezuzot & Tephillim sine ullis punctis scribendi; unde manifestum est, eos Masorethicam punctorum & accentuum inscriptionem hactenus privatim tantum amplexos esse, atque in gratiam ignaræ plebis, ut in lectione juvaretur, tamen nunquam esse admissam.
units.tr: 3. The same thing is shown by the constant custom of the Jews and the Karaites, who write not only the Synagogue book of the Law but also the Mezuzot and Tephillin without any points. Hence it is clear that they had embraced the Masoretic inscription of points and accents only privately until now, and that, although it was admitted for the sake of the ignorant common people, to help them in reading, it was never admitted into the public text.

units.la: 4. Omnes Judæi Karaitæ quoque, licet traditionum & cabbalæ sint hostes, credunt ut certis-simam traditionem, librum legis, quem Moses Israelitis tradidit, sine punctis & accentibus fuisse; ita Moses Bar Nachman in proœmio legis, Elias Levita in 3. præfat. & apud Cozri, l. 3. c. 29. & 30, Rabbanitæ & Karaitæ communi consensu, quo effato concidunt omnes avorumdam Judæorum, atque etiam Theologorum nonnullorum ratiunculæ. 5. Propter literas aliquas, in aliquo folio malè aut non regulariter scriptas, propter Parafchas clausas & apertas nō bene observatas libros privatos non secus ac publicos censent prophanos:verū id propter puncta non faciunt. Horum unumquodq; nedū omnia simul evidenter punctorum novitate demonstrant. Quamobrem liber sine punctis in Synagoga, sià Mose data sunt, quamobrem propter puncta male scripta liber prophanus non judicatur, si puncta affigere soliti erant antiqviRabbini? Quare punctis & accentibus nova nomina, eaque barbara indere, eaque paulatim addere & augere, si à Mose aut ab Esdra hæc omnia acceperunt? Denique Samaritanorum consuetudine id demonstratur, apud quos nullum est punctorum vestigium, sed hactenus lectionem orali traditione conservarunt.
units.tr: 4. All the Jews, the Karaites too, although they are enemies of tradition and of the Kabbalah, believe as the most certain tradition that the book of the Law which Moses gave to the Israelites was without points and accents. So Moses bar Nachman in the preface to the Law, Elias Levita in his third preface, and Cozri in book 3, chapters 29 and 30, both Rabbanites and Karaites with common consent. This assertion overthrows all the petty arguments of certain Jews and also of some theologians. 5. Because of some letters written badly or irregularly on some page, or because the closed and open paragraphs were not well observed, they consider private books profane just as they do public ones; but they do not do this because of the points. Each of these alone, let alone all of them together, clearly shows by the novelty of the points that the case is otherwise. Why, then, is a book without points in the synagogue held to be given by Moses, while a book is not judged profane because of badly written points, if the ancient rabbis were accustomed to attach points? Why should they impose new and barbarous names on the points and accents, and gradually add to and increase them, if they had received all these things from Moses or from Ezra? Finally, this is shown by the custom of the Samaritans, among whom there is no trace of points, but who have so far preserved the reading by oral tradition.

units.la: Plura potuissent addi, eandem sententiam partim confirmantia, partim illu-stranstrantia : sed hæc sunt Postulatis tuis satis superqve, jamqve Epistolæ modum longe supergressi sumus ; velim autem, eruditissime Buxtorfi, accipias à me ista, non ut decretorie dicta. Feram facile, qvi aliter senserit, licet caducis admodum rationibus niti mihi videatur.
units.tr: Many more things could have been added, some confirming the same opinion and some clarifying it, but what I have said is more than enough for your requests, and I have already gone well beyond the proper length of a letter. I would like you, most learned Buxtorf, to take these points from me as suggestions, not as final judgments. I will easily tolerate anyone who thinks otherwise, although he seems to me to rest on very feeble arguments.

units.la: Natura non possumus non amare opus qvod excolui-mus, & amanti τὰ μὴ καλὰ, καλὰ πειράντα, hæc περιλήψις[?] exuat animum suum necesse est eum, qvi oppositæ sici sententiæ refutationem aggreditur, alioqvin id, qvod adversarius asserit, capere vix potest, nedum refutare. Licet ea, qvæ retuli, videantur mihi admodum perspicua, omnemqve solutionis ansam præripere, amico tamen animo ea refutantem, non modo facile feram, sed etiam de me bene mereri existimabo.
units.tr: We cannot help loving the work we have cultivated, and a lover tries what is not good as good [τὰ μὴ καλὰ, καλὰ πειράντα]. Whoever sets out to refute the opposing view must strip his mind of this grasp [περιλήψις], otherwise he can scarcely understand what his opponent asserts, let alone refute it. Although the points I have set out seem to me very clear, and although they take away every opening for a reply, I shall not only bear it easily but also consider that I have done a service to myself if you refute them in a friendly spirit.

units.la: Falli possum & nonnunqvam expertus sum, ea qvæ judicabam admodum perspicua, aliter se habuisse.
units.tr: I can be mistaken, and I have sometimes found that things I judged to be quite clear were otherwise.

units.la: Allatas rationes si in libro, cujus editionem paras, dissolveris, & mihi & aliis multis magnum operæ pretium feceris : Hoc vero si irrito canatu aggrediaris, conclamatum est, frustraque alter Elias hæc revelaturus expectabitur. Vale vir Clarissime, & me ama, omniaque mea ut boni consulas,etiam atque etiam rogo.
units.tr: If you should answer my arguments in the book whose edition you are preparing, you will do me and many others a great service. But if you attack them with an empty challenge, it will be declared a defeat, and another Elijah will be waited for in vain to reveal these things. Farewell, most distinguished sir. Love me, and I earnestly ask you again and again to take all that is mine in good part.

units.la: Idibus Novembris, Anno 1646.
units.tr: On the Ides of November, in the year 1646.

units.la: EPIST. LXXII.
units.tr: EPIST. LXXII.

units.la: J. Morinus Cardinali Barberino con- gratulatur, quod Barberinorum fa- milia cum summo Pontifice in gra- tiam redierit.
units.tr: J. Morinus congratulates Cardinal Barberino that the Barberini family has been reconciled with the Supreme Pontiff.

units.la: Eminentissimo Cardinali,Barberino
units.tr: To the most eminent Cardinal, Barberino

units.la: J. Morinus, S. P. D.
units.tr: J. Morinus sends his most hearty greetings.

units.la: LÆtatus sum plurimùm, cùm primum ante paucos dies omnium sermone percrebuit, Illustrissimam familiam Barberinam in gratiam cum summo Pontifice rediisse. Verùm qua ratione ego Eminentiæ tuæ deditissimus lætitia non exultarem, cum omnium ora, audito hoc fausto nuncio, lætitiâ gestirent? Ut reconciliationem istam viri boni omnes à Deo summis votis efflagitarunt, ita æterternam exoptant. Conquerebantur a-pud omnes literarum amantes Musæ Charitesque, cum Româ pulsum, quem donis philtrisque suis omnibus ornavesrant, quem alium novum suorum asylum elegerant.
units.tr: I rejoiced greatly when the news spread through everyone's mouths a few days ago, that the most illustrious Barberini family had been restored to favour with the supreme Pontiff. Indeed, how could I, who am most devoted to your Eminence, fail to exult in joy, when the mouths of all men were leaping for gladness at this happy news? Just as all good men have earnestly begged God for this reconciliation, so they desire it to be eternal. The Muses and Graces, lovers of letters, complained everywhere that the man whom they had adorned with all their gifts and charms had been driven from Rome, and that they had chosen another new refuge for themselves.

units.la: Redeunti igitur cum Musis & Charitibus plaudit universus literas profitentium chorus, hisque immistus ego cumulatus gaudio Eminentiæ tuæ pristinos honores & opes recuperanti prospera omnia & immota precor, benevolentiaque perpetua ut me complectatur, submississimè rogo.
units.tr: So now, as the Muses and Graces return, the whole chorus of those who profess letters applauds, and I, mingled among them and overflowing with joy, pray that every blessing and unbroken prosperity may attend your Eminence as you recover your former honours and wealth, and I humbly and earnestly beg that you will keep me in your lasting goodwill.

units.la: Patres domus Congregationis nostræ recens autoritate summi Pontificis Avenione tenuiter fundatæ scripserunt ad :ne[?] Eminentissimum Card. à J. Onuphrio E. V. patruum summam pecuniæ grandem in opera pia autoritate & arbitrio E. V. collocandum legasse. Eminentiam vestram humillime & obnixissime precor, ut in pecuniarum istarum distributione & erogatione Domus Avenionensis patrum Oratorii Jesu Christi non sit immemor. Congregationem nostram E. V favore & benevolis multis officiis saepius defensam & auctam hoc beneficio magis ac magis habebit sibi devinctam & devotam, amplissimamque Jesu Christo, cui nos omniaque nostra consecramus, sustentatae familiae suae mercedem reportabit. Deus & Reip. Christianæ, & literariæ quâm diutissime & felicissime conservet.
units.tr: The fathers of our Congregation, recently and modestly founded at Avignon by the authority of the supreme Pontiff, have written to me that the most eminent Cardinal J. Onuphrius, your Eminence's uncle, has bequeathed a large sum of money to be applied to pious works at the authority and discretion of your Eminence. I most humbly and earnestly beg your Eminence not to forget the house of the Avignon fathers of the Oratory of Jesus Christ in the distribution and disbursement of that money. Our Congregation, often defended and advanced by your Eminence's favour and many kind services, will hold itself ever more closely bound and devoted to you by this benefit, and will obtain as its reward for supporting your household the most ample gift to Jesus Christ, to whom we and all that is ours are consecrated. May God preserve you and the Christian Commonwealth and the republic of letters for as long and as happily as possible.

units.la: Parisiis 16. Kal. Dec. 1646.
units.tr: Paris, 16th day before the Kalends of December, 1646.

units.la: EPIST. LXXIII.
units.tr: Letter LXXIII.

units.la: J. Morinus Lud. Capello quid Buxtorf- io rescripserit recenset, alia non- nulla quæ ad Rabbinorum libros pertinent. A MONSIEUR
units.tr: J. Morinus to Lewis Cappel, recounting what Buxtorf wrote back, and some other matters pertaining to the books of the Rabbis. TO MONSIEUR

units.la: Monsieur Cappelle,
units.tr: Monsieur Cappelle,

units.la: Monsieur,
units.tr: Monsieur,

units.la: ILy à quelque Jour, que M. vostre fils me rendit, une lettre de vostre part, par la quelle vous me remerciez de quelques services, que je vous avois rendus, il n'estoit point besoin de ce remerciement en mon endroit, deux considerations bien fortes m' obligeoient à faire ceqve J'ay fait, une de la verité qve vous maintenez en la these, qve defend voftre ecrit; l'autre de voftre propre merite & du renom, qve vous vous estes justement acqvis parmi ceux, qvi font profession des lettres; qvand au reste qve vous desiries de moy, je le feray toujours avec affection & sincerité en toutes les occasions qvi se presenteront.
units.tr: Some days ago your son handed me a letter from you, in which you thank me for some services I had rendered you. That thanks was not at all necessary on my part. Two very strong considerations obliged me to do what I did: one, the truth you maintain in the thesis your writing defends; the other, your own merit and the reputation you have justly earned among those who profess letters. As for the rest of what you ask of me, I shall always do it with affection and sincerity on every occasion that arises.

units.la: Le Sr- Buxtorfe m' escrivit une lettre assez honneste, qve je receus, il y a enuiron trois mois qvi contenoit plusieurs choses, premierement de excusas de ce qv'il avoit parlé fort indignement de moy en son liure des lettres hebraiqve, & me promettoit de retrancher tout cela en une seconde impression; puis il me marqvoit six ou sept endroits, ou il croioit qve je miestois[?] trompé; apres il m' imputoit, qve j'a vois escrit, qve la pluralité des Rabbinis cloioit, qve leurs an-ciennes lettres estoient Samaritaines, non Assyriennes; outre céla il me prioit de luy envoier ce que J'avois de particulier touchant l'antiqvité des poincts, me temoignant qu'il avoit presqve acheve d'imprimer un liure contrevous sur ce su jet, enfin il me demandoit quels auteurs Juifs j'avois avant EliasLevite, qui cussent esté de son opinion ; si j'avois quelqve Grammaire Manuscrite de R. Sonas, ou oe R. Juda Chiug, qui sont les premiers Grammairiens des Juifs, si les liuresd' Aben Esdra שפה רבורח & יסוד מירא [?], quels auteurs Karaites J'avois entre mains, & l'origine de leur schisme avec les autres Juifs ; quant au premier je luy respondis le plus honnestement, qu'il me fut possible, comme en effetes paroles de mesoris me touchent fort peu, si elles ne passent jusqves à des calomnies atroces ; pour le second je luy avoüe franchement, que je me suis trompè en deux ou trois endroits, dont il y en a un ; où luy & moy nous nous sommes trompes, comme il se voit sans difficulté par le texte lors que je l'ay confideré de plus pres ; il y en a un, où il me reprend de n'avoir voir pas marquè que c'estoient des mots tirés du texte de l'escriture Ste ; en ce cas plusieurs interpretes manqueroent souvent ; car il suffit,que l'interprete le reconnoisse sans le dire ; en un endroit J'ay veritablement pris le texte de l'escriture pour celuy de l'auteur, ce qui à embarrassé mon inter pretation, quoi que le sens soit le mesme que celuy qu'il donne, ce que l'advoue franchement estre une fauce, il y en à deux qui peuvent porter l'une & l'autre interpretation ; il le prend en un sens, & moy en un autre ; si cela estfauce[?], combien y en a t'il dans les 70 comparez a St. Jerofme ou en St. Jerome comparé avec les 70, & en tous les interpretes de l'hebreu comparez[?] l'an avec l'autre, & de plus son interpretation ni la mienne ne font rien au sujet, pour lequel je les alegue,il me semble que, velut α”λΦα[?] penulatorum facile ὀβελίζ[?]; il y en á une,s'il dit vray, qui merite d'estre reprise, car j'aurois pris un passage, qui dit tout le contraire de ce pourquoy je l'ay emploié. Il feroit long maintenant d'axaminer cela, mais qvoy qve-es en soit de la faute, que je ne croy pars, I'ay pour moy l'autorité de son Pe-re, du feu Sr. de Muis & du Rabbin commentateur de Cozri, qvi l'ont tous interpreté au mesme sens que moy, il est pris de Cozri, & rapporté en mes exercitations Samarit. p. 3, 4, 5.
units.tr: Monsieur Buxtorf wrote me a rather courteous letter, which I received about three months ago. It contained several things. First, he excused himself for having spoken very unworthily of me in his book on Hebrew letters, and promised to cut all that out in a second edition. Then he pointed out six or seven passages where he believed I had been mistaken. Next he charged me with having written that the majority of the Rabbis held that their ancient letters were Samaritan, not Assyrian. Besides this, he asked me to send him what I had of my own concerning the antiquity of the points, saying that he had almost finished printing a book against you on this subject. Finally, he asked me which Jewish authors before Elias Levita I had who held his opinion; whether I had any manuscript grammar of R. Sonas or of R. Juda Chiug, the first grammarians of the Jews; whether I had the books of Aben Ezra, Safah Berurah [שפה ברורה] and Yesod Mora [יסוד מורא]; and which Karaite authors I had in hand, and the origin of their schism from the other Jews. As to the first point, I answered him as courteously as I could, since the insults of Buxtorf touch me very little, unless they go so far as atrocious calumnies. As to the second, I frankly confess that I have been mistaken in two or three places. In one of them he and I have both been mistaken, as is plain without difficulty from the text when I examined it more closely. In one place he blames me for not having marked that these were words taken from the text of Holy Scripture; in such cases many interpreters would often fail, for it is enough that the interpreter recognise it without saying so. In one place I did indeed take the text of Scripture for that of the author, which embarrassed my interpretation, although the sense is the same as the one he gives; this I frankly admit to be a mistake. There are two passages which can bear either interpretation: he takes one in one sense, and I take it in another. If that is a fault, how many such are there in the Seventy compared with St. Jerome, or in St. Jerome compared with the Seventy, and in all the interpreters of the Hebrew compared with one another? Moreover, neither his interpretation nor mine has any bearing on the subject for which I cite them; it seems to me that, as with penultimate syllables, it is easy to mark them with an obelus. There is one, if he speaks truly, which deserves to be rebuked, for I would have taken a passage that says the exact opposite of what I used it for. It would be long to examine this now. But whatever the fault, which I do not believe is there, I have on my side the authority of his father, the late Sieur de Muis, and of the Rabbi commentator on Cozri, who all interpreted it in the same sense as I did. It is taken from Cozri and reported in my Samaritan Exercitations, p. 3, 4, 5.

units.la: התראה שמעשיהם בוה לריק ולשלה א השתרלות כדברי חובה [?] nunquid vides quod opus eorum in hoc vanum fuerit & supervacaneum & diligens occupatio in re damnabili. Il traduit l'un, videaturne tibi (vel an videatur tibi, an existimas) quod opus illorum in hoc vanum fuerit, & supervacaneum, aut occupatio circa rem debiti, hoc est, honestam & necessariam. Mais le commentateur hebreu l'entend comme moy; en second lieu l'auteur conclud les choses dites precedemment, & peu apres, &c. d'une mesme facon de parler qvand au mot התראה; Mais son Pere l'a interprete comme moy au chap. 20. de son Tiberias; au reste en ces corrections on pourroit trouver à redire, il s'imagine avoir tire la qvintesfence de cet auteur me repetant, qv'il l'a leu fort diligemment, je pense neanmoins, qv'il s'est eloigne bien fort de son but, non pour n'estre pas assez exerce dans la lecture des Rabbins, car comment ne le seroit il pas veu qv'il ne fait autre chose, & qve des son enfance il a esté instruit d'une si bonne mai ı[?] ? Mais d'autant qv'il à plus de soin d'establir l'opinion, dont il est prevenu, qve de rechercher la verité ;je me figure affez aisement, qv'il fait pour cet auteur comme son Pere, qvi dit en sa Bibliotheqve Rabbiniqve, qve c'est un liure multiplicis doctrinæ, conscriptus in laudem regis cujusdam, quem vocat Cozar;c'est une forme de Catechisme ou Dialogue, où il instruit le Roy Cozar en la Religion Judaiqve, & luy preuve qv'elle doit estre preferee à toutes les Religions, & il semble ou il feint, qve ce Roy Cozar avoit inclination aux Karaites ; c'est pourqvoy il y a aussi une longue dispute contre eux, en laqvelle il monstre, qu'ils doivent estre postposes aux Rabbinistes, la maniere de parler du Jeune Buxtorse me fait estimer, qu'il est de l'humeur de Ciceron, qui escrit de luy mesme à son frere, que à puero adamabat ἀιὲν ἀ-ξιξεύεον ἡ ὑπερέχον ἐμμένας ἄλλων[?].
units.tr: התראה שמעשיהם בוה לריק ולשלה א השתרלות כדברי חובה [?] Do you not see that their work in this was vain and superfluous, and a diligent occupation in a matter that is condemned? He translates the one clause as Does it seem to you (or do you think) that their work in this was vain and superfluous, or an occupation concerning a matter of duty, that is, honourable and necessary. But the Hebrew commentator understands it as I do. Secondly, the author concludes the things said previously, and shortly after, etc., with the same manner of speaking, as regards the word התראה. But his father interpreted it as I do, in chapter 20 of his Tiberias. Moreover, in these corrections one could find fault: he imagines he has extracted the quintessence of this author, repeating that he has read him very diligently. I think nevertheless that he has strayed very far from his aim, not for want of practice in reading the Rabbis, for how could he be unpractised, seeing that he does nothing else, and has been trained from childhood in such a good method? But since he takes more care to establish the opinion with which he is preoccupied than to seek the truth, I imagine quite easily that he does for this author what his father did, who says in his Rabbinic Bibliotheca that it is a book of many-sided learning, written in praise of a certain king whom he calls Cozar. It is a form of catechism or dialogue, in which he instructs King Cozar in the Jewish religion and proves to him that it ought to be preferred to all religions; and it seems, or pretends, that this King Cozar was inclined to the Karaites. That is why there is also a long dispute against them, in which he shows that they must be placed below the Rabbinists. The manner of speaking of the young Buxtorf makes me judge that he has the temper of Cicero, who writes of himself to his brother that from boyhood he always loved to aim at the best, or at least to excel others [ἀεὶ ἀριστεύειν ἢ ὑπερέχειν ἐμμενὰς ἄλλων].

units.la: 3. Pour ce qui est des lettres Hebraiques, J'ay rapporté trois opinions des Juifs, & en ay mis deux en une apres les avoir distinguées, a scavoir celle qui tient, qu'il n'y ayoit que le liure de la loy donné par Moyse & gardé dans l'arche, qui fust escrit en lettres Assyriennes, & celle qui dit absolument, que toutes les lettres estoient Samaritaines. Pour la premiere opinion j'avois cité neuf ou dix Babbins, & d'autant que j'estime, comme je luy ay mandé la premiere opinion ridicule, & quand elle seroit vraye, entierement inutile, & mesme occasion de soumettre toute la Religion & la police aux caprice du grand Prestre, qui seul eust eu droit de lire ce liure, l'ay dit en mes Exercitations, que la plus grande partie des Juifs croioit, que les anciennes lettres estoient Samaritaines, & ay conjoint les auteurs de ces deux opinions en un, estimant à la facon des jurisconsultes la restriction de la premiere pour nulle. Mais Buxtorf a voulu entendre mes paroles, comme si je n'avois point fait mention du grand nombre des Juifs, qui suit cette ridicule opinion.
units.tr: 3. As for the Hebrew letters, I reported three opinions of the Jews, and put two of them together after distinguishing them: namely, the view that only the book of the law given by Moses and kept in the ark was written in Assyrian letters, and the view that asserts absolutely that all the letters were Samaritan. For the first opinion I had cited nine or ten Rabbis. Since I hold, as I have written to him, that the first opinion is ridiculous, and even if it were true entirely useless, and moreover an occasion for subjecting the whole religion and polity to the whim of the high priest, who alone would have had the right to read this book, I said in my Exercitations that the greater part of the Jews believed the ancient letters were Samaritan. I joined the authors of these two opinions into one, judging, in the manner of the jurisconsults, the restriction of the first to be void. But Buxtorf wanted to understand my words as if I had made no mention of the large number of Jews who follow this ridiculous opinion.

units.la: Quant au 4. je luy ay fait un assez long discours des raisons, qui me portoient à croire, que les points estoient de nouvelle invention; je seray bien aise, qu'il y responde; ce que je ne croy pas possible. Car il me semble, qu'il y a des preuves si evidenies, que les points n'estoient point inventés du tems de St. Jerome, du Talmud, & des auteurs de leurs Midraschim, qu'on n'en scauroit pas defirer d'avantage pour preuver une negation, où l'absolue ignorance de quelq; chose. Je luy ay aussi marqué plusieurs auteurs ou qui reprennent les Maforethes, ou comme leur oeuvre estant inutile ou comme s'estant tropes, & qui ne font plus difficulté de les reprendre, qvoy qv'ils les estiment, qv'ils feroient de reprendre un autre Rabbin, qvi les auroit precede, qvi est un argument tre;certain qv'ils les croioient posterieurs aux Talmudistes, bien esloignes de les croire les asseseurs d'Esdras. La preuve est encore plus conclu-ante par la comparaison des Karaites. Les Juifs parlent des Karaites, qvi sont leurs heretiqves, comme des plus impies du monde; la raison est qve les Karaites n'adjoustent pas egale foy aux traditions Talmudiqves, qv'au texte Bibliqve; Car d'ailleurs ils sont estat du Talmud, le lisent, s'en servent, & firent de la plusieurs ceremonies, mais ils disent, qv'il se sont trompez qvelqve fois & n'estiment point pecher en reprenant; à cette occasion les Juifs s'accorderoient plutost avec un Christien qv'avec un Karaite ; ou plusieurs insignes Rabbins depuis six cens sont mocqvés de la plus grande part du travail des Masorethes', plusieurs autres les ont repris comme ils feroient leurs compagnons, & sus-qves ques ici pas un ne s'est avisé de les avoi en detestation, & de l' un de, ces deux avis ont esté presqve tous le Juifs, qvi ont escrit avant deux cens cinqvante, ou trois cen sans dautant, qv'ils les reprennent sans s'objecter, qv'il y en ait d'entre eux, qvi les egalent aux Talmudistes, ou qvi croient un crime deles reprendre, il seroit ennuyeux d'entrer plus avant en cette matiere ; je vous diray seulement, qv' Aben Esdra qvi escrivoit il y apres de 5oo[?], apres a-voir dit, qv'il avoit leu treze ou qvatorze Grammairiens, qvi l'avoient precedé à fait une liste des ses docteurs selon l'ordre dit il, qv'il sont vescu, Moyse, les Prophetes,Esdras,la grande Synagogue, les auteurs, dont est compilé les Misnaioth, les Talmudistes, les Masorethes, enfin les Grammairiens, dont, dit il, je suis du nombre & assigne à un chacun son oeuure principal. Je seray fort aise de voir ce qv'il[?] pourra respondre à cela & à qvantité d'autres raisons; car il n y à rien, qvi me soit plus important, qve la veriverité, & l'embrasseray quand il me la monstrera, ce que je ne croy pas possible au fait, dont il est question.
units.tr: As for the fourth point, I gave him a fairly long account of the reasons that led me to believe the vowel points were a recent invention. I shall be glad to see him answer it, though I do not think he can. There seem to me to be such clear proofs that the points were not invented in the time of St Jerome, or of the Talmud, or of the authors of their Midrashim, that one could hardly ask for more to prove a negative, that is, complete ignorance of something. I also pointed out to him several authors who either criticise the Masoretes, as if their work were useless or corrupt, or who have no hesitation in criticising them, although they esteem them, just as they would criticise another rabbi who had gone before them. That is a very certain argument that they believed the Masoretes came after the Talmudists, and were far from believing them to be the associates of Ezra. The proof is more conclusive still from the comparison with the Karaites. The Jews speak of the Karaites, who are their heretics, as the most impious people in the world. The reason is that the Karaites do not give equal faith to the Talmudic traditions and to the biblical text. For otherwise they are learned in the Talmud, read it, make use of it, and observe many of its ceremonies, but they say that its authors have sometimes erred, and they do not think it sinful to criticise them. On this point the Jews would sooner agree with a Christian than with a Karaite. Several eminent rabbis for six hundred years have mocked most of the work of the Masoretes, and several others have criticised them as they would criticise their own companions, and yet not one has thought to hold them in detestation. Nearly all the Jews who wrote before two hundred and fifty, or three hundred years ago, took one of these two views: either they criticised the Masoretes without scruple, or they did not think that any of them should be put on a level with the Talmudists, or that it was a crime to criticise them. It would be tedious to go further into this matter. I will only say this: Aben Ezra, who wrote about five hundred years ago, after saying that he had read thirteen or fourteen grammarians who had preceded him, drew up a list of his teachers in the order, as he says, in which they lived: Moses, the Prophets, Ezra, the Great Synagogue, the authors from whom the Mishnayot were compiled, the Talmudists, the Masoretes, and finally the grammarians, of whom, he says, I am one, and I assign to each his principal work. I shall be very glad to see what he can reply to this, and to many other arguments. For there is nothing more important to me than truth, and I will embrace it when he shows it to me, though I do not think that possible in the matter in question.

units.la: Enfin pour les liures de Karaites nous n'en avons quun, qui est un commentaire manuscrit sur toute la loy, du quel comme aussi du liure de Cozri on voit clairement,que lesKaraites ont tousiours fait {*}grand estat des Masorethes, {†} l'auteur de ce commentaire vivoit quelque tems apres Kimhi, & escrivoia Constantinople, c'est cequi a donné occasion à plusieurs Juifs de mesprifer bien fort les Masorethes,par une antipathie naturelle à ceux, qui s'entrehaissent.
units.tr: Finally, of the books of the Karaites we have only one, a manuscript commentary on the whole Law. From this, as also from the book of Cozri, it is clearly seen that the Karaites have always held the Masoretes in great esteem. The author of this commentary lived some time after Kimhi and wrote at Constantinople. This is what has given many Jews occasion to despise the Masoretes very strongly, from a natural antipathy among those who hate one another.

units.la: Pour les Masorets, pont[?] vous m'escrives, il me semble que je prouve clairement deux choses, premierement qu'il y en a eu de deux sortes, qui ont esté en divers tems, sans m'arrester aux auteurs de la petite Masore, qui ont esté en divers tems & qui sont posterieurs à toutes les deux ; les premiers ont reveu le texte de la Bible, l'ont repur-gé, &
units.tr: As for the Masoretes, which you write about, it seems to me that I prove clearly two things. First, there have been two kinds of them, who lived at different times, without my dwelling on the authors of the Lesser Masorah, who lived at various times and are later than both. The first reviewed the text of the Bible, purged it,

units.la: {†} Cela n'est pas vray. gé, & sont les auteurs de la beaucoup plus grande partie du Keri,&Chetib; car il y en avoit deja une partie notable remarquée avant eux & le Talmud,& quelque peu dans le Talmud; les seconds sont les auteurs des points & des accens, & de la distinction des versets, qui ne s'accorde nullement avec la distinction, que l'on peut receuillir de S. Jerome & autres, ni avec celle que les Talmudistes avoient par tradition; la seconde est,que le Talmud n'apoint esté achevé devant l'année 680. au plutost; cequi se proue par quelques tres anciennes histoires partialles des Juifs, qui temoignent que R[?] Aser fut interrompu de sa collectionTalmudiq; par la ruine de l'Empire des Perfes, fait par les Mahumetans ou Agariens, & les grandes perfecutions, qui furent alors excitées par les Agariens, de sorte qu'ils demeurerent plus de 70. ans sans l'achever, or le liure Trastatus Sophrim suit le Talmud'& precede la veuue da tente Bibliqve,com-me il se peut demonstrer clairement; par consequent les premiers Maforets ne s'auroient avoir plutost commencé que le 8. siecle ; il est vray aussi & peut estre demonstré par les propres paroles des Maforets, que les points n'ont pas esté tous inventés par les Maforets, in les figures & moins encore les noms, vous avez, si l'ay bonne memoire, traitté de cela en voftre Arcanum ; quant à la conjecture, que vous faites, que les Juifs ont pris leurs points des Arabes, je la croy tres vraye & pense le pouvoir demonstroir. Mais tout cela demande un long discours, que se cessions tous à faiut il y a plus de dix ans.
units.tr: {†} This is not true. purged it, and they are the authors of by far the greater part of the Qere and Kethib. For a notable part of these had already been noted before them, both in the Talmud and in a few places in the Talmud. The second kind are the authors of the points and accents, and of the division into verses, which agrees in no way with the division that can be gathered from St Jerome and others, nor with that which the Talmudists had by tradition. The second point is that the Talmud was not finished before the year 680 at the earliest. This is proved by some very ancient partisan histories of the Jews, which testify that R. Aser was interrupted in his compilation of the Talmud by the ruin of the Persian Empire, effected by the Mahumetans or Agarenes, and by the great persecutions which were then stirred up by the Agarenes, so that they remained more than seventy years without finishing it. Now the tractate Tractatus Sophrim follows the Talmud and precedes the reviewing of the biblical text, as can be clearly demonstrated. Consequently the first Masoretes could not have begun before the eighth century. It is also true, and can be demonstrated from the very words of the Masoretes, that the points were not all invented by the Masoretes, still less the figures, and even less the names. If my memory serves, you treated of this in your Arcanum. As for your conjecture that the Jews took their points from the Arabs, I believe it to be very true, and I think I can demonstrate it. But all this requires a long discussion, which we were both putting off some more than ten years ago.

units.la: Quant au Zohar, je n'ay pas entendu parler de Leo Juda pour les raison, que vous m'escriviez, mais d'un Juif Africain appellé Leo, qui vivoit il y a peutestre trois cens ans, que quelque Historien Juif temoigne avoir esté accusé des lors de contreservir cela pour le profit, qu'il recevoit debitant cette marchandise. J'ay autrefois perdu du tems à lire ce liure, non pour y apprendre ses resueries, mais pour y remarqver hiftoires ou di-fcours non convenables au tems qu'on luy donne, dont J'ay remarqué grande quantité, qui me confirme en la pensée de la suppofition.
units.tr: As for the Zohar, I have not heard of Leo Judah for the reason you write about, but of a Jewish African called Leo, who lived perhaps three hundred years ago. Some Jewish historian testifies that he was then accused of having falsified this work for the profit he got from peddling this merchandise. I once wasted time reading this book, not to learn its fancies, but to note the stories and discourses unsuitable to the period to which it is assigned. I have noted a great quantity of these, which confirm me in the opinion that it is a forgery.

units.la: Vous remarqverés aussi fon dialecte bien different de celuy d'Onkelos, & messe de termes & manie-res de parler de la phrase de Jonathan Uzielis & du Targ. Hierofol. & d'autres, qui ressentent entierement le dialecte Talmud; ce qui prouve clairement que l'auteur apris fon language de la lecture de tous ces auteurs ensemble. Mais je passe de beaucoup les bornes d'une let-tre; c'est pouiquoy je finis apres les of-fices de mon tresh. service, & vous avoir supplié de prendre en bonne part la fran-chife avec la quelle vous escrit celuy qui est veritablement M.
units.tr: You will also notice its dialect, very different from that of Onkelos, and mixed with the terms and modes of speech of the phrase of Jonathan ben Uziel, of the Targum of Jerusalem, and of others, which are entirely of the Talmudic dialect. This clearly proves that the author learned his language from reading all these authors together. But I have far exceeded the limits of a letter. That is why I end here, after the duties of my most honoured service, and after begging you to take in good part the frankness with which he writes to you who is truly M.
