units.la: Bartholdus Nihusius Jo. Morino. Cur in Provinciis unitis pauci libri eruditio- ne referti ex Galliis adsportati com- pareant.
units.tr: Bartholdus Nihusius to John Morinus. Why few learned books from France turn up in the United Provinces when they are imported.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo Joanni MorinoS. P.D. Bartholdus Nihusius.
units.tr: To the Very Reverend John Morinus, greetings from Bartholdus Nihusius.

units.la: REdditæ omnino sunt mihi tuæ, prid. Id. Novembr. datæ; quæ supra modum placent, etiam amicis, imo & Gerardo Joanni Vossio, licet non Catholico: nam & huic legendas dedi. Gratias ago immortales, de beneficio illo maximo; neque enim interpretari ali-ter possum; ac spero non me peccaturum, si data opportunitate, tuam istam Epistolam luce donem, qui copiam hic facio Chartulæ de Cruce. In quo negotio, si quid istic vobis occurrat, non observatum aliis, doceri id optem. Fieri enim potest, ut manus admovendæ sint ei rei denuo. Profitebor publicè, per quos prosecerim: sicuti & ad Bartholinum & Sal-masium profiteri me vides, quòd libri eruditi ex Galliis comparcant hîc rarissi-mi, Vossius inde ait esse, quia paucissimi in Provinciis hisce unitis reperiantur homines docti, adeoque multitudine illæ talium vincantur longe à [?]Iola Lutetiâ. Et hinc fit, ut, si Bibliopolæ Batavi emunt in Francia libros, in Poloniam & similia loca eos devehi curent. Interim vehementissimo nos laboramus desiderio videndi suo temporePraxin SacramentiPœniten-tiæ, cujus spem facis. Deus det suam gratiam, ut feliciter partus ille in luminis auras exeat. Salve plurimum.
units.tr: Your letter, dated the day before the Ides of November, has reached me at last, and it pleases me beyond measure, as it has my friends, and indeed Gerard John Vossius, though he is not a Catholic; I have given it to him to read too. I give immortal thanks for that very great kindness, for I can take it in no other way. I hope I shall not be wrong, if at a suitable opportunity I publish your letter, since I am making a copy here of the little paper on the Cross. In this business, if anything occurs to you there that others have not noticed, I would be glad to be told of it, for it may be that my hand must be put to the matter again. I shall acknowledge publicly those through whom I have made progress, just as you see I do also to Bartholinus and Salmasius. That learned books from France arrive here so rarely, Vossius says, is because very few learned men are found in these United Provinces, so that their numbers are far outdone by Lutetia alone. Hence it happens that when Dutch booksellers buy books in France, they arrange to have them carried on to Poland and similar places. Meanwhile we are suffering from a most intense longing to see, in due time, the Praxis of the Sacrament of Repentance, whose coming you hold out to us. May God grant his grace, so that that birth may come happily out into the breezes of light. Farewell, most heartily.

units.la: Quia hæc diriguntur per me; obsequia mea tibi duxi unico verbo offerenda, &si-mul rogandum an veré ad nostras partes accesseritMeleteri[?]o,de quo Nihusio antehac recordor te scripsisse; aliud nec otiû modo permittit, sed finio ac permaneo.
units.tr: Since these things are being sent through me, I have thought to offer you my respects in a single word, and at the same time to ask whether Meletius has really come over to our side, of whom, as I recall, you wrote to Nihusius before. Time allows nothing more, so I finish and remain.

units.la: J. Morinus Card. Barberino. Apologia Domini Feronii Canonici, & Archidiaconi Ecclesiæ Carnutensis ac Doctoris Sorbonici, cui summus Pontisex concedere noluerat diplomata Bullarum Abbatiæ Sti Laudomari Blesensis, eó quòd doctor ille ob Jansenianas opiniones apud Aulicos urbis male audierat.
units.tr: J. Morinus, to Cardinal Barberini. An apology for Lord Feronius, canon and archdeacon of the Church of Chartres and doctor of the Sorbonne, to whom the Supreme Pontiff had refused the papal bulls for the abbey of St Laumer at Blois, because that doctor had been ill spoken of at the papal court on account of his Jansenist opinions.

units.la: Eminentissimo Cardinali Francisco Barberino J. Morinus S.P.D.
units.tr: To the most eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini, J. Morinus sends greetings.

units.la: FAma non vulgarihîc increbuit, sanctissimum Dominum nostrum diplomata suis Bullis Abbatiæ S. Laudomari Blesensis concedere nolle in favorem viri admodum reverendi, & apud nos celebris; Domini FeroniiCanonici & Archidiaconi Carnutensis Ecclesiæ, Doctoris Sorbonici, & Illustrissimi Carnutensis vicarii & officialis ad eam regendam summo Pontifici à rege nominati, eo quòd Cornelii Jansenii Iprensis librum cui titulus est Augustinus, suffragio suo comprobaverit Calumnia, quæ huic viro,optimo,doctissimo,& de Ecclesia Catholica bene merito impingitur, impulit me ad hanc Epistolam Eminentiæ vestræ scribendam, ut veritati testimonium debitum perhibeā, &innocentiam à malevolis iniquissimè appetitam, quantum in me est asseram, verum equidem est, nec diffiteor, librum [illegible, ~3 letters]lum cum plurimis aliis & doctoribus & Episcopis se probasse. Sed id factum est, cum primùm Galliæ innotuit, antequam turbines, qvi postea illius causa commoti sunt, in orbe Christiano excitati fuissent; videbat librum ab Episcopo Catholicæ communionis compositum, cujus autor omnes labores suos Ecclesiæ Romanæ emendandos & expungendos humillimé subjiciebat; videbat librum in Belgio á librorum Censoribus examine facto probatum & commendatum, & duplici privilegio Imperatoris & regis Catholici munitum; videbat librum á multis viris doctis in Gallia magni fieri, á nemine tum attentatum.; librum legit, quæstiones varias&populares præsertim attendit;est enim D. Feronius prædicator celebris,&sermonibꝰ quadragesima libus continuis in plerisque Galliæ dioecesibus nedum Carnutensi notissimus, videt eas pié& devoté variisS.Augustini testimoniis resolvi & decidi. Suffragium rogatus libro dare non recusat, quem amplecti tot argumenta suadebant,nullum adhuc dissuadebat; sed consideretur[?], qualem postea se præstiterit: excitis quæstionibus Jansenistarum factioni nunquam fuisse auditum est; ab eo tempore innumeros Sermones ad populum variis locis habuit,nullus unquam Episcopus aut quivis alius Novationis Jansenianæ eum accusavit: in Gallia notum est illustrissimum Episcopum Carnutensem doctorem Sorbonicum & olim in ea Theologiæ Professorem regium Janse-nianis opinionibus maxime adversum esse; Feronium tamen post librum hunc ab eo probatum&vicarium suũ& officialem constituit, hoc est, universum totius Diœcesis regimen ipsi commendavit, quod sane præsul religiosissimus & prudentissimus nunquam fecisset,si quid Jansenianæ labis ipsi adhærere conjecisset, nec cum eo familiari & continuo contubernio conviveret; unde est,quod Bullam Pontificiam de quinque Propositionibus Jansenio tributis nuper editâ, ipsi commisit per dioecesim promulgandam & exequendam; quo munere ita functus est, ut qui impias illas Propositiones maximè aversantur, nihil ultra id, quod fecit, desideraverint; denique Abbatiæ illius nominationem obtinuit non aulicorum more, ambitu, & importuna amicorum intercessione, sed nihil de ea cogitans à sereniss. Duce Aurelianensi, ad quem pertinet,ad illam Abbatiam nominatio ex antiqua cum Rege Christianissimo conventione quæsitus est atque ut illius curam gereret rogatus. Religiosissimi autem Principis intentio est, quinque millia redituum annuorum ex illo sacerdotio provenientium in seminarium pro Dioecesi fundandum è mensa Abbatis eximere; hoc autem cum nunc fieri non potuerit, Rege & quibusdam Consiliariis non approbantibus, Feronius e-lectus est, qvi Abbas factus magnam Abbatiae fructuum partem in Seminarium illud fundandum spontaneus & volens impenderet, donec Regis consensus obtineretur, & à summo Pontifice confirmaretur. Hæc Eminent. Card. tibi nota esse volui, ut calumniam viro optimo & qvacunqve Catholico iniqvisime inustam ex officii mei debito abstergerem, atqve ut negotium pietatis, cujus causa hoc sacerdotium illi donatum, qva potis sum, adjuvem & promoveam; cùm autem variis experimentis certissime sciam Eminentiam vestram juxta Apostoli Pauli mandatum, qvaecunqve sunt vera, qvaecunqve pudica, qvaecunqve ju-sta, qvaecunqve sancta, qvaecunqve a-mabilia, qvaecunqve bonae famae, si qva virtus, si qva laus disciplinae, eum cogitare, pluribus illi hoc negotium non commerdabo, rei aequitas, justitia, Ecclesiae necessitas verbis meis longe efficacius apud eum intercedunt. Deus diutissimè te conservet, Eminentissime Cardinalis, & inimicos tuos triumphatos pedibus tuis sternere pergat.
units.tr: A report, not a small one, has spread here that our most holy Lord is unwilling to grant the papal bulls for the abbey of St Laumer at Blois in favour of a man most reverend and well known among us, Lord Feronius, canon and archdeacon of the Church of Chartres, doctor of the Sorbonne, and vicar and official of the most illustrious Bishop of Chartres, who was named to govern that church by the King to the Supreme Pontiff. The reason given is that he lent his approval to the book of Cornelius Jansenius of Ypres entitled Augustinus. This slander, thrown at a man so good, so learned, and so deserving of the Catholic Church, has moved me to write this letter to your Eminence, so that I may bear the testimony due to the truth and, as far as lies in me, assert the innocence that malicious men have most unjustly attacked. It is true, and I do not deny it, that he approved the book together with many other doctors and bishops. But this was done when the book first became known in France, before the storms that were later raised across the Christian world on account of it had broken out. He saw that the book had been composed by a bishop of the Catholic communion, whose author humbly submitted all his labours to be corrected and expunged by the Roman Church. He saw that in Belgium the book had been examined and approved and commended by the censors of books, and fortified by a double privilege from the Emperor and the Catholic King. He saw that the book was held in high esteem by many learned men in France, and at that time no one had attacked it. He read the book, and attended especially to its various questions as they bear on popular teaching. For Lord Feronius is a celebrated preacher, well known not only in the diocese of Chartres but in most dioceses of France, through continuous Lenten sermons, and he saw that these questions were resolved and decided in a pious and devout manner by various testimonies of St Augustine. When asked for his judgment on the book, he did not refuse to give it. Many arguments urged him to embrace it, and nothing as yet dissuaded him. But let it be considered what he has since shown himself to be. Although the questions were raised by the Jansenist faction, it has never been heard that he was of that party. Since that time he has preached innumerable sermons to the people in various places, and no bishop or anyone else has ever accused him of the Jansenist innovation. In France it is well known that the most illustrious Bishop of Chartres, a doctor of the Sorbonne and formerly royal professor of theology there, is strongly opposed to the Jansenist opinions. Yet after approving this book, Feronius was appointed by him as his vicar and official, that is, he entrusted to him the whole government of the diocese. A most devout and prudent prelate would certainly never have done this if he had suspected any taint of Jansenism to cling to him, nor would he have lived in such familiar and constant intimacy with him. Hence it is that he entrusted to him the papal bull on the five propositions attributed to Jansenius, lately published, to be promulgated and enforced throughout the diocese. In discharging this office he so acquitted himself that those who most abhor those impious propositions could desire nothing beyond what he did. Finally, he obtained the nomination to that abbey not by the usual courtly methods of canvassing and importunate intercession by friends, but, thinking nothing of it, through the most serene Duke of Orléans, to whom the nomination to that abbey belongs by an ancient agreement with the Most Christian King, and he was sought out and asked to take charge of it. Now the intention of this most religious Prince is to take five thousand yearly revenues arising from that benefice out of the abbot's table, in order to found a seminary for the diocese. Since this could not be done now, the King and some of his councillors not approving, Feronius was chosen, so that as abbot he might, of his own accord and willingly, devote a large part of the abbey's revenues to founding that seminary, until the King's consent should be obtained and it should be confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff. I wished your Eminence to know these facts, so that, in discharge of my duty, I might wipe away from an excellent man, and from any Catholic, a slander most unjustly branded upon him, and so that I might help and advance, as far as I can, the work of piety for whose sake this office was bestowed upon him. Since I know most certainly from various experiences that your Eminence, according to the command of the Apostle Paul, thinks on whatever things are true, whatever things are chaste, whatever things are just, whatever things are holy, whatever things are lovable, whatever things are of good report, if there be any virtue and if there be any praise of discipline, I will not commend the matter to him at greater length; the fairness of the case, justice, and the needs of the Church plead with him far more effectively than my words. May God preserve you for a very long time, most eminent Cardinal, and may He continue to lay your enemies, conquered, at your feet.

units.la: Parisiis xj. Kal. Sept. 1653.
units.tr: Paris, 22 August 1653.

units.la: EPIST, LXXVI.
units.tr: Epistle LXXVI.

units.la: J. Morinus Card. Barberino congra- tulatur ob triumphatos abeo hostes.
units.tr: J. Morinus congratulates Cardinal Barberini on the defeat of his enemies.

units.la: Eminentissimo Cardinali Francisco Barberino J. Morinus S. P. D.
units.tr: To the most eminent Cardinal Francesco Barberini, J. Morinus sends greetings.

units.la: ELapsæ sunt jam aliquot septimanæ cùm in dies singulos expecto viri clarissimi D. Conæi domestici tui Romam á nobis discessum, ut testatam tibi facerem eam, quam animo concepi de tua familiæque tuæ illustrissimæ reconciliatione cum summo Pontifice lætitiam, luxerunt acerbé viri boni omnes, cùm calumnias innocentiæ tuæ tante arte instructas viderunt, ut summo Pontifici alias tibi multis nominibus maximè devincto tam atrociter imponerent.Sanguine collachrymaruntMusæ,cùm audierunt unicum hoc seculo justum æstimatorem & defensorem suum bonis spoliatum, patriâ profugum, ne exul quiescere iniquis litibus post fugam appetitum ; quis tam ferrei & feri pectoris, qui cùm videat nobilissimam familiam tota Europa celebrem honoribus amplissimis ubique decoratam derepente cum teneris & dul-cissimis pignoribus sese miserabiliter æ-stibus maris intempestivo cœlo committentem, nullum periculum quantumvis eminens & capiti impendens detractantem, ut eos fugeret, quos summis beneficiis & honoribus cumulaverat, temperet à lachrymis? ita quoque serenitate & tranquillitate rebus tuis reddita exultantem animo lætitiam comprimere nec potui nec debui ; qua ratione enim quem afflictum & extorrem summa cum animi tristitia conspexi, malis superstitem & tandem de invidia triumphantem sine ingenti animi lætitia & exultatione conspicere possem? Nec etiam permittit ea benevolentia, qua me à tot annis complecteris, ut gaudium de restitutione tua toto pectore exundantem apud me contineam: accipe igitur Eminentissime Card, hoc Epistolium, ut lætitiæ argumentum. qua propter triumphatos à te hostes tuos exulto & gestio, atque etiam ut gratitudinis qua tibi arctissime devinctus sum, qualecunque monumentum, meiqve tibi obsequentissimé addicti ne sis immemor. Deus vota tua, & consilia secundet, & Eminentiam tuam Ecclesiae suae & literis incolumem diutissime conservet.
units.tr: Several weeks have now passed since I have been expecting, day by day, the departure from us for Rome of the most distinguished Mr. Conaeus, your household servant, so that I might show you the joy I have conceived at the reconciliation of you and your most illustrious family with the Supreme Pontiff. All good men have mourned bitterly when they saw the calumnies against your innocence contrived with such skill that they could impose them so atrociously on the Supreme Pontiff, who is otherwise bound to you by so many ties. The Muses wept tears of blood when they heard that this one just judge and defender of our age had been stripped of his goods and had fled his homeland, an exile seeking no rest from unjust lawsuits after his flight. What man has a heart so hard and savage that, when he sees a most noble family, famed throughout Europe and everywhere adorned with the highest honours, suddenly and wretchedly committing itself, with its tender and most dear pledges, to the waves of the sea and an untimely sky, not shrinking from any danger, however great and hanging over its head, in order to flee those whom it had loaded with the greatest benefits and honours, could hold back his tears? So too, when your affairs were restored to calm and tranquillity, I could neither restrain the joy that exulted in my mind nor ought I to have. For by what reasoning could I look upon with no great gladness and exultation him whom I had seen afflicted and exiled with the deepest sorrow of mind, surviving his troubles and at last triumphing over envy? Nor does that goodwill, with which you have embraced me these many years, permit me to keep within myself the joy overflowing from my whole heart at your restoration. Accept, therefore, most eminent Cardinal, this little letter as a token of my joy. For this reason I exult and rejoice in the enemies you have defeated, and also offer this, whatever its worth, as a memorial of the gratitude by which I am most closely bound to you, lest you forget one who is most devotedly attached to you. May God favour your wishes and counsels, and keep Your Eminence safe for his Church and for letters for a very long time.

units.la: Parisiis 7. Idus Septembr. 1653.
units.tr: Paris, 7 Ides of September, 1653.

units.la: EPIST. LXXVII
units.tr: EPIST. LXXVII

units.la: Card. Barberinus ad[?] Morino.D. Feronii Pietas & Doctrina commendatur.
units.tr: Cardinal Barberini to Morinus. The piety and learning of Feronius are commended.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo Patri D. Joanni Morino Presbytero.
units.tr: To the most reverend Father John Morinus, priest.

units.la: ADmodum Reverende Pater, D. Feronium Illustrissimi Carnutensium Episcopi Vicarium generalem suae virtutes ac doctrina commendare sat poterant; maxima tamen iis accessio facta est ex luculento adeo testimonio, nam quem tanta judicii sui[?] laude exornat ornatissimus Morinus, eum plurimi ab omnibus faciendum censeo; video itaque, ad quam me officii rationem excitet, & tanti pondus judicii, & praecipuus meus erga P. Tuam amor; qvamobrem P. Feronius qvidqvid in me est, vel à me proficisci poterit, sibi certo promittere potest, ea enim omnia testimonia libentissime dabo atqve officia adhibebo qvae ad ipsius commendationem magis facere intelligam; caeterum si ego DoctissimumMorinum à me amari dixerim, nihil novi dixerim.
units.tr: Most reverend Father, the virtues and learning of Feronius, Vicar General of the most illustrious Bishop of Chartres, could certainly recommend him well enough; yet a very great addition has been made to them by so brilliant a testimony. For I judge that the man whom the most distinguished Morinus adorns with such praise of his judgment is to be esteemed greatly by everyone. I see, therefore, both the weight of so great a judgment and my particular affection for your Reverence, which urge me to the duty I owe. Wherefore, Feronius may confidently count on whatever lies in my power or can come from me: I will most willingly give every testimony and perform every service that I understand will serve to commend him. Moreover, if I were to say that I love the most learned Morinus, I would be saying nothing new.

units.la: Romae die 29. Septembris 1653.
units.tr: Rome, 29 September 1653.
Your Reverence's

units.la: Addictissimus Card. Barberinus.
units.tr: most devoted servant, Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: EPIST. LXXVIII.
units.tr: EPIST. LXXVIII.

units.la: J. Morinus Card. Barberino obsequium suum testatur.
units.tr: Jean Morin testifies his devotion to Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: Eminentissimo & Reverendissimo Principi, Francisco Cardinali Barberino Joannes Morinus Congreg. Orat. Presb. salutem obsequiosissime dicit.
units.tr: To the most eminent and most reverend Prince, Francesco Cardinal Barberini, Jean Morin, of the Congregation of the Oratory, presbyter, sends his most dutiful greetings.

units.la: QVanqvam ante paucos dies abeunti[?] Domino Coneo literas ad Eminentiam vestram perferendas dederim, qvibus devotum illi obseqvium meum testarer, credidi tamen officii mei esse R. Patre Goezaldo Romam redeunte eum hinc abire insalutata Eminentia vestra non sinere ; Cùm enim ei sit a multis annis cognitus, eumqve sæpius colloqvio suo benigne honoraverit, literas meas merito deferentis illi gratiores fore existimavi. Religio mihi est,& quidem verecundus pudor Eminentiam vestram rebus arduis occupatissimam interpellare, & dum mente versat, & disponit negotia totius orbis Christiani maxima & difficillima,mei homuncionis plane inutilis mentionem injicere. Sed cùm in memoriā revoco eā qva me semper complexus es benevolentiam,cujꝰ argumenta qvam plurima mihi dedisti,animū & confidentiā resumo,mihiq; persuadeo,frequens obseqvii mei testimonium. Eminentiae vestrae non fore importunū.
units.tr: Although a few days ago I gave letters to be carried to your Eminence by Signor Coneo, on his departure, in which I bore witness to my devoted obedience to him, I nevertheless thought it my duty not to allow Father Goezaldo, who is returning to Rome, to leave here without greeting your Eminence. For he has been known to me for many years, and has often honoured me with his kind conversation, so I judged that my letter would be all the more welcome to you through one who deservedly carries it. I feel scruple, and indeed modest shame, in interrupting your Eminence, who is most heavily occupied with weighty affairs, and while you are turning over in your mind and arranging the greatest and most difficult business of the whole Christian world, in introducing any mention of me, a wholly useless little man. But when I call to mind that kindness with which you have always embraced me, of which you have given me very many proofs, I take courage and confidence, and I persuade myself that a frequent testimony of my obedience will not be unwelcome to your Eminence.

units.la: Vale Eminentissime Cardinalis. Deus Eminentiam vestram incolumenEcclesiae quàm diutissime conservet.
units.tr: Farewell, most eminent Cardinal. May God preserve your Eminence, for the good of the Church, for as long as possible.

units.la: Parisiis viij. Id. Octob. Anno MDCLIII.
units.tr: Paris, 6 October, in the year 1653.

units.la: EPIST. LXXIX.
units.tr: EPIST. LXXIX.

units.la: J. Morinus Abrahæ Ecchellensi. Quærit nonnulla de gente Samaritanorum.
units.tr: J. Morinus to Abraham Ecchellensis. He asks several things about the people of the Samaritans.

units.la: Clarissimo Viro Dn. Abrahæ Ecchellensi J. Morinus Congr. Orat Pr. S. D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished man, Mr. Abraham Ecchellensis, J. Morinus of the Congregation of the Oratory sends greetings.

units.la: Patre Goezaldo quem nosti Romam redeunte te insalutatum nolui dimittere, sed veteris amicitiæ nostræ memorem te volui monere; an è Svria responsum acceperis de Samaritanis, qua ratione legere solent Pentatcu-chum, Hebraicasque voces rescire velim. Multæ quæstiones hac in causa elucidanda fieri possunt, olim eas sigillatim descripsi tibique dedi, & jam dudum est cùm mihi rescripsisti, te eas conservasse, atque in patriam misisse; præcipuæ sunt, an ut Arabes utantur punctis, an ut Judæi, an vero nulla habeant; quid sentiant de punctis Judæorum & de eorum pronuntiandi ratione; qua ratione pueros & mulieres, si puncta non habent, doceant legere, an Grammaticarum usum habeant; & si fieri posset una ab eis GramGrammatica Hebræa comparetur; haberetur quoque exemplar pronuntiationis eorum decem aut duodecim versuum è Pentateucho latinè, si fieri posset, ab aliquo Syro latinæ lingvæ perito expressorum, ut, qua ratione pronuntient, melius judicari possit; iterum à te expostulo pauca quædam, quæ ad Samaritanam pronuntiationem spectant, quæque Parisiis è Chronico quodam Samaritano excerpsisti; pauca ea sunt & brevissima paginula possunt inscribi; pervelim ea ad me mitti, ut mihi sint velut præludia amplioris messis expectatæ; hæc si concesseris non modo me, sed & Remp. literariam magno beneficio cumulabis; amicitiæ tuæ admodum confidens familiariter tibi scribo, pluraque quàm petierim spero. Vale vir Clarissime, meiqve semper esto memor.
units.tr: When Father Goezaldo, whom you know, was returning to Rome, I did not want to let him go without greeting you, but I wished to remind you of our old friendship. I would like to know whether you have received a reply from Syria about the Samaritans: in what manner they are accustomed to read the Pentateuch, and I would like to learn their Hebrew words. Many questions can be raised in order to clarify this matter. I wrote them out separately some time ago and gave them to you, and it is long since you wrote back to me that you had kept them and sent them to your homeland. The chief ones are these: whether they use points as the Arabs do, or as the Jews do, or whether they have none; what they think of the points of the Jews and of the Jewish manner of pronunciation; by what method they teach boys and women to read if they have no points, and whether they have the use of grammars; and, if it could be managed, a Hebrew grammar should be obtained from them. I would also like to have an example of their pronunciation: ten or twelve verses from the Pentateuch, rendered into Latin, if it could be done, by some Syrian skilled in Latin, so that it may be better judged how they pronounce. Again I ask you for a few things concerning Samaritan pronunciation, which you extracted at Paris from a certain Samaritan Chronicle. They are few and can be set down on a very short page. I would very much like them sent to me, as a kind of prelude to the larger harvest I hope for. If you grant this, you will heap great kindness not only upon me but also upon the literary commonwealth. Relying confidently on your friendship, I write to you familiarly, and I hope for more than I have asked. Farewell, most distinguished man, and remember me always.

units.la: Parisiis viij. Id. Octob. An. 1653.
units.tr: Paris, 8 days before the Ides of October, 1653.

units.la: EPIST. LXXX.
units.tr: EPIST. LXXX.

units.la: Card. Barberinus Morino gratiam habet, quòd tam liberaliter in se laudes conjecerit.
units.tr: Cardinal Barberini thanks Morinus for having heaped praises upon him so generously.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo Patri J. Morino Congregationis Orat Presbytero.
units.tr: To the Most Reverend Father J. Morinus, Presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory.

units.la: ADmodum Reverende Pater ; quod me meamque domum summus Pontifex novo benevolentiae nexu devinxerit, in partem felicitatis meae ponō ; verum etsi non aliud honoris ac fructus ea mihi res peperisset, hoc certe abunde apud me esset, quod te Vir Clarissime, ad gratulationem excitavit, ut quam animo conceperas laetitiam ; tuis ornatissimis literis testatam mihi faceres ; id mihi quam gratum accideerit, vix assequi verbis possum ; tibi facilius conjectandum erit. qui noris quoapud me sint loco eximiae tuae virtutes, eloquentia, doctrina, ingenium a vulgaribus longe semotum ; ac profecto & majorem tibi habeo gratiam, quod etiam perspexerim, quam liberaliter ac plena manu laudes in me conjicias, quo enim minus eas demereri possum, id eo majus tui in me amoris esse argumentum sentio ; quo in amore respondere tibi quantum cupiam, repotius, quam verbis declarare vellem. Vale optime Morine, ac pro me Deum precare.
units.tr: Most Reverend Father: that the highest Pontiff has bound me and my household to him by a new tie of goodwill, I count among the chief points of my happiness. Yet even if that event had brought me no other honour or profit, this alone would surely be enough for me: that it moved you, most distinguished Sir, to congratulate me, and to make me aware, by your most elegant letter, of the joy you had conceived in your mind. How welcome this was to me I can scarcely express in words; you will find it easier to imagine. You who know what outstanding virtues I hold in you, your eloquence, your learning, and a talent far removed from the ordinary, will understand. Indeed I am the more grateful to you because I have also perceived how generously and with full hand you heap praises upon me. The less I am able to deserve them, the greater, I feel, is the proof of your affection toward me. How much I long to answer that affection I would rather show by deeds than declare in words. Farewell, best Morinus, and pray to God for me.

units.la: Romæ die 24. Novembris 1653.
units.tr: Rome, the 24th day of November 1653.

units.la: Amore, quo semper me devincis, leges quæ in seposito folio addere ausus sum, eruditione & bonitate tua allectus
units.tr: Drawn by the love with which you always bind me, and by your learning and goodness, I have ventured to add certain remarks on a separate sheet.
Your most Reverend Fatherhood,

units.la: AddictissimusCard. Barberinus.
units.tr: Your most devoted servant, Cardinal Barberini.

units.la: EPIST. LXXXI
units.tr: EPISTLE LXXXI

units.la: Card. Barberinus J. Morino. Jucundas sibi esse illius literas testatur.
units.tr: Cardinal Barberini to J. Morinus. He says that the letter from him gave him pleasure.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo P. P. Joanni Morino Congregationis Oratorii Presbytero.
units.tr: To the Most Reverend Father P. P., John Morinus, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory.

units.la: ADmodum[?] Reverende Pater ; nullæ mihi litteræ tuis jucundiores accidere solent neque ego promptiori manu calamum unquam arripio, quam cùm ad te Vir clarissime, scribendi occasio se mihi præbet; quod ideo significandum duxi, ut vel hinc intelligas, quanto te amore prosequar, quantiqve tuas singulares virtutes faciam. Patrem Goezaldo ad nos redeuntem, qui tuas mihi reddidit, libeulibentissimé vidi, & amanter sum complexus, cùm tui, vestræqve Congregationis causa, tùm ob amicitiam, quæ á plurimis annis mihi cum eo est, cui propterea, quidquid á me Proficisci potest, ultro exhibui; cæterùm me velim, ut facis, amare pergas.
units.tr: Most Reverend Father, no letters are ever more welcome to me than yours, and I never take up my pen more eagerly than when the chance to write to you, most distinguished man, presents itself. I thought this worth saying, so that you may understand from this alone how greatly I love you and how highly I esteem your singular virtues. I was very glad to see Father Goezaldo, who is returning to us and who brought me your letter, and I embraced him warmly, both for the sake of you and your Congregation and because of the friendship that has existed between us for many years. For that reason I have readily offered him whatever can come from me. For the rest, I would like you to go on loving me, as you do.

units.la: Romæ die prima Decembris 1653.
units.tr: Rome, 1 December 1653.

units.la: P. T. Addictissimus
units.tr: Your Reverence's most devoted,

units.la: EPIST. LXXXII.
units.tr: Letter 82.

units.la: Card. Barberinus J. Morino significat' Criticam Sacram Lud. Cabelli materiâ disputationis Romæ suppeditasse, & cur non errores solùm, sed curiositatem omnem & audaciam, quibus ad novos errores via sternatur, depellere curent Romani Aulici.
units.tr: Cardinal Barberini writes to J. Morin that Ludovicus Cappellus's Critica Sacra supplied the material for a disputation at Rome, and why the Roman courtiers take care to repel not only errors but every curiosity and audacity by which a way is paved to new errors.

units.la: Admodum Reverendo P. P. J. Morino Congr. Orat. Presbytero.
units.tr: To the Most Reverend Father J. Morin, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory.

units.la: VIx tibi gratias egi ob præcipuam benevolentiam, quam in tuis literis exhibuisti, cum nova præberetur occasio & tibi per istam singularem tuam eruditionem cum summa pietate conjunctam, nullisqve privatis affectionibus obnoxiam perpetuo benemerendi, & mihi ob expertam toties humanitatem tuam grati animi significationes renovandi. Ludovici Capelli Critica Sacra materiem disputationibus his diebus suppeditavit propter SacriConcilii Tridenti[illegible, ~2 letters]de vulgata Bibliæ editione decretum, & contra malos interpretes & contra illos, qui sibi facultatem arrogant libros sacros proprio Marte emendandi & edendi; adversam vero sententiam non tantumCriticæ Auctor affirmat & docet, sed ex pluri-bus ejus dictis induci asserunt, illud ab eo privatæ auctoritati tribui, quod Ecclesiæ, & summo Pontifici reservatum videtur, etiamsi in minima dictione auc[?] vocula correctio esset adhibenda: præsertim post editionem á Clemente VIII, factam summo cum plausu&unanimita-te Ecclesiæ Catholicæ receptam; quam opinionem sequitur inter cæteros Auctò[?]res magnæ notæ Melchior Canus, qui in suo locorum Theologicorum opere, quam religiosissime cesnet a nullo attingendam Sacram Bibliam esse, nec quæ le-visfima forte videntur in dubium revocanda. Apud me alicujus momenti est, q od cùm apud vos agerem, acceperim diu hæsitatum fuisse circa libri editione, nam ab ea deterrebat nimius Censoris rigor in[illegible, ~2 letters]extum Hebraicum ob hiftoriæ s[illegible, ~3 letters]itatem & in violabile Sacramentum, cùm tamen omni studio contenderetur, ideo hoc opus dandum in lucem esse, quod perspicuè demonstraret, hæreticos abusos Hebraico textꝰ ita ut si publici juris hoc opus fieret, verisimile effet, illos id ægrè laturos, præsertim homine ejusdem farinæ hæc docente, ut postea evenit; cæterum quid ageret de vulgata Versione nihil audivi; apud accusatores, auget operis suspicionem auctor extra Ecclesiæ sinum mortuꝰ (nulla habita ratione quod ejus filius quippe Catholicus & Sacerdos anteqvam librum ederet, probabiliter emendandum curare potuerit) auget inqvam suspicionem in hac urbe præsertim, in qua ob Dei gratiam ab hæresibus re-motifmotissimi cùm simus, dare operam debemus, ut non errores modo, verùm etiam curiositatem omnem & audaciam, quibus ad novos errores via sternitur, depellamus. Liceat mihi tutis[?] auribus tuis, amicissime Morine, hæc pauca deponere, & qvale sit etiam judicium tuum de isto opere, efflagitare.
units.tr: I could hardly thank you enough for the especial goodwill you showed in your letter, since it gave me a new occasion both to you, whose learning is joined with the greatest piety and free from all private partialities, and always deserves well, and to me, who have so often experienced your kindness, to renew the expressions of my grateful feeling. The Critica Sacra of Ludovicus Cappellus has in these days supplied the matter for disputations, on account of the decree of the Sacred Council of Trent concerning the Vulgate edition of the Bible, and against bad interpreters and against those who arrogate to themselves the power of emending and publishing the sacred books on their own authority. Indeed the author of the Critica not only affirms and teaches the opposite view, but from many of his statements they claim it can be inferred that he attributes to private authority what seems reserved to the Church and the supreme Pontiff, even if the smallest word or particle required correction, especially after the edition made by Clement VIII, which was received with great applause and unanimity by the Catholic Church. Among other authors of great note, Melchior Canus follows this opinion; in his work On the Theological Places he holds that the Sacred Bible must be touched by no one, with the utmost reverence, and that even the slightest things perhaps seeming trivial ought not to be called into doubt. It is of some importance to me, which I learned while I was with you, that there was long hesitation about publishing the book; for it was deterred by the excessive strictness of the censor concerning the Hebrew text, on account of the sincerity of history and the inviolable Sacrament. Yet it was urged with every zeal that this work ought to be brought to light, because it would clearly demonstrate that heretics abused the Hebrew text; but if the work were made public, it would probably be that they would take it badly, especially since a man of the same stripe teaches these things, as later happened. As for what he would do concerning the Vulgate version, I heard nothing. Among the accusers, the author, having died outside the bosom of the Church (no account being taken of the fact that his son, being a Catholic and a priest, could probably have arranged for it to be emended before the book was published), increases the suspicion against the work. I say this increases the suspicion, especially in this city, in which, since by the grace of God we are very far removed from heresies, we ought to take care to drive off not only errors but also all curiosity and audacity by which the way is paved to new errors. May I be permitted to lay these few words before your friendly ears, most dear Morin, and to ask for your own judgment of this work.

units.la: P. T,
units.tr: Your Paternity,

units.la: Addictissimus
units.tr: Most devoted

units.tr: Fr. Card. Barberini.

units.la: EPIST. LXXXIII
units.tr: EPIST. LXXXIII

units.la: J. Morinus Card. Barberino. Judicium suum de Critica Sacra Capelli, & in eum Anima versiones, cur Parisiis cum privilegio Regis edita, quibus Approbationibus, quid in ea laude dignum, quid vituperio, quis sit sensus Concilii Tridentini pro definitione vulgatæ.
units.tr: J. Morinus, Cardinal, to Barberino. His judgment on Ludovicus Capellus's Sacred Criticism and the animadversions upon it, published at Paris with the King's privilege: by what approvals it was supported, what in it is worthy of praise and what of blame, and what is the sense of the Council of Trent concerning the definition of the Vulgate.

units.la: Eminentissimo Principi Francisco Cardinali Barberino.
units.tr: To the most eminent Prince Francesco Cardinal Barberino.

units.la: CUm Eminentia tua postremis tuis ad me literis testetur, tantopere sibi placuisse, qvòd officio meo Satisfacere qvalicunqve modo conatus fuerim, mi-
units.tr: Since Your Eminence, in your most recent letter to me, bears witness that it greatly pleased you that I tried in whatever way I could to satisfy my duty,

units.la: hiqve tanta cum humanitate demonstret, se boni consuluisse, imo gratias mihi habere, qvòd lætitiam de summi Pontificis benevolentia in illustrissimam familiam Barberinam rediviva animo meo exundantem per Epistolam meam affluere siverim, mihi profecto magna confidentia est, gratum & acceptum multo magis Eminentiæ tuæ fore, si illius commodis inservire qvomodo possem, & opera mea obsequium aliqvod illi præstare; qvapropter cum iisdem literis hujus rei occasionem mihi dederit, non lubens modo, sed alacer eam amplector.
units.tr: and shows me with such courtesy that you took it in good part, and indeed that you thank me, because I allowed the joy I felt at the Supreme Pontiff's goodwill toward the most illustrious Barberini family, which welled up in my mind freshly reborn, to flow out in my letter, I am certainly confident that it will be far more pleasing and acceptable to Your Eminence if I can in any way serve your interests and render you some service by my labour. Therefore, since in the same letter you have given me the occasion for this, I embrace it not only willingly but eagerly.

units.la: Postulat à me[?] Eminentia tua sententiam meam de Ludovici Capelli Critica Sacra; qvanqvam E. V. sit literarum omnis generis ornamentis politissima, virisqve doctissimis undiqve circumdata, atqve in medio mundi sole constituta, tamen qvoniam jubet, lumen soli mutuum dabo, & facula mea meridiem illustrabo; de sacra igitur Capelli Critica dicturus ut ordine procedat sermo noster, eum in tres partes dividam; primùm de Capello dicam & ejus in Critica scopo; deinde rationes explicabo, quibus persvasi viri quidam docti privatim institerunt apud Franciæ Cancellarium, ut imprimendæ Criticæ facultatem concedederent; postremo quæstioni de qua sententiam meam postulat Eminentia tua respondebo: nec enim ei planè nisi duobus prioribus explicatis satisfieri potest.
units.tr: Your Eminence asks my opinion of Ludovicus Capellus's Sacred Criticism. Although Your Eminence is most polished in every kind of ornament of letters, surrounded on all sides by the most learned men, and placed in the very sun of the world, nevertheless, since you bid it, I will lend my light to the sun and illumine the noon with my little torch. So, to speak of Capellus's Sacred Criticism, and that our discourse may proceed in order, I will divide it into three parts. First I will speak of Capellus and his aim in the Criticism; then I will explain the reasons by which certain learned men privately pressed the Chancellor of France to grant permission to print the Criticism; lastly I will answer the question on which Your Eminence asks my opinion, for it cannot be fully satisfied unless the first two points are explained.

units.la: Ludovicus Capellus adhuc vivit, annum agens ultra 70; non modo hæreticus est, sed etiam hæreseos Minister & Prædicator, atqve in Academia Salmuriensi Hugonotica linguæ HebraicæProfessor; itaqve quod dicebat Anastasius Pontifex Epist. 3. de Ruffino, multo magis de Capello videtur mihi dicendum, Ruffinum scito ita haberi à nostris partibus alienum, ut quid agat, ubi sit, ne scire cupiamus; ipse denique viderit, ubi possit absolvi. Quid Capellus dixerit aut scripserit, bene an male, non mihi videtur magis esse Magistratui Ecclesiastico curandum, quàm curare solet aliorum Ministrorum libros, qui penè innumeri quo-tidie tidie eduntur in Gallia, Germania, Anglia, aliisque regionibus haeresi infectis. Quis sufficeret omnibus recensendis & censura notandis? quos sane ut dicitur, ναῦς μὴ μία πάντας ἀγ[?], deinde hac censurā Capello magnum & optatum beneficium conferetur,nam haeretici decem & amplius annis, diligenter cave-runt, ne liber iste ederetur; diu Genevae Manuscriptus haesit,sed ut imprimeretur, obtinere non potuit,diu Sedani, diu Lugduni Batavorum: sed repulsam quam Genevae passus erat,illis quoq; locis, licet Lugduni editionem Salmasius urgeret, passus est; sentiebant scilicet Ministri validissimum argumentum ac pene unicū, quo hacten9 in vulgatam usi fuerant, validissime subduci,hoc nempe, Texus Hebraeus est plane incorruptus,qualis à Mo-se & Prophetis est Spiritu S. dictante su-sus; ergo translatio omnis huic primigenio textui non consentiens ad hunc textum corrigenda est; at translatio vul-gata innumeris locis ab Hebraeo Textu differt, ergo innumeris locis castiganda est,& tota reficienda. Assumptionem plurimis exemplis docent; speciosum istud fontiū nomen, à quo Translationū rivuli fluunt, veros Catholicos multos aut decepit, aut suspensos tenuit; totus est Capellus in hoc fundamento evertendo, quod sanè magno molimine tentat & feliciter exequitur; res erat probatu admodū difficilis; antiquissimi codices Hebræi nulli sunt. Mirificus enim est Bibliorum Hebraicorum editorum consensus; ideo qui ab uno codice discedit, ab omnibus æquo spatio distat. Quid ille ut hoc assequatur ? Varios Testamenti veteris libros, in quibus eadem repetuntur inter se comparat, indeq; necessario variantes lectiones colligit; idem præstat in locis novi Testamenti ex vetere desumptis; deinde ad Keri & Ketib Judæorum digreditur, pleraque salebrosæ & seconditæ Masorethicæ Criticæ arcana denudat; postea varia testimonia 70 Interpretum cum hodierno textu Hebræo comparat, quorum differentia aliunde provenire non potest, quam ex differentia exemplaris, quo usi sunt 70, ab hodrerno textu Hebræo; idem facit in Paraphrasi Chaldaica atque in variis locis, quæ supersunt, antiquarum translationem Græcarum Aquilæ, Symmachi, & Theodotionis, quibus & inter se & cum hodierno textu Hebræo collatis evincitur tot codicibus usos & inter se, & cum hodierno textu non ita consentientibus, ut Biblia Judæorum Neoterica inter se nunc consentiunt: Denique vulgatam cum textu Hebræo plurimis locis comparat, ex qua rursus comparatione demonstrat differentiam, quæ multis locis conspicitur, Hebræum textum inter & Latinum, nec ab errore interpretis, nec à mendis librariorum manare, sed à varietate codicis Hebræi, quo usus est S.Hieronymus ab eo, qui nunc vulgatus est; lectionem autem S.Hieronymi hodiernā tanto certiorem esse, quanto S. Hieronymi codex hodierno Hebræo antiquitate præstat; hoc ipsum adnotavit præsatio præposita editioni vulgatæ autori-tate Clementis VIII, editæ, Facile fieri posse credendum est, ut majores nostri, qui ex Hebraeis & Graecis latina fecerunt, copiam meliorum & emendatiorum libro-rum habuerint, quam ii, qui post illorum aetatem ad nos pervenerunt, qui fortasse tam longo tempore identidem describendo minus puri atque integri evaserunt.Idem nos in novo Testamento fecimus duorum antiquissimorum codicum manuscriptorū ope freti, quorum comparatione cum[?] vulgata quadringenta & quadraginta loca protulimus, in quibus vulgata versio ab hodierno textu Graeco discedit, sed cum istis exemplaribus mirificè consentit;unde manifestum fit, quod vult ista praefatio, varietatum causam, quae inter vulgatam&Originarios textu intercedit, ab errore aut mendis in vulgatam irreptitiis non esse petendam, sed ut plerumque à mendis in Originarios textus illapsis, quae nunc ab antiquo puriore, quem vulgatae interpres prae manibus habuit, difformes reddunt ; omnium autem Catholicorum sententia est, fontes nunc plurimum turbidos fluere, ut latè demonstravimus in iisdem exercitationibus c.2,3,4,5 primæ Exercit. Huic veritati qui contradiceret, neminem legi, nisi forte unum aut alterum Catholicum stultè Hebraizantem, ne professioni suæ derogaret; cùm igitur viderent ministri hoc suum fundamentum planè corruere, illius libri editionem qua arte & authoritate valuerunt impedire conati sunt; cùm autem editum audierunt, Capello plurimi succensuerunt, ut qui Catholicis arma ministraret, & suas ad autoritatem Ecclesiæ ut aliquid certi habere possent, confugere cogeret; itaq; libri censura Capello gratissima erit, ut pote quæ illi occasio erit cum suis in gratiam redeundi; ea ratio, quæ tantopere Ministrorum animos adversus hujus libri editionem commovit, nonnullos viros Catholicos doctrina præstantes, in quorum manus Critica ista pervenerat, plurimum ad procurandam privatim istam editionem incitavit; videbant enim argumentum hoc de mendis in Hebræos codices illapsis doctè admodum & cum varia penitioris litteraturæ Hebraicæ supellectile enarrari & in omnem partem versari, hacq; dissertatione Achilleum hæreticorum argumentum contra vulgatam penitus convelli; alia insuper ratio ex Priore consequens eos ad id suadendum non parum commovebat; inde enim consequitur, hoc semel dato, nihil plane certum esse posse, cum Ecclesiæ authoritati nihil prorsus deferunt; nam si tam multis scatet mendis id, quod est solum eorum fidei columen, fidem eorum necesse est esse caducam ad modum & prorsus ficulneam; hoc consequens opposuerunt Capello sui & varie animum versat & in omnes partes torquet, ut ei respondeat, ut videre est pag. 12. p. 186. & præsertim pag. 387 sect. 5, 6. & aliis locis, sed semper incassum fumumque fugiens in ignem incidit; faverunt huius libri editioni viri docti complures, quos intererant viri celebres Dionysius Petavius & Marinus Mercennus è minimorum familia, à quorum sententia nec ego alienus eram; hurū testimoniis adiutus Capellus & Bibliopolam invenit & privilegium in Bibliopolæ commodum, ne videlicet di-spendium aliquod editione ab alio atten-tata pateretur. Nullus enim Doctor Ca-tholicus publico suffragio librum istum probavit aut commendavit; cæterùm autoris filius, qui Catholicus est, impres-sioni præfuit, diligenterque cavit, ne quid atrox in Religionem Catholicam patri elaberetur; multa equidem omittit, quæ Catholicus expressisset, sed nihil mihi oc-currit, quod Religioni Catholicæ sit aper-tè infestum; si, quæ hac in causa Eccle-siæ auctoritati tribui debent, edidisset, non fuisset hereticus, aut si addita fuissent, fi-dem apud suos non invenisset, quorum tamen gratia editioni privilegium con-cedebatur. Postremò scribit ad me Emi-nentia tua, nonnullos dicere autorem i-stum docere unicuique licentiam esse sa-cros libros emendandi & edendi, sicque contra Concilii Tridentini autoritatem Sacri textus correctionem privatæ auto-ritati submittere; quid de hac re mihi videtur E. V. scisscitatur; ab ea igitur justus aperto pectore quid sentiam elo-quar[?] qvar ;hæc accusatio duplici sensu intelligi potest, qvorum prior Catholicus est ab omnibus Catholicis probatus & usurpatus nedum à Capello : Posterior audax, temerarius,pœnaCanonica dignus,in qvẽ [?] non animadverti Capellum incidisse ; imo animadverti audaciam istam exhorrentes eum ideo laudasse : Prior igitur accusationis sensus est,nemini licere post Concilii Tridentini decretum saltem post Clementis VIII. correctionem scri-benti commentaria in sacrum Tex-tum,aut qvovis aliomodo de re Theolo-gica tractanti asserrere,in vulgata editione in esse aliqvem librarii errorem aut varias lectiones ex antiqvis Manuscriptis colligere,aut tueri lectionem aliqvam antiqvam esse significantiorem ea, qvæ re-tinetur in vulgata, aut comparare textus Hebræum,Chaldaicū,Translationes Græ-cas cum textu vulgatæ, licet sint plane diversi aut etiam contrarii , & horum textuum aliqvem videri hoc loco commodiorem textu vulgatæ ; deniqve nun-qvam licere dictionem aliqvam vulgatæ, irreptionis accusare, Si hic est accusationis sensus, omnes accusandi sunt Catholici tractatores; vix enim aliquis est, qui in hunc occasione data non impegerit, imò contrarium omnes asseruerunt & occasione data fecerunt. Cardinalis Bellarminus l. 2. de verbo Dei c. ii. quatuor occasiones refert, in quibus ad fontes confugere licet. 1. Quando in nostris codicibus videtur esse error librariorum.
units.tr: Ludovicus Capellus is still alive, aged over seventy. He is not only a heretic but also a minister and preacher of heresy, and professor of Hebrew at the Huguenot Academy of Saumur. So what Pope Anastasius said in his third letter about Rufinus seems to me to apply even more to Capellus: "Know that Rufinus is held by our side to be so alien that we do not want to know what he is doing or where he is; let him see for himself where he can be absolved." As to whether what Capellus has said or written is good or bad, it does not seem to me that the ecclesiastical magistrate should concern himself with it any more than he usually troubles himself with the books of other ministers, which are published almost innumerably every day in France, Germany, England and other regions infected with heresy. Who would suffice to list them all and mark them with censure? "One ship does not carry them all" [ναῦς μὴ μία πάντας ἀγ…]. Then, by this censure, a great and desired benefit will be conferred on Capellus. For the heretics, for ten and more years, took careful precautions that this book should not be published. It lay long in manuscript at Geneva but could not obtain permission to print; long at Sedan, long at Leiden. The rejection he suffered at Geneva he suffered in those places too, although Salmasius pressed for an edition at Leiden. The ministers evidently felt that the strongest and almost only argument they had hitherto used against the Vulgate would be most thoroughly undermined, namely this: the Hebrew text is wholly uncorrupted, such as Moses and the Prophets wrote under the dictation of the Holy Spirit; therefore every translation that does not agree with this original text must be corrected to it. But the Vulgate differs from the Hebrew text in countless places; therefore it must be censured in countless places and entirely remade. They support the assumption with very many examples. That splendid name of fountains, from which the streams of the translations flow, has deceived many true Catholics or kept them in suspense. Capellus is wholly engaged in overturning this foundation, which he attempts with great effort and carries out successfully. The matter was very difficult to prove, since there are no very ancient Hebrew codices. For the agreement of the printed Hebrew Bibles is remarkable, so that whoever departs from one codex is equally distant from all of them. How does he achieve this? He compares the various books of the Old Testament in which the same passages are repeated, and from them necessarily gathers variant readings. He does the same with passages of the New Testament taken from the Old. Then he turns to the Keri and Ketiv of the Jews, laying bare many of the rugged and abstruse secrets of Masoretic criticism. Afterwards he compares various readings of the Seventy Interpreters with the present Hebrew text, and their differences can arise from no other source than the difference between the exemplar the Seventy used and the present Hebrew text. He does the same with the Chaldee paraphrase and with the surviving passages of the old Greek translations of Aquila, Symmachus and Theodotion. By comparing these both with one another and with the present Hebrew text, he shows that they used codices which did not agree with one another or with the present text, just as the modern Jewish Bibles now agree with one another. Finally he compares the Vulgate with the Hebrew text in very many places, and from this comparison again demonstrates that the difference seen in many places between the Hebrew and the Latin text arises neither from an error of the translator nor from the faults of scribes, but from the variety of the Hebrew codex that St Jerome used, which differs from the one now in common use. St Jerome's reading is more reliable than the present one by as much as his codex surpasses the present Hebrew text in antiquity. The preface prefixed to the Vulgate edition published by the authority of Clement VIII itself noted this: "It is easy to believe that our forebears, who made the Latin text from the Hebrew and Greek, had a supply of better and more correct books than those who came after their age, who, through so long a time of repeated copying, perhaps became less pure and whole." We did the same for the New Testament, relying on the aid of two very ancient manuscript codices. By comparing them with the Vulgate we brought forward four hundred and forty places where the Vulgate version departs from the present Greek text but agrees remarkably with those exemplars. Hence it is plain what that preface means: the cause of the variants between the Vulgate and the originals is not to be sought in error or faults creeping into the Vulgate, but, as is usually the case, in faults slipped into the original texts, which now make them differ from the older and purer text the Vulgate translator had before him. The opinion of all Catholics is that the sources now flow very muddied, as we have widely shown in the same exercises, chapters 2, 3, 4 and 5 of the first Exercise. Whoever contradicted this truth would be read by no one, except perhaps one or another Catholic who foolishly Hebraizes, lest he undermine his own profession. Since, therefore, the ministers saw their foundation plainly collapsing, they tried by whatever skill and authority they had to prevent the publication of that book. But when they heard it had been published, many were angry with Capellus, as one who supplied arms to Catholics and compelled them to take refuge in the authority of the Church in order to have something certain. Therefore the censure of the book will be most welcome to Capellus, since it will be an occasion for him to return to favour with his own people. The reasoning that so stirred the ministers' minds against the publication of this book greatly moved several Catholic men eminent in learning, into whose hands the Criticism had come, to procure this edition privately. For they saw that this argument about faults slipped into Hebrew codices was treated learnedly and with a rich store of deeper Hebrew literature, and was examined from every side, and that by this dissertation the heretics' Achilles-argument against the Vulgate would be utterly torn away. Another consideration, following from the first, moved them no little to urge it. For from it follows that, once this is granted, nothing at all can be certain, since the heretics give no weight whatever to the authority of the Church. For if that which is the sole pillar of their faith abounds with so many faults, their faith must necessarily be unstable, and altogether like a fig tree. Capellus's own people raised this consequence against him, and he turns it over in many ways and twists it in all directions in order to answer it, as may be seen at p. 12, p. 186, and especially p. 387, sections 5 and 6, and in other places; but always in vain, fleeing smoke and falling into fire. Several learned men favoured the edition of this book, among them the famous Dionysius Petavius and Marin Mersenne of the order of Minims, and I was not opposed to their opinion. Aided by their testimony, Capellus found both a bookseller and a privilege for the bookseller's benefit, so that no loss would be suffered from an edition attempted by someone else. For no Catholic doctor approved or commended this book by public vote. Moreover, the author's son, who is a Catholic, oversaw the printing and took careful care that nothing atrocious against the Catholic Religion slipped in from his father. Indeed he omits many things which a Catholic would have expressed, but nothing occurs to me that is openly hostile to the Catholic Religion. If he had published what in this matter ought to be attributed to the authority of the Church, he would not have been a heretic; or, if those things had been added, he would not have found belief among his own people, for whose sake the privilege for the edition was granted. Finally, Your Eminence writes to me that some say this author teaches that everyone has the licence to emend and publish the sacred books, and so, against the authority of the Council of Trent, submits the correction of the sacred text to private judgment. You ask what I think of this matter, so with an open heart I will justly tell you my view. This accusation can be understood in two senses. The first is Catholic, approved and used by all Catholics, and not least by Capellus. The second is bold and rash, and deserving of canonical penalty; I did not notice that Capellus fell into it, and indeed I noticed that he condemned that boldness. The first sense of the accusation, then, is this: that after the decree of the Council of Trent, and at least after the correction of Clement VIII, no one is permitted, when writing commentaries on the sacred text or treating theological matters in any other way, to assert that there is some scribal error in the Vulgate edition; or to gather variant readings from ancient manuscripts; or to maintain that some older reading is more significant than the one retained in the Vulgate; or to compare the Hebrew text, the Chaldee, and the Greek translations with the Vulgate text, even though they are plainly different or even contrary, and to hold that one of these texts seems more suitable in a given place than the Vulgate text; and finally that it is never permitted to accuse any word of the Vulgate of corruption. If this is the sense of the accusation, then all Catholic writers must be accused, for there is hardly anyone who, when the occasion arose, did not stumble into these things. Indeed all of them have asserted the contrary, and when the occasion arose have acted accordingly. Cardinal Bellarmine, in book 2 of On the Word of God, chapter 11, reports four occasions on which it is permitted to have recourse to the sources. 1. When in our codices there seems to be an error of the scribes.

units.la: 2. Quando Latini codices variant. 5. Quando verba aut sententia in Latino est anceps. 4. Ad energiam & proprietatem vocabulorum intelligendam. Paulo ante de approbatione Concilii ita edixerat, nec ita tamen approbavit, ut asseruerit nullos in ea librariorum errores reperiri, sed certos nos reddere voluit in iis praeser-tim, quae ad fidem & mores pertinent, nulla esse in hac versione interpretum errata. Idem Cardinalis litteris scriptis ad Lucam Brugensem Anno 1603. Scias velim, vulgata non esse à nobis accuratissimè castigata, multa enim de industria istis de causis pertransivimus, quae correctione indigere vibebantur, variæ lectiones, quæ in Bibliis Lovaniensibus habentur, & in quas tu librum utilissimum scripsisti, mihi videbantur omnino addenda,&c. Hæc Lucas in Epist. quam præposuit variis novis lectionibus in vulgatam, quæ editæ sunt in fine Bibliorum Antverp. Anno 1618. Puta etiam in aliis anterioribus & posterioribus. Ibid ex Card. Baronio; Fateor in Bibliis nonnulla adhuc superesse, quæ in melius mutari possunt. Idem Lucas initio Ep. Etiam in Vaticana eaque prima horum Bibliorum editione, impressores non pauca errata admiserunt, quæ passim in priore libello adnotavimus. Etiam ipsi correctores à Pontifice deputati idem testantur in Epistola editioni Vaticanæ liminari; quid ipse Lucas Brugensis omnibus probantibus, & separatim & simul cum Bibliis varias lectiones publicavit; si quis numerum inire vellet Tractatorum Ecclesiasticorum, qui occasione data aliter interpretati sunt, vel ex Græco vel ex Hebræo, quam ferat vulgatæ textus, qui varias vulgatæ lectiones à textu diversas adnotarunt & amplexi sunt, qui eas cum Græcis, Hebraicis, Syriacis & Chaldaicis codicibus comparârunt, edisserunt convenientioresque aliquando textui sacro χ[?] ἐμφατικωτέρας quàm sit eo loco vulgatæ textus, multitudine sane obruere-tur; satis erit unius aut alterius, qui hanc quæstione excusserunt, testimonium producere. Sixtus Senensis in postrema Pag.† Bibliothecæ suæ fatetur in vulgata non-nullas inveniri mendas, &c. Postea docet hæc omnia nec fidem nec bonos mores lædere, causasque explicat, ob quas errores & mendas in Scripturis Ecclesia patiatur. Melchior Canus lib. 2. Locorū Theologi, in fine cap. 14. & toto cap. 15. docet utiliter ad fontes sæpe recurri. Inter eas quinta utilitas est ejusmodi, ut mendæ, quæ in vulg. irrepserunt, fontium ope corrigan-tur, quod multis exemplis demonstrat; idem argum. fusè prosequitur lib. II. c. 5. resp. ad argum. 11. & 12, &c. Joannes Mariana in opusculo de editione vulgata c. 21. sic interpretatur Concilii Tridentini decretum, Vulgatæ editionis vitia non non probantur, quæ multa in esse ex codicum varietate colligebamus, librariorum certè incuria, sed ipsa tantùm interpretis versio probatur, ubi constiterit aut ex codicum omnium consensione, aut Ecclesiæ auctoritate locum aliquem ab illo ita esse conversum; addo tamen, nec verbis quidem illis ita esse probatam nostram editionem, ut eadem magis proprie aut magis aperte exprimi posse, nonnullis locis negent.Hanc Concilii mente fuisse probat testimonio Jacobi Laines Societatis Jesu Præpositi Generalis, qui Concilio interfuit, & paulo post Gallos Italos, atque Germanos Scriptores, qui libris de Theologia editis non dubitabant sæpe editionis vulgatæ vitia accusare, & nostri interpretis oscitantiam[?]; grave est universos quasi impios & de Religione male sentientes criminari, præsertim cum validis argumentis eorum sententia fulciatur, &c. Multa superiori[?] in Hebraicis & Græcis codicibus vitia esse ostendimus, multa mendacia in rebus minutis, eorum pars aliqua non exigua in nostra editione Vulgata extat.Hoc postea multis exemplis dedemonstrat idem Andræas Vega lib. 15. in Concil. Trident. cap. 9. ubi asserit' hanc fuisse Concilii mentem, sæpius à Cardinale Sanctæ Crucis audivisse. Idem argum. fuse persequitur l. 11. cap. 5. Resp. ad argum. 11. & 12 ubi non modo mendas multas irrepsisse fatetur, sed nonnullas, quæ falsum inducunt, quod tamen nec ad fidem nec ad bonos mores spectat. Idem Lindanus de optimo genere interpretandi l. 3. c. 24. sed præcipue 13. Gouelser. pro Bellarmino l. 2. cap. 10. Ita Capellus abstinenter de his vulgatæ ab Hebræo varietatibus locutus est, ut alió ferè semper recurrat, quàm ad mendarum in vulgatam illapsum, ut legere est pag. 371. sect. 6. pag. 356. sect. 2, ideo rectè ait pag. 12. se à sententia Card. Bellar. cujus verba fusè refert, non longè discedere. Imo concessô, quod nulli contendunt vulgat. Interpretem suisse prophetam & θεόπνευστον interpretationem condidisse (quam sententiam ut probabiliorem amplexi sumus Exercit. nostrarum Biblicarum l. 1. Exercit. 7. c. 4.) nec sic tamen conseqveretur, nævos in vulgata nullos esse, errores & ofcitantias nullas; seqveretur eqvidem,nihil horum ab Interprete commissum esse, sed Amanuenses in ea describenda nunqvam aberrasse, cespitasse, oscitasse,qvis præstare audebit? hoc esset in hæreticorū insaniā ruere, qvi Græcos & Hebræos codices, præsertim hos posteriores, volunt eadem puritate nunc excellere,qvâ primùm fusi sunt, ut vulgata Ecclesiæ editio secundū eos absolutè corrigatur ; contra hanc hæreticorum suorum insaniam validissimè scripsit Capellus & prope innumeris exemplis demonstravit, in codices Hebræos plurimas mendas irrepsisse, tantūqve abest ut vulgatæ injuriam intulerit, ut ex comparatione vulgatæ cū Hebræo textu plurimas in Hebræum textum irrepsisse mendas colligit, ut videre est lib. §[?] c. 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. nos de Græco textu idem variis modis fusè demonstravimus in Exercitat. Biblicis lib. 1. tota Exercit. 2, & multis annis ante Capellum de Hebræo textu ex ipsa Masora variisqve autoribus quam adducit, sed semper praetermittit, Verum tamen de S. Hieronymo & ejus versione magnifice & vere Catholicè loquitur p. 354. 355. Omnibus praecedentibus longè praefert, affirmatq; contra omnes haereticos eam esse S. Hieronymi, & a plurimis hoc esse evidentissimè probatum, inter quos Augustinum, Steuchum, Eugubinum, & Joannem Marianā nominat, ut videre est pag. 355. optimas insuper & viris Catholicis passim enar-ratas causas reddit dissensionis ejus a textu Hebraeo, ut videre est p. 356, 357, atque etiamnum p. 402 sect. 8. Imo tanti facit vulgatam, ut postea ex illa dissensione textum Hebraeum colligat esse mendosum; si errata librariorum aut etiam interpretis, quod rarissimum erit, in vul-gata superesse aliquando admittit, nihil mirum, cum Catholici plurimi id fateantur; optat equidem p. 434. sect. 10. versionem fieri novam veteris Testamenti ex Hebraeo textu, in cujus margine variae lectiones undique selectae collocarentur, sed hoc, ut mihi videtur, non praejudicat Concilii decreto, quod tantum vult vulgatam Latinam Editione cæteris Translationibus præferri&,authentica haberi, atq; in officiis Ecclesiasticis solam usurpari,& indisputationibus à nemine rejici; sed ex Hebræo aut Græco interpretationem ad Originarii textus illustrationem condi nunquam prohibuit; quamquam certò conjiciatur, Capellum utpote hæreticum decreti istius-rationem non habuisse; mihi attentè consideranti, quod à me per Epistolam quæsierat E.V. visum est ita probabiliter responderi posse, multa poterant addi: hæc enim quæstio spinosis obscuritatibus fœcunda est, sed Epistolam, non librum postulas, jamque justam Epistolæ mensuram ex-cessi; si Eminentiæ Vestræ expectationi feci satis, id quod vehementer desiderabam, assequutus sum, sin minus, mihi bono animo conanti, ut soles, favebis.
units.tr: (2) When the Latin codices vary; (3) when a word or sense in the Latin is ambiguous; (4) for understanding the force and proper meaning of words. Shortly before this, Bellarmine had declared about the approval of the Council: yet he did not so approve it as to maintain that there are no scribal errors in it, but he wished to assure us that, especially in those matters which pertain to faith and morals, there are no errors of the translators in this version. The same Cardinal, in a letter written to Lucas of Bruges in 1603: I would have you know that the Vulgate has not been corrected by us with the greatest care, for we purposely passed over many things which seemed to need correction; the variant readings found in the Louvain Bible, on which you wrote a most useful book, seemed to me altogether to be added, etc. These are the words of Lucas in the letter he prefixed to the various new readings for the Vulgate, which were published at the end of the Antwerp Bible in 1618. Think also of other works, earlier and later. Likewise, from Cardinal Baronius: I admit that some things remain in the Bibles which can be changed for the better. The same Lucas, at the beginning of his letter: Even in the Vatican edition, the first of these Bibles, the printers have admitted not a few errors, which we have noted here and there in the earlier booklet. The correctors appointed by the Pope themselves bear witness to the same in the preface to the Vatican edition. What Lucas of Bruges himself published, with the approval of all, both separately and together with the Bibles, were various readings. If anyone wished to count the ecclesiastical writers who, when the occasion arose, translated differently from the Greek or the Hebrew than the Vulgate text bears, and who noted and embraced the various readings of the Vulgate differing from the text, who compared them with the Greek, Hebrew, Syriac and Chaldee codices, and who sometimes explained the sacred text as more suitable and more emphatic [ἐμφατικωτέρας] than the Vulgate text is in that place, he would be quite overwhelmed by the multitude. It will be enough to produce the testimony of one or two who have examined this question. Sixtus of Siena, in the last page of his Bibliotheca, admits that some blemishes are found in the Vulgate, etc. Afterwards he teaches that none of these things harms either faith or good morals, and he explains the causes for which the Church allows errors and blemishes to stand in the Scriptures. Melchior Canus, in the second book of his Loci Theologici, at the end of chapter 14 and throughout chapter 15, teaches that it is often useful to return to the sources. Among these, the fifth advantage is of this kind, that the blemishes which have crept into the Vulgate are corrected with the help of the sources; he demonstrates this by many examples. He pursues the same argument at length in book II, chapter 5, in reply to arguments 11 and 12, etc. John Mariana, in his little work on the Vulgate edition, chapter 21, interprets the decree of the Council of Trent in this way: The faults of the Vulgate edition are not approved, which we gathered to be many from the variety of the manuscripts, certainly through the carelessness of scribes; but only the translator's version itself is approved, where it has been established, either from the agreement of all the manuscripts or by the authority of the Church, that some passage has been so translated. I add, however, that our edition is not approved in those words in such a way that some deny the same things could be expressed more properly or more clearly in some places. He proves that this was the mind of the Council by the testimony of James Laynez, Superior General of the Society of Jesus, who was present at the Council, and who shortly afterwards, against the French, Italian and German writers who, in theological books published, did not hesitate often to accuse the Vulgate edition of faults and the carelessness of our translator, said: It is grievous to accuse all of them, as if they were impious and thought badly of religion, especially since their opinion is supported by strong arguments, etc. We have shown that many faults exist in the Hebrew and Greek codices, and many falsehoods in small matters, some part of which is not small and is found in our Vulgate edition. Later, Andreas Vega demonstrated this by many examples in book 15 on the Council of Trent, chapter 9, where he asserts that this was the mind of the Council, which he had often heard from the Cardinal of Santa Croce. The same author pursues the argument at length in book 11, chapter 5, in reply to arguments 11 and 12, where he admits not only that many blemishes have crept in, but some which introduce falsehood, which nevertheless bear neither on faith nor on good morals. The same Lindanus, in De optimo genere interpretandi, book 3, chapter 24, and especially 13; Gouelser, for Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 10. Capellus also spoke of these variants of the Vulgate from the Hebrew so cautiously that he almost always has recourse to anything other than the intrusion of blemishes into the Vulgate, as can be read on page 371, section 6, and page 356, section 2; therefore he rightly says on page 12 that he does not differ far from the opinion of Cardinal Bellarmine, whose words he reports at length. Indeed, granting what no one disputes, that the Vulgate translator was a prophet and produced a translation inspired by God (an opinion which we have embraced as the more probable in our Exercitationes Biblicae, book 1, exercise 7, chapter 4), it would still not follow that there are no blemishes in the Vulgate and no errors or oversights. It would indeed follow that none of these things was committed by the translator, but who would dare to guarantee that the copyists in transcribing it never went astray, stumbled or nodded? To assert this would be to rush into the madness of the heretics, who want the Greek and Hebrew codices, especially the later ones, to excel now in the same purity in which they were first poured forth, so that the Church's Vulgate edition may be absolutely corrected according to them. Against this madness of their heretics Capellus wrote most forcefully and demonstrated with almost countless examples that very many blemishes have crept into the Hebrew codices; and so far is he from doing wrong to the Vulgate, that from the comparison of the Vulgate with the Hebrew text he gathers that very many blemishes have crept into the Hebrew text, as can be seen in book [?], chapters 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. We have demonstrated the same about the Greek text in many ways at length in our Exercitationes Biblicae, book 1, the whole of exercise 2; and many years before Capellus, about the Hebrew text from the Masora itself and from various authors whom he cites but always passes over. Yet he speaks magnificently and truly, and in a thoroughly Catholic manner, of St. Jerome and his version, pages 354 and 355. He places him far above all the others, and affirms against all heretics that it is St. Jerome's, and that this has been most evidently proved by many, among whom he names Augustine, Steuchus, Eugubinus and John Mariana, as can be seen on page 355. Moreover, he gives excellent reasons, explained throughout by Catholic men, for the disagreement of the Vulgate with the Hebrew text, as can be seen on pages 356 and 357, and still on page 402, section 8. Indeed he values the Vulgate so highly that afterwards, from that disagreement, he concludes that the Hebrew text is faulty. If he admits that errors of scribes, or even of the translator, which will be very rare, sometimes remain in the Vulgate, that is no wonder, since very many Catholics acknowledge it. He indeed wishes, on page 434, section 10, that a new version of the Old Testament be made from the Hebrew text, in whose margin various readings chosen from every side would be placed. But this, as it seems to me, does not prejudice the decree of the Council, which only wills that the Latin Vulgate edition be preferred to other translations, that it be held authentic, and that it alone be used in public Church services and not be rejected by anyone in disputations; but it has never forbidden a translation made from the Hebrew or Greek to illustrate the original text. Although it may certainly be conjectured that Capellus, as a heretic, did not take this decree into account. As I considered carefully what you, Your Eminence, asked of me by letter, it seemed to me that it could be answered probably in this way, though many things could be added. For this question is fruitful of thorny obscurities; but you ask for a letter, not a book, and I have already exceeded the just measure of a letter. If I have satisfied Your Eminence's expectation, I have attained what I very much desired; if not, you will, as you usually do, favour my honest efforts.

units.la: Vale Eminentissime Cardinalis, Deus omnia Consilia tua prosperet & ad optatum finem perducat.
units.tr: Farewell, most eminent Cardinal; may God prosper all your counsels and bring them to the desired end.
