units.la: R. Goezaldus J. Morino de Moribus Ur- bani octavi aliqua, Abraham Ecchelensis apud Romanos Aulicos male ha- bitus, quòd Cardinalem Antonium Barberinum titulo Episcopi Pictavorum in opere à se edito insigniat.
units.tr: R. Goezaldus J. Morinus on some matters concerning the manners of Urban VIII; Abraham Ecchelensis ill-treated by the courtiers at Rome because, in a work he published, he styled Cardinal Antonius Barberinus with the title of Bishop of Poitiers.

units.la: A Reverend Pere Morin Pestre de la Congregation de L'Oratoire,
units.tr: A Reverend Father Morin Pestre of the Congregation of the Oratory,

units.la: Mon Reverend Pere,
units.tr: My Reverend Father,

units.la: LA Grace de Jesus pour Jamais, je receus hier la vostre du 27. du passè avec le paqvet pour le Sieur Abraham, que je fus chercher par deux fois sans le pouvoir rencontrer, je tacherai à le trouver ce matin peut estre devant de fermer la presente & luy dire ce,que dessus & l' asseurerey de luy bailler ou rembourser tout ce qui sera necessaire pour vostre service, Je vous remercie de la response touchant vos liures præcedens & l'avis sur ce que vous faites imprimer, je ne manq;ray pas de le faire sçavoir à Monseigneur le CardinalBarberin a la premiere occasion, que je luy pourray parler ; Ce qui est assez difficile à present estant grandement employez, par le Pape, qui devient bien caduc quoiqs il tache à faire voir le contraire & vouloit aller aux champs ce jourdhui à son St. Martin pres Viterbe sans les pluies froides, qui ont commencé depuis deux jours apres une assez grande Secheresse pour la saison ; il continue toujours d'en rechercher contre ceux de sa Maison & de sa famille & principalement le Card. Astali autrefois surnommé Pamphilio & in Angelis suis reperit pravitatem. J'avois escrit ce qve dessus des hier jour de la reception de la vostre à l'heure mesme vint le Sieur Abraham & summes ensemble qvelqve tems, il leut tuote la lettre qve luy escriviés & me promit de satisfaire à vos desirs le plustost qv'il luy sera possible, mais qv'il vous prie de patienter un peu parce qv'il travaille pour son restablissement. Le Card. Barberin luy a promis de parler au Pape : dans peu de Jours tout les Cardinaux luy portent compassion de ce qve le Pape s'est ainsi efmeu concontre luy pour si peu de chose, qui eft seulement pour avoir qualifié le Card. Anthoine Evesque de Poictiers en son Epistre dedicatoire du liure qu'il nous envoia, vous l'aures sceu du R. P. Gassot au quel le P. Beruidi l'escrivit pour vous le dire, ce que jen'avois voulu faire pour ne vous attristrer, sur l'esperance que j'avois que cela s'accommoderoit promptement; il dit, que si cela ne s'accommode, il veut retourner ne France : le Pape comme l'ay dit est grandement facile à presentà la cholere. Je demeure apres vous avoir presenté nos tres humbles re-commendations de tous à vos S. prieres & de tous de vostre Maison.
units.tr: By the grace of Jesus, forever. Yesterday I received yours of the 27th of last month, with the packet for Signor Abraham. I went looking for him twice without being able to find him. I will try to find him this morning, perhaps before closing this letter, and tell him what is above and assure him that he will pay or reimburse whatever is needed for your service. I thank you for your reply concerning your earlier books and your advice on what you are having printed. I will not fail to let Monsignor the Cardinal Barberini know at the first opportunity that I can speak with him. That is rather difficult at present, since he is greatly occupied by the Pope, who is becoming quite decrepit, although he tries to show the contrary. He wanted to go to the country today, to his St. Martin's near Viterbo, but the cold rains that began two days ago, after a rather long drought for the season, prevent him. He continues always to search for faults in those of his house and family, and especially in Cardinal Astalli, formerly called Pamphili, and he finds wickedness in his angels. I had written the above on the day I received yours, and at that very hour Signor Abraham came, and we were together for some time. He read the whole letter you wrote to him and promised to satisfy your wishes as soon as he is able, but he asks you to be patient a little, because he is working toward his recovery. Cardinal Barberini has promised him to speak to the Pope. In a few days all the Cardinals will pity him, because the Pope has been so stirred up against him over such a small matter, which is only that he called Cardinal Antonio, Bishop of Poitiers, by a title in the dedicatory epistle of the book he sent us. You will have learned this from the Reverend Father Gassot, to whom Father Beruidi wrote to tell you; I had not wanted to do so, so as not to sadden you, in the hope that the matter would be settled quickly. He says that if it is not settled, he will return to France. As I have said, the Pope is very easily moved to anger. I remain, after presenting to you our most humble recommendations, from all of us, to your holy prayers, and from all of your house.

units.tr: EPIST. LXXXV. Abraham Ecchellensis to John Morinus. Some things concerning John Maron and his works, whence the sect of the Maronites takes its name

units.la: unde Maronitarum nominatur secta: de Joanne Darensi syro; qui nam sint Melchitae,& qua in re à Jacobitis difsentiant; de aliis sectis in Oriente; Judicium de Originibus Alexandrinis à Seldeno editis.

units.la: Clarissimo Doctissimoque viro Joan. Mo-rino, Congreg. Orat. Presb. Abraha-mus Ecchellensis Maronita S.P.D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and learned man John Morinus, of the Congregation of the Oratory, priest: Abraham Ecchellensis, Maronite, sends greetings.

units.la: Nullae profecto sunt mihi gratiae agen-dae, Morine doctissime,quòd libellum meum de scriptoribus Chaldaeis{a} ad te miserim, & quòd misionem non distulerim; sed tibi duplices à me rependen-dae, quòd illum legere ac perlegere non sis dedignatus, ad quaestiunculas autem, quas subinde moves, breviter pro temporis angustia ac præsentium rerum statu, qui te haud latet, sic respondebo.
units.tr: I owe you no thanks at all, most learned Morinus, for sending you my little book on the Chaldean writers{a} and for not delaying the dispatch; rather, I owe you a double thanks, because you did not disdain to read it through. As for the little questions you raise from time to time, I will answer them briefly, given the shortness of time and the present state of affairs, which you are not unaware of.

units.la: I. Joannes ille Maro, qui Commentarios confecit in Liturgiam S. Jacobi, & à me eo nomine laudatur in meis notis pag. 135. & alibi, plures quoque alias doctissimas edidit elucubrationes contra Nesto-
units.tr: I. That John Maro, who composed commentaries on the Liturgy of St James, and whom I praise on that account in my notes at p. 135 and elsewhere, also published several other most learned works against the Nestorians{b}

units.la: {a} Intelligit catalogum Hebed Jesu. Nestorianos, Monophysitas, aliosqve antiqviores hæreticos qvarum vetustissimum exemplar, Syriacè, & Arabicè extat apud me. {b}Qvòd verò is viveret sex-culo sexto vergente ad septimum, habemus non solùm ex Masoretarum Monumentis, sed etiam ex Jacobitarum, Melchitarum, aliarumqve gentium historiis; hunc autem fuisse hæreticum Monothelitam, ac in sexta Synodo damnatum, sunt qvi scribunt; sed qvàm oscitanter, & frigidè versatis in actis Synodorum plane constat, {c}cùm hujus rei nec vestigium, nec vola in actis illius Synodi, aut aliarum occurrat; imò Jacobitæ, qvi Monothelitæ sunt, uti & omnes reliqvi Monophysitæ, diris hunc Maronem devovent, tanqvam duarum naturarum, voluntatum, & operationum asserto-rem,
units.tr: {a} He means the catalogue of Ebed Jesu, of the Nestorians, Monophysites, and other more ancient heretics, of which the oldest copy, in Syriac and Arabic, exists with me. {b} That he lived at the end of the sixth century, approaching the seventh, we know not only from the monuments of the Masorites but also from the histories of the Jacobites, the Melchites and other peoples. Some write that he was a heretical Monothelite, condemned at the Sixth Synod; but how carelessly and coldly they write is plain to anyone versed in the acts of the Synods, since no trace or mention of this matter occurs in the acts of that Synod or of others. Indeed, the Jacobites, who are Monothelites, as are all the remaining Monophysites, curse this Maro with dreadful curses as an asserter of two natures, wills and operations, and that most vehemently.

units.la: {b} Non ita profecto antiqvus est scriptor ille, vel ejus scripta, qvæ nondum in lucem edita, sunt suppositicia.
units.tr: {b} That writer, or his writings, which have not yet been published, are certainly not so ancient; they are spurious.

units.la: {c} Frustra contendunt Maronitæ, Maronem suum, qvem ut sanctum venerantur, non fuisse hæreticum; de his consulatur ipse Morinus libro de ordinationibus. rem, & quidem acerrimum; affirmant quippe, illum hac de re multa disseruisse, ac disputasse cum Cyni discipulis, quod notatur etiam in praefatione professionis fidei ejusdem, quae illius dissertationibus adversus Nestorianos, & Monophysitas hisce verbis praefixa legitur, [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] [illegible, ~30 letters] Cum autem motum esset dogma illud dividens unitatem sive unionem Domini no-stri, à Nestorio, atque ab Eutychete stulto commixtione & confusione adversus duas naturas gloriosas, & unitas Domini nostri, & cùm susceptum esset à discipulis horum duorum, tunc cœpit ipse Joannes, qui cognominatus est Maro monere illos, atque demonstrare eis claris testimoniis, quæ po-steà describemus; quemadmodum & contra discipulos Cyni, qui unam profitebantur voluntatem. Argumenta autem, quibus horum refutat dogmata certè tanti sunt ponderis, ut affirmare non dubitem, omnibus hunc palmam in hoc genere e-ripuisse; hæc omnia forsitan operâ no-strâ lucem aliquando videbunt. Quæris præterea, an Joannes iste Maro Pa-triarcha Antiochenus auctor Commen-tariorum in Liturgiam S. Jacobi sit idem cum illo, qui inter sextum & septimum seculum vivebat? Respondeo eundem esse. Quæris denique utrum Maronitæ suæ denominationis originem referant ad Joannem istum Maronem, an verò ad MaraMaratam Episcopum Tagritensem, cujus Liturgia impressa legitur in Maronitarum Missali ? Dico ad neutrum istorum, non ad Maratam Episcopum & Martyrem, qvia is vixit multo anteqvam hæc denominatio audiri cœpit inter nostros Orientales ; nec præterea illius nominis Analogia id ullo modo admittit, vel admittere potest; non ad Joannem Maronem, qvia is post inditam nostris denominationem floruit, eandemqve ob causam Maro seu Maronita cognominatus est ; qvandoqvidem id nominis tam illi, qvàm nationi universæ attributum est paulo post [?]celebratam Chalcedonensem Synodum ; ex nomine Monasterii D. Maronis Abbatis, de qvo Theodoretus in Relig. Histor. cap. 16. & 21, 24, 30. & alii ; Ex hujus qvippe D. Maronis nomine denominati primò sunt omnes Monachi secundæ Syriæ, ({d}) deinde mox post laudatam Synodum omnes illi Syri,
units.tr: {c} The Maronites vainly contend that their Maro, whom they venerate as a saint, was not a heretic; on this let Morinus himself be consulted in his book on ordinations. For they affirm that he discussed and disputed this matter at length with the disciples of Cyrus, which is also noted in the preface to his confession of faith, prefixed to his dissertations against the Nestorians and Monophysites, in these words: [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] [illegible] When the doctrine dividing the unity or union of our Lord had been set in motion by Nestorius and by the foolish Eutyches, through a mingling and confusion against the two glorious natures and the unity of our Lord, and when it had been taken up by the disciples of these two, then John, who was surnamed Maro, began to admonish them and to demonstrate to them by clear testimonies, which we shall set out afterwards, as also against the disciples of Cyrus, who professed one will. The arguments with which he refutes their doctrines are certainly of such weight that I do not hesitate to affirm that he has carried off the palm in this kind over everyone. Perhaps all these will one day see the light through our labour. You further ask whether this John Maro, Patriarch of Antioch and author of the Commentaries on the Liturgy of St James, is the same as the one who lived between the sixth and seventh centuries? I reply that he is the same. Finally, you ask whether the Maronites trace the origin of their denomination to this John Maro, or rather to Marata, Bishop of Tagrit, whose Liturgy is printed in the Maronite Missal? I say neither. Not to Marata, bishop and martyr, because he lived long before this name began to be heard among our Eastern people, and moreover the analogy of that name does not and cannot admit it in any way. Not to John Maro, because he flourished after our denomination had been introduced, and for that reason was himself surnamed Maro or Maronite, since that name was attributed both to him and to the whole nation shortly after the Council of Chalcedon was celebrated. It derives from the name of the monastery of St Maro the Abbot, of whom Theodoret speaks in the Religious History, chapters 16, 21, 24, 30, and others. Indeed, from the name of this St Maro, all the monks of Second Syria were first named, and then, soon after the said Synod, all those Syrians{d}

units.la: {d} Hæc non sunt ex omni parte vera, Syri, qui contra Eutychianos, Dioscorianos, & Acephalos Conciliorum defensitarunt Decreta, & fidem accitam, quemadmodum plane constat ex Epistola Archimandritarum Syriae se-cundae ad Hormisdam Papam, libello Monachorum Tractus Apameensis ad Syriae secundae Episcopos & aliis: Epistolae primo loco subscribit Alexander hisce verbis. Alexander Presbyter, & Archimandrita Monasterii S. Maronis. Rem istam paucis complectitur titulus Dissertationum ejufdem Joannis Maronis in haec verba,
units.tr: {d} These things are not wholly true. The Syrians who defended the decrees of the Councils and the received faith against the Eutychians, the Dioscorians and the Acephali, as is plain from the letter of the Archimandrites of Second Syria to Pope Hormisdas, and from the little book of the monks of Tractus Apameensis to the bishops of Second Syria and others. The letter is signed first by Alexander, in these words: Alexander, Presbyter and Archimandrite of the Monastery of St Maro. The title of the dissertations of this same John Maro sums up the matter briefly, in these words:

units.la: اعتقاد البيعة الرسولية الذي كتبه القديس يوحنا بطريرك انطاكية في بير مارون علي نهر العاصي بلل[?] حماد وحمص واوردا ذلك الي جبل لبنان ولاجل هذ[?] سموا اهل الجبل المذكور موارنة [?] علي اسم الدير مارون وبسمي [?] يوحنا المذكور مارون هو ايضا علي اسم الدير ۞
units.tr: I'tiqād al-bī'a al-rasūliyya alladhī katabahu al-qiddīs Yūḥannā biṭrīrak Anṭākiya fī Bayr Mārūn ʿalā nahr al-ʿĀṣī [Hasi] bi-l-qurb min Ḥamā wa-Ḥimṣ, wa-awradā dhālika ilā jabal Lubnān; wa-li-hādhā sammaw ahl al-jabal al-madhkūr Mawārina ʿalā ism al-dayr Mārūn, wa-yusammā Yūḥannā al-madhkūr Mārūn huwa ayḍan ʿalā ism al-dayr.

units.la: idest, Professio fidei Ecclesiae Apostolicae, quam scripsit S. Johannes Patriarcha Antiochiae in Monasterio Maronis sito ad flumen Hasi, (Latinis Orontes dicitur), Provinciae Apameæ, & Hemes eamque misit ad Montem Labanum, ex quo nominantur incolæ memorati Montis Maronitæ ex nomine Monasterii Maronis, & Joannes quoque ipse Maro nominatur ex nomine Monasterii. Ad hujus Monasterii judicium provocarunt nostri Syri, cùm propositum illius esset Monothelitarum dogma, testis est Thomas Caphortabensis Episcopus Tractat. 4. suarum dissertationum de voluntatibus Christi hisce verbis,
units.tr: That is, the Profession of Faith of the Apostolic Church, which St John, Patriarch of Antioch, wrote in the Monastery of Maro situated on the river Hasi (in Latin called Orontes), in the province of Apamea and Hemesa, and sent to Mount Lebanon; from which the inhabitants of the said mountain are called Maronites from the name of the Monastery of Maro, and John himself is also called Maro from the name of the monastery. Our Syrians appealed to the judgement of this monastery, since the purpose of that writing was to refute the Monothelite doctrine. Thomas, Bishop of Caphartab, is witness in the fourth Treatise of his dissertations on the wills of Christ, in these words:

units.la: جبنيد [?]
units.tr: Jabnīd

units.la: حبنيد قالوا اهل الشلم نحن[?] واحعين لي حكم دير مارون ديو[?] السوريان الذي تاويله ديار الوب[?] لان كانت صفة هذا النير علي شط العاص خارج مدينة حماد[?] وكانت جبلة وهبانه ثمانماية
units.tr: Ḥabnīd. Qālū ahl al-Shām: naḥnu rājiʿūn ilā ḥukm dayr Mārūn, dayr al-Suryān alladhī taʾwīluhu diyār al-Rabb, li-annahu kānat ṣifat hādhā al-nayr ʿalā shaṭṭ al-ʿĀṣī khārij madīnat Ḥamāh, wa-kānat jamāʿatuhu thamānimāʾa rāhib.

units.la: واهب قليسين Tunc responderunt Syri; nos redimus ad judiciũ Monasterii Maronis, Monasterii Syrorũ, quod interpretatur domicilium Domini (ex Etymologia nominis id significat) erat ante id Monasterium situm ad ripam Hasi, extra urbem Hemat, eratque numerus illius Monachorum 800. Sanctorum, & paulo infra subditi: عند ذلك ثبتوا اهل جبل لبنان وحمص وحماه وحلب علي المغالة [?] المقدم ذكرهما وعلي واب [?] الجامع المقدسة وانتسبوا باجبعهم الي دير مارون وسيبوا [?] موارنة علي اسم الدير ۞ Tune per-manserunt incolæ Montis Libani & Hemes Hemat, & Aleppi in memorata jam sententia, & in decretis seu mente Sanctorum Conciliorum, ac relati sunt omnes ad Monasterium Maronis, ac nominati sunt Maronitæ de nomine Monasterii. Et hæ[?] paucis de Maronibus, & Maronitis, e[?] quibus planissimè patescit, quàm frivol[?] sunt, quæ de illis nonnulli scripserunt.
units.tr: Wa-rāhib qlīsīn. Then the Syrians answered: we return to the judgement of the Monastery of Maro, the Monastery of the Syrians, which is interpreted as the dwelling of the Lord (this is what the etymology of the name signifies). That monastery stood before on the bank of the Hasi, outside the city of Hemat, and the number of its monks was 800 holy men, and a little further on it is added: ʿInda dhālika thabatū ahl Jabal Lubnān wa-Ḥimṣ wa-Ḥamāh wa-Ḥalab ʿalā al-maqāla al-muqaddama dhikruhā, wa-intasabū bi-ajmaʿihim ilā dayr Mārūn, wa-summū Mawārina ʿalā ism al-dayr. Then the inhabitants of Mount Lebanon, Homs, Hamath and Aleppo remained in the aforesaid opinion, and in the decrees or mind of the holy Councils; and all were referred to the Monastery of Maro, and were named Maronites from the name of the monastery. And from these few things about the Maroni and the Maronites it is quite plain how frivolous are the things some have written about them.

units.la: II. Quæris quo argumento probo Joanem Episcopum Darensem Syrum, cu[?] mentio fit in meis notis pag. 131. & ali-[?] claruisse seculo quarto & Commentar[?] in libros D. Dionysii de utraque Hiechia conscripsisse? Quandoquidem nullibi gentiū apud Græcos & Latinos mentio sit librorum Dionysii ante annum 530 regnante Justiniano{e} Respondeo Joannem Darensem eo seculo vixisse constare ex Syrorum historiis, neque hac de re ab illis dubitatur; ejus quoque scripta id ultro confirmare videntur, cùm omnes, quos citat Sriptores, eo seculo anteriores sint; eos verò libros Dionisii notissimos fuisse apud Syros ante Justiniani tempora, certissimum est ex D. Isaac Syro S. Ephrem discipulo, qui floruit seculo tertio ad quartum vergente; is enim in suis libris de Angelis passim hos Dionysianos laudat, & sequitur. Scio non deesse Doctos & Criticos viros, quibus hæc neque probantur neque placent; at ego lecta refero, & aliorum scripta, non judicium fero; his addis, nimirum Maronitas nostros antiquiores hos Dionysii contempsisse libros, quia in Liturgiis & ritualibus non eundem servunt ordinem.Respondeo, ta-
units.tr: II. You ask by what argument I prove that John, Syrian Bishop of Dara, who is mentioned in my notes at p. 131 and elsewhere, flourished in the fourth century and wrote a commentary on the books of St Dionysius on the Celestial Hierarchy? Since nowhere is there mention among the Greeks and Latins of the books of Dionysius before the year 530, in the reign of Justinian{e}. I reply that it is established from the histories of the Syrians that John of Dara lived in that century, and they do not doubt this; his own writings also seem to confirm it of their own accord, since all the authors he cites are earlier than that century. That those books of Dionysius were very well known among the Syrians before the time of Justinian is most certain from St Isaac the Syrian, disciple of St Ephrem, who flourished at the turn of the third to the fourth century; for in his books on the Angels he cites and follows these Dionysian works throughout. I know that there are not lacking learned and critical men to whom these things neither seem proven nor please; but I report what I have read and the writings of others, and do not pass judgement. To this you add, namely, that our older Maronites despised these books of Dionysius because they do not keep the same order in their Liturgies and rituals. I reply, ta- [e]

units.la: {e} Orientales rei Criticæ minimè periti, metsi non eundem servant ordinem, eandem tenent Doctrinam, nec repugnant Dionysio, nec libros ejus contemnunt; mentionem enim faciunt Angelorum in ritualibus & Liturgiis, ut res fert, ac modo à superioribus descendunt ad inferiores, modo ab inferioribus ascendunt ad superiores, modo habent rationem significationis, & Etymologiæ, modo Metri & Carminis; ex quo si res diligentius discutietur, comperies, non eundem ordinem, & modum servari in ipsis Liturgiis, & ritualibus.
units.tr: {e} The Orientals, who have little skill in critical scholarship, although they do not keep the same order, hold the same doctrine. They do not contradict Dionysius, nor do they despise his books. For they mention the angels in their rituals and liturgies as the matter requires: sometimes they descend from higher to lower, sometimes they ascend from lower to higher, sometimes they follow the sense of a word or its etymology, and sometimes the metre and the verse. If the matter were examined more carefully, you would find that the same order and method are not observed in the liturgies and rituals themselves.

units.la: III. Quæris, quinam sint Melchitæ, & in quo potissimum dogmate à Jacobitis dissentiunt? Respondeo, Melchitas nunc esse Syros, Arabes, Ægyptios, seu Cophtitas, & quoscunque alios, qui cùm non sint genere Græci, Græcorum tamen sequuntur placita, & ritus; dissentiunt quidem isti à Jacobitis in Mysterio Incarnationis Verbi Divini, cùm Melchit[?] teneant cum Concilio Chalcedonensi[?] & sexta Synodo duas in Christo Domi[?] esse naturas, duas voluntates, & du[?] operationes; Jacobitæ verò unam du[?] taxat naturam, unam voluntatem, & unam operationem; discrepant praeterea Jacobitæ à Melchitis, quòd Jacobitæ {f} Spiritum S. à Patre Filioque procedere credant, & id dogmatis in Concilio Ephesino determinatū constanter affirment,uti ex eorum Catechismo notavimus olim ad Synopsin, seu praefationem Concilii Nicæni,qvam Latinè cum argumentis Canonum, & constitutionū illius Concilii fecimus; ubi Melchitæ nonnulli contrarium cum nonnullis Græcis sentiunt. Addubitas praeterea, an iidem sint cū Maronitis Melchitæ, & id ex eo,qvod p.168. mearum notarū videar tibi utrosq; copulare,dum dico: Verba ipsa sunt apud Melchitas & Maronitas. Ad qvæ dico, Melchitas Syros qvibꝰ[?] primò nomē Melchitarum inditū fuit,tū in alias qvoq; derivatū gentes, eosdē fuisse cū Maronitis, usq; ad Justiniani Junioris tempora, eademq; utrisq; dogmata, uti hisce verbis testatur David Archiep. Tract.de Orientalium sectis & opinionibus c. I. de fide,
units.tr: III. You ask who the Melkites are, and on what doctrine above all they differ from the Jacobites. I answer that the Melkites are now the Syrians, Arabs, Egyptians (or Copts), and any others who, though not of Greek descent, follow the tenets and rites of the Greeks. They do differ from the Jacobites on the mystery of the incarnation of the Divine Word, since the Melkites hold, with the Council of Chalcedon and the Sixth Synod, that there are in Christ our Lord two natures, two wills, and two operations, whereas the Jacobites admit only one nature, one will, and one operation. Moreover the Jacobites differ from the Melkites in that the Jacobites believe the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, and they constantly affirm this doctrine as determined at the Council of Ephesus, as we once noted from their Catechism in the Synopsis, or preface, of the Council of Nicaea, which we translated into Latin along with the arguments of the canons and constitutions of that Council; there some Melkites hold the contrary, with some Greeks. You further doubt whether the Melkites are the same as the Maronites, because on page 168 of my notes you seem to yoke them together when I say: The very words are among the Melkites and the Maronites. To this I answer: the Syrian Melkites, to whom the name Melkites was first given, and which was afterwards extended to other peoples, were the same as the Maronites until the time of Justinian the Younger, and both had the same doctrines, as David, Archbishop, testifies in his treatise on the sects and opinions of the Orientals, chapter 1, on the faith.

units.la: {f} Id falsum est, nam orientales omnes hac in parte consentiunt cum Græcis.
units.tr: {f} That is false, for all the Eastern churches agree with the Greeks on this point.

units.la: وثبتت هذه الفرق الاربعة علي انما الفرقتين الملكية والمارونية اللتان ذكوناهما فرقة واحدة ورايهما في الاتحاد والاقنوم واي واحد
units.tr: These four sects persist, but the two sects we mentioned, the Melkite and the Maronite, are one sect, and their view on the union and on the person [hypostasis] is one and the same. [wa-thabatat hadhihi al-firaq al-arba'a ... al-Malakiyya wa-l-Maruniyya ... firqa wahida wa-ra'yuhuma fi l-ittihad wa-l-uqnum wa-ayy wahid]

units.la: Constat itaq; has sectas esse quatuor, quoniam illæ duæ sectæ nimirum Melchitarum, & Maronitarum, quas memoravimus, sunt una eademq; secta, eorumq; opinio circa unionem & personam una eademque est, fusius hac de re scribit in Epistola ad Arsenium Episcopum Haincurensem sub An Alexandri 1370, qui est Christi Domini 1053. Schismatis ac tantorum malorum, quæ inde sequuta sunt; quæqve hactenus tanto nostro damno experimur, Justiniani fuit petulantia, seu potius ignavia, & inertia quemadmodum ex Græcis literis consignârunt Theophanes, Zonaras, Cedrenus, & alii: quandoquidem Maronitæ nostri Libani incolæ, quos laudati mox Græci auctores ap-pel-pellitan[?] [illegible, ~2 letters] qv Arabun[?] rio ita Arabiæ tos fe eff niano pe tionibus rent Ror M equu[?] Mardait fiones, & Gedreni no audi inquit, a Arabum nitque ut in Libar ret, eoqu rent in f[?] ferv[?]um. ad Abim gratia i[?] hensam[?] pellitant Mardaitas ex Syriaco vocabulo [illegible, ~5 letters] qvasi dicas rebelles & indomitos, Arabum incursiones ab Romano imperio ita coercebant armis, ut vix intra Arabiae suae terminos ac deserta loca tutos se esse crederent: hinc pacem à Justiniano petere coacti sunt, quam his conditionibus obtinuere, nimirum, ut penderent Romanis in singulos dies nummos M equum, & servum, si Imperator Mardaitarum, seu Maronitarum impressiones, & irruptiones compesceret. Sed Gedreni hac de re verba in ipso Justiniano audire juvat. Primo anno Justiniani, inquit, ad eum nuncios mittit (princeps Arabum) confirmandae pacis causa, convenitque ut imperator Mardaitarum agmen in Libano, ejusque impressiones compesceret, eoque nomine Arabes Romanis penderent in singulos dies nummos M equum & servum. Imperator Paulum Magisterianū ad Abimelecum mittit pacti confirmandi gratia idque scripto & testibus est comprehensum: deinde Imperator misso legato duodecim millia Mardaitarum revocat, quæ quidem factoRomanam potentiam accidit, quidquid enim hodie Arabes tenent à Mopsuestia usque ad quartam Armeniam, id enim omne infirmum erat, culturibusque vacuum ob incursiones Mardaitarum: quibus repressis ingentia damna Arabes Romano imperio in hunc usque diem intulerunt. Ex his facilè quisque deprehendere potest, qui qualesque semper fuere Libani incolæ, & quamChristianæ Religionis acerrimi extitere defensores. Certè nisi in suarum victoriarum, & imperii salutis auctores arma convertisset Justinianus, & qui sequuti illum imperatores, Mahometana forsitan lues, quæ ex Arabum illorum cæno emersit non multo post, nec universum pene infecisset orbem tanto Christianæ Religionis & reip. damno, nec tam latè longeque grassata esset; verùm enimvero res ex animi sententia Justiniano haud usquequaque evenit; quia etsi Libani accolæ arma dePosuêre, incolæ neqvaqvam; hinc quidem factum est, ut qui imperatoris mandatis acqviaeqvieverint , Melchitæ dicti sunt & hactenus hoc nomine dignoscuntur,qvasi dicas imperiales seu Regii ; qvi verò non , & Mardaitarum, seu rebellium, & Maronitarum nomen retinuere ; hacqve de causa multa prælia cum Justini-ani ducibus inierunt, ut præter Maronitarum testantur Melchitarum , Jacobitarum , aliarumqve gentium orientalium monumenta ; nec profectò ab avita virtute, aut Religione degenerârunt Maronitarum posteri etiam sub immani Turcarum jugo ; etenim illi soli inter omnes Orientales Christianas gentes arma tractant & Catholicam profitentur fidem ; bellicæ virtutis præclarissimum testimonium nobis facit præliū illud, qvod ante biennium illatum est á Prorege Damasci Amiro ( ut de antiqvioribus nihil nunc dicam ) in qvo Amiri acies, qvæ ex diversis componebatur gentibus, Turcarum multitudine, ac numero pene oppressa jamjam in fugam inclinaverat, nisi nostrorum Maronitarum incredibilis ac invicti animi magnitudo gravissima pericula contemnentis adfuisset, hoftumqve obstitislet conatibus ; siqviden tanto impetu, ac tam impavido anim[?] in hostem irruit dexterum cornu, qvod ex qvinq; Maronitarum millibus constabat, ut illum non modò fuderit ac in turpissimam converterit fugam, verùm etiam Turcarum octodecim millia ferro interemerit, gloriosissimâ suo Principi partâ victoriâ ; sed hæc nostrum sunt præter institutum, ac aliud tempus, alium locum, aliudqve otium reqvirunt; tandem ut ad rem nostram redeam, Melchitæ nunc differunt à Maronitis in iis omnibus dogmatibus, in qvibus differunt Græci à Latinis.
units.tr: It is therefore clear that there are four such sects, since those two sects, the Melchites and the Maronites that we have mentioned, are one and the same sect, and their opinion concerning the union and the person is one and the same. He writes more fully on this matter in his Epistle to Arsenius, Bishop of Haincurensis, under the year of Alexander 1370, which is the year of Christ the Lord 1053. The schism and the great evils that followed from it, which we have experienced to our great loss ever since, were the fault of Justinian's wantonness, or rather his sloth and inertia, as the Greek writers Theophanes, Zonaras, Cedrenus and others have recorded. For our Maronites, inhabitants of Lebanon, whom those Greek authors just mentioned call Mardaitae, from a Syriac word meaning, as it were, rebels and untamed people, checked the raids of the Arabs by force of arms on behalf of the Roman Empire, so that they hardly believed themselves safe within the bounds of their own Arabia and its deserted places. Hence they were compelled to seek peace from Justinian, and they obtained it on these conditions: that they would pay the Romans each day a thousand gold coins, a horse and a slave, if the Emperor would restrain the attacks and incursions of the Mardaitae, that is, the Maronites. But it is worth hearing Cedrenus's own words on this matter about Justinian. In the first year of Justinian, he says, the prince of the Arabs sends envoys to him to confirm the peace, and it was agreed that the Emperor would restrain the army of the Mardaitae in Lebanon and their raids, and on that account the Arabs would pay the Romans each day a thousand gold coins, a horse and a slave. The Emperor sends Paul the Magisterian to Abimelech to confirm the treaty, and this was recorded in writing and with witnesses. Then the Emperor, having sent a legate, recalls twelve thousand Mardaitae; and this indeed brought harm to Roman power, for whatever the Arabs now hold from Mopsuestia as far as Fourth Armenia, all of that was weak and without cultivation because of the incursions of the Mardaitae; and once these were checked, the Arabs have inflicted huge losses on the Roman Empire down to this day. From these things anyone can easily see what sort of people the inhabitants of Lebanon always were, and what most fierce defenders of the Christian religion they have been. Certainly, if Justinian and the emperors who followed him had not turned their arms against the authors of their victories and the safety of the empire, perhaps the Mahometan plague, which emerged from that filth of the Arabs not long afterwards, would not have infected almost the whole world, to such great loss of the Christian religion and of the commonwealth, nor would it have spread so widely and far. But in truth the matter did not turn out at all as Justinian wished, for although the inhabitants of Lebanon laid down their arms, the inhabitants did not do so in any way. Hence it came about that those who had complied with the emperor's commands were called Melchites, and are still known by that name, as if to say "imperial" or "royal"; but those who did not kept the name of Mardaitae, that is, rebels, and of Maronites. For this reason they fought many battles with Justinian's generals, as the records of the Maronites, the Melchites, the Jacobites and other eastern peoples attest. Nor indeed did the descendants of the Maronites fall away from their ancestral valour or religion, even under the savage yoke of the Turks; for they alone among all the eastern Christian peoples bear arms and profess the Catholic faith. A most distinguished proof of their martial courage is given to us by that battle which, two years ago, was fought by the Prorector of Damascus, the Emir (to say nothing now of older examples), in which the Emir's line, composed of various peoples, was nearly overwhelmed by the great numbers of the Turks and was already inclining to flight, had not the incredible and unconquered greatness of spirit of our Maronites, who scorned the gravest dangers, come to its aid and resisted the enemy's attempts. For the right wing, which consisted of five thousand Maronites, rushed upon the enemy with such impetus and such fearless spirit that it not only routed them and turned them into a most shameful flight, but also cut down eighteen thousand Turks with the sword, winning a most glorious victory for its prince. But these matters are beside my plan, and require another time, another place and another leisure. Finally, to return to our subject: the Melchites now differ from the Maronites in all those doctrines in which the Greeks differ from the Latins.

units.la: IV. Paucis scire velis, qvid censeo de Originibus Alexandrini à Seldeno editis, & Commentariis illustratis? Respondeo Seldenū plura admisisse in iis Originibus peccata cūm vertendo qvàm commentando; in versione ad suas adstruendas sallacias &propositaargumenta pro universalibus particularia interpretatus est, & vice versa; exemplo nunc esto.Eutychius loquens de Ordinationibus Demetrii ait,
units.tr: IV. You would like to know briefly what I think of the Origines Alexandrinae published by Selden, with its illustrated commentaries? I answer that Selden admitted many errors in those Origines, both in translating and in commenting; in the translation, to establish his own fallacies and the arguments he had proposed, he interpreted universal statements as particular, and vice versa. Let an example be given now. Eutychius, speaking of the ordinations of Demetrius, says:

units.la: وهو اول بطويبك بالاسكندرية
units.tr: And he is the first patriarch at Alexandria (wa-huwa awwal Biṭrīk bi-l-Iskandariyya)

units.la: عمل الاساقفة[?] qvæ ad verbum & fidelissimè sic reddenda sunt: Et est primus Patriarcha, qvi in Alexandria fecit Episcopos. Ea tamen sic infidelissimè reddit Seldenus; & primus fuit hic Patriarcha Alexandrinus, qvi Episcopos fecit. Prosecto Demetrius non fuit primus Patriarcha Alexandriius, qvi Episcopos fecit; sed primus, qvi fecit Episcopos in urbe Alexandrina, qvemadmodum pluribus adductis testimoniis ex antiqvissimis illius Ecclesiæ monumentis, & Scriptoribus in responsione ad ipsum Seldenum ostendimus; & hoc qvidem mirum in modum consonat iis, qvæ in Alexandrino Chronico de Episcoporum antiqvitate leguntur in Juliano Demetrii prædecessore; sed eo tempore nulli poterant[?] Alexandriæ commorari; at nos Episcoporum originem & successiones à D. Marco, & Anania arcessimus; sed nec nomine Ægypti universa Patriarchalis Dioecesis accipienda, & intelligenda est apu[?] Eutychium, ut nos clarissimè demon-stramus.
units.tr: "ʿamal al-asāqifa", which must be rendered word for word and most faithfully as: And he is the first patriarch who made bishops in Alexandria. Seldenus, however, renders it most unfaithfully: "and this was the first Alexandrian patriarch who made bishops." Surely Demetrius was not the first Alexandrian patriarch who made bishops, but the first who made bishops in the city of Alexandria, as we showed in our reply to Seldenus himself, with many testimonies drawn from the most ancient monuments of that Church and from its writers. This agrees remarkably with what the Alexandrian Chronicle says about the antiquity of bishops under Julian, Demetrius's predecessor, though at that time no bishops could be stationed at Alexandria. We, however, trace the origin and succession of the bishops back to St Mark and Annianus. Nor should the whole patriarchal diocese be understood and taken under the name of Egypt in Eutychius, as we demonstrate most clearly.

units.la: Quintum quod attinet, nihil mihi dicendum occurrit; nam versionem tuam cum textu originario contuli, & menda omnia exscriptoris ad marginem adnotavi & ad te misi; ad illa autem, quæ asseris de primo titulo, quod scilicet in fronte ferat tantum Diaconorum Ordinationes, tamen exhibet lectorum & subdiaconorum, uti integrum legendo te animadvertisse, ais, dico hoc nomen ܫܡܫܢܐ[?] Syris significare ministrum, adeoque aliquando accipi pro Diacono, aliquando pro omnibus inferioribus ordinibus, atque ita passim tam Subdiaconus quàm lector caeteriqve alii minores appellantur ܫܡܫܢܐ[?] ministri, quanquam præcipue pro Diacono sumi & usurpari soleat; hinc qui vocis hujus usus ignorant, addubitant de numero minorum ordinum apud Orientales, existimantes eam significare apud illos solum Diaconum uti apud Latinos,
units.tr: As for the fifth point, I have nothing to add, for I have compared your translation with the original text, noted all the copyist's errors in the margin and sent them to you. As for what you say about the title on the first page, that it bears only the ordinations of deacons, yet (as you observed on reading it through) it also contains those of readers and subdeacons: I say that this word shamshanā in Syriac means minister, and so is sometimes taken for a deacon and sometimes for all the lower orders. Thus subdeacons, readers and the other minor orders are everywhere called shamshanā, "ministers", though it is commonly used and applied chiefly to the deacon. Hence those who do not know how this word is used doubt the number of the minor orders among the Orientals, supposing that among them it signifies only deacon, as it does among the Latins.

units.la: VI Asseris, verba [illegible, ~6 letters] & [illegible, ~6 letters] in ordinatione Diaconi esse tertias personas praeteriti atque Latinè explicanda, Ordinatus est, separatus est, quod quidem verisimum est; attamen posse quoque esse secundas personas imperativi praesentis, & vertenda separare ordinare, nequaquam ambigendum est; quod autem ad haec reponis, nempe Syros non habere praesens tempus in imperativo, sed tantum futurum, uti & Hebraei, ac Chaldaei, verum est in primis & tertiis personis, non quidem in fecundis, nisi adsit particula [illegible, ~2 letters], ne prohibitiva, uti loquuntur, tunc enim futuro utuntur, ut [illegible, ~7 letters], ne occidas, alioquin praesenti, uti [illegible, ~3 letters] fac [illegible, ~3 letters] legito [illegible, ~4 letters] esto, & sic de caeteris, idem quoque Arabibus solemne est; ea tamen verba, quae notas, in Nestorianorum rituali nullo modo imperativa esse possunt, quia adjungitur iis verbum [illegible, ~6 letters] quod est praeteriti temporis' vertendumqve, perfectus est, cuju[?] imperativus est [illegible, ~5 letters] perficere. I[?] Maronitarum autem Rituali verbum hoc abest, adeoqve possunt illa redd[?] qvoqve imperativè, & constare hoc vi[?]detur ex ordinatione Episcopi, ubi e[?] verba sunt praesentis temporis modi i[?] indicativi, legiturqve [illegible, ~6 letters] or[?]dinatur, &c. Sed hoc in tuo exemplari Ritualis Maronitarum diligenter animadverte, scilicet illud esse imperfectum & quasi compendium & indicem nam plures preces indicantur tantùm tamqvam ex alio codice recitandae. Confer illud cum exemplari Illustrissimi D[?] Cancellarii Petri Seguierii, & hoc verissimum esse comperies.
units.tr: VI. You assert that the words [illegible] and [illegible] in the ordination of a deacon are third-person past tenses, to be explained in Latin as ordinatus est, separatus est ("he was ordained, he was separated"). This is indeed probable. Yet it is by no means doubtful that they may also be second-person imperatives of the present tense, to be rendered separa, ordina ("separate, ordain"). As for your objection, that the Syriac, like the Hebrew and Chaldee, has no present tense in the imperative but only the future, this is true of the first and third persons, but not of the second, unless the particle [illegible] is present, the so-called ne prohibitiva; then they use the future, as in [illegible], ne occidas ("do not kill"). Otherwise they use the present, as in [illegible] fac ("do"), [illegible] legito ("read"), [illegible] esto ("be"), and so on for the rest. This is also customary among the Arabs. Yet those words you note cannot in any way be imperatives in the Nestorian ritual, because the verb [illegible] is joined to them, which is a past tense and is to be rendered perfectus est ("is completed"), whose imperative is [illegible], perficere ("complete"). In the Maronite ritual, however, this verb is absent, and so those words can also be rendered as imperatives. This seems to be confirmed by the ordination of a bishop, where the words are in the present tense, the indicative mood, and read [illegible], "is ordained," etc. But in your copy of the Maronite ritual, take careful note that it is incomplete, a kind of abridgement and index, since many prayers are only indicated, to be recited as from another codex. Compare it with the copy of the most illustrious Chancellor Pierre Séguier, and you will find this to be most true.

units.la: VII. [illegible, ~4 letters] apud Nestorianos & Orientaliores Syros accipitur pro Amictu, qvi est pars indumenti Sacerdotalis, qvo tegitur caput; at apud nostros usurpatur pro pallio Sacerdotali[?] [illegible, ~4 letters] Amictus. [illegible, ~3 letters] Epho tuni-ca Saca Sacerdotalis, indusium Sacerdotale, album [illegible, ~3 letters] cingulum, Zona [illegible, ~3 letters] cucullus, hac voce utitur Ritualis inordinationibus Monachorum [illegible, ~3 letters] sunt Cancelli, quibus altare includitur, quapropter ea verba nostri Hebed Jesu de Scriptoribus Chaldæis Page 84.
units.tr: VII. [illegible] among the Nestorians and the more eastern Syrians is taken for the amictus, which is the part of the priestly vestment with which the head is covered. Among us, however, it is used for the priestly pall: [illegible] amictus; [illegible] ephod, tunica sacerdotalis, indusium sacerdotale, albus, [illegible] cingulum, zona, [illegible] cucullus. The Maronite ritual uses this word in the ordinations of monks. [illegible] are the lattice screens by which the altar is enclosed. Therefore our Hebed Jesu's words in his account of the Chaldean writers, page 84, [illegible].

units.la: [illegible, ~12 letters] [illegible, ~14 letters] [illegible, ~5 letters] [illegible, ~6 letters] ita reddimus: Ejusdem sunt capita, quæ metro decantantur ad portam cancellorum Accipitur quoque dictio hæc non semel pro ipso altari; particula [illegible, ~4 letters] quæ passim occurit in Rituali Nestorianorum, denotat, verba, quæ sequuntur eodem tono esse decantanda, & nequaquam mutandum esse tonum, uti non raro fieri solet; hinc in Rituali Maronitarum occurrit non semel verbum [illegible, ~5 letters], hoc est muta, nempe tonum; his vocibus [illegible, ~3 letters] apud Nestorianos hoc est Magnus, & [illegible, ~5 letters] apud Maronitas id est princeps sacerdotum, designatur Episcopu verbum [illegible, ~3 letters] quod passim quoque occurrit, significat, versiculum repetendum esse, & est à verbo [illegible, ~3 letters] repetit, iter vit,[?]
units.tr: [illegible] We render it thus: These are the chapters which are sung in metre at the gate of the screens. This word is also taken more than once for the altar itself. The particle [illegible], which occurs everywhere in the Nestorian ritual, indicates that the words that follow are to be sung in the same tone, and that the tone must not be changed, as is often done. Hence in the Maronite ritual the word [illegible] occurs more than once, meaning muta, that is, change the tone. By the words [illegible] among the Nestorians, that is, "Great," and [illegible] among the Maronites, that is, princeps sacerdotum ("chief of the priests"), the bishop is designated. The word [illegible], which also occurs everywhere, signifies that the little verse is to be repeated, and it comes from the verb [illegible], "to repeat."

units.la: VIII. Quæris an Presbyteri, & Episcopi Maronitæ Romam venientes Missa celebrent in collegio suo more ac lingu sua, uti Græci in collegio suo & æqu fruantur privilegio. Respondeo, Maronitas non modo in suo collegio sacro celebrare more & lingua sua, sed etiam quandoque extra collegium, quod ab facile non permittitur.
units.tr: VIII. You ask whether Maronite priests and bishops who come to Rome may celebrate Mass in their own college, in their own manner and language, as the Greeks enjoy the same privilege in theirs. I answer that the Maronites may celebrate sacred rites in their own college in their own manner and language, and sometimes even outside the college, though this is not easily permitted.

units.la: IX. Quæris an viri conjugati Diaconatui & Sacerdotio initiantur? Respondeo, omnino, sed non ita ut cœlibes his ordinibus arceantur, uti & apud [?] aliquos Orientales mos est, imo ipso exemplo Apostoli summopere laudantur. De hoc argumento multa mihi dicendi essent contra nostri temporis hæreticorum latratus.
units.tr: IX. You ask whether married men are admitted to the diaconate and priesthood? I answer: certainly, but not so that the unmarried are excluded from these orders, as is the custom among some Orientals. Indeed, by the Apostle's own example, they are greatly praised. Much could be said by me on this subject against the barkings of the heretics of our own time.

units.la: X. Quæris, num infantes à Presbyteris Chrismate confirmentur, ut apud Græcos? Respondeo maximè, antiquitus enim uti adulti baptizabantur, sic continuata actione confirmabantur.
units.tr: X. You ask whether infants are confirmed with chrism by the priests, as among the Greeks? I answer most certainly, for in ancient times, just as adults were baptized, so they were confirmed in one continuous action.

units.la: XI. Num Sacerdotes in azymis, uti Latini, an in fermentato, uti Græci corpus Christi conficiant? Respondeo in azymis, ut Latini; at nemini suspicandum est, morem hujusmodi nuper introductū fuisse, ut quidam falso putarunt; etenim antiquissimus fuit mos iste apud duas Orientales Nationes, nempe Maronitas, (g) & Armenos, hinc Azymitæ à quibusdam Scriptoribus Græcis dicti & appellati sunt. Christum autem Dominum, cujus exemplar singuli sequi existimant, suum instituisse corpus in Azymis testatissimum est apud Maronitas; vide nunc, quæ hac de re, etsi præter propositum, attulimus ex cap. 10. Libri constitutionum ejusdem Ecclesiæ Maronitarum in nostris notis ad Tract. de Scriptoribus Chal-
units.tr: XI. Do priests consecrate the body of Christ in unleavened bread, as the Latins do, or in leavened bread, as the Greeks do? I answer: in unleavened bread, as the Latins do. But no one should suspect that this custom was recently introduced, as some have falsely thought. For this custom is most ancient among two Oriental nations, namely the Maronites (g) and the Armenians, and hence some Greek writers called and named them Azymites. That Christ the Lord, whose example each one thinks he should follow, instituted his body in unleavened bread is most amply attested among the Maronites. See now what we have brought forward on this matter, though beside our purpose, from chapter 10 of the Book of Constitutions of the same Maronite Church, in our notes on the treatise on the Chaldean writers.

units.la: (g) Illud ex Latinis sumpsere Maronitæ. Chaldæis pag 144. Sed profecto nihil liud freqventi9 eccinitur in officio fer quintæ de institutione hujus Sacramei quàm Christum Dominum in Azymis um confecisse corpus.
units.tr: (g) The Maronites took this from the Latins. Chaldaeis p. 144. But surely nothing else is sung more often in the Friday office on the institution of this sacrament than that the Lord Christ consecrated the body in unleavened bread.

units.la: Animadverte dum tamen, formam seu figuram pai Eucharistici ab aliquibus annis commu ditatis gratia immutatam fuisse & fig ram Latini introductam,unde falso ar trati sunt nonnulli,cum figura immut tam quoque fuisse qualitatem nempe nis fermentati Azymum,quia antiqua nis usualis, & fermentati speciem ferebat. Verba autem illa libri Cons[?] tutionum relata pag.144.notarum:Et accepit tunc ex illo pane azymo, recte op nuntur, Jacobitarum & Nestorianorum verbis,quæ vel in ipso Missæ Canone leguntur : Et accepit ex illo pane fermentato, Hoc de argumento variæ sunt int Orientales controversiæ.
units.tr: Note, however, that the form or figure of the Eucharistic bread was changed for some years, for the sake of uniformity, and the figure of the Latins was introduced. From this some were falsely led to think that the quality was changed too, namely that unleavened bread was used instead of leavened, since the ancient and usual form had the appearance of leavened bread. Those words of the Constitutions cited on page 144 of the notes, Et accepit tunc ex illo pane azymo ("And then he took from that unleavened bread"), are rightly opposed to the words of the Jacobites and Nestorians, which are read even in the Canon of the Mass itself: Et accepit ex illo pane fermentato ("And he took from that leavened bread"). On this subject there are various controversies among the Orientals.

units.la: XII. Demum quæris, an pluries in c super idem altare,ut Latinis mos est, m sa c
units.tr: XII. Finally you ask whether Mass may be celebrated several times on the same altar, as is the custom among the Latins.

units.la: {h} Nata, multa libris Maronitarum adjectis esse,& plerosque non esse integros. sa celebretur? Respondeo, semel tantum missam celebrari in die super idem altare, nisi vel adsi urgeatque necessitas aliqua, vel id Episcopi obtineatur auctoritate. Vale Doctissime atque Doctissime Vir meque tui colentissimum amare perge. Romæ 13. Julii 1654.
units.tr: ...many things have been added to the books of the Maronites, and most of them are not complete. ...is celebrated? I answer that Mass should be celebrated only once a day on the same altar, unless some urgent necessity arises or the permission of the bishop is obtained. Farewell, most learned sir, and continue to love me, who am most devoted to you. Rome, 13 July 1654.

units.la: Quæstiunculis hisce tuis utcunque potui respondi. nunc restat, ut etiam atque etiam te rogem, ne meam hanc responsionem edas, & in eruditorum evulges theatrum; at si hoc tibi aliquo modo libuerit, eam ut castiges, enixe efflagito, ac tua summa eruditione, sapientiaque limatam facias addendo, diminuendo mutando, expoliendoque, ut proprius auctor, & amici perhumaniter ignoscas ruditati.
units.tr: I have answered these little questions of yours as well as I could. It remains for me to ask you again and again not to publish this reply of mine or make it public in the theatre of the learned. But if it should please you in any way, I earnestly beg you to correct it, and with your great learning and wisdom to polish it by adding, removing, changing and refining, so that, as its author's friend, you may kindly pardon its crudeness.

units.la: EPIST. LXXXVI.
units.tr: EPISTLE LXXXVI.

units.la: J. Morinus Card. Barberino commen- dat negotia aliqua suæ Congregatio- nis.
units.tr: J. Morinus commends some business of his Congregation to Cardinal Barberino.

units.la: Eminentissimo Cardinali Barberino.
units.tr: To the Most Eminent Cardinal Barberino.

units.la: RPater Valencon nomine, qui has litteras Emin. Vestræ reddit, Con-gregagregationis seu Capituli nostri genera[?] decreto mittitur ad sedem Apostc[?] cam, ut ei exponat quasdam constit[?] tiones nostras jam à sacra Congregati[?] ne regularium examinatas & approb[?] tas, atque ut earundem constitutione[?] confirmationem apud sedem Apostoli[?] prosequatur negotium, cujus causa R[?] mam legatur, personamq; ipsam quan[?] possum animi effectu E V. commend[?] negotium illi curæ fore dubitare non[?] nit ea E.V. benevolentia, quam in omn[?] bus rebus suis experta est Congregat[?] nostra. Personam autem ipsam cum pr[?] bitatis & scientiæ omnis generis lau[?] præstet, gratiosam illi futuram confid[?] Ejusmodi homines apud E. V. lon[?] commendatione opus non habent; e[?] enim eorum asylum & columen;quapr[?] pter cæteris, quæ in eo laudari possu[?] omissis, Deum Opt. Max, precor, ut [?] minentiam Vestram quam diutissimè E[?] ecclesiæ suæ conservet.
units.tr: Father Valencon, who delivers this letter to Your Eminence, is sent to the Apostolic See by decree of our Congregation or Chapter. He is to set out before it certain of our constitutions, already examined and approved by the Sacred Congregation of Regulars, and to pursue their confirmation at the Apostolic See. That is the business for which he is going to Rome. I have no doubt that this business will be a care to Your Eminence, given the goodwill our Congregation has always experienced from you in all its affairs. The man himself excels in every kind of probity and learning, and I am confident he will be welcome to you. Men like him need no recommendation to Your Eminence for long, since you are their refuge and support. So, leaving aside the other things that could be praised in him, I pray God, the Best and Greatest, to preserve Your Eminence for the Church for as long as possible.

units.la: Parisiis 14. Kal. Nov.
units.tr: Paris, the 14th day before the Kalends of November.
In the year 1654.

units.la: EPIST. LXXXVII.
units.tr: EPIST. LXXXVII.

units.la: J. Morinus Lucæ Holstenio antiqvam amicitiam renovat.
units.tr: J. Morinus renews an old friendship with Lucas Holstenius.

units.la: Clarissimo & Eruditissimo D. Holstenio Bibliot. Vatic. custodi Joann. Morinus Cong. Orat. Presbyter.
units.tr: To the most illustrious and learned Mr. Holstenius, keeper of the Vatican Library, from Joannes Morinus, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory.

units.la: JAm longum tempus elapsum est, clarissime Holsteni, cùm literis tecum non egi; non ideo tamen existimo mei oblivionem te cepisse, nam non modo tanta cum amicitiæ & familiaritatis demonstratione me Romæ viventem complexus es, verum etiam anteqvam Romā accederem, me æstimatione & laude tua ita commendabilem reddidisti, ut mei memoriam in animo tuo nunqvam aboleri posse confidam; his ergo fretus antiqvam amicitiam nostrā hac Epistola renovaturus nihil tibi injucundum aut importunum me facturum spero. Vive igitur felix mei nonnunqvam memor, amicitiæ & obseqvii mei securus; nihil tibi tam honorificum & eminens contingere potest, qvod votis non præcipiam & præoptem. Parisiis xvij. Kal. Nov. An. MDCLIV.
units.tr: It is now a long time since I last wrote to you, most illustrious Holstenius; yet I do not think you have forgotten me, for not only did you embrace me while I was living in Rome with such a display of friendship and familiarity, but even before I came to Rome you so recommended me by your esteem and praise that I am confident my memory can never be erased from your mind. Relying therefore on this, I am writing to renew our old friendship by this letter, and I hope I shall do nothing unpleasant or troublesome to you. Live happily, then, and now and again think of me, secure in my friendship and devotion; nothing so honourable and distinguished can befall you that I shall not wish for it and desire it with my prayers. Paris, 17th day before the Kalends of November, in the year 1654.

units.la: EPIST. LXXXVIII.
units.tr: EPIST. LXXXVIII.

units.la: Abr. Ecchellensis Jo. Morino. Errores Seldeni in sua Eutychii interpretatione.
units.tr: Abraham Ecchellensis to John Morinus. Selden's errors in his interpretation of Eutychius.

units.la: Viro Clarissimo Doctissimoqve ac mihi Colendissimo Joann. Morino Congreg. Orat. Jesu Christi Presb. Abrahamus Ecchellensis S.P.D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and learned John Morinus, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus Christ, and my most esteemed friend: Abraham Ecchellensis sends greetings.

units.la: SEcundis tuis litteris primum respon-deo, ita te exigente. Certe utrumqve Eutychii locum falsa & adulterina interpretatione depravavit Seldenus. Primum qvod attinet, Eutychius neqvaqvam dicit: ab Hanania usq; in tempora Demetrii nullum fuisse in Provinciis Ægypti E-piscopum: sed habet in provincia Ægypti; & qvidé loqvitur juxta lingvam & moré Conciliorum, Patrum, & Scriptorum Ecclesiasticorum, qvi passim Ægyptū accipiunt pro peculiari Provincia Dioecesis Alexandrini Patriarchatûs, nimirum pro insula Niliaca, qvæ Delta ex similitudine Græcæ litteræ dici consuevit, qvemad-momodū Francia pro insula Francia qvandoqve usurpatur ; exempla habes apud Concilia & Patres obvia, qvi passim scribebant: Episcopi, qvi sunt in Ægypto, Thebaide, Libya, Pentapoli, &c. ex qvo liqvidò patet, Ægyptum non esse accipiendam pro tota Patriarchatûs Dioecesi, sed pro peculiari illius Patriarchatûs Provincia. Eutychius itaqve hoc negat duntaxat, sc. nullum Patriarcham ab Ha-nania usqʒ ad Demetrium in Alexandria & ejus Provincia constituisse, qvam peculiarem assertionem universalem interpretatur malitiosè Seldenus, & alterum committit mendum substituens personam, seu dignitatem personæ pro loco. Electio autem, impositio manuum, benedictio & constitutio Patriarchæ, qvæ ab illis duodecim Presbyteris Alexandrinis fiebant, nullum prorsus facessunt ei negotiū, qvi vetusta illius Ecclesiæ evolvit monumenta & mores ac ritus probè intelligit. Electio enim denotat apud Alexandrinos privatam, & qvæ intra parietes ab illis solis duodecim, & ex solo duodenario illo numero ex vigore instituti fiebat. Impositio manuum designationem personæ publicè coram populo, & Christiana plebe. Benedictio congratulationem quæ verbis quibusdam benedicendi concipiebat. Demum dicebatur Patriarcha constitutus ab illis Presbyteris, quia iis cæremoniis pro constituto habebatur ex vi antiqui juris peculiaris. Ordinationem tamen proprie acceptam sive consecrationem semper ac perpetuo pertinuisse in ea ipsa Ecclesia ad solos Episcopos ab ejus orgine exemplis manifestissimis, & evidentissima deductione ostendo in responsione ad Seldenum, & quidem omnia ex Alexandrinis Monumentis producta habeo; ea Seldenus aut nescivit aut nescire simulavit ac suorum more, & instituto. Hæc Doctissime Morine, æqui bonique consule, & si minus literatè, certè satis verè. Dat. Romæ 11. Januarii 1655.
units.tr: I answer your second letter first, as you asked. Selden has certainly distorted both passages of Eutychius by a false and corrupt interpretation. As to the first point, Eutychius by no means says that from Hananiah down to the time of Demetrius there was no bishop in the provinces of Egypt; he says in the province of Egypt. He speaks in the language and usage of the Councils, the Fathers and the ecclesiastical writers, who everywhere use "Egypt" for the particular province of the diocese of the Patriarchate of Alexandria, namely the Nile island which is commonly called Delta from its resemblance to the Greek letter. In the same way France is sometimes used for the island of France. You will find examples in the Councils and Fathers, which are everywhere to be met with, where they write: the bishops who are in Egypt, Thebaid, Libya, Pentapolis, and so on. From this it is clear that "Egypt" is not to be taken for the whole diocese of the Patriarchate, but for the particular province of that Patriarchate. Eutychius therefore denies only this, namely that any Patriarch from Hananiah down to Demetrius was appointed in Alexandria and its province; and Selden maliciously interprets this limited statement as a universal assertion, and he commits another error by substituting the person, or the dignity of the person, for the place. The election, the laying on of hands, the blessing and the appointment of the Patriarch, which were performed by the twelve Alexandrian elders, cause no difficulty at all for anyone who has studied the ancient records of that Church and understands its customs and rites well. For election among the Alexandrians denotes a private act, carried out within closed doors by those twelve alone, and by virtue of the institution, from that number of twelve alone. The laying on of hands denotes the public designation of the person before the people and the Christian congregation. The blessing denotes the congratulation which was expressed in certain words of blessing. Lastly, he was said to be appointed by those elders because by those ceremonies he was regarded as appointed, by virtue of an ancient peculiar right. However, I show in my reply to Selden, from the order of that Church by the clearest examples and the most evident deduction, that ordination properly so called, or consecration, has always and continually belonged in that same Church to the bishops alone; and indeed I have all these points drawn from the Alexandrian records. Selden either did not know these things or pretended not to know them, as is his way and custom. Most learned Morinus, please take this in good part, and if it is not written elegantly, at least it is fairly true. Given at Rome, 11 January 1655.

units.la: PAtere qvæso, Eminentissime Cardinalis, hac tantula Epistola negotia tua negotiosissima tantillum interpellari, meiq; memoriam redeunte anno in animum tuum redire, atqve humillimi obsequii mei votajam dudum E.T. nuncupata me renovare; qvamqvam oblivione mei securum reddant continuo benevolentiæ tuæ testimonia, ita ut contra qvàm in proverbio dicitur, ἀεὶ[?] τὰ πέρυσι βέλτίω sperare debeam anno vertente benevolentiæ tuæ gratiam præcedétibus effusiorem fore. Præter hæc enim interrogasti paucis abhinc diebus R. Patrem Goezaldum, qvî valerem, qvid agerem, qvid elaborarem? Hac interrogatione nihil optatius nihil honorificentius mihi contingere poterat, Ista E.T. de me rebusqve meis solicitudo certissimum est argumentum, mei memoriam in ejus animo nunqvam intermori, sed semper vivere. Officiossimæ huic de rebus literariis curiositati ut faciam satis, & eam qviqvibus occupationibus distinear&implicer, qvadantenus informem;ad eam mitto titulum operis, qvod à multis annis elaboro præcipua capita, qvæ in eo edisse-runtur, continentem; operis jam media pars desudata est: qvod restat, sub duobus prælis sudat; opus consummatum iri intra qvadrimestre spero; in his qvæ-stionicus Theologicis & Polyhistoricis, qvas titulus exhibet, recensendis, dispun-gendis, & enucleandis altum otium, qvo abundo, consumpsi, & qvotidie in his emaculandis& edendis consumo. De-us E. T. salvum & in columen Ecclesiæ suæ conservet, summumqve dignitati qva splendes fastigium imponat.
units.tr: Pardon me, most eminent Cardinal, for troubling you, though only briefly, in the midst of your very busy affairs, and for renewing, as the year turns, my memory in your mind, and my vows of most humble devotion, which I have long since dedicated to Your Eminence. Yet the continual tokens of your goodwill assure me that I need not fear being forgotten; and so, contrary to the proverb, I ought to hope that, with the year turning, the favour of your goodwill will be more lavish than before. For a few days ago you asked Reverend Father Goezaldus how I was, and what I was doing and working on. Nothing could have come to me that was more welcome or more honourable than this question. This solicitude of Your Eminence for me and my affairs is the surest proof that my memory never dies in his mind but always lives there. To satisfy this most dutiful curiosity about my literary pursuits, and to show with what occupations I am distracted and entangled, I send you, to some extent, the title of the work which I have been labouring at for many years, containing the principal heads treated in it. The middle part of the work has already been sweated over; what remains is being sweated over in two presses; I hope the work will be finished within four months. In reviewing, disputing and elucidating the theological and polymathic questions that the title sets out, I have spent the leisure in which I abound, and every day I spend it in correcting and publishing them. May God keep Your Eminence safe and a pillar of His Church, and set the highest summit of dignity upon the splendour that you already enjoy.

units.tr: Abraham Echellensis to J. Morinus, On the Rite of Anointing Priests among the Orientals.

units.la: Clarissimo, Doctissimo; Viro Johann. Morino Congreg. Orat. Presb, Abrhamus Ecchellensis S. P. D.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and most learned man Johann Morinus of the Congregation of the Oratory, presbyter, from Abraham Echellensis, who sends his greetings.

units.la: Postremis tuis litteris exigis à me, vir observantissime, ut quid Orientales sentiant de Sacerdotum unctione, paucis tibi aperiam; negotium facessunt tibi imprimis ea Maronitarum ritualis verba, [illegible, ~12 letters] qvæ sic reddenda censes: Et metitur ad eum, qui ordinatur, & ponit super caput ejus, & ei adaptat. Ratio hujus tuæ versionis est, qvia ungere non videtur congruere cum vetusta & universali Orientalium consuetudine, qvi nullam in Ordinationibus agnoscunt unctionem; qvamobrem sciendum est, qvotiescunq; in eorū ritualibus aut alibi occurrit unctionis mentio, id de mystica & spirituali unctione accipiendum intelligendumqve esse; Ex nostris hoc tradit Joannerensis lib. Hierach. Eccles.cap. 12. cui titulus est, [illegible, ~10 letters] de magnitudine, præstantia, & celsitudine Sacerdotii Ecclesiastici, ubi antiqva legis) oleo materiali perficieba-tur; hoc secundum (novæ legis Sacerdotium ] oleo Spiritus immaterialis manus impositione absolvitur.
units.tr: In your last letter, most respected sir, you ask me to explain briefly to you what the Orientals think about the anointing of priests. The words of the Maronite ritual cause you particular difficulty, [illegible in the scan], which you think should be rendered: And he measures it to the one who is ordained, and places it upon his head, and fits it to him. The reason for your translation is that to anoint does not seem to agree with the ancient and universal custom of the Orientals, who recognise no anointing in ordinations. Therefore it should be understood that whenever a mention of anointing occurs in their rituals or elsewhere, it must be taken as referring to a mystical and spiritual anointing. Among our own writers, Joannerensis gives this in the book Hierarchia ecclesiastica, chapter 12, whose title is [illegible in the scan], On the greatness, excellence and eminence of the ecclesiastical priesthood, where he says that the ancient priesthood (of the Law) was completed with material oil, and the latter (the priesthood of the New Law) is completed by the immaterial oil of the Spirit through the laying on of hands.

units.la: Ex his; quæ pro temporis angustia notare nunc licuit, facile videre est, unctio-nem, de qua in Orientalium Ritualibus, mysticè accipiendnm esse, & spiritualiter-ter, & in eodem sensu verbum sive illud vertas ungere sive metiri, sive admovere, movere motare, adaptare, & si quid aliud.
units.tr: From these points, which the shortness of time allows me to note now, it is easy to see that the anointing spoken of in the Oriental rituals is to be understood mystically and spiritually, and that in the same sense the word, whether you translate it to anoint, or to measure, or to apply, move, bring near, fit, or anything else.

units.la: Rogo enixè, ut plurimam dicas salu-tem meo nomine Clarissimo, atque mihi observantissimo viro D. Le Jay, & aliquid & amantissimis filiis mihi rescribas, & an modo degat Parisiis, ut illi scribam, nam plurimum virum illum optimum diligo, amo & colo, quemadmodum & omnes suos; nec non D. Vitray & ejus genero Durando, & uxori, quibus multa debeo.
units.tr: I earnestly ask you to give my very warm greetings to the most distinguished man, and my most respected friend, Mr. Le Jay, and to write back to me with news of yourself and your most loving sons. Also tell me whether he is still living in Paris, so that I may write to him, for I greatly love, esteem and honour that excellent man, as I do all his family; and likewise Mr. Vitray, his son-in-law Durand, and his wife, to whom I owe much.

units.la: ACcepi à Luca Holstenio, viro mihi multis nominibus obseruando & colendo, Eminentiam tuam inter tot bel-lorum tumultus perplexasq; pacis com-ponendæ difficultates, mei tamen me-morem esse, ut & qua ratione me bonis honoribusq; Ecclesiasticis augeat & hone-stet solicitam; tot benevolentiæ erga me suæ argumenta mihi hactenus dedi-sti, ut verba, quibus animi mei gratitudi-nem tibi testatam faciam, mihi non sup-petant; quanquam enim nonnulla impe-diant, ne beneficium illud acceptare pos-sim, bellorum videlicet strepitus, quibus nulla spe pacis affulgente, à tot annis ar-deret universa illa regio, deinde ipsius be-neficii natura, quæ ipsissimam possessoris præsentiam exigit cum Ecclesiasticarum functionum necessitate, cui multis de cau-sis parere non possum, rem tamen à bene-vola & continua animi tui in me propensione ut debeo, atque par est, æsti- mans ξενίων γὰρ θυμὸς ἀρίστῳ [?], Emi- nentiam tuam me tibi novo hoc titulo devinctissimum habere æternumqve ha- biturum profiteor; velim, optime Cardinalis, non verbis tantum demonstrare, qvantas pro tuis in me meritis tibi gratias habeam, sed maxime velim reap- se, si hoc opis esse meæ daret Deus, ali- qvas referre, & obseqviosissimis officiis meis qvam alte animo meo propensissi- mæ erga me voluntaris tuæ memoria inhæreat, aliqvo specimine comprobare. Verùm mihi præter vota nihil adest, qvo prodesse possim tibi, nec ea, qva fulges, eminentissima dignitas, referendi vicem desiderat; in vota igitur precesqve qvod mihi solum superest, pro salute tua nun- cupandas nusqvam cessaturus, ab Eminentia tua pro ea, qva est in litterarum studiosos humanitate & munificentia, ut mei semper memor esse velit enixissime contendo; χάρις χάριν γὰρ ἔστιν ἡ πίπτως [?], ἀεὶ, ut vulgo ex Sophocle usurpant, Gra- tia ea est, quæ gratiam semper parit, sic gratiam tuam & benevolentiam, quibus me semper amplexq; es, & cumulasti, nunquam mihi defuturus confido. Eminentiam tuam Deus Ecclesiae suae & litteris quam diutissime incolumem conservet.
units.tr: I received from Lucas Holstenius, a man whom I esteem and honour in many respects, the news that Your Eminence, amid so many tumults of war and the difficulties of establishing peace, nevertheless remembers me and is concerned to advance and honour me with good offices and ecclesiastical dignities. Until now you have given me so many proofs of your goodwill towards me that the words with which I might make my gratitude to you known fail me. For although certain things prevent me from accepting that benefice, namely the clamour of wars, under which that whole region has burned for so many years with no hope of peace shining forth, and then the very nature of the benefice, which demands the actual presence of the holder together with the duties of the ecclesiastical office, which for many reasons I cannot perform, still I estimate your kindness, constant and well-disposed towards me, as I ought and as is fitting. For "the spirit of hospitality is the best" [?], and I declare that I hold Your Eminence bound to me by this new title, and that I shall always hold you so. Most excellent Cardinal, I would wish not only to show in words how great thanks I owe you for your merits towards me, but above all I would wish, if God gave me the means, to repay something, and by some specimen of my most dutiful services to prove how deeply the memory of your will, so well disposed towards me, clings to my mind. But I have nothing beyond my prayers by which I might be of service to you, nor does that eminent dignity which shines in you require any return; therefore, what remains to me alone are the vows and prayers I shall never cease to offer for your welfare, and I most earnestly beg that Your Eminence, in that humanity and generosity which you show towards students of letters, will be pleased always to remember me. "Gratitude is that which always begets gratitude" [?], as people commonly quote from Sophocles; so I confidently trust that I shall never lack your favour and goodwill, by which you have always embraced and heaped benefits upon me. May God preserve Your Eminence, a help to His Church and to letters, safe for as long as possible.

units.la: JAm ab aliquot diebus fama hic percre-buit de summi Pontificis in Eminentiam vestram favore & benevolentia; Cùm primum optatissimi mihujus nuntii rumor ad me pervenit, à domesticis E. V. qui hic supersunt, sedulus & gratulabun-dus quid rei esset, inquisivi, secundoque nuntio à viris Clarissimis D. Ricardo, & E. V. Medico didici E. V, tenero paternoque animo à summo Pontifice non modo exceptam, sed etiam dignitatibus bonisq; restitutam spemq; magnam esse Eminentissimum Cardinalem Antonium eadem gratia ornatum iri, aut dignitatis suae exerexercitiumE.V.committendum fore Statim hæc audiens incredibili gestivi lætitia nec ego tantum, sed quotquot hic sunt pietatis &literarum amantes; sicut enim omnes in calamitate indoluerunt, CharitesMusasqueRomâ fugisse credentes;sic te diis hominibusque plaudentibus Romam redeunte eadem ab exilio revocatas sibi persuadet. Jovis taxilli inquiunt Græci, bene semper cadunt ἀεὶ γὰρ ἓν πίπτοσιν διὸς νύβοι[?]. Calamitate tua tam fortiter tolerta ex illustrissimo apud omnes Christianos longe factus es illustrior, & commendatior. Numquid in æternum projiciet Deus, aut non apponet ut complacitior sit adhuc? Complacitior erit adhuc, nec obliviscetur misereri Deus. Præparabitur, ut ait Isaias c.16. in misericordia solium, & sedebit super illud in veritate in tabernacu-lo David. Nam te major agit Deus atque opera ad majora remisit. Hoc adeo efflagitant universa Ecclesia hæreticorum armis & insidiis non modo truculenter appetita, sed etiam percussi piorum omniũ Preces&virorum literatorum vota, qui-bus bus ego gratus, officiorumq; tuorum volens lubensque me adjungo.
units.tr: For some days now the report has spread here that the supreme Pontiff has shown favour and goodwill toward your Eminence. As soon as this most welcome news reached me, I eagerly and joyfully asked your Eminence's household who remain here what was happening. Then, from a second report by the distinguished men Richard and your Eminence's physician, I learned that your Eminence was received by the supreme Pontiff with a fatherly and tender heart, and was not only restored to your dignities and goods, but that there is also great hope that the most eminent Cardinal Antonio will be honoured with the same favour, or that the exercise of his dignity will be entrusted to him. Hearing this, I rejoiced with incredible gladness, and not only I but all lovers of piety and letters here did too. For just as everyone grieved at the calamity, believing that the Graces and the Muses had fled from Rome, so they are persuaded that they have been recalled from exile now that you return to Rome, to the applause of gods and men. The Greeks say, "the dice of Jove always fall well" [ἀεὶ γὰρ ἓν πίπτουσιν διὸς κύβοι]. Having borne your calamity so bravely, you have become far more illustrious and commended to all Christians. "Will the Lord cast off for ever, or will he be favourable no more?" He will be even more favourable, and God will not forget to show mercy. "A throne," as Isaiah says in chapter 16, "shall be prepared in mercy, and one shall sit upon it in truth, in the tabernacle of David." For God has raised you higher and turned you to greater works. This the whole Church, assailed fiercely by the arms and snares of heretics, urgently demands, and the prayers of all the pious and the vows of learned men also demand it; and I, grateful for your services, gladly and willingly join my own voice to theirs.

units.la: Vale Eminentissime Cardinalis, & me E-minentiae tuae divinctissimū amare perge.
units.tr: Farewell, most eminent Cardinal, and continue to love me, who am most closely bound to your Eminence.

units.la: Perdiu est, cum officii mei, quo erga Eminentiam tuam multis nominibus devinctus sum, nullum apud te specimen edidi. Concurrunt plures causae, primum nonnihil veritus sum, ne frequentioribus litteris Eminentiae tuae seriis in negotiis semper occupatissimae importunus esse; deinde ea, quae scribere possum, tam levia sunt, ut[?] quo rarius, eò prudentius scribā; his accedit operis nostri de administratione poenitentiae retardatio; hujus coro-nidem cùm in dies speraremus, ut simul cum litteris nostris Exemplar aliquod possemus Eminentiae tuae offerre, spem meam non diebus, sed aliquot mensibus operae fefellerunt; tantopere tamen confido benevolentiae in me tuae, cujus argumenta, toties mihi demonstrasti, ut facile mihi persuadeam, diuturnitate temporis nihil de ea in animo tuo imminutum esse, aut refrigeratum; opus igitur hoc nostrum longum & laboriosum animo, ut mea soles, benevolo suscipe, illiqve ut à cliente & domestico tuo proficiscenti benignus aspira; cum praeterita mente revolvo, vana spe me non delusum iri, certissima spes est, Morinumqve tuum & quidquid ab eo procedit, solito favore & benignitate te amplexurum & probaturum. Deum Opt. Max. etiam atqve etiam rogo, ut Eminentiam tuam & Ecclesiae & litaris incolumem quam diutissimé conservet.
units.tr: It is a long time since I last gave any evidence of my duty to Your Eminence, to which I am bound by many obligations. Several causes have combined. First, I was somewhat afraid of being a nuisance to Your Eminence by writing too often, since you are always occupied with very serious business; then, what I can write is so trivial that the less often I write, the more prudent I shall be. To this is added the delay in our work on the administration of penance. While we hoped day by day to finish its conclusion, so that we could send Your Eminence a copy along with this letter, my hope was disappointed, not by days but by several months of labour. Yet I trust so much in your goodwill towards me, of which you have so often shown me proof, that I easily persuade myself that, though much time has passed, nothing of it has been diminished or cooled in your mind. Therefore, receive this long and laborious work of ours with your customary benevolent spirit, and graciously favour it as coming from your client and household servant. As I look back over the past in my mind, I am certain I shall not be disappointed in vain hope; it is most certain that you will embrace and approve Morinus, and whatever proceeds from him, with your usual favour and kindness. I pray God, the best and greatest, again and again, to keep Your Eminence safe and sound for the longest time, for the good of the Church and of letters.
